en: Salutations to Śrī Hayagrīva, who is the essence of the illustrious Hanumān, Bhīma, Mādhva, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Vedavyāsa.

May Viṣṇu, the Lord of the Universe, who is distinct from all things by virtue of His inherent independence and all other attributes, be victorious. *Bhedojjīvana* (The Revival of Difference), composed by Śrī Vyāsatīrtha.
I worship Vyāsa, whose pair of lotus-hands grant fearlessness to consciousness, who is the lamp of existence that revives the distinctions created by the obstacles of worldly life;
who is eternally free from defects, distinct from all that is conscious and unconscious, and perfectly full of all excellent qualities such as incomparable bliss through his own inherent sovereignty;
and who dwells permanently within the lotus-heart of the illustrious Pūrṇaprajña, the king of gurus. 1.
Having prostrated before the glorious lotus-feet of Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha, and before Jayarāja Muni, Vyāsa Muni, and our own gurus as well; ||2||
By His grace, I shall expound the restoration of the divisions,
relying upon the great words [of the scriptures], for the pleasure of Hari, according to my own understanding.

The venerable Śrīmad Vyāsatīrtha, while composing this work titled *Bhedojjīvana* (The Revival of Difference) which cuts through the Māyā-vāda system, offers praise to Viṣṇu—endowed with attributes relevant to the task—as a means to ward off obstacles and to introduce the treatise that is about to be composed; he does so by praying for the knowledge of His pre-eminence. [He says: "By His very nature... The construction is as follows: "May Viṣṇu, the Lord of the universe, be victorious"—that is, may He abide in a state of excellence.
Although the root *ji* (to conquer) is transitive, here it is used intransitively because its meaning is the attainment of pre-eminence.
As it has been said: "In the sense of victory and defeat, this [root *ji*] is intransitive in its primary meaning;
the attainment of excellence is the primary meaning, while in its secondary meaning it is transitive.

Here, even though the Blessed One possesses eternal excellence, his prayer for the attainment of excellence—as in "Victory! Victory! O Unconquered One, conquer the Unborn!"—is appropriate because it is intended as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) of that [excellence].
As it has been said: "The victory of Viṣṇu, who is ever-victorious, consists in his manifestation;
hearing, seeing, and so forth are requested as the means for making that known.
For he himself hears, sees, conquers, and so on, by his own nature."
"Victory! Behold! Listen!"—this is merely for the purpose of making those respective things known.

However, some say that although the excellence of the Blessed One is eternally established, the imperative suffix *loṭ* in "may he be victorious" (*jayatāt*) is appropriate because it expresses a desire for excellence in relation to a future time; this desire for excellence is a cause of the Blessed One’s pleasure.
This is because one observes that a king’s pleasure arises when those who desire his excellence wish for him to remain so even in the future.
That is to be considered.

While the excellence of the Blessed Lord is eternally established, the excellence of kings and others regarding their future time is uncertain; thus, although affection for a king is appropriate in those who desire his [future] excellence, such a desire cannot be a cause of affection regarding the eternally established excellence of the Blessed Lord, and therefore it is not something that ought to be performed.

For this very reason, in the *Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya*, it is stated that the blessing pronounced by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and Satyabhāmā upon Aditi was rooted in ignorance due to the influence of an asura-possession: "Not knowing him [Kṛṣṇa] and Satyā—who are the source of all and the lords of the world—due to the power of asura-possession..."

"Aditi gave them auspicious blessings whose sole essence was faultless happiness, just as she did for her own sons"; otherwise, since even Aditi’s blessing would—according to the aforementioned reasoning—result in being a cause for the Lord's displeasure, it would be illogical to state that it was rooted in the possession of Asuras and the like. Some, however, explain the meaning as: "May Viṣṇu conquer (jaya-tāt) the world—that is, may he overcome the universe consisting of obstacles created by the wicked. Others, however, say: "May he conquer the world—that is, may he defeat the host of Advaitins who are ignorant of the purport of the Śruti, by reviving the doctrine of difference established by me."
They have explained that this [verb] contains an implied causative sense (*antarṇīta-ṇij-artha*).

Now, one might object: "How can Viṣṇu be the Lord of the world, given that the relationship between the governed and the governor is pervaded by difference (*bheda*), and that [difference] is based on the possession of distinct attributes? To this, [the author] establishes the difference of Viṣṇu from that [world] by virtue of His possessing attributes distinct from those of the world.
By the phrase "headed by independence" (*svatantratva-pramukhaiḥ*), etc.:
"entire" (*nikhila*) means without remainder (*niḥśeṣa*); they are not "fragmentary" (*khila*) or incomplete, thus they are entire, and each one is also limitless.

By those qualities—serving as the instrumental causes such as knowledge, bliss, power, and so forth—the Lord is distinct from the universe consisting of both sentient and insentient beings on all sides.
The prefix *vi-* is used to refute the view that [the self] is both different and non-different;
its meaning is "absolutely distinct.
To refute the view that difference is produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as ignorance (*avidyā*), it is stated that this is "by nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*).

The connection is with the word "vibhinna" (distinct). This is merely an explanation of the meaning obtained from the prefix *vi-*; for there is a rule that absolute difference must be non-conditional (*anaupādhika*).

If it is argued that Viṣṇu is not possessed of all perfect qualities because he is conscious, like Devadatta, we say no; for this inference is vitiated by the fallacy of the "limiting condition" (upādhi) consisting in the lack of independence. With this intention, it is stated [in the original text] "by means of independence and so forth. Independence is called "foremost" because it serves as the basis for establishing the possession of all perfect qualities.

As it is stated in the *Nyāyavivaraṇa*: "Because there is a rule that for one who is independent [of others], there must be a fullness of qualities. And as it is said in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "Since both qualities and defects depend entirely upon him, how could he not possess qualities? And how, moreover, could he have defects?"
And by "independence" (svatantratva), what is intended is either the state of not depending on anything else with respect to its own existence and so forth,
or the state of having an activity that depends solely upon its own will.
Some, however, say that independence is intended simply as the state of not being subject to another's control.
That is to be considered;
for that [meaning] is not obtained by the word *svatantra*.
For one who is dependent on his own tantra (system) is indeed *svatantra*.

Because the Blessed One possesses self-dependence (*svādhīnatva*), there is an absence of non-dependence (*anadhīnatva*); since this would lead to the impossibility [of the definition], dependence on another (*parādhīnatva*) must necessarily be intended [as its opposite].
For this very reason, it is stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "The wise know that independence (*svātantrya*) is indeed the state of acting according to one's own will.
And in the *Tattvodyota-ṭīkā*: "One who is independent is one whose activity is governed by his own will."

By this, the objection that the relationship between the constrained (*niyamya*) and the constrictor (*niyāmaka*) is necessarily pervaded by difference, and therefore how self-dependence in the form of autonomy (*svātantrya*) can be established in the one Lord, is refuted;
for the meaning of the word "autonomy" is simply activity according to one’s own will.

And although there is no difference between will and activity, because there exists a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) acting as its representative, the status of being the constrictor and the constrained is established on the strength of that [distinction]. On this point, some say:
Since His status as Lord would be impossible in the absence of a relationship with the world that is to be ruled, it is said, "Viṣṇu is everywhere.
They explain this to mean that He is pervaded throughout the universe.
That too should be considered.
For it is possible for the Lord to exercise control even while not remaining within the world;
indeed, the Lord’s presence in the world is solely for the sake of his divine play (*līlā*).
As it is stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "In various places, Viṣṇu remains present, awakening the respective powers [of those beings]."

"Even from afar, that Lord is exceedingly powerful; he acts merely as a matter of sport. Thus ends the *Bhedacintāratna* composed by Ānanda Tīrtha Ācārya, the son of Mudgalārya: "The glorious Hari, the Supreme Lord, ever victorious in this world—He who, through His own multitude of attributes such as natural sovereignty, knowledge, bliss, beauty, and compassion, is far more intense than the mass of worldly beings; He who is eternally the manifest Ruler over this universe which is divided by a most firm distinction from Him. (1)
Having bowed to Pūrṇabodha, Añjanācārya, and also Vyāsarāja and his teachers,
I shall, by their grace, compose this detailed exposition on the Revival of Dvaita.

Intending to clarify the fivefold expansion of differentiation—which, though previously elaborated at length, was presented here in a scattered manner—by means of a summary and other methods, and thus generating a desire to know while introducing that very subject for the sake of completing the work he has begun, he invokes a blessing upon his chosen deity: "By nature... (*svabhāvataḥ*). Here, the preeminence of "independence" (*svatantratva*) consists in its being the accomplisher of all qualities other than itself.
As the Teachers have said: "He is full of qualities preceded by the powers of bliss, existence, and knowledge, due to His independence.
The connection [of the verse] is: "[He is] distinct from everything on all sides" (*viśvato vibhinnaḥ*).
The prefix *vi-* is used for the purpose of negating both difference and non-difference.
By the statement "on all sides" (*viśvataḥ*), a further internal distinction is suggested therein,
because it is impossible for a single entity to possess the quality of being "all-sided."
"Because of the attainment of truth through false qualities by its very nature"—the word "attainment" (*prāpteḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Alternatively, the connection is: "because it is distinct by its very nature."
That too is for the purpose of negating the dependence of difference upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Viṣṇu is the locus of a real difference whose counter-correlate is the universe, because He is the locus of real qualities that do not subsist in the universe.

Whatever is the locus of qualities possessing the same ontological status (*sattā*) as a certain thing, and which do not subsist in that thing, is the locus of a difference from that thing, where the difference possesses the same ontological status as those qualities.
Just as a pot is the locus of its distinction from a cloth;
and the ultimate reality of the qualities is established by such authoritative means [of knowledge] as "This greatness of his is true," which is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, he will state later that the fallacy of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) is not a defect.
The phrase "O Lord of the World" expresses another logical reason for the distinction [between the two].
Alternatively, the meaning is "may he overcome the enemies," with the word "enemies" (*śatrūn*) being supplied;
or it may be the second person singular, with the word "you" (*tvam*) being supplied.
Based on the grammatical rule, "The *liṅ* and *loṭ* [moods] are used in the sense of benediction (*āśis*)," the *loṭ* suffix here denotes a blessing.

Since Viṣṇu’s very victory is what he himself desires to be wished for, it should be understood that "you are his" (*tasyāsi*) means you belong to him from his own perspective, and not from Viṣṇu’s perspective.
By this, the objection—"How can there be a benedictory statement addressed to one whose desires are already fulfilled?"—is refuted.

May he who assumed the body of Narasiṃha, bestowing Sarasvatī upon me, a fool— may he, who dwells in the Dharma that coexists with the Pramitas, be present within me, as envisioned by Kumbhāri Vāsudevācārya in his *Bhedacandrikā*. (1)

May the fire of Vyāsa—born from the kindling wood of the glorious hands and feet of Brahmā, who wanders to sacred fords, and fanned by the wind of Madhva’s words—be for the destruction of my ignorance. 2.
May Vāsudeva, the enemy of the temples of the intoxicated elephant Māyin, bring joy to my heart; may he, who is supported by Hari, compose this commentary on the *Bhedojjīvana*. 3.

The venerable Vyāsatīrtha Paramahaṃsa, intending to revitalize the distinction between Viṣṇu and the ocean of milk, offers praise to Viṣṇu—endowed with attributes that serve as the thematic connection for the treatise he is about to compose—in order to ward off obstacles and for other purposes, and thus expresses his aspiration with the words beginning "By His very nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*). May the Lord of the Universe (*jagadīśvara*) be victorious; may He abide in excellence. This verb is intransitive when used in the sense of attaining excellence, because the object is included within the root itself.

An action is intransitive when the verbal root functions in a sense other than its primary meaning, when it includes the object within the meaning of the root itself, when the object is well-known, or when the object is not intended to be expressed. In the case of the root *ji*, which signifies both victory and conquest, it is intransitive in its first sense.

It is stated that the primary meaning [of the root] is "attaining excellence" (*utkarṣaprāpti*), while in the second sense, it is "transitive" (*sakarmaka*). Although the imperative (*loṭ*)—which signifies a benediction consisting of a prayer for the attainment of an unestablished desired object—is not appropriate here because the Lord's abiding in excellence is eternally established, nevertheless, since the identity of the Lord with the universe has been proven by wicked disputants (*durvādin*), the virtuous (*sādhu*) lack the realization of His attainment of universal excellence. Therefore, the imperative is appropriate in accordance with the worldly perspective, just as in expressions such as "Victory! Victory! O Abandoner of Ignorance! (*jaya jaya jahyajā*).
Alternatively, this is the *loṭ* (imperative) suffix expressing a desired purpose (*abhīṣṭārthaka*).
Or rather, let the class of Advaitins—who are ignorant of the intended meaning of the Śruti, [claiming] that "the Lord moves through the world according to the path of the Śruti"—be conquered.

The root *ji* here contains the sense of the causative (*antarbhūta-ṇij-artha*); the meaning is that he should overcome them, or, by reviving the doctrine of difference established by me, he should cause their defeat.
And thus, the word *loka* is also connected exactly as it is heard [in the text].
Since His status as Lord (*īśvaratva*) is not possible in the absence of a relationship with the world that is to be ruled (*īśitavya*), it is said: "Viṣṇu is everywhere" (*viśvato viṣṇuḥ*).
The suffix *-tasi* is used here from a locative form (*saptamyanta*).

The meaning is that he is pervaded throughout the universe; or rather, the connection is "may Viṣṇu be victorious. The term "Lord of the World" (jagadīśvara) is intended to indicate the evidence for his existence.

If there were a difference between Viṣṇu and the universe, then either pervasion (*vyāpti*) or lordship (*īśvaratva*) would have to exist therein; therefore, it is said that he is "distinct by nature, but not through limiting adjuncts" (*upādhi*).
[The suffix] *tasi* is used here for the ablative case.
The word "from all sides" (*viśvataḥ*) connects with both [parts of the sentence], like a lamp placed on a threshold.
In this regard, what is the proof? Therefore it is said: "by all qualities, foremost among which is independence by nature.
Alternatively, since the third-case nominal stems function as instruments of cognition (*jñapti-sādhanatva*), there is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) toward cognitions;
or else, the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the third case.

By their very nature—that is, by those qualities which constitute their essential form, and not merely those induced by limiting adjuncts such as ignorance—independence (*svatantratva*) is the foremost and primary attribute of these [qualities], namely omniscience, omnipotence, perfect bliss, and so forth; through them, there is the cognition of their respective names.
Thus, independence is also included within the meaning of the compound.
Furthermore, these [qualities] are the causes for the differentiation of the universe, being distinct from one another.

There is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*), because both the distinction of volition (*cetanabheda*) and the distinction of non-volition (*acetanabheda*) are individually well-established and are adduced as proofs for Viṣṇu.
Nor is there the fallacy of being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*),
because the reason does not exclude that which is ascertained as possessing the property delimited by the probandum-qualifier (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), namely, the nature of duality (*dvitva*).

This is because, although the probandum (sādhya) delimited by the delimitor of the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) might not be established within the inclusion of a single locus, it is nonetheless established within the inclusion of two locuses.
Otherwise, the position of others—that thirteen absences are the probandum in the case of earth—would also be untenable.

Alternatively, since the probandum in the case of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) where the probandum is an absence consists in the absence of identity with the universe (*viśvatādātmyābhāva*), as will be explained later, the non-establishment of the probandum is not a defect in such a case.
Since an inference having the probandum as its qualificand (sādhyaviśeṣyaka) is possible first, there is no inconsistency.
What remains will be explained later.
Now, what is this "independence" (svatantratva)?
If it is argued that [the definition] is "dependence on oneself," we say no.

Since there is no single entity that is self-identical (anugata) across all things, the dependence on the Lord ultimately results in a relationship of the governed and the governor. This relationship is pervaded by difference; therefore, its existence in a single entity is impossible, leading to both non-establishment [of the definition] and contradiction. Furthermore, if the qualification [of being distinct from the Lord] is not included, there is a fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra), as this property exists even in the entire universe [if taken as a whole].

Nor should it be argued that independence (*svatantratva*)—as in the expression "the ascetics are themselves slaves" (*svayaṃ dāsāstapasvinaḥ*)—means being devoid of a controller other than oneself (just as being devoid of slaves other than oneself), and that since this exists in the Blessed Lady, there is neither non-establishment (*asiddhi*) nor contradiction (*virodha*);
nor that since this does not exist in the universe, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

For, relying on a designation based on uniqueness—as in "one who drinks only water" (*abbhakṣaḥ*) or "one who breathes only air" (*vāyubhakṣaḥ*)—independence means being dependent on oneself alone (*svamātrādhīnatva*).

Since the word *sva* (self) can bring to mind the state of being independent of others while being self-dependent, the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) [of the definition] is redundant and thus not intended to be expressed. Consequently, although independence from others can be brought to mind through the word, the state of being devoid of any regulator other than oneself is what is actually conveyed by the term *svatantra* (independent).
Nor should it be argued that independence from others is itself the definition of independence because it possesses the same ontological status (*tattulyasattāka*) as the former;

for this would fail to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since even the state of not being dependent on others—such as the Blessed Lord—is present in the universe just as it is in the Blessed Lord himself.
Nor should it be argued that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because the state of being dependent on another superior to the Blessed One does not exist in this universe;
for even so, that [dependence] cannot be avoided in the case of Lakṣmī.
To this, it is said:
Because the aspect of being dependent on others other than the Blessed One is as redundant— and thus not intended to be expressed— as the aspect of self-dependence;
independence itself is autonomy,
and that exists in the Blessed One.
And because there is nothing else in the universe, there is no minor affliction whatsoever.
By this very verse, the subject matter and so forth are indicated:
Viṣṇu, who is distinct from the universe, is the subject (*viṣaya*).
Knowledge of that is the intermediate purpose;
liberation is the supreme purpose;
one who desires that is the qualified candidate.
The connection is as appropriate [to the context].
The *Bhedasañjīvinī*, composed by Hulagīśrīnāthācārya— *Hariḥ Om*.
Salutations to the son of Satyavatī, by whose grace even a worm attained unwavering prosperity and wisdom that causes wonder to the world. 1.
Having bowed to the true gurus, beginning with Nanda, Jaya, Vyāsa, and the Munis,
the one named Śrīnātha composes this auspicious *Bhedasañjīvanī*.

Although there are many commentaries on this work, nevertheless, this [present] composition of mine should not be disregarded, because it sets forth even a fraction of the meaning not mentioned therein. (3)

Having performed the auspicious invocation at the beginning of the work, he composes [the verse] starting with "By nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*). In the expression "May He be victorious" (*jayatāt*), the optative suffix (*loṭ*) expresses a wish (*icchārtha*) in relation to a future time (*bhāvikāla*).
Since that future time does not exist at present, the wish is indeed connected to it.
Even though such a wish is not the cause of that [victory], divine grace certainly arises toward those who possess such a wish; therefore, such a wish must certainly be made.

Because we observe that kings desire, "May there be such excellence for me even in the future," there is no room for the doubt: "Since the excellence of the Blessed One is established at all times, how could He have such a desire here?

In the word *vibhinna* ("distinct"), the prefix *vi-* conveys that the difference is real (*satyatva*), non-conditional (*anaupādhikatva*), and for that very reason, it is irreversible even in liberation (*mukti*) and is not co-referential with non-difference (*abheda-sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
To establish that, the phrase "by its very nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*) and so forth is employed.

If there were a state of possessing contradictory attributes by its very nature, then since non-difference would never exist, it follows that non-difference could never exist in any way whatsoever, because the very essence [of the entity] would have to cease.

To illuminate that the experience of suffering caused by distinctions dependent on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is absolutely impossible for one who is independent, the controller of all, and omniscient, independence (*svātantrya*) is mentioned first.

With the commentary composed by Kāśītimmaṇṇācārya: We worship that supreme Brahman, known as Viṣṇu, who is superior, from whom the origin and so forth of this world proceed, who is accessible through the scriptures, and who is distinct [from all else] through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Commencing this treatise (*prakaraṇa*) for the purpose of establishing the distinction between the two [realities] preceded by the negation of the conflicting misconceptions regarding difference—which are obstacles to the realization of the supremacy of the Supreme Deity, the cause of liberation desired by all—the venerable sage Vyāsatīrtha prays to the Supreme Lord for the sake of completing the work without hindrance and for its widespread propagation: "By nature... (*svabhāvataḥ*). Although the distinction, along with its supporting arguments, has already been established by the venerable Bhagavatpāda (Śaṅkara), it is not redundant here; for that very same point is being summarized and demonstrated in brief in this context.
"May Viṣṇu be victorious; may he exist as known through his pre-eminence over the universe.

It is not therefore illogical to pray for the pre-eminence of Viṣṇu, who is eternally established. But how is it that he possesses this very pre-eminence over the universe? To this he says: "The Lord of the World. But how can one who is non-different from the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, which lack lordship, be the Lord of the World? To this he says: "Distinct from the universe. The word "universe" (viśva) refers to the sentient (jīva) and the insentient (jaḍa).
Since that difference, being merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), is not the determining factor [for its reality], the word "inherently" (*svābhāvika*) is used to ensure its non-contingent nature.
The phrase ending with "by means of qualities" (*guṇaiḥ*) provides the reason for possessing such a difference; "by means of qualities" refers to those which establish [the self] as unique.

The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of a characteristic (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*). The meaning is: "possessing the manifold distinctions of the universe as made known by such qualities. To the question, "What are those means of proof? [the author] says: "By independence and so forth" (*svatantratvapramukhaiḥ*). Since imagined [qualities] such as independence—consisting of a state of existence that does not depend on another and the like—are incapable of establishing an intrinsic difference, he says: "by nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*). This means: "by those that are inherent" (*svābhāvikaiḥ*).
By this, the subject matter and other factors that serve as prerequisites for the listener’s engagement are also indicated.
Viṣṇu alone, who possesses the manifold distinctions of the universe, is the subject matter;
the knowledge of His preeminence over the universe is the purpose.
Therefore, the qualified person desires that;
the connection is according to what is appropriate.
With the commentary composed by Śarkara Śrīnivāsācārya:
Salutations to Lakṣmī-Hayagrīva, who is the essence of the illustrious Hanumān, Bhīma, Madhva, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Vedavyāsa.
Hari Om!
Having bowed to Rāma, the Lord of Ramā; to the illustrious Madhva, the master of victory;
and to Vyāsatīrtha, my guru who revives the doctrine of difference, I shall now provide this exposition.

In this world, indeed, for one who desires liberation—thinking, "May there be only happiness for me, and may even the slightest suffering not occur"—and who has realized the fivefold divisions [of Viṣṇu] as well as His non-difference from oneself: [The verse continues: "Having understood the fivefold divisions of Viṣṇu and His very identity with oneself..."

Knowing that liberation occurs through the realization of the faultlessness [of Brahman] and the preponderance of its qualities—and not otherwise—Vyāsatīrtha Muni, desiring to uplift the dull-witted, composed this treatise titled *Bhedojjīvana* (The Revival of Difference). This was done by collecting and condensing the very proofs for difference taught in the ancient scriptures; for although those ancient scriptures were composed for that purpose, they do not easily make difference known to the dull-witted due to their extreme extent and profundity. He thus sought to generate the knowledge of difference by means of this work.

Having performed the auspicious rite (*maṅgala*)—consisting of praise and prayer to the chosen deity, which is established by the authority of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) and has as its fruit the completion of the work he intends to begin—he composes at the beginning of the treatise [this verse] in order to cause his students to grasp it, starting with the words "By its own nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*). Now, one might object: since we observe that the root *ji* (to conquer) is transitive in such expressions as "Devadatta conquers his enemies," how can there be an absence of an object here? We reply: no;

for although the root *ji* is transitive when it means "to overcome" (*abhibhava*), it lacks transitivity when it means "to excel" or "to rise superior" (*utkarṣa*). As it has been stated in the passage beginning with "of the root *ji*," and so forth.
And in the present context, excellence alone is intended to be expressed.
Thus, "May Viṣṇu conquer" means "may he become excellent.

Although the Blessed Lord is eternally excellent, nevertheless, because a prayer for excellence is being made here with reference to a particular manifestation, the use of the imperative suffix *loṭ* in the sense of a benediction (*āśīḥ*) is justified.

Alternatively, according to the principle of *tantra* (economy of expression), the word *jagat*—whether taken distributively (*vyasta*) or collectively (*samasta*)—is connected with both the preceding and the following terms through a difference in intended meaning (*vivakṣābheda*).
Thus, the meaning is: "May Viṣṇu conquer the world," that is, may he overcome the entire universe, including evil obstacles and the like.

Indeed, it is improper to perform acts such as praise toward one whose essential nature (*svarūpa*) has not been determined; nor can the determination of essential nature occur without a definition (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, he states the definition of Viṣṇu: "The Lord of the World" (*jagadīśvara*). Here, by the word "world" (*jagat*), derived from the etymology "that which goes to birth" (*jam utpattim gacchati*), the phenomenal universe consisting of sentient and insentient beings is denoted. Since birth—in the form of the acquisition of particular qualities dependent on another—is common to all things, there is no minor flaw here.
By this, the defining characteristic of being the controller of the world is stated.

Now, one might object: since the relationship between the governed (*niyamya*) and the governor (*niyāmaka*) is pervaded by difference, and since there is no difference between the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and the Lord (*Īśvara*), this definition is not possible. To this, he says: "distinct" (*vibhinna*). Here, the word *viśva* (world/universe) refers to the universe consisting of sentient beings. For this very reason, he will immediately state that [the Lord] is distinct from the universe consisting of both sentient and insentient entities. Thus, the meaning is that [the Lord] is absolutely distinct from the phenomenal world composed of both the sentient and the insentient.
Here, by the prefix *vi-* expressing absolute difference, Yādavaprakāśa—the proponent of both difference and non-difference—is refuted.

Now, one might object: "Since difference is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), it would not exist in the state of liberation; consequently, the Lord could not be the controller of liberated souls. To this, he says: "by His very nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*). This means "by His essential nature" (*svarūpataḥ*).
It is to be construed with the word "distinct" (*vibhinnaḥ*).

Since difference is necessarily determined by distinguishing attributes, he states them with the words "by the qualities" (guṇaiḥ). To the question of how these can serve as distinguishers when they are common to the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), he qualifies the qualities with the phrase "headed by independence" (svatantratvapramukhaiḥ). The meaning is: among the three kinds of existence, independence is the state of not being dependent on another; those qualities in which this very independence is primary or principal are "headed by independence," and it is by means of these that [the Lord is distinguished].

Now, since these qualities are adventitious (aupādhika), they do not exist in the state of liberation; therefore, they cannot be the determinants of difference in the essential nature (svarūpa). To this, he says: "by their own nature" (svabhāvataḥ). The suffix *tasi* is used here in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārthe*), according to the Vārttika rule *ādyādibhya upasaṅkhyānam*.
Thus, the meaning is "by those [qualities] which constitute the essential nature.
The word "entire" (*nikhilaiḥ*) is a mention of the essential nature itself. || 1 ||
Now, how can the Supreme Brahman, known as Viṣṇu, be inherently distinct from the universe consisting of both sentient and insentient entities?
For there is a lack of evidence for such a distinction. To explain:
To begin with, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not possible regarding the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

This is because a difference whose locus is the Lord, or whose counter-correlate is the Lord, cannot be perceived, since the Lord himself is not an object of perception. He raises an objection—beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*)—in order to support the qualification of Viṣṇu as being "distinct from the universe," for by the word "universe" (*viśva*), the entire world consisting of both sentient and insentient beings is intended; hence it is said to consist of "sentient and insentient beings."

Thus, since it is the Supreme Brahman alone that is intended by the word "Viṣṇu," it should be understood that the phrase "of the Supreme Brahman named Viṣṇu" has been stated. Why is there such an objection? To this he says: "Because of difference. If one accepts that the Brahman named Viṣṇu is distinct from the universe, then one must also accept that the universe is distinct from Him. For it is not possible that Viṣṇu is different from the universe while the universe is non-different from Him.
In this way, the mutual distinction between the universe consisting of the sentient and the insentient must also be admitted;
otherwise, even the designation "consisting of the sentient and the insentient" would be untenable.
Likewise, the mutual distinction between sentient beings and insentient things must also be admitted.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of the futility of employing the word "viśva" (the universe) as a term denoting the whole.

Thus, the meaning is that there is no evidence for a difference having Viṣṇu as its locus and the conscious and unconscious universe as its counter-correlate, nor for a difference having the universe as its locus and Viṣṇu as its counter-correlate, nor for the mutual difference among the members of the universe, nor even for the mutual difference between conscious and unconscious entities.

For this very reason, although the difference having Viṣṇu as its locus was the subject under discussion, the term "difference" is mentioned again in order to include all types of difference—answering the question: "How can Viṣṇu be distinct from the universe?"
Otherwise, it should be understood that its [the opponent's argument] would result in futility.
Although in the first verse the means of valid cognition known as inference was mentioned by way of "independence" and so forth,

nevertheless, that statement was made solely for the purpose of raising an objection, since one will subsequently state the refutation of that inference precisely through the sequence beginning with perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And he will state this refutation by anticipating the inference that "the two are distinct because they are subjects of dispute.

He establishes this very point in sequence with the words beginning "tathā hi" (for instance). The word "tāvat" signifies sequence. The phrase "na tāvat pratyakṣam" (first of all, not perception) is to be connected with both [the alternatives]. Regarding the phrase "jīveśvarabhede": it means either the difference of the Lord from the individual soul, or the difference of the individual soul from the Lord.
It becomes perception;
the word "valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) is to be supplied.

Why is it not the case that perception is the valid means of knowledge in that instance? To this he says: "of that which has God as its subject" (*īśvaradharmikasya*). This means: of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and God, or of the difference between God and the individual soul.
The point is that for the perception of difference (*bhedapratyakṣa*), the perceptibility of both the locus (*dharmī*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is required.

By this, one should note that there is no room for the objection that the statement regarding the absence of evidence for a difference having Viṣṇu as its counter-correlate is irrelevant, since the doubt raised was merely whether Viṣṇu is different from the universe—that is, a difference having Viṣṇu as its locus.

However, some explain the phrase "in the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)" as meaning "in the difference of the Lord having the individual soul as its counter-correlative. Having raised the objection—"In that case, why is there this irrelevant statement regarding 'or [the difference] having the Lord as its counter-correlative'?"—they explain that such a statement was made for the sake of providing an illustration (*dṛṣṭāntārtham*). This, however, is to be considered; for, according to the method already stated, the difference having the Lord as its counter-correlative is also indeed relevant.

Furthermore, does "being different from the universe" mean possessing a difference whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is the universe, or does it mean being the counter-correlate of a difference residing in the universe?

Neither of these two is possible, because there is no evidence for either of these two types of difference; with this intention, the passage beginning "first of all, the difference between the individual soul and the Lord" should be taken exactly as it stands. As for that other interpretation offered here, it too must be considered.
When it is said that [Viṣṇu] is "distinct from the universe," there appears only a difference whose counter-correlative is the universe;
there does not appear the state of being the counter-correlative of a difference residing in the entire universe.

Thus he sets forth the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "Now, [is it... (nanu). Since the opponent has stated that Brahman alone is non-different from the universe, the statement "Viṣṇu is distinct" would be syntactically inconsistent (vyadhikaraṇa); therefore, he specifies "of him who is named Viṣṇu. He asks "How?"—that is, is it because there is evidence for difference, or because there is a lack of evidence for identity?
In the first case, [the knowledge arises] from perception, inference, or scripture;
in the second case, it means from the absence of perception, the absence of inference, or the absence of scripture. "Sentient and insentient" is the explanation of the word *viśva* (the universe).
The phrase "consisting of sentient and non-sentient" is intended to indicate the introduction of its internal subdivisions;

otherwise, he would have simply said "divided by internal differences. Regarding the term "diversity" (*bhinnatva*): it means being the locus (*dharmitva*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) with respect to difference.
Herein lies the point of contention (*vipratipatti*).

It should be inferred whether or not consciousness (cit) as characterized by lordship (īśvaratva) possesses an unconditioned, absolute difference (kevalabheda) that exists at the same level of reality (samānasattāka) as the substratum (dharmin) whose counter-correlative is consciousness as characterized by individuality (jīvatva). Regarding the phrase "due to the non-perceptibility of the Lord" (īśvarāpratyakṣatvena): in the perception of a relational entity, the perception of the relata is a necessary condition;
otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence of perceiving either the conjunction between air and space or the conjunction between air and a jar.
Here too, by the term "Lord" (īśvara), pure Brahman itself is intended.

If it is argued that there is a discordant dispute—since those who know reality declare that the Lord with attributes (*saguṇa*) and form (*sākāra*) is distinct, whereas the Brahman intended by the opponent is without attributes (*nirguṇa*)—we say no. For that which is without attributes for the opponent is, in reality, the very same Lord who possesses attributes and form; He is not something separate from Him. Thus, because they are identical in their specific nature, they stand in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
By this, perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of knowing the mutual difference between living beings and insentient things, whether they be beyond the senses or not beyond the senses, is refuted.

Nor can it be argued that yogic perception is the authority in all such cases, on the grounds that it is well-known from such scriptural passages as "When he sees that which is adored... (*juṣṭaṃ yadā paśyati*).
Because it is intended to be refuted precisely by the refutation of [the opponent's] approach;

and because the subsequent section of the text is for the purpose of establishing the Lord’s difference from the universe, the "connection" (*saṅgati*) is simply the state of being the means of establishment—this is the intention with which he raises an objection regarding the Lord’s difference from the universe, beginning with "But surely... (*nanu*). He states that the objection does not concern Viṣṇu himself, but rather the [alleged] difference, saying: "because there is a lack of evidence for difference. Although evidence was indeed stated in the form of "by all attributes, foremost among which is independence," nevertheless, since Brahman is taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), those attributes which serve as logical reasons (*hetu*) are unestablished (*asiddhi*) in the case of a qualityless (*nirguṇa*) Brahman.

This statement is made with the intention that if the qualified [Brahman] (*saguṇa*) were taken as the subject, there would be the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*) due to the distinction arising from limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Wishing to establish through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) the absence of any proof for the difference between the conscious and unconscious universe, he first refutes perception regarding the difference among conscious beings—stating "not, first of all" (*na tāvat*). Regarding the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), that is, the difference having the Lord as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*): the construction is that a difference whose locus (*dharmin*) is the Lord and whose counter-correlative is the individual soul cannot be perceived, because the locus in the form of the Lord is not perceptible. Alternatively, the phrase "having the Lord as its counter-correlative" may be intended as an illustrative example.
The word *vā* is used in the sense of *iva* (like).

Consequently, the meaning is: "just as" there is non-perceptibility of a difference whose locus is the individual soul (*jīva*) and whose counter-correlate is God (*īśvara*), due to the absence of perception of the counter-correlate in the form of God and the absence of perception of the locus in the form of another individual soul;
for otherwise, since that [other case] would not be under discussion, it would be inappropriate to refute the means of knowledge regarding it.

Alternatively, being different from the universe (*viśvabhinnatvam*) might mean either possessing a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the universe, or being the counter-correlate of a difference residing in the universe.

Neither of these two is possible, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for either type of difference; with this intention, the passage beginning with "First of all, there is no difference between the individual soul and the Lord" is to be taken exactly as it stands.

What must be said here will be stated at the occasion of the refutation. The following begins with the words "Now, indeed" (*nanu*) in order to strengthen the meaning already stated by means of the rejection of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). This is done to dispel the doubt: "Since the opponents do not admit that Viṣṇu—known as Viṣṇu and variegated by *māyā*—is identical with the entire phenomenal world, as we [Advaitins] do, how can the prima facie view arise with reference to him? Thus, the glorification of Viṣṇu’s status as Brahman is intended to remove this objection.

The sense is that since the two terms *viṣṇupada* and *brahmapada*—which signify pervasion (*vyāpti*) and expansion (*vṛddhi*) consisting of the absence of the three kinds of limitation—are synonymous, they are one and the same; it is on this basis that the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises. Furthermore, because the distinction between the sentient and the insentient will be examined later, the term "consisting of the sentient and the insentient" is used as a qualification of the universe (*viśva*) to indicate that the universe is already present as its referent. Regarding the phrase "having Īśvara as its counter-correlative": difference, like conjunction and other relations, resides in both [relata]; it has as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) the entity contained within that relation, and as its substratum (*anuyogin*) the other relatum.

This is because there exist uncontradicted cognitions such as "these two are distinct" and "this is distinct from that," just as there are cognitions like "these two are conjoined" and "this is conjoined with that.
It is accepted that a single difference possesses both the state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) and the state of being the substratum (*anuyogitva*) relative to a jar.

Furthermore, the undesirable consequence (absurdity) that "a jar is distinct from itself" does not arise, precisely because the locus-ness of a difference qualified by having itself as its counter-correlate—which necessarily appears in such a cognition—is contradicted in relation to itself.
This is according to the view that [the cognition] would result in the apprehension "the jar is conjoined with itself.

For this very reason, relying on this very position, he will—when seeking to establish the cognition "there are two moons" by resorting to a difference in the moon—avoid the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example.

Thus, since difference is one and the same—whether it appears in the cognition "the world is different from God" as having God as its counter-correlative, or in the cognition "God is different from the phenomenal world of individual souls (jīvas) and so forth"—it follows that this difference is not perceived, because God Himself is not perceived.

The point is that for the perception of a relation, such as the conjunction between a jar and space, the perception of all its substrata is a necessary cause, just as in the case of the conjunction between a jar and the ether.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "Since in the preceding verse it was only the difference of the world from God that was relevant and upon which the inquiry had commenced, the statement that the difference of God [from the world] is not perceptible is incoherent;

furthermore, if the non-perceptibility of the counter-correlative necessitates the non-perceptibility of the difference, then the perception of the difference in the case of 'the pillar is not a ghost' would be impossible. Thus, the argument is set aside.

In the previously mentioned view, since it is accepted that even a difference having God as its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) resides in God as its locus (dharmin), there is no lack of relevance to the inquiry; furthermore, in this view, the cognition "the pillar is not a ghost" is admitted to be of the nature of inference, verbal testimony, and so forth, rather than being admitted as perception.

The word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Alternatively, this statement proceeds according to the view established by all [schools], namely: "A difference which has a certain thing as its counter-correlative does not reside in that thing, but resides only in the locus (anuyogin)."
If it is asked, "In that case, how is the demonstration of the non-perceptibility of difference relative to God (Īśvara) of utility?"—it is as follows:
Just as in the view of Bhāskara, there is absolute non-difference between the jar and the clay, whereas there is absolute difference of the jar from the clay;
thus, difference and non-difference are established between cause and effect.

Likewise, although there is absolute non-difference between the Lord, who has become the cause, and the world, the word "distinct" (*bhinna*) is used to refute the view that [the Lord] is absolutely non-different from the world.
Furthermore, specific distinctness consists in possessing an absolute difference relative to the world with which He is absolutely non-different.

This [concept of distinctness] follows from what was introduced in the preceding verse; accordingly, the meaning of the term "distinctness" (*bhinnatva*) in the passage concerning the doubt regarding His being different from the universe is also this very same thing.
And thus, since both types of difference are under discussion, it is appropriate to establish that this particular difference—having God as its counter-correlate—is not perceptible.

Nor does the non-perceptibility of a difference follow from the non-perceptibility of its counter-correlate, for that would entail the impossibility of perceiving the difference between a pillar and a piśāca; however, such an outcome is acceptable [to us].
This is because, according to the manner previously stated, it is admitted that [the cognition of difference] takes the form of verbal testimony and so forth.
Nor is there a lack of grounds for this here;

for we experience that the knowledge of a property contradictory to a property residing in the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is a cause for the perception of difference. Thus, if the counter-correlate itself is not perceived, the property residing in it is also not perceived, and consequently, it would be impossible to apprehend its contradiction within another property.

Alternatively, the determination of the counter-positive as qualified by the delimiting property of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) is the cause of the cognition of difference; since [entities] such as *piśācas* are determined through worldly consensus and usage, the perception of difference having them as its counter-positive is established.

As for the Lord qualified by independence and other attributes as you conceive Him, He cannot be known through inference and the like, because such arguments are rendered non-conclusive by being countered by equally strong opposing reasons (*satpratipakṣa*).

However, since the scriptures, by means of their introductory indications (*upakrama-liṅga*), have as their sole purport pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), what remains is nothing but direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The intention [of the author] is that even such perception is not possible regarding the aforementioned Lord, because of the absence of the cause consisting in the determination of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*); thus, the perception of the difference from the aforementioned Lord is not tenable.
[Objection: But surely, since the substratum (*dharmin*) in the form of the Lord is not perceptible, it is improper to state that the difference residing therein (*tadvṛtti-bheda*) is imperceptible.

If it is argued that even though the sky (*gagana*) is not perceptible, the absence of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) residing therein is accepted by the experts as an object of perception; and even though a flower is not an object of the sense of smell, the absence of the campaka fragrance residing in it is admitted to be an object of olfactory perception—this is not so.

For while such a state of affairs may be possible in the case of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) because the non-perception of a perceptible counter-positive (*yogyapratiyogyanupalabdhi*) serves as the cause, the intention [of the author] is that in the perception of difference (*bheda*), the perception of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) itself is the cause, as established by positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
Alternatively, the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) is indeed mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
In that case, the cause [of non-apprehension] is the non-apprehension of identity with that which is fit for perception.
And "fitness" consists in having a counter-positive whose existence would entail the presence of that counter-positive.

Thus, since it is impossible to posit the apprehension of identity with anything other than that [object] residing in a locus that has become perceptible, there is no non-apprehension of the fit in the present instance; such is the intended meaning. Enough of this.
However, some explain that the word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of a comparison;
thus, the difference having God as its counter-correlative is presented as an example, and it is not an irrelevant statement.

They further maintain that this [difference] must be understood as having another living being (*parajīva*) as its counter-correlative and something beyond the senses (*atīndriya-jaḍa*) as its substrate, because such a difference is directly perceived by oneself (*svapratyakṣatvāt*).

In this regard, since the Advaitins and the Naiyāyikas both accept a single difference having God as its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) that resides in universals other than God, there is a dispute regarding whether the difference from God is an object of perception in the case of the self, a jar, and so forth; thus, the illustrative example is inconsistent.
Even if one were to say "this" by accepting a difference based on the distinction between substrata (dharmin), it remains inconsistent to claim the apprehension of difference in general.
Furthermore, one must consider how to resolve such issues as the refutation of the perception of a difference from God where the self is the locus (anuyogin).
Nor should it be argued that because [the opponent's position] is not even relevant, its refutation is unnecessary.

For even so, since in our own second explanation the perception of difference having God as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) must also be refuted, the fault stated therein remains unaddressed. Thus, the attempt to somehow reconcile the text by establishing the opponent’s conviction—that the perception of the counter-correlative is a cause for the perception of difference in general—is a desperate resort. Furthermore, in the explanation we have provided, this [conviction] does not exist.

Here the proponent of non-duality (advaitavādin) raises an objection: "Now [nanu]... By the phrase "of the Supreme Brahman," he indicates that if difference were admitted, the status of being the Supreme Brahman—which consists in the non-limitation of reality—would be untenable. "Sentient and insentient" refers to the individual soul (jīva) and the insentient (jaḍa).
The term "by nature" is also to be construed with the word "difference."

Although the distinction between the Lord (*īśvara*) and the subject (*dharmin*) is the primary topic here, the term "distinction" (*bheda*) is employed in its general sense in order to include the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and insentient matter (*jaḍa*), which is indicated by the word "universe" (*viśva*). Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of proof": this is based on the conviction that the aforementioned proof is merely fallacious (*ābhāsa*).

He demonstrates this very point with the passage beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*) and ending with "in brief" (*saṅkṣepaḥ*). As for the phrase "not, first of all": [an objection is raised] "But this is inconsistent; since the inference based on contradictory properties such as independence was stated in the first verse, it is precisely that which ought to be refuted.
Do not say so.

In this context, because the term "principal" (*pramukha*) is intended to include being the object of perception and scripture that apprehend differentiation, only the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are obtained. Although perception and scripture are inherently more powerful, in the present case, perception pertaining to the Lord is subject to dispute because it is the very thing to be proven (*sādhya*), and scripture is dependent upon reasoning; therefore, inference alone is primarily adopted. Thus, by prioritizing inherent strength, perception is refuted first.

For this very reason, even in the Siddhānta (the final conclusion), the three means of valid cognition beginning with perception (*pratyakṣa*) will be demonstrated. Regarding the phrase "the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)," the meaning is a difference whose locus is the self and whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is another self. This amounts to saying: the difference of the individual soul from the Lord, the difference of the Lord from the individual soul, and the mutual difference among individual souls.
It is precisely for this reason that there is a logical connection (*saṅgati*) in refuting the inference that establishes the plurality of selves in general.
The term "Īśvara" (the Lord) is an indicator for other selves as well.

As for the claim that Viṣṇu’s being distinct from the universe would mean either possessing a difference whose counter-correlate is the entire universe, or being the counter-correlate of a difference residing in the entire universe—neither of these two is possible. With this intention, the perception of difference is refuted in both cases.
That is not so; for since the word "different" (bhinna) does not denote that which is the counter-correlative of difference, such a conceptual construction is untenable.
Otherwise, there would result the absurdity of the usage "a jar is different from a jar."

Furthermore, even if one does not accept a difference whose counter-positive resides in a part of that [whole] which has as its locus a property occurring distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), there would still be the undesirable consequence of the usage: "The pair consisting of a jar and a cloth is different from the jar. "Because it is not perceptible" (*apratyakṣatvāt*): The sense is that the perception of the substrate (*dharmin*) and the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) are causes for the perception of absence (*abhāva*).

He raises an objection in order to establish that Viṣṇu is by his very nature different from the universe consisting of sentient and insentient beings—starting with "But surely" (*nanu*). "Consisting of sentient and insentient" (*cetanācetanātmaka*): This means "consisting of sentient and insentient beings that are mutually distinct."
Therefore, it should be understood that what follows later—the refutation of the mutual difference between living beings (*jīva*) and the body (*jaṭha*)—is consistent [with this].
Otherwise, there would be an inconsistency with the subject matter at hand. "In difference" means in difference by their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*).
The same applies to what follows.

Keeping in mind the alternatives—that the means of proof for difference (*bheda*) is either perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), or scripture (*āgama*)—the author first refutes the first by saying "no" (*na*). The word "first" (*tāvat*) is used with the intention that he will later refute perception even regarding the difference between insentient things (*jaḍa*); or it is used with the intention that he will refute both of the latter two positions as well. "The difference between the individual soul and the Lord" (*jīveśvara-bheda*) means the mutual difference among individual souls (*jīva*) and the difference between the individual soul and the Lord (*īśvara*).

Is it asserted that perception has as its object a difference qualified by the Lord (īśvara) and counter-correlative to the individual soul (jīva)—that is, "The Lord is not the soul"—or does it have as its object a difference qualified by the soul and counter-correlative to the Lord—that is, "The soul is not the Lord"? He refutes the first alternative: "Of that which is qualified by the Lord. The grammatical connection is: "Because a difference qualified by the Lord—that is, having the Lord as its locus—is not perceptible. He states the reason for this: "By virtue of the non-perceptibility of the Lord. This means: because the Lord, who serves as the substantive locus (dharmin), is not an object of perception.

The point is that in the perception of absence (*abhāva*), the perception of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is a necessary cause. Now, it might be argued that there is no such rule regarding the perception of the locus for the perception of absence, because the absence of sound in space (*ākāśa*) is perceived even though space itself is not perceived.

If it is argued that because the absence of color in air is perceptible, and since only the cognition of the locus is required, the perceptibility of the difference residing in that [air]—even though that [cognition of the locus] regarding God is non-perceptual—is not compromised; we say no. For while there is no rule requiring the perception of the locus for the perception of an absolute absence (atyantābhāva), which is a relational absence, there is a necessary requirement for the perception of the locus in the perception of mutual absence (anyonyābhāva), which is called "difference" (bheda).

For this very reason, it was stated by Rucidatta in his exposition of the Upādhyāya’s view: "Mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) that possesses color, even if it is [otherwise] perceptible, is not apprehended when air is the locus, because of the lack of perceptibility in that locus; for such perceptibility is a necessary condition for the apprehension of mutual absence. And this was also stated by the author of the *Ṭīkā* in the third chapter.
"In the apprehension of relational otherness (*saṃsargānyonyābhāva*), the fitness of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and its locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is, respectively, the governing factor.

He refutes the second [position] with the words: "of that which has God as its counter-correlate" (*īśvarapratiyogikasya*). The syntactical connection is: "because a difference having God as its counter-correlate is not perceptible. He states the reason for this: "due to the non-perceptibility of God" (*īśvarāpratyakṣatvena*). The meaning is: "due to the non-perceptibility of God, who is the counter-correlate."
The point is that the perception of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is a cause for the perception of a non-existence (*abhāva*).
This is an elliptical indication;

it should also be understood that a difference whose counter-correlate is another living being, or which resides in another living being, is not perceived because that other living being is not perceived.

For this very reason, the Siddhānta texts establish that the mutual difference between individual selves (*jīva*) is perceptible, stating that "the difference residing in Viṣṇumitra, having Yajñadatta as its counter-correlate, is perceived by Viṣṇumitra," and so forth.
It is for this same reason that the refutation of inference regarding the difference of the self-in-general—beginning with the words "Nor is there inference"—is logically consistent;

otherwise, after refuting perception regarding the difference between the individual self and the Lord (*jīveśvara-bheda*), the subsequent refutation of inference would have been more appropriately directed toward that specific difference, rather than being irrelevantly applied to the difference of the self-in-general.

Nor should it be said that "if the difference between the individual selves (*ātman*) is not established, the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is also not established," for even so,
one must consider that the refutation of the suspicion regarding the mutual difference of individual souls— as expressed in the phrase "the body of Caitra" and so forth— would remain untenable.
Nor is there proof by inference (*anumāna*).
The argument that "selfhood (ātmatva) resides in multiple individuals because it is a universal (jāti), like earthness (pṛthivītva)," is unestablished;
for those who maintain the oneness of the self, the difference between individuals is sublated, and thus they do not accept that selfhood is a universal.
Furthermore, the argument that "the self is the locus of a difference whose counter-correlative is another self, because it is a substance, like a jar," is also unestablished.
This is because we do not accept that the self, which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*) characterized by being a substratum for qualities.
Furthermore: "Pleasure (*sukha*) resides in multiple individual instances, because it is a quality, like color.
The nature of pleasure (*sukhatva*) resides in that which resides in multiple individual instances, because it is a genus residing in a quality, like the nature of color (*rūpatva*)."
Nor is there any deviation [of the reason] with respect to sound (*śabda*) or the nature of sound (*śabdatva*), because that [sound] is a substance (*dravya*).
Even in the case where it is not a substance, the reason is qualified by being "other than that" (*tad-anya*); if this is argued, we say no.

Since pleasure, pain, and so forth reside in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and because there is a plurality of internal organs, the argument commits the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

However, if one intends to refer to intrinsic happiness (*svarūpasukha*), that is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it is not a substance (*dravya*). Furthermore, in the inference "Caitra’s body has a master distinct from the master of Maitra’s body, because it possesses activity contrary to that [other body]," there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Because even in the case of a jar and a cloth—which have the same owner (or even if they have different owners)—contradictory activities are observed.
If the reason is qualified by the term "being a body," the example fails to prove the point.
If it is argued that "the two subjects under dispute are distinct because they are substrata of contradictory properties, like fire and snow," this is not correct.
Because in proving an ultimate (pāramārthika) distinction, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva);
and because in proving a non-ultimate (vyāvahārika) distinction, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatva).
Therefore, inference is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the distinction between the Self (ātman) and the individual soul (jīva).

"Nor is it inference" means that it does not serve as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Regarding "selfhood" (*ātmatva*): although this inference establishes the difference of the self in general, it is stated here with the intention that the specific difference between the individual soul and the Lord is also established by it.

Just as when the quality of being a possessor of attributes (*guṇitva*) is established for substance in general, it is thereby established for its particular instance, the jar; so too, since it has been demonstrated that the mutual difference between individual souls is as relevant to the context as the difference between the soul and the Lord, it should be understood [that the reason applies] with reference to that. "Because it is a genus" (*jātitvāt*): the meaning is that a genus is characterized by subsisting in multiple individuals. "Because of non-establishment" (*asiddheḥ*): the sense is that it is unestablished for one or the other party.

He establishes that very point with the words "by the proponent of the identity of the self" (ātmaikyavādinā). The connection [of the phrase] is: "because the status of being a universal (jātitva) is not admitted. Regarding the phrase "of the difference between individuals" (vyaktibhedasya): the meaning is "because the difference between individuals called 'selves' is sublated by the proofs to be stated later."

He demonstrates the very non-establishment [of the reason] with the words: "of the attributeless self" (*ātmano nirguṇasya*). To the question, "Why is the substantiality (*dravyatva*) of the attributeless self not accepted?", he replies: "because its definition is being the substratum of attributes" (*guṇāśrayatvalakṣaṇa*). He then anticipates two inferences regarding the plurality of the self, starting with: "Now, pleasure... (*atha sukha...*). Having raised the objection of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in these two inferences, he refutes it with: "And not... (*na ca*). The meaning is that in the first inference there is deviation in the case of sound (*śabda*), and in the second inference there is deviation in the case of the nature of sound (*śabdatva*).
The underlying point is that because the individual instance of space (*ākāśa-vyakti*) is one, there is no plurality [of instances].

To the question "Why is there no deviation (vyabhicāra)? he says: "Of that" (*tasya*). Thus, since sound lacks the quality of being a quality (*guṇatva*), and since "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) lacks the status of being a genus residing in qualities, the reason itself is absent; this is the sense of why there is no deviation.

Even if, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, sound is a substance (*dravya*), the absence of deviation remains well-established in the view of the Naiyāyikas and others because of its quality-status; therefore, he says: "Even in the case of its not being a substance. [The phrase] "by being other than that" means: in the first inference, by being other than sound; in the second inference, by being other than sound-ness.

Thus, in order to refute these two suspected inferences, the author sets forth the following alternative in his mind: "Is the word 'pleasure' here intended to mean ordinary pleasure, which is an attribute of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), or is it the pleasure that is one's own essential nature (*svarūpasukha*)? Having thus formulated the dilemma, he refutes the first position with the words: "Of pleasure, pain, and so forth. Here, the mention of "pain and so forth" is for the sake of providing an illustrative example. He refutes the second position with the words: "Pleasure as essential nature. The meaning is this: since the status of being an essential nature is untenable if there were a difference between a quality and its possessor, one must admit their non-difference; and if they are non-different, then like the Self itself, that pleasure which is non-different from it cannot logically be a quality, and thus the reason [of the opponent] is unestablished (*asiddhi*).

By this, the following refutation is indicated regarding the second inference as well: if "the state of being pleasure" (*sukhatva*) resides in the attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*); if it resides in the attribute that is the nature of intrinsic pleasure (*svarūpasukha*), there is non-establishment (*asiddhi*), because since that [intrinsic pleasure] is not a quality (*guṇa*), it is impossible for it to be a genus (*jāti*) residing in a quality.
This is merely an illustration.
In this regard, is it being asserted that there is only one pleasure residing in various individual instances? Or is it many? In the first case, there is a contradiction.
Furthermore, there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example;
for it is not the case that a single pleasure or form resides in multiple individuals, as that would contradict experience.
Moreover, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the number one.
In the second case, the reason is unestablished (*aprayojaka*),
because we observe that a single self can be the locus of multiple pleasures at different times,
and because we observe it to be so even simultaneously through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*avacchedaka*) such as the feet and other limbs.

Furthermore, for those who maintain the identity of bliss with its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) because they do not accept that "bliss-ness" is a genus (*jāti*).

Moreover, regarding the position that a single bliss or a single form resides in multiple individuals, does it reside in multiple individuals by way of pervasion (*paryāpti*), like a genus, or by way of non-pervasion (*aparyāpti*), like a cloth spread over the tips of many blades of grass? Neither of these two [alternatives] is tenable.
Because this contradicts experience.

And thus, since it is untenable for pleasure to reside in multiple individual instances, the possibility of the universal "pleaseness" (sukhatva) residing in those [individuals] that reside in multiple instances is also cast far aside;
for the latter's existence is dependent upon the former.
By this, the claim that the property of "pleasurability" (*sukhatva*) itself is being proven to reside in multiple individuals through a relation mediated by its own substratum is also refuted.
One should also observe that, according to the aforementioned reasoning, the argument is unestablished (*aprayojaka*), and so forth.
For this very reason, it should be understood that these two inferences—being beset by many such defects—have been resolved by the text of the Siddhāntin.

Having raised the objection regarding the inference for the difference between individual souls (*jīva*), he refutes it with the words "Caitra’s body" and "Maitra’s body. The meaning is as follows: Maitra is the owner of Maitra’s body, and Caitra is distinct from him; therefore, [the body] belongs to that [distinct] owner. "Contrary to that" means contrary to the activity of Maitra’s body.
Here, the example is that of rams, cocks, and the like, which fight one another while being kept by their owners.
The intended general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) is: whatever possesses an activity contrary [to another's] has an owner distinct from that [other's] owner.
He establishes the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words: "of two [things] having a single owner. Regarding this, some read "of two [things] having a complete single owner";
however, the ancients state that this is an error.
Furthermore, this is merely an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
If one intends to express a distinction that is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).

If one seeks to prove a non-ultimately real distinction, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); this objection, which will be stated later, should also be understood here. Regarding the phrase "absence of an example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*): since the words *caitra* and *maitra* are employed merely for the sake of illustration, and because all bodies are intended to be the subject (*pakṣa*) due to their different arrangements, there is no example.

Some proponents of the doctrine of the oneness of the self (*ātmaikyavādin*), however, explain that there is an absence of an example because even in the body of Yajñadatta and others, the state of having an owner distinct from the owner of Maitra’s body is not admitted.

He anticipates another inference regarding the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), stating: "In the two subjects under dispute... [and] "...because they are the substrata of contradictory attributes. Here, in the subject (*pakṣa*), the contradictory attributes are omniscience and non-omniscience, and so forth;
in the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), heat and cold, and so forth, are to be understood.
The nature of contradiction, however, will be explained in the text of the Siddhānta.

Regarding that which ought to be stated, it will be explained at the very occasion of its commentary. "Because the qualification is unestablished" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatvāt*): the sense is that I have not accepted ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*) anywhere. "Because it would be proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatvāt*): the sense is that I have accepted the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) as being merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).
He concludes the refutation of inference with the words: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Regarding the phrase "the nature of the Self": although the mere distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) was introduced by the words "even though not yet," etc., nevertheless, since all five types [of distinctions] were introduced at the outset, the proof of the general distinction of the Self is considered here incidentally.
Now, one might ask: how is it that the distinction is fivefold?

Is it due to a difference in the substratum (*dharmin*), a difference in the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), a difference in the delimitors of the substratum (*dharmitāvacchedaka*), or a difference in the delimitors of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*)?
It cannot be the first two, because the three— insentient matter (*jaḍa*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and the Lord (*īśvara*)— alternately serve as both the counter-correlate and the substratum.
However, if one were to grasp the internal subdivisions, the number five would be untenable due to their infinity; for this very reason, the latter two [classifications] are not accepted either.
This is because the three categories—insentient matter (jaḍa), the individual soul (jīva), and the Lord (īśvara)—alone encompass all such states through their various permutations.

Therefore, in this context, only three types of distinctions should be stated. Even if there were fivefold divisions such as the "property-bearer" (*dharmī*) and so forth, one should state that there are exactly ten types of distinctions,
because there are ten [combinations] consisting of five counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*) and five sub-correlatives (*anuyogin*).
In this regard, the difference between absences shines forth solely due to the difference in the delimiters of the counter-correlates (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*).
