For this very reason, even though jars are infinite, there is no infinity of jar-absences on the ground because the delimiter is one and the same.
As for antecedent and destructive absences, however, although the counter-correlate is identical, they differ due to the difference in their delimiters in the form of prior and posterior time.

In the case of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there are five delimiters (*avacchedaka*): lordship (*īśatva*), individuality (*jīvatva*), insentience (*jaḍatva*), the property subsumed under insentience (*jaḍatvavyāpyadharma*), and the property subsumed under individuality (*jīvatvavyāpyadharma*).
Although the subsumed properties are many, there is no fault because they are unified by their respective natures (*tattvena*).

For instance, in the cognition "the individual is distinct from another individual" or "insentient matter is distinct from insentient matter," individuality and insentience are not the delimiters, because these properties also reside in the individuals and insentient things that serve as the substrata (*dharmibhūta*).

Regarding the statement "the insentient is distinct from the sentient," they say that although there is no fivefold absence for each individual factor—such as the substrate, the counter-positive, and so forth, since "sentience" and the like alone serve as the delimiters, the fivefold distinction is nonetheless established from the fivefold absence of the collective aggregate of both.
Furthermore, the tenfold classification when analyzed is indeed accepted;

since it is possible to unify them by considering the distinction as relating to both the sentient and the insentient, whether as the substrate or as the counter-positive, there is no loss of the fivefold nature.
[Objection: Even so, because of the distinctness of Ramā, there would be an eightfold nature consisting of the Lord and Ramā, the individual soul and Ramā, and the insentient matter and Ramā.
And it must be said that since "being untouched by suffering" is the definition of lordship (*īśatva*), she too would be included within the category of the Lord.
If that were the case, then by the phrase "the difference between the two Lords," there would be only six types. [Reply: This is not so.
Because it is intended that "jīvatva" (the state of being a living soul) means "having a consciousness that is not independent," she too is included by the term *jīva*.

Here, "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) means "consciousness" (*cittva*). "In various individuals" means: residing in a locus of absolute difference that is non-conditional and possesses the same ontological status as the substrata whose properties are mutually applied. This should be understood accordingly in the subsequent cases as well. Regarding "because it is a genus" (*jātitvāt*): [Objection] But "genus-ness" (*jātitva*) is not itself a genus; rather, it is the state of being eternal, unitary, and inherent in many.
In that case, the phrase "because it follows many" is sufficient; and if only that much were stated, there would be the fallacy of the probandum being non-different from the reason. Not so.

The state of being followed by many (*anekānugatatva*) consists in existing as that which possesses a number other than unity. The property to be proven (*sādhya*), however, is the state of existing in distinct individuals (*bhedavadvṛttitva*); thus, there is a difference [between the two].

Alternatively, the nature of a genus (*jātitva*) is the state of being the determinant for a cognition of recurrence (*anugatadhīniyāmakatva*) independently [of other factors]. [The phrase] "because the distinction between individuals is sublated" means that for this very reason, it is impossible for there to be either a state of being recurrent or a state of being the determinant for a cognition of recurrence. This is the intended sense.

Now, one might object: since for those who know reality (*tattvavid*), a genus (*jāti*) subsists in only a single individual, how can it be established by that [genus] as residing in multiple individuals?
And how can the rebuttal be effective against them, given that the property of "subsisting in many" is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to them?
To this, it is said:

By them as well, in order to establish that "spaciousness" (*ākāśatva*) and the like are not universals (*jāti*), it must be stated that a universal resides in multiple individuals or is concomitant with many [individuals]. However, when "residing in multiple individuals" is expressed by means of a term (*yatpada*) in conjunction with another term (*yadabhivyāhṛtya*), this "residing in multiple individuals" consists precisely in residing in specific individuals that fall within the midst of various individuals which are substrata of those respective properties, each of which is distinct from the others yet similar to them, [all] being delimited by the property that serves as the delimitor of the denotation of that term.

"Being followed by many" means residing in a particular individual that falls within the midst of many individuals which serve as the substrata for various properties similar to the property already mentioned.

Thus, by means of the property of "selfhood" (ātmatva), since non-difference is obtained through the inclusion of all fragments (khaṇḍa) via the various self-natures (ātmatva) that resemble the single selfhood, there is no defect whatsoever.
If it were stated simply by the term "selfhood," the probandum would be deficient; therefore, the recourse was made to the general [term] "that which... (yattat).
Because there is no other similar property (sadṛśadharma) for the nature of space (*ākāśatva*) in the form of "space-ness," it does not reside in multiple individuals.
Now, one might ask: what is this similarity?
If it is argued that it is "the state of possessing many properties belonging to that [object] while being distinct from it," we say no.
Because it would entail an abandonment of one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
Nor is it the possession of a property similar to that property, because that would involve the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
Nor can it be said that [similarity] consists in possessing a property as defined by that [other] property;
for in cases such as "the gavaya is like a cow," the form residing in the cow would be defined by the form residing in the gavaya, and so forth.
If that were the case, Yajñadatta—who possesses sonship as defined by Devadatta’s fatherhood—would incur the undesirable consequence of being similar to Devadatta.
Nor should it be said that "that which is the locus of a property as determined by another property—such as fatherhood and so forth—is similar to that [other property].

For if, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the property that serves as the determiner of similarity were also included, an impossibility would result. Nor should it be said that "[the property] must be different from its relatum," and so on.
Because similarity, like fatherhood and so forth, is a specific type of relation since it is defined by both [the similar entities],
and because it is difficult to define relationhood in relation to fatherhood and the like alone. To this, it is replied:
That which is the locus of a property as defined by a property residing in the ultimate [substratum] that determines a qualified cognition is similar to that [object].
Since properties such as "fatherhood" determine qualified cognitions such as "one who has a son," there is no over-extension [of the definition] to them.
However, in cases of similarity, such as "the gavaya is like a cow," the form (ākāra) and so forth do not determine a qualified cognition.

This is because there is no such cognition as "the cow is like a gavaya. Nor should it be argued that even in the case of "the cow is similar [to the gavaya]," there exists a qualified cognition (viśiṣṭapratīti);

for in that instance, what determines the cognition is specifically a particular relation between the intrinsic natures (svarūpa) residing in the two mutually related terms, and not the generic form (ākāra) and so forth.

Now, in your view, since there is no indivisible universal (*jāti*) that persists [through all individuals], and since divisible persisting properties exist even in color (*rūpa*) and so forth, it would be simpler to account for the cognition of persistence in jars and the like by means of those very properties; what, then, is the point of accepting a "universal"?

One might argue: "Let it be that any property whatsoever which does not over-extend (*anatiprasakta*) is the referent of the term 'universal'. But this cannot be said, because it would contradict the separate mention [of categories] in such rules as "preceded by quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), or universal" (*jāti*). If this is raised, we say: No.
For we do not postulate a genus (jāti) on the basis of some practical purpose.
In the case of a jar and the like, a genus distinct from qualities and so forth is established by direct perception itself.
In the cognition "this is a jar," the jar-ness (ghaṭatva) which is the object of that cognition is certainly not [the color] form (rūpa) and the rest.
Nor can it be the state of being a receptacle for water, because that would lead to the absurdity of perceiving "pot-ness" even in a cloth and the like, due to their existence there; furthermore,
the perception [of pot-ness] occurs even when one does not attend to this [property of holding water].
For that [definition] would result in the undesirable consequence of its application even to a pond and the like;
furthermore, it would result in the impossibility of applying it to a perforated jar.
Nor is it the state of having a broad base and a bulbous belly.

For [if it were defined as such], the cognition of that [earth] would erroneously apply to a painted image or a particular type of casket and so forth. Nor can it be qualified by the condition "while being produced from clay," because this would result in the impossibility of that cognition applying to a golden pot and similar objects.
Furthermore, because that [object] is perceived even when these [qualities] are not correlated [with it].
Moreover, if these alone were the grounds for the application of the word "pot" (ghaṭa), it would follow that the aforementioned words would be synonyms of the word "pot.

Alternatively, there is no fault, as this inference proceeds according to the Nyāya system. Regarding the term "Self" (ātman): nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction with the initial proposition (pratijñā).
Because that [property] is absent during the state of doubt regarding the unity or plurality of the self.
He demonstrates its non-establishment with the words "of the self. Nor, in that case, should it be said that "substantiality" (dravyatva) is the state of being an inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇatva);
for that must be predicated only of a quality in relation to the self, which is changeless and actionless.

Nor should it be said that "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) consists in being distinct from the six categories beginning with quality (*guṇa*); for such a statement is empty, as the property of being a substratum of qualities—which would effect that distinction—is absent [in the subject].
Nor, then, should it be said that substantiality itself is the reason (*hetu*).
Because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a difference whose counter-correlative is the self;
for since it is impossible for a thing to reside in itself, the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) exists [therein].
Furthermore, this is because "being a real entity" (*vastutva*), as common to both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), is not admitted [by the opponent].

Regarding the term *sūkṣma*: the sense is that because this [pleasure] is dependent upon a self (*ātman*), the plurality of selves is established by the force of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
Now, an objection: if one takes the pleasure of a single self as the subject (*pakṣa*), there is a contradiction (*bādha*);
if one takes the pleasures of multiple selves as the subject, the qualification of the subject is unestablished (*asiddhi*).
Even if [the universal] were generally included within the category of pleasure (*sukhapakṣīkāra*), there would still be a contradiction;
for it is logical that what resides in every particular (*viśeṣa*) should also be absent from the general [universal].

Therefore, although a resolution might be possible by means of a "partless inclusion" (*khaṇḍānugati*), the author—accepting "partless inclusion" (*akhaṇḍānugati*) for the sake of argument (*tuṣyatviti*)—employs another method, stating: "pleaseness" (*sukhatva*). The sense is this: in this way, it is easily established that "pleaseness"—which follows after each respective pleasure existing in a single instance—is that which resides in what resides in multiple individuals (*nānāvyaktyāśritāśritatva*). Regarding the phrase "in sound, soundness," the remainder of the sentence is: "of the two aforementioned reasons, respectively."

The sense is that this is because the space which serves as its substratum is one. "Because it is a substance" (dravyatvāt)—the remainder [of the sentence] is "of the portion consisting of color" (varṇabhāgasya).

Therefore, it should also be understood as: "because the nature of sound (śabdatva) resides in a substance. "Because it is not a substance" (adravyatve)—the remainder [of the sentence] is "of the portion consisting of resonance" (dhvanibhāgasya).

The statement "because of being a substance" (*dravyatvāt*) is a bold assertion (*prauḍhavāda*) intended to express only a partial aspect. Regarding the phrase "by being other than that": it should also be understood as an admission that even sound alone possesses that same nature. Regarding the example "Caitra’s body": one should provide the following illustration—"Whatever is the locus of an action incompatible with another is possessed by a master different from that [other's] master; for example, Caitra’s pot has a master different from the master of Maitra’s pot. Now, an objection may be raised: since pots and cloths, like bodies, are not established as having masters different from those [of others], this [example] is deficient in its probandum (*sādhyavikala*). Nor should it be argued that there exists a conventional distinction (*vyāvahārika-bheda*).
If that were the case, it would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) by that very same [reason].

Nor should it be argued that "only a negative instance (*vyatirekadṛṣṭānta*) should be cited here" (or "let it be cited"), because that would contradict the subsequent text which states, "due to the absence of an instance. If this is objected:

In general, since it is precisely the state of having different owners that is the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). And in the present case, if the ownership of the body belonged only to those [selves] as conditioned by the body, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*); therefore, the difference of the unconditioned [self] must necessarily be natural, and since the conclusion rests upon the subject (*pakṣa*) itself, one obtains nothing other than ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*), so there is no proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

Nor should it be argued that the ownership of the body belongs only to those conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and thus the difference between the pure self (*śuddhātman*) is not obtained.
For even in that case, it is established by proof that Caitra’s internal organ has a master distinct from the master of Maitra’s internal organ.

Nor should it be argued that the status of being a master of an internal organ belongs only to those [masters] as conditioned by another; for it is likewise established that such a condition itself possesses a distinct thing to be conditioned.

It should be understood that making the body the subject of the proposition (pakṣīkāra) amounts to accepting it as its very first limiting adjunct (upādhi). Furthermore, if one were to postulate an infinite series of such adjuncts, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress (anavasthā).

If it is argued that because the two [the self and the body] are merely characterized by the body, they possess the relationship of owner and owned, and thus there is neither a difference between the pure self and [the adjunct] nor the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya), we say no.
If the indicator (*upalakṣaka*) is merely extrinsic (*taṭastha*), then some specific property sought by the indicated object (*upalakṣya*) must be stated;
for example, although a crow is extrinsic, it indicates a house only as qualified by its being associated with grass, the conjunction with it, its destruction, and so forth.
And thus, by taking such a qualified entity as the subject (*pakṣa*), if one proves that [the self] has a different locus, the difference between the pure self (*śuddhātman*) is established.

Nor should it be argued that even though such a distinction exists, because it is merely indicative (*upalakṣakatva*), it does not constitute a pure substratum (*śuddhāśraya*), for that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

He clarifies the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*): "In all cases" (*sakala*). The meaning is as follows: when two things have owners who are both entirely distinct from one another, those who are the owners of the jar are also the owners of the cloth; thus, they possess non-distinct owners.

"Even devoid of internal distinctions of ownership and so forth" means that if it were stated simply "possessing a single owner," one might argue that there is no deviation [from the rule] due to internal distinctions of ownership even when the primary owner is one; therefore, the word "sakala" (all/entire) was used. "Due to the absence of an example" means that the mere body is of the same nature as the subject (*pakṣa*). "Unestablished" should be understood as being stated according to his own system, even though it does not constitute a valid objection. "Ultimate" means: in the sense of "mere difference" as qualified by the attribute of ultimacy (*pāramārthikatva*), without that qualification being included.

Regarding the term "selfhood" (*ātmatva*): Now, it might be argued that "being a universal" (*jātitva*) consists in being inherent in many individuals while being eternal and unitary. However, this [property] would be doubtful regarding selfhood during a state of doubt as to whether it resides in multiple individuals; furthermore, once there is certainty, inference would be redundant.
Moreover, the phrase "while being eternal and unitary" would be superfluous. To this we reply: no.
This is because *jātitva* (the state of being a universal) is an indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) adjunct (*upādhi*).
Alternatively, it is the property of being a feature that is free from the six subverting factors, such as non-difference with the individual (*vyakti*).
Nor should it be argued that even here, since the mere absence of non-difference with the individual is sufficient to indicate [the universal], the inclusion of the specific qualifiers is redundant.
This is because [the qualification] is not redundant, as it serves to constitute the absence of being undivided;
furthermore, in the present context, that much alone constitutes the reason (*hetu*).
Nor should it be argued that even there, there is the fallacy of "doubtful unestablishedness" (*sandigdhāsiddhi*) or "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatā*).
Because this very point is stated immediately hereafter. Regarding the phrase "like a jar" (*ghaṭavat*):

although the opponent does not admit that even a jar is the locus of a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the Self—thus making the example deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*)—nevertheless, this is stated with the intention that its establishment is like that of the jar, based on the unimpeded perception that "the jar is not I."

Alternatively, it should be understood that this objection—which accepts the meaning of "in a well-known instance" as "because the probandum is unestablished"—is indeed the very same refutation that will be stated later. Regarding the phrase "of the Self": although it is possible for the Self, which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), to possess substantiality (*dravyatva*) in the form of being a substratum of qualities, such substantiality cannot exist in the sense of a universal (*jāti*) within that which is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*).
This is because being a substratum of qualities is pervaded by [the presence of] attributes.
This is stated with the intention that when that [substratum] ceases, this [universal] also cannot exist;
for it is sublated that a single entity can reside in multiple individuals.

Thus, because there is a lack of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example, he says—due to this underlying unease—"pleasure-ness" (*sukhatva*). For even in this case, whether by the complete pervasion (*paryāpti*) of a single form of pleasure (or color) across many individuals, or by its non-pervasion (*aparyāpti*) like a cloth spread over the tips of many blades of grass, the fact that it resides in multiple individuals is not sublated.

In this way, [the opponent might argue] that for "form" (*rūpa*) as well, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "The state of being pleasure" (*sukhatva*). Even here, whether by way of pervasion (*paryāpti*)—like a genus (*jāti*) residing in various instances of pleasure or form—or by way of non-pervasion (*aparyāpti*)—like a cloth spread over the tips of many blades of grass—it does not reside in multiple individuals; thus, there is once again a sublation [of the reason] and the example remains deficient in the property to be proven.

Nevertheless, since the property of residing in an individual is to be proven for "pleasurability" (sukhatva) by means of a relation mediated by its own substratum, there is no minor flaw whatsoever. Regarding the phrase "residing in a quality" (guṇaniṣṭha): the term "being a universal" (jātitvāt) is used to exclude deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of that very nature [of pleasure];
the term "residing in a quality" is used to exclude deviation in the case of "mind-ness" (manastva);
and in the inference beginning with "sound," as well as in the subsequent inference regarding "sound-ness" (śabdatva), the term "being other than that" (tadanyatvena) is used.

In the first inference, [the reason is] "by being other than sound" (śabdānyatvena); in the second, it is "by being other than the nature of sound" (śabdatvānyatvena). Regarding the first inference, one must keep in mind the following alternatives: is the pleasure intended as the subject (pakṣa) a mental modification (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) or the innate bliss of the self (svarūpasukha)? Regarding the second, is it a property of a mental modification or a property of the modification of innate bliss? Having set these alternatives in mind, he states the critique of the first two cases: "of pleasure, pain, and so forth. The mention of "pain" is for the sake of providing an illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).

And with the intention that this same refutation should be understood to apply likewise even to the inference belonging to the side of suffering, he states [the objection] regarding the last two [inferences]: "svarūpa... (intrinsic nature...). In the second inference, it should be understood that for one who maintains the identity of intrinsic nature and pleasure (*svarūpasukha*), there is also non-establishment (*asiddhi*) because the property residing therein cannot be a universal (*jāti*).
In the phrase "contrary to that" (*tadviruddha*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the bodily movement of Caitra.

The reading "because of performing an action contrary to that [intended] action" is correct. Regarding the phrase "of those with multiple or single owners," the intention is that by the word *ceṣṭā* (action), mere movement is expressed.
For this very reason, the objection concerning the logical reason (*hetu*) based on the qualification "by way of being a body" is also appropriate.
In this context, the word *sakala* (multiple/all) is a scribal error.

By the phrase "of two things having a single owner," the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is established; and by the phrase "due to the observation of contrary activity," the presence of the reason (*hetusadbhāva*) is demonstrated.

Alternatively, if one were to argue that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the probandum also exists in the case of a jar and a cloth that have one primary owner and two secondary owners respectively, [the author] says "entirely" (*sakala*). This means that for both of them, there is only one single owner, whether primary or secondary. As for the claim "there is no example" (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*): for a proponent of the doctrine of the oneness of the self (*ātmaikyavādin*), even in the body of Yajñadatta and others, there is no admission of an ownership distinct from the owner of Maitra’s body.

The meaning is that in the case of a specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*), there is an absence of an example for the reason (*hetu*) as qualified by corporeality (*śarīratva*). Likewise, in the case of a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*), one should understand that there is an absence of an example for the reason as qualified by corporeality.
Similarly, one should understand that even for the unqualified reason, there is an absence of an example in both types of pervasion.

And thus, even if the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is excluded by qualifying the reason (*hetu*) with "being a body," the absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*) remains indeed difficult to overcome; such is the meaning of the text. One must not, however, be deluded into thinking that there is an illustrative example when there is no qualification, and an absence of an illustrative example when there is a qualification. Regarding the phrase "because they are the substrata of contradictory properties" (*viruddhadharmādhikaraṇatvāt*): if "contradiction" here refers to the relationship between the slayer and the slain, then there would be an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) due to the relationship between slayer and slain existing between knowledge and desire, even though they reside in the same locus, according to the maxim: "One that is not yet born does not kill another, nor does one that resides in a different locus."

If it is argued that the relation of counter-positive and substrate (pratiyogyanuyogibhāva) [is the defining characteristic], then there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntyam), because such a relation is possible even between knowledge and its prior absence when they share the same locus. If it is argued that there is a rule of non-coexistence (sahānavasthānaniyama), then there is a lack of proof (asiddhi) under the doctrine of a single self (ekātmavāda). While this objection stands, he states another refutation: "pāramārthika... [the ultimate...]

Regarding the phrase "the nature of being a self": the delimiting condition of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) is merely the state of not occurring in anything other than a self, and not the state of occurring in all selves as well.
This is because, since the plurality of selves is unestablished, there would otherwise follow for the opponent the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi).

However, according to the aforementioned delimiting condition (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*)—namely, that the purpose is fulfilled merely by establishing the probandum (*sādhya*) through co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which establishes the plurality of selves—there is no requirement for establishing the probandum under the specific delimiting condition (*avacchedakāvacchedena*). Consequently, even though the probans (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) are absent in pleasure, pain, and so forth—which are indeed covered by the aforementioned delimiting condition consisting in "not occurring in anything other than the self"—there is neither partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*) nor sublation (*bādha*) regarding those parts. Alternatively, the delimiting condition may be defined as "occurring in all selves" while being characterized by the absence of being a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of any difference residing in a self; thus, there is no lack of establishment regarding the subject (*pakṣāsiddhi*).

In order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking [the property of] substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth as the subject, the probandum must be proved with respect to the delimiting factor (*avacchedakāvacchedena*).

Even if the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum with respect to the delimiting factor, if one adopts the view that there is the fault of partial establishment (*aṃśe siddhatādoṣa*), then the property of "not occurring in anything other than the self" (*ātmetarāvṛttitva*) must also be included within the scope of the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

Now, an objection: in this position—or under the alternative position where the delimiting factor of the subject is merely "occurring in all selves"—since even the plurality (*bahutva*) occurring in all selves would be included within the scope of the subject, it would be impossible for the nature of a "universal" (*jāti*) being refined here to exist [in all such cases], and thus there would be the fallacy of partial non-establishment (*bhāgāsiddhi*).

If it is argued that, since plurality is established in one's own view, a difference characterized by a delimitation residing in selfhood (ātmatva) as delimited by the relation of objectness exists in the self; and therefore, because the relation of inherence must necessarily be included in the delimitation of the counter-correlativity of that difference in order to include such [other] selves, the aforementioned plurality would not be excluded—this is not so.

For the meaning of the term "residing in all selves" is simply the state of not being the counter-correlative of an absolute absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of inherence and resides in the self; thus, plurality is indeed excluded.

Because even the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of that [entity] exists in the self at the moment immediately preceding its own production, since destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), and absolute non-existence are mutually contradictory. The phrase "residing in multiple individuals" means either: (1) being qualified by difference (*bheda*) through the two relations of "subsisting in the locus of its own counter-positive" and "subsisting in its own substratum"; or (2) being qualified by duality (*dvitva*) through the relation of "pervading itself."

Therefore, the objection that there would be *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) or *arthāntara* (irrelevance) because—when "subsisting in a substratum of duality" or "subsisting in something distinct" is the probandum—one could take the duality of two selves (*ātman*) and so forth, as well as the difference from a pot residing in the self, thereby establishing the probandum even in the case of the oneness of the self, is refuted. The phrase "because it is a universal" (*jātitvāt*) means "because it possesses a qualifierhood delimited by an unrestricted inherence relation.
It does not mean "because, while being eternal, it is inherent in multiple things."

Since "subsisting in many" (*anekavṛttitva*) is precisely what is to be proven (*sādhya*) at this point, even if something additional were included in the body of the reason (*hetu*), the problem of the reason being non-different from the probandum (*sādhyāvaiśiṣṭya*) would not be avoided.

Nor should it be argued that the non-difference from the probandum—occurring when there is doubt regarding the probandum in the subject (*pakṣa*)—results in the reason being "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*), and that you yourself will later state that this fault does not apply because "being a universal" (*jātitva*) is not established; for such an objection is not worth considering now, because at the outset no such groundless doubt could have arisen, and because you will later state, on the basis of your own view, that it is only "ascertained unestablishment" (*niścitāsiddhi*) that applies, while "doubtful unestablishment" (*sandigdhāsiddhi*) is not mentioned.

Nor is its meaning "being an object of conventional usage by virtue of being a genus" (*jāti*), because there is no way to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the fact that even in the case of "unreal rejoinders" (*asaddūṣaṇa*), such usage is observed among the experts (*tāntrika*). Nor is it "being so [an object of usage] in a primary sense."

Since it is impossible to determine that the term "jāti" (universal) is primary here due to the absence of [the six] criteria such as being a *kośa* (repository), while it is secondary there, nor can its meaning be defined as "being a property (*dharma*) while being devoid of the six subverters such as non-difference from individuals," because the term "being a property" would fail to exclude deviation in the case of the ether (*ākāśa*). This is because the six subverters are likewise absent in the case of "ether-ness" (*ākāśatva*) and so forth, resulting in deviation there as well.

Nor can the absence of the sixfold sublation be the probans, because for one who maintains the identity of the Self, the absence of being a single individuality is unestablished; consequently, the group of six factors constituted by that [absence] cannot escape being unestablished as well.

In our own view, regarding the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*)—which possess an unconditioned modehood (*prakāratā*) in their own part through identity—in the case where the "pot-ness" residing in those particulars appears as a non-particularized essence through its own nature (as a relation), the inclusion of "being delimited by the relation of inherence" (*samavāyasambandhāvacchinnatva*) within the modehood is intended to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to them.

The proponent’s assumption is that, by the force of the experience "the pot" (just as the reason was stated for the pot), by the force of the experience "the self" (ātman), the [subject] is established as being the self even during the state of doubt regarding the aforementioned probandum.

It should be understood, however, that because that experience is denied on the basis of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), there is a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) later on. Regarding the phrase "of the self": the reading is *ātmano nirguṇatvena*.
The qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) of the self is stated as the reason for the sublation of the distinction between individuals.
In the case of the qualityless (nirguṇa), since there is an absence of qualities in the form of mutually exclusive attributes, mutual difference is not possible;
otherwise, a jar would be different from itself—this is the sense.
Regarding the phrase "because the difference between various individuals is sublated," the word "nānā" (various) is a scribal error, as the status of being a universal (jāti) is not admitted.

The point is that because the inherence [of difference] is not admitted, its modehood—whether delimited by inherence or undelimited—is not established, as is the case with its being of that nature (*tadrūpatva*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "having the self as its counter-correlative" (*ātmapratiyogika*): since a difference delimited by a property that exists distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) does not exist in its own locus, the qualification "not residing in the counter-correlative" (*pratiyogyavṛttitva*) must be added to the definition of difference.

Therefore, the sense is that by taking the difference between both [the self and] the pot, there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatā*). Regarding the phrase "like a pot": at the time of proving the difference of the self within the self, the dispute concerns only that [self] and nothing else; hence, the example "like a pot" is appropriate.
Otherwise, since the inferences found in the author's own Siddhānta texts are for the most part constituted by differences, they would fail to arise—this is the sense.

Furthermore, the sense is that there is a non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) in the form of being the locus of qualities, as well as the "substantiality" indicated by that.

Since this passage is intended to refute the two types of reasons based on substantiality (*dravyatva*) preceded by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the term "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa-pada*) in this section should also be applied as having both senses—that which makes known the essential nature (*svarūpa-jñāpaka*) and that which serves as the object [of proof]. Regarding the word "pleasure" (*sukham*): here, one should not fear that there would be a lack of a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*) and a contradiction (*bādha*) because the probandum (*sādhya*)—taken literally as consisting of the state of being various individuals (*nānā-vyaktitva*)—is already established according to the previously mentioned method; for if one were to apply the aforementioned refinement, that [state] would be absent in pleasure in any form whatsoever. Thus, there is no room for such a doubt.

In this world, individual instances such as blue, yellow, and so forth, are joined with and separated from their respective manifestations through the power of causal complexes (*sāmagrī*); the same principle applies to pleasure and other qualities. It is by relying on this view that this inference proceeds. Alternatively, "subsisting in multiple things" (*nānāvṛttitva*) here consists in possessing a genus (*jāti*) that is subordinate to the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) which delimits the pervasion of some duality. By taking the genus "pleasure-ness" (*sukhatva*), the probandum is established in the case of pleasure. And in the case of color, this is established by taking the genus "color-ness" (*rūpatva*). Furthermore, since this does not reach its conclusion without a distinction between selves (*ātmabheda*), the distinctness of the self is proven.

By including "guṇatva" and "sattā," the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) is avoided; by specifying "subsisting in something less extensive than quality-ness" (*guṇatvanyūnavṛtti*), the same fault is likewise excluded. Following the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), he states another inference: "pleasure-ness" (*sukhatva*). The meaning is that it is pervaded by some instance of duality through the relation of "inherence in that which inheres in its own inherent substrate. Thus, there is no minor flaw regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
The term "residing in qualities" (*guṇaniṣṭha*) is included to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of "mind-ness" (*manastva*).

The term *jāti* (universal) has the meaning of "merely inherent. Regarding the phrase "by being other than that": in the first inference, it means "by being other than sound" (*śabdānyatvena*); in the second inference, it means "by being other than sound-ness" (*śabdatvādanyatvena*).

Although even so, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) residing in [qualities] such as *katva* remains difficult to avoid, nevertheless, because the intended meaning is "being distinct from what resides in sound," there is no fault whatsoever.
The final logical reason (*hetu*) is established as "because of being inherent in a quality other than sound," since the other part [of the compound] is redundant.

Having placed in his mind the dilemma within his own school—whether the happiness under discussion is of the nature of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or of the nature of the Self—he refutes them in succession, beginning with "sukham" (happiness). "Because it is not established as a quality by this [reason]" means that it is not an object of establishment characterized by the mode (qualifier) of being a quality.
Thus, the sense is that the reason consisting of the form of "being a quality" is unestablished (*asiddha*) in that case.
The reading "because it is not established as non-quality" is easy to understand.

Regarding the phrase "Caitra’s body": Now, for those who maintain the identity of consciousness (*caitanyaikya-vādin*), since only consciousness possesses the status of owner (*svāmitva*) to some extent, the probandum (*sādhya*)—which involves an owner distinct from the owner of Caitra’s body—is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*). Nor should it be argued that this is established by resorting to a conventional distinction (*vyāvahārika-bheda*);
for alas, in that case, there would result the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhanatā*).

If it is argued that, in order to avoid this [fallacy], one must add the qualification "ultimately real" (*pāramārthikatva*) to the difference, and that this would result in the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), we say no.

Even when the difference between the bodies of Caitra and Maitra is perceived, the difference between the internal conscious beings is not perceived; therefore, at the time of debate concerning mere difference—unqualified by ultimate reality—the aforementioned inference proceeds. Thus, there is no non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) due to the inclusion of ultimate reality. Nor should it be said that, even so, the fallacy of an unestablished qualification remains.

Since the probandum (sādhya) is precisely the owner of Maitra’s body through the relation of being owned by one distinct from [the body] itself, ownership (*svatva*) functions merely as a qualifier within the scope of that relation; thus, the mere fact of having a distinct owner is well-known as a relation for things such as jars and the like. Regarding the phrase "because of possessing activity contrary to that": the meaning is "because of possessing activity contrary to its own activity. Now, one might object: "In this context, contrariety (*viruddhatva*) consists in not residing in the same locus (*tadadhikaraṇāvṛttitva*)."

There is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) because the two bodies belonging to Caitra during childhood and youth are distinct from one another and possess mutually contradictory activities; thus, the probandum (*sādhya*) as stated is absent [in the reason]. Even if one accepts their non-difference by relying on the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), there remains an inconsistency when taking the bodies of previous and subsequent births into account. Furthermore, if the body is included in the reason by way of the general property (*sāmānyadharma*) of being "Caitra’s body," then for those who maintain the identity of consciousness (*cidaikya-vādin*), Caitra’s body would also be Maitra’s body [due to the unity of consciousness], resulting in the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*).
But anything beyond that is not useful for the present context and is not worth defining.
Furthermore, let the mere fact of not residing in that body be the reason;
any charge of inconclusiveness (vyabhicāra) is not even worth considering.
If it is argued that even if [the body] is included as "action" (*ceṣṭātvena*), since a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) will be stated later, it should not be considered at this point—[we reply] no.
The body of Maitra is included precisely as a perceptible body (*paridṛśyamānaśarīratvena*), and not in its general form; therefore, there is no unestablished reason (*asiddhi*) for the opponent.

Since the reason is "possessing action that does not reside in the locus of that [action] at the very time of the action of the perceptible body," there is no deviation by taking into account the body of a previous birth, the body of childhood, or the body in the state of youth.

There is no deviation [in the inference] because the cause of the friend who is not a yogi resides in his body; this is established by taking as the probandum the action of two bodies belonging to him at the same time when he has attained the state of being a yogi.

If "action" (*ceṣṭā*) were not included [as the definition], or if it were included as "being a property residing in that which resides in a substratum of that [action]," there would be a lack of proof (*asiddhi*).

This is because the state of being a locus for "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and the absence of "space" (*gagana*), which reside in that [friend's] body, exists in Caitra’s body, and because the action of Caitra’s body exists therein.

If mere non-occurrence in that [body] were the reason, it would be improper to employ as a reason [the property of] color and so forth—which do not occur in Maitra’s body but do occur in many of his clothes and such—since they clearly possess deviation; therefore, it is introduced as "volitional effort" (*ceṣṭātva*). In that case, such "volitional effort-ness" exists only in actions accomplished by effort through the medium of the body, and these do not exist at all in things other than the body.

The proponent of the inference intends that since other bodies are similar to the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) anywhere. If one were to include merely "the state of possessing activity not occurring in that [subject]," the reason would be inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).

There might arise the suspicion that even the activity of this very body could be produced by that [other] self; therefore, at that very time, the contradiction—consisting in the state of not residing in the locus of that [other] activity—is included within the activity that serves as the reason.

Since two contradictory actions cannot arise from a single effort at one time, and since two specific qualities (*viśe�ṣaguṇa*) do not arise simultaneously in a self without the effort that originates life (*jīvanayoni-yatna*), another individual soul (*jīvātman*)—as the substratum of the effort conducive to those respective actions—is established. Because the effort of God (*īśvara-yatna*) is common to all, the argument does not conclude by taking that into account; therefore, there is no failure to establish the intended subject, which is the distinction between individual souls. This is the core of the inference. Granted that the action of the body as conceived by you may indeed be such [an action], in what form is it to be included within the body of the reason (*hetu*)?
There is no evidence for its inclusion [in the definition] by way of a distinct genus (*vaijātya*).

Furthermore, if it is included as "action-ness" (*kriyātva*), the intended general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) in the present context is: "Wherever there is the possession of an action incompatible with some particular action, there is ownership by one different from the owner of that [particular action].

Alternatively, the specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*) is: "Wherever there is the possession of an action incompatible with an action subsisting in Maitra’s body, there is ownership by one different from Maitra’s owner."

He states that neither [of the two] is possible because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), saying: "In this case" (*atre*). He demonstrates the deviation, saying: "Of the whole and the one" (*sakalaika-*) etc. The analysis of the compound is: "those two of which the master is one and the same for the whole.
The word "one" (*eka*) refers to the primary master. Thus, the meaning results in: "of those two established by the two systems as having Īśvara alone as their master."

Nor should it be asked how there can be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*). According to the opponent's view, since even with respect to everything, the single *jīva* alone is the owner, there is no one at all who possesses a different owner; thus, there is an absence of any cognition of deviation. If it is argued: "In order to avoid the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), we accept that the probandum (*sādhya*) is 'the owner of Maitra’s body' related through the relation of being the owner of a body distinct from oneself. Therefore, there is no deviation in the specific pervasion, because the probandum can be established by taking the Lord (*Īśvara*) as the owner. This is not so.

In the view of the opponent who maintains the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*), even God is—by his very nature—merely imagined, like a king seen in a dream; therefore, according to that very school’s own principles, they accept the presence of a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*).

As for the absence of an example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*), it is indeed difficult to overcome whether one posits action as such in the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) or the specific pervasion, or whether one posits it as action residing in a body, all according to the opponent's system.
However, in our own system, an example is possible by taking God himself as the possessor (*svāmin*); it is with this intention that the possibility of this inference being subject to doubt arises.

Otherwise, even in one's own system, an argument that lacks an illustrative example would be baseless and thus incapable of being subject to doubt. If it is argued that [the inference] cannot be a locus of doubt because it is swallowed by the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*)—taking the Lord as the possessor (*svāmin*)—we reply: by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), which consists in the sublation of other possibilities according to the previously stated method—namely, the impossibility of two uncommon volitions (*prayatna*) that produce two contradictory activities arising simultaneously in a single self—it results in the conclusion that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the possessor.

Therefore, there is no fault in stating that very [body] as the example (dṛṣṭānta), based on the following considerations: either with the intention that the probandum is not unestablished (*asiddhi*) because the "soul" (*jīva*) is included; or with the intention that even if the reason (*hetu*) is taken as "being an action of a body," the probandum is easily established in the bodies of Ḍittha and others at the time when Caitra’s body alone is the subject (*pakṣa*), by including the Lord (*Īśvara*) as its owner; or with the intention that the inference has been brought within the range of doubt. However, since the proponent does not accept the existence of God (*Īśvara*), and because there is no basis for ascertaining the aforementioned probandum in other bodies, the absence of an example remains a settled fact. Thus, there is no defect whatsoever.

Nor should it be argued that, even if the probandum (*sādhya*) is established for one who suspects inference, the emendation of the probandum as stated by you is irrelevant because—given the possibility of error according to his own system—it might be possible to state the probandum exactly as heard.

For, having set aside the most obvious fault in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*), which ought to have been pointed out first, to speak instead of [logical fallacies such as] deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth is extremely contrary to the context; therefore, the author’s intention was for the probandum to culminate in the formulation we have provided.

Alternatively, in the case of inference regarding God (*īśvara*), the term "owner" (*svāmī*) is included in the probandum (*sādhya*)—specifically as that which is delimited by ownership consisting in the possession of either pleasure or pain caused by being the determiner of ownership residing in oneself—in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). Furthermore, the relation [of the probans] is made to include that [ownership]. As for the lack of establishment in the instance (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*), it arises from the delusion that one's own view alone is tenable, namely, the belief that another living being (*jīva*) resides within other bodies. If that were the case, one should observe that even according to one's own view, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*) regarding objects such as pots, which are governed solely by God.

Alternatively, in order to avoid the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), one may take as the subject-qualification (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*) the state of being owned by Caitra with respect to Caitra’s body; thus, the probandum (*sādhya*) would be simply the absence of being the counter-correlate (*nirūpakatvābhāva*) of the ownership residing in the owner of Maitra’s body. Furthermore, the ownership included in the probandum within the subject must be understood in the aforementioned sense as being distinct from that of God (*īśvara*). This qualification is introduced in the subject to prevent the conclusion from terminating in [the ownership of] God and to avoid the contradiction (*bādha*); for if it were not so qualified, the argument would result in the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratā*) by terminating in the conclusion that the body has no owner at all. Therefore, its inclusion is necessary.

However, the probandum (sādhya) stated in the treatise is established by taking into account the conclusion of the probandum as the object of an inference that is dependent upon a subsumptive reflection (parāmarśa) consisting in the apprehension of the sublation of other particulars, which is assisted by a general cognition in the form of the cognition of the qualification of the subject (pakṣaviśeṣaṇa), according to the method previously described.

And this has been stated in the *Pratyakṣamaṇi*: "In the case of an inference with many probanda (*bahusādhyaka*), validity is apprehended by means of the property 'having fire as its qualificandum and fire-ness as its qualifier' (i.e., *vahnitvavad-viśeṣyakatvāvacchinna-vahnitva-prakārakatva*), even though it is not apprehended as the delimitor of the pervasion of the causal complex for inference (*anumiti-sāmagrī*)—by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—through the absence of the property 'having fire as its qualificandum and fire-ness as its qualifier' delimited by the state of having as its qualificandum that which possesses the non-production of burning (which is the pervader) and is delimited by the state of having as its qualificandum that which is qualified by fire-pervasion (*vahni-vyāpyavat-viśeṣyakatva*)," [this absence] being of the nature of the apprehension of sublation (*bādhagraha*), namely, the absence of the property 'having fire as its qualifier' delimited by the state of having as its qualificandum that which stands before one and lacks fire-ness (*vahnitvābhāvavat-purovṛtti-viśeṣyakatva*).”

Just as that [other particular] is established by the production of an inference of another particular through the causal complex for the inference of a general property accompanied by the apprehension of the sublation of one particular, so too is the other particular established—even if its pervasion has not been grasped—by the causal complex for the inference of the absence of one particular accompanied by the cognition of the possession of the general property.
This is because the non-arising of doubt regarding another particular is established by experience in both cases.
All of this, as stated by Dīdhiti and others, should be understood as having been restated here.

And since, in this way, misconceptions regarding other bodies—just as with Caitra’s body—are possible, those [other bodies] cannot serve as examples; therefore, what is intended by the term "volitional activity" (*ceṣṭā*)? If it were merely "action" (*kriyā*), then even according to the Advaita view, objects situated in the forest that have no owner such as Maitra could not possibly serve as examples.

Alternatively, keeping in mind the two alternatives—whether to include "residing in a body" as a qualification or not—the proponent of the doctrine of a single soul (ekajīvavādin) states, according to his own view, that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in both the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) and the specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*), just as in the case of jars and cloths owned by Caitra, Maitra, and others, [stating] "of those belonging to a single owner.

In that context, the opponent who refutes the inference provides a qualification containing the reason (*hetugarbhaviśeṣaṇa*). Even from the perspective of the one who employs the inference, there is a deviation in the general pervasion with respect to jars and other objects owned solely by God (*īśvara*), because the probandum (*sādhya*) as formulated—which consists of being miserable as determined by Him—is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*) insofar as it involves ownership residing in a body.

Furthermore, regarding the pervasion by a specific property (*viśeṣavyāpti*), the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—namely, that [the reason] exists in a jar owned by Maitra which possesses an action contrary to the action of Maitra’s body—is already almost established by the aforementioned statement.

And if one follows the second alternative, since action residing in a body does not exist in things other than bodies, and because other bodies are equivalent to the subject (*pakṣatulya*), there is no deviation; however, there is a failure of the example (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*).

And since there is indeed a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) when [the reason] is restricted to mere action, there is no lack of proof for the example; thus, there is no contradiction between the preceding and following sections of the text. Regarding the phrase "by being a body" (*śarīratvena*): the meaning is that "given that it is a body" (*śarīratve sati*) is a qualification of the reason (*hetu*).
The point is that if the qualified portion were not included, there would be a deviation in Maitra’s very body.
In some manuscripts, the reading *ekasvāmikayoḥ* ("of two having the same owner") is observed.
And that [point] is easy to understand.

Regarding the phrase "in case of doubt" (*vimatau*): one might object, "Since the difference between the two has not yet been established, how can there be the status of being the subject (*pakṣatā*) by virtue of being 'two'? For this would result in the fallacy of the subject being unestablished for the opponent.

This is not so; because the duality residing in the bodies of Caitra and Maitra is established through perception, we follow the principle that it serves as the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) by means of the relation of possessing experience delimited by its own substratum.

Even in the view that there is only one single Self delimited by both bodies, there is no sublation [of the reason]. Regarding the term "contradictory" (*viruddha*): contradiction does not mean "not existing in the same locus," because prior to the establishment of difference, it is impossible for the reason to be established for both parties.
Rather, it means being of the nature of mutual absence, or being pervaded by mutual absence.
And this is accepted even by the opponent on the strength of common worldly experience regarding specific pleasures, their absence, suffering, and so forth.

Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of all worldly transactional activity (*laukika-vyavahāra*). The intended meaning is that its non-establishment does not occur in either of the two views. Regarding the term "non-ultimate" (*apāramārthika*): the sense is that, having set aside the qualification of "ultimacy," it refers to being established either in the form of the general property of "difference-ness" (*bhedatva-sāmānya-rūpa*) or in a form consisting of "transactionality" (*vyāvahārikatva*).
It should be noted that this critique is stated precisely at the conclusion of the refutation of inference in order to demonstrate its applicability to all inferences that establish difference.

It should not be argued that, this being the case, the refinement of the probandum (*sādhyapariṣkāra*) in the previous inference and the refinement of the subject (*pakṣapariṣkāra*) made here are redundant, since such statements could have been made incidentally simply by not considering the aforementioned refutations.

For if that were so, the very occurrence of the inference would be rendered redundant—since the previous inference would have achieved its purpose through the mere establishment of the probandum and this one through the mere establishment of the subject—and thus, according to the stated reasoning, the refinement is indeed necessary.

However, since after that [point] the refutation—that because suffering and so forth exist only in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to a self devoid of attributes—is evident according to both the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*) and the doctrine of many souls (*bahujīvavāda*), it is not stated [again].
Instead, this refutation is stated according to the view of the doctrine of many souls, as something common to all inferences that establish the distinction between conscious and insentient entities.

This is done to make it clear that even if the doctrine of a single soul were refuted regarding that specific subject by merely establishing some kind of distinction between conscious entities, the "distinctness from the universe" (*viśvabhinnatva*) intended by you would still not be established; thus, everything is consistent.

Although the inference establishing the difference of the universe from God—which has as its subject (*dharmin*) God and as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) the universe—stated in the first verse, is precisely what should have been refuted first; nevertheless, [the author] first refutes the inferences establishing the difference of [any] sentient being in general, in order to indicate that if an inference establishing the difference of sentient beings in general is fallacious, then an inference establishing it in a specific case is all the more so. He does so with the words: "The nature of self" (*ātmatvam*). This means: the ground for the application of the term "self. By this, if the nature of self (*ātmatva*), which is a universal (*jāti*), were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be the fault of the subject being unestablished (*pakṣāprasiddhi*).

And since its nature as that individual [the universal] is thus established, there is no room for the objection that this would constitute a contradiction (*bādha*). "Residing in multiple individuals" means being inherent (*samaveta*) in many;

that is to say, it exists in that which possesses a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is its own substratum. Nor should it be argued that this results in a shift of the subject matter (*arthāntara*), because by this it would be established that *ātmatva* (the nature of selfhood) is inherent in both the self and the pot.

Because inherence in the self (ātmatva) is unestablished due to its being contradicted in the case of jars and so forth; or, if it were established, the intended goal would be achieved through the establishment of the plurality of the substrata of selfhood. And this is according to the method of the logicians (Tārkikas).
It should be understood that, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), this is because a universal (*jāti*) is not inclusive (*ananugata*).

In reality, however, the state of occurring in that which possesses the aforementioned difference consists in the fact that [the universal] is not, per se (*svarūpataḥ*), a delimiting factor (*anavacchedakatva*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference occurring in that which possesses such a difference.

And although "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) differs with each individual instance, there is no fault, because—due to the absence of such cognitions as "this is a self" or "this is not a self"—it is not, per se, a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of the differences occurring in each respective self.

Because of the qualification "by its own nature" (*svarūpataḥ*), there is no defect even if the property of being a self (*ātmatva*)—in its specific individuality—is the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in other selves. This should be understood similarly in what follows as well.
Furthermore, the "genus-ness" (*jātitva*) employed as the reason is not defined as "being inherent in multiple eternal entities."

Because [the property] would be either redundant due to its eternality, or because it would be indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*). However, it should be understood that [the reason] is either an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) or the state of being denotable by the word "universal" (*jāti*). Thus, "because this is unestablished" (*ityasyāsiddheḥ*) means: because the reason (*hetu*) to be established by the *nyāya* is unestablished.
The meaning is that the distinction between individuals (*vyaktibheda*) refers to an inherent distinction between selves (*svābhāvikātmabheda*).

The intention is that an inherent distinction between individuals serves as the determinant for a universal (*jāti*), in order to preclude [universals such as] "sky-ness" (*gaganatva*) from being classified as universals.
This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be understood that if one posits a difference qualified by ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) within the body of the probandum (*sādhya*), there is the fallacy of the unestablished probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*). Conversely, if one posits a difference without that qualification, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), as this would merely involve a non-ultimate difference.

Regarding the term "Self" (*ātman*): here, the phrase "having a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) that is not ultimate" is used to exclude the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*)—namely, the mere difference from pots and the like. Its meaning is: "having a counter-correlativity delimited by a nature (*rūpa*) that is pervaded by selfhood (*ātmatva*)."
Therefore, by taking the difference between the self and the pot, there is no "different subject matter" (*arthāntara*).
Some also say that the probandum (*sādhya*) is a difference that does not reside in the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) which has the self as its own counter-correlate.
Although in this case even [the property of] knowability (*prameyatva*) and so forth could potentially serve as a logical reason (*hetu*), [it is not used].

Nevertheless, because an inference based on that [mere observation] depends upon extensive and frequent observation common to both substances and non-substances, it is not easily accomplished; with this intention, the author has followed the view that "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) alone is the logical reason (*hetu*).
Since there is dispute regarding whether "substance-ness" is a universal (*jāti*), it is described as having the definition of being the substratum of qualities (*guṇāśrayatva*).

If, however, one does not accept that "being the substratum of qualities" (*guṇāśrayatva*) is the reason because it is more cumbersome than "being a substratum" (*āśrayatva*) alone, then it should be understood that the reason is simply "the quality itself by virtue of being its substratum. Others also maintain that the universal "substantiality" (*dravyatvajāti*) alone is the reason, on the grounds that "being the substratum of qualities" is merely the definition or the manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*) of that universal. Regarding the phrase "because it is not accepted": although [the argument] is not established even for that which is naturally devoid of qualities, since it possesses a superimposed (*āropita*) substratum of qualities—given that one accepts that even a superimposed state of "smokiness" can prove the existence of fire.

Nevertheless, the sense is as follows: in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), since it is precisely an ultimate (*pāramārthika*) difference that is to be proven, and because being the substratum of superimposed qualities is irrelevant (*aprayojaka*), that [difference] must also be stated as being ultimately real; thus, [the reason] remains unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Regarding the statement "pleasure does not reside in multiple individuals": although there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example because color (*rūpa*) and so forth do not each reside in multiple individuals, and even if conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like could serve as examples, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding color and so forth.

Nevertheless, there is no fault, because the probandum (*sādhya*) consists in a universal belonging to a genus that resides in various individuals, specifically defined as possessing a universal subordinate to *guṇatva* (the property of being a quality) which resides in the delimitors of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the differences residing in the substrata of its own substratum.

This is because, in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), *rūpatva* (the property of being color) and so forth reside in yellow color, which is a delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in a blue jar—the substratum of itself.

And in the subject (*pakṣa*), when the probandum is established by taking *sukhatva* (the property of being pleasure), the difference between the selves (*ātman*), which are the substrata of those [pleasures], is proven.
The term "pervaded by quality-ness" (*guṇatvavyāpya*) is included to exclude other possible objects [of the definition] by taking into account universals such as quality-ness itself.

It should not be argued that the fault of "otherness of the object" (*arthāntaratā*) remains because quality-ness itself is also pervaded by quality-ness, since it does not subsist in that which is devoid of quality-ness;

for by the phrase "pervaded by quality-ness," what is intended is subsistence in a locus smaller than quality-ness, which amounts to being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the difference residing in qualities.

There is no fault here, because the property of being pleasure (*sukhatva*) and so forth is pervaded by the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*), since it serves as the delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of the difference residing in qualities such as odor. Regarding this position, [the author] states "or pleasure-ness" (*sukhatvaṃ vā*) because of the complexity of the probandum (*sādhyagaurava*). The meaning of the phrase beginning with "not manifold" (*nānā*) is: "residing in that which is the locus of the difference residing in its own locus. By this, even though the property of being colored (*rūpatva*) and so forth does not possess the property of being resident in conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other such things that reside in multiple individuals, there is no fault as before.

The phrase "residing in a quality" (*guṇaniṣṭhā*) is used because the mere state of being a genus (*jātitvamātra*) is deviant with respect to *manastva* (the nature of the internal organ) and so forth.
The word "genus" (*jāti*) is used because that much alone [i.e., residing in a quality] is deviant with respect to its own form (*tadrūpatva*) and so forth.

It should be noted, however, that when it is stated that [the property] inheres in a quality (*guṇasamavetatva*), the term "genus" (*jāti*) is included precisely for the sake of obtaining that [specific property]. Regarding the term "deviance" (*vyabhicāra*): the point is that since the ether (*gagana*), which serves as the substratum of sound, is a single entity, the first probandum (*sādhya*) is absent from sound, and the second probandum is absent from the nature of sound (*śabdatva*).
He states [the view] according to the Mīmāṃsaka position: "of that" (tasya). This means "of sound" (śabdasya).

Thus, the sense is that since there is no reason [for deviation] either in sound or in the nature of sound (śabdatva), there is no inconstancy (vyabhicāra). He also states [the view] in the Nyāya system: "in the case of the position that it is not a substance" (adravyatvapakṣe). "By its being other than that" (tadanyatvena) means: in the first case, by being other than sound; and in the second case, by being other than the nature of sound (śabdatva).

Nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the second [reason], namely the genus "katva" and so forth; for by the phrase "being other than that," what is intended is "not subsisting in that which possesses it.
They also say that the reason should be further qualified by the condition "not being terminated by katva and so forth."
In reality, in both alternatives (*kalpa*), the phrase "as being other than that" means precisely "as being other than the word.

The intention is that since the phrase "because it is a qualifier of the reason" means "because it is a qualifier of a quality (*guṇa*) contained within the reason," there is no aforementioned defect; for properties such as *śabdatva* (word-ness), which reside solely in the word, do not reside in qualities other than the word.

Here, either *vṛttisukhatva* (the state of being pleasure consisting in occurrence) or *svarūpasukhatva* (the state of being intrinsic pleasure) serves as the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

With the intention that the universal "being a pleasure" (*sukhatva*) which follows both [pleasure and pain] is impossible due to its commingling (*saṅkara*) with [the universals] such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), he refutes the first [position] with the words: "of pleasure, pain, and so forth," beginning with "consisting of a function" (*vṛttyātmaka*).

Although pleasure (*sukha*) alone is the subject under discussion here, the mention of pain (*duḥkha*) and so forth is intended to indicate the refutation of other inferences that take pain, desire, and the like as their subjects. "Because they reside in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)"—the meaning is that these [pleasures and pains] are modifications (*pariṇāma*) of the internal organ. "Because it would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*)"—although even on the view that pleasure, pain, and so forth reside in the self (*ātman*), proving what is already established is indeed possible by taking recourse to an indefinable (*anirvacanīya*) distinction within the self;
and if the distinction were qualified by "ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatva*), the probandum (*sādhya*) would be unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).
Furthermore, if it were held that [the self] resides in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*),
because even the distinction between them is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*).
Nevertheless, the residence in the internal organ was stated solely in accordance with the way things appear to common experience.

In reality, according to the method to be explained, since the difference whose existence is co-extensive with the existence of the substratum (dharmin) constitutes the body of the probandum (sādhya), there is no room for the charge of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) under the view that [pleasure] resides in the Self; therefore, that statement refers only to the view that it resides in the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
He refutes the second position with the words "svarūpa... (in its own nature). This means "the nature of the Self.

The sense is that since pleasure is a quality (guṇa) only when it is inherent in a substance (dravya-samaveta), and the pleasure of one's own nature (svarūpa-sukha) is not so, there is a failure of the essential nature of the reason (svarūpāsiddhi).

In the Siddhānta, however, it should be understood that although [the body] is the very nature of the self, it nonetheless possesses the status of an attribute (*guṇatva*) by virtue of being a specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) of the self. Regarding the phrase "Caitra’s body": here, "being its owner" does not mean "being the enjoyer of the experiences delimited by it," for that would contradict the subsequent text which speaks of "a jar and a cloth having a single owner."
For the experience delimited by a jar or the like is not established [in the case of the Self].
Rather, it is a specific attribute characterized by being the regulator of the conventional usage of the relationship between owner and owned, and so forth, which regulates its existence.
Although, according to the opponent's view, the state of having an owner distinct from that [owner] is unestablished.

Nevertheless, there is no fault, because the delimiting factor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) is precisely "being distinct from its own owner," which is common to well-known objects such as jars.
Furthermore, the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatā*) is by way of the relation of "owning one's own [object].
Consequently, the difference between the selves of Caitra and Maitra is established as a result.
Because it is impossible for a jar or the like to be established by such a relationship.

Here, [the opponent], considering that "possessing an action contrary to that" means either possessing an action that does not occur in that [object] or possessing an action of a different genus from its action, offers a refutation with the words "In this case... He demonstrates the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words "Of two things belonging to one owner," which means "of two things owned by Maitra."

And thus, since a jar or similar object—which possesses an activity contrary to the body of Maitra—lacks ownership by anyone other than its own master, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even in the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) that "whatever is the locus of an activity contrary to X lacks ownership by anyone other than the owner of X," because a cloth or similar object—which possesses an activity contrary to a jar—also lacks ownership by anyone other than the jar's master.
[Objection: But surely the reason (*hetu*) is simply "possessing an activity contrary to that [body] while being a body";

therefore, the aforementioned deviation does not occur. To this, he says: "Even as a body" (*śarīratvena*). This means: even if the reason is "possessing the aforementioned activity qualified by being a body."

Although it might be argued that the aforementioned defect can be avoided simply by intending to define the category of *ceṣṭā* (volitional action) as an activity produced directly by effort— such that the separate mention of "bodiness" (*śarīratva*) defined as being the locus of such an activity would be unnecessary—
