it should not be said that there is no complexity [in the definition] because bodiness is a universal (*jāti*).
This is because it would result in a logical overlap (*saṃkara*) with earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and other such universals.

Nevertheless, since it is not accepted that *sāṅkarya* (overlapping) constitutes a sublation of a universal (*jāti*), "body-ness" (*śarīratva*) is mentioned separately because of the possibility of parsimony (*lāghava*). Regarding the phrase "absence of an example": the sense is that even if there is no apprehension of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) which opposes the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the apprehension of pervasion remains impossible due to the impossibility of apprehending the concomitance (*sahacāra*) that serves as its cause; thus, inference is not possible. He anticipates the method of inference that establishes all disputed differences with the words "in the two under dispute" (*vimatau*). This means the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), who are subjects of dispute regarding their being different or non-different.
Here, the number "two" is not intended to be restrictive.

Because being the object of dispute (*vimatatva*) alone serves as the delimiting condition for the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). "Distinct" means mutually distinct; that is to say, they possess a difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by a property pervaded by being the object of dispute. This is because they are substrata of contradictory properties, i.e., because they possess properties that are counter-correlates of absences residing in one another.
This means: "because it possesses a property that is the counter-positive of an absence co-located with the state of being doubtful" (*vimatatva*).

Here, by means of a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*)—namely, "whatever possesses a property that is the counter-positive of an absence co-located with a given property (*yaddharma*), possesses a difference whose counter-positiveness is delimited by a property pervaded by that given property (*taddharma*)"—just as *tuṣāra* (frost) and the like possess a difference whose counter-positiveness is delimited by *dahanatva* (firehood), which is pervaded by the state of being both fire and frost (*dahanatuhinobhayatva*), because they possess coldness and so forth, which is the counter-positive of an absence residing in fire and the like, which are loci of the state of being both fire and frost.

The intention is as follows: since the subject under discussion, such as Īśvara, possesses independence (svātantrya) and other qualities that are the counter-correlates of the absence residing in the individual soul (jīva) and others—which serve as the locus of the aforementioned state of being doubted—it is established that [Īśvara] possesses a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "jīva-ness" and the like, which are pervaded by such a state of being doubted.
Alternatively: This [Īśvara] is different from that [the jīva], because he possesses a quality that is the counter-correlative of an absence residing in that [jīva];
and that [jīva] is different from this [Īśvara], because he possesses a quality that is the counter-correlative of an absence residing in this [Īśvara].

The intended meaning of the collective inference (*samūhālambanānumāna*) is as follows: whatever possesses a property that is the counter-positive of an absence residing in *x* is distinct from *x*, just as ice, which is the locus of coldness—the counter-positive of an absence residing in fire—is distinct from fire.

Therefore, by taking both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) as the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no room for such defects as: (1) *arthāntara* (shifting the meaning) when proving mere difference by taking the difference from a pot (*ghaṭa*) and so forth; (2) *bādha* (contradiction) in part even when proving mutual difference, because that [mutual difference] consists in each case of the difference of the soul and so on; (3) *bhāgāsiddhi* (partial unestablishedness) in respect of properties such as possessing attributes contradictory to the soul, since these apply to each individually; and (4) the lack of concomitance between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*) in the subject and the example. In this context, the probandum is difference, whether qualified by ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) or not so qualified.

He states the fault in the first case: "pāramārthika" (ultimately real). He states the fault in the second case: "apāramārthika" (not ultimately real). The meaning is "unqualified by ultimate reality," and not "qualified by non-ultimate reality.
This is because, by not rejecting the position that establishes difference unqualified by either [of these two], there would be the consequence of an omission.
Whether that [inference] is qualified by "not being ultimately real" or not is another matter.

He concludes the refutation of the inference proving a distinction between the self [and Brahman] with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is: because, according to the manner explained, every inference attempting to prove difference is fallacious. The meaning is that inference is not a valid means of knowledge regarding the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

He announces the refutation of the second [position] with the words, "Nor... The phrase "the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)" is understood to carry over. Therein, he first restates and then refutes two inferences that seek to prove the mere plurality of the self, beginning with the words "The nature of being a self... Here, it is argued that the property of being a self (*ātmatva*) cannot reside in multiple individuals without the plurality of selves; thus, the difference between selves is established. [The opponent replies: "Because it is unestablished" (*asiddheḥ*). This means it is unestablished for one or the other party (*anyatarāsiddhi*). He demonstrates this very point with the words, "For those who maintain the oneness of the self... The word "in the opinion" (*mate*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

In the reading "by the proponent" (*vādinā*), the syntactical connection is with the phrase "due to non-acceptance. Regarding the phrase "of the distinction between individuals": the meaning is that the distinction—that is, the plurality—within the individual called the self (*ātman*) is sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
For if there were a plurality of selves, then "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) would constitute a universal (*jāti*), because it would reside in multiple instances.

The point is that since there is no difference [between individual instances], and because the subverting factor known as the non-difference of individuals exists, "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*), just like "space-ness" (*ākāśatva*). Regarding the phrase "of that which is devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇasya*): the point is that this is based on the scriptural text, "He is the witness, the knower, solitary, and devoid of qualities. Regarding the phrase "characterized by being a substratum of qualities": the point is that the nature of being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇatva*) is not accepted by one who maintains the doctrine of changelessness (*nirvikāratva*).

He anticipates two inferences regarding the diversity of the self with the words "Now," and so forth. Having raised the objection that these two inferences are fallacious (*vyabhicāra*), he refutes them with the words "And not," and so forth. The meaning is as follows: since space is a single entity, sound does not reside in multiple individual instances; thus, the first inference is fallacious in that case.
For this very reason, because the universal "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) does not reside in that which resides in multiple individuals, the second inference is also fallacious in that case.

Relying on the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, he says: "of that" (*tasya*). Relying on the view of the Naiyāyikas, he says: "due to being non-substantial" (*adravyatvena*). Regarding the phrase "by being other than that": the meaning is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because of the qualifications applied to the reason "being a quality" (*guṇatva*), namely "while being different from sound," and to the property of "being a genus residing in a quality" (*guṇaniṣṭhajātittva*), namely "while being different from the nature of sound" (*śabdatva*).
[The opponent asks: Is it the manifoldness of instances (*nānāvyaktyāśritatva*) of ordinary pleasure that is being proven, or rather the nature of absolute bliss (*svarūpasukha*)?
He states the fault in the first case: "of pleasure, pain, and so forth. The intention is based on the Vedic scripture: "All this is indeed the mind alone" (*etatsarvaṃ mana eva*).

Even when pleasure alone is taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), it should be understood that the inclusion of suffering and so forth here is for the purpose of refuting inferences based on the side of suffering and the like, according to the method previously stated. Anticipating a second objection, he refutes it with the words "intrinsic pleasure" (*svarūpasukha*). The sense is that if intrinsic pleasure were a quality (*guṇa*), the Self would consequently possess qualities, which would contradict the scriptural texts stating that the Self is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). Anticipating an inference regarding the mutual difference between individual selves (*jīva*), he refutes it with the words "Caitra’s body" (*caitraśarīra*) and "Maitra’s body" (*maitraśarīra*). The meaning is: Maitra is the owner of Maitra’s body; [the inference would be] that there is something belonging to an owner other than him (i.e., other than Maitra).

By this, the distinction of Caitra from Maitra is established in respect to the owner of Caitra’s body—namely, "being opposed to that" (*tadviruddha*). This means having an activity opposed to the activity of Maitra’s body. Here, the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) is to be understood as follows: whatever possesses an activity opposed to the activity of [something else] has an owner distinct from the owner of that [other thing]; for example, a jar, which possesses an activity opposed to the activity of a cloth, has a potter as its owner who is distinct from the weaver, the owner of the cloth.

He demonstrates a possible deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with the words, "even in the case of two [bodies] having a single owner. By the phrase "by being a body," he means "by being a locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*)."
"The example is unestablished" (dṛṣṭāntāsiddhiḥ) means that the example itself is not established. There is also a reading: "due to the absence of an example" (dṛṣṭāntābhāvāt).

He raises an objection regarding the inference for the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—namely, "in the case of the two under dispute" (*vimatau*). In the subject (*pakṣa*), contradictory properties such as omniscience and limited knowledge are to be understood; in the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), however, they are to be seen as heat and cold.
*Dahana* means fire, and *tuhina* means snow.
Here, is it an ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) difference that is to be proven, or a conventional (*vyāvahārika*) one?

Regarding the first [position], he says: "ultimately real" (*pāramārthika*). The sense is that, in my view, the qualification of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaṇa*)—namely, ultimate difference, which is intended as the probandum—is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). Regarding the second [position], he says: "conventional" (*vyāvahārika*). The sense is that conventional difference is accepted by me.

He concludes the refutation of inference with: "therefore. "The difference between the Self and the individual soul" (*ātmajīvabheda*) means the difference between the Supreme Self and the individual soul, as well as the mutual difference among individual souls.
Scriptural passages such as "Two birds" and "Two Brahmans" merely restate the difference established by worldly experience;
and this restatement serves to facilitate the subsequent negation in the passage, "There is no diversity here.
By this, one should understand that even in the case of the difference between a jar, a cloth, and so forth, perception is not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Because perception is invalid due to its being erroneous,
the inference based upon it is likewise not a valid means of knowledge.
However, in the case of non-difference, perception is indeed easily obtained.

Because of the experience [of the self] in the single form of "I" (i.e., from the experience of the self). And there is an inference: "The selves under dispute do not differ from the Supreme Self in ultimate reality, because they possess the nature of being a self, like the Supreme Self.

Having thus refuted both perception and inference regarding difference, he anticipates and refutes scripture (*āgama*) as a means of valid knowledge as well: "Two birds... This means that the two called the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are like two birds. "Two Brahmans": the meaning is that the two Brahmans in the forms of the supreme and the subordinate—namely, the Lord and the individual soul—are to be known. "[Scripture is] merely restating a difference established in the world."

The meaning is that the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), which is established through worldly convention, is merely restated [by scripture] and not established [as a new truth]; furthermore, worldly convention is based on a blind tradition and is not rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Now, one might object: since there is no purpose in providing additional instruction, a mere restatement would be useless; therefore, this [scripture] must indeed be an original establishment. To this, he says: "And the restatement... The sense is that it is like a restatement by an opponent in a debate for the purpose of refuting what has been asserted by the proponent.

Now, he refutes the mutual distinction even among insentient things with the words "by this" (*eteneti*). The meaning is that since all distinction whatsoever has been negated by the scriptural text, "There is no diversity here" (*neha nānāsti*).

Some, however, argue that because the mutual distinction between insentient things is not under discussion, the phrase "the distinction of jars and so forth" refers either to a distinction residing in God (the counter-correlate) regarding jars, cloths, etc., or to a distinction residing in God regarding jars, cloths, etc. They further claim that, as a consequence, this also serves to refute the evidence for the mutual distinction between insentient things. That view is to be considered.

This is because the mutual difference between insentient objects (*jaḍa*) has already been demonstrated previously. The mention of "the difference between pot and cloth" is merely illustrative; one should also understand it to include "the difference between the sentient and the insentient. Regarding the phrase "of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*): the meaning is that it refers to perceptions such as "a cloth is not a pot" or "I am not a pot," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because of being an error" (*bhrāntitvāt*): the sense is that what contradicts the flawless Śruti cannot possess validity. Regarding the phrase "for this very reason": the meaning is precisely because the perception that serves as the root [of the argument] is itself an error. Regarding the phrase "inference and so forth" (*anumānādi*): by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), scripture (*āgama*) is included.

In this regard, inference is rooted in perception because it takes as its subject (dharmin) and other factors those things established by perception; scripture, however, is rooted in perception because it merely restates distinctions already established by perception—this is the distinction. Not only is Viṣṇu’s difference from the universe unproven according to the aforementioned method, but it is also contradicted by the means of valid cognition that apprehend non-difference. With this intention, he states three proofs for non-difference in sequence, beginning with "But in the case of non-difference. This means: in the case of the non-difference between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman).

The word "tāvat" (so much / for that long) should also be applied here, because the proof for the non-difference of the insentient [matter] will be stated later. Regarding the phrase "in the single form of 'I'": for the Self of all is indeed experienced as one through the form "I.
If the Supreme Self were also present along with the individual soul as a subjectivity (*pratyaktva*) like the individual soul, then the experience would have to be "the two of us."
But this is not the case.

Therefore, the sense is that the non-difference (*abheda*)—in the form of the absence of difference—between individual selves and the Supreme Self is established. Regarding the phrase "and inference": the term "non-difference" carries over from the previous context.

Since even [the author] himself accepts empirical difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*), the qualification "in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthataḥ*) is stated in order to avoid invalidation (*bādhā*) and other such faults.
"Anuvādaka" means that which presents the category of what is to be negated.
It is said to be "established by worldly consensus" because a negation of what has not been previously established is impossible;
this means it is established by the perceptions and so forth of those under delusion.

Or rather, this is stated to demonstrate that the statement regarding difference lacks novelty (*apūrvatva*). By the phrase "by this," there is a general reference to the refutation of defects as previously explained.
It should be understood that "difference from pots and so forth" refers to [the difference] of the Lord from the individual soul (*jīva*) and their mutual difference.
Although, in the case of insentient objects (*jaḍa*), a difference is admitted that is co-extensive in existence with the existence of the substratum (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*).

Nevertheless, it should be understood that the intent is to refute the ultimate reality of both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*). Regarding the phrase "as being erroneous": this means either because [the cognition] is deviant in one respect and thus lacks universal validity, or because it is contradicted by powerful scripture (*āgama*).

Regarding the phrase "for this very reason": this means because the foundational perception (*mūla-pratyakṣa*) is erroneous. Regarding the phrase "inference as well": the inference is as follows—"A pot is the locus of a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is a cloth, because it is the locus of a property that does not reside in a cloth; otherwise, it would be like a cloth."

The meaning is that there is the traditional scripture stating, "Nature is divided eightfold. He refutes the second position—that there is no evidence for unity—with the words, "But in the case of non-difference" (*abhede tu*). The sense of the phrase "oneness" (*ekatva*) is that no diversity is perceived, since all [cognitions] have the same mental imprint (*ullekha*), namely, "I am. Regarding the term "the subjects of dispute" (*vimatā*): it should be understood that the plural number and the status of being the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) may be based either on empirical difference or on difference according to the opponent's view; furthermore, the doubt regarding the object of apprehension is not a defect, so the plural may be used even with a doubtful or merely apparent difference. The phrase "in reality" (*paramārthataḥ*) is used to preclude sublation (*bādha*) and the fallacy of an unestablished tenet (*apasiddhānta*).

One might object: "Since it has been stated that 'In case of contradiction, there is a figurative statement (guṇavāda); when [the fact] is already established, there is a restatement (anuvāda); and the statement of an existing fact (bhūtārthavāda) is the restatement of reality—thus it is considered threefold,' and since we observe the validity characterized by non-contradiction of the meaning even in cases of restatement intended for the purpose of enjoining something additional, why should there not be non-contradiction of the meaning even in the case of a restatement? To this, he says: "And the restatement... The intention is that there is no contradiction of the meaning because it is a restatement for the purpose of negation.

Having thus refuted the difference [of the Self] from the conscious universe, he now refutes its difference from the unconscious by the words "by this" (*etena*). This also serves to refute the means of knowledge for a mutual difference residing in one thing or another, which would otherwise result in the contingency of a difference between a jar and a cloth, or a difference residing in the Lord with the jar and cloth as counter-correlates, or a difference residing in the jar and cloth with the Lord as the counter-correlative. Regarding the phrase "of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*): the meaning is that it refers to such perceptions as "I am not a jar," "this is not a jar," and "a jar is not a cloth."

"Exactly for this reason" means that since perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), the inference based upon it—which would grasp the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—is not authoritative; likewise, the word-based [inference] which grasps the nature of sound and so forth, and the word upon which it is based, are also not authoritative.
Now, one might object: "Difference (*bheda*) is indeed the negation of identity (*tādātmya*).
Identity is non-difference (*abheda*); therefore, the very absence of a means of knowledge regarding it will serve as the means of knowledge for difference."

One might argue that no separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) needs to be stated; therefore, he says: "But in the case of non-difference" (*abhede tu*). The intended meaning is that, in this way, there is no absence of a means of valid cognition regarding that [non-difference].

By this—namely, by establishing the absence of a means of valid cognition for the postulation of the difference of the universe—it should be understood that the objection that it is irrelevant to state the means of valid cognition for non-difference is refuted.

Now, one might object: just as there is a difference among jars even though they are experienced with a single form such as "this is a jar," so too there would be a difference among selves even though they are experienced with a single form such as "I."

The mere form of "I-ness" (ahantva) would have absolute identity [with all], just like "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva). In that case, just as there is an absence of difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by pot-ness, so too here, even though there is an absence of difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by selfhood (ātmatva), there might still be difference in terms of this or that specific self. Anticipating this lack of conviction, he says: "Inference. To ward off sublation by accepting conventional difference, he adds: "in reality" (paramārthataḥ). [He cites] "Two birds... [Ṛgveda 1.164.20]. Now, one might ask: how can this [scriptural passage] serve as a means of valid knowledge for difference?
Even though duality has been mentioned, difference (*bheda*) has not;
nor should it be argued that because duality is pervaded by difference, difference is established by the mention of the former.

For if that were the case, this [statement] would result in being a producer of inference (*anumāna*), and thus it would be improper to present it as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the form of scripture (*āgama*).
Nor should it be argued that the difference between the two, insofar as it is expressed by the phrase "not other than those two," becomes the object of verbal cognition;

for if that were so, since only that specific portion [of the meaning] would be the example, it would be inconsistent to cite a portion that is not useful. Furthermore, the citation of "the two Brahmans" would be entirely irrelevant. If this is objected, we say no.

In this context, the word *dvau* (two) itself possesses the capacity to convey a cognition qualified by mutual difference; otherwise, there would result the redundancy of one of the two words—either *suparṇau* (the two birds) or *brahmaṇī* (the two Brahmans)—since resorting to one being merely a repetitive reference (*anuvādaka*) is a desperate measure of last resort. It is with this intention that the present example is consistent. If it is asked, "By what mode of operation (*vṛtti*) does the word *dvi* convey a cognition qualified by difference?", the answer is: either by means of conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) or by its primary denotative power (*śakti*).

We say that the semantic potential (*śakti*) [of the word *dvaita*] is established by the statement in the *Nānārtharatnamālā*: "The word *dvi* is employed in the sense of the number two and also in the sense of difference.

If one asks how this is so, it is because, from time immemorial, the word *dvi* as a constituent of the term *dvaita* has been used in common linguistic practice precisely in the sense of that which possesses difference (*bhedavat*).

Otherwise, since the word *dvi* primarily denotes a state (*bhāva-pradhāna*), and the word *dviti* signifies an object qualified by difference (*bheda-viśiṣṭārtha*), it would be impossible for the suffix *aṇ*, which expresses a state (*bhāva-artha*) following that [word], to convey the notion of difference.

This is because there is a rule that a suffix expressing a state must convey the delimitor of the meaning of its base (*prakṛtyarthatāvacchedaka*); consequently, it would necessarily follow that it conveys only duality (*dvitva*).

And this word has been explained as having the sense of "difference" alone, according to the method stated in the *Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya-ṭīkā* and other works during the occasion of explaining the Śruti passage, "Where there is, as it were, duality. Thus, there is nothing inconsistent here. Regarding the phrase "neha nānā": the negation—"here, in Brahman, there is nothing whatsoever characterized by manifoldness or difference"—culminates in the negation of difference in general; its purport is to convey that the world (prapañca) is of the nature of Brahman, insofar as it is superimposed upon Brahman. Regarding the word "etena" (by this): [it refers to the aforementioned reasoning].

The meaning is: because every form of difference has been refuted by means of a faultless scripture (*āgama*). Now, one might ask: how can there be a rejection of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? For perception exists, as do those inferences—rooted in it—that consist in the fact of being substrates for contradictory properties; on the contrary, due to their contradiction with such [perception], the scripture itself would not be intent upon its own meaning. To this he says: "of perception. This means: of knowledge in the form of perception. "By way of being erroneous" (*bhrāntitvena*): in the reading *bhrāntatvena*, the suffix *-kta* denotes the abstract state (*bhāve*). Because it is non-authoritative since it is an object of the possibility of being erroneous, it is impossible to determine it as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And thus, since it is observed that the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and similar cases is an error rooted in defects of the sense organs and so forth, it is impossible to ascertain its validity in other instances as well due to the possibility of such defects.

Since scripture, being of non-human origin, is determined to be free from defects and thus possesses established authority, it subverts perception itself; and by extension, it subverts even more decisively the inference upon which that perception is based—this is the intended meaning.

It should be understood that if one does not accept that the word "etena" (by this) has the meaning already stated, but instead accepts it as being merely an elaboration of what is about to be said, then there would be the undesirable consequence of deficiency: having proposed the refutation of the means of knowledge in general, one would fail to refute both perception and inference.

It should be understood that the refutation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the difference between a pot and a cloth is either incidental, or it is intended to dispel the following doubt: "If there were an absolute mutual difference between a pot, a cloth, and so forth, how could Brahman be non-different from such a world? For it contradicts experience for two things that are absolutely distinct from one another to be of the nature of a single reality.
[The opponent objects: "But if Brahman is different from the universe, how can there be an absence of proof [for that difference]?"

In order to dispel the doubt that "the difference between the two is established by the force of the very reason consisting in the absence of evidence for their non-difference," he states the proofs for non-difference: "But as for non-difference... Alternatively, having refuted the proofs for the opponent's position, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin) states the proofs for his own position: "But as for non-difference..."—meaning, regarding the oneness of consciousness and so forth. "By the single form 'I'... [is the meaning].

Since the uniformity of a recurring cognition cannot be accounted for without its having a single object, it is logical that the consciousness appearing in all such cognitions is one and the same; any contradiction arises only regarding the objective (viśeṣya) portion.
In cases such as the cognition "this is a jar," the recurring form must be explained by taking the identity of the qualifiers (prakāra) into account;
however, this is not the case here.
The sense is that [the distinction between] perception and the other means of knowledge has already been refuted.

(Regarding Brahman as well,) since its cognition as "I" is established by such scriptural passages as "He knew only Himself as 'I am Brahman'" and by such Smṛti passages as "I am beyond the perishable," perception itself is the means of valid knowledge even in the view that [Brahman] is one with consciousness—this is the sense. Regarding the term "disputed" (*vimatā*): because conventional difference is admitted, the phrase "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*) is used to exclude the charge of contradiction when proving the absence of that [conventional] difference; it means "as ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatvena*).
Nor should it be argued that even if empirical difference exists, since its non-existence is also accepted in accordance with its falsity (*mithyātva*), how can there be sublation (*bādha*)?

For, in order to avoid the fallacies of proving something already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) or proving a different thing (*arthāntaratā*) by taking into account non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*), one must necessarily include the condition of "residing in a different locus from the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivaiyyadhikaraṇya*) within the absence of difference; thus, sublation remains unavoidable.
Alternatively, the absence included in the definition of falsity is not opposed to the knowledge of the empirical existence of the counter-positive.
Since that [difference] is not excluded [from the world], there is no possibility of contradiction (*vipratipatti*) and so forth in the world by taking that as the subject.

And thus, because a contradiction regarding the two alternatives of difference from the Supreme Self and its absence has as its basis an absence that contradicts the difference established in the world, and since such an absence of difference is the probandum (*sādhya*), there is indeed a sublation (*bādha*) due to the existence of the conventional difference which is opposed to it. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total destruction of all reasons where an absence is the probandum, because statements such as "fire is not hot" would result in being uncontradicted.
Therefore, it must indeed be stated that they are "intent upon that" (tatparāḥ).

Nor can it be argued that because the counter-positive—consisting of difference qualified by ultimate reality—is unestablished, the side of its absence is likewise unestablished; for it has been stated in the *Advaitasiddhi*, its commentary (*ṭīkā*), and other works that even in one's own system, as in the case of the Naiyāyikas and others, the existence of an absence presupposes the existence of its counter-positive. Consequently, how could such [difference] be the subject of dispute (*vipratipatti*) or the probandum (*sādhya*)? This is what must be addressed.

Since only the absence qualified by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*) is accepted, it is possible for the absence whose counterpositiveness resides in a difference qualified by ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) to be both the subject of the dispute and the probandum (*sādhya*).

In this view, one should understand that "counterpositive-inherence-in-a-different-locus" (*pratiyogivaiyyadhikaraṇya*) consists precisely in the subsistence [of the absence] in a locus that possesses a difference whose delimitation of counterpositiveness is delimited by the same delimitation of counterpositiveness as that which delimits its own counterpositive; thus, a difference whose delimitation is delimited by a property residing in a different locus is admitted.

If that [definition] is not accepted, however, the counter-thesis (vipratipatti) regarding the absence of that [property] would be: "The general locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatāsāmānya*) residing in individual selves (*jīvātman*), which fall under the delimitors of the subject matter of the counter-theses to be stated hereafter—namely, those [selves] in which there is the absence of both 'being defined by ultimate reality' and 'being defined by a difference having the Supreme Self as its counter-correlate'.

The first alternative (the affirmative side) belongs to the Advaitins. If the general locus-ness residing in the individual self possesses the absence of both [properties], then the difference having the Supreme Self as its counter-correlate (and being ultimately real) is effectively negated in the individual self.

The inclusion of the term "universal" (*sāmānya*) is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), which would occur by taking any locus-ness whatsoever residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) as defined by the absence of a jar and so forth.

In the Advaita system, being defined by ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-nirūpitatva*) is well-known in relation to the inherence (*ādheyatā*) and other properties residing in the purity and other attributes that are the qualities of Brahman.

For those who maintain the doctrine of difference (*bhedavādin*), the alternative of non-existence is untenable; for the absence of such universal locus-ness in the individual soul could not otherwise be resolved than by the existence of an ultimately real difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*) having the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

Thus, since the probandum (*sādhya*) is precisely the state of having the aforementioned commonality, there is no fault whatsoever. Furthermore, if it is considered that the probandum lacks uniformity (*ananugama*) because "one's own-ness" (*svatva*) is not uniform, then the probandum is the absence of both [the properties of] being qualified by ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*) and being qualified by the difference whose counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This absence has as its counter-correlative the locus of the property of being the substratum of a qualifier delimited by itself, related through the relation of non-residence in the locus of the property of being the substratum of a qualifier delimited by itself.

If there were an ultimate difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), then the locus-hood (*adhikaraṇatā*) characterized by a relatum-ness delimited by that "bothness" (the property of being both), which resides in the locus-hood of the difference characterized by those two, would be the locus-hood residing in the soul with respect to such a difference.

Because "bothness" exists [in the soul] through that relation, the probandum—which consists in the absence of such "bothness" whose counter-correlativity is delimited by that relation—would be difficult to establish in the subject (*pakṣa*); therefore, the proof of the negation of such a difference in that [soul] follows.
Because "selfhood" (svatva) serves as a delimiting indicator (*paricāyaka*) at the level of the relation, there is no lack of uniformity (*ananugama*).
In the view of the dualists (*dvaitin*), the aforementioned relation is indeed a relation of different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*) for the aforementioned "duality" (*ubhayatva*).
For instance, the duality of being determined by a jar and being determined by a cloth is well-known as a relation in such things as the ground.

Nor should it be argued that even if an ultimate (paramārthika) difference characterized by (nirūpita) the Supreme Self as its counter-correlate exists in the individual soul (jīva), the stated probandum is still established;

for since difference itself is what is characterized as ultimate, the dual nature [of being both ultimate and having the Supreme Self as counter-correlate] is absent from the locus of difference, and thus the absence of such a duality is possible in the subject (pakṣa).
This is not so, because there is a distinction between "being characterized by ultimacy" and "having as its characterizer a difference delimited by ultimacy."

Alternatively, if there is no difference [between the two], there is no fault, for the probandum (*sādhya*) is simply the absence—defined by a locus-relationship qualified by its own [absence] and having as its counter-positive a locushood determined by a determinerhood that is itself determined by both "ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatva*) and "the state of being delimited by such difference" (*tādṛśabhedatvāvacchedyatva*).

Or rather, the intended meaning is the proof of the absence of both: (1) having a determinerhood delimited by ultimate reality, and (2) having a determinerhood delimited by the state of being a difference whose counter-positive is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), with respect to the locushood residing in the individual soul (*jīva*).
In accordance with that, the logical reason (*hetu*) and other members of the syllogism should be inferred.
The same should be understood in other cases as well.
Let it be, then, that the scripture beginning with "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) is indeed the authority for the difference between the selves;

for in that passage, regarding the two birds called the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), duality—which is pervaded by difference—is heard in the statement "two Brahmans," where they are described as the higher and lower Brahman.

Anticipating the objection that the difference between the two is explicitly stated in the passage, "One of them eats, while the other does not eat," and that the plurality of individual souls (*jīva*) is understood from the statement, "Many creatures have been produced from the Puruṣa," he says: "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*). In the phrase *dvau suparṇau*, the vowel *au* is substituted for the vowel *ā*. Now, since it has been stated that difference is not established by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can scripture be merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*) of it? To this, he replies: "established in the world" (*loka-siddha*).
The meaning is that [the distinction] is established by worldly convention. And the point is that this [distinction], being in contradiction with the proofs to be stated later, is indeed invalid.
Now, one might ask: how can difference be refuted merely by restating [an opponent's position]?

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of rejecting even the sacrifice and so forth that are being restated in such injunctions as "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*) for the purpose of prescribing qualities such as the form of curd; therefore, he says: "And [it is] a restatement. "For the sake of negation" means for the sake of negating difference in Brahman by way of its ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*).
Thus, since the purport of the restatement of difference is precisely its negation, the meaning is that the scripture has no authority regarding that [difference].

Having thus refuted the distinction between the Self [and the non-Self], he now refutes the mutual distinction between the Self and the non-Self, as well as among the various non-Selves, in order to establish that mere difference is not ultimately real—by the words "by this" (*eteneti*). This means: by the fact that all mere difference has been negated in the passage, "There is no diversity here. "The difference between pot, cloth, etc. means: the difference of the Self from pots, cloths, and so forth, as well as the mutual difference among those [non-Selves] themselves.

In that case, what is the status of the perception "the jar and the cloth are distinct," and so forth? To this he says: "of perception. The sense is that when there is a contradiction with a faultless scripture, it is logical that a perception suspected of possessing defects lacks authority. For this very reason—namely, because the perception grasping difference is erroneous—it is said to be "rooted in that," meaning it depends upon corroboration by such a perception. By the phrase "inference and so forth," human-authored scripture (*pauruṣeya-āgama*) is included.

The point is this: since inference and the like taken alone are not established as valid because their authority is suspected, their validity must be asserted only through corroboration by means of perception and other such pramāṇas.
Furthermore, if that perception and so forth lack validity, it is difficult to establish the validity of an inference or other means directed toward the same object.

Others also explain that inference and the like, being rooted in the perception of concomitance (*sahacāra*) that grasps pervasion (*vyāpti*), cannot be a valid means of knowledge because that perception is an error.
In this regard, even if there is an error regarding the coexistence of fire and water, the validity of the inference of fire—based on the mark of water—in a mountain or similar location still exists.
Nevertheless, the intention is that when there is an absence of both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the presence of the mark in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), validity is difficult to ascertain.

Having thus established the subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against identity, he shows the threefold supporting evidence for its firmness, stating: "But as for identity... [The opponent might argue: "Since there is simply an absence of evidence for identity, that very absence will serve as the evidence for difference. To this he says: "But as for identity... This [objection] is to be considered.
By the same logic, it can be asserted that the very absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for difference is itself the means of valid cognition for non-difference;

furthermore, since the absence of a means of valid cognition for non-difference establishes difference by way of inference, it must be refuted at the very occasion of refuting that [inference]. Now, one might object: "Since it has been stated that a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is another self is not perceptible when that counter-correlate is not perceived, how can non-difference—which is of the nature of the absence of such difference—be perceptible? To this, he says: "In a single form" (*ekākāreṇa*). This means: "by way of identity with a single entity."
The point is this:
the absence of difference is indeed identity with the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitādātmya*).

Thus, if experiences of the single form "I" have a single entity as their object, then by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), how could the perception "I"—which apprehends identity with a single consciousness—possess validity regarding non-difference?

"Those who are of divergent opinions regarding the self (*ātman*). The use of the plural number is intended to indicate that the subject of the proposition (*uddeśya*) is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) with respect to each specific delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), for otherwise, the identity of all selves would not be established.

Since the conventional distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) is admitted, there would be a contradiction (*bādha*) if one were to deny difference in general; therefore, it is specified as "in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthataḥ*). Nor should it be argued that, because an ultimately real difference is unestablished, the probandum itself remains unestablished.
This is because the absence of difference in an ultimate sense (*pāramārthikatva*) is what is to be proven;

for in that system, the probandum is established through the existence of an absence qualified by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*). By this, the view that "ultimate reality" is a qualification of non-difference is also refuted.
Because the stated objection has been refuted. Nor should it be argued that there is a shift in the subject matter (*arthāntara*) due to the establishment of a merely apparent non-difference;
for what is to be proven is precisely non-difference in the ultimate sense.

The claim that by the phrase "they do not differ from the perspective of ultimate reality" (paramārthataḥ), what is intended to be proven is precisely an ultimate identity (pāramārthika-tādātmya), is not correct.

This is because it would be inconsistent with the similarity of the fallacious arguments (abhāsa) to be stated later, namely that "they do not differ even from the perspective of conventional reality" (vyavahārataḥ).

In that case, since a conventional identity with the Supreme Self (paramātman) does not exist in the example—the Supreme Self itself—it is impossible for such an identity to be the probandum (sādhya).

Since the absence of ultimate difference is unestablished for the proponent (siddhāntin) in a general sense, the phrase "having the Supreme Self as its counter-correlate" is used as a qualification of difference. He refutes the third position with the words: "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*).

The meaning of the sūtra *supāṃ sulukpūrvasavarṇāccheyāḍāḍyāyājālaḥ* is that, within the domain of Vedic literature (*chandasi*), in place of the case endings (*supām*), these substitutes— *su*, *luk*, *pūrvasavarṇa*, *āt*, *ā*, *śe*, *yā*, *ḍā*, *ḍyā*, *yāc*, and *āl*— may occur. An example is as follows:
"May the paths be straight," and so forth.
Here, by the substitution of the vowel *a* for the diphthong *o* in the word *dvau*, the form *dvā* and so on arises.
Consequently, this is the meaning [of the passage].
"Sayujau" means joined together;
"sakhāyau" means friends;
"dvausuparṇau" refers to the two birds, the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (Īśa), who take the form of birds by virtue of their perching upon the tree.
One is common; they have both embraced— that is, they have clung to— the single tree called the body, the *aśvattha*.
Between those two birds,
the other is the individual soul (jīva);
it eats, as it were, with relish the fruit of actions produced by the body, which is like a pippala tree, though it is actually tasteless.
Another is the Lord.
That, not eating.
Toward; on all sides.
It "shines forth" (cākaśīti) means it manifests; however, it does not depend upon that [manifestation] for its own subsistence.
The meaning of the statement "two Brahmans are to be known" is that the two things denoted by the terms "higher Brahman" and "lower Brahman" are to be understood.
The meaning is that [the scripture] merely restates a distinction, but does not establish a distinction, whereby the authority of this scripture regarding distinction would be undermined.
Now, one might object: "A restatement of what is already established is possible."

Therefore, since the very fact that difference is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—which is accepted for the sake of proving that scripture is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*)—is itself our proof for establishing difference, he says: "Established in the world" (*lokasiddha*). This means "established through worldly convention.
The point is that worldly convention is not a [valid] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Now, an reiteration is made for the purpose of prescribing something additional, just as in the case of "one offers with curd" (*dadhnā juhoti*), where, having reiterated the sacrifice already obtained by the injunction "one should offer the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhuyāt*), the quality characterized by curd is prescribed by the word "with curd" (*dadhnā*).

Regarding the statement "that which one offers is with curds," there is no further injunction here by virtue of which it would be appropriate for the scripture to be a mere restatement of a difference; therefore, he says: "And [it is] a restatement. The word "and" (ca) has the sense of "but" (tu). Furthermore, a restatement is sometimes made even for the purpose of negation; for example, the restatement "there is a jar here on the ground" is made in order to negate its existence.

Likewise, here too, by the statement "not here, not manifold" (*neha nānā*), the meaning is that for the purpose of negating—whether in this world or in Brahman—any kind of manifoldness (*nānā*) even as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of any given entity, the scripture beginning with "two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) restates the difference already established in common worldly experience. Having thus refuted the evidence for a difference between selves (*ātman*), he now refutes it regarding the difference between non-selves (*anātman*). The phrase "by this" (*etena*) means by the statement that the sentence "not here, not manifold" negates difference.
To the question "How so?", he says: "of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*). That cognition which is sublated by a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is an error (*bhrānti*).

The point is as follows: just as the cognition "this is silver" is recognized as an error because it is sublated by the authoritative statement "this is silver" [which negates the previously perceived silver], so too in the present case, the difference between a jar and a cloth and so forth—previously apprehended by the cognition "the jar is not the cloth"—is sublated by the statement "not here, no diversity," and thus its erroneous nature is unavoidable.
In the reading *bhrāntatvena*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*).
The meaning is "as being an error. "For this very reason" means "precisely because the perceptual cognition upon which [the other] depends is invalid.

It is not merely that difference is absent due to a lack of validity; rather, with the intention that non-difference itself is accepted as being established by valid means of knowledge, he states three proofs for non-difference: "But in the case of non-difference... The sense is that [if there were difference], there would be a cognition of a single form, i.e., oneness; whereas if there were difference, there would be a cognition such as "we two" or "we [many]."
Since a conventional distinction from the Supreme Self (paramātman) has been accepted by [the author] himself, the term "in reality" (paramārthataḥ) was employed.
Now, one might ask: what is the delimiting property of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) here? It cannot be "selfhood" (ātmatva).

Furthermore, since the Supreme Self would also fall under the category of the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding that part.
Nor can it be qualified by "being other than the Supreme Self," because there is a contradiction between the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) and the probandum (*sādhya*).
Nor can it be qualified by being perceived as other than the Supreme Self through error;

for since the possibility of such an error regarding "otherness" could also occur with respect to the Supreme Self itself, one would not escape the defect mentioned in the first alternative. If this is argued, we say no: because the very state of being the subject of a dispute—namely, whether they are different from the Supreme Self or not—is what constitutes the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).
Otherwise, since they would also be distinct from your own supreme self (*paramātman*), it would be impossible to establish their difference.
Furthermore, "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*);
rather, what is it? It is self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).

Therefore, there is no contradiction between the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*). Now, one might object: "Since the specific nature of the subject (*dharmin*) is established by the word 'selves' (*ātmānaḥ*) alone, the inclusion of the term 'disputed' (*vimata*) is redundant. To state its purpose, he raises this objection with the words "Now... (*nanu*). "Because [the probandum] would be already established in part" (*aṃśe siddhasādhanāt*): the meaning is that the absence of ultimate difference—where the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the Supreme Self—is already established in one portion of the subject, namely, in the Supreme Self itself. "The qualification 'other than the Supreme Self'" (*paramātmetaratvaviśiṣṭam*): the term "selfhood" (*ātmatvam*) is understood to carry over here.

And thus, since the property of being other than the Supreme Self (*paramātmetaratva*) is absent in the Supreme Self itself, it does not qualify as the subject (*pakṣa*), and therefore the aforementioned defect does not apply; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the delimitant of subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*)," the meaning is that there is a contradiction because the probandum is non-difference from the Supreme Self, while the delimitant of subjecthood is the state of being a self other than that [Supreme Self]. Regarding the word "by error" (*bhrāntyā*), the meaning is: being the object of a cognition in the form of an erroneous apprehension whose qualifier is the property of being other than the Supreme Self.

And thus, since the probandum is ultimately real while the state of being other than the Supreme Self is imagined through delusion, there is no contradiction; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "the defect stated in the first position": it means the defect consisting of *siddhasādhanatā* (proving what is already established) with respect to a portion [of the subject].

He now states the purpose for which this objection was raised: "of the Supreme Self. The word "only" (*eva*) implies that no other delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) need be sought here.
And since this [property] exists in the Supreme Self, the intention is that there is neither *siddhasādhanatā* regarding a portion nor any contradiction.

Out of respect [for the opponent's position], he states "otherwise" because it is not appropriate for *ātmatva* (selfhood) to be the delimiting condition (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) of the subject (*pakṣa*). The meaning is as follows: if *ātmatva* were the delimiting condition of the subject, there would be a sublation (*bādha*) in the case of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which is a part [of the subject].
If one qualifies [the subject] by being distinct from that [Supreme Self], then if that [distinct self] is already established, it results in proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*);
if it is not established, the subject itself remains unestablished (*apakṣaprasiddhi*).
Some, however, [hold that it] is not the nature of the individual self (*ātmatva*), because that is sublated in part;
nor is it qualified by being the supreme self (*paramātmatva*),
because that remains unestablished even now.

Nor can it be that [the world] is perceived through error as something other than the Supreme Self, because—as before—there would be a sublation regarding a part within the Supreme Self; this is what they mean. But that is to be considered.

If "being perceived through the error of being other than the Supreme Self" were the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), then the very perception of non-difference from the Supreme Self would necessarily result in being a valid cognition (*pramā*); consequently, there would arise a contradiction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the delimiting factor of the subject itself.

In this context, since it would be improper to state that the reason (*hetu*)—the nature of selfhood (*ātmatva*)—is unestablished (*asiddhi*) in the previously mentioned inference (that "selfhood resides in multiple individuals because it is a universal" [jāti]), he states "And the nature of selfhood... in order to define selfhood by another means. Regarding "self-luminosity": the meaning is that it consists in being the object of immediate empirical usage while being non-cognizable [by another].

If one accepts that "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is of the nature of a universal (*jāti*), what is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) by which its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) is asserted? To this, he says: "By that" (*tena*). If selfhood were a universal, then since a universal must be said to inhere in many [individuals], it would follow that one must accept multiple individual selves; and since multiplicity is pervaded by difference, there would be a contradiction between the reason and the probandum.
Therefore, the sense is that this selfhood is not of the nature of a universal.
The statement that there is no contradiction between the reason and the probandum is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be understood that there is no contradiction in stating the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the character of a futile rejoinder (*jāti*) in the previously suspected inference. He says "nanu" (but surely) in order to explain the utility of employing the term "under dispute" (*vimata*). Regarding the phrase "because of proving what is already established in part" (*aṃśe siddhasādhanāt*): here some maintain that even if the non-difference of the Supreme Self from the Supreme Self is established in its form as the Supreme Self, this fault does not apply because it is not established in its form as the *ātman*.
This is because the fault lies only in the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) in a location co-extensive with the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka-sāmānādhikaraṇyena*).

Otherwise, since the probandum would be established even at the stage of grasping the pervasion—namely, that "wherever there is a reason, there is a probandum"—it would follow that inference as a whole is rendered useless.
Therefore, they say that this fault occurs only in cases where the delimiters of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) are multiple.
That is not correct.
Establishment [of the probandum] even by way of a property that is either the delimitor of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka) or a property pervaded by or pervading it, is indeed a defect;
for there exists the seed of defectiveness consisting in futility (vaiyyarthya).
In that case, if it is by way of a pervaded property, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā) with respect to the "this" (idaṃśe).
Since "smoke-possessingness" and the like are neither the pervaded (*vyāpya*) nor the pervader (*vyāpaka*) with respect to "mountain-ness" and the like, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

However, in cases such as "earth is distinct from others," although the distinction of earth from water and so forth is established through specific properties like "pot-ness" in pots and the like, the formulation of "earth" as the subject (*pakṣa*) is appropriate because, at a time when the relationship of pervasion and pervader between "pot-ness" and "earth-ness" is unknown, a dispute (*vipratipatti*) exists as to whether "earth is distinct from water and the like or not.
But once that knowledge [of the pervasion] is attained, the doubt exists only in cases other than pots and the like; therefore, taking it as the subject in a general sense would indeed be a fault.

And here, there is no disagreement regarding the specific nature of selfhood; rather, the question is whether individual souls (jīvas) are distinct from the Supreme Self (paramātman) or not. Thus, even in the case of the entry of the Supreme Self, there is indeed a fault, because of this contradiction.

It should be understood that there is a contradiction in attempting to prove non-difference from that [Brahman] by qualifying it as being "other than that. This means that the very same fault mentioned in the first position applies: namely, *siddhasādhyatā* (proving what is already established). Regarding the term "disagreement" (*vipratipatti*):
for this very reason, it should be understood that the word "contested" (*vimata*) is employed at the outset.
Now, is there some property that serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the state of being an object of disagreement, or not?
In the first case, let that very [property] be the delimitant of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).
In the second case, since its belongingness is not apprehended, there would be the consequence of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) and so forth.
Nor should it be argued that a non-uniform delimitant is easily grasped through the analogy of grass, fire-sticks, and gems, as a doubt resting on diverse subjects is easily resolved.
[Objection: In that case, the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) would be redundant.
[Reply: Not so.

If the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) as co-located with the delimiting factor of the subject, then that factor must necessarily be stated; for if it were not stated, there would be the consequence of the failure to establish what was intended. Even though the delimiting factor of the dispute (*vimatyavacchedaka*) is not explicitly stated, since [otherwise] there would follow the undesirable consequence that the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and so forth would also be subjects of dispute, it is easily grasped that the probandum applies only to things other than those. Thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
But even so, doubt is not the delimiting condition of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka), because it is that very doubt which constitutes the state of being the subject (pakṣatā).
As they have said:
"The subject (pakṣa) is that which possesses a doubtful probandum"—
this is because the word "doubtful" (sandigdha) must necessarily have the sense of "disputed" (vimata).
Not so.
Because here, "being the subject" (pakṣatva) consists in the state of being desired to be proven as possessing the property to be proved (sādhyavattayā siṣādhayiṣitatva).

The phrase "it has been made the reason" (hetūkṛta) refers to "selfhood" (ātmatva); this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Regarding the statement "there is no contradiction": the meaning is that since there is a rule that a universal (jāti) must inhere in many [individuals], there is no contradiction in the form of a pervasion by the opposite of the property to be proved—which is non-difference from that [universal].

Although one might raise the doubt here: "How can there be a contradiction, given that the absolute absence of the property to be proved has not been ascertained as being pervaded by selfhood in its specific form?"

Nevertheless, the point is that since the pervasion of the absolute absence of the probandum in the probans—when considered under the aspect of the property that delimits its status as a probans—is also a matter of contradiction, there would be a general contradiction such that "wherever there is a universal (jāti), there is an absence of non-difference from the individual (vyakti)."

Thinking that the term "those who hold different opinions" (*vimatāḥ*) would not serve as a differentiator if the specific nature of their disagreement were not made clear, he raises an objection: "But what is the point here? [The answer is: "Because there is proof of what is already established in part. Although, if the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), then even if the absence of difference having the Supreme Self as its counter-correlate is established in the Supreme Self, it is not a case of proving what is already established in part—since such an absence is not established as delimited by "selfhood" (*ātmatva*).

However, if the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum as co-located with the delimiting factor of the subject, then the proof is complete; thus, in neither case is there the fault of proving what is already established in part.

However, this [objection] is not tenable; for while there is scope for [the objection] when the delimiters of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) are multiple, there is no such scope when the delimiter of the subject is non-different.

Nevertheless, in a case where the pervasion by the delimiter of the subject and the relation [of the probandum] delimited by the delimiter of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) appear within the sphere of the relation in the aspect of the probandum, that constitutes the establishment of the probandum as delimited by the delimiter of the subject.

Where the probandum (*sādhya*) appears in that which possesses the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) by means of the relation that delimits the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakasambandha*), but it is not intended as the goal for every instance possessing the delimitor of the subject, that is "establishment of the probandum through co-occurrence with the delimitor of the subject" (*pakṣatāvacchedakasāmānādhikaraṇyena sādhyasiddhi*). According to the intention of the ancients (*prācīna*), where the intended establishment is a proof that has all subjects as its qualificandum (*viśeṣyaka*) in the form of the delimitor of the subject and has the probandum as its qualifier (*prakāra*) by means of the relation that delimits the probandum—distinct from both of the aforementioned types—even if the probandum is established in only one subject, there occurs the fallacy of "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatā*) in part.

The sense is that even in such a case, partial *siddhasādhanatā* (proving what is already established) is indeed appropriate. This is because there is a contradiction between the *pakṣatāvacchedaka* (the delimiting condition of the subject) and the *sādhya* (the probandum). The meaning is that there is a contradiction between the *sādhya*, which is non-difference (*abheda*), and the *pakṣatāvacchedaka*, which contains difference (*bheda*) within its nature.

That is to say, there is a contradiction between the *sādhya*, which is non-difference from the Supreme Self (*paramātmābheda*), and the *pakṣatāvacchedaka*, which is "being other than the Supreme Self" (*paramātmetaratva*).
In some places, however, the reading is: "because of the contradiction between the *pakṣatāvacchedaka* and the difference (*bheda*) [of the *sādhya*]."
In the view that there are six types of fallacies (*ṣaṇṇigraha*), this contradiction (*pratijñāvirodha*) is included within the category of "contradiction" (*virodha*).
In the position of the opponent, however, this is simply "sublation" (*bādha*).
As for the defect of speech, it is "self-contradiction" (*vyāghāta*).

The phrase "those who are in doubt" (vimatāḥ) clarifies the nature of that doubt: namely, whether [these souls] are different from the Supreme Self or not. Regarding the word "otherwise": if "selfhood" (ātmatva) were the delimiting property of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka), there would be a contradiction regarding a part [of the subject].
If the subject were defined as being qualified by "otherness from the Supreme Self," then if that qualification is established, it results in proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā);
if it is not established, the subject itself remains unestablished (pakṣāprasiddhi). This is the meaning.

[Objection: If the "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) made the reason is a *jāti* (universal), then it must have multiple substrates. Consequently, there would be a contradiction in establishing the identity of the substrate [of the self] by means of that [universal]. To this, he says: "And as for selfhood... The meaning is that selfhood consists in being self-luminous, which takes the form of being the object of non-occult discourse while not being an object of cognition (*avedyatva*). [Regarding the phrase] "because of proving what is already established in part": even if the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) with respect to the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), the fault of proving what is already established in part (*aṃśe siddhasādhanatā*) remains indeed a defect.

An inference that has a greater scope regarding the subject (*pakṣa*), the probandum (*sādhya*), and other components, is not obstructed by a cognition (*siddhi*) that has a lesser scope; however, this does not mean it merely possesses a scope encompassing some additional entity.

For if that were the case, there would arise the undesirable consequence that at the time of a consideration (*parāmarśa*) of a jar—by the force of a consideration of smoke that constitutes a *siddhi*—there would be an inference of both a jar and fire.

Furthermore, in an inference where the delimitation is by the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), all individual instances that are the substrata of the delimitor of the subject appear [in the cognition], but [in the case of the probandum] the property of being pervaded by the delimitor of the subject and so forth do not appear.

In an inference based on grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), however, only a few individuals appear [in the cognition]. It is with the intention of the ancient view that this distinction between the two is stated. But according to the modern view, since there is the appearance of an additional element within the scope of the probandum (*sādhya*), this is not a fault; this should be kept in mind. Regarding the phrase "non-difference from the probandum" (*sādhyābheda*): non-difference that constitutes the probandum is "non-difference from the probandum. And because there is a contradiction between that and the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), such is the meaning.

The meaning is as follows: since conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*) and so forth are not yet established, if one says "other than the Supreme Self" (*paramātmetara*), only a non-ultimate difference having the Supreme Self as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*) is obtained; thus, there is a contradiction. Regarding the phrase "of being the object of disagreement" (*vipratipatti-gocaratvasyaiva*): the ellipsis is "by way of an inexpressible [definition] that does not over-apply. Because it is the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), it is possible to state its status as the delimiting factor of the subject.

Now, the status of being the delimiting factor of the subject for the disagreement is not by virtue of being a disagreement whose modes (*prakāra*) are the difference from or identity with the Supreme Self.

Nor can it be [the object] by way of its being the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), for since the aforementioned two types of disagreement (*vipratipatti*) could still occur regarding the Supreme Self as qualified by "this-ness" (*idantva*) and so forth, the stated fault cannot be avoided. Nor can it be [the object] by way of its being that particular individual (*tadvyaktitva*),
because it is impossible to gain acquaintance with its occurrence [in the subject] through its exclusion from others (*itaravyāvṛttatva*).

And thus, the statement that this [property] is the delimiting condition (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) for the subject (*pakṣa*) is indeed improper; therefore, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). This refers to the refutation of its status as the delimiting condition for the subject by means of such an objection. "In your case too" (*tavāpi*): the word "too" (*api*) conjoins the possibility of what is about to be stated, meaning that not only is the proof of non-difference possible for me, but for you as well. "Of the proof of difference" (*bhedasādhanasyāpi*): here the word "too" (*api*) is intended to include the proof of non-difference. To explain:

If "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is taken as the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) in proving difference, then if the probandum (*sādhya*) is established as being co-located with that [delimiting factor], there would be a failure of the intended goal (*uddeśyāsiddhi*), because the difference from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is not established in all individual souls (*jīva*). If it is established by way of the delimiting factor itself (*avacchedakāvacchedena*), there is sublation (*bādha*) in part, because the difference from the Supreme Self does not exist in the Supreme Self itself. If "being other than the Supreme Self" is included within the delimiting factor of the subject, then prior to the stated inference, that [property] is unestablished; consequently, the subject qualified by the delimiting factor is unestablished (*apakṣadharmatā*), otherwise the inference would result in futility.

Since the appearance of being distinct from the Supreme Self occurs even with respect to the Supreme Self itself due to delusion (*bhrānti*), there would again be a sublation (*bādha*) regarding that part.

Therefore, you must accept as the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) either the aforementioned disagreement whose qualificandum is consciousness delimited by the state of being a sentient being characterized by suffering, bondage, and so forth—either in its inclusive form or as distinct from that—or something equivalent to it.
This is the sense: "The same applies to me as well."

Although it is possible for such states as being a sufferer (*duḥkhin*) to serve as the delimitors of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), nevertheless, since the operation of inference is impossible when there is certainty regarding either alternative (*anyatarakoṭi*) with respect to that delimited [subject], and since such a doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) arising from the aforementioned conflicting assertions (*vipratipatti*) is necessarily required, it is more appropriate—on account of parsimony (*lāghava*)—to take that very doubt as the delimitor of the subject by virtue of its specific individuality (*tadvyaktitvena*). This is the underlying intention.
Regarding "self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatvam*): it consists in being the object of immediate linguistic usage (*aparokṣavyavahāra*) while not being an object of cognition (*avedyatva*).

Alternatively, the conceit that—in both systems—the state of being the agent of some verbal usage regarding its own object that does not depend on a consciousness distinct from itself is established by taking into account the usage occurring after the period of deep sleep, thereby refuting the objection that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) in the view of the opponent because the Self lacks the nature of being a cognition whose object is itself—[is as follows]: "There is no contradiction. The sense is that otherwise, if one were to accept that "Selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is a universal (*jāti*) and employ it as the reason, it would be contradictory to the probandum (*sādhya*), since [the probandum] is the oneness of the individual (*vyaktyaikya*).

Regarding this inference, he raises the objection that the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) is difficult to define—introducing it with "Now, [it may be objected]... (*nanu*). Since the property of being a self (*ātmatva*) has been refuted as the delimiting condition of the subject according to the method to be explained, and since its pervader—namely, the state of being a locus of dispute (*vimatatva*) in a general sense—and the selfhood qualified by that [dispute] are already virtually refuted, he refutes *ātmatva* itself with the words "Not, first of all" (*na tāvad iti*). [The phrase] "by the consequence of being the subject" (*pakṣatvāpattyā*) means by the consequence of being occupied by the delimiting condition of the subject. [The phrase] "because of proving what is already established in part" (*aṃśe siddhasādhanāt*) refers to the fallacy of proving what is already admitted in some respect.

Even though, when the objective is the establishment of the probandum (sādhya) by way of its delimiting property (avacchedaka), partial proof of what is already established (*aṃśataḥ siddhasādhana*) is not a fault— since a proof whose scope is narrower does not contradict the inferential cognition (*anumiti*)—
nor is it a fault because it destroys the "subjecthood" (*pakṣatā*), which is characterized by a doubt regarding the presence or absence of the probandum with respect to that delimiting property.

Even if there is partial proof of the probandum (*sādhyasattva*), since doubt is possible—which apprehends the probandum through the relation of co-existence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) while apprehending its absence through the delimitation of the delimitor (*avacchedakāvacchedena*)—that very state constitutes "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*) in that case.

Nor should it be argued that this would lead to the undesirable consequence that, in an inference such as "Speech and mind are non-eternal," the proof of the probandum in speech alone would not be an obstacle [to the inference]. For, while proof delimited by the delimitor of subjectness is an obstacle to an inference delimited by that same delimitor, proof delimited by "speech-ness" (*vāktva*) can indeed be an obstacle to an inference delimited by that same "speech-ness."

For this very reason, the author of the *Maṇi* says: "Indeed, when there is a plurality of delimiters of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), partial proof of what is already established (*aṃśataḥ siddhasādhana*) is a defect. Nevertheless, this was stated following the view that, regarding an inference having a certain object as its content, the general state of having a proof (*siddhi*) regarding that same object acts as an obstacle. Now, one might raise the objection: "Let the delimiter of the subject be simply 'selfhood' (*ātmatva*) qualified by otherness from that [individual self], which excludes the Supreme Self (*paramātman*.
