He refutes this with the words "nor even" (*nāpi*). [He gives the reason: "because of contradiction" (*virodhāt*). Due to the contradiction between difference and non-difference, it is impossible for the property to be proved (*sādhya*) to coexist with the delimiter of the subject.
The sense is that [the opponent] does not admit a mediated (parokṣa) cognition whose qualifier is the subject-qualifier (dharmitāvacchedaka) of a property that is contradictory to itself.

Although, in their view, there is no contradiction between the general category of difference and the absence of ultimate difference, nevertheless—since illusory difference lacks the capacity to exclude [an object], and since empirical difference is unestablished for the opponent—the only difference that can be included within the scope of the subject (pakṣa) is ultimate difference; thus, contradiction is certain.

In reality, since the established doctrine (siddhānta) does not accept a threefold existence (*sattātraividhya*), and since mere difference alone is the antithesis of non-difference, it should be understood that this statement is made according to that [conventional] method.

Since the term "subject of dispute" (*vimata*) intends precisely the state of being the object of a specific doubt, there is no inconsistency in taking that much alone as the delimiting condition for the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*); thus he says: "of the Supreme Self," etc. The phrase "Caitra and others" follows.

Here, because Caitra-ness and so forth are not inclusive (*ananugata*), one follows the view that the delimiting condition for the subject is the state of being the object of a collective doubt (*samūhālambana-vimati*) regarding those [individuals] as its locus.

[Objection: But surely, if one takes "selfhood" (ātmatva) and so forth as the delimiting condition of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka), then for one who maintains the difference from the Supreme Self (paramātman), it would be incoherent to prove non-difference with respect to that which is delimited by a property other than those; therefore, he says: "Otherwise. This means: if the proponent of difference were to take selfhood and so forth as the delimiting condition of the subject. [He says] "because of impossibility."

The sense is as follows: if one attempts to prove the difference from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) by means of its co-occurrence with the universal property of selfhood (*ātmatva*), that [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) across all individual selves (*jīva*). If one attempts to prove it by delimiting [the subject] to those [selves], there is a contradiction (*bādha*) regarding the Supreme Self itself. Furthermore, if one qualifies the subject (*pakṣa*) as "other than that" (i.e., other than the Supreme Self), this qualification is unestablished for the opponent. And if one states that it is "perceived as other than that," there arises the fault of tautology and contradiction. Therefore, even by the proponent of difference, the very state of being the object of the aforementioned disagreement must be adopted as the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

Now, one might object that since the universal *ātmatva* (selfhood) is restricted to distinct individuals (*vyakti*), it is impossible for it to be pervaded by the aforementioned probandum (*sādhya*), which culminates in the non-difference of the individual; to this, he says: "Selfhood... By "self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatva*), what is intended is "non-knowability" (*avedyatva*), and not "the illumination of itself as its own object," because [in the latter case] the self itself would remain unestablished.
The opponent's lack of proof will be stated later.

Now, one might ask: even if the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is established by such an inference, how is the mutual non-difference of all individual souls established? If this is asked, the answer is no; for the non-difference of one [Self] from all [souls] necessarily results in the unity of all.
This is an illustration;
one should also include such inferences as: "The selves under dispute do not differ from Caitra’s self, because they possess selfhood, like Caitra’s self."

He raises an objection in order to state the purpose of employing the term *vimata* (doubted): "But surely... [and so on]. Regarding the phrase "because of proving what is already established in part" (*aṃśe siddhasādhanāt*): one might object that where there is a plurality of delimiters for the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), as in the case of "speech and mind are non-eternal," there is partial proof of what is already established because the intended cognition—"speech is non-eternal"—is already established; since the author of the *Maṇi* has stated this, how can there be partial proof of what is already established here, given that "self-ness" (*ātmatva*) alone is the single delimiter of the subject? To this, the following must be asked: [The answer follows: Here it must be asked. What is the nature of the cognition "speech is non-eternal"? Is it a cognition whose qualifier is "non-eternality" and whose qualificandum is "speech," or is it a cognition whose qualifier is "speech" and whose qualificandum is "non-eternality"? In the first case, even if the cognition "speech is non-eternal" is not established, the cognition "that which is speech is non-eternal" is indeed established, because the property of being a speaker (*vaktṛtva*) is co-extensive with the property of being speech (*vāktva*). In the second case, however, there is no proof of what is already established in part, because the cognition "speech is non-eternal" is not established. Therefore, the term *vimata* is employed to indicate that the cognition "the self is eternal" is not established. Is it only the multiplicity of the delimiters of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) that serves as the cause for partial proof of what is already established (*aṃśe siddhasādhana*), or is it also the establishment of the intended cognition?
It cannot be the first, because there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) both through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For instance,

there is no such rule that where there is a plurality of delimiters of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), there must be proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) with respect to some part [of the subject].

This is because, in the case of "The forest and the mountain possess fire, because of smoke," even though there is a plurality of delimiters of the subject in the form of "forest-ness" and "mountain-ness," there is no proof of what is already established with respect to any part.

Nor is there a rule that where there is an absence of multiplicity in the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), there is an absence of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) with respect to that part. [For example:
"Substances are non-eternal, because they are the locus of qualities.

Nor is there a rule that where there is an absence of multiplicity in the delimiting condition of the subject, there is an absence of the fallacy of proving what is already established with respect to that part.

In the argument "Substances are non-eternal because they are the substrata of qualities, like a pot," although the delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), namely "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), is a single entity, there exists the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in part, since non-eternality is already established in the case of produced substances such as earth.
Regarding the second [alternative], however, let it be that the very establishment of the intended cognition (*uddeśyapratīti*) is the motivating factor;
for this is necessary, simpler, and free from deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

But this does not apply even to the multiplicity of the delimiters of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), because that is unnecessary, involves prolixity (*gaurava*), and is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Now, one might object: "In this case, there is not even the establishment of the intended cognition (*uddeśyapratīti*)."

To explain: here, is the intended object of proof (*uddeśya*) a single, collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) whose content is the non-difference of the Self everywhere through its co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "Self-ness," or is it one that remains indifferent to such universality and so forth?
In the second case, since the non-difference [of the individual self] from the Supreme Self is already established, this would be a mere proving of what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*).

Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) even partially; for since the intended object is precisely that cognition which is universal (*sārvatrika*), even if one part were established, it would still constitute *siddhasādhana*.
If it is asked: "In the first case, how can there be *siddhasādhana* even partially?
For even if one part is established, the intended object—a cognition that takes everything as its collective object (*samūhālambana*)—is not yet established," we reply as follows:
For even the establishment of the cognition of the subject (*uddeśya*) does not, by its own nature, result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Rather, it functions solely as an obstacle to inference by way of destroying the status of the subject (*pakṣatā*). And this [obstructive function] exists in some cases even when the probandum (*sādhya*) has been established.

In some cases, when the probandum (*sādhya*) is already ascertained, doubt and the absence of proof regarding that constituent part (*tadaṃśa*) are impossible; consequently, there is an absence of "pakṣatā" (the state of being a subject of inference), which is constituted by both of those factors. Here, when the probandum is established in relation to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there is an absence of *pakṣatā* regarding that constituent part. Therefore, there cannot be a single collective cognition (*samūhālambana*) in the form of an inference whose qualificand is the entire self and whose qualifier is non-difference from the Supreme Self. Thus, by virtue of obstructing such an inference, "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) in that specific part remains indeed a logical defect. Nor should it be argued that during the state of a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), the establishment of the probandum does not obstruct the inference, and thus there is no obstruction to the inference regarding that part.
Because this [inference] does not apply when there is an absence of the desire to prove [the point];
otherwise, according to the aforementioned reasoning, even "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) would not constitute a logical fault.

Nor should it be argued that, although the non-difference of the Supreme Self from the Supreme Self in the form of "Supreme Self-hood" is ascertained, doubt and so forth regarding it in the form of "Self-hood" are still possible.

Because a specific ascertainment (viśeṣaniścaya) is generally opposed to doubt and the like, when such an ascertainment exists, it is impossible for that kind of doubt and so forth to occur. Otherwise, if one had ascertained [the mountain] as possessing fire by way of its being this particular mountain, there would arise a doubt regarding it by way of its being a mountain; consequently, one seeking fire would not engage in it with confidence. All of this is clearly explained in the *Tarkatāṇḍava*; this is the summary.
"Distinct" (viśiṣṭam): the term "selfhood" (ātmatvam) carries over here.

The intended meaning is that the aforementioned fault does not apply in this case. "By the probandum" (sādhyena): the meaning is that there is a contradiction between selfhood and the state of being other than the Supreme Self—which serves as the delimiting condition for the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka)—insofar as it is non-different from the probandum (abhedena).

And thus, since it is observed that mountain-ness (*parvatatva*) and the like, which are co-located with fire and so forth, serve as the delimiters of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), the meaning is that "self-ness" (*ātmatva*)—which is not co-located with non-difference from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—cannot serve as the delimiter of the subject when qualified by "being other than the Supreme Self. Regarding the phrase "by way of error" (*bhrāntyā*): the meaning is that because being other than the Supreme Self is unreal (*avāstava*), it does not stand in contradiction to real non-difference. Regarding the phrase "due to the possibility of error" (*bhrāntisambhavena*): [the meaning follows accordingly].

The point is that the quality of being perceived as distinct from the Supreme Self—the very cause of the aforementioned delusion—is common even to the Fish [incarnation] and others who possess His form.

He states what is obtained through the use of the term "matter of dispute" (*vimata*): "from the Supreme Self. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that being a subject of disagreement—namely, whether they are different from the Supreme Self or not—is not the *pakṣatāvacchedaka* (the delimitor of the subject), because it is cumbersome?
We say no; for cumbersomeness is a defect only when there exists another, lighter delimitor.

Just as when "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) is simpler, "blue-smokeness" (*nīladhūmatva*), being more complex, cannot be the delimitor of the probans (*hetutāvacchedaka*). Nor is there any other simpler delimitor here by virtue of which this [complex one] would be discarded due to its complexity; such is the sense. He strengthens this very point with a counter-argument against the opposite view—namely, "otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means: in the event of not accepting the aforementioned delimitor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).
For one who asserts the truth, it must be proven that the disputed selves are ultimately distinct because they possess contradictory properties.
In this regard, one must ask: what is the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) here?

If it is "selfhood" (*ātmatva*), then since the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is also delimited by that [property], it would follow that it too is the subject; consequently, there would be a partial sublation (*bādha*) because the difference from the Supreme Self does not exist in that case.
Nor is it qualified by being other than the Supreme Self,
because the state of being other than the Supreme Self remains unestablished even now.
Nor is it the state of being perceived as other than the Supreme Self through delusion.

Since the possibility of the delusion that even the Supreme Self (paramātman) is other than the Supreme Self exists, that too would be subject to the same defect stated in the first position by virtue of being a "subject" (pakṣa). Therefore, one must accept that the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) is simply the state of being an object of dispute—namely, whether they are different from the Supreme Self or not—and the defect encountered therein must be avoided according to the aforementioned method. Since the avoidance of the defect is equal in both cases, it is improper to show partiality toward one side over the other.
As they say: "When a fault is equal for both sides, or the remedy is likewise equal, one should not be subjected to censure in such an investigation of meaning.
But surely, in order to account for the subsistence of the universal *ātmatva* in multiple instances, the multiplicity of selves must be admitted.
And the absence of multiplicity is being established.

Therefore, to dispel the doubt that the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is untenable due to the mutual contradiction between the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*), he says: "The nature of selfhood" (*ātmatva*). [Objection: If it is not a genus (*jāti*), then what is it? He asks this. [Response: He gives the answer: "Self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatva*). The self-luminosity of the Self is intended as the state of being non-objective (*avedyatva*); it is not, however, the state of being manifest to itself (*svaviṣayaprakāśatva*).
It should be understood that this is because, due to the contradiction between agent and object, the proponents of Māyā do not accept that the Self is the illuminator of itself.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "By that" (tena). This means by the non-acceptance of "Selfhood" (ātmatva) as a universal class (jāti).
Furthermore: "The bodies under dispute are the substrates of experience for Devadatta alone, because they are bodies, like Devadatta’s own body."
In this context, the probandum (sādhya) is the state of not being a locus for the absolute non-existence of the substratum of experience;
by this, there is no sublation (bādha) with respect to bodies that are asleep, in a swoon, or dead,
nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra).
(There is neither contradiction nor inconclusiveness.

Now, in the phrase "of Daivadatta alone," since it is impossible to exclude the insentient—which is not even suggested as a potential enjoyer—by means of the particle *eva*, one must state that another sentient being is what is excluded by it;
thus, the existence of another self is established.

If it is argued that by abandoning the restrictive particle *eva*, it would follow that all bodies—even those with their own specific experiencers—could serve as the locus of experience for Devadatta, and thus there is the fallacy of proving something other than the intended point (*arthāntara*), we say no; for the restrictive particle *eva* excludes precisely another experiencer who might be accepted according to the opponent's view. Furthermore, he states another inference regarding the non-difference of the Self: "Moreover, the subjects of dispute... and so forth.
In this context, the term "under dispute" (*vimatāni*) is stated to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) regarding Devadatta’s body.

Thus, it is understood as "bodies other than Devadatta’s body. The underlying intention is that if one were to prove that these [bodies] are the locus of experience for Devadatta alone, it would follow that all selves, such as Yajñadatta and others, are non-different from Devadatta.

Now, one might object: if the bodies of those who are asleep, unconscious, or dead are included within the subject (*pakṣa*), there is a contradiction (*bādha*) because they lack the status of being a locus of experience; yet if they are excluded from the subject, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). To this, he says: "due to the absolute non-existence of being a locus of experience. Although the status of being a locus of experience is absent during states such as sleep, since that status is possible either prior to or subsequent to those states, those bodies are not loci of the absolute non-existence [of that status]. Thus, even though they are included within the scope of the subject, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, precisely because they are included within the scope of the subject, there is no deviation either—this is the meaning.
"Is it not the case that this inference is intended to prove the non-difference of selves?

In that context, by the very use of the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase 'of Devadatta alone,' that which is excluded—namely, the establishment of a consciousness distinct from Devadatta—is achieved. Therefore, this [inference] is self-contradictory. Thus he raises the objection with "Is it not the case? (nanu). To the question, "Why could that which is excluded not be simply the insentient [body]? he replies: "Of that which is not even suspected to be an enjoyer. The word "insentient" (*acetanasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

To the objection that the word "only" (*eva*) is therefore redundant, he says: "The word 'only'... The meaning is that even for those whose enjoyers are restricted [to specific bodies], it is possible for them to serve as the locus of Devadatta's enjoyment by way of the analogy of possession by a spirit (*bhūtāveśanyāya*); thus, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*). Regarding the phrase "of that which has reached the position of the opponent": the sense is that since the exclusion applies only to another conscious being (*cetanāntara*) as it might be suggested by the opponent's view, there is no self-contradiction. "The disputed ones" means the bodies of Yajñadatta and others.
The sense is that the establishment of non-difference follows from the force of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

The particle *eva* is used to exclude the possibility of a different object, such as Devadatta’s entry into another body. "Neither sublation (*bādha*) nor deviation (*vyabhicāra*)" means that if there is no sublation regarding the subject, then there is no deviation either. He refutes the inference even with the employment of the particle *eva*: "But surely... The phrase "establishment of another self" implies that otherwise, the particle *eva*, which functions as a differentiator, would be inappropriate because [the self] would already be excluded by its own nature.
The intended meaning is that the attainment of negation alone is the essential factor, not the existence of an intrinsic nature (*svarūpasattva*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "the disputed [entities]":

although by this inference the mutual non-difference of individual souls (*jīva*) may be established, it does not serve the purpose at hand in establishing their non-difference from the Lord (*īśvara*).
Nevertheless, this should be understood as having arisen by way of a contextual implication (*prasaṅga*).

Alternatively, based on the statement, "That Hari always drinks what is auspicious, he would not drink what is inauspicious," those who maintain the doctrine of the difference between the Self (*ātmabheda-vādin*) must admit that the Blessed Lord is the enjoyer of the essence delimited by that body.

The intention is that by means of this inference, when establishing [the body] as the locus of enjoyment for Devadatta alone, the non-difference from the Lord (*īśvarābheda*) is established. Regarding the phrase "the absolute absence of being a locus of enjoyment": although here the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is spatial (*daiśikī*).

Furthermore, when the bodies of those who are asleep, unconscious, or dead are taken as the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), there is neither sublation (*bādha*) nor deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because even though there is an absence of experience in those respective states, the status of being a locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*) still exists at some time.

Nor should it be argued that because there is a difference in substance due to a difference in dimension, the sleeping and other bodies are distinct from the preceding and succeeding bodies, and thus they never possess the status of being a locus of experience—thereby resulting in sublation and deviation;
for if that were the case, one could not escape the problem even by means of intended reference (*vivakṣā*).

This is because those bodies, being the loci of enjoyment and its prior non-existence as well as its destruction, cannot be the locus of its absolute non-existence. Nevertheless, this inference proceeds by means of two pervasions (*vyāpti*); it is with this intention that [the author] says "nanu" (but...). [The opponent objects: By the use of the restrictive particle "eva," since it is impossible to exclude insentient matter—which is not even suggested as a potential enjoyer—the exclusion must be of another sentient being who *is* suggested as a potential enjoyer. Consequently, the resulting meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) is: "being the locus of Devadatta’s enjoyment while not being the locus of the enjoyment of any sentient being other than Devadatta."
And thus, by means of the present inference which establishes the existence of such a probandum, there would be the establishment of a conscious being distinct from Devadatta.

Furthermore, if the particle *eva* (only) is abandoned, then even for those specific experiencers [of other bodies], it is possible for them to serve as the locus of experience for Devadatta—according to the logic of possession by a spirit (*bhūtāveśa*). Thus, the meaning is that there would be the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*), because the conclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) would be reached even without [proving] non-difference. Regarding the phrase "the view of others" (*paramatā*): thus, the meaning of the probandum is "being the locus of Devadatta’s experience while not being the locus of the experiences of another conscious being intended by the opponent as distinct from Devadatta. Consequently, neither [of the two disputants] establishes the existence of a conscious being distinct from Devadatta.

The sense is that [the author] says this very thing because the inclusion of the probandum within its own delimitation (*paramatāvacchedakatvena*)—as in the case of "this person speaks"—does not extend to the actual existence of the object.

Thus, having established the non-difference of all individual souls from the Supreme Self according to the doctrine of many souls (*bahujīvavāda*), he now relies on the doctrine of one soul (*ekajīvavāda*) and proves the identity of the soul in all bodies, beginning with the words "The subjects of dispute... (*vimatāni*). The meaning is: all bodies other than the visible physical aggregate of Devadatta.

This is stated with the intention that even if the probandum (sādhya) mentioned is already established in the bodies belonging to other births of Devadatta, there is no fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) when the proof is conducted by way of the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*). Alternatively, if through the mouth and so forth of a person possessing knowledge (*jñānin*), there is some manner of apprehending a form common to all the bodies of others—excluding the entire series of prior and posterior bodies related to Devadatta—then either that form, or the subject of dispute (*vipratipatti*) delimited by it, serves as the delimiting factor for the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*); therefore, there is no room for the fault of proving what is already established in part.
However, such a doctrine cannot enter the path of the intellect for the ignorant.

For, on the view that all embodied beings are the body of Devadatta, properties such as being produced by the karma of Devadatta would also be possible even in those bodies that constitute the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*).

Alternatively, according to the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*), there is only one soul named Hiraṇyagarbha who, assuming the identification with the body, has existed from beginningless time as the presiding agent over all bodies.
The position of the doctrine of the single soul (*ekajīvavāda*) is that until this present time no one has attained liberation, and after his liberation, nothing of the world will remain.
Consequently, in this context, the term "Devadatta" does not refer to one who identifies with a body;
rather, it is established by scripture that the physical aggregate (*piṇḍa*) consisting of the body of Hiraṇyagarbha has existed from beginningless time.

It should be understood that since it is established that Hiraṇyagarbha alone is the locus of experience (bhogāyatana) as delimited by the state of having a body other than those [others], there is no room for the fault of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā) in part.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "Since in this manner, even when proving by means of a delimiting factor (avacchedaka) in the preceding and subsequent texts, the admission of the fault of *siddhasādhanatā* in part exists, your refusal to accept it here in the middle [of the argument] constitutes a contradiction with the context. "Of Devadatta alone" means that being a locus of experience is the state of being a delimiting factor of experience (*bhogāvacchedakatva*).

[The opponent argues: "Experience (*bhoga*) is something other than [the self], because—according to the logic of the possession (*āveśa*) by pleasure and so forth—it is possible for Devadatta’s experience to occur even in a body that delimits the experience of someone other than Devadatta; therefore, the identity of all living beings (*jīva-ekya*) as the intended object is not established. To prevent this shift in meaning (*arthāntara*), the definition must be restricted. Its meaning is: "being qualified by the absence of being the locus of experience belonging to anyone other than Devadatta. [The proponent replies: But since there is no conscious being other than Devadatta, and since experience caused by an insentient agent is unestablished, the counter-positive (the thing whose absence is to be proven)—namely, experience caused by another agent—is itself unestablished. Consequently, its absence cannot be established according to the view of the inferer.

Nor should it be argued that one must introduce "the absence of being the locus of experience produced by that [Devadatta]" by introducing [the subject] as "consciousness intended by the opponent" under the qualifier "being consciousness other than Devadatta's.

For the inclusion of something in the category of the probandum (*sādhya*) merely as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for what is intended by the opponent does not imply its actual existence, just as in the expression "this person says so.
Even if the opponent's intention is erroneous, the objective reference (*viṣayatā*) of that intention must be stated as residing either in consciousness or in the insentient.

If it is argued that in the first case there is no escape from the contradiction in proving the absence of being the locus of experience for Devadatta’s consciousness— since that consciousness itself is the object of the delusion of being distinct from itself— and in the second case there is no established instance of experience produced by an insentient agent, we say no; for what is included [in the definition] is simply the qualification of being distinct from others, where the counter-positiveness is delimited by the relation of possessing experience whose agent is oneself.

Nor should it be argued that [the probans] is non-excluding because it is a *kevalānvayin* (universally present) due to being an absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by a relation with a different locus;

for the author will state immediately below that it is purposeful as a refutation of the "different subject matter" (*arthāntara*) contingency in the view of others who accept that Devadatta has experiences caused by an agent other than himself, since for them there is no such relation with a different locus.

According to the view of the Cārvāka school, specifically the position of those who maintain the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*), it is accepted that only one body possesses a living soul while all others—like bodies seen in a dream—lack a soul; or, according to that same system, the qualifying portion [of the definition] is meaningful to prevent the conclusion that [all else] is insentient.
But even so, it may be argued that the exclusion of other unintended objects (*arthāntara*) remains impossible.

Even in a body that delimits the enjoyments of someone other than Devadatta, at a particular time, there exists the absence of those [enjoyments] due to their non-existence; thus, the absence delimited by the relation constituted by them also indeed exists there. Consequently, the probandum—in the form of being the locus of enjoyments qualified by that [absence]—is not sublated in that case.

Nor should it be argued that an absence whose counter-positiveness is delimited by the aforementioned relation is necessarily an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*), because the counter-positiveness of antecedent absences (*prāgabhāva*) and the like is not delimited by any relation.

Since it will be made clear later in the text itself that [the self] is contradictory with both the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of that [enjoyment], just as it is with its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*),—because at some time there exists the delimitation of another enjoyment, the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of that [enjoyment] does not exist; thus, how could the absolute non-existence of "other" (i.e., different from that) as delimited by a relation containing that [enjoyment] reside therein? Even though the absolute non-existence of enjoyment is impossible there, because the prior absence and destruction of enjoyment themselves do not constitute the relation [required for the definition of absolute non-existence], while enjoyment alone constitutes the relation.

For even the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) delimited by the relation constituted by that [connection] exists, with respect to the delimitation of time and space that are not the locus of experience.

Even on a floor that possesses the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of the conjunction with a jar, there arises the cognition "the jar does not exist by way of conjunction" during a state devoid of conjunction; in accordance with this, Gadādhara and others have established—in their *Pūrvapakṣa* sections and elsewhere—that just like the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar, there also exists a prior absence of fuelhood and the like as delimited by the relation of conjunction. Since this applies to both prior absence and destruction, they too possess the property of being delimited by a relation. Therefore, [if it is argued that] the fallacy of proving something other than the intended subject (*arthāntaratā*) is unavoidable, we say: no.

This is because there is no risk of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*), since the aforementioned qualified probandum—or the probandum related by the aforementioned relation—is impossible if its qualifier exists at some time, provided that either (1) being delimited by the time of its own locus is accepted as a qualifier of the probandum, or (2) the nature of the probandum is accepted as being related by a relation not delimited by time.
[Objection: In that case, since the substantive (*viśeṣya*) lacks existence at all times, there would be a contradiction (*bādha*) and a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in Devadatta’s body.

Even if one intends to refer to Hiraṇyagarbha, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because, being asleep during the dissolution (*pralaya*), he lacks experience (*bhoga*); therefore, the author says: "being the locus of experience" (*bhogāyatanatva*). Since the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the delimitation of experience is incompatible with its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*)—according to the view that these are opposed to absolute non-existence—the probandum (*sādhya*) or its relation cannot possibly occur at any time; thus, there is no possibility of sublation (*bādha*) or deviation.
Even under the aforementioned intended meaning, the qualification in the form of the sense of the particle *eva* must indeed be supplied.

Otherwise, even in a state where the experience is produced by another agent, the aforementioned subject-portion remains intact; thus, one cannot escape the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*).

Alternatively, in order to avoid the difficulty of the meaning of the restrictive particle (*evakāra*)—namely, that Devadatta alone is the locus of experience—the meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) is: "the state of being resident in Devadatta, which pervades the experience delimited by itself."

The final conclusion is that the probandum (*sādhya*) is "enjoyment qualified by a body" through two relations: (1) the relation of being the locus of an absence whose counterpositiveness resides in that [body] itself, and whose counterpositiveness is delimited by the relation of being delimited by itself and the relation of being delimited by a counterpositiveness residing in that [body] which is delimited by itself; and (2) the relation of being delimited by [the body].

This serves to exclude the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), because if at some time another person's enjoyment were delimited by that [body], then since Devadatta’s presence would be absent from that enjoyment, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) would be violated.

One might raise the objection: "In states such as deep sleep for Devadatta and others, since there is an absence of experience delimited by such a body, the probandum (sādhya) which includes that [experience] would be absent; thus, there would be both sublation (bādha) and deviation (vyabhicāra). He dispels this doubt with the words: "bhogāyatanatve" (in being the locus of experience). The meaning of that term is simply "not being a substratum for the absolute non-existence of being such a locus of experience. And since, according to the method stated, that [property] does not subsist pervasively throughout time (akālikavyāpyavṛtti), there is no sublation or deviation—this is the intended sense.

Although there is no possibility of *bādha* (contradiction) or *vyabhicāra* (inconstancy) merely by the existence of the probandum (*sādhya*) at some time or other in the subject (*pakṣa*) or in the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*), because the condition of "non-co-occurrence with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivaiyyadhikaraṇya*) is included in the definition of both the body of *bādha* and the body of *vyabhicāra*;
otherwise, even the argument "this is in contact with a monkey, because it is this tree" would result in being fallacious.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that although stating the purpose of the "non-occurrence in the same locus as the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivaiyyadhikaraṇya*) and so forth would result in unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) when refuting that doubt, the refutation of the stated doubt was nevertheless carried out by first establishing the conclusion regarding a pervadingly present probandum (*vyāpyavṛttisādhya*).
Others, however, explain that "probandum" (*sādhya*) means "equal to the probandum" (*sādhyatulya*), which signifies "co-extensive with the probandum" (*sādhyasamaniyata*).

And thus, in order to exclude the invalidity (*bādhitatva*) of such inferences as "the earth possesses fragrance because it is earth" (*pṛthivītvāt*), since absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) itself is posited for both sublation (*bādha*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*), there can be no such sublation or deviation, because the absolute non-existence of those [reasons] is possible at some time even in that which possesses the aforementioned probandum (*sādhya*) as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). The point is that the probandum, namely the state of being a locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*), is exactly as it was stated in the original formulation; so they say. Some, however, argue that although the pervasion (*vyāpti*) here is spatial (*daiśikī*) regarding the absolute non-existence of being a locus of experience...

And thus, even though in the state of fainting there is no existence as a locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*), there is neither sublation (*bādha*) nor deviation (*vyabhicāra*), precisely because [the property] exists at some time in both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Nor should it be argued that this is so by accepting a difference between prior and subsequent bodies based on the observation of differences in the size of the body's parts;

for even in such cases, since all three—experience, its prior non-existence, and its destruction—are absent in certain bodies, an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is necessarily required, and thus the aforementioned defect remains as it was even when the intended probandum (*sādhya*) is formulated in that way.
Nevertheless, they say this with the intention that this inference proceeds by means of two pervasions (*vyāpti*).
Here, this must be analyzed:
the second pervasion is not temporal (*kālika*).

In this context, because the relationship between "being a body" (*śarīratva*) and "being a locus of experience" (*bhogāyatana-tva*) does not constitute a probans-probandum (*hetu-sādhya*) relation by way of temporal connection (*kālika-sambandha*), a pervasion (*vyāpti*) based on that connection is of no use for the present argument. Nor can it be argued that a probans-probandum relation also exists by way of temporal connection; for since temporality (*kālatva*) is absent in a body, the probans and probandum do not exist therein through a temporal connection.

In any case, having accepted that time possesses the status of a locus (*upādhi*), and having relied on its being the locus of something through the relation of temporal connection (*kālika-sambandha*), if one accepts the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*) there by way of temporal connection, then since even a jar (*ghaṭa*) and the like could potentially be the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no reason for excluding them.

Furthermore, if "embodiment" (*śarīratva*) is taken as the reason through the relation of temporal connection, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even in the case of a jar or similar objects—which are times that are loci of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) [of embodiment] because they are not loci of experience, its prior non-existence, or its destruction—since the specific probandum [of being a self] is absent there.

If it is argued that because saṃsāra is beginningless, the destruction of the enjoyments obtained by Devadatta since time immemorial exists there [in the body] by way of a temporal relation, and therefore its absolute non-existence is not asserted therein; then, even though the enjoyment produced by an agent other than Devadatta exists at the time the body exists, the aforementioned probandum remains uncontradicted. Consequently, since the identity of the conscious being is not established, this results in nothing but a "proving of the already proven" (arthāntaratā).

Even if one accepts that the exclusion of an "extraneous object" (*arthāntara*) is achieved by including in the probandum (*sādhya*) the absolute non-existence of enjoyment by a creator other than Devadatta—on the grounds that such non-existence is impossible at the time when the existence of Devadatta’s enjoyment or its destruction is present, which is the meaning of the particle *eva*—then, since the desired conclusion is established by that much alone, the qualifier portion (*viśeṣyabhāga*) is redundant. This is because even for one who maintains that [the self] is insentient, it is impossible to deny enjoyment as established by experience; therefore, it is impossible for the argument to terminate by taking the non-existence of enjoyment in general as its final point.

Furthermore, if one accepts that the body is time and proceeds with the inference, then for those who maintain the identity of the conscious self across all bodies—which are of the nature of time—there would arise the problem of sublation (*bādha*), since Devadatta’s experience exists at some time or other through a temporal relation in all bodies. [Objection: But surely, a body existing solely in times that are not the locus of any experience is well-known; thus, how could there be the possibility of sublation there? Moreover, the author’s pointing out sublation in the case of bodies that have entered states such as deep sleep or fainting would be utterly inconsistent.

Furthermore, since absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is incompatible with both antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) at a given time, if existence were [defined as] such, then the general category of absolute non-existence—having as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) any impermanent entity—would never touch time; this would result in their being unreal. Consequently, such a doctrine cannot withstand scrutiny, and thus it is improper to refine the probandum (*sādhya*) in that manner. Indeed, in the Nyāya statement "the bodies under dispute," there is nothing whatsoever that indicates a relationship between the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of temporal connection (*kālikasaṃbandha*).

Nor can it be said that even if others have stated such things in their own works, this would necessarily lead to the authors being subject to the process of raising doubts and providing resolutions [based on those sources].

For this very reason, the following is refuted: the objection of "sublation" (*bādha*) regarding the probandum—defined as being the locus of the aforementioned experience at all times—which would otherwise be established by force [of the argument], namely, that "whenever there is the state of being the locus of a body at a particular time, then at that same time it is the locus of experience for Devadatta alone," or the objection of "inconstancy" (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Because time does not enter into the body of the probandum (*sādhya*) which is established by the reason (*hetu*), it is impossible to state a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) that includes it.

Even if the probandum were to include time according to our stated method in order to exclude the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*), there would be no purpose whatsoever in introducing it into the reason.

Furthermore, if it were introduced into the reason, only a single spatial pervasion (*daiśikavyāpti*) would result in being a constituent of the inference; consequently, statements such as "this inference proceeds by means of two pervasions" would be entirely inconsistent.
Therefore, we do not understand this intention; rather, the great ones must be consulted.
Here, the following appears [as the solution]:
the meaning is by means of two types of pervasion (*vyāpti*), one consisting of and one not consisting of the heterogeneity of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi-vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Since both types of pervasion (*vyāpti*) are possible when the probandum (*sādhya*) is a pervasive presence (*vyāpyavṛtti*), the statement regarding the sublation of the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāraśaṅkābādha*)—even in a definition of pervasion that does not incorporate the absence of coreferentiality with the counter-positive (*pratiyogivaiyyadhikaraṇya*)—is made with the intention that the sublation in the subject (*pakṣa*) consists merely in the absence of the probandum, and that the absence of coreferentiality with the counter-positive need not be included in its definition. Thus, according to his own system, having raised the objection that the restrictive particle (*eva*) is redundant, he maintains that it serves a purpose on the grounds that it has utility even within the view of either the proponent or the opponent.

He demonstrates the purpose, which consists in the exclusion of an irrelevant conclusion (*arthāntara*) according to the opponent's view, with the words beginning "Now" (*nanu*). The sense is that since the inference intended to prove the identity of the conscious being actually establishes only the difference between conscious beings, it results in the proof of a thing utterly undesired; thus, because the desired [conclusion] is not established, there is indeed an irrelevant conclusion. Although this inference appears, at first glance, to be inconsistent with the present context—since it is intended to prove the oneness of the individual soul (*jīva*) rather than the oneness of the individual soul and the Lord (*īśvara*)—it is nonetheless relevant here.

Nevertheless, the underlying intention is that even the bodies of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others—which are the bodies of the Lord assumed for the sake of divine play (*līlā*)—are included within the scope of the subject (*pakṣa*), and thus they serve the present purpose by establishing the intended point.
On this very point, he states another inference: "Furthermore" (*kiṃ ca*). Experience (*bhoga*) means perception;
the "abode" (*āyatana*) means the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*).
And thus, the meaning is: "being the delimiters of Devadatta's enjoyments while not being the delimiters of enjoyments distinct from Devadatta's.
The exclusion of the first part of the definition (the *satyanta*) will be stated by [the author] himself.
The qualificand portion (*viśeṣyabhāga*) is for the purpose of establishing that the enjoyer is Devadatta.

Now, one might ask: even if the identity of the enjoyer is thus established, how is the non-difference of the non-enjoying Lord (Īśvara) from the individual soul (jīva) established? To this, he replies: "The identity [of the Lord] is established because the Lord also is the enjoyer of the rasa delimited by each respective body. This, however, is to be considered.
This is because it is impossible for the body of someone such as myself to serve as a specific limiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*) for the experience of God;

otherwise, even the body of Devadatta would possess both types of experiencers, which would render it unfit to serve as a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*). Furthermore, it should be understood that when the unity of all conscious beings is established through the force of favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*)—namely, parsimony (*lāghava*)—the intended goal is achieved.
Some also say that the intended objective here is merely the establishment of the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Now, one might ask: in this context, is the delimitor of the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) the state of being the body of Caitra and so forth—which serves as the delimitor of the locus of dispute—or is it simply the state of being under dispute? In the first case, there would be a sublation (*bādha*) regarding the body characterized by states such as deep sleep or fainting.

Even if one accepts that at that time there is an experience of pleasure and pain dependent on the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), there is no evidence for the body being its delimiting adjunct (*avacchedaka*).
Furthermore, this would lead to the same defect of contradiction in the case of a dead body. Thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Devadatta’s dead body.

Nor should it be argued that there is no such fault because the qualified entity is not distinct from the qualificandum, and since the probandum (sādhya) exists at some time within the body that serves as the qualificandum, [the definition holds].
This is because the qualified entity, being adventitious (*aupādhika*), cannot be non-distinct from the bare qualificandum.

Nor should it be argued that, by this logic, there would be the undesirable consequence of sublation (*bādha*) and so forth in cases such as "The tree is in contact with a monkey, because it is this [tree]," since the absence of the probandum exists in the tree delimited by its base (*mūla*).

If the probandum (*sādhyatā*) is delimited by "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*), this is accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it is not a fault when the probandum is established through co-inherence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In the second case, however, since the qualified entity is not the object of dispute, it falls outside the scope of the subject (*pakṣa*); thus, even though there is no opportunity for sublation (*bādha*) there, there is nevertheless a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that very instance.

Nor should it be argued that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) simply because the nature of being a body (*śarīratva*), defined as possessing movement (*ceṣṭāvattva*), is absent in dead bodies and the like. For, in order to avoid the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*) in the case of a body in deep sleep which is devoid of movement, it is necessary—as before—to define "being a body" either as a specific genus (*jāti*) or as the state of not being a locus for the absolute non-existence of movement. Therefore, he says: "insofar as it is the substratum of experience (*bhogāyatana*). [He adds: "there is no sublation (*bādha*). The sense is that bodies in deep sleep and so forth are loci for the destruction of their status as substrata of experience; therefore, they are not loci for the absolute non-existence of that status. This might be so.

There would be a contradiction [in the opponent's position] because, by accepting a mutual conventional difference between Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and others, the bodies of Yajñadatta and the rest lack the property of not being the locus of experiences distinct from those of Devadatta and the rest.
Nor can the difference be qualified as being "ultimately real" (*pāramārthika*);
for if that were the case, it would entail the establishment of Yajñadatta and others as ultimately distinct from Devadatta, which would result in an abandonment of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

Nor should it be argued that, because the probandum (sādhya) culminates in the fact that [the Self] is not the non-delimiting factor for the enjoyment of objects such as jars—which are distinct from Devadatta—there is no undesirable consequence of proving a difference between individual souls (jīva-bheda). For the objection is raised: "But surely... [nanu]. [The opponent might say: "In the aforementioned probandum, since the term 'satyam' (real/actual) is not included, there is no room for this fault. To this, he replies: "...by the word 'eva' (only/exclusively). [This refers to] those whose enjoyers are restricted, meaning those whose enjoyers are mutually distinct.
The meaning is that, since the inference would conclude with the establishment of two distinct experiencers within a single body, the identity [of the self] is not thereby established.

Nor should it be argued that even with the inclusion of the qualification "being existent" (*satyanta*), the fallacy of proving something other than what is intended (*arthāntaratā*) remains unavoidable—because the identity of the experiencer of deep-sleep experience (*sauṣuptika-bhoga*) who is unconditioned by a body with Devadatta has not been established.

The point is that such a difference is not established, as it would contradict the recollection of identity expressed by one who has awakened from sleep: "I slept happily. [Regarding the phrase] "of that which has reached the position of the opponent's view": this is the underlying intention.
Even if the difference that constitutes the object of negation is qualified by its being ultimately real (*pāramārthikatva*), there is no consequence of establishing another individual soul (*jīva*).
This is because it is the very thing to be negated,
just as one says, "ultimately real silver in a mother-of-pearl shell does not exist."

Nor should it be argued that here only the state of being a locus for experience (*bhogāvacchedakatva*) is negated, but not another experiencer (*bhoktrantara*); for a qualified negation regarding that which possesses the state of being a locus for experience results precisely in the negation of another experiencer. Furthermore, this negation is intended to refute the perception of another experiencer as established by the doctrines of opponents. As for the claim that the meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) here is "being the locus of Devadatta’s experiences while not being the locus of the experiences of any conscious being other than Devadatta, as maintained by opponents"—[this is rejected].
That is not correct;

for it would entail the undesirable consequence of contradicting the Māyāvādin, who accepts that the consciousness of Devadatta itself is what is intended by the opponent as being distinct from that [body]. Furthermore, since the matter is established by the aforementioned method alone, the inclusion of the phrase "as intended by the opponent" is redundant.
He announces another inference that establishes non-difference with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). The meaning is that yet another inference proving non-difference is now stated.

To the question "What is that inference?", he replies: "The subjects under dispute" (*vimatāni*). Here, if the body in general were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), then Devadatta’s body would also fall within the subject, resulting in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding a portion [of the subject].
Therefore, he specifies "the subjects under dispute."

In this context, the fact that these disputed bodies serve as the instruments for Devadatta’s enjoyment is not possible without their belonging to Devadatta; and that [belonging] is not possible without the identity of the self residing in those bodies, because it is impossible for two experiencing souls (*bhoktṛ-jīva*) to exist in a single body. Thus, the identity [of the self] is established.
Now, one might ask: do the bodies of those who are asleep, unconscious, or dead constitute the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*), or not?
Regarding the first [alternative], there is partial sublation (*bādha*) because those [bodies] lack the status of being a locus for experience (*bhogāyatana*).

Regarding the second, there is the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since the reason (*hetu*) exists in the sons who lack the probandum (*sādhya*). To dispel this doubt, he says: "In this case" (*atrety*). [The meaning is: "There is neither sublation nor deviation. The distinction is that sublation occurs if they are the subject (*pakṣa*), while deviation occurs if they are not the subject.

The point is that although those [bodies] do not possess the status of being a locus for experience at that time, they do so at another time; thus, because the absence of the absence of being a locus for experience exists in them, the probandum—defined as not being a non-locus of that [experience]—is present.
Now, it may be argued that experience (*bhoga*) is the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of either pleasure or pain.
While this is not possible in a dead body, it is indeed possible in those who are asleep or in a state of fainting;
for, upon waking, one has the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), "For such a long time I slept happily," through which the direct perception of pleasure during sleep is understood.

If it is argued that "delusion (*moha*), by process of elimination, should be understood as 'attaining half [of the fruit],' because there is only the recollection of suffering"—and that this implies the realization of suffering within delusion—it is not so.

For the bliss of deep sleep (*sauṣuptika-sukha*) experienced by one fit for liberation is the very nature of the Self (*ātman*); since it is produced merely by the embrace of the *prājña* (the supreme consciousness), the body has no causal role therein.
Thus, because the pain of fainting is produced by previous beating and the like, the body in a state of fainting is not the cause of it.

[Objection: Even so, how can sublation (*bādha*) be a defect in part? For in the case of "The tree is conjoined with a monkey, because it is a substance," one observes the arising of an inference regarding the uncontradicted part—the upper portion—without abandoning the rooted part which is contradicted. [Response: This is not so.

In that case, while the sublation (*bādha*) regarding a specific part of a tree—such as its conjunction [with a bird]—is not a defect because it does not obstruct the intended cognition of "tree-ness" (the universal) as co-present with that part, one should note the following: in the present context, since the intended cognition is the understanding that all bodies, by virtue of being co-present with the state of being a body under dispute, are instruments for Devadatta’s experience, the sublation regarding dead bodies and the like acts as an obstacle to inference in that respect. Consequently, because it obstructs the intended object, such sublation constitutes a defect. Furthermore, it must be considered whether the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "of Devadatta alone" is necessary or unnecessary.

Regarding the first [alternative], he says: "Now, indeed" (*nanu*). The particle *eva* (indeed) excludes the possibility of anyone other than Devadatta being the enjoyer. In that regard, no other [entity] can be non-conscious, because such a thing is never even suggested as an enjoyer, since it is entirely incapable of enjoying.
Since a negation is impossible regarding that which is not applicable,
therefore, by the word "only" (*eva*), the one to be excluded must be stated as the conscious Devadatta himself;
yet that is not tenable.

The meaning is "because of [falling into] an unestablished tenet" (apasiddhāntāt). In this context, by the word *eva* being present, that which is excluded by the *eva* is what is to be excluded (*tadvyāvartyam*).
By that statement explaining the other consciousnesses excluded by the particle *eva*;

but regarding the second [case], he says: "by the particle *eva*. And the connection is that when the particle *eva* is abandoned, there is the consequence of a different meaning (*arthāntara*). To demonstrate that, he says "of all," and so forth.
Although each respective body is a means for the experience of its own specific self, it is nonetheless possible for it to be a means for the experience of Devadatta as well.

The point is that we observe female bodies serving as instruments for the enjoyment of males, and bodies such as those of horses serving as instruments for the enjoyment of riders and others. Regarding the phrase "of those belonging to specific enjoyers": this means [the argument applies] even to those who possess selves that are restricted to being the enjoyers within each respective body. Regarding the phrase "precisely as it follows from the opponent's view": this means it serves to exclude a sentient being other than the enjoyer who is reached in the doctrine of the Proponents of Reality (Tattvavādins)—namely, a non-sentient entity such as another enjoyer distinct from Devadatta. The point is that there is no fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), because I do not accept the existence of another sentient being [other than the self].
Moreover, difference is false because it is a difference, like the [apparent] difference in the moon.
And falsity consists in being sublated by the knowledge of the true nature of the substrate.
If it is objected that the reason is unestablished because there is no common universal (*sāmānya*) underlying both what is authoritative and what is non-authoritative, we say no.
Because the very state of being perceived as distinctness is the probans (*hetu*),
there is thus no room for the aforementioned fault.
For "being perceived" (*pratīyamānatva*) means being an object of cognition (*pratītiviṣayatva*).
And that [property] is the state of being related to cognition;

for in this case, since the relation to cognition is nothing other than the essential nature itself, there is no requirement for it to depend upon being established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

If it is objected: "But since one moon is superimposed upon the moon being perceived, and because the difference between the superimposed and non-superimposed moons is real (*satya*), the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*)," we say: no.

Since the cognition of duality is established merely by the superimposition of difference upon the moon (or merely by the superimposition of the moon), it would be cumbersome to accept the superimposition of a second moon.

[Objection: In that case, since the cognition "this is silver" is established merely by the superimposition of non-difference with silver upon the mother-of-pearl, the acceptance of the superimposition of silver is useless. [Reply: This is not so;
for in that instance, because the substrate is not silver, one must accept the superimposition of silver in order to bring the silver to mind.
For when silver is not present, it is impossible to superimpose non-difference with silver;
this is not the case here, because the substratum is actually the moon.
He states another inference with the words "api ca" (furthermore). The meaning is: "all difference whatsoever is under dispute.

Thus, since difference and non-difference are contradictory, once the falsity of mere difference is established, the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and so forth, is proven.

Therefore, one should understand that there is no room for the objection that, having proposed the presentation of evidence for non-difference, it is inconsistent to present evidence for the falsity of difference.
Now, what indeed is this so-called falsity?
If it is non-existence, then it is a departure from one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
If it is indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*), then there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).

And because there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example, he says: "and falsity" (*mithyātvaṃ ca*). The intention is that since this [falsity] is already admitted in the case of the difference between two moons, there is no room for the aforementioned defect. Now, one might object: unlike *ātmatva* (selfhood) or *śarīratva* (bodiness), this "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*) cannot be employed as a logical reason (*hetu*), because in those cases a commonality (*anugatasāmānya*) is possible, as both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).

Having raised the objection that—although the difference between the objects of dispute (*vimatabheda*) is authoritative because it is empirical (*vyāvahārika*), the difference between the moon seen in the example (*dṛṣṭāntabhūcandrabheda*) is non-authoritative because it is merely illusory (*prātibhāsika*), and thus a commonality consisting of "the state of being a difference" (*bhedatva*) shared by both is impossible—the author refutes this with the words: "Of the authoritative and the non-authoritative... [The phrase] "of the state of being perceived as a difference" means that the expression "because of being a difference" is intended to signify "because of being perceived as a difference" through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). To the question, "How does this also remove the stated defect? he says: "For the state of being perceived... and so forth.

[Objection: Even so, the aforementioned defect remains exactly as it was, because it is impossible for the state of being an object of cognition (*pratītiviṣayatā*) to reside in the locus of the contact that produces that cognition. To this, he says: "And that [is]... [The meaning is: "And the relation is the very nature (*svarūpa*) itself. It is not something additional in the form of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), but rather its intended meaning is that it consists solely in the capacity to differentiate the cognition, characterized precisely by being what is delineated by the cognition.
And the point is that this is common to both what is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) and what is not.

He raises an objection: "of that which is perceived" (*pratīyamānasya*). [This refers to] the difference between the superimposed and non-superimposed moons—the illusory moon and the empirical moon. The sense is that if they were false (mithyā), it would follow that they would have mutual identity (*tādātmya*) with one another.
This deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) would occur only if the superimposed second moon were distinct;
but this is not the case.
This is because there is simply no superimposition of another moon.
The perception of duality, such as "these two moons," is accounted for merely by the superimposition of difference upon a single moon.
Even by one who accepts the superimposition of another moon, the perception of the difference between the two must necessarily be accepted.
Since the cognition "these two are distinct" is also established by experience,
it is better to postulate the superimposition of difference upon a single entity;
otherwise, there would be the consequence of unnecessary complexity (gaurava).

He offers a rebuttal, stating that since that difference is false, how can there be any deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*)—namely, "merely by the superimposition of difference upon the moon. He raises an objection by way of a counter-argument (*pratibandī*): "In that case...

Thus, just as in that instance, having accepted the superimposition of silver as well as its non-difference from the [shell], it is said that the resulting complexity (*gaurava*) is not a fault because it is established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*);
so too here, it is more appropriate to accept the superimposition of both.
The point is this: since the distinction between the superimposed (*āropita*) and the non-superimposed (*anāropita*) is real, the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) is difficult to avoid.
Nor should it be argued that by accepting such a distinction, there is no deficiency of the probandum because the superimposed is necessarily false;

for even though the difference superimposed upon a single moon is false, the difference whose counter-positive is another superimposed moon and whose locus is the non-superimposed moon is real. It is with reference to this very [real] difference that the deficiency of the probandum is stated here.

If it is argued that there is no room for the suspicion of a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) because it is precisely the superimposed difference in the moon that is intended here as the example, then let there be no deficiency in the probandum regarding the superimposed difference.
However, we maintain that there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) with respect to the difference between the superimposed and non-superimposed moons—this is our intention.
But if one accepts the superimposition of another moon in this way, then its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth must be stated.
For it is said: "An error never occurs anywhere—even in cases such as dreams and illusions—without a substratum consisting of two similar and real entities.
And in this case, there is no such substratum.

Because the moon is perceived as distinct from the object of superimposition (āropya), it cannot function as the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna); for it is impossible for that which is perceived as distinct from the object of superimposition to be its substratum.
Indeed, in the delusion of mother-of-pearl, the substrate is not perceived as distinct from the silver.
Furthermore, no substrate other than the moon is possible,
nor is there any primary cause (pradhāna) here,
because there exists no other real moon.
Furthermore, since the substratum cannot be mentioned separately when the visible moon is the primary object,
and because such a substratum does not exist,
how can the superimposition of another moon be admitted?
Not so;
for in the case of an error consisting in the delusion of identity, that [identity] is absent due to the necessary restriction of the substratum and other factors.

It is simply the moon, already perceived by the rays of the eyes that are not obstructed, which is perceived again by those same rays when they are obstructed and inverted, thereby perceiving it in a different location.

Thus, when two cognitions arise with respect to the single object of the moon by means of the two eyes, an error such as "these are two moons" occurs to the perceiving person. In that case, what need is there for a locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth?
Nor should one dispute regarding the two cognitions.

For when the eyes are closed without being pressed, there is no cognition of two moons; whereas that cognition occurs precisely when the eyes are not closed. Nor should it be argued that, since both cognitions would then be valid cognitions (*pramā*) because they have a real moon as their object, there would be no room for error.

This is because this cognition, which arises through the non-discrimination of the two cognitions that link them together, is logically established as an error (*bhrānti*) precisely because it is distinct from those two.

For this very reason, the argument—that in the third cognition, that which appears as distinct must be superimposed (*āropita*), since the difference relative to that [superimposed object] and its counter-correlate, the real moon, is real, and thus there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*)—is also valid. Enough of this. He releases the counter-objection (*pratibandī*) with "No. If it is asked: "In that case, why is the presence of the superimposition of silver (*rajatāropa*) in the instance of the error 'this is silver' even accepted?"
We say that in the absence of that [identity], the very cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—namely, "this is silver"—would not occur.

If it is argued that this is possible precisely through the superimposition of non-difference from silver, he replies to that: "In the absence of the presentation of silver," and "because the substratum is the moon. Thus, since the presentation of the moon is already possible through the perception of the substratum itself, one need not admit the superimposition of another moon for that purpose.

The point is this: since the superimposition of mere difference (*bhedamātrāropa*) is indeed possible upon the moon—which is presented as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) even without the superimposition of another moon—how can there be any room for the objection that the probandum (*sādhya*) is deficient? Regarding the word "difference" (*bheda*): what here constitutes falsity (*mithyātva*)? If it means empirical reality (*vyāvahārikatva*), then the probandum is deficient; if it means non-illusory appearance (*aprātibhāsikatva*), then there is sublation (*bādha*). Therefore, he provides a definition of falsity that applies universally. Furthermore, if the reason (*hetu*) is "the state of being a false difference," then there is unestablishedness (*asiddhi*); if it is "the state of being a real difference," then there is deficiency in the proof (*sādhanavaikalya*).

Nor is the universal (*sāmānya*) the cause [of cognition], because there is no universal that pervades both the false and the real; having raised this objection, he provides the resolution: "prāmāṇika... [and so on]. Now, one might object: "being perceived" means being the objective factor (*karmakāraka*) of a cognition; that is not tenable for what is non-existent. To this, he says: "For 'being perceived'... and so forth.

Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is non-existent to be within the scope of the contact between the sense organ and its object; therefore, he says: "And [the status of being] an object. Being related means being the locus of a relation.

Since even that is untenable, he says: "And the relation. Even though the non-existent is devoid of all causal power, it is designated as the object of cognition by virtue of a relation consisting in its own nature, which is dependent upon the majesty of its own causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

The meaning is that this very [difference] is what constitutes the appearance of a non-existent thing. "Of the superimposed and non-superimposed moons" means of the apparent (prātibhāsika) and the empirical (vyāvahārika). "By way of existence" means by way of non-apparent existence. "Deficient in the probandum" means that since every empirical difference is delimited by the delimiting condition of the subject (pakṣatāvacchedaka), the probandum remains doubtful. "In the case of the justification for the cognition of duality" means in the case of the justification for the cognition having the form "two."

The sense is that since it is precisely the difference (*bheda*) that is superimposed, and since that alone is of an illusory nature (*prātibhāsika*), the aforementioned defect does not arise. Regarding the phrase "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*): the sense is that the postulation of a substratum possessing attributes (*dharmī*) is more cumbersome than [postulating] the attributes and the substratum themselves.

Alternatively, the meaning is that while the mere duality is sufficient to account for the cognition of duality, it is more complex to assume that a pair of substrata qualified by duality is the cause. Regarding the phrase "in accounting for the cognition 'this is silver'": this should be explained as meaning "in accounting for the fact that the cognition takes the form 'this is silver'."

Therefore, there is no room for the doubt: "How can it be said that this [error] is explained by the fact that the cognition 'this is silver' is precisely the superimposition of non-difference? Regarding the phrase "for the sake of presentation" (*upasthity-artham*): although the superimposition (*āropa*) and its presentation (*upasthiti*) are one and the same, the statement that it is accepted "for the sake of that" (i.e., the presentation) should be understood as being intended in the sense of a general category and its specific instance (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).

Now, one might ask: "Why could there not be a superimposition of identity (*tādātmya-āropa*) upon the silver presented by memory? If this is asked, the answer is no; because for the direct perception (*aparokṣa*) of an identity, the direct perception of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) itself is the necessary condition.

"Moreover" (*api ca*): if mere difference were false, then the difference between Viśva and Viṣṇu would also be established as false; thus, it is relevant to the present topic. Now, if falsity means non-existence or being merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), then there would be a contradiction, because the difference under dispute is admitted to be of a conventional (*vyāvahārika*) nature.

In the first example, there is a deficiency regarding the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*); therefore, he says: "and falsity" (*mithyātvaṃ ca*). The intention is that this [falsity] is common to both the apparent (*prātibhāsika*) and the empirical (*vyāvahārika*), so there is no room for the aforementioned defect. Furthermore, since being perceived as distinct between the valid and the invalid—namely, the empirical and the apparent—is itself perceived, how can it be common to both? To this, he says: "For being perceived... (*pratīyamānatvaṃ hi*).

The point is that being perceived as distinct, or having a relation thereto, is possible in the case of the *prātibhāsika* (illusory) just as it is in the case of the *vyāvahārika* (empirical). Regarding the phrase "being perceived": in instances such as "these two moons," there is a moon perceived other than the empirical moon; since this is *prātibhāsika*, and because according to the opponent's view there exists a difference between the *prātibhāsika* and the *vyāvahārika*, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). Regarding the phrase "merely by the superimposition of non-difference with the moon": [the meaning is as follows].
