In the expression "these two moons," since the cognition of duality is established merely by superimposing a difference upon the moon currently perceived—without superimposing another moon—it is unnecessary to postulate such a [second] moon.
Likewise, even according to the opponent's view, the difference therein is false; thus, that example is not devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*).
This is what should be understood here.

Due to the pressure of the finger, one might think, "These two are moons; this [other thing] is not the moon," yet a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "moon-ness" is not superimposed upon the object on the ground.

This is because there is no such cognition as "this is not the moon," and because such a superimposition of difference could not serve as the basis for the superimposition of duality expressed in "these two are moons."

However, even though there is a presence of the moon-cognition regarding the empirical lunar portion residing in a specific location—where the counter-correlativity is delimited by that particular "moon-ness"—one must nevertheless admit the superimposition of another moon for the sake of the moon-cognition regarding the lunar portion residing in a different location.
This effort to refute the superimposition of another moon is futile;
for since the superimposition of a difference between moons upon the production of what is contradictory is well-known, the opponent himself accepts the falsity of the difference between moons.

For it is not tenable that the opponent does not accept falsity (*mithyātva*) in any particular instance. As for the word "then" (*tarhi*): this is merely superficial. For, according to both the dualist (*dvaitavādin*) and the proponent of reality (*tattvavādin*), since the non-difference from silver consists in being of the nature of silver, if one accepts the superimposition (*āropa*) of that [non-difference], the superimposition of silver itself becomes unavoidable.

For the Naiyāyika, however, silverness (*rajatatva*) is either non-difference from silver or the absence of difference from silver. Thus, the superimposition of silver is not established otherwise than through the superimposition of silverness. The superimposition of silverness occurs through the causal complex of error accompanied by the presentation of silver as qualified by silverness.
Alternatively, the superimposition of silverness occurs through the respective causal complex accompanied by the presentation of silver as qualified by a property residing in silverness.

This is because it is accepted that when both [the substrate and the superimposed object] exist, there is a superimposition of both. Consequently, since the difference between the superimposed and the non-superimposed is not admitted to be real, it is improper for that [difference] to enter into this discussion. Regarding the phrase "of the substrate" (*tatrādhiṣṭhānasya*): this too is merely superficial, according to the previous reasoning. Regarding the phrase "in the absence of the presentation of silver" (*rajatānupasthitau*): this too is quite gross;

for since the superimposition of non-difference with silver is possible through the very presentation of empirical (vyāvahārika) silver, there is no need for the superimposition of illusory (prātibhāsika) silver for that purpose.

With the intention that the proof of all one’s own desired positions occurs through this single inference establishing the falsity of difference and generality (*sāmānya*), he says: "Difference" (*bheda*). Here, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) with respect to a portion [of the subject] by taking the difference between the moon and so forth as the example, the term "disputed" (*vimata*) should be supplied. Furthermore, the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) should be understood as "the state of being a difference not sublated by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman. However, if it is held that there is no fault in applying that [delimiting property] to each individual instance (*avacchedakāvacchedena*), then "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*) alone should be understood as the delimiting property of the subject.

[Objection: Is it not the case that if falsity (*mithyātva*) means non-existence (*asattva*), there is a contradiction with one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) and a sublation (*bādha*) because [the object] possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*)? To this, he says: "And falsity... [and] "The substrate... "The substrate" refers to the unique form (*asādhāraṇākāra*) which is the object of the knowledge that removes [the error] by revealing the true nature (*yāthātmya*). In the case of Brahman, this is its very own nature; elsewhere, it is such things as the "shell-ness" (*śuktitva*). Thus, falsity is the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of a destruction whose causality is delimited by a property consisting of "being an object of knowledge" (*jñānatva*); the rest is a description of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). There is no impossibility [of this definition], because based on cognitions such as "silver has perished due to the knowledge of the shell," the destruction (*nāśa*) of silver is accepted.
The disappearance of the state of existence of a jar or similar object in the form of its cause—due to the falling of a hammer or other such means—is not what is meant by "destruction" (dhvaṃsa).
Since it is accepted that [true] destruction occurs only through the knowledge of Brahman, there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in that case.

The phrase beginning with "jñānatva" (the nature of knowledge) is included to exclude the conventional usage of "falsity" regarding prior desires and so forth, which are to be sublated by subsequent cognitions, on the grounds that they are specific qualities of the self.

This should be further investigated in my own commentary on the *Tattvodyota*, titled *Dvaitadyumaṇi*. Regarding the phrase "of being perceived precisely as difference": one might object, "How can 'being perceived'—that is, being the object of a cognition—be possible for that which lacks any basis in valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*)? For such a thing, being devoid of all causal capacity, cannot possess the status of an object as defined by its inclusion within the category of a causal factor (*kāraka*). To this, he says: "Being perceived. The meaning is that we accept the cognition qualified by the mode "difference-ness" as the cause [of the appearance] by virtue of its being the objective content (*viṣayatā*).
The intention is that there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*), because we accept the manifestation (*bhāna*) of even that which is non-existent.
Objection: Is there not a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) and the like, since the possibility of an error regarding their being "difference" exists?
Nor should it be argued that there is no deviation because falsity (mithyātva) also exists therein;
for if that were so, the argument would be redundant, as the point would be fully established by the mere fact of being an object of cognition (pratītiviṣayatva). Response: No.

This is because what is intended [by the definition] is the state of possessing an objectivity (*viṣayatā*) determined by a mode (*prakāratā*) whose nature is difference (*bhedatva*), as delimited by identity (*tādātmya*) or relation (*saṃsarga*).

One should not suspect that the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) remains unavoidable by taking into account the superimposition (*āropa*) of difference—qua difference—upon prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth elsewhere;

for even in those cases, in order to justify the linguistic usage "this is the difference being superimposed," it is accepted that there is an error regarding difference (*bhedabhrama*) there, wherein difference-ness (*bhedatva*) appears precisely through the relation of identity.

Furthermore, since there is the possibility of a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to the falsity of the difference being superimposed therein, it follows that where the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) appears as the primary qualifier itself, the nature of difference appears through identity, and difference itself appears. Even in such an error, it is not accepted that the difference is not apprehended; rather, by the force of the linguistic usage "this is a difference," the error consists precisely in [taking] the difference to be the prior absence.

Since it is accepted that in that very [cognition] the nature of difference (*bhedatva*) appears, there is no possibility of doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*). To exclude deviation—taking into account the difference between the cognition of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and others by means of "temporal object-ness" (*kālikaviṣayatva*) and so forth—the qualification "delimited by the relation of identity" (*tādātmyasaṃsargāvacchinna*) is introduced into the qualifier-role (*prakāratā*) of the nature of difference. Furthermore, as for object-ness (*viṣayatva*), it consists in being the locus of a sense-contact which is the instrument having a cause not common to [other] cognitions; how then could this be appropriate for that which is non-existent? To this he says: "And that... This too is just like that; therefore he says: "The very nature itself" (*svarūpameva*). The meaning is: "the very nature of cognition."

This is according to the view that since the nature of what is non-authoritative (aprāmāṇika) is impossible, the very nature of the knowledge itself constitutes its "objectness" (viṣayatā), and this very fact of being its determiner (*tannirūpakatva*) is the cause for the conventional usage "this is the object of this [knowledge]. Here, the word "therein" (*tatra*) refers to the determination of that [knowledge] residing in the intellect. The sense is that because there is no requirement for authoritativeness (*prāmāṇikatva*), such a position has been established in the original treatises (*ākara*). Furthermore, the sense is that since even the "indescribable" (*anirvacanīya*) is non-authoritative according to the opponent's own system, this does not constitute a departure from their tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Regarding the phrase "by the existence of difference": the meaning is that otherwise, there would be the consequence of non-difference between the superimposed and the non-superimposed.

It has been established elsewhere that the difference between the superimposed and the non-superimposed, being perceived as distinct from that [superimposition], is therefore truly existent. Regarding the phrase "merely by the superimposition of a difference in the moon": this means by the mere superimposition of a difference perceived as being related solely to the essential nature of the moon, and by the mere superimposition of a difference having the essential nature of the moon as its counter-correlative.

In the view that difference is a pervasive property (vyāsajyavṛtti) belonging to both [entities] and that the relation of counter-positive and substratum (pratiyogyanuyogibhāva) also exists between both, the cognition "these two moons are different from this" is established even without the superimposition of another moon, provided that the nature of the moon itself is superimposed with the pervasive property of difference along with its status as counter-positive and substratum.

The point is this: even on the view that difference is not manifested due to its non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāsajyavṛttitā*), since the manifestation of a particular instance of difference possessing a counter-correlate is experienced elsewhere due to some defect, such linguistic usage and so forth are accounted for by the mere fact of its being superimposed as being conjoined with that [actual] moon; thus, there is no need to posit the superimposition of the moon in another location.

But surely, if this difference were superimposed upon that very [moon], there would result the cognition "this is different from that," even though it is the same moon and the same individual. This is not so, because at that time, due to the influence of a defect (*doṣa*), the difference appears, and the two forms are mentioned separately as the delimitors of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) and the delimitors of the substratum-correlativity (*anuyogitāvacchedaka*). Since the property that constitutes the nature of the moon does not appear as the delimitor of that counter-correlativity, there is no resulting cognition such as "this is not the moon" or "the moon is not the moon. Nor should it be asked why the superimposition of another moon in a particular location is not accepted.
If that were the case, would there be a superimposition (āropa) of the moon as it is being perceived, or a superimposition of the moon as it is being remembered? Not the first;
for in this instance, what must be asserted is simply the superimposition of a connection with another location upon the moon appearing here.

Since all worldly transactions can be accounted for by the superimposition of a relation upon the object currently being experienced, it is more cumbersome (gaurava) to postulate the superimposition of both [the moon and its distance].
Furthermore, in that case as well as here, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the single moon appearing as elongated,
just as when two nearby mango and jackfruit trees are perceived as "this is one great mango tree."

Furthermore, in the case of "Is this a mango tree on the path? But of these two, one is a mango; however, this is indeed a jackfruit," there is no sublation (bādha) regarding the mode [of inquiry], yet there is sublation regarding the identity with a mango. Similarly, there arises the sublation: "The moon is not there, but right here," rather than the sublation of mere difference, such as "This is one and the same moon, not two.
Moreover, superimposition (āropa) in the form of a memory is also not possible through conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
This is because, while the powerful causal complex for the perception of the moon is present there, it is impossible for the cause of a superimposition in the form of a memory to exist there.

Furthermore, in cases where superimposition is dependent on the contact between memory and the object, one does not observe the fulfillment of the subsequent reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) in the form "I perceive this [object] directly. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence that the cognition "I perceive two moons" could not be accounted for.

In the case of the superimposition of remembered silver, the cognition "I perceive silver directly" is fulfilled by the very fact that the silver exists as a worldly object (*laukika-viṣayatā*) while being perceived through identity with that [shell].
However, in the present case, there exists nothing whatsoever that is perceived through identity with the remembered moon and yet constitutes a visual object.
It is precisely a particular pure location that appears as being within the moon,
because it is experienced as distinct from the moon.
The justification for this is that even in the location occupied by the moon, a delusion of difference arises when one presses with a finger.
By this, it is refuted [by the opponent] that a specific defect (*doṣaviśeṣa*) alone is postulated as the basis for the objective referent (*viṣayatā*) that sustains such a cognition;

otherwise, since one would have to speak of a superimposition (*āropa*) of what is being remembered in order to establish the falsity of the nature of difference (*bhedasvarūpa*), you too would face an insurmountable difficulty.

Furthermore, because no substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) can be identified when another moon does not appear through identity (*tādātmyena*), and because the perception of a moon in another location is accounted for by the aforementioned method itself, there is no seed for that superimposition, and thus the previously mentioned sublation (*bādhā*) is untenable.
Therefore, since [the required cognition] occurs through the mere superimposition of difference alone, the postulation of the superimposition of another moon is entirely redundant.

Here, although it might appear that one must speak of the superimposition of the relation (*saṃsarga*) of this difference of the moon—which is experienced in things other than the moon—onto the moon itself;
and thus, since that [superimposition] would be real and therefore unfit to serve as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), how can there be an articulation of that position?
Nevertheless, its status as an illustration for falsity is established by way of its mixed form (*saṃsṛṣṭarūpa*).

In reality, however, it should be understood that the author’s primary emphasis lies in this very point: that only a difference (*bheda*) residing in a distributed manner (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) is superimposed; and that, due to the influence of a specific defect (*doṣaviśeṣa*), it possesses an objectivity (*viṣayatā*) that effects the perception of being directly manifest (*sākṣātkāritva*), while being false in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

Although the effort [of the author] appears futile—since there is no dispute regarding the delusions of difference such as "this is not Caitra" in relation to Caitra seen previously at another time, and thus those instances could serve as examples—nevertheless, because there is no reason to abandon what has been explicitly stated when it is possible to do so, and because the purpose is to instruct the student, the effort is not in vain. Some say that the effort is indeed in vain because there is no dispute regarding the delusion of difference in the moon for one who is separated from his beloved. [The author replies: "In that case... and so forth.

One might object: "In the views of both the dualist and the non-dualist, since the non-difference of silver is itself the very nature of silver, its superimposition would necessarily result in the superimposition of that [nature] itself; therefore, this doubt is groundless.

This objection should not be raised, because the aforementioned doubt remains valid given that, in order to account for cognitions such as "the non-difference of silver," one must—according to their respective systems—accept either a postulated difference or a specific attribute (*viśeṣa*).

In that context, the phrase "by the superposed silver being the substrate" (*adhiṣṭhānatvena*) is used; alternatively, some manuscripts read: "by the silver being the substrate there" (*rajatasyādhiṣṭhānatvena*).
The meaning here is as follows:

because of the manifestation of two forms—namely, "this is silver" and "silver is this"—the superimposition of the identity of the mother-of-pearl upon the silver is as necessary as the superimposition of the identity of the silver upon the mother-of-pearl.

Thus it is stated in the *Saṅkṣepaśārīraka*: "The object 'this' (*idamartha*) may also be imagined within the silver, and the object 'silver' may be imagined within 'this'. Consequently, for the sake of the appearance of silver based on the mother-of-pearl as its substrate through the identity of the mother-of-pearl, there is also the superimposition of the silver upon the aspect of the mother-of-pearl in the error; such is the meaning.
The meaning of the term *upasthiti* is "manifestation.
Regarding the phrase "rajatasyānadhiṣṭhānatve," the reading "tatrārajatasyādhiṣṭhānatve'pi" is more appropriate; and if that were the case, this would be the correct interpretation of the meaning.

The reason for not accepting the superimposition (*āropa*) of the moon [in the case of the double moon] is that, since the moon itself is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) there, a cognition such as "there are two moons" can occur through the superimposition of difference and so forth in the manner described. In the present case, however, silver is not the substratum; rather, it is the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) alone that is the substratum. Since a cognition of that [silver] is impossible through ordinary sensory contact (*laukika-sannikarṣa*), it is necessary to accept the superimposition of silver at that very time in order to establish the existence of the cognition that accounts for the linguistic usage "this is silver" at that moment. Therefore, this does not constitute an obstacle to that [superimposition]. This is the intended meaning.

He states—“In the absence of the presentation of silver”—that if one does not accept the superimposition (*āropa*) of silver, not only is the empirical usage “this is silver” untenable, but even the superimposition characterized by the identity with silver as intended by you cannot be established. This means that in the case of the aforementioned error, if the absence of a cognition having silver as its object is admitted—that is to say, if the error is held to have silver as its object—then [the following follows]. Regarding “non-difference from silver”: the meaning is that such a cognition is impossible because [silver] would have to be known as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of a non-difference. Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
The activity of one seeking silver cannot be accounted for by a cognition of mere identity (*tādātmya*) alone.

Nor should it be argued that, in that case, it is the aspect of non-difference itself that appears as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), making the superimposition (*āropa*) of silver onto the mother-of-pearl redundant;

for since the appearance of silver in an error is necessary, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to postulate its appearance in the mother-of-pearl through the relation of non-difference, rather than postulating an additional object of cognition.
Furthermore, it is due to parsimony (*lāghava*) that [the non-difference] itself is the cause for the activity directed toward silver.

There is no parsimony in assuming that identity (*tādātmya*) is a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the part consisting of the mother-of-pearl and then postulating silver as a qualifier therein. This is because there would necessarily be the manifestation of a relation (*saṃsarga*) between silver and its non-difference, as well as between the mother-of-pearl and its non-difference; thus, there is the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) resulting from the postulation of additional objective relations (*viṣayatā*), and such a view fails to account for the causality of the activity. This is the intended meaning.

One should not suffer mental distress due to a misconception regarding the refutation [of our position]. For, while there might be a misconception regarding the meaning—that since the superimposition of non-difference with silver is impossible if silver is not previously present, the prior superimposition of silver is necessary—there is actually no such necessity for the superimposition of silver because the manifestation of that identity can occur through the mere presence of empirical (vyāvahārika) silver, even in the absence of a prior superimposition of silver.
This is because the aforementioned refutation does not touch upon the meaning of the sentence as we have explained it.

Regarding the statement that "there is no cognition of silver" when one superimposes the cause of activity (pravṛtti) and so forth upon someone seeking silver: since it would be useless and irrelevant to establish the prior superimposition of silver for such a person, it is an act of extreme audacity to suggest that the aforementioned sentence intends such a meaning. This is the general direction [of the argument]. To establish the non-difference of all things, he states the inference for the falsity of difference alone: "Difference... and so on. The phrase begins with "the subject of dispute" (*vimata*).
By this, there is no *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) in part, as was the case previously, regarding the difference between two moons.

Now, if "falsity" here means "non-existence," it would constitute an *apasiddhānta* (a deviation from one's own tenets), because the world is accepted as being distinct from both existence and non-existence; therefore, he says: "And falsity... Alternatively, since the opponent might object that there is no established instance (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) for proving falsity in the form of being distinct from existence and non-existence, he says: "And falsity..."

Alternatively, if falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in not being the locus of existence (*sattva*), then—just as in the case of Brahman which is devoid of attributes—it would be possible to deny that difference, even though it is of the nature of existence, from being the locus of existence; thus, the argument would result in proving what is already established (*arthāntara*). To this, he says: "And falsity... Alternatively, falsity is indeed simply the state of being sublated (*bādhyatva*).
And that [state of being sublated] is simply the state of being correctly known after having been known otherwise; thus, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Because one might accept that the world, known as momentary and so forth, is also known as permanent and so forth, he says: "And falsity. Alternatively, if the probandum is falsity in the form of being either ignorance or its effect, there would be a deficiency of the probandum in the example for the opponent, since in his view things like the moon in the sky—which are absolutely non-existent—are not included within ignorance or its effects; therefore, he says: "And falsity."

Since the mere quality of being removable—just as a jar or similar object is removed by the blow of a mallet—is possible even on the side of its reality, [the opponent might argue that] it is "removable by knowledge. However, this too, like a prior cognition that is removed by a subsequent cognition, does not contradict its reality; thus, the term "substratum" (adhiṣṭhāna) is employed.

It might be argued that this is a different point (arthāntara), because while the existence of things like "silver in a mother-of-pearl shell" (śuktirajata)—which are sublated by the knowledge of the true nature of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna-yāthātmyajñāna)—is not observed, their existence is possible insofar as they are sublated by that delusion. To this it is replied: "by the term *yāthātmya* [the objection is answered]. Nor should it be said that there is a deficiency in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntavaikalya*), on the grounds that although the difference between two moons and so forth can be sublated according to the Māyā-vāda because it is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), its sublation is impossible according to the Viśiṣṭādvaita school because it is non-existent (*tuccha*).
For what is meant by being "sublatable by that" is being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absence whose establishment is dependent upon that [knowledge].

The non-existence of the difference between the moon and its reflection, and so forth, is established in dependence upon the cognition of the oneness of the moon; thus, there is no fault. Regarding the term "authoritative" (*prāmāṇika*): the meaning is that, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the property of "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*)—which would have to be common to both the existent and the non-existent—is not established. Regarding the phrase "the reason is unestablished" (*asiddho hetuḥ*): if "difference-ness" as a feature common to both [the real and the unreal] were taken as the reason, the reason itself would be unestablished (*hetvaprasiddhi*). If "difference-ness" as residing only in the existent were taken as the reason, the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be unestablished. And if "difference-ness" in the form of being the object of an erroneous cognition of difference, which resides in the corroborative instance, were taken as the reason, there would be a lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*). This is the meaning.
Is it not the case that being "cognized" (pratīyamānatva) consists in being the object of cognition?

And since this [status]—which takes the form of being the locus of the fruit produced by cognition—is not common to both the existent and the non-existent, he says: "being the object of cognition" (*pratītiviṣayatvam*). This alone constitutes being the object of cognition, and not the aforementioned form [of being the locus of the fruit].
The point is that [the status of being the locus of the fruit] is impossible because the fruit in the form of "knownness" (*jñātatā*) has already been refuted.

One might object: "Is it not the case that being the object of a cognition—defined as possessing a contact (*sannikarṣa*) or similar condition that generates that cognition—is also common to both the existent and the non-existent? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And that... One might further object: "Since a relation depends upon the existence of its relata, how can there be a relation of cognition with something non-existent, such as a distinction between [two] moons? To this he replies: "And the relation... This would indeed be so if the relation were something other [than the cognition itself].
But this [relation] is simply the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the cognition. The point is that since this nature does not depend on the existence of an external object, there is no fault.

This might be the case: according to the opponent's view, because the difference between moons is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), the illustrative example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*).
Nor does it follow that the cognition of the difference between moons would thereby become a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*).
He raises the following objection: "But surely... [The opponent argues: Since the moon appearing as distinct from [the real] moon is itself superimposed, there is a sublation of the qualified object;

for if the distinction from the moon were itself superimposed, the perception of two moons would be untenable, because such a perception depends upon a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) directed toward two distinct entities. He replies: "As being real. The sense is that otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of identity between what is superimposed and what is not superimposed.

With respect to the cognition of duality, a cognition whose object is two actually distinct things is not the cause; for otherwise, the cognition of duality would result even when the difference between two distant trees is not perceived. Rather, it is the perception of difference itself [that is the cause]. Thus, there is no inconsistency in accepting the superimposition of the difference between two moons upon a single moon.

Nor is there an absence of a subverting argument (bādhaka) even if one accepts the superimposition (*āropa*) of another moon; for in cases such as "the moon is different from the moon," the difference from the moon is directly a qualifier of the locus (*dharmin*), whereas [if one were to posit] that which is different from the moon as being so [a qualifier] through identity (*tādātmya*), there would be a lack of parsimony due to the excess of objective relations (*viṣayatā*). With this intention, he provides the solution: "merely by the superimposition of the difference from the moon. Here, he raises an objection by way of a counter-argument (*pratibandī*): "But surely... Although there is no room for this counter-argument because the superimposition of non-difference with silver is more cumbersome than the superimposition of silver due to the excess of objective relations, [the author proceeds].

Nor should it be suspected that the conceptualization of the property (*dharma*) is lighter than the conceptualization of the substratum (*dharmin*); for a conceptualization of a property that is constituted by its substratum cannot be considered light. Nevertheless, the intention is that since the non-difference from silver consists in the nature of silverness (*rajatatva*), there is lightness in the superimposition (*āropa*) of that [silverness] when one superimposes the qualified [silver].

Furthermore, silverness (*rajatatva*) cannot be the object of superimposition in its own right, because that would contradict the recollection expressed as, "It was precisely false silver that appeared. Moreover, if silver were superimposed by way of being non-different from [the substrate], then the superimposition of silver itself must necessarily be admitted; this is stated in the passage beginning with "tatra" (therein). Even if one accepts the superimposition of non-difference from silver, the superimposition of silver must necessarily be accepted for the sake of presenting the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), which serves as the cause for that [superimposition of non-difference].
Nor is there such a necessity for the superimposition of another moon,
because the very cognition of the moon, which serves as the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), constitutes the knowledge of the counter-correlative (pratiyogin).
Nor can it be argued that here too [in the case of the shell-silver], the explanation is achieved merely by the presentation of silver existing in a marketplace.

If that were the case, since the non-difference between them alone would result in being the object of superimposition, it would contradict the aforementioned recollection (*anusmṛti*). Thus, the intention is that since the phenomenon is adequately explained by the necessary superimposition of silver alone, accepting the superimposition of their non-difference is both redundant and cumbersome. Furthermore, the phrase "apica" (moreover) is to be interpreted as equivalent to "kiñca" (furthermore). Regarding the term "bheda" (difference): it means the difference in question (*vimatabheda*).

Otherwise, since even the difference between the moon [and its reflection] would fall within the scope of the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding that part.
It should be understood here that once the falsity (*mithyātva*) of difference is established, its opposite—non-difference (*abheda*) itself—is thereby established.
Now, one might ask: what is this "falsity"?
[The world] would either be non-existent or indescribable.
Not the first, because it would contradict your own established tenets.

Not the second [alternative], because since that [second type of difference] is not established anywhere, it would result in the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). To this he says: "And falsity [is known] through the substrate... The meaning is that in the case of a shell-silver [illusion], it is well-known that [the silver] is removable by a true cognition whose object is the shell, which serves as the locus of superimposition (*āropādhiṣṭhāna*).
Now, one might object: "In this context, is the reason (*hetu*) the 'state of being a difference in dispute' or the 'state of being a difference of moons'?"
Not the first,
because the probans would be deficient due to the absence of the property of being different from the subject of dispute in the example.
Not the second.

Because the reason (*hetu*) is absent from the subject (*pakṣa*), there is a failure of its essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*). Now, one might object: just as smoke belonging to a mountain cannot serve as the reason due to the deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*), while smoke belonging to a kitchen cannot serve as the reason due to the failure of its essential nature, so that—both to avoid such doubts—a universal "smokeness" (*dhūmatva-sāmānya*) common to both types of smoke is made the reason; likewise, here too, a universal "differenceness" (*bhedatva-sāmānya*) common to both the difference between the moon under dispute and [other] differences should be the reason. If this is argued, we say no. For in that case, since both types of smoke are established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*), a universal common to both types of smoke is possible. However, here [in your case], that is not the case.

Regarding the present case, one might raise the objection that since the difference under dispute (*vimatabheda*) is authoritative (*prāmāṇika*), whereas the difference regarding the moon (*candrabheda*) is not, there is no common universal of "difference" that encompasses both the authoritative and the non-authoritative; thus, the reason would suffer from the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddhi*). Anticipating this, the author refutes it with the words: "But surely... (*nanu*). The statement that the difference under dispute is non-authoritative is made either in the sense of being merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) or according to the perspective of the proponent of ultimate reality (*tattvavādin*). The phrase "if this were so" (*evaṃ cet*) implies that the property of being perceived as a difference (*bhedatvena pratīyamānatva*) is common to both cases.

[Objection: Is it not the case that "being perceived" (*pratīyamānatva*) means being the object of a cognition whose nature is valid (*pramā*); and since this alone constitutes "being established by valid means" (*prāmāṇikatva*), how can this apply to the difference between moons, which is not established by valid means? To this, he says: "For 'being perceived'... [The meaning is: it is the state of being an object of cognition (*pratītiviṣayatva*), and not the state of being an object of a cognition whose nature is valid; for if it were the latter, the aforementioned fault would follow. [Objection: Surely, that which is known by means of a sense-organ in proximity to which a cognition arises becomes its object.
Thus, in this context, "being an object of cognition" must be defined as being in contact with the instrument that produces the cognition;
and such contact with the instrument consists of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.

Since this [contact] belongs only to what is real (*prāmāṇika*), how could it possibly apply to what is unreal (*aprāmāṇika*)? To this he says: "And that... [meaning] "being related to cognition," and not "being in contact with the instrument that produces the cognition"—the sense being that [if the latter were meant], the aforementioned defect would follow.

[Objection: But surely, since our relation [of inherence] must necessarily be either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), the aforementioned defect remains as it was. To this, he says: "And the relation... [The relation] is the very nature (*svarūpa*) itself, not something additional such as conjunction and so forth.
The definition of a relation of nature (*svarūpasambandha*) is that which determines a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭadhī*) without depending on an additional relation.
[Objection: But if it lacks a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would follow that it does not exist; how then can there be even a relation of nature? [Reply: No.

The point is that, by accepting the apparent difference between the two moons as merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*), one does not accept its non-existence. Regarding the phrase "in this way": the meaning is that when something is perceived as having the aforementioned difference, it does not require, according to the stated reasoning, to be established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).

To the question, "Why is the difference between the two moons real? he says: "between the superimposed and the non-superimposed. The point is that if the difference between the superimposed and non-superimposed moons were false, there would be a mutual identity (*tādātmya*) between them; and this is not possible for two things that serve as the substrata of contradictory attributes.

To the question, "Why is the superimposed nature (āropitatva) not accepted for both? it is said: "Because [the second moon] is superimposed upon the perceived moon. The implication is that if the other moon were not superimposed, it would be perceived even in the absence of pressing with a finger. This might be so if the other moon were indeed superimposed;
however, this is not the case.
Nor should it be argued that, if this were the case, the cognition of duality in the form "these two moons" would be untenable,
because one does not admit the existence of another moon that is superimposed;
for the cognition of duality is established merely by the superimposition of difference upon a single moon.

Nor should it be argued: "Why not assume the superimposition of another moon itself? He refutes this by stating: "By the mere superimposition of difference upon the moon. The meaning is: "By the mere superimposition of a difference having the moon as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) upon the moon. This is because, according to the maxim that "the postulation of a property (*dharma*) is simpler than the postulation of a substratum (*dharmī*"), once the moon is established, the perception of duality is accounted for by accepting the superimposition of the property alone in the form of difference; thus, there is the burden (*gaurava*) of assuming the superimposition of an entire substratum called "another moon."

He raises an objection by way of a counter-argument: "If that were so... If, on the grounds that the cognition of duality is accounted for merely by the superimposition of difference upon the moon, one does not accept the superimposition of a second moon, then there would be no superimposition of silver upon the mother-of-pearl.
Nor would there be an inconsistency in the cognition "this is silver" under such circumstances;
for that cognition is accounted for merely by the superimposition of non-difference between the mother-of-pearl and silver.

Nor should it be argued: "Why not assume that it is silver itself that is superimposed? For, according to the maxim that "the postulation of a property is simpler than the postulation of a substratum," since the cognition can be accounted for by the mere superimposition of the property called "non-difference from silver" upon the mother-of-pearl fragment, it is more cumbersome (gaurava) to accept the superimposition of a substratum called "silver.

If one were to accept the superimposition of silver there on the grounds that it is supported by valid means of knowledge (prāmāṇika) and thus its cumbersomeness is not a defect, then here too one must likewise accept it and admit that it is simply another moon that is superimposed upon the moon. This is the intended meaning.

He releases the counter-objection with "No. Regarding that cited instance, it might be asked: why should the presentation of silver not occur through the very cognition of the locus? To this he says, "because the locus is not silver.
The meaning is that since the locus of superimposition is [actually] mother-of-pearl, the presentation of silver is impossible upon seeing it as such.

To the question "Why is there even the presentation of silver? he says: "In the absence of the presentation of silver. The meaning is that since the knowledge of the counter-correlate is a cause for the knowledge of a relational entity (sapratyogika-padārtha), the superimposition of identity with that [silver] as its counter-correlate is impossible in the absence of the knowledge of the counter-correlate, which is silver. If, however, because identity is a relational entity, the superimposition of silver is admitted for the sake of presenting the counter-correlate;

In that case, since difference (*bheda*) is likewise [non-existent], one must admit the superimposition (*āropa*) of another moon for the sake of presenting its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); to this he says: "Not so. The meaning is: just as the superimposition of silver must be admitted for the sake of presenting silver, so too the superimposition of another moon need not be admitted for the sake of presenting the moon.

Why? To this he says: "Of the substratum" (*adhiṣṭhānasya*). For in that case, since the substratum is perceived as being of the nature of mother-of-pearl (*śukti*), the presentation of silver is impossible upon seeing it; therefore, the superimposition of silver is admitted.

The point here is that since the moon—the substratum for the superimposition of difference—is already present when it is perceived as the moon, the further superimposition of another moon for that same purpose is redundant.
Furthermore:
"The subject of dispute [is real] because it is devoid of any intrinsic internal difference in reality."
Whatever is thus is so; just as space is, so is this, and therefore it is thus.
Just as the sky is not ultimately divided by the spaces within jars, huts, and so forth— which are themselves devoid of ultimate mutual difference—
so too the entity called the "world" is not ultimately divided by its own parts, such as jars and the like, which are themselves devoid of ultimate mutual difference.

If it is objected that the example is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because one must admit an ultimate mutual difference between the spaces within jars, huts, and so forth, we say no.
If they were distinct by their very nature, then the cognition of their difference would occur even prior to the connection with a jar or other such objects.
If it is argued that there is no fault because jars and the like are merely manifestors [of the difference], we say no;
for we observe that sometimes a jar is perceived through touch even in the absence of manifestors such as lamps.
This [clarified butter] is the manifestor of the fragrance of saffron, just as clarified butter is for the fragrance of saffron.
If it is argued that, likewise, difference is not perceived even in the absence of a jar or other such objects, we say no;

for while fragrance is established there by its nature as earth, it would be cumbersome to assume that the fragrance is merely unmanifested (anudbhūta), and thus clarified butter is accepted as the manifestor.
But this is not the case with the subject at hand, because there is no evidence for a difference in space (*ākāśa*).

Now, he summarizes with a verse the inference regarding the absence of mutual difference among insentient things: "The disputed [entity]," etc. Some, however, say that the entire collection of sentient and insentient things constitutes the object of dispute (*vimata*).
That is to be considered.

For, whether in the text of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) or the text of the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), one hears only words such as "pot" which denote insentient things, and no word denoting both [sentient and insentient] is heard. Furthermore, since the removal of the lack of connection has already been shown previously by demonstrating the logical consistency, he explains the verse: "Just as the sky... By this, it is meant that the object under dispute, known as the "water-jar," is devoid of any real internal differentiation.
It possesses jars and so forth that occupy its own parts and are devoid of any real mutual difference;
that is to say, it is not ultimately different from those jars and so forth which occupy its own parts and are themselves devoid of any real mutual difference.
Why?
Because it is seen as being of the nature of the cognized.
Whatever is thus seen is such—that is, like its own object.
The sky does not, in the ultimate sense, differ from the spaces within jars, huts, and so forth, which are empty of mutual ultimate difference.
And this world is likewise perceived as such;
therefore, because it is an object of perception, it is in reality devoid of internal differentiation—thus the meaning of the verse is clarified.
[This would not hold] if those [entities] were distinct by their very nature.
This means, in short, the absence of having a limiting adjunct (upādhi) such as a jar.

He raises an objection with the thought that even if the parts of space are inherent, their cognition occurs only when there is a connection with a jar or the like, because it is accepted that they act as manifestors (vyañjaka) like a lamp; thus he says: "Of jars and so forth. [The phrase] "even in the absence of manifestors such as lamps" is used.
And thus, in this case as well, there would occasionally be a cognition of a portion of space even in the absence of a jar or the like;
but such is not the case.
Therefore, the point is that these [factors] are not manifestors (*vyañjaka*), but rather merely limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Now, one might object: "These [manifestors], unlike a lamp and so forth, are not non-specific manifestors; rather, like ghee which manifests the fragrance of saffron, they are indeed specific manifestors.

Therefore, in the absence of such a manifestor, the difference, though existing in space, is not perceived. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words: "Of the fragrance of saffron. It is reasonable to assume that ghee is a specific manifestor of the fragrance of saffron, because while the fragrance exists there, it is not perceived, and no other cause for this non-perception is observed.
Nor is it the case that there is no fragrance at all in saffron;
rather, even though it exists, let it be unmanifest, as in the case of stones and the like.
Therefore, one must say that through contact with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the fragrance residing in that [butter] alone appears in the saffron.
Because the presence of fragrance in saffron is established by the reason of its being earth (*pṛthivī*), there is no evidence for postulating that it is unmanifest (*anudbhūta*). Furthermore,

since only a manifest fragrance is perceived in saffron through contact with clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the postulation that the fragrance resides in the clarified butter alone is likewise lacking in authority.
But it is not so in the case at hand;

for there is no evidence for the existence of an intrinsic difference in space, by virtue of which—just as with ghee—the absence of that [space] would result in the non-perception of difference, given that [space] acts as a fixed manifestor of things such as jars. This is the intended meaning.
"Vimatam" means "the world.

The term "tāttvika" (real) is used to prevent sublation [of the probandum]. Since everything is included within the world, and it is already established that the world is not the locus of a difference from the world, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*); therefore, the term "svāntaḥ" (within itself) is added. "Matatvataḥ" means because it is known.
"Just as the sky" means "just as space"; this is the application (*upanaya*). "Therefore, so it is" is the conclusion (*nigamana*).

He explains the example with the word "yathā" ("as"). Regarding the term "bheda" (difference): according to the view of the *ekadeśin* (partialist), it should be understood that the word "bheda" refers to a specific quality (*viśeṣa*). Regarding the word "prāk" (before): this is an indication of the time when the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is absent. Regarding the phrase "because of being a manifestor": thus, even though there is a rule of following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the limiting adjunct with the cognition of difference, the fact that difference is adventitious (*aupādhika*)—in the sense of being produced by the limiting adjunct—is not established.

The meaning is that positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established otherwise. Regarding the phrase "by means of touch" (*spārśanena*): thus, even at a time when there is an absence of light and so forth, the existence of a jar is accepted on the basis of another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

In the present case, however, since there is no means of knowledge for a difference existing at a time when the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is absent, the conclusion is that the difference is produced by that very adjunct. Regarding the phrase "saffron" (*kuṅkuma*): just as the natural fragrance of saffron is never perceived without a manifesting agent such as clarified butter (*ghṛta*), let difference be the same.

The sense is that otherwise, even that [manifestation] would not be inherent (*svābhāvika*). Regarding the phrase "by way of earth-ness" (*pṛthivītvena*): the point is that even at a time when its manifestor is absent, although there is no perception of the odor through direct perception, its existence is indeed established.
An objection is raised: let it be granted that odor exists by way of earth-ness, but let it be unmanifest (*anudbhūta*) in stones and the like;
however, that which is perceived upon contact with ghee must be something else entirely, produced by a temporary adventitious condition (*upādhi*).

And thus, even in that case, why is it not accepted that there is no occurrence of following an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*) for that which is intrinsic? To this it is said: "not arisen" (*anudbhūta*). The sense is that, according to the maxim that "the postulation of a property (*dharma*) is better than the postulation of a substratum (*dharmī*"), it is more cumbersome for a distinct odor to arise merely from the manifestation of what was already present. "Disputed" (*vimata*) means: the entire range of sentient and insentient beings, which has become the object of doubt regarding the alternatives of whether they possess real internal differentiation or lack it.

In this context, although the sky is included within the subject (*pakṣa*), it is still appropriate for a jar alone to serve as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) in the inference of the difference from others (the counter-correlates) qualified by "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*). Similarly, there is no partial *siddhasādhanatva* (proving what is already established). As for the presentation of the five-membered syllogism, it follows the method of Nyāya; thus, by way of an incidental argument (*prasaṅga*), the absence of difference—relative to its constituent members—in the aggregate known as the "world" has been established. It should be understood, however, that what is relevant to the present topic is the absence of ultimate difference (*tāttvikabheda*) among the constituents themselves: Viṣṇu, the individual soul (*jīva*), and insentient matter (*jaḍa*).
Having in mind the alternative that the manifestor—such as a jar or a hut—is either indefinite or definite, he says "not the first" with the words "lamp, etc.
The ellipsis is: "for here too, even in the absence of a manifestor, there would be the undesirable consequence of the perception of difference at some time.
He raises the second objection with the words "of the fragrance of saffron. To this, he replies "by its being earth," which is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

In the present context, it should be understood that the perception of the fragrance of saffron cannot be accepted as being merely adventitious (aupādhika), in the same way as the perception of adventitious difference [is held to be], because such a fragrance does not exist in its substrate, namely the ghee. He states another method for proving the falsity of the general difference residing in the world: "The subject of dispute" (*vimatam*). The subject (*pakṣa*) is the collection of the world consisting of sentient and insentient beings, which is the object of disagreement due to the presence or absence of the general property of difference having as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and substratum (*anuyogin*) the constituent categories that are devoid of reality.

A whole (*samudāya*) is something distinct yet non-distinct from its constituents (*samudāyin*), characterized by being the object of a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). Therefore, since space lacks such a qualified nature, it is excluded from the subject (*pakṣa*), and its status as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is established. Regarding the term "real" (*tāttvika*): it means "ultimately real" (*paramārtha*) according to the method previously stated.

Since [the opponent] Bhāskara accepts inference, and since in his view there is no absence of difference that is not ultimately real, [the reason] would fail to be excluded [from the counter-example]; thus, the phrase "by way of being unconditioned" (*anaupādhikatvena*) is used.
In both systems, the probandum (*sādhya*) is indeed the absence (*abhāva*) qualified by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*).

This is because, in the view of Bhāskara, a difference that is non-conditional (*anaupādhika-bheda*) is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*). The phrase "with respect to itself" (*svāntara*) means a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and sub-correlate (*anuyogin*) are its own parts.

The essential point is this: just as threads are parts with respect to a jar, so too the individual members of the aggregate—such as jars—which constitute the world-form, are merely parts of that aggregate. Similarly, the spaces delimited by conditions such as jars are merely parts of the great space (*mahākāśa*). This is the underlying intention (*hṛdaya*).

The phrase "having as its counter-correlate one of its own parts" (*svāṃśapratiyogika*) is included to prevent the charge that the example is unestablished (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*), since opponents admit the existence of a real difference between the sky and things such as jars. The phrase "having as its substratum one of its own parts" (*svāṃśānuyogika*) is included to prevent the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because it is not admitted that a difference exists between a whole and a part of itself. The meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) is: "possessing a collection of absences of those differences—each qualified by reality—that reside in each respective thing, where the differences have as their counter-correlates and substrata their own parts. The reason for following this formulation of the probandum as a "collection" (*kūṭa*) is to establish the falsity of all differences intended in the thesis.

Since the absence of the aforementioned property delimited by its own difference—which is superimposed upon the jar—and the absence of the aforementioned form of the difference conditioned by adjuncts such as saffron (*mahārajana*) are already established, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*).
Therefore, the purpose [of the qualification] is to exclude that.
The phrase "by way of being considered" (*matatvataḥ*) means "because of being observable" (*dṛśyatvāt*).

Since it has been stated by Brahmā that the probandum (sādhya) must be accepted by both the proponent and the opponent, there is no possibility of the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the probandum in the case of the reason "being perceptible" (dṛśyatva).

Because the reason is simply cognition in its capacity as an object (viṣayatayā jñānam), there is no suspicion of the redundancy of the "cognition" (jñāna) component within the reason, which consists in being the object of cognition.
The example is: "Whatever is thus [perceptible] is such [non-existent]."
The meaning is: "Having established the probandum (sādhya) as stated in the sky, I shall employ it as an illustration.
Likewise, "this is so" is the application (upanaya). Thereafter, "therefore, it is so" is the conclusion (nigamana).

He explains the verse with the words beginning "yathā" (just as). The phrase "due to the consequence of the cognition of difference" means that when there is contact between the sense organ and the object, the absence of such a cognition would lack a causal basis.

Although the sky (*gagana*) is not perceptible by the eye, it is nonetheless perceptible by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*); therefore, the logical consequence (*āpādana*) is entirely appropriate.

Since cloth and other objects are perceptible by the eye, one should observe that by the same principle, if one were to admit that the parts of the cloth are inherent [to it], the possibility of the consequence of their being visually perceptible (*cākṣuṣatva*) would likewise arise.

Considering the two alternatives—whether the absence of some particular manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the absence of its perception because it is a constituent of the causal complex for that perception due to being a manifestor, or whether it is the absence of the general class of its own manifestors—he refutes the first with the words "dīpa" (lamp), etc. He raises the second alternative with the words "kuṅkuma" (saffron), etc.

The point is as follows: since the absence of ghee—which is the very manifester—results in the absence of its perception, the relationship between the manifestor and the manifested is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Thus, when ghee is absent, there is necessarily an absence of its own manifester (the universal), and consequently, just as there is no perception of odor at that time, so too here, because it is accepted that the substance possessing a specific dimension is invariably a cause for the perception of a specific part delimited [by that dimension], the absence of perception is indeed logical when the jar and so forth are absent, due to the presence of the absence of that which delimits its own manifestation.

Since that [pot] exists prior to the time of the object that serves as the cause of its perception, and since there exists a more robust means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [establishing its existence], the presence of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) sublates the notion that the manifestor of perception is the cause of its production; thus, one postulates that the manifestor is the producer of that perception.
In its absence, however, one postulates only its capacity to produce it.
Otherwise, the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) such as the staff and so forth would be the cause for the production of the perception of the jar, rather than the producer of the jar itself.

And thus, since there is no evidence for the existence of the part prior to its connection with the jar and so forth, the perception of the part occurs at the time of its connection with the jar and so forth;
it is this very fact that leads one to postulate that the part is produced by the jar and so forth—as he says with the words beginning "therein" (*tatra*).

Demonstrating another inference that establishes the non-difference of all things, he cites an ancient *kārikā* in the form of a five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava*) according to the method of logicians (*tārkika*), in order to make known the manner of its application: "The subject of dispute... He explains it as follows: "For example... Thus, the world under dispute is devoid of ultimate difference from any part of itself that stands in a relation of mutual opposition, because it is an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*). Whatever is an object of perception possesses such a probandum (*sādhya*). For example, elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*).
And the world is visible;
therefore, the meaning of the formal argument (prayoga) stated is "like that which possesses the probandum (sādhya).
Here, the absence of difference in general is unestablished (aprasiddha).

Therefore, [the definition] is "having as its counter-positive a part of itself. The term "ultimate" (*pāramārthika*) is included to avoid sublation (*bādha*), since such conventional differences do exist.

The qualification of "part" (*ekadeśa*) by the word "void" (*śūnya*) is intended to avoid the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), namely, the non-difference [of the whole] from mutually distinct parts.
The phrase "mutually," and so forth, is included as before to exclude the charge of unestablished nature (*aprasiddhi*).
Nor does the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) follow from the non-establishment of ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*),
because it has been stated that a negation can be established by the mere admission of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) by the opponent.

If, however, what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is the absence—by way of ultimate reality—of a mutual difference between [the whole and] its own parts, qualified by that very absence of such a difference by way of ultimate reality, then there is not even the suspicion of non-establishment (*aprasiddhi*).
This is because the absence of a difference delimited by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*) is well-established.
Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of partless entities such as qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth.

This is because a partless entity is not admitted at all; or, even if it were admitted, the very fact of having parts would constitute the reason for its being manifold. One might object: "Even if the objects in the form of distinctions exist within the parts of space prior to their connection with jars and so forth, there is no contingency of perceiving those distinctions simply because of the absence of other causes. To this, he raises the following doubt: "Just as in the case of lamps and the like during the perception of a jar... [The full phrase is: "...even in the absence of a manifestor such as a lamp. The sense is that since an effect is seen to arise through one cause even when another specific cause is absent, there might occasionally be a perception of distinction even in the absence of a manifestor for the jar and so forth.
By the term "manifesting agency" (*vyañjakatva*), it is not intended merely to be the cause of a specific cognition;
rather, it is intended to be the cause of that [cognition] in general.

Therefore, with the intention that the aforementioned fault does not apply, he raises an objection: "As in the case of saffron," etc. This rebuttal of the objection would indeed be valid if there were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [their] difference, as in the case of the fragrance of saffron and so forth.

He states that this very [reason] does not exist [in the counter-example]: "In that case" (*tatra*). Although the property of being earth (*pṛthivītva*) deviates from odor in a composite whole produced by parts consisting of both fragrant and non-fragrant [substances], nevertheless, it should be understood that the property of being earth is a valid reason provided it is devoid of any obstructer of odor. And in the case shown, there is no deviation because the obstructer—in the form of a contradictory odor—is present.

[Objection: But even if the mere existence of odor is thus established, how can the manifest odor manifested by clarified butter (*ghṛta*) be established by means of valid cognition? To this he says: "not manifest" (*anudbhūta*). [He adds] "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*); the meaning is that because one would have to postulate both the destruction of the previous odor and the production of a manifest odor upon the occurrence of contact with the clarified butter, there is complexity. Nor should it be argued that a manifest odor, though previously non-existent, is perceived due to its connection with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the clarified butter;
for, in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is impossible for such a perception to be an error.

In this context, it should be supplemented [in the commentary] as follows: "Because the odor is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) as being indeed manifested (*udbhūta*), the perception of it even prior to its connection with the clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is thereby precluded. Regarding the phrase "due to a lack of evidence" (*mānābhāvāt*): one should not argue that the very perception of the difference between the space within a jar and the space in a hut serves as the proof for that [manifestation]; for that perception can be accounted for as an error (*bhrama*), and there is the principle of parsimony (*gaurava*) against postulating a separate entity. Now, he summarizes in a verse (*kārikā*) the five-membered inference (*pañcāvayavopeta-anumāna*) that establishes the difference from the Self (*anātman*), so that it may enter the intellect. Regarding the term *vimatam*: the meaning is "that which is other than the Self and space."

In reality, it is devoid of internal differentiation; from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is a single locus free from mutual distinctions, being ultimately without division because it is, by its very nature, an object of perception. Whatever is such is an object of perception.
That is so in reality, being devoid of internal differentiation within itself;
just as the sky, that is, like space,
so too is this— the visible world— like space.
Then, because it is thus perceived as such in reality, [the author] explains the verse as being devoid of internal differentiation—
by way of the admission "just as," [meaning] by me, the proponent of difference.

The meaning is as follows: if the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*) and the space of a hut (*maṭhākāśa*) were ultimately distinct, then the illustrative example would be "deficient in the probandum" (*sādhyavikala*). This is because the probandum—namely, the state of being devoid of ultimate difference due to parts that are themselves ultimately devoid of mutual difference—is absent from the [space of the] sky. Regarding the phrase "prior to connection with the jar, etc.": if the difference between the jar-space and the [great] space were indeed caused by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) known as the jar, then one could rightly say that the connection with the adjunct called "jar" is perceived [only when it exists], and not otherwise. However, if the difference were intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), it would not depend on the connection with an adjunct; consequently, its perception would be unavoidable even in the absence of such an adjunct. This is the intended sense.

Now, it might be argued that even if the distinction between the space within a jar and [universal] space lacks the status of being caused by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the jar, it is nonetheless logical for that distinction to have a cognition dependent upon the jar; for the jar acts as its manifestor (vyañjaka),
and the cognition of the manifested (vyaṅgya) is necessarily dependent upon the manifestor.

He raises the objection: "Just as a jar, even in the absence of being conditioned by a lamp, has its cognition dependent upon that [lamp] because it is manifested by the lamp and so forth"—this is expressed by the words "of the jar and so forth. "There is no fault" means that there is no fault known as the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of cognition occurring even in the absence of that [lamp].
Let it be granted that the jar is the manifestor of the distinction from space;
nevertheless, the cognition of that [distinction] would still occur even when the jar is absent.

Nor should it be argued: "How can there be cognition of the manifested (vyaṅgya) in the absence of a manifestor (vyañjaka)? He refutes this by stating "No," because such a rule does not exist; for we observe that even in the absence of a manifestor called a lamp, there is cognition of a manifested object called a jar by means of the tactile sense-organ in the dark. Now, one might object: "A manifestor is of two kinds—restricted and unrestricted. That which exists invariably in the cognition of the manifested is restricted."
Just as cow's ghee is invariably present when the fragrance of saffron is perceived,
that which does not invariably exist when the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is perceived is "inconstant" (aniyata);
for example, a lamp or similar object in relation to a jar.

In this regard, just as cow’s ghee is accepted as the necessary manifestor of the fragrance of saffron, so too is the pot accepted as the necessary manifestor of the distinction of the space within the pot (*ghaṭākāśabheda*). Therefore, one might object that even in the absence of the pot, there would be no contingency of perceiving that distinction—this is the doubt expressed by the words "of the fragrance of saffron. Here, "distinction" refers to the distinction of the space within the pot. The author refutes this, saying "No. It is indeed possible for ghee to be the necessary manifestor of the fragrance of saffron, because that fragrance is not perceived in its absence.
Nor should it be said that the non-perception of the fragrance of saffron is not due to the absence of ghee, but rather because of the absence of fragrance in the saffron itself;

for since the presence of fragrance there is established by the inference "saffron possesses fragrance, because it is earth," it is improper to claim that the non-perception of fragrance results from the absence of fragrance.
Nor should it be argued that even if the fragrance of saffron is established by inference, its non-perception is possible because it is unmanifest (anudbhūta), like the fragrance of stone.

The meaning is that since the perception of smell through its connection with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is established by experience, to accept that the smell is unmanifest (*anudbhūta*) would entail the fault of abandoning what is authoritative and imagining what is not—namely, the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).

Now, one might object: "In this case, since the distinction of space (*ākāśabheda*) is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the jar's status as a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*) is postulated. To this he says: "And not... The sense is: [there is no such distinction] by which the jar could be a manifestor.
One might further ask: "How can there be a lack of proof for the distinction of space?"
If it is argued that the very cognition "there is a bird here" and "there is no bird here" is itself the proof [of space], we say no;
for that cognition has the circle of light as its object.
This is because, in the case of the perception "light here," the term "here" refers to the constituent parts of the light.
In the phrase "here is light," because of the reference to the sky,
the cognition "here is light" is either metaphorical,
like the cognition "here is the sky," or [it refers to] "here is a bird."

The sense is that, in this way, a distinction of parts is established: one part has the bird as its substratum, and another part has the absence of that [bird] as its substratum. Regarding the phrase "the circle of light" (*ālokamaṇḍala*): the sense is that in this case, there is no cognition of a portion of space, but rather the circle of light itself is the object of the cognition "here.
If that is so, what is the status of the cognition "here" in the case of the expression "light here"?
For it cannot be said that even there, it is the circle of light itself that is cognized as "here."
Because it would entail the consequence of [the cognition] residing in itself (*ātmāśrayaprasaṅga*).
Therefore, one must say that in that case, only a portion of space is the object of the cognition "here.

Having raised the objection—"In the same way, why is it not accepted that in the case of 'the bird is here' as well, that very [portion of space] is the object?"—he states that this too can be explained otherwise: "not because there is no light here" (*nehāloka iti*).
The point is that, just as there is the cognition "cloth" with respect to these threads, so too the cognition "light" is logically established with respect to the parts of light.
If that were so, then in the case of "there is no light here," what is cognized would be the absence of light;
yet even in that case, the parts of light cannot be the object of the cognition "here."

Since the cognition "there is no light here" would be untenable while the parts of the light are manifesting, one must therefore admit that in that case, it is only a portion of space (*ākāśa*) that is the object of the cognition "here. To this he says: "There is no light here. The meaning is that in that instance, the sky itself is the object of the cognition "here," not its part.
[Objection: But in the case of "there is no light here," the parts of the light are the objects.

In the phrase "there is no light here," the sky is the object; thus, there is no basis for postulating a twofold division [of space]. Due to the lack of internal consistency—specifically, because of the absence of partiality toward one's own view—the author states: "the cognition that 'there is light here. The point is as follows: just as the sky, despite lacking the property of being supported by the sky, is conventionally perceived as being supported by the sky—as in the expression "the sky here"—so too, although light lacks the property of being supported by light, its perception as being supported by light (in the expression "light here") can be explained as merely figurative (*aupacārika*). Consequently, this cognition does not establish a real division of parts within the sky.

In this context, what is called the "metaphorical nature" (aupacārikatva) of the cognition consists in its having as its object a non-primary meaning, by virtue of its apprehending a relationship between locus and located (ādhārādheyabhāva) even in the absence of actual difference.
For the relationship between locus and located is primary when it is co-referential with difference; that which is not co-referential with difference is intended here as non-primary.
Thus, since metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is understood as a property of words, there is no room for the doubt as to how its metaphorical nature could be established.
Some, however, say that the cognition which gives rise to the employment of a metaphorical word is itself metaphorical, and thus the word is called "metaphorical.

This is incorrect; for since an employment that possesses the same form as the cognition [of the object] cannot be metaphorical, it is all the more impossible for the cognition that produces it to be metaphorical.
The meaning is: "because of the cognition that 'this [is] here'.

Although it should have been stated simply as "because its object is conditioned by limiting adjuncts" (*aupādhika-viṣayatvāt*), this is because the opponent accepts that the two—[the tree] characterized by the presence of the bird and [the same tree] characterized by its absence—are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Nevertheless, there is no fault in this being a theory of poetic imagination (*utprekṣā*) proposed by some in order to account for its imperceptibility as well. Regarding the phrase "here, light": the sense here is that, as before, if light were to enter [the body], it would lead to the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Now, because there is an inconsistency in the statement "here, a part of light," he says "here" out of a sense of unease. Regarding the term "figurative" (*aupacārikī*): according to his own system, this should be understood as follows: in reality, based on the scriptural statement, "The Lord, the directions, and time are always inherent in Himself," that perception is actually primary (*mukhya*).

He anticipates an objection regarding the proof for the difference in space, asking: "But how? Even if by this cognition both the bird and its absence are apprehended in space, yet not their difference, how can this [cognition] serve as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for difference?
