Nevertheless, according to the older view, because a substance lacks the property of non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*), which consists in being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is co-locative with itself, it is impossible for a single locus to be the substratum of both the bird and its absence. Therefore, through the framework of inference (*anumāna*), difference is established by this [cognition].

Nor is it proper to say that this [cognition] has as its object the conjunction of a bird and its absence; for, like the cognition of sound, it is impossible to provide such an explanation. It should also be understood that there is a cognition of difference in the form: "this possesses a bird" and "this does not possess a bird. Regarding the phrase "the orb of light": the point is that since this [cognition] has the orb of light as its object in the capacity of a locus (adhikaraṇa), there is no difference in the nature of space (ākāśa) resulting from it.
Now, the cognition "there is light here" and "there is no light here" establishes a distinction in space.

However, the designation of "light" as being "here" is not possible in this context, because that would involve the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya). To this, he says: "Light here. Even here, the sky is not the object as a locus.

Because the sky, being formless, cannot be the object of visual perception; and because, in the absence of any fixed bringer-forth (upanāyaka), it is impossible to postulate an act of bringing-forth (upanaya). The sense is that it is only the constituent parts of light that can appropriately be the object. [Regarding the term] "metaphorical": The meaning is as follows: since the sky is devoid of form, it lacks the fitness to be an object of visual cognition (*cākṣuṣa*). Furthermore, because there is no determinate factor that brings the object into proximity, it is impossible to conceive of an act of presentation (*upanaya*). Therefore, the intended sense is that only the particles of light are fit to be the object. [The term] "metaphorical" (*aupacārikī*)...
Now, one might object: "Is figurative usage (*gauṇī vṹttih*) distinct from indication (*lakṣaṇā*), or is it included within it?

Since that [figurative usage] is a function of words, how could it apply to cognition? We say no; for the cognition that serves as the motivator for the use of a figurative word is itself metaphorically designated as "figurative" (*aupacārikī*).

The point is this: just as in the case of the cognition "the sky is here" when one asserts that the sky is the locus in such statements as "there is no bird here,"—since it is impossible for the sky to be the locus of itself due to self-dependence (ātmāśraya), one must somehow describe the relationship between the container and the contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) as non-primary even though there is some kind of difference—the same applies to the present case.
This is the intended meaning. [Regarding the phrase] "here is a bird":

The meaning is as follows: since it is impossible for existence and non-existence to appear in a single location due to their mutual contradiction, this cognition must take the difference between the two spatial parts—consisting of the portion of space itself—as its object, and thereby apprehend existence and non-existence therein; thus, perception itself is the proof for the difference in parts.

Now, one might object: even if the aforementioned cognition has the difference in parts as its object, it is not established that it has a natural (intrinsic) difference in parts as its object, because it is possible that it is merely apprehending a difference in parts produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the form of the bird.
Not so.

Even if one accepts that in the portion related to the bird there is an appearance of difference caused by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of the form of the bird, it is impossible to speak of a spatial difference in that [portion] which is devoid of the bird, because of the absence of connection with any corporeal substance; for if that which is non-existent there were to act as a differentiator, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Nor is the mere absence of the bird itself the differentiator.

Even previously, since [the sky] exists there, even according to your own view, it would follow that it is distinct; thus, its cognition as something distinct would have occurred already. Nor is this a desired consequence, because if that existence were beginningless, the assumption that it is caused by an adjunct (*upādhi*) would entail the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), thereby establishing that it is intrinsic—this is the underlying intention. Regarding the phrase "a circle of light": since the perception [of the sky] is experienced as visual, it is more reasonable that its object is light within the range of the eye, for the sky itself is not an object of visual perception.
Nor should it be argued that, once a natural part (svābhāvikāṃśa) is established in light through this perception, that same logic would establish such a part in the sky as well;

for the sense is that the orb of light is produced by its source, and thus its parts—just like the parts of a cloth—are dependent upon the producer of the orb of light which is their own whole (svāṃśin).
[Objection: Even so, in the case of "light here" and "no light here," there is no other way to account for it than by the manifestation of distinct parts of the sky.

Raising the objection that since light cannot reside in light, the cognition "there is light here" would be untenable unless one were to posit a distinction between different instances of light, [the author] shows the distinction of the object as it appears as the locus by stating, "here is light," and so forth. Now, one might argue: since light is perceived as inhering in its own parts, one must say that in this case the sky is being indicated, and thus the absence [of light] is perceived as delimited by its relation to that [sky]. If that were so, then even in the sky connected to the orb of light, there exists an absence of light delimited by that same relation; consequently, the cognition "there is light here" would result [absurdly].

Since the sky is not an object of visual perception (*acākṣuṣa*), there would be a contradiction with the experience of its being a locus that is visually perceived; therefore, he says: "as in the case of 'the sky here'. Whether this cognition is verbal or mental is another matter. In any case, because the self-bearership of a thing upon itself is sublated by the consequence of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), it must be stated that [the cognition] takes as its object the connection with another corporeal entity situated in that location. The point is that the cognition "light here" is analogous to that.

The meaning is that figurative [cognition] does not have the primary locus as its object, but rather has as its object another non-primary relation, like the verbalized cognition "knowledge in the jar" or "cows in the banyan tree.

Therefore, since the two types of non-primary function (vṛtti) which constitute the objects of figurative usage are dependent on words, there is no deficiency even if they are impossible in the case of perception.

The phrase "mānam" (the means of knowledge) refers to the difference in space (*ākāśabheda*), and so forth. Although this [space] is not the subject here— since the cognition "there is a bird here" and "there is no bird here" does not apprehend the presence of the bird and its absence as residing in space, and thus space-difference lacks the status of being the means of knowledge for that— nevertheless, such a cognition has as its object the subsistence [of the two] in different locations, because its object consists of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharma*).

Its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) should be understood through its capacity to give rise to inference, such as the cognitions "here there is potness" and "here there is no potness.

In reality, however, it should be noted that since the absence of a bird is invariably concomitant with a location distinct from one containing a bird, and is thus non-different from that [location], the cognition apprehending it possesses validity regarding that [absence].
Here, although it could be argued that the adventitious condition (*upādhi*), such as light, merely manifests a spatial distinction in the ether (*ākāśa*) that does not actually exist;

Nevertheless, following the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), he says: "Light... [etc.]. Now, even so, let the very cognition "there is light here" and "there is no light here" be another means of knowledge (*māna*).

For, since it is impossible for a thing to be its own substratum, that cognition—just as before—cannot have the orb of light as its object. To this he replies: "There is light here. The sense is that, because the sky lacks the status of being a substratum for light, it is impossible for that [cognition] to have the sky as its object. As for the phrase "of the sky": the sense is that since it is impossible for the parts of light to be the substratum of the absence of light, it is untenable for them to be the object [of such a cognition].
But in that case, there would be no cognition here of "light" as involving a relation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*),
because such a relation does not exist between a part and its whole.
Nor can it be that the sky alone is the object of that cognition.

Even though there is a conjunction between the sky and light, there is no relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) by virtue of that conjunction; therefore, he says: "or it is figurative" (*aupacārikī vā*). The meaning is that here, [the expression] has as its object a secondary sense (*gauṇa-artha*) consisting in the state of being related to the sky. To the question, "In the absence of a specific purpose, why is there a figurative usage?", he states: "just like the cognition 'here is the sky'. The meaning is that just as in that case the use of the word "here" (*iha*)—meaning "in this"—is a conventional metaphor (*rūḍhopacāra*) and does not require a particular purpose, so it is here as well.

Alternatively, one might object: surely the conventional usage of the relation between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*) regarding a part and its whole is contrary to experience, since such cognitions as "the jar is in the potsherd" are not established. Therefore, how can there be a designation of "here" with respect to the parts of light? To this, he says: "Or it is metaphorical" (*aupacārikī vā*). The intended meaning is that even in this case, the sense is simply "this light [belongs] here."
Regarding the objection "How so?":
there is no evidence for a division in space; how could it not be so?
It means that, on the contrary, such a division certainly exists.
To the question "What is the proof for that?", he says: "In this case, 'the bird'... For this cognition grasps both the bird and its absence within the space specified as "here.
Indeed, the existence of both in a single space is not logical, because of the contradiction between a counter-positive (pratiyogin) and its absence in one and the same place.

Therefore, the sense is that the distinction [of space] is established within a region of space (*ākāśapradeśa*). He states—beginning with "āloka"—that this cognition does not serve as a means of knowledge (*māna*) for the distinction of space, because it apprehends the presence and absence of light within the circle of light (*ālokamaṇḍala*). Now, one might object: the cognition "there is light here" and "there is no light here" apprehends light and its absence in the very space pointed out by the word "here. Nor should it be said that even here, the word "here" refers merely to the circle of light.
If that were the case, it would lead to the absurdity of "light in light," resulting in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Therefore, [the opponent] might argue that the distinction between space is established by this very cognition, "light here. To this, he says: "Light here" (*ihāloka*). Following the word "of the sky" (*gaganasya*), the term "here" (*iha*) is understood to carry over. Now, one might object: since the singular reference "here" is established by experience in both instances, if one accepts the aforementioned distinction based on such usage, there is a contradiction with experience. Dissatisfied with this, he says: "Light here" (*ihāloka*). Just as in the expression "not light here" (*nehāloka*), so too in "light here" (*ihāloka*), the word "here" refers exclusively to the sky.
Nor is there any inconsistency in the counter-positive and its absence having the same locus,
for we do not admit that space (*gagana*) is the locus of light. Nor is there any inconsistency in the cognition "light is here."

The point is that there is no contradiction in accepting a figurative cognition (aupacārikapratīti), just as one might say "there is space" in space even when space is absent, so too one might say "there is light" here even in the absence of light.
Alternatively, it cannot be said that in the cognition "there is light here," the word "here" refers to a part of the light;
for ordinary people lack the notion of a whole (avayavin) based upon its parts.

For people do not conventionally designate the hands and so forth as "the body," but rather as being of the very nature of that [body]; therefore, he says: "here, the light" (*ihāloka*). In the expression "here, the light," the word "here" (*iha*) refers specifically to the light.
Nor is this a case of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
This is because it is accepted that this cognition is metaphorical (*aupacārika*).
Since the purpose of the metaphor must be stated, it is said here: "like the cognition 'the sky [is here]'".
The meaning is: just as there is the cognition "the sky" with respect to the sky even when there is no sky, so too is it here.
The sense is that because the metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is well-established, there is no requirement for a specific purpose.

Now, even so, does the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) such as a jar touch the entirety of space, or only a portion of space? It cannot be the first case, for otherwise, every instance of "jar-space" would be [identical with] the whole of space.
If it is argued that in the second case the establishment of the essential part (*svābhāvikāṃśa*) follows, we say no. What would it mean for "all space" to be "pot-space"?
Does it mean that it would become related to a pot? Or that it would possess a dimension similar to the dimension of a pot? Or that even the entire great space (*mahākāśa*) would become pot-space?
Not the first, because that would entail an undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti). Not the second.

Because an adjunct (*upādhi*) necessarily sides with the reflection—meaning it must side with the reflection—the jar, as an adjunct, imparts its own dimension to the space that occupies the position of the reflection.
However, since the great space (*mahākāśa*) occupies the position of the original object (*bimba*), the adjunct does not color it with its own properties.
For this very reason, the third alternative is not tenable.

Because the property of being a "colored jar"—which is the ground for the application of the term "jar-space" (ghaṭākāśa)—is absent in the "great space" (mahākāśa), just as it is in a limited space, that term is not applied there.
Furthermore, the coexistence of conjunction with its own absolute non-existence is accepted on the strength of valid evidence;
indeed, that very evidence will resolve the contradiction.
"For consciousness alone, the venerable lady, is our refuge in establishing the existence of objects," according to this principle.

Now, as for the phrase "even so": even if a natural part [of space] is established in the sky by the aforementioned method, the construction is that the establishment of the natural part occurs when the second alternative among the two alternatives is accepted. The phrase "mere sky" means the entire sky.

Accepting the first position for the time being, he asks by means of an alternative in order to refute the objection stated therein: "Is every space [the same]? This is to be construed as: "Would every pot-space be the great space (mahākāśa)? or "Would every great space be the pot-space?
In some places, however, the reading is exactly as such.

The phrase "it would be the space within a jar" (ghaṭākāśaḥ syāt) means that it would be designated by the term "space within a jar. Regarding the expression "by imparting the cognition of its own dimension": the meaning is that, having taken its own dimension—such as a span (*vitasti*)—and applied it to the space within the jar, it generates the cognition thereof.
For this very reason, the author will later state that "therein, it does not color [the object] with its own attributes.
This means it does not attach its own attribute, namely the nature of having a dimension such as a span.

He explains what was stated by the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*): "of being a property of the jar colored [by the adjunct]" (*uparañjitaghaṭadharmatvasya*). This means: "of having as its properties the jar's dimensions such as a span (*vitasti*) and so forth, which have been attributed [to it].

Regarding the phrase "because there is no usage of that term for it" (*tatra tadavyavahārāt*): the meaning is that the term "jar-space" (*ghaṭākāśa*) is not used with respect to the great space (*mahākāśa*).

Although the first position is not accepted by the proponent of non-duality (*advaitavādin*), it should be understood that he entertains it here in order to demonstrate that the aforementioned refutation does not apply to it.
For this very reason, accepting the second position, he refutes the objection raised therein with the words: "of conjunction" (*saṃyogasya*). This is the underlying intention:
we accept precisely the position that the adjuncts such as a jar touch a single part of space.
Nor should one be satisfied by the thought that, in that case, no intrinsic parts are established.
This is because the statement "it touches a portion of space" does not accept the meaning that it possesses a conjunction with a portion of space;

rather, its intent is that the conjunction with the jar is co-located with its own absolute non-existence in space. Nor is it the case that, even if this were so, the proof of an inherent part would be unavoidable.

It should not be argued that because the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and its absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) are contradictory, their coexistence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible, and therefore a distinction between parts must necessarily be admitted in order to resolve this contradiction;

for we perceive, by direct experience, the simultaneous presence of both a jar and its absolute absence even in the sky, just as we perceive the conjunction of a monkey and its absolute absence in a tree.
Furthermore, once an object is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no room for the suspicion of contradiction.
In this regard, he states the agreement with the Nyāya logic: "Consciousness alone... [and so on]. The venerable [consciousness] is worthy of respect;
that is to say, it is not subject to denial.

Having stated the impossibility of intrinsic difference, he addresses the unity of those possessing adventitious differences, beginning with: "But surely... He asks by means of the words "the pot," etc., intending three possibilities: the space of the pot, the pot as space, and the space belonging to the pot alone.

The meaning is that, according to the third position, there would be no distinction in conventional usage such as "the space of a jar" and "the space of a hut. Regarding the term "reflection": this is the secret here.
The adjunct (*upādhi*) alone manifests the single reflected object (*bimba*) in two ways; it is in this way that it imparts the dimensions and other qualities of the reflection.

And thus, just as the one and only great space (*mahākāśa*), by way of being reflected as the "space within a jar" (*ghaṭākāśa*), attains the status of being another space; that very same [great space] is spoken of as having the dimensions of the jar. "For this very reason" means: because it favors the position of reflection. "Of the ground for application" (*pravṛttinimitta*): the sense is that since the mere connection with a jar is not the [actual] ground, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

If all of space were related to the pot, there could be no cognition of its absence in another location; therefore, he says: "of conjunction" (*saṃyogasya*). The meaning is that there is no evidence for co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such that "in that location space is conjoined with the pot, but here it is not. Nor should it be argued that here a difference of locus is actually perceived, because in both cases—"space is conjoined" and "space is not conjoined"—space appears as the substantive (*viśeṣya*).
In this context, the phrase "therein" (*tatra*) functions merely as a delimiter. [The opponent] thinks: "The means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself will establish the element of contradiction.
For indeed, contradiction is to be grasped by a means of valid cognition that apprehends a lack of common locus (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*).
If that very same [cognition] were to apprehend a common locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), then how could there be contradiction? This is the intended meaning.

"Only the sky" means the entire sky. "The establishment of the intrinsic part" (svābhāvikāṃśasiddhiḥ) is the meaning; thus, the point is that the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavaikalya). Or, "every pot-space would be the great space," which is to be construed as: every great space would be a pot-space, i.e., denotable by the term "pot-space."

In some places, the reading is exactly as follows: "Because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is partial toward the reflection. The sense is that, since one observes the emergence of the mirror's own impurities and so forth specifically in the reflected face, one postulates such a nature [for the adjunct].

The connection is made by changing the case ending and repeating the word: "The jar, which colors it with its own qualities, is the limiting adjunct. Now, an objection: there can be no relationship of original and reflection between the limited space and the great space according to the logic of the face and its reflection.

Because the jar is an opaque substance and space is formless (*nīrūpa*), it is impossible for the latter to be reflected in the former. Even if such a reflection were possible, just as the impurity residing in a mirror appears in the entire reflection of a face and not in its specific parts such as the ears, so too here, the cognition would arise that "the entire space is the size of the jar," just as one might think "the entire face is dirty.
Therefore, it must be stated that the connection with the jar occurs only in a single part of space.
If that partiality were also adventitious (*aupādhika*), there would be an infinite regress; therefore, it must be said to be inherent (*svābhāvika*).

And thus, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*); to this he says: "of conjunction," etc. "Mere ether" means the ether as established by convention. "The dimension of the jar," etc., refers to the great ether (*mahākāśa*) and so forth.

The point is that if the Great Space (mahākāśa) were to acquire a dimension equal to the dimension of the jar, it would follow that it lacks greatness, and consequently, there would be no cognition of it as distinct from the jar. Or, [if one argues] "the Great Space would be [so]," the point is that the very space delimited by the jar would result in being perceived as having greatness.
Furthermore, since the portion of space that serves as its own cause cannot impart its own attributes [to itself], there is no basis for the dimension of the jar to be attributed to the Great Space.

He states the resolution—namely, that the distinction between the two is produced solely by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)—by first presenting an illustration: "Of the limiting adjunct" (*upādheḥ*), "of the reflection" (*pratibimba*). Even though there is identity between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), the meaning is as follows: since it is observed that the reflection alone manifests its own attributes such as turbidity through the appearance of difference therein caused by the adjunct, the nature of the adjunct is to favor the side of the reflection. [Objection: Let this be so; what does it have to do with the present case?

Since there is no relationship of original and reflection between the great space and the space within a jar—because the jar and such things are not transparent—it is said: "standing in the place of a reflection. The meaning is that it is similar to a reflection by virtue of possessing distinctions caused by itself and so forth.

Thus, because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) possesses distinctions and is imagined by itself, its status as a substrate for its own attributes is accepted on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), and not as being delimited by the state of being a reflection qualified by that [adjunct], due to the resulting complexity (*gaurava*).

The meaning is that [the reflection] does not possess that nature (tathātva) merely by virtue of being a reflection, because it would follow that even reflections imagined by oneself would likewise possess it. Regarding the phrase "colored by its own attributes" (*svādharmoparañjaka*): the word *upādheḥ* (of the limiting adjunct) is understood here as a nominative case ending (*prathamānta*). Regarding the phrase "the state of having the attributes of a jar colored by [it]": *uparañjita-ghaṭa* means "a jar colored by [something].
The inversion of the order of words in this instrumental *tatpuruṣa* compound—similar to the *rājadanta* class—is permissible.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which is both *sa* (it) and *dharma* (attribute)."

Alternatively, the analysis of the compound *uparañjitaghaṭa* is as follows: it is a "pot" (*ghaṭa*) which is "colored" (*uparañjita*) by a certain property (*dharma*), such as "being the space of a pot" (*ghaṭākāśatva*). That [property] and that [pot] together constitute the compound. The point is this: because the property of "being the space of a pot"—which is defined by its occurrence in the pot (i.e., *ghaṭavṛttitva*) and serves as the delimitor of the referent of the term "space of a pot"—is not present in the great space (*mahākāśa*) due to its being perceived only through the coloring of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the form of the pot, there is no co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "being the space of a pot" and "greatness. Therefore, the objection that "the space of a pot would be great" is untenable.
Why is that [property] absent from the great space?

This is because it has been stated that an adjunct (*upādhi*), by virtue of its partiality toward the reflection, does not impart its own attributes to the original object (*bimba*). "Because there is no such usage in that case" means that there is no usage of "greatness" (*mahattva*) with respect to the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*).

In this very context, the reason for the absence of co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "greatness" and "jar-space"—which was established in the preceding sentence—is the intended meaning up to this point in the previous statement. That is what must be stated.

To the question, "Why is the state of being the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśatva*) not accepted in the great space (*mahākāśa*)," he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). The meaning is: because there is no conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of the term "space within a jar" with respect to the great space.
The word "conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as the cognition that is the basis of that usage.

If the inherent part (*svābhāvikāṃśa*) were not admitted, then the absence of the jar [in the space]—which is perceived precisely at the time when the jar is not in conjunction with the space—would not be possible.

Because existence and non-existence are contradictory in one and the same place, if one were to admit a natural distinction of parts, it would be possible for both to exist through a systematic arrangement; therefore, he says: "Of conjunction... Some, however, maintain that there is no relationship between a reflected face and its original (bimba-pratibimba) between the limited space (*paricchinnākāśa*) and the great space (*mahākāśa*), according to the maxim of the face and its reflection. This is because space is formless (*nīrūpa*) and a jar is not transparent (*asvaccha*). Alternatively, if such a connection were admitted, then just as "all faces are dirty," there would be the cognition of the jar's dimensions throughout the entire space. Therefore, it must be stated that the jar merely possesses a connection with space.

And because a "natural part" (*svābhāvikāṃśa*) is required in order to avoid establishing that [conjunction] exists as a partial inherence (*aṃśavṛtti*), he says: "of conjunction" (*saṃyogasya*). They say that the sense is this: since it is not accepted that conjunction exists as a partial inherence, there is no requirement for parts. Having raised the first position, he says "because it would be an admitted consequence" (*iṣṭāpatteḥ*). However, if the conjunction with a jar were admitted, then establishing that [position] by means of this refutation would be useless.
Since its definition as being "in the state of a reflection" has already been stated,
it is inconsistent to raise an objection against it by failing to mention its nature as a reflection. Furthermore,

even on the view that accepts the existence of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and subjects it to criticism, just as the reflection itself produces the conventional usage that "the face is entirely soiled," here too, the production of the cognition of that [limited] dimension exists in the "pot-space" (*ghaṭākāśa*), whereas the factor that brings about that [cognition] in the "great space" (*mahākāśa*) simply does not exist.

One must consider how to resolve such issues as: since the reflection of luminosity is observed in a mirror situated in light, the fact of being a reflection therein does not contradict its relation to that [light], and thus the refutation of its being a reflection is useless for establishing that relation;
and how can two contradictory [propositions]—such as "even without the distinction of parts" in the phrase "its own absolute non-existence," etc.—be accepted on the strength of valid cognition?

Because it is impossible for that which apprehends an object contradictory to its own objective domain to possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he says: "It is indeed a valid means of knowledge. [The opponent] will refute this, meaning he will eliminate it. Contradiction (*virodha*) consists in not occurring in the same locus (*ekādhikaraṇāvṛttitva*);
however, that is not established, because the two do not appear as co-located (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) within a single cognition.
And thus, the meaning is that there is no contradiction between those two at all.

If it is argued that, because "that which lacks fire" and "that which possesses fire" appear in a single cognition as "this," it would follow that this perception destroys the contradiction between all absences, [the author] says: "For consciousness alone is the blessed one.
This means: uncontradicted consciousness.
Thus, it is only an uncontradicted cognition (*abādhitabuddhi*) that establishes the nature of a thing, not cognition in general.

The point is this: while in cases such as "fireless fire" or "possessing fire," one subsequently observes the sublation of one or the other part and thus no contradiction is established, here, because no sublation is observed regarding either aspect later on, there is indeed no contradiction.
This might be so.

The distinction between spaces will be established precisely because it is otherwise impossible for a jar or the like to serve as the cause for the conventional usage of "the space within a jar" and so forth.

To explain: if a jar or similar object were the cause of such usage while being either unconnected to space or connected to all of space, then all of space would result in being the "space within a jar"; therefore, it must be stated that it is only when connected to a specific part [of space] that it functions in this way.

He raises an objection: "But surely... (*nanv iti*). If a portion [of space] is considered adventitious (*aupādhika*), then because this would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in the same manner, one must admit that it is indeed intrinsic (*svābhāvika*); thus, an intrinsic difference (*svābhāvikabheda*) that accounts for that [portion] is established. Alternatively, even if one does not accept the establishment of non-difference (*abheda*) based on the aforementioned cognition, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is the cause for the conventional usage of "pot-space" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "it touches the mere sky," does it mean that it touches the entire sky, or that the sky exists in all its parts, or that the sky is delimited by all the adjuncts, or that it is the sky unconditioned by any adjunct? It cannot be the first.
Because space is one;
not the second [alternative], because it is partless.
Not the third,
because it contradicts experience.
For now, the fourth [alternative] is accepted.

And since the aforementioned fault does not apply there, he says: "No. [The meaning is: "It would have a measurement equal to that of the jar"; that is, it would have to be treated as possessing such a measurement. The sense is that an adjunct (upādhi) is the cause for the attribution of its own properties to that which it qualifies. "The great space (mahākāśa) would become the jar-space (ghaṭākāśa)" means that even though it is not delimited by the adjunct, it would have to be treated as the jar-space.
The sense is that the connection with the adjunct, which is the basis for such usage, would obtain in the great space itself.

One might object: "In cases involving the relationship between an original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), it is indeed the case that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) favors the side of the reflection;

for we observe that a mirror or similar medium imparts its own impurity specifically to the reflected face. However, in the present case, since that [reflection] is absent, it would follow that even the great space (*mahākāśa*) would receive the dimensions of a jar. Anticipating this objection, it is said: "standing in the place of a reflection. The meaning is that the nature of the limiting adjunct is such that it favors only that imagined portion [of reality] which corresponds to the reflection. For this very reason, it means that the limiting adjunct, such as a jar, imparts its own qualities only to that which is conditioned by itself.

He explains this very point with the words "uparañjitā" (colored/affected). Thus, the sense is that there is no conventional usage of the term [for that state] precisely because of the absence of the grounds for the application of that word.

[Objection: But in that case, the non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) of the conjunction of a jar or the like with space would not be possible; for that [non-pervasive occurrence], defined as "co-occurrence with its own absolute absence," must be sustained by a difference in location. To this, he says: "of conjunction... [The phrase] "by the force of valid cognition" means: by the force of the perception "here there is conjunction with a jar, here there is not," and by the force of the inference: "the conjunction of a jar and space is the counter-positive of an absence residing in all its own loci, because it is a conjunction, like the conjunction of a tree and a monkey."

It should be considered as follows: having resolved the objection by accepting the first position—that the adjunct (*upādhi*) touches the entirety of space—and then providing an explanation for that by accepting the second position—that it touches a single part of space—through the passage beginning with "its own absolute non-existence" (*svātyantābhāva*), [the author] intends the primary meaning consisting in the relation to a constituent part of space;
for it was proposed that "it touches a part of space" precisely with that primary sense in mind.
It is not possible to accept that position merely by accepting the aforementioned figurative sense.
Furthermore, since this [definition] is accepted even in the first position, it is impossible for it to constitute a separate alternative.

Now, one might object: "If this were so, there would be a contradiction with the means of knowledge that apprehends the opposition between a counter-positive and its absence in general—namely, the principle that 'whatever is the counter-positive of something is opposed to it. To this he replies: 'The very means of knowledge itself... The meaning is that it will sublate the portion concerning opposition by removing the apprehension thereof; the sense is that the universal pervasion is rendered fallacious by a specific means of knowledge.

He confirms this very point through the consensus of the elders with the words, "For consciousness alone... By the term "Bhagavatī" (the Blessed One), he expresses its worthiness of respect due to its being uncontradicted.
"Refuge" means the cause.

He raises a doubt regarding a division of space in another manner with the word "nanu" (but). The meaning is: "even though," that is, even if a division of space is not established by the aforementioned method, it is nevertheless established by the method about to be described.

To the question, "What is this manner that is about to be described?", he says: "The jar," and so forth. If that which is unrelated were the differentiator, then even saffron (*mahārajana*) that is unrelated to a cloth would result in being a differentiator; therefore, it must be stated that only that which is related can be a differentiator.

And thus, the meaning is: does the connection with the limiting adjunct (upādhi) called "jar" subsist in the entire space, or does it subsist in only one part? [The phrase] "the whole [is so]" means that since the aforementioned saffron dye is related to the entire cloth, the result is that everyone perceives the cloth as being red; this is the intended sense. [Regarding the phrase] "the establishment of an inherent part": [an objection might be raised: "Let there be no inherent part in the ether. Even if that were the case, it would not be impossible for the jar to act as a differentiator by connecting with one part of the ether. For, by admitting an adventitious part (aupādhikāṃśa), its function as a differentiator upon connecting with that part is logically consistent. If this is argued, we say: no.
Because if one accepts that parts are produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To explain:
for a part produced by a limiting adjunct is itself "produced by a limiting adjunct."

In this regard, it must be asked: does this limiting adjunct (upādhi) touch the entire space, or only a portion of it? Not the first, because it would entail the consequence that all of space is itself a limiting adjunct.
Regarding the second [alternative], one must ask whether that partiality is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*) or adventitious (*aupādhika*). It cannot be the first,
because it is not admitted.
The sense is that in the second case as well, there is a sequence of refutations based on the dilemma of whether that limiting adjunct (upādhi) is coextensive with everything or only a part of it.

Accepting the first alternative, he asks in order to refute the objection stated therein: "sarvo 'pi" (even all...). The meaning is that the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*) would have to be designated by the term "space within a jar. [The opponent replies: "Because this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). The sense is that since no spatial parts are admitted in space, the connection with the jar resides in the entirety of space. [The author replies: "Of the adjunct (*upādhi*), [the nature is] regarding the reflection... For it is the very nature of an adjunct to project its own attributes onto the reflection itself;
just as the adjunct in the form of a mirror projects its own attributes, such as dirtiness, onto the reflection which is the face.
For when a mirror is dirty, the reflection in it is also perceived as dirty;
yet even when the mirror is dirty, the face itself is perceived as clear.
Likewise, here too, the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the jar superimposes its own dimension upon the space within the jar (ghaṭākāśa), which is its reflection.
But not in the reflected image within the great space;
therefore, the point is that it does not possess a dimension equal to that of the jar.
[The term] *ādhānāt* means from attachment or association.

"In that great space" (*tatra mahākāśe*). "Precisely for this reason" (*ata eva*): the meaning is that it is precisely because the adjunct (*upādhi*) of the jar does not impart its own dimension to the great space. Now, one might ask: even if the adjunct of the jar does not impart its own dimensions to the great space, why should the conventional usage of the term "great space" not still apply? To this he says: "because [the space] possesses the quality of the jar as an imposed attribute" (*uparañjitaghaṭadharmatvasya*). That which has the quality of the jar—namely, its dimension—imposed upon it (*āhita*) is "that which is so characterized"; the state of being such is "that-ness" (*tatvam*). This is the meaning of the phrase.
In the delimited space, that is, the space within a jar;
therein, in the great space (mahākāśa),
because of the absence of the conventional usage of the term "space within a jar" (*ghaṭākāśa*).
This is the meaning:
for the linguistic usage of a term is indeed caused by, and has as its basis, the ground for the application of that term.

Just as, in the case of the space within a jar, the linguistic usage of the term "jar-space" occurs because of the presence of the property called "limited dimension," which is the ground for applying the term "jar-space."

Furthermore, there exists no property or form residing in the great ether (*mahākāśa*) that could serve as the basis for the application of the term "pot-ether" (*ghaṭākāśa*), by which the term "pot-ether" might be applied to the great ether. Having thus accepted and resolved this first position, he now accepts the second position—that the conjunction with the pot resides in a single part of the ether—and resolves it according to the Nyāya method, beginning with the words: "Of the conjunction... Indeed, the residence of the conjunction with the pot in a single part does not mean its existence in a single part [of the pot].
However, it is the state of having a common locus with the absolute non-existence of itself.
The meaning of this is as follows:
"self" (sva) refers to conjunction; the absolute non-existence that has that as its counter-positive is the absolute non-existence of conjunction.
That which has a single substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) identical with that [other thing] is described as such; the state of being so is its "nature" (*tattva*).
The fact that the word *samāna* (identical) signifies a single object is seen in the expression "the same tree" (*samānaṃ vṛkṣam*).

Now, one might ask: since a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and its absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) are contradictory in one and the same place, how can this be? To this it is replied: "by the force of valid cognition" (*pramāṇabalāt*).

The meaning is: "on the strength of the evidence consisting of such cognitions as 'here there is conjunction with the space within the jar,' or 'here at the root there is no conjunction with the monkey, nor at the tip,'" and so forth.
The intention is that there is no possibility of contradiction with what is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
In this regard, he states the agreement with the logic of the Naiyāyikas: "For consciousness alone... [and] "for us" (*naḥ* = *asmākam*).
Upon the admission of the existence of objects— that is, upon accepting the reality of entities—
consciousness alone, which is to say cognition alone, is the venerable one, the worshipful one.
"Refuge" means a protector;
"it is the authority" (pramāṇa) is the meaning according to the logical principle.
Thus, it is established that since there is no evidence for a division in space, a jar cannot be the manifester of a division in space.

If it is argued that the difference already exists but is merely not manifested by the jar and so forth, then one must say that it is produced; yet that is incorrect, because difference is innate and not adventitious. If this is said, then, in order to avoid these two faults, let it be that the limiting adjunct (the jar and so forth) causes the non-existent difference to appear.
If this were so, we would have achieved our purpose;
moreover, the scriptures—such as "There is no diversity here"—teach non-difference.
Therefore, Viṣṇu is not different from the universe by his very nature. This is the summary of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Thus, it has been stated that when a limiting adjunct (upādhi) such as a jar exists in space, its capacity to manifest [the inherent difference] is logically established.

To this, an objection is raised with the words “nanu” (but surely). Here, the word “yadi” (if) must be supplied, because of the presence of the word “tarhi” (then). The phrase “it must be said that it is produced” implies that no other effect is observed to arise from a limiting adjunct apart from manifestation and production. The term “autpattikatvena” (by way of being innate) means by way of having the same ontological status as the substratum (dharmisamasattākatvena);
that is, because it is not adventitious and does not come into existence in the interim.

The sense is that, since one must somehow avoid the aforementioned defect by relying solely on the position of manifestation (*abhivyakti*), the author resolves the doubt by resorting to a third position, because the defects stated for both [the previous] positions are unavoidable. He says: "Then... [and] "Regarding the two defects":
under the position of manifestation, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving difference even when the mirror and other such [reflective surfaces] are sometimes absent.

The meaning is that there are two faults: [first,] the consequence that difference would not be adventitious on the view that it arises; and [second,] the consequence that its non-existence would be undermined.

One cannot say, "Let it be exactly so," with this intention he says: "If it were thus" (*evaṃ cet*). The point is that if one accepts the appearance of a difference that does not actually exist, then—just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—it is established as being merely false; thus our aforementioned inference becomes entirely faultless, since the probandum is not lacking in the example.

Having thus established the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as well as among the individual souls themselves, by means of the first two inferences; and having, for the sake of stabilizing that [non-difference], declared the falsity of mere difference by means of the third; and having stated the absence of mutual difference even among insentient things by means of the fourth; he now cites the Śruti scriptures as authority for that very point: "And the Śrutis... The meaning is that within this aggregate of sentient and insentient beings, there is not the slightest thing that is diverse or distinct. Thus, they are "those which teach non-difference."

The meaning is that [these texts] teach the absence of any ultimate difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as well as among individual souls and insentient objects (jaḍa).
He concludes with the words "therefore" (tasmāt): the meaning is that there is no evidence for difference, whereas there is such evidence for non-difference.
[An objection: Even so, in both the thesis (pakṣa) and the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta), it follows that difference is merely adventitious (aupādhika).
Intending to state that "it is not false" by way of resolving this doubt, he says, beginning with "nanu" (but surely), etc. Regarding the phrase "doṣadvaya" (two faults):
if [the cognition] were manifested by an adventitious adjunct (*upādhi*), there would be the impossibility of its being necessarily bound to follow that adjunct;
if it were produced from it, there would be the loss of its innate nature—this is the meaning of "two faults. Regarding the phrase "pratibhāsayati" (it causes to appear):

The sense is that [the world] is false because it is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. Regarding the phrase "their purpose is fulfilled": the meaning is that we need not exert ourselves to prove its falsity.
It is accepted that the connection between the adjunct (*upādhi*) and the pot exists as a non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛtti*) in space;
however, it is not an occurrence in a single part (*ekadeśavṛttitva*), which would imply a real internal division within space itself.
Rather, [the definition is] "having a common locus with its own absolute non-existence.
Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction between a counter-positive and its absence in a single locus without a difference in their delimiters (*avacchedaka*);
for the meaning is that the cognition of the Blessed Lady herself serves as the dispeller of such contradiction.

"By being innate" means by virtue of being eternal; "by pervading the substratum throughout time. Regarding the phrase "and the scriptural texts": the sense is that since there is an abundance of evidence for non-difference, one should not suspect that the absence of evidence for non-difference constitutes evidence for difference. Regarding "by being innate": the meaning is by virtue of being natural (*svābhāvikatvena*). Regarding "because it is not adventitious": the meaning is because it is unproduced (*ajanyatvāt*).

The sense is that its definition is being an eternal absence (*nityābhāvatva*) while being non-different from absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Regarding "the two defects": [this refers to the defects of mutual dependence and infinite regress].

The meaning is that there are two defects: first, the defect of the impossibility of prior existence because it is perceived only as having limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); and second, the defect of [impossible] origination because of its eternality.

To the question, "What follows when the means of knowledge are non-existent in the case under discussion? he says: "And thus" (*evañca*). The sense is that since all distinctions would possess our intended falsity—defined as being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a threefold negation while being perceived—it is already established that which we intend.

One should not suspect that dry arguments are unproving; thus he says: "And the Śrutis... By the first word, passages such as "where there is, as it were, duality" and "the knowledge that produces differentiation" are included.
He concludes the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) with: "Therefore... Thus ends the explanation of the prima facie argument.

[The opponent] objects that since the view of difference being merely adventitious (aupādhika) is untenable, its inherent nature (svābhāvikatva) must be established: "Now, if... [This is answered] by the established conclusion (siddhānta) that because [difference] is innate, it persists as long as its substratum is perceived.

The meaning is that because it is not adventitious (*anāgantuka*), it is impossible for it to be produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). He says, "Then," [meaning]: if, due to the aforementioned logical inconsistency, the view that difference is adventitious is not established, then for that very reason, its being natural (*svābhāvika*) is also not established; thus, its falsity (*mithyātva*) alone is established. "Regarding the avoidance of two defects": the meaning is that this is for the purpose of avoiding the two defects consisting of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and a contradiction with one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says, "If it is so. This means: if the difference in space (*ākāśabheda*) is false, then...
The meaning is that [the arguments] have achieved their purpose and established their own position;

for, since there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) or other defects in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of the previously stated inference, it is possible for it to prove the probandum in the form of being devoid of internal differentiation.

Having thus established non-difference through perception and inference, he also cites scripture (*āgama*)—namely, "But the Śrutis... Since it was previously stated that Śrutis such as "There is no diversity whatsoever here" and "One only, without a second" are intent upon negation, and because they are therefore more authoritative, their sublation of the Śrutis concerning difference will be established; it is with this intention that this was not demonstrated [separately] earlier.

He concludes the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that, according to the reasoning stated, there is an absence of both a probans (*sādhaka*) and an absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*) for the opponent's position, whereas for our own position, these two are present.
By the phrase "the summary of the prima facie position," the existence of further arguments to be refuted is indicated.

We shall elaborate upon those later on, in the form of [showing] how the non-dualistic scriptures (*advaita-śruti*) possess the sixfold marks of intention (*tātparya-liṅga*), such as the introductory context (*upakrama*) and so forth. This concludes the section on the prima facie position.

Now, by stating the refutation regarding the opposing view, he raises the objection that a jar manifests the distinction of space—beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*). After the word "then" (*tarhi*), the phrase "by means of jars and so forth" (*ghaṭādibhiḥ*) is understood to follow.
The sense is that there is no other possible mode [of manifestation].
The term "intrinsic" (*autpattikatvena*) means being natural (*svābhāvikatvena*).

"Because it is not adventitious, and because there is no attainment [of difference] in the interim. Regarding "the two faults": the first fault stated by me is the contingency that difference would sometimes be perceived even in the absence of [manifesting conditions] such as a jar; the second fault stated by you is the impossibility of its arising if it were not manifested. Such is the meaning of "the two faults.
The first fault is avoided because difference is not admitted prior to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as a jar.
The sense is that the second fault does not apply because the arising of jars and so forth is not admitted.

It is not merely that by accepting this [position] one avoids two faults; rather, what follows? To this he says: "If it were so... (evam cet). The sense is as follows: if one accepts that [consciousness] manifests a difference that does not exist, then difference is established as being false (mithyā), and thus we, who are proponents of non-difference (abheda-vādinaḥ), have achieved our purpose.
This is because, since difference lacks ultimate reality, there is no deficiency in the probandum (sādhyavaikalya) regarding the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta).

Having thus described perception and inference regarding non-difference, he speaks of scripture as well: "The Śrutis. He concludes: "Therefore. The meaning is that there is an absence of evidence for difference and the existence of such evidence for non-difference. Here is the rebuttal: first, as for what was said—that perception is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—to that we reply: the difference whose locus is the Lord and whose counter-correlate is the individual soul is perceived by the Lord.

Regarding that [Lord], the existence of such a direct perception is established by His own word: "But the Supreme Person is another. Since the Lord possesses the capacity to directly perceive the individual soul (*jīva*), there is no room for objection. However, the distinction having the Lord as its counter-correlative and the individual soul as its locus (or the difference residing in the individual soul) is directly perceived by the individual soul.
In the perception of an object that possesses a counter-correlate (*sapratiyogika*), the perception of that counter-correlate is not the necessary condition (*tantra*).

This is because there are instances of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), such as: "This cow is similar to a gavaya," "That cloth does not exist here" (or "There is no jar here"), and "The pillar is not a *piśāca*.

By this, the following view is refuted: that the fitness for the perception of absence (specifically the fitness for the perception of mutual absence) is dependent upon the fitness for the perception of the counter-correlate; for if that were so, how could there be perceptual fitness for a mutual absence whose counter-correlate is the Lord (*Īśvara*), who is himself beyond the reach of perception?

Because there is deviation [of the reason] in cases such as "the pillar is not a piśāca" (based on the experience that "the pillar is not a piśāca"), and because that [cognition] has mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as its object (since that [pillar] has mutual non-existence as its object).

In this way, it should be inferred that the difference having Yajñadatta as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and Viṣṇumitra as the locus (*dharmin*) belongs to Viṣṇumitra, and the difference having Viṣṇumitra as the counter-correlative and Devadatta as the locus belongs to Devadatta; all such cases are to be understood accordingly.

Thus, he begins to refute the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) that has been established [with the words]: "In this regard, this... The meaning is that what is about to be stated should be understood as a rebuttal consisting of the removal of objections regarding the means of knowledge for difference, and a rebuttal consisting of objections regarding the means of knowledge for non-difference.

Regarding that, the phrase "we say" means that we state the reply to the objection raised there—namely, that a difference whose locus is God (*īśvara*) or whose counter-correlate is God is imperceptible because God is not perceptible. [The response is: "It is perceptible to God. The sense is this: although such a perception by God is imperceptible to us, it is nonetheless perceptible to Him.
[Objection: But from what source is the existence of such a perception for God known?

Because another's consciousness is not perceptible [to oneself], he says: "Of that" (*tasya*). The subsequent statement, "Since I am beyond the perishable," should also be cited here. By this, the perception of the Lord as distinct from the individual soul (*jīva*) is established. Now, one might object: even if the Lord possesses the perception of himself as the subject (*dharmin*), how can there be a perception of difference characterized by himself as the subject and having the individual soul as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), given the absence of a perception of the individual soul as the counter-correlate? To this he says: "Of the Lord. The implication is that otherwise, his omniscience would not be established.

Although, according to the method to be explained later, in the perception of difference (*bhedapratyakṣa*), the perception of the locus alone (*dharmimātrapratyakṣa*) is the requisite factor and not the perception of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogipratyakṣa*) as well, nevertheless, this statement is made by accepting the position [of the opponent] for the sake of argument, following the maxim "let him be satisfied" (*tuṣyatviti nyāya*). "In the locus that is the individual soul" (*jīvadharmika*): the word "difference" (*bheda*) is understood to carry over. "Of the individual soul" (*jīvasya*): the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is understood to carry over. Now, one might object: since there is no perception of the Lord (*īśvara*) by the individual soul, how can the difference having that [Lord] as its counter-correlate and the soul itself as its locus be perceived? To this he says: "along with its counter-correlate" (*sapratiyogika*). The intended meaning is as follows:
In the world, there are many categories of objects that possess counter-correlates (*sapratiyogika*), such as similarity, conjunction, and so forth.
Among these, while the perception of conjunction necessarily requires the perception of its counter-correlate, such necessity does not exist for the perception of similarity and the like. To explain:
First, the perception of similarity arises in the form: "This cow is similar to a gavaya.

In that case, there is no perception of the counter-correlative (the gavaya), because the gavaya previously seen in the forest is at that time remote and thus serves only as an object of memory, lacking direct perceptual presence.

Thus, in this case, the direct perception of the absence of a jar arises in the form "there is no jar here," yet there is no direct perception of the jar, which is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), therein. Similarly, in the case of "the pillar is not a *piśāca*," the difference characterized by the counter-positive *piśāca* is perceived in the pillar.
Furthermore, there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a *piśāca* therein;
rather, it occurs solely through indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) regarding that object.

Therefore, because such deviation is observed, the direct perception of God is not a necessary condition for the direct perception of a difference whose counter-correlate is God, but rather mere knowledge of Him is sufficient.
That [omniscience] is established by such scriptural authority as "He who is omniscient," and so forth.
However, in some places here the reading is "na sa paṭaḥ" (not that cloth).
For this very reason, they say that the use of the word "sa" (that) is employed to indicate the non-perceptibility of the cloth.
They also say that in the case of "similar to a gavaya," it should be understood as "similar to that gavaya.

Although here, the demonstration of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) would have been more appropriate in a single instance such as "the pillar is not a *piśāca*," because the perception of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is required as a necessary condition for every perception of difference.
This is because, in cases other than those involving similarity and the like, the perception of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is not suspected to be a necessary factor.
Nevertheless, it should be understood that its mention is intended either for the sake of instructing the student or as an illustrative example.
Now, one might object: we do not claim that the perception of the counter-positive is the sole requisite for the perception of absence (*abhāva*).
By this, there would be no deviation (vyabhicāra) in cases such as "there is no jar here";
rather, [the condition is] merely the perceptibility of the counter-positive (pratiyogin).
And in cases such as "there is no jar here," just as the jar lacks perceptibility at that time, its perceptibility (pratyakṣayogyatā) likewise does not exist.

Furthermore, if one accepts that in the present case difference—consisting of mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) having God as its counter-correlative (pratiyogin)—is perceptible, then it must be accepted that the counter-correlative, namely God, is perceptible;
yet that is not the case.

Therefore, he dispels the doubt—namely, how the perception of a difference whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is God, who is unfit for perception, could possibly occur—by means of an extended application (*atideśa*), stating: "By this [it is refuted]... because it depends on the perceptibility of the counter-correlate. This means: because it is dependent upon the perceptibility of the counter-correlate. "In God, who is unfit" means: in God, who is unfit for perception. "How is there perceptibility? means: how is there perceptibility for perception?

He clarifies what was already stated by the word "by this": "A pillar is not a ghost. The sense is that a ghost does not possess the fitness for perception (pratyakṣayogyatā) in the same way that a jar or similar object does.

Now, one might raise the following weak objection: "This experience does not have non-existence as its object, but rather has as its object a difference (bheda) whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is the ghost;
therefore, how can this serve as an example here? He dispels this doubt with the words: "mutual non-existence" (anyonyābhāva). For it is mutual non-existence itself that is called "difference."
Therefore, the point is: how could this experience not have non-existence as its object?

Having thus established that both types of difference—the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—are proven by perception, he now states that the mutual difference between individual souls must also be considered proven by perception: "In this way" (*evam*). The sense is that once the presence of a self in another's body has been established by the sign of [observed] activity, there exists the experience "I am not Devadatta" in Viṣṇumitra, who possesses activity contrary to that [of Devadatta].

He establishes the conclusion: "In this regard" (*atre*). His word is authoritative because, in the *Īśvarāvatāra*, Kṛṣṇa—having declared his own superiority by saying, "But the Supreme Person is another," and having stated, "Since I am beyond the perishable"—has shown that his own distinction from others is directly perceived by himself; this is the sense. Nor should it be argued: "Could there not be a difference for him as well, whether heard or inferred? For the powerful causal complex for direct perception, such as the direct perception of the substratum (*dharmin*), obstructs inference and other means of knowledge.

In reality, however, those who know the truth maintain that the Lord possesses only non-perceptual knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). "Nor is there an objection" means: what objection could there be as to how it can be perceptual, given the absence of perception of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)?

Although he will state immediately below that the perception of the counter-correlate is not an essential factor, this [present statement] is nonetheless a concessionary argument (*aṅgīkāravāda*), and thus there is no fault.
Furthermore, difference is even directly perceived by yogis, according to the scriptural statement: "When he sees the other, the Lord, and His majesty.

Although the perception of the Lord and so forth can be established as proof for difference in general, this specific statement is nevertheless made to demonstrate that such difference is not perceptible to those like us. The phrase "of the individual soul" (jīvasya) means "of each respective individual soul."

The meaning is that this is because of such experiences as "I am not the Lord" or "I am not free from suffering. To the question, "How [can there be a perception of similarity] when, like the Lord, the individual soul lacks the direct perception of a counter-correlate (pratiyogin)? he says: "Having a counter-correlate... [He gives the example: "As in the case of a *gavaya*... The point is that at that time, the [counter-correlate, the cow], is not directly perceived. Even if the existence of similarity having the *gavaya* as its counter-correlate is established because it is a positive entity (*bhāva*), it is not established for a negative entity (*abhāva*); therefore, he says: "In this case... Now, one might object: "But this rule applies only to mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)."
Furthermore, even though a gavaya and the like are not perceived at that time, it is their very *yogyatā* (perceptibility) that is the determining factor.

But in the case of God (*īśvara*), even that does not exist; therefore, he says: "a pillar" (*stambha*). [Objection: If this were so, then even though the conjunction of air and space is imperceptible, the conjunction of air and a jar would be perceptible, because that [conjunction], as defined by air and having the jar as its locus, has a locus that is perceptible.
If it is argued that in our view the subjecthood (*dharmitva*) of both is not admitted,
on account of the statement, "All entities are indeed distinct and possess distinct properties," we reply:
True.
For conjunction, although it has one thing as its counter-positive and another as its locus, its existence depends upon the existence of both things;
for when either one is destroyed, the conjunction is destroyed.
Similarity and the like are not thus.
For there is the cognition: "The cow is similar to the gayal, even though the gayal is lost.
However, [the existence of] conjunction depends solely upon the existence of its locus (*dharmin*).

And thus, since the existence of conjunction depends upon the existence of both its locus and its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the perception of that [conjunction] is also dependent upon the perception of those two.

The perception of similarity and so forth is dependent upon the perception of the locus (*dharmin*) alone; therefore, that [example] does not constitute a valid counter-argument (*prati-bandī*). By the phrase "by this" is meant: because there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of *piśācas*. Regarding the phrase "of the fitness for the perception of absence": the sense is that difference consists in the nature of mutual non-existence.
By this, the following doubt is refuted. To explain:

Difference (*bheda*) is not, first of all, separateness, division, plurality, or distinctness; for these are positive entities (*bhāva*), whereas difference is cognizable through negative cognition (*niṣedhadhī*) such as "the pot is not the cloth" and so forth. Nor is it mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), nor is it an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is delimited by identity (*tādātmya*), nor is it an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by relation (*saṃsarga*).
Not the first [alternative],
because it would result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of such identity;

and furthermore, in the cognition "the jar is not a cloth," there is a contradiction with the understanding of the cloth as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), since it is precisely the cloth that functions as the object of negation.
By the same logic, even in the case of a relational absence (saṃsargābhāva), it would follow that the relation itself is the counter-positive (pratiyogin). Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for it would result in over-extension (ativyāpti) to an absolute absence (atyantābhāva) which is understood as being non-existent in the form of that [relation].

Furthermore, in the case of "the cloth does not exist," there is no mention of identity (*tādātmya*) other than the cloth and the property of being a cloth within the body of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*).
This is because only that which is mentioned as residing in the counter-positive can serve as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of counter-positiveness.
Moreover, since the identity with a jar does not reside in the cloth, it cannot logically function as such a delimiting condition.

Furthermore, by parity of reasoning, even in the case of a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), it would follow that the relation itself is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), which would result in the undesirable consequence that "pot-ness" and so forth could not serve as delimiting factors.
Nor is the third [alternative] tenable; for there is no pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) as understood in the cognition: "A pot is related, but a cloth is not."

By the logic already stated, even in the case of non-occurrence (saṃsargābhāva), there is over-extension (ativyāpti) because the relation itself cannot be its own delimiting factor (anavacchedaka). Nor is there any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for it;
for the cognition "the jar is not other" is supported by parsimony (lāghava) and by the maxim that "when a qualification is present, [the cognition refers to the qualified]."

The purpose [of the definition] is fulfilled by the absolute absence of "cloth-ness" (paṭatva) in a jar; thus, it is undesirable for those who maintain that a property's co-existence with its own absolute absence—that even that which is devoid of difference from [the jar] should be the locus of the absolute absence of properties residing therein.
Furthermore, regarding the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) of cloth, the counter-positive (pratiyogin) must be either the cloth, cloth-ness, or identity (tādātmya). It cannot be the first.
Because there is no contradiction with its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the cloth;
for "contradictoriness" (*virodhitva*) itself is the meaning of the word "counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*).
If being a counter-correlate were based on any mere relation whatsoever, then even the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth would result in being such [a counter-correlate].
The second and third [alternatives] are not [tenable],

because the fault already stated— that the cloth itself would be perceived as the object of negation— cannot be avoided. Here, it is evident that difference is indeed mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Reality (tattva) is the state of being the absence of a relation that serves as the superimposed identity. And the absence of relation is that which has a relation as its superimposed object.

In the case of the expression "it does not exist through identity," although identity functions as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka), it does not possess the status of the superimposed relation; rather, it is only the [other] relation that constitutes the superimposed relation.
In this way, the opposite should also be inferred for the case where "it is not mixed.

Identity (*tādātmya*) is neither the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) nor the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) therein; furthermore, there is a distinction between relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) due to the difference in the relationship of the superimposed object.
Mutual non-existence is opposed only by the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity, not by the counter-correlative itself.

And since counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) consists in being the locus of a property that does not coexist with mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Alternatively, difference is simply that mutual non-existence wherein the counter-positive does not exist by way of the relation of identity (*tādātmya*) as the superimposed [object]; thus, there is indeed a contradiction with the counter-positive. Or else, identity is a property of the cloth and so forth, sharing the same status as a relation (*saṃsarga*).

And the representation of that [negation] occurs in the case of "the jar is not the cloth" through the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words; for, by virtue of linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*), even though it is an absence of relation (*saṃsargābhāva*), and even though the relation does not appear as a relation, it appears merely by way of the mode of relation (*saṃsargamaryādayā*). Thus, here too, although there is no appearance as identity (*tādātmya*), it is logically established as the relation of the superposed object (*āropya-sambandha*).
Nor is there a lack of evidence for this.

It should be understood that for one who is being taught "there is no cloth-ness in the jar," the superimposition consists in the relation of cloth-ness as delimited by the universal *paṭatvatva*; whereas for one who is being taught "the jar is not a cloth," the superimposition consists in the identity with cloth as delimited by the universal *paṭatva*. Thus, there is no difference between these three types of superimpositions—each having the delimiter of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) as its object—since the purpose is served by that very [superimposition]. Furthermore, it is accepted that the absence of a cloth differs from the absence of a jar by virtue of each individual [delimiting property]; otherwise, the absence of a jar delimited by fluidity would not differ from the absence [of a jar] delimited by jar-ness. Enough of this.
Regarding this, the following objection has been raised by the modern [opponent] against the perception of difference:
"The mind is not a means of valid cognition for us, as it is known through non-apprehension of the unperceivable;
this difference, residing in adventitious conditions (upādhi), does not fall within the range of direct perception."

"Because it functions as a concomitant to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because its object also lacks existence, and because it is the substratum for error and the like, the mind (*manas*) is not a means of valid cognition for us," and so forth.
This is the summary of that [position].
"It is not the case that the mind does not perceive the difference from God even when [the world] is not real;
nor is it the case that even if such were so, that difference does not reside in pure consciousness.
This is trivial.
If the mind were not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), it would follow that the self (*ātman*) and other categories could not be established.

If it is held that the mind is known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedya*), then its distinction [from the self] must likewise be so known; what then is the use of this elaborate refutation of the mind’s status as a means of valid knowledge?
Furthermore, why should it be invalid? If you argue that it is like time (*kāla*), being merely an auxiliary to the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-sahakārin*), we say no.

Because there is deviation [from the rule] in the case of a sentence acting as a cooperative factor for a presented perception, and in the case of inferential marks such as the commencement [of an action], which act as cooperative factors for bringing about [an object]; therefore, it must be stated that [the cause] is "that which acts as a cooperative factor for whatever constitutes a means of valid knowledge. This is because the witness (sākṣin) is not established as being otherwise with respect to itself.
