Nor should it be argued that [the reason] holds because of its dependence on the cooperation of external means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for this would result in a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of your own witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).
Furthermore, this reason is unestablished (*aprasiddha*).
Furthermore, "not being a sense organ" (*anindriyatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

As for the argument that, because the mind is a cause of cognition in some instances, parsimony (*lāghava*) would lead to its being the cause of the cognition of color and so forth, and that consequently the eyes and other organs would become mere auxiliary factors— just like light— and thus their status as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would not obtain—
that is not correct.

Since the excellence (*atiśaya*)—defined as possessing a genus that delimits the causal capacity (*kāraṇatā*) relative to an effect delimited by some property (*dharma*) pervaded by perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*)—resides only in the eye and other [senses], it is appropriate that these alone possess the status of being the cause.
Furthermore, since light and so forth are not causes with respect to visual cognition, such an excellence is impossible for them.

If one were to insist on the mere conventional usage of "causality" even in the absence of the aforementioned excellence, that would result in nothing but verbal quarreling; therefore, it should be disregarded.

And as for what was stated: "Because conjunction and the other [means of contact] are impossible, and because nothing else is established, this [cognition] is merely a designation of difference based on proximity"; by such statements, it was shown that there is no proximity between the mind and the two distinct [objects].
This is not superior;
for since both are of the nature of the Self, their identity itself constitutes the sense-contact through the very apprehension of difference by the witness-consciousness.
Furthermore, as it has been stated, identity does not require a further relation of proximity (*pratyāsatti*).
Let there be no relation of identity (*tādātmya*) as the means of contact.

Let that very same relation—such as "qualifier-ness" (*viśeṣaṇatā*) and so forth—which exists when the witness (*sākṣin*) perceives the absence of pleasure in the self, serve also for the perception of difference in the form of the absence of identity.
Or, let the perception of difference there be by the mind alone, with the relation of contact-qualifier-ness (*saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇatā*) and so forth serving as the means of contact.
As for what was stated— that there is no evidence for the fact that qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*) and so forth constitute a means of proximity (*pratyāsatti*)—

that is not correct, because their status as such is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other relations when perceiving a jar or similar objects.
And as for what was here prattled on:
It is argued that perception cannot apprehend the mutual absence of God because it lacks the auxiliary condition of the non-perception of a perceptible object (*yogyānupalabdhi*).

This is unsound; for if the non-perception of a perceptible object were the cause [of negative cognition], there would follow the impossibility of any valid cognition of a general absence regarding objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).

Because atoms and the like are not perceived due to the absence of their being perceptible, mere non-perception is the reason [for their non-existence]. There is no over-extension [of the argument], because even when the counter-positive is not perceived, the cognition that the locus possesses the capacity to serve as the substratum for that counter-positive acts as an obstacle.

Even if that were the case for the apprehension of an absolute absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), there is no fault, because even in the apprehension of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), non-apprehension alone is the cause.

If it is argued that otherwise the inference "the pillar is not a *piśāca*" would not occur—[we reply] no; for in the case of a perceptible subject (*dharmin*), even if the object exists as a real entity through a relation consisting of a superimposed connection, it may not be perceived due to unfitness (*ayogyatā*). In a certain case where the relation is a superimposition of identity (*tādātmya*), since the subject is not perceived as being of that nature, the qualification of "fitness" (*yogyatā*) here is redundant.
For in the perception of a jar or similar object, one observes that its own self (the substrate) is not perceived in turn.

Nor should it be argued that even when the mountain is perceived, the non-perception of its substrate—the fire-possessor—is observed due to its lack of perceptibility; for we do not admit an absolute difference between the mountain and the fire, as we do not admit between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).
Nor should it be argued that the apprehension of Kṛṣṇa is seen upon the apprehension of Rāma.
Neither the sense organs nor inference [are sufficient],
because it is determined that only those belonging to the white faction possess the proficiency for perceiving Īśvara,
due to the presence of a specific obstacle to the perception of the identity of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
However, in the case of the perception produced by Jāmbuvant, there is no obstruction of that [perception] due to the presence of an auxiliary factor (*uttejaka*).

Nor, for the opponent who maintains the doctrine of unqualified consciousness (*nirviśeṣita-caitanya*), can non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) alone be the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) because of its parsimony (*lāghava*).

For in the case of a mere absence of relation (*saṃsargābhāva*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, "fitness" (*yogyatā*) must be included. Or, let it be that fitness is indeed included.
In this context, the meaning is "the non-apprehension of that which is capable [of being perceived].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the absence of earthness in an atom being perceptible.
Nor should it be argued that the fitness of the locus (*adhikaraṇa-yogyatā*) is also a cause [for perception].
Out of respect [for the opponent's view]:

Is "fitness for non-apprehension" (anupalabdhi-yogyatva) the state of being simultaneous with the entire collection of conditions for apprehension, excluding the contact with one's own counter-positive?
And is "fitness for apprehension" (upalambha-yogyatva) the state of having an apprehension entailed by the presence of the counter-positive, even when that presence has not been considered?

In this context, if the individual soul (*jīva*) were indeed the Lord (*īśvara*), then the mind, which grasps the soul, would grasp it precisely as the Lord; thus, the apprehension would be simultaneous with the mind that possesses the capacity for such apprehension.
Alternatively, the fitness for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-yogyatva*) consists in being opposed to the existence of a counter-positive (*pratiyogi*).

Opposition (*virodhitva*) is the state of being the counter-positive of an absence that can be logically entailed (*āpādanīya*), such that if the counter-positive were present, the [non-apprehension] itself could not exist.
As for what was said— that how can the existence of a non-existent counter-positive function as a reductio (*āpādaka*)— that is weak,
because such a status applies even in the case of a mere *tarka*.

As for what was said— that the capacity to bring about [an effect] belongs to the non-existent by virtue of the object's own greatness and not by virtue of the greatness of the knowledge of its pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth— the first [alternative] is not tenable,
because the non-existent is devoid of even the slightest power (*śakti*).

"In the second case, the counter-positive is not perceived there; thus, because non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is invariably preceded by the knowledge of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), it indicates absence solely as an inference, and therefore there is no perception of difference therein. But that is merely a source of intimidation. For even if one accepts pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth in order to establish the definition of "fitness" (*yogyatā*), such factors are not required for non-apprehension to produce the cognition of absence.
This is because there is a dispute regarding whether non-apprehension functions as an instrument of knowledge (*jñānakaraṇa*).
This has been stated by way of concession;
however, in reality, when non-existence is apprehended through perception, no function for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is observed.
Nor should it be argued that the cognition of non-existence would arise even while the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and its apprehension are present.
Because the object itself does not exist.
Nor should it be argued that, according to your own view, since the object is not a cause [of cognition], what need is there for it;
for, due to the absence of the object, the causal complex consisting of the sense-faculty's contact [with the object] is obstructed.

Nor should it be argued that in a place devoid of a counter-positive, there would be a cognition of absence during the state of non-perception of the counter-positive, because the perception of the [counter-positive] acts as an inhibitor.
Nor should it be argued that this implies non-apprehension functions as a cause by virtue of being an "absence of an inhibitor.
For in my view, the absence of an inhibitor is not accepted as a cause.
Because the very meaning of the term "causality" (*kāraṇatva*) is the restriction of [the cause's] existence to a time prior [to the effect].
If it is asked, "How can that [restriction] be causality?", we say no;
for its meaning is precisely the specific capacity (*śakti*) to produce an effect.
Otherwise, it would follow that even the color of a thread and so forth would possess that status [of being a substance].
Nor should it be argued that this [color] is established otherwise;
for it can be said that this [thread] also is established in that same way.

Now, one might ask: among the three types of extraneous determination (*anyathāsiddhi*), which applies here? [The first is: that which is extraneously determined by something with which it is grasped as having a prior existence toward a certain effect; [the second is:
that whose prior existence toward a certain effect is understood only when its prior existence toward another thing is already known;

[the third is: that which is extraneously determined because the effect can be accounted for by something else that has a fixed prior existence elsewhere, while this [third factor] merely co-exists with it. We reply: it is precisely this [third type].

Fire accompanied by the absence of a jewel is the antecedent condition for burning, because the antecedence of the absence of the jewel and so forth is apprehended only together with the fire and so forth;
for there is no experience of a separate apprehension such as "the absence of the jewel is the cause of burning.

Furthermore, in the case at hand, since the apprehension of the absence is established by the very same sense-object contact and other means already postulated for the apprehension of the positive entity (bhāva), it is appropriate that non-apprehension (anupalabdhi), which coexists with them, constitutes a third type of extraneous condition (anyathāsiddha).

Otherwise, even in that case, non-apprehension of absence would have to be considered a cause. Furthermore, since the mere procedure lacks a foundation and the aforementioned "establishment by another means" (anyathāsiddhi) is inapplicable, one should instead postulate a fourth type of "establishment by another means": when a thing which serves as the causal condition for the absence of an effect is apprehended as being antecedent to something else by virtue of its being the counter-correlative of an absence, it is established by another means through that [absence].

Is the absence of an obstructer merely the removal of a covering over the causal power residing in the cause? In that case, since the removal of the covering—which is the actual factor for the existence of the effect—is possible through the mere cessation of the obstacle (the karma) by its own nature, it would be cumbersome to grant causal status even to the absence of the obstructer.
Furthermore, it is otherwise established as being merely an "activator" (*uttejaka*) of the causal power residing in the cause.

Therefore, since non-apprehension of the fit (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is not a cause, it has been stated that in the present case, even in the absence of that [non-apprehension], the perception of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is established due to the absence of an obstructer in the form of the apprehension of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
As for what was stated— that even if a person is apprehended, because of the absence of auxiliary factors, only the oneness of Brahminhood itself is established— that is inconsistent;
for it is proven that difference exists precisely because the apprehension of oneness is untenable.
However, it is stated that "I am not God" is known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For one who maintains the identity of the perceived individual soul (*jīva*) with the pure essence (*tanmātra*), even that analogy is inappropriate.
By this, the argument that there is no perception [of the Self] because its oneness is the subject matter of the Upaniṣads or because it is unknown, is refuted.
As for what was said— that because the cognition "I" arises through limiting adjuncts (upādhi), this difference does not reside in the undivided, pure Self—
that is not so;
for it is precisely the state of being a locus for the insentient and the Lord that constitutes the very nature of the individual soul (jīva).
Surely, in this case, it is precisely the aforementioned experience that constitutes the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Nor should it be asked how this can be the nature of the unlimited Brahman-Ātman,
for even now that state remains unestablished.
Furthermore, that which has been prattled—that "I am not the Lord" is a cognition of egoism—is utterly feeble;
for it would entail the dissolution of such [Vedic] declarations as "I am Brahman.
Moreover, unlike the statement "I am not the Lord," there is an absence of the mention of "I" in such cases as "one remains as the Lord."

Since the usage of the word "I" (aham) is established in such expressions as "the speaker [is] 'I'," and since it is well-known that the meaning of the word "I" is non-different from the meaning of the pronoun "we" (asmad), enough with this weak [objection regarding] injury. Regarding the phrase "in this way": the ellipsis is to be supplied as "at the time when Devadatta, through yoga, perceives another living being.
In this manner, one may infer: "Devadatta am I; Yajñadatta am not; I am not an insentient jar; I am not the Lord," and so forth.

Therefore, since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for difference, even though difference as a property of God (*īśvara*) is not an object of our perception, it might still be an object of His perception; to this he says: "as a property of God" (*īśvaradharmika*). [He adds] "of God" (*īśvarasya*). This is said by way of a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*).

In reality, however, since in produced worldly perception the fitness (*yogyatā*) of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and so forth is the determining factor, and divine perception is not of such a nature, there is no dependence on that here.

Even if dependence [on perception] were required, there is no room for objection because, as will be explained later, we observe the perceptual apprehension of the mutual absence of a *piśāca* in a pillar; thus, it is precisely the non-apprehension of the counter-positive—where the existence of that counter-positive has been hypothetically introduced by reasoning—that is required. And since such non-apprehension can occur even due to the non-perception of the living self (*jīva*), the objection finds no footing. The word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is to be supplied with "of the living self."

Now, one might object: "Since God is not an object of perception, how can difference having Him as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) be perceived? Anticipating this, the author sets forth a dilemma in his mind—whether the perceptibility of the counter-correlative is a cause for the perception of any object having that counter-correlative, or for the perception of absence (*abhāva*) in general, or specifically for the perception of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*)—and states the following instances of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in succession, beginning with the words "sapratyogika" (having a counter-correlative). This is merely illustrative;
in reality, both of the two alternatives should be understood.

The word "that" (*sa*) is used for the purpose of indicating the perceptibility of the cloth. Regarding "that": it is said, "The form of *idam* refers to what is perceived and situated nearby; the form of *etad* likewise; but one should know that *adas* refers to what is remote, and *tad* to what is beyond the senses. Similarly, in the case of "one who resembles a gavaya," it should be understood as "one who resembles that gavaya."

One might object: "Is it not the case that for a person, the perceptibility of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) by that person's own perception is the necessary condition for the perception of its absence? While this condition exists in the case of perceiving the absence of a jar that is otherwise imperceptible, it does not exist in the case of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and God (Īśvara), since God is not an object of sensory perception; how then can there be such a perception? He dispels this doubt by means of the fault stated in the final position, using the phrase "by this" (*etena*). "Perceptibility of the counter-positive" (*pratiyogipratyakṣayogyatā*) means the capacity of the counter-positive to be perceived.

For this very reason, he says later, "in an unsuitable Lord. By the word "by this," he shows what was stated: "the pillar. Although a refutation was offered during the occasion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by relying on the position that difference (*bheda*) subsists in multiple loci (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), at the occasion of stating the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), he provides the resolution by relying on the actual state of things, beginning with "residing in the Lord" (*īśvaradharmika*).

The sense is that since it is reasonable to say that perception is a means of valid knowledge regarding difference merely through the perceptibility of something for a particular person, the non-existence of that [perceptibility] for all people does not constitute a sublation (*bādhaka*).
If it is argued that, when we inquire about the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes that [object], the presentation of that perception is irrelevant, we say no.
For it is possible here as well, just as there is certainty regarding an object located in another place through a perception established by the words of a reliable person (*āpta*).

If it is argued that this perception does not serve as a cause for the destruction of doubt by way of being a direct perception—like the perception of a jar—but rather by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*), [we reply:]...

In this case as well, let it be so; what harm is there? Just as in an assembly, when a specific object is presented, the perception of an ordinary person is adduced as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of a neutral observer, so too there is no contradiction in stating it here.

To the question, "What is the proof for the existence of God’s perception? he says: "Of God... [and] "That statement... The sense is that just as His perception is established by the word of a reliable authority (*āpta*), so it is here as well.

Now, regarding the causal efficacy of the perception of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) for the ordinary perception of a produced difference (*janyabheda*): if it is held that difference is "pervasive" (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) such that it resides in both [relata] simultaneously, then it must be stated that its perception is impossible without the perception of all its substrates;
otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence (*āpatti*) of perceiving the duality, conjunction, and so forth, between the sky and a jar.

Even in the view where difference resides only in the locus (*dharmin*) because it does not reside in the counter-correlate, the prior existence of the perceptions of both the counter-correlate and the locus is necessarily required in some other form as a cause, in order to account for the uniformity of experience.
For this very reason, even the difference between a pillar and a *piśāca* is not perceptible.

In other systems of thought, since the non-perception of that [difference] is necessary due to the absence of perception of the substratum (*āśraya*) which is the form of the *piśāca*, it is appropriate to accept the same [explanation] in this system as well, in order to account for the similarity of such experience.

Likewise, with respect to the ordinary perception of a difference, "being a perception possessing a worldly objectivity residing in both its locus and its counter-correlate" is the pervading property (*vyāpaka*).

This is because, through the observation of an invariable concomitance (*sahacāra*), there is a certainty regarding that [nature], just as there is a certainty regarding fire being the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of smoke.

And thus, since the knowledge of God consists of a modification of *māyā* and is therefore produced (*janya*), it is necessary that the perception of both the individual soul (*jīva*) and God must have existed prior to it.

Even if that [divine knowledge] were eternal, in order to maintain the aforementioned relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, it is necessary that both possess the status of ordinary objects (*laukika-viṣayatva*) within that perception as well.
But that [conclusion] is not tenable here;
for since the individual soul (jīva), being atomic, is unfit for ordinary visual perception, it cannot possibly appear even in the visual perception of the Supreme Self.
Furthermore, since the Supreme Self is never observed to be an object of the mind, it is impossible for [the jīva] to be an object of the Lord's mental cognition. Therefore, he says:
"Because the Lord possesses the capacity for presiding over the individual soul (jīva). This means because He possesses the capacity—that is, because He is capable.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of losing the very nature of Lordship, which consists in the power to bring about the impossible.
For this very reason, the phrase "of the Lord" (*īśvarasya*) is a qualification containing a logical reason (*hetugarbha*).
[Objection: "In that case, it should be able to produce even a conscious pot, or even make itself into a living soul.
[Reply: Not so.

For while a pot is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being perceived through worldly convention as something devoid of consciousness, its capacity [to produce such things] is established by such proofs as "possessing diverse powers" (*vicitraśakti*), since it acts as the producer [of those effects].

The meaning is that the Supreme Self’s status as the direct perceiver of all objects is established by thousands of scriptural and traditional texts, such as "The Witness, the Knower, solitary and devoid of qualities" and "He who is omniscient is all-knowing. Thus, there is no room for objection. Now, regarding the objection raised based on the claim that the Lord’s perception does not have the individual soul (jīva) as its object, the refutation of the view that the perception of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is a cause [of non-apprehension] is found elsewhere.

Even if one were to admit such causality, there would be no occasion to discuss the irrelevance of the perception of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) therein, following an investigation into the eternality of God’s perception;
for at the outset, even that doubt does not arise,
because no proponent whatsoever accepts any entity that is beyond the scope of His perception— whether His omniscience be considered illusory (*māyika*) or natural (*svābhāvika*).

Therefore, the objection that—even though the existence of a cognition that motivates his own linguistic usage is established by the aforementioned statement of the Lord—its nature as perception (*pratyakṣa*) remains unestablished, is refuted.
Since that very [perceptual nature] is obtained first, there is no reason to reject it.

Consequently, because the refutation of the requirement for the perception of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogipratyakṣa*) as a causal factor and so forth is unnecessary for the purpose of that [objection], it is not performed here; rather, it is addressed immediately following this, at the occasion of establishing the perception of difference (*bhedapratyakṣa*) regarding the individual soul (*jīva*).

The sense is that one should not feel mental distress on the grounds that the context would be corrupted by performing now what was desired but not done previously; for that would result in the corruption of the literary composition (*sandarbha*).

Some, however, say that since the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogijñāna*) is a cause for perceptual knowledge produced by a sentient being (*janya-pratyakṣa*), it does not follow that it is a cause for God’s perception (*īśvara-pratyakṣa*); and since that [position] has been refuted by the reasoning about to be stated, there is no occasion for such an objection. Thus, their statement—that the mention of the cause consisting of perception directed toward a living soul (*jīva*) merely serves to show that [the objection] finds no footing—is nothing more than a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*).

Since this [objection] can be resolved according to the method we have stated, and since it is possible—despite the refutation of its causality in the subsequent text—to now accept the doubt that arises from the misconception that God’s perception is produced, and thereby provide an easy resolution, one must ask those very people: how can this work be characterized as a mere *prauḍhivāda* (bold assertion) that results in a statement made without due reflection?
Regarding the phrase "having God as its counter-correlate" (*īśvarapratiyogika*), the meaning is "of the individual soul" (*jīvasya*). That is to say, it applies to the individual soul as well.

Now, one might object: "Since the causal efficacy of the perception of a counter-positive (*pratiyogipratyakṣakāraṇatā*) has been established according to the method stated in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), how can the perception of that [absence] be possible for the individual soul (*jīva*), given its absence [of such a cause]? Anticipating this, and keeping in mind the two alternatives—whether the causal efficacy of the perception of a counter-positive applies to all perception whatsoever, or only to the perception of absence—one states an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the first alternative: "This is a cow."

The sense is that this [definition] is not tenable because it suffers from deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the perception of the similarity of a forest gavaya in a nearby cow, even though one has a memory of the forest gavaya.

Regarding the second [alternative], he states the deviation in both cases—namely, in the locus of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and in the locus of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)—for the sake of strengthening the argument: "Here is that cloth. The use of the word "that" (*sa*) is intended to indicate that the cloth is at that time beyond the range of perception;
by this, the absence of the cause consisting in the perception of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is established for that time.

One need not provide an introduction [to the following argument] by keeping in mind the alternatives—whether it be the perception of a counter-positive (*sapratiyogika-pratyakṣa*), the perception of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva-pratyakṣa*), or the perception of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva-pratyakṣa*)—and then refuting them in succession.

This is because, regarding the perception of absolute non-existence, the alternatives of whether the perception of the counter-positive is a cause or not a cause are irrelevant to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*); thus, it is inappropriate to include "perception of absolute non-existence" as a category within the alternative set.

It is also logical to provide the following introduction: having postulated the second alternative (vikalpa-koṭi) as the perceptibility of non-existence (*abhāva*), and having assigned the third alternative as the perceptibility of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), [the author] refutes them in succession. Regarding the term "pillar" (*stambha*): one might object that it has already been stated that this [perception] is not of the nature of perception; however, this must be addressed because, according to our own position, since difference (*bheda*)—which has a single entity as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and all other entities as its substrates (*anuyogin*)—is a property that subsists collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), there is only one difference between the counter-correlate and the individual substrate, just as in the case of duality (*dvitva*).

Thus, when there is a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and distinct manifest instances of other correlates (*anuyogin*), it is said that there is a single difference (*bheda*). When there is the aforementioned counter-correlate and all [other] correlates, it is said that there is only one difference.

In the first case, there would follow the unwarranted assumption of a plurality of differences belonging to the correlate of a difference whose counter-correlate is a jar—a plurality that lacks any basis in valid cognition.
In the second case, it would follow that the difference of a jar from its parts is not perceptible;
for even in a thousand lifetimes, it is impossible to perceive all the individual instances that serve as its substrata simultaneously.

Furthermore, in both positions, one must assume—according to the previously mentioned method—that the jar is "distinct from itself" in order to prevent such a cognition, which leads to the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Since his view is thus to be rejected on these grounds, the similarity of experience accepted by him is irrelevant. Consequently, the perception of the difference between a pillar and a *piśāca* (demon), which is established by the experience of everyone, cannot be denied.

Furthermore, since the perception of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) is not a cause for the perception of difference, but rather the mere cognition of it is the cause, it is entirely logical that there could be a perception of difference from God in the form "I am not omniscient" or "I am not the Lord of All," even without divine perception, because such recollection can occur through knowledge produced by scripture (*āgama*).
[The opponent’s claim] that no certainty regarding God is possible because scripture refers only to pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is incorrect;
for that position will be refuted later by establishing that scripture indeed has difference as its purport.

Furthermore, since the knowledge of that [negation] can arise through the mere cognition of those terms— even before the purport of the scripture is determined— by means of Vedic words such as "omniscient" (*sarvajña*),

the direct perception of the counter-positive need not be the cause. Nevertheless, even so, one must state that the cause for the perception of absence (*abhāva*)— whether defined as the perception of absence in general or specifically the perception of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*)— is the knowledge of the counter-positive as an object of ordinary sensory perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the perception of the absence of a *piśāca* on the ground and such locations.

Thus, one might suspect that because God is not an object of perception, His knowledge cannot bring about the perception of difference from Him; however, such a causal relationship holds in the case of the perception of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), but not in the case of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), because there is a deviation in cases such as the perception of the difference of a *piśāca* from a pillar.
Rather, the causality consists in the perceptibility of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and the knowledge of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
He states with the words "by this" (*etena*) and so forth that there is no inconsistency in the present case, because the establishment of all categories is accepted in accordance with experience.
By this [statement], [he refers to] the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the perception of the difference between *piśācas*.
[The phrase] "the fitness for the perception of absence" (*abhāvapratyakṣayogyatā*) means the fitness for perception residing in the absence (*abhāva*).
Whether this [fitness] is objecthood (*viṣayatā*) or something else that persists as long as the substance exists is another matter.

This is because [the absence] is dependent on the perception of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), and thus, according to the stated method, it is contingent upon the perception of the counter-positive. If the cause is defined as the cognition of the counter-positive which is the object of perception, then the perception of the counter-positive serves as a remote factor (*paramparayā*)—either by being included within the delimiting condition (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) of the cause, or through fitness (*yogyatā*) equivalent to it—which functions as the delimiting condition for the effect, namely the objecthood of the positive entity (*bhāva*). Thus, its causal efficacy remains unimpeded. Regarding the phrase "in the pillar" (*stambhe*): it refers to that fitness for perception residing in the counter-positive.
The word "ca" (and) is a conjunctive particle that collects the previously mentioned deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

The portion ending with "because it is not the object of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), because it is not a non-requisite factor for the perception of mutual non-existence, and because it is experienced in that very [case]" constitutes the logical reason (*hetu*).

And thus, because of the aforementioned deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and because—following actual experience—one does not postulate a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in cases of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), the doubt based upon that [causal relationship] is refuted; this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, the feminine ending in the phrase "because that [doubt] has mutual non-existence as its object" (*anyonyābhāvaviṣayatvācca tasyāḥ*) is an error, since the masculine ending is seen in many manuscripts. And in that case, the meaning is as follows:

He explains what was stated by the word "by this" with the words "stambha" (the pillar). To the question, "Even if such an experience exists, what relevance does it have to the present case? he says: "of that. The connection is "and of that. The particle *ca* has the sense of "but" (*tu*). Thus, the intended meaning is that this [argument] is not tenable because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Even under the view that the non-apprehension of what is capable [of being perceived] (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is the cause for the direct perception of absence, the non-apprehension of the counter-positive—which consists in the apprehension capable of being adduced as "if I were omniscient, I would have been so experienced"—is certainly intact here; thus, there is no inconsistency in the direct perception of difference.
As for the nature of non-apprehension, it has been examined on the occasion of defining existence as being perceptible in the *Dvaitadyumaṇi*; it should be sought out therein.

Thus, having established that perception is capable [of apprehending] the primary objects—the difference between the soul and its attributes (*jīvadharmika-bheda*) and the difference between God and His attributes (*īśvaradharmika-jīvabheda*)—he now demonstrates the difference whose counter-correlate is the soul and whose locus is the soul (*jīvapratiyogika-jīvadharmika-bheda*), which arises either incidentally or through a traditional sequence as being somehow useful for that purpose: "In this way," etc.

The reading "In this way, the difference whose counter-correlate is Yajñadatta and whose locus is Devadatta is perceptible to Devadatta," and so forth, is universally found and is perfectly consistent.
However, in some places, the reading is "In this way, the difference whose locus is Viṣṇumitra and whose counter-correlate is Yajñadatta," and so forth, is to be inferred.

Although the difference between the bodies of Yajñadatta and Viṣṇumitra—which are being perceived by Devadatta—is indeed experienced, the difference between their respective conscious selves (*cetana*) is not directly perceived.

Because it is unsuitable for the eyes and other sense organs, it is impossible for it to be an object of visual perception (*cākṣuṣa*). Furthermore, since the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*)— which perceives the individual soul (*jīva*) of that [body] as its own object— is also not operative therein,
this appears to be incorrect.

Nevertheless, it is not the case that in the perception of an absence produced by a particular sense organ, the cause is simply the non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) of a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) consisting of a perceptual cognition produced by that very sense organ, which is itself rendered impossible by the contingency of the existence of that counter-positive. Rather, the referent of the term "non-apprehension of the capable" (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is the absence of a counter-positive whose nature is a certainty characterized by the capacity to entail its existence;
that alone is the cause for the perception of an absence.
Even when that [consciousness] exists, the absence of a certainty produced by it is the cause for the perception of its absence there.

And thus, the non-difference between the conscious being residing in Yajñadatta’s body at a previous time—characterized by that prior period—and the one existing at this present time, is ascertained through such means as the recollection of what was experienced then, and through signs such as the absence of activity that would contradict the results intended at that time.
Yet, there is no non-difference between Yajñadatta and Viṣṇumitra.

The sense is this: if there were non-difference [between the two], then such inferential marks (*liṅga*) and the resulting inference would exist; however, by means of the visual organ itself—conjoined with the absence of that very inference which is being adduced as a reductio ad absurdum, and accompanied by the sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) of "qualified-objectness" (*viśeṣaṇatā*) in some manner through its connection with the difference residing therein, along with the presentation of the substratum (*dharmin*)—there arises a perception whose form is "the difference between the conscious Yajñadatta and the conscious Viṣṇumitra," which is of the nature of an *upanaya* (application) regarding the substratum and is of a worldly (*laukika*) nature regarding the aspect of difference.

Just as it is accepted that even when the locus is imperceptible, the perception of absolute non-existence—such as "the absence of manifested color in the sky"—is possible by the force of perceptual experience, and that in such a perception of absolute non-existence the fitness (*yogyatva*) of the locus is not a necessary factor but rather merely the non-apprehension of what is fit for perception (*yogyānupalabdhi*); so too, by the force of the perceptual experience "the difference from that which possesses manifested color in the sky," it is necessary to accept the same principle here as well.

Nor should it be argued that in that case, the difference from that which possesses manifested color is merely the object of an inference based on a manifested mark (*liṅga*), and not the object of perception.
For it could be argued that the reverse is equally possible due to the absence of any decisive factor (*vinigamakābhāva*).

Furthermore, since there is identity between a pervasive property's absolute absence (*vyāpyavṛttidharmātyantābhāva*) and the difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by that absence, this [difference] would be unavoidable under the view of their identity. Alternatively, after the existence of a self (*sātmakatva*) has been established in Yajñadatta’s body and Viṣṇumitra’s body through the mark of movement (*ceṣṭā*), the mutual difference between those two bodies as qualified by their respective selves appears in ordinary perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*) through an extra-ordinary contact (*alaukikasannikarṣa*), wherein even the difference between both delimiters of the qualification (*viśeṣaṇatāvacchedaka*) is manifested.

This is because, following that [realization], one experiences the non-arising of any doubt regarding the mutual non-difference between those two, just as one does not experience such a doubt regarding one's own self and the Self of another.

Otherwise, for ordinary people, there would follow the consequence of the cessation of worldly activity due to doubt and the like, even in the absence of any suspicion of invalidity arising from your scripture.
And thus, even though there is a difference between those two, Devadatta’s perception certainly proceeds.
However, in that respect, it is devoid of worldly character (*laukikatva*).
And that [non-worldly perception] is useless for us, because we do not claim that it is exclusively worldly.

Nor should it be argued that if even non-worldly perception were to establish an object, then "temporality" (*kālatva*) would also be established in the sky, since such a presentation through mental intuition (*upanītabhāna*) is possible at some time.
It would indeed occur if there were sublation by another stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
however, that is not the case here.
In the present instance, there is simply no sublation by another stronger means of valid cognition.

On the contrary, since difference itself is established here through statements such as "I am indeed distinct from this" and by means of logical marks (liṅga) such as the possession of contradictory attributes, it is precisely that [perception] which exists in this case.
Alternatively, if Devadatta were a yogi, then a perception whose object is the difference between two conscious entities would indeed be appropriate, just as in the case of the Lord (Īśvara);
for even the perception of a yogi serves to account for his own conventional usage, such as "I perceive directly."

Since it is indeed equivalent to ordinary worldly perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*), it is appropriate to present that [perception] as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this context, just like the perception of the Lord (*īśvarapratyakṣa*).

With the intention that the difference—characterized by having one's own self as its locus and another self as its counter-correlate—is certainly an object of everyone’s own worldly perception and thus requires no further proof, he says: "and so forth should be inferred."

He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "In this regard, this... and so forth. Here, in response to the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), "this" means the following refutation, which is the removal of the objection that is about to be stated.

He first declares the removal of the first objection in order to indicate that the presentation of the established conclusion follows the very sequence of the prima facie arguments. [He says: "As for that which... [and] "having God as its subject. Although difference-in-general is an object of God’s perception, and regarding that perception, the scriptural statement "There are these two persons in the world," etc., is itself the proof.

Nevertheless, this has been illustrated with the intention of referring to the general rule that "a difference whose locus is itself and whose counter-correlate is other than itself is perceptible to itself.
Alternatively, it may be because in the first verse, the difference having God as its locus was primarily introduced.
Although even the difference having an insentient entity as its counter-correlate was also under discussion there.

Nevertheless, since at the outset the absence of the means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the very difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) was suspected, it was stated that [the difference] has the individual soul as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
In this way, the consistency of the subsequent mention of the Lord as the counter-correlative and so forth should be understood.
Now, one might object: there is an absence of evidence for the existence of such a perceptual cognition of difference in the case of the Lord.
This is because another's cognition is not perceptible.

Nor should it be argued that the inference—"God does not possess the perception of the difference between Himself and others residing in Himself, because He is a self, like us"—is the valid means of knowledge;
for such an argument is inconclusive due to the absence of a supporting reason (*anukūlatarka*).

Nor is there [reliance on] scripture (*āgama*), because its authority regarding such a matter has not been ascertained; therefore, he says: "Of the Lord" (*īśvarasya*). "His word" (*tadvacanam*) means the word of the Lord in the form of Kṛṣṇa.
And thus, this sentence is preceded by the Lord’s direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) concerning the meaning of the sentence.
Because it is a statement of authoritative knowledge concerning God,
like other such statements;
or because God, though devoid of indirect cognition, possesses knowledge of the meaning of this sentence.
Because of being the speaker of this sentence;
for whoever is the speaker of a particular sentence possesses knowledge of its meaning—

just as in the case of Yajñadatta— and such inference is the proof for the existence of direct perception of the meaning of the sentence [stating] that God is distinct from the individual soul and primordial matter (*prakṛti*).
The authority of this statement is established for both disputants;
the underlying intention is that because it is supported by such scriptural testimony, the aforementioned inference is also indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Although it would be more parsimonious to establish difference by means of that very statement—having first established the perception of it through the statement that propounds difference—rather than establishing difference by relying on that perception [subsequently], [the author proceeds as follows].

Nevertheless, since it has been stated by the opponent that perception as a means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) is impossible regarding the difference between the individual soul and the Lord, one resorts to a traditional succession [of authorities] in order to negate that [possibility].

Now, if it is argued that because only conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*) is the object of the Lord’s perception, ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*) is not established thereby—[we ask: is that [difference] perceived as being ultimately real, or only as being conventionally real? Not the first.
For this would result in the fallacy that even Īśvara is subject to error.
As for the second alternative, is its conventional validity sublatable or unsublatable?
In the first case, because it would grasp a sublatable object, that same defect [of error] would ensue.

Furthermore, it would follow that difference is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) in reality; moreover, in the end, this results in a contradiction with one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

Moreover, since it is untenable for the aforementioned statements to have conventional difference as their purport according to the method to be explained, how could the perception of that difference—which is the object to be inferred from those statements—have a conventional object? This is the direction of the argument.

[Objection: But has not the perception of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) already been refuted on the grounds that there is no perception of the counter-positive (pratiyogin) and so forth? How, then, can this [present argument] be valid? To this he says: "Of the Lord" (īśvarasya). The sense is that otherwise, His omniscience would be untenable. This was stated merely as a concession; for the requirement of perceiving the aforementioned counter-positive will be refuted immediately below, and because the perception of the Lord does not depend upon such causes, there is no room for the objection. To indicate this, he did not say "there is no room for the fault" (na doṣāvakāśaḥ), but rather "there is no room for the challenge" (na codyāvakāśaḥ).
The connection is that the distinction whose locus is the living being (jīva) is directly perceived by the living being;
the sense is that this is because of the experience: "I am not omniscient" and "I am not free from suffering."

If it is objected: "Since God is not perceptible, how can there be perception of a difference having Him as its counter-correlate (pratiyogin)?"—then is the perception of the counter-correlate the cause for the perception of any object possessing a counter-correlate, for the perception of absence in general, or specifically for the perception of mutual absence? Or rather, since the non-perception of a capable object is the cause of the perception of absence, is it maintained that the capability of the counter-correlate is a necessary condition for the capability of the absence? He refutes the first three positions with the words: "sapratiyogika... (possessing a counter-correlate).
The point is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in such cases as perception;
for even in the absence of the perception of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as a gavaya, at the preceding moment, such a perception [of the non-existence] is produced.

He refutes the fourth [definition] by extending the third fault, saying: "By this... He explains this very point with the words: "In the case of a pillar... and so forth, beginning with: "even though the counter-correlate, the *piśāca*, is unperceivable (*ayogya*)."
"From such experience" means from the production of a perception in the form "it is thus.

And so, since there is a deviation [of the rule] in that case, it is impossible for non-perception of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*) to be the general cause of the perception of absence; therefore, the meaning is that the capability of an absence does not depend upon the capability of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

Alternatively, one might object: "But surely there is no perception at all of the difference from a *piśāca*, so the aforementioned deviation does not occur"; to this he says: "In a pillar. "From such experience" means because the perception is established by experience.
The sense is that otherwise there would be a contradiction with experience.

[Objection: Let the cognition "it is not a piśāca" have as its object precisely that contradiction, since contradiction (*virodha*) is also the meaning of the negative particle *na*. To this he says: "mutual absence" (*anyonyābhāva*). The sense is that even when no other entity is present, that [absence] is established by experience.

[Objection: But if the fitness for the cognition of a non-existence (*abhāva*) were not dependent on the fitness of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of perceiving the non-existence of gravity (*gurutva*) and the like.

Nor can it be said that the fitness of the counter-positive is the causal factor for the perception of a relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*), while the fitness of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the causal factor for the perception of a mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*);

for otherwise, the perception of the absolute non-existence of a *piśāca* in a pillar, or the difference from something possessing manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*) in air, would be impossible. [Reply: This is not so.

Because, according to experience, it is precisely the state of being the absence of this or that [object] that serves as the determinant for the fitness (yogyatā) of this or that [cognition]. "Of Viṣṇumitra" means: the sense is that this is based on such experiences as "I am not Yajñamitra. By the phrase "and so forth," there is the inclusion of the fact that for everyone, the difference—having itself as its locus and having something other than itself as its counter-correlate—is directly perceived. He establishes the final conclusion with the word "here": "In this regard" refers to the subject of the refutation of the proofs for difference.
This refers to what is about to be stated.
"Refutation" (parihāra) means the method of removing objections;
furthermore, in this context regarding the means of valid cognition that establish non-difference, it also means the method of refutation.

In this regard, he first demonstrates the method for refuting the critique regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for difference, beginning with the words "As for that which... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "perception of the Lord" (*īśvarasya pratyakṣa*): the intended meaning is that [the distinction] is established by experience in the form, "I am not the individual soul" (*jīva*).

[Objection: "But since the intellect of the Lord (*īśvara-buddhi*) is not perceptible to us, how are we to know that such a perception exists for the Lord? To this he says: "Of him" (*tasya*). Having described the two types of persons—the perishable (*kṣara*) and the imperishable (*akṣara*)—in the form of Kṛṣṇa through such passages as "These two persons exist in the world," it was stated [in the *Bhagavad Gītā*]: "The Supreme Person is other than these two, and is not one of these two. Now, such a statement would not be possible if He lacked such a perception.
Therefore, the sense is that it is known that the Lord possesses such a perception.

To the objection—how can there be perceptibility of a difference whose counter-correlate (the *jīva*) is imperceptible due to its atomic nature—he says: "Of the Lord. This is because of His capacity, that is, His power;
the sense is that it is due to His omniscience.
And this has been stated provisionally, for the sake of argument.

It should be understood that such a restrictive rule has been refuted immediately following [the statement] beginning with "having a counter-correlate" (*sapratiyogika*). Regarding the phrase "of the individual soul" (*jīvasya*): the intended meaning is that there exists the experience of that soul in the form, "I am not omniscient, nor am I free from suffering."

To the objection—“If the Lord, who serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), is not perceptible, how can the difference having Him as its counter-correlate be perceptible?”—the author says: “*Sapratiyogika-etc.*” This means “defined by a counter-correlate. Regarding the word “*iyam*”: after experiencing a *gavaya* in the forest, when one sees a cow upon reaching the city, the perception of similarity having the *gavaya* as its counter-correlate arises in the form, “This cow is similar to a *gavaya*. Yet, in that case, there is no perception of the *gavaya*, which serves as the counter-correlate, because it is situated in the forest and is thus spatially remote (*vyavahita*).
Therefore, the meaning is that because there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in this case, the aforementioned rule does not hold.

Now, one might object: "In the perception of an entity that is non-existent (abhāva) and possesses a counter-correlate (sapratiyogika), the rule that the perception of the counter-correlate is necessary is accepted;

since similarity (sādṛśya) is a positive entity (bhāvarūpa), there is no deviation in its perception. To this, he says: "There is no jar here. Here, on the ground, the perception of the absence whose counter-correlate is a jar arises in the form, "A jar does not exist here."
Furthermore, there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the counter-positive— the jar— on that ground,
because there is no sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) with it due to the absence of the jar on the ground.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that the aforementioned rule does not hold, as there is an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) here.

[Objection: Surely, in the perception of a category of entity (apadārtha) that consists of mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) and possesses a counter-correlate (sapratiyogika), a rule is accepted that there must be perception of the counter-correlate. And the perception "there is no jar here" has as its object the absence of the relation (saṃsargābhāva) with a jar; therefore, there is no deviation [from the rule] in that case. To this, he says: "The pillar... The perception of mutual non-existence having the piśāca as its counter-correlate arises in the form: "The pillar is not a piśāca. Yet, in that case, there is no perception of the piśāca, who is the counter-correlate.
Because that [absence] is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no such stated rule here due to this deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Now, one might object: "In the case of the perceptibility of an absence, the perceptibility of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is the necessary condition."

Just as the absence of a jar is perceptible because the jar itself is perceptible, so too the absence of an atom is imperceptible because the atom itself is imperceptible. Therefore, since the Lord—who is the counter-positive (pratiyogin)—is imperceptible, how can the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) that has Him as its counter-positive be perceptible? Furthermore, if there is an absence of perceptibility, what could possibly be perceived? Anticipating this objection, he refutes it by way of extension: "By this" (etena). "Imperceptible" (ayogyā) means "imperceptible to direct perception" (pratyakṣāyogyā).
He explains what was stated by the word "by this" with the term "pillar. To begin with, there is perceptibility for the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) that has a *piśāca* as its counter-correlate;
however, the *piśāca* itself lacks perceptibility in that context.
Therefore, because of this deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the aforementioned rule does not hold true. This is the meaning.

One might object: "In that case, would it not follow that the absence of atoms is perceptible? To this we reply: Do you intend to establish the perceptibility of the absence of conjunction with atoms, or rather the absence of mutual identity (*anyonyābhāva*)? It cannot be the first.

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because the perceptibility of the counter-positive is a cause for the perceptibility of the non-existence of relation, and that [perceptibility] is absent in that case. Nor is the second, because it would entail an undesired consequence (iṣṭāpatti).

The meaning is that since one accepts the perception of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of atoms, such as "the jar is not an atom. He states that the difference between individual souls (*jīva*) is likewise established by perception with the words "In this way": the meaning is that there exists the experience, "I am not Yajñadatta, [but] Viṣṇumitra.

If it is objected: "In the experience 'I am not free from suffering' or 'I am not omniscient,' only the non-existence of a relation (*saṃsargābhāva*), such as freedom from suffering, is experienced in the self, and not the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) having the Lord (*Īśvara*) as its counter-correlative," we say no.
The very experience that "in me there is no state of being free from suffering, omniscience, and so forth" has as its object the absence of the relation [of those qualities] to me;
for it is the state of being free from suffering itself that is presented there as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
Nor is the absolute non-existence of the state of being free from suffering the object of this [experience].

Because identity between the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is first established through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), and then that very identity is negated.
Furthermore, the validity of perception has been firmly established by us elsewhere.
Now, as for what was stated—that the difference having God as its counter-correlate and the individual soul as its substratum is indeed perceived by the individual soul—this is addressed as follows:
That is not so;
for there is no experience of anyone to the effect that "I am not the Lord.
Nor is there such an experience shared by everyone as "I am not free from suffering" or "I am not omniscient."
For that very experience—"I am not the Lord"—must be said to have the Lord as its object, since the Lord is defined by those characteristics.

One might raise the objection: "But this experience has as its object the absence of a relation such as 'freedom from suffering' and so on; therefore, it cannot have as its object the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) whose counter-positive is the Lord, who is of the nature of being free from suffering and so forth. Anticipating this, he replies: "Not so," with the underlying thought that one who entertains such an objection is neither a common person nor an investigator.

The point is this: if this experience were to proceed by taking "freedom from suffering" (nirduḥkhatva) or "omniscience" (sarvajñatva) as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—just as in the case of the cognition "there is no jar here"—then it would have a non-occurrence relation (*saṃsargābhāva*) as its object.
But it is not so.

Rather, because it negates the identity between the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—namely, the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)—through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in "I am free from suffering and omniscient," its object is exclusively mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

In this context, "grammatical coreferentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya) refers to the co-location of "I-ness" (ahantva) and "freedom from suffering" (nirduḥkhatva) within a single substratum, and not merely the state of having the same case-ending;
for in the cognition [of these qualities], there is an absence of case-endings and the like,
since those are properties of words.
Nevertheless, some have explained that what is intended here by "grammatical coreferentiality" (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is simply the state of having the same case-ending.
Now, even if the experience "I am not devoid of suffering" has difference as its object, this does not establish [the existence of] that [difference].

Because that [position] lacks validity, being contradicted by many means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establish non-difference, he says: "But as for the validity of perception... This means that it has been demonstrated with great precision in nine chapters—beginning from the discussion on establishing the superiority of perception through such arguments as its being a genus (*jāti*) and so forth in the first chapter of the *Nyāyāmṛta*, up to the discussion on establishing that perception grasps ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-sattva*). In this regard, the distinction is as follows:
external perception is not sublated by anything other than a stronger perception.

The direct perception of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*) cannot be sublated by anything. In this regard, the realization "I am not free from suffering" and "I am not omniscient" is indeed the direct perception of the witness-consciousness;
therefore, there is no sublation of it by anything whatsoever.

Since the validity of the uncontradicted direct perception of the witness-consciousness is certain, the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is established by it—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the term "non-existence through non-connection" (*saṃsargābhāva*): the sense is that, by virtue of the maxim *saviśeṣaṇe hi* (for when there is a qualification), it is possible for it to be perceived because its counter-positive is capable [of being perceived]—namely, the absence of pain and so forth—and because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in having a single type of non-existence.
Now, one might object: "Even so, it follows that [the world] is non-different from the attributes of God.
To this we reply: even if that were the case, the perception of difference would still be sublated.
In reality, however, there is no fault whatsoever in accepting that those attributes coexist with their own absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
[One might object that] identity (*tādātmya*) would follow from such coexistence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

[The response is: In the case of "I am not free from suffering," the meaning is that identity is superimposed upon the two terms "I" and "free from suffering" by virtue of their grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

And thus, regarding the statement "in me there is neither freedom from suffering nor omniscience," since the connection between different substrates (*vyadhikaraṇānvaya*) is understood as a relation (*saṃsarga*), it is logical that this [cognition] makes known a relation by virtue of its being a superimposer of a relation. However, since the aforementioned cognition is a superimposer of identity (*tādātmya*), it must be stated that its object is simply an absence distinct from that [identity]; thus, there is no fault.
To the objection that "the perception of difference is erroneous," he says: "perception... [and so on]. "Elsewhere" means...
The meaning is "in the *Nyāyāmṛta*.
To explain: the validity of perception is either sublated or remains silent.
In the first case, [it would be sublated] either by perception, inference, scripture, or by the mere suspicion of a sublation.
Not the first,
because that [perception] is absent.
Or, because the opposite is possible regarding existence;
and because the first [alternative] is stronger due to its lack of contradiction.
Not the second.
Because this would result in the total abolition of the "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) fallacy;
and because perception, as the apprehender of the subject (dharmin), is that upon which [all other means of knowledge] depend.
Nor is it the third [alternative].
The scriptural statement "the sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ) is logically consistent with the sublation of that [scriptural] difference by direct perception.

However, the direct perception of the moon's size is sublated by scripture even before it arises, because it is weak—due to the absence of the causal conditions for transformation established elsewhere—and thus, having arisen, it is subsequently sublated by scripture.
This does not apply to the fourth [type of sublation].
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For this very reason, the second [alternative] is not tenable.
If it is argued that existence at a later time is not established by perception, which grasps only the present, we say no.
Even by that much, falsity—in the form of a negation across the three periods of time—is not established.
As for the word "in me" (*mayi*): the sense is that the locative case in the correlate (*anuyogin*) is invariably associated with the indication of a relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*).

[Objection: "Surely, statements such as 'I am not free from suffering' must have difference (*bheda*) as their object; nevertheless, non-duality is not established by this, because it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). To this, he replies: "The validity of perception. This is because this [perception] is of the nature of the Witness (*sākṣin*), and the Witness is of the nature of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); furthermore, there is no sublation [of it].

As for scriptural texts such as "There is no diversity here" and "That thou art," they do not constitute a sublation in your own view, since they are intended to convey an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārtha*).

Moreover, due to conflict with the foundational perception (*upajīvya-pratyakṣa*), these texts can only have a figurative meaning (*gauṇārthatā*), just like the scriptural statement "The sacrificer is the sacrificial grass-bundle" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*).

The meaning is that in the *Nyāyāmṛta*, the validity of perception is established by such arguments as: "The individual souls (*jīvas*) are distinct, and the Supreme (*para*) is likewise distinct; nevertheless, they are everywhere declared in the Vedic doctrines to be of the nature of Brahman," and because it has been stated in both the *Smṛti* and the *Sūtra*—namely, "Because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated as such"—that this [identity] is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*). Thus, the validity of perception is demonstrated.
Now, if the perception of the counter-positive is not a cause for the perception of absence due to its lack of invariable concomitance, what then is the operative factor in the perception of absence?

If you say it is simply the "qualifier-ness" (*viśeṣaṇatā*) of that which is in contact with the sense organ, we say no; for this would lead to the absurdity of the absence of a *piśāca* (a ghost) being perceptible.

Nor is it the case that having a fit counter-positive (*yogyapratiyogikatva*) is the determining factor for the perception of a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), nor is having a fit locus (*yogyādhikaraṇatva*) the determining factor for the perception of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*). Therefore, it should not be said that the absence of a piśāca and so forth is not perceptible,
nor that the mutual absence of a piśāca in a pillar is imperceptible.
Otherwise, it would follow that the absolute absence of "mind-ness" (*manastva*) in a jar would not be perceptible,

and it would follow that the difference from atoms and so forth would be perceptible in a jar. Furthermore, is it the fitness of some particular counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) that constitutes the criterion, or is it the fitness of all such counter-positives?

In the first case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the perception of the absence of the universal "materiality" (mūrta-sāmānya). In the second case, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the perception of the absence of the universal "color" (rūpa-sāmānya) in a large volume of air.
The same dilemma applies regarding the fitness of the locus as well.
If it is argued that in the first case (the universal of corporeality), there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of piśācas,
and in the second case (the universal of being large), there would follow the perception of the mutual absence of that which possesses color in the great wind (*mahat*); to this,
the teacher Udayana replies:

They say that in the case of non-existence through relation (*saṃsargābhāva*), fitness (*yogyatā*) consists in the presence of all other means of perceiving the counter-positive and everything pervaded by it.
Consequently, there is no unwanted consequence of the non-perception of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) when its counter-positive is beyond the senses,
nor is there the undesirable contingency of the perception of the absence of a *piśāca* and the like.
That is not correct.

Since no other specific fitness (*yogyatā*) has been stated for the perception of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), if one were to accept that the cause in that case is merely the particularity of sense-organ contact and so forth, it would follow that mutual absence would not be perceptible in cases such as gravity (*gurutva*).

Furthermore, when it is possible to account for all the factors that bring about its apprehension, then the co-presence (*samavadhāna*) of those factors delimited by whatever constitutes the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the apprehension of those factors is likewise [the cause].

In the case of the perception of the absence of a jar on the ground, there is an absence of the substrata of those properties—such as being a particular reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), being a cognition of a particular word, or being a particular mental impression (*saṃskāra*)—which serve as the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) for the apprehension of every jar.
Furthermore, does the "pervasion by the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivyāpyatva*) occur through a temporal relation or a spatial relation? It cannot be the first.
Because it would follow that the contact with a jar is not pervaded by the jar;
because it would perish upon the destruction of the jar;

and because, since nothing other than an eternal entity is established as being temporally pervaded, there would follow the absurdity of perceiving a relational absence whose counter-positive is eternal.

Not the second [alternative], because it would follow that even the contact between the jar and the sense organ is not pervaded by the jar; consequently, due to the absence of such a conjunction, the non-existence of the jar would result in being imperceptible.
If it is argued that what is intended by the term "pervaded" (*vyāpya*) is a unique cause characterized by the presence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), we say no.

Because it is difficult to state that [the cause] is unique by virtue of being excluded from light and so forth; furthermore, there is no decisive reason (vinigamanābhāva) as to whether the causal status consists in being the absence of all those factors that bring about its perception when they are present together, or whether it consists in being all those factors that bring about its perception when accompanied by an absence.

Because the absence of the sense organs and so forth cannot be included within the scope of the causal determinant (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) in the form of *yogyatā* (fitness) as a cause for the perception of absence;

and because the non-perception of a destruction produced by the destruction of a conjoined object occurs due to the lack of the coexistence of the conjoined object or its perception with the perception of the conjunction, since [the former] does not pervade [the latter] through that conjunction—this is the general direction. However, according to the author of the *Maṇi*:

The capacity (*yogyatā*) common to both relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*) and mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) consists in the presence of an absence of that which would perceive the counter-positive, were the existence of that counter-positive to be logically entailed.

The meaning is this: an absence is "capable" in a given locus when, by the entailment of the existence of its counter-positive—constrained by a relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or identity (*tādātmya*)—it is possible to entail the perception of that counter-positive through that same relation in that locus.

Furthermore, the "existence of the counter-positive" refers to the existence of the counter-positive in its non-perishing state; by this, the perception of the destruction of conjunction caused by the destruction of the conjoined object is accounted for.
They say that for *piśācas*, the perception and non-perception of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) are thus established.
That too is not correct;
for it is as follows:

The property of the existence of the counter-positive being a subsumer (*prasañjaka*) of the perception of that counter-positive consists either in its being conditioned by it (*tadupahitatva*) or in its being suitable for it (*tadyogyatva*).
It cannot be the first, because such [subsumption], being of the nature of a reductio (*tarka*), is not invariably present prior to the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the absence.
Not the second [alternative], because that which is distinct from being pervaded cannot be defined.
If it is asked, "Let that very thing be so; what is the subverting argument (bādhaka)?"
It is replied: Is the existence of the counter-positive intended as pure, or as qualified by the pervader?
In the first case, the perception of the absence of cloth and so forth would not occur.
Because the apprehension of pure existence (*sattva*) alone does not pervade [the object];
and in the second case, because it would follow that the absence of earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) in a water-atom would be imperceptible,
since even there, earth-ness qualified by magnitude (*mahattva*) is what is pervaded by apprehension.

Nor should it be argued that what is intended as the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is not the existence of the counter-positive as delimited by a specific property residing in the locus (*dharmyavṛttiviśeṣaṇāvacchinnapratiyogisattva*), and that since largeness (*mahattva*) and so forth do not reside in atoms (*paramāṇu*), the aforementioned fault does not apply.

For the existence of earthness (*pṛthivītva*) when conjoined with such factors as sensory contact and the difference from the earthly atom would likewise [be a pervaded], and thus the stated fault would not be avoided.
Nor can it be said that in that locus, that which is the perceiver of the counter-positive, being unconditioned by anything else, is such [a pervaded].
It should not be argued that there is no such fault because the state of being distinct from earth-atoms (*pārthivāṇu*) and so forth is something over and above that [absence].

For in that locus, while the existence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi*) as a pure, unconditioned entity—distinct from the perception of the counter-positive—is not the case, the pervaded (*vyāpya*) must be stated as being delimited by whatever conditions the perception of the counter-positive. Furthermore, since even that which is delimited by some particular condition for perceiving the counter-positive is not the case, it must be stated as being delimited by whatever conditions the perception of the counter-positive.

And thus, by distinguishing between what is attained and what is not attained, it would be said that "capacity" (*yogyatā*) is simply the presence of all the conditions for the perception of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). And that [capacity] has already been addressed by the ancients here as being the absence of defects (*doṣa*).
Furthermore, is the perception of the object to be sublated (*apādya*) worldly (*laukika*) or non-worldly (*alaukika*)?
Not the first [alternative],
because it would follow that the mutual absence of piśācas in a pillar would not be perceptible,
since such a perception is not established in that case.
Not the second [alternative],
