because the existence of a *piśāca* as a sentient being is not pervaded by its being perceived in a manner transcending the world (*alaukika*).
Not the second.

This is because the existence of a *piśāca* as a sentient being is not pervaded by worldly perception through identity (*tādātmya*). Nor should it be argued that its existence is such [i.e., pervaded] when accompanied by a cause of extraordinary perception; for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of *piśācas*. This is the general direction of the argument.

If it is argued that, since there is no distinction regarding the contact of the sense organs and other factors, it is impossible to state a restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) for why only a certain absence is perceived by a certain person—and thus what hope can there be for the perception of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of God?
It is replied:
There is simply no single, pervasive restrictive rule (*anugata-niyāmaka*) among absences.
However, just as in the case of positive entities (*bhāva*), the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that determines the perception of each respective absence (*abhāva*) is distinct.
Some absences are non-perceptible precisely because they are by their very nature unfit for perception, like gravity (*gurutva*) and other such qualities.
The specific causal complexes are to be inferred accordingly through the methods of agreement (*anvaya*) and difference (*vyatireka*).

The possibility that the non-existence of another (anyonyābhāva) is not perceived does not arise from the experience of a pillar saying, "I am not a Piśāca," nor from [the experience] "I am not omniscient.
Otherwise, what hope would there be for the perception of the non-existence of even a jar? Thus, everything is well-established.

"And not of this" (*na cāsya*): Just as in the cognition "Now I am not wearing a topknot" (*na śikhī*), even though the locus is not expressed by a word ending in the locative case, the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) appears within the portion of the locus; so too, even though the locus is not expressed by a word ending in the nominative case, it is possible for the cognition to have the absence of the relation with that [counter-positive] as its object.
Furthermore, there is no dispute regarding the example;

the intention is that because difference (*bheda*) is a non-pervasive property (*avyāpyavṛtti*), it is impossible for the difference from fire (*śikhibheda*) to appear therein. Regarding "identity" (*tādātmya*): this is by virtue of the mention through words in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) having the same case-ending.
"From negation" means from the experience of negation.
The third case-ending here serves as the reason.
For difference (*bheda*) is indeed the very absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*).

The point is that, regarding the example, since there is no other way [to account for it], one must either accept that such conventional usage is merely technical (*pāribhāṣikatva*), or that it somehow conveys absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), or else—having accepted that difference is a non-pervasive property (*avyāpyavṛttitva*)—one must admit its capacity to sublate [the notion of identity].

An objection is raised: "Surely all perception is invalid due to its contradiction with Śruti, and thus it cannot be a means of proof; for even the perception of Īśvara is rooted in the defect of Māyā, which possesses the power of projection. To this, he says: "The validity of perception" (*pratyakṣaprāmāṇyam*). The meaning is that the validity of perception has been firmly established in the *Nyāyāmṛta* on the grounds of its being subservient to Śruti, its lack of scope [for sublation], its inherent strength, and so forth.

It might be argued that the aforementioned distinction could indeed be perceptible if the perception "I am not free from suffering," and so forth, were to have distinction as its object; however, this is not the case, and thus he raises an objection with the word "nanu" (but). The phrase "because it is presented as a counter-correlate" means that it functions as a qualifier in the aspect of non-existence through the relation of counter-correlation (*pratiyogitā-saṃsarga*). This refers to the perception "I am not free from suffering," and so forth. The phrase "of the locus and the counter-correlate" is to be understood in connection with the statement "I am not free from suffering," and so on.
Having superimposed the identity (*tādātmya*) of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), namely God, upon the locus (*dharmin*), namely the individual soul (*jīva*)—
the sense being that the words for the locus and the counter-correlate are expressed with identical case-endings (which generates such a superimposition of identity)—
one negates that very identity; that is to say, one brings about the cognition of its absence.
This is the intended meaning:
from a particular word, a particular object is understood; thus, in a cognition reflected by that particular word, that very same object appears.
Wherever a certain property is perceived when a word is not accompanied by the negative particle (*nañ*), the absence of that property is understood when it is so accompanied.

And thus, since in the cognition "there is freedom from suffering in me" there is the manifestation (*bhāna*) of freedom from suffering with respect to the locus (*dharmin*), it is possible for the absence of that [freedom from suffering] itself to manifest in the cognition "there is no freedom from suffering [in me]. Nor should it be argued that because words such as "there is freedom from suffering in me" convey only the existence of freedom from suffering as qualified by the locus, how can there be a manifestation of freedom from suffering in the locus in the aforementioned cognition? For when the existence of freedom from suffering is manifested as qualified by the locus, the manifestation of freedom from suffering in the locus is also established by experience (*anubhavasiddha*).

Thus, since in the cognition "I am free from suffering" and the like, there is the manifestation of identity with freedom from suffering (*nirduḥkhatādātmya*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*), whereas in "I am not free from suffering" and the like, there is the manifestation of the very absence of that [identity], it is necessary to accept that mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is perceptible.
This is because mutual non-existence is nothing other than the negation of identity.

Nor should it be argued that this is merely the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of freedom from suffering, since freedom from suffering is itself the nature of identity with freedom from suffering.

Since mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) consists in the negation of identity (*tādātmya*) by way of [the relation of] identity itself, so too in cases such as "I am not free from suffering," when a difference appears as having freedom from suffering as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), there also appears the fact that identity has that [freedom from suffering] as its counter-positive. However, in cases such as "freedom from suffering does not exist," this is not the case; thus, one should note that there is no identity of object [between these two types of cognition].

Granted that there may be a perception of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), yet it is simply not a valid means of knowledge (apramāṇa), because it is sublated by the aforementioned proofs. To this he says: "The validity of perception. This has been very firmly established in works such as the *Nyāyāmṛta*, by demonstrating that it cannot be sublated by other means of knowledge.
The point is that otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the sublation (*bādha*) [of the reason] being destroyed in cases such as "fire is not hot because it is produced.
Since this meaning was stated by the ancient teachers themselves, the author did not say "it was stated" but rather said "it was established.
Furthermore, it will be explained later that there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

Alternatively, the validity of the very perception of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), which is the subject under discussion, has been firmly established as being non-erroneous;
the sense is that this is because it is a perception by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), and the witness-consciousness possesses inherent validity.
As for what was stated—that the difference, having the Lord as its counter-correlate and the individual soul as its locus, is perceived by the individual soul—that is not correct.
This is because such a perception does not exist for him.

Furthermore, one should not argue that the very perception, "I am neither omniscient nor free from suffering," apprehends a difference from the Lord; for that perception has as its object the absolute absence of freedom from suffering in the individual soul (*jīva*), and thus lacks the status of having the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the Lord—who is free from suffering—as its object. Thus he raises the objection: "But surely... (*nanu*). If the aforementioned perception were to have the absolute absence of freedom from suffering as its object, then one would first posit freedom from suffering as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) by saying, "Freedom from suffering exists in me," and only then could its negation be performed.
But this is not the case;

rather, in the statement "I am free from suffering," the identity of the individual soul (jīva)—denoted by the word "I"—with the Lord (Īśvara), who is denoted by the term "free from suffering," is presented as a counter-correlative and then negated.
And this negation, being of the nature of a denial of identity, is indeed a mutual absence (anyonyābhāva).

Therefore, this [perception] has as its object precisely the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is God. He provides the rebuttal: "In me... This refers to the perception, "I am not free from suffering. Regarding the phrase "of the locus (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate": the locus is the individual soul (*jīva*), denoted by the word "I";
the counter-correlate is God, designated by the term "free from suffering.

That which makes known the contingency of identity (*tādātmya*) has been stated. Regarding the phrase "by way of grammatical coreferentiality" (*sāmānādhikaraṇyena*): here, coreferentiality consists in having the same case-ending.

The point is that, just as in the case of "the cloth is white" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*), the two expressions "I am free from suffering" (*nirduḥkho 'ham*) and [its counterpart] also convey identity (*tādātmya*) because they both terminate in the nominative case.

Now, an objection may be raised: the perception grasping the blueness of the sky, such as "the sky is blue," is contradicted by the inference that "the sky is colorless because it is all-pervading (*vibhu*), like the Self. Similarly, the perception apprehending the moon's limited extent, such as "the moon is the size of a span (*prādeśa*)," is contradicted by [scriptural statements]: "Its width is known to be eighty-eight thousand *yojanas*, and its measure there is exactly fifteen digits (*kalā*s)."

Just as [the notion of difference] lacks authority because it is sublated by such scriptural passages (*āgama*), so too the perception that apprehends a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) lacks authority. This is because it is sublated by the inference: "The disputed selves do not differ in reality from the Supreme Self, because they are selves, like the Supreme Self," and because it is sublated by the scriptural passage, "Not here is plurality" (*neha nānā*). Therefore, he says: "The authority of perception. Nowhere has it been observed that perception is unsublatable by inference or scripture;
rather, the perception that apprehends the blueness of the sky or the moon's small size arises as something defective due to being affected by defects such as distance.
Subsequently, inference and scripture, having been granted an opportunity by that [perception], are said to be its sublaters.

However, there is no evidence for the lack of acuity in perception that apprehends difference, such that it would be invalid according to the aforementioned method; this is what is established elsewhere in the *Nyāyāmṛta*.
And as for the inferences:

The individual soul (*jīva*) is the locus of a difference whose ontological status is equal to the ontological status of its own existence as a subject relative to Brahman, because it experiences suffering not experienced by Brahman; the counter-example being Brahman itself. Alternatively, Brahman is the locus of a difference whose ontological status is equal to the ontological status of its own existence as a subject relative to the individual soul, because it does not experience the suffering experienced by the individual soul; the counter-example being the individual soul itself. Herein, there is no fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), because differences relative to the individual soul and Brahman—which possess an ontological status equal to the conventional status of a pot—are well-established in the case of a pot as conventional differences.

Since the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman are ultimately real, the difference established as having the same ontological status as their existence is itself established as ultimately real; thus, there is no "proving what is already proven" (*siddhasādhana*).
Furthermore, although suffering and the like reside in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), they are experienced by the individual soul as the one who synthesizes experience.

If Brahman were the synthesizer of suffering, it would follow that liberation—defined as the absence of such suffering—would not be a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*); moreover, since the absence of suffering is necessarily required to avoid contradicting scriptural texts concerning its stainlessness (*nirañjana*), the reason is not unestablished (*asiddhi*).

Having thus stated perception as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the mutual difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as among individual souls, he also states the inferences (*anumāna*s), saying: "And the inferences... The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "they are presented as the means of valid knowledge for the difference between the individual soul and the Lord, and among individual souls and insentient things (*jaḍa*). Regarding the phrase "having the same ontological status as the subject" (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*): the meaning is that it has the same ontological status as the subject (*dharmin*) itself, which is the individual soul. Regarding the phrase "not apprehended by Brahman" (*brahmānanusaṃhita*): [it refers to that which is not realized as non-different from Brahman].

In this context, what is called "conjunction" (*anusandhāna*) does not mean mere direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*), which would leave room for the doubt: "Since Brahman is omniscient, how could suffering not be conjoined with it?
Rather, it refers specifically to the experience "I am happy" or "I am miserable.
For the Lord has no such experience of suffering.
How indeed could one directly perceive pleasure and so forth residing in the individual soul (jīva), as one perceives color and other qualities residing in a jar?
Therefore, it is logical that [the soul] is not conscious of Brahman.

However, some maintain that regarding suffering and the like, because of the conceit of ownership (*svātmīyatva-abhimāna*), there is indeed an experience consisting of a modification (*vikriyā*) characterized by the soul’s fluctuation between states of lowness and highness caused by those [afflictions].
That is to be considered;
for transformation is inseparable from experience,
and it is not possible for that which is produced by it to possess its true nature [as the experiencer].
Nor does a state of being "low" or "high" appear in such instances as "I am happy," as it does with pleasure and the like;
for, unlike the experience [of pleasure], modification (vikriyā) is not experienced as a transitive action.

Indeed, the transitivity of a modification such as "I am low"—which is the object of a cognition like "I am low"—does not manifest in the same way that the experience which is the object of the reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) "I experience pain" or "I experience pleasure" possesses transitivity.
The statement, "The very state of being low or high is called the experience (*bhoga*) of suffering and so forth," is figurative (*gauṇa*), like saying "the cucumber is a fever.
This is because, even when those who possess knowledge (*jñānin*) experience suffering and the like, the cognition "I am low" and so forth does not arise at times.
As it has been said:

"Even for Brahman there might be slight suffering, yet even that would not exist due to the absence of egoistic identification (*anabhimāna*); it does not exist because of the lack of connection with a self. This is also supported by the words of Jaḍabharata in the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa*: "Sleep, pleasure, anger, egoism, and pride do not belong to me, who am indeed born with a body."
"Born with a body" means one who possesses identification with the body (*dehābhimānin*).
Now, an objector might say that even for the Lord (*īśvara*), the reflection "I am possessed of happiness and so forth" is possible;
however, the meaning of the phrase "possessed of happiness and so forth" is simply the state of being the owner of happiness and so forth.
But there is no inherence of those [qualities] [in the Lord],
because they are attributes of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and thus do not exist even in the individual soul (jīva).
And yet, the Blessed One possesses lordship over them.
On the contrary, it is primary even with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*).
Therefore, if it is asked how it can be qualified as "not being contemplated as Brahman," we say no;
for what is called the contemplation of "I am happy" and so forth is the experience that "non-differentiated happiness is favorable" and "non-differentiated suffering is unfavorable."
For it has been stated that [the Lord is] "supreme" by virtue of His similarity to other forms of bliss and His favorability toward them;
however, the Lord does not possess such a nature of experiencing suffering,
because the suffering of individual souls (jīvas) is not contrary to the Lord.
Therefore, it is appropriate that "not being connected with Brahman" (*brahmānanusaṃhita*) is a qualification of suffering.

However, some say that what is intended to be expressed as the cause is either the connection with the suffering of others (*paratantra-duḥkhānusandhāna*), or the connection with suffering that does not encompass all objects (*asarvaviṣaya-duḥkhānusandhāna*), or the state of possessing inferiority caused by suffering through the relation of non-primary ownership (*amukhya-svāmitā-sambandha*).
That too must be considered.

Since the word *anusandhāna* signifies a specific type of experience according to the method already stated, no purpose for the qualification "dependent on another" (*pāratantrya*) and so forth is observed.

Now, if it is argued that this reason is "uniquely inconclusive" (*asādhāraṇa*) because it is absent in the insentient, which constitutes the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), as well as in Lakṣmī, we say no;
for when a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*) exists, that [inconclusiveness] does not constitute a defect, as it does not lead to the emergence of a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*).
Furthermore, since favorable arguments (*anukūlatarka*) will be stated here [later], one might object:

"In this context, since the mere fact of being a recollector of suffering is sufficient to establish the reason, the qualification 'not recollected by Brahman' is redundant. We reply: No, for it serves to clarify the favorable argument in order to avoid the charge that the reason is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).

Just as in the case of the sūtra "Because of seeing [it is not so], for it is not based on scripture" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*), where there might be a doubt regarding the lack of logical necessity—namely, that "let there be the state of being seen, but let there not be the state of being denotable"—the qualification "provided it is not known through perception and other means" is added for the purpose of establishing a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*) consisting in the sublation of the reason (*hetūcchitti*).

Similarly here as well, if there were no difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman even though the soul experiences suffering, then Brahman—which is non-different from that soul—would likewise experience suffering. Since the subject of the inference is the soul alone, there is no positive example (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*); therefore, he says: "by way of negative concomitance" (*vyatirekeṇa*). Having thus stated the inference regarding the difference where the soul is the subject and Brahman is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), he states the inference regarding the difference where Brahman is the subject and the soul is the counter-correlative: "or Brahman... (*brahma vā*).
Thus, regarding these two types of inference as well, is an ultimately real difference being established, or a conventional one? Not the first.

Because the qualifier would be unestablished [in the first case], and because it would result in proving what is already established [in the second case], the qualification "having the same ontological status as the existence of the subject" (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*) is employed for both parts of the probandum (*sādhya*) in order to resolve these objections.

Therefore, how is the avoidance of these two faults achieved? To this, he demonstrates the avoidance of both in sequence with the words "herein" (*atre*). Regarding the phrase "of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman": the words "as the substrata" (*dharmibhūtayoḥ*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis. Now, an objection may be raised: since suffering and so forth are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), how can the individual soul be their experiencer? And conversely, how is it that Brahman does not experience them?

Since there is no subverting argument against accepting that [the self] is a substratum for the experience of suffering just as the living body is, the reasons in both of these two inferences are unestablished (*asiddhi*). To this he says: "Of suffering and so forth" (*duḥkhādīnām*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), pleasure and other such things, as well as the attributes of the body, senses, hunger, thirst, and so on, are included.
In the phrase "the internal organ and so forth" (*antaḥkaraṇādī*), the word "and so forth" includes the body, the senses, and the rest.

Although only a portion of suffering (*duḥkha*) is under discussion here, pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest are included as examples. Regarding the phrase "because the individual soul (*jīva*) is the synthesizer (*anusandhātṛ*)," this connects with the subsequent statement that there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*) in the first inference. For there is no restrictive rule that only what pertains to the soul must be synthesized by the soul and not what pertains to another;
since the meaning of the word "synthesis" (*anusandhāna*) consists merely in the experience of "this is contrary to me" and so forth.

The sense is that this [reason] is possible even in the case of suffering and so forth residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). "Characterized by the state of being That" means characterized by the state of being Brahman as the one who experiences suffering and so forth;

the sense is that in the Māyā-vāda system, liberation is accepted precisely as the attainment of the state of Brahman. "The absence of That" means the absence of being the experiencer of suffering and so forth. "There is no unestablishedness" means that this applies to the second inference as well.

"The individual soul has Brahman as its counter-correlative" means that consciousness qualified by the nature of an individual soul (*jīvatva*) has consciousness qualified by the nature of Brahman (*brahmatva*) as its counter-correlative.

The phrase "having Brahman as its counter-correlative" (*brahmapratiyogika*) is used to exclude the inclusion of insentient objects (*jaḍa*), which are not the subject under discussion. The phrase "the substratum," etc., is used to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
The meaning is that the substratum is the living consciousness (*jīvacit*), and its existence is ultimately real and identical to that [of Brahman].
Furthermore, it should be understood that "identity of level of reality" (*samānasattva*) is determined by a property directly pervaded by the universal "existence-ness" (*sattātva*).

By this, the objection that there is a "proving of what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatā*) because [the subject] is similar to [other things] by virtue of the property of being an object (*padārtha*) through conventional existence (*vyāvahārikī sattā*) is refuted. As for the statement that "ultimate existence" (*pāramārthika*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), even so, the ultimate nature is established by the force of the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should be understood that even if one substitutes the term "having the same ontological status as the existence of the locus" (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*) with "not being an effect of the cognition of the locus" (*dharmijñānākārya*),

or "not being sublated by the cognition of the locus" (*dharmijñānābādhya*), or "persisting for as long as the locus exists" (*yāvaddharmikālamanuvartamāna*), or "being non-conditional" (*anaupādhika*), the aforementioned distinction is established.
The reason is simply "because he does not contemplate Brahman. The term "suffering" (duḥkha) is included for the purpose of manifesting the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā).
The reason is simply "because he does not contemplate suffering."
The remaining words are intended to indicate the causal agency (*prayojakatā*).
This statement is made with reference to two distinct inferences (*anumāna*).
Alternatively, what is intended here by "realization" (*anusandhāna*) is simply direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*).
And thus, according to our view, the property of being a pursuer of suffering is deviant with respect to the omniscient Brahman.
"Brahmānanusaṃhitam" (not pursued by Brahman) is an adverbial modifier meaning "because of being a pursuer of suffering in such a manner.
Its sense is: "because of possessing a cognition that is of a different genus from the knowledge of Brahman and which serves as a cause for baseness."

If it is argued that even so, the statement regarding suffering is redundant, we say no; for what is intended to be expressed is the state of being a sufferer, which is established by the logical reason (*hetu*) in the sentence. The same applies to the subsequent syllogisms as well.
Although in the second application (of the argument) the positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) alone is easily grasped in the case of a jar and so forth,

nevertheless, even if the qualification "ultimately real" (*pāramārthika*) were occasionally added, this would not constitute the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), because it is possible to grasp the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*). It is for the purpose of indicating this that the negative concomitance is demonstrated.
He states the intended meaning of the qualification "the subject" (*dharmin*) and so forth with the words beginning "herein" (*atretyādi*).

Now, one might object: "In that case, since the reason (*hetu*) is absent in a jar—which possesses a difference having the same ontological status as the existence of the subject whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is Brahman—the reason would be 'uniquely inconclusive' (*asādhāraṇya*). This is not so, because of the disagreement among disputants (*vādivipratipatti*).

Some maintain that being uncommon (*asādhāraṇya*) is not a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*); others hold that it is included within the "unestablished due to lack of pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddha*). Yet others argue that only a reason for which no similar instance (*sapakṣa*) exists is such [an uncommon one], whereas a reason for which a similar instance does exist is "inconclusive" (*vyabhicārin*). This is because, just like occurring in an inappropriate place, not occurring in an appropriate place also constitutes the meaning of "inconclusiveness."

Some, however, say that even though [the reason] exists elsewhere, because one does not perceive the relation between the probandum and that [reason], it produces doubt regarding the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and is therefore a distinct fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).
In reality, however, this is not a fallacy of the reason, because pervasion is possible through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Nor does it produce doubt, since such doubt is precluded by the establishment of a favorable logical argument (*anukūlatarka*).
Otherwise, there would be an equality of doubt regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*) even for smoke and the like, which exist in only a few similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Or, let this fault remain;
what is intended by "being a subject of suffering" is "being a locus of defects.
And since that exists in a jar, there is no fault whatsoever.

If it is argued that, in the doctrine of the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, the reflection (*anusandhāna*) residing in the soul cannot be established as residing in Brahman, we say no.

For if this were so, one would be unable to establish even conventional difference through contradictory attributes in cases such as snow and fire, because the heat residing in the fire would then have to reside in the snow as well. Furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) under discussion is not "unestablished" (*asiddha*) in the sense of being certain; rather, it is seized by doubt induced by the doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
And thus, it is precisely the natural doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) that is not induced [by anything else].

Consequently, when there is a doubt induced by a doubt regarding the probandum, the reason’s being a non-object of such a doubt constitutes what is called the "unestablished" (*asiddhi*) of the reason.
Otherwise, even a doubt regarding smoke induced by a doubt regarding fire would likewise be [an instance of unestablishedness].
Even in that case, it is logical that there should be doubt regarding the smoke, which is the effect, based on the doubt regarding the fire, which is its cause.
Now, some might argue: "Even if the fire is doubted, it does not invalidate the doubt regarding the smoke perceived through direct perception;

rather, by the force of the certainty regarding the cause, that very doubt [of the fire] dissolves. If that is so, then here too, by the force of scriptural texts such as "without a second," the doubt regarding non-difference itself dissolves. Now, an objection is raised: in the second syllogism, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason—defined as the absolute absence of non-apprehension—with respect to the individual soul (*jīva*).

If it is argued that [the reason] is unestablished because it is co-located with its own absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), we say no; for what is intended is an absolute non-existence that is not co-located with its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Thus, there is no lack of establishment (*asiddhi*). The meaning is as follows: by stating "because the individual soul (*jīva*) is a cognizer" in the first inference, the nature of the reason itself is established; and by stating in the second [inference] that "there must necessarily be an absence of that [cognizing nature] in Brahman, which is the qualification of that [reason]," the nature of the first qualification is established in the second, and thus there is no lack of establishment.

"And the inferences" means that these are the proofs for the primary distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as the incidental distinctions between individual souls among themselves and between insentient objects (*jaḍa*) among themselves. Regarding the term "individual soul": the examination of the subject (*pakṣa*) will occur later in the root text itself.

The phrase "not being contemplated as Brahman" is intended to indicate a supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*) for the reason (*hetu*), but it is not part of the formal structure of the reason itself, as that would be redundant.
But there is no deviation with respect to Brahman,
because, being omniscient, He is the one who experiences all suffering.
Nor does His experience of suffering entail that liberation— characterized by the cessation of that [suffering]— would fail to be a human goal (apuruṣārtha).
In your view, since that state is not liberation, your position suffers from the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*).
Nor should you argue that we do not admit Brahman to be a partaker of suffering because it would contradict the scripture stating, "He is without blemish, without fault";
for such an argument would contradict other scriptures such as "He who is all-knowing," and would constitute a departure from your own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

Nor should it be argued that, although the Blessed Lord is the one who experiences all suffering, the intended meaning is not that He experiences suffering through a relationship of ownership—such as "it is not my suffering"—but rather that the *jīva* is of such a nature; for there would thus be neither a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) nor a lack of proof (*asiddhi*).

This is because, according to your own view, the primary status of being the master of all belongs exclusively to the Supreme Lord, while that of the *jīvas* is secondary and granted by Him, as established in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "But the presiding over fire and so forth belongs to Him, because of His meditation" (Brahma-sūtra 2.4.15). Furthermore, it is said: "Even though dwelling in hell, the Lord is not said to be an enjoyer of suffering."

It should not be argued that there is no deviation [from the rule] because the state of being subject to suffering and so forth—consisting of the experience of lowliness and loftiness caused by suffering—is restricted solely to the individual soul (*jīva*), on the basis of the statement: "For the experience of suffering and so forth is called 'lowliness and loftiness'; the Lord does not undergo such lowliness and loftiness, for He always perceives [it].
This is because [the text speaks of] lowliness and loftiness...

Furthermore, because the state of residing in the senses, the body, and so forth does not exist in the individual soul (*jīva*) through a direct relationship, whereas it exists in the Lord (*bhagavat*) even through the relationship of ownership; moreover, just as Arjuna—who does not experience the pleasure produced by the union with Śacī residing in Indra—remains non-different from Indra, why should Brahman, despite experiencing the suffering residing in the individual soul, not be non-different from the *jīva*? Thus, [the opponent's reason] lacks probative force.
Furthermore, is "insentience" (jaḍatva) and "Lakṣmī" the subject (pakṣa) or the co-subject (sapakṣa)? Not the first,
because since those two lack the capacity for the apprehension of suffering, there would be the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (bhāgāsiddhi).
Not the second [alternative],
because it would result in the fallacy of being an uncommon (asādhāraṇa) reason.

Nor should it be argued that since the uncommon reason is a defect only insofar as it obstructs the apprehension of positive concomitance (anvayavyāpti), it is not a defect in the case of a purely negative inference (vyatirekin).

If it is argued that where the probandum (sādhya) is present, the absence of the reason (hetu) constitutes a counter-inference (satpratipakṣa) by virtue of being a negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti) with the absence of the probandum— and thus remains a defect even there—
it is replied: in this case,
the reason is either the nature of experiencing suffering dependent on others, or the nature of experiencing suffering that does not encompass all objects.
Nor should it be said that "being dependent" (*paratantratva*) or "not having all things as its object" (*asarvaviṣayatva*) is the probans, as these are merely qualifiers of the subject;
for by the two terms "dependent" and "not having all things as its object," there is an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of a specific class-character (*vaijātya*) residing in the experience of suffering.
Alternatively, the probans is the state of possessing inferiority caused by suffering through the relation of non-primary ownership (*amukhyasvāmitva*).
Since that too is indeed the individual soul (jīva), there is no deviation [from the rule].
This has been explained by us in detail in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*) of the *Madhvatantramukhāloka*.
Nor is the reason [for our position] unestablished (*aprayojaka*).

In your own view as well, since Arjuna must necessarily be pervaded by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) that constitute Indra’s individual soul (jīva) due to being an incarnation of Indra, you must assert that he possesses only a single empirical soul. Consequently, it follows that his failure to experience the pleasure arising from the enjoyment of Śacī and so forth must be necessitated by factors such as his connection with human food and bodily constituents. Furthermore, it cannot be said here that Brahman’s non-experience of suffering is caused by limiting adjuncts, because He is entirely free from all limiting adjuncts.
Furthermore, the suffering arising from Indra’s worship and so forth was not experienced by Arjuna at all, whereas everything residing in Arjuna was experienced by the sense organ;
and since this is not the case in the present instance, how can there be non-difference?
Nor is there any lack of commonality [between the two cases].

Since favorable *tarka*s will be stated [later], there is no emergence of an unestablished counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) based on the uncommon (*asādhāraṇya*) [reason] in a negative inference (*vyatirekin*).
For this very reason, the elders say that "uncommonness" is a defect only in a particular state [of knowledge].
Or, out of fear of such uncommonness, he says: "Or Brahman. Here too, the phrase "conceived by the individual soul" is for the purpose of making favorable *tarka*s manifest.

Just as in the previous case there was an avoidance of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), here in our own system there is an avoidance of the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the subject (*svarūpāsiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "and the inferences": this refers to the previously mentioned distinctions and so forth. Regarding the term "having Brahman as the counter-correlative" (*brahmapratiyogika*): this is stated because we do not accept a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a property that exists distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*) over [Brahman] itself. Therefore, there is no consequence of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*) through the objection that the subject would be unestablished, since there is no difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by such properties as "that particularity residing in Brahman" (*tadvyaktitva*) or "Brahman-hood" (*brahmatva*).

Furthermore, since the difference having Brahman as its counter-correlative is a purely positive (kevalānvayi) entity, there is no possibility for negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), because the absence of that which is delimited by the probandum-delimiting property—which would be common to that [Brahman]—is unestablished.
However, there is no fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

Because no [distinction] coexistent with the reality-level (*samānasattāka*) of consciousness—characterized by the "living-ness" (*jīvatva*) to be described later—is admitted by the opponent, the probandum (*sādhya*) lacks the status of being established for both parties. Regarding the phrase "not apprehended by Brahman": although the mere quality of being an apprehender of suffering does not suffer from fallacies such as deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the specific qualification "not apprehended by Brahman" serves to state the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of suffering and so forth. This is intended to evoke a favorable logical argument (*anukūlatarka*) based on the fact that, if there were identity [between the individual soul and Brahman], it would be impossible for Brahman to lack the apprehension of the suffering apprehended by the individual soul.
The same applies to the subsequent inferences.

Alternatively, even though it serves to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*), its inclusion in the body of the reason (*hetu*) is indeed proper because it is useful for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by way of generating the aforementioned favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*).

However, this is according to the view of the Navyas (the Neo-logicians), who hold that a mere qualification which is not useful for that purpose is useless and thus has no place in the body of the reason.

This has been explained by us on the occasion of refuting the inference proving reality (*satyatva*) in the *Guru-Advaitacandrikā* and elsewhere, as well as in our *Tattvodyota-ṭippaṇī* and in the *Dvaitadyumaṇi* during the investigation of the reason "being liberated" (*muktatva*).

The inclusion of the condition "having the same ontological status as the locus" (*dharmisattāsamānasattākatva*) in both parts of the probandum (*sādhya*) is intended to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) for the opponent, by taking into account the mutual empirical difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.
He himself will state later that the establishment of the probandum occurs only in the case of objects such as a pot.

Regarding the phrase "by way of negative concomitance, like the individual soul": [This refers to the formulation of the inference where the absence of the probandum is shown in the case of the individual soul.]

In this context, although positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyāpti*) is possible regarding [the example of] a jar and so forth, it has not been stated with the intention that it can be understood by the students themselves; rather, negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) alone has been stated in accordance with the association with the preceding and following inferences.

Alternatively, it should be understood that even if the aforementioned reason (*hetu*) exists in the absence of existence (*asati sattve*), because the probandum (*sādhya*)—which is constituted by the existence of its own locus (*svadharmin*)—would be unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), the property of "sentience" (*cetana-tva*) must be introduced into the reason for the sake of simplicity (*lāghava*) in order to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*); therefore, since positive concomitance is not possible, only negative concomitance has been stated.

Now, since suffering and the like are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the capacity for "synthetic unification" (*anusandhātṛtva*)—whether defined as being a knower of suffering residing within oneself or as the nature of direct perception thereof—is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the individual soul (*jīva*) with respect to the first inference.

Furthermore, in the second inference, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the absence of being a cognizer of suffering associated with the living self (*jīva*) exists in the living self as well; therefore, he says: "of suffering and so forth. [This means] even though [suffering] is dependent on the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it resides therein through identity (*tādātmya*). "Of the living self" means: because of its being the cognizer thereof. The sense is that, within the constitution of being a cognizer, residing in oneself through identity is not intended in the case of suffering and so forth. Now, one might object: "Being a cognizer thereof" must mean "possessing direct perception of that," since defining it by the nature of knowledge (*jñānatva*) would be over-extensive (*atiprasakta*)."

And thus, since even your Lord—who is the very essence of the category of Brahman—possesses direct perception, there is no established instance of suffering that He does not keep in mind; consequently, in the first inference, the very nature of the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Furthermore, if the qualification "not kept in mind by Brahman" is included within the body of the reason, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Brahman itself, because the quality of being a cognizer of suffering exists in Brahman as well.
If it is argued that there is a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) regarding the second inference, we say no;
for the act of recollection (*anusandhāna*) is distinct from that direct perception (*tatpratyakṣa*).
And its nature [as such] consists in possessing modifications such as depression (*nīcatva*) and so forth, which are induced by that direct perception.
And that [distinction] exists only in the nature of the individual soul (jīva), not in the Supreme Self (paramātman).
As it is stated in the Bhāṣya:
"The very state of being low or high is designated as the experience of suffering and so forth."

In the *Sudhā*, on the very occasion of commenting on the *Anuvyākhyāna* passage, "If there were falsity (*mithyātva*) regarding suffering and so forth," it is stated: "The individual soul experiences only real modifications characterized by lowliness and loftiness; and such a modification does not result in the loss of the soul's essential nature.
[Objection: But how is this [point] incorporated into the body of the formal argument (*hetuśarīra*)?

Nor should it be argued that the reason—namely, "possessing a modification dependent on the direct perception of suffering"—is not established because of the absence of being a generator of a modification of Brahman’s state;

for in that [Advaita] system, since a modification of Brahman’s state is not admitted and an absence whose counter-positive is not recognized as valid is not accepted, the reason consisting in the absence of being its generator remains unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).

If it is argued that there is no proof (*asiddhi*) because I do not accept [the existence of] that [agency] in the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), when the reason is refined by either (1) incorporating the absence of producing a modification of its own function as delimited by association, or (2) incorporating the direct perception of suffering as being identical with Brahman which possesses the absence of a modification produced by itself—then this is not so.

Even in your own view, since it is established by hundreds of scriptural and Puranic texts that the qualified Brahman who is the object of worship—such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa—is eternally free from suffering, and since the suffering of individual souls (*jīvas*) is established by direct experience, you too must accept this distinction. Therefore, I am also able to refine my reason (the *hetu*, i.e., the body of the argument) by incorporating what has been established by you. Furthermore, I do not define "being a cognizer" (*anusandhātṛtva*) as possessing a perceptual mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) whose object is suffering and so forth; rather, such a state exists for the individual souls.

It cannot be argued that the Lord’s perception consists of a modification of *māyā* and therefore He lacks the capacity for synthetic recollection (*anusandhātṛtva*), whereas [the individual soul] possesses it;
for if that [Lord's perception] were capable of withstanding such an argument, I too could certainly have included that very point within the body of my own reasoning. However, that is not possible.
This is because, since suffering and the like are known by the Witness (*sākṣin*), neither you nor I admit the existence of a mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) in that regard.

Or, if it were admitted [that such a perception exists], then since even for yogins there exists a perception—consisting of an internal mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) directed toward another's suffering—which serves as the basis for the linguistic usage "direct perception" (*sākṣātkāra*), it would follow that they too would be experiencers of that suffering.

Nor can it be argued that one should accept, within the perception of a sufferer, either a "worldly objectivity" (*laukika-viṣayatā*) or some distinct "specific universal" (*vaijātya*)—excluded from the perceptions of yogins, lords, and so forth—and that it is only when delimited by this that the subsequent reflective awareness (*anusandhāna*) is said to occur.

This is because, according to the refined final position (*niṣkṛṣṭa-siddhānta*) that suffering and the like are cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣivedya*), there would be no other way to account for the phenomenon.

Furthermore, even under the view that [the reflection] is accepted as real, since the mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) is a property of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇadharma*), the individual soul (*jīva*) cannot be its "experiencer" (*anusandhātṛ*) by virtue of possessing that property.

If it is argued that possessing that property occurs through the relation of ownership (*svāmitā*), then since you yourself accept that the Lord (*īśvara*) possesses ownership—as seen in such scriptural passages as "He is the controller of all, the lord of all"—it would be impossible to avoid the conclusion that He too is a sufferer.
If you claim that being an experiencer consists merely in having ownership dependent on another, then let that very same [dependent ownership] be included in my reason (*hetu*) regarding the body.

It should not be argued that even if I do not accept the perception of suffering and so forth as being of the nature of a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), I must nevertheless include "the state of possessing the perception of suffering" in the body of the reason by means of the relation of ownership dependent on another;
for otherwise, it would follow that Lakṣmī is a sufferer according to your own view.

This is because the perception of the suffering belonging to another—which constitutes her very nature—exists in Lakṣmī as well, just as it does in the individual soul (*jīva*), by virtue of a specific power through the relation of ownership that constitutes her nature and is dependent upon the Lord (*īśvara*).

How is it so for you as well? Because it is impossible to abandon both the dependence on the Lord established by numerous Śrutis and Purāṇas, and the state of being free from suffering, which follows from having no other master.

One might object: "In reality, I do not admit anything at all; I accept all these arrangements merely as a conventional appearance, so there is no need for such fine-grained scrutiny (atikṣoda) regarding my position.
To this we reply: if that were the case, since one would end up abandoning scrutiny in every instance, your very act of inquiry would fall into futility.

Furthermore, since Bhāskara, who accepts the reality of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), must necessarily establish a systematic order (*vyavasthā*), the two aforementioned inferences apply primarily against him alone. For it has been stated elsewhere by the commentators (*ṭīkākāra*): "Since the Māyāvādin accepts that everything is imagined (*kalpita*), a conceptual order might indeed be possible for him; however, this is not the case for Bhāskara, and therefore these [inferences] result in the undesirable consequence (*duḥkhānusandhāna*) of [proving] his position. And so forth.
This refutation was already stated in the *Upādhikhaṇḍana* during the occasion of rejecting the view of Bhāskara.
Likewise, it is found in the *Tattvodyota*.

Similarly, in the *Anuvyākhyāna* as well—wherein, having accepted the reality of the world, one proceeds to refute the doctrine of both difference and non-difference regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self—it is stated precisely during the commentary on the sūtra, "And for this very reason, there is a comparison such as that of the sun's reflection and so forth."

In the *Gītātātparya* as well, after stating the objections against the view that the adjunct (*upādhi*) is real—such as the undesirable consequence of one person experiencing the pleasure, pain, and so forth of another—it is stated that these same defects apply even to the view that the adjunct is illusory (*mithyā*). Accordingly, there arises the contingency of applying the same argument regarding the restriction of the experience of suffering and so on, even against the proponent of illusoriness (*mithyātvavādin*).

And thus, since even he must accept the conventional status established by the world, the aforementioned inconsistency remains indeed in force. If it is argued that "being a cognizer of suffering" consists merely in having the relationship of ownership dependent on both the Supreme Self and His power in the form of His consort—a state which exists only in the individual soul (*jīva*)—then let that very factor be included within the body of my reason (*hetu*).
For even by that much, my desired conclusion is established.
In reality, however, let the direct perception of suffering, or suffering itself, be the cause by virtue of the relationship of being a master dependent on another.
Even if there exists the direct perception of individual suffering, or that suffering itself, in Lakṣmī by virtue of the relationship of being released [from bondage], it does not cause us any harm;
for, due to the absence of any contemplation of the suffering accepted in our own tenet, it is logically established that her consciousness remains untouched by suffering.

Nor should it be argued that, on the view that perception is the cause [of rebirth], the qualification "having suffering as its object" (*duḥkhaviṣayakatva*) in the definition of perception is redundant;
for, by means of the aforementioned relation, mere perception is not subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

This is because, by accepting that suffering itself is the cause through the relation of being perceived by one who possesses ownership dependent on another, there is no redundancy in the formulation as it stands.

Alternatively, let suffering (*duḥkha*) be the cause by way of the relation of "possessing an inferiority brought about by one's own direct realization. In my view, such an inferiority arises at that time and is distinct from that which is eternally established. Even by others, an inferiority consisting of being miserable and so forth—which is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*)—must be admitted in accordance with scriptural authorities such as "I have transcended the perishable" (*yasmāt kṣaramatīto 'ham*). Therefore, since it is included in the body of the relation delimiting causality (*hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha*) under the form of "inferiority common to both," its perception is not established [for the opponent].

In reality, however, there is no fault whatsoever, because this inference must be employed by first establishing—on the strength of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa)—against the opponent as well, our proposed reason consisting in the state of being subject to modification (*vikriyāvattva*), which is distinct from God. This is the essential point.
Now, even so, the quality of being a cognizer of suffering not experienced by Indra exists in Arjuna;
and the quality of being a cognizer of suffering not experienced by Arjuna exists in Indra.
Since there is no difference between these two, how can this be tenable?
Do not say so. What is meant by this?

If it is argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) intended to subvert the pervasion (*vyāpti*) necessary for the inference under discussion, that is simply not the case. For such a deviation would occur only if one were to follow the general pervasion: "Whatever does not experience the suffering associated with something is distinct from it. But this is not the case here.
Since it has been stated that the negative concomitance (vyatirekavyāpti) itself is constituted by the reason and the probandum under discussion,
if the intention is that this reason is "unproving" (aprayojaka) according to that method,
then the illustrative example (dṛṣṭānta) itself is unestablished (asiddha).
Because Indra possesses the capacity for the continuous experience (*anusandhāna*) of all pleasure and pain delimited by Arjuna’s body;

and because Arjuna likewise possesses the status of being an enjoyer of pleasures and other states, such as the great fruits resulting from worship and other practices performed while delimited by Indra’s body—does the general rule that the non-experience of any slight pleasure, pain, or the like [by one] is due to the Lord’s power (the power of the Lord who accomplishes the impossible), which is augmented by the enjoyment of human food and so forth, thereby causing the non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) of that experience of suffering etc. defined by their difference, become sublated?

Because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is characterized by the presence of a limiting condition (*sopādhika*), it is not a defect; this has been stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the *Bhaktipāda*: "That which is established even as a general rule (*utsargataḥ*) and is free from exceptions will indeed become a means of valid knowledge (*māna*) through the exception of deviation," and this was further explained in the *Sudhā* during the commentary on that passage.
Now, one might ask: how can even what is stated in the *Sudhā*—namely, that deviation accompanied by a limiting condition is not a defect—be logically justified?

Even if the deviation (vyabhicāra) is due to a limiting condition (sopādhika), its capacity to obstruct pervasion (vyāpti) is unavoidable. Otherwise, even a deviation that is without a limiting condition (nirupādhika) would not be a defect, as there would be no distinction between the two cases.
This is not so.
For it appears thus here:
pervasion (vyāpti) is the rule of concomitance (sāhacarya-niyama),
because it has been stated exactly so in the *Paddhati*.

The meaning of the *Paddhati* is as follows: pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in the possession of that which qualifies as the locus of non-occurrence in that which lacks the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavadavṛttitvādhikaraṇatāyogyatāvattva*), within the general class of loci possessing such a delimitor of the reasonhood (*hetutāvacchedaka*) as belongs to the substratum of the delimitor of the reasonhood in question; it is the possession of such a delimitor of reasonhood within the general class of substrata of the delimitor of reasonhood in question. Pervasion in a specific instance must be defined by incorporating those specific locations and so forth where, when the reason is qualified by its occurrence in such locations, the inference of the probandum occurs as a matter of experience. In cases of purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) inference where the absence of the probandum is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), pervasion as defined by that [absence] is easily available even for those who maintain that absences have unestablished counter-correlates (*aprāmāṇikapratiyogikābhāvavādin*).
In every instance where there is a valid reason (*saddhetu*), such fitness (*tādṛśayogyatā*) exists;

for it is established by the common experience of all people that its ascertainment occurs through means of knowledge such as perception—accompanied by favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*)—due to the non-perception of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and other such defects.

Even if, in some cases, due to specific causes such as mantras or medicinal herbs, a particular individual instance of the reason (*hetuvyaktiviśeṣa*) should come to reside in a locus where the probandum is absent—as in the case of a barren woman—the fitness established by the means of knowledge with respect to the reason in its general form (*hetusāmānya*) is not thereby removed.

Although this individual instance is indeed capable of possessing the relation of not occurring in the locus of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvādhikaraṇāvṛttitva*), nevertheless, due to the force of powerful causes, its connection with the absence of the probandum is established through the universal experience of all people.

Otherwise, even when the causal complex consisting of eating and so forth is present, if satisfaction does not occur due to the power of potent mantras, medicines, and the like, it would follow that all worldly practice would lose its validity—on the grounds that "this [instance], though fit for satisfaction, has become incapable of producing satisfaction due to the power of potent mantras, medicines, and so forth."

Nor is there any powerful subverting argument against the validity of the aforementioned cognition and linguistic usage, by which [the opponent’s position] would result in an undesired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). Furthermore, compatibility (*yogyatā*) is a specific property residing in each respective [term], which constitutes their very nature;
and it serves as the determinant for the locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatā*) of such a relation as resides in those respective [terms].

To the question, "Why is it that smoke alone—and not jars or other things—does not occur where fire is absent? everyone must reply that its very nature (*svabhāva*) is the regulating factor. Furthermore, since nature itself is dependent upon God, as established by the authority of the scriptural passage: "By whose grace these [factors] exist, and by whose neglect they do not exist: nature, the individual soul, karma, substance, time, the Vedas, and action."

It should not be argued that the aforementioned status of being a locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) might be directly governed by God, rather than by an intermediate power in the form of *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature),
for there are many instances observed where the power of the Lord brings about an object only through the mediation of external causes.
Otherwise, one would be forced to deny even the power conducive to a jar that resides in a clay rod.

Nor should it be argued that "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*) itself is precisely of the nature of such fitness (*yogyatā*); for smokeness lacks the status of being a determinant (*prayojaka*) because it does not subsist in a domain narrower than the locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatā*) residing in light and other such things. On the contrary, since it is perceived through the cognition "this [light] is unfit to possess such non-occurrence" (*avṛttitva*), it is perceived precisely as an indicator of such fitness, and thus it is distinct from it.

And thus, even when [the reason] possesses such an occurrence that depends on a powerful cause—thereby overriding its own intrinsic nature—there is no possibility [of the fallacy], because such fitness exists therein.
For this very reason, there is no obstruction to the cognition of pervasion, since [the presence of such fitness] does not have a contradictory object;
rather, it is the cognition of the absence of such fitness alone that constitutes the contradiction.
Nor should it be argued that because the object is not sublated, the knowledge of pervasion residing in that locus is not erroneous;
nor that if it were valid, then the inference arising at a time when no sublation has occurred regarding the object of exception would have to be valid,
since a correct consideration of the mark (*liṅga-parāmarśa*) lacks the capacity to produce an erroneous inference.

This is because it is possible for [the reason] to produce error through the power of generating a misconception caused by the defect consisting in having as its object that which lacks the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavat*).

This is since the Naiyāyikas accept that even the inference of smell in a jar at the moment of its production—which is produced by a *parāmarśa* based on the valid mark of "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*)—is of the nature of an error.

If it is argued: "Why not simply include 'being different from the cause whose object is the exception' (*apavādaviṣayahetubhinnatva*) within the scope of the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*), rather than this elaborate effort?", we say: No.

Because it is impossible to ascertain the absence of exceptions—whether they take the form of sensory or non-sensory counter-instances, such as mantras or medicinal herbs—that pertain to both past and present times, it is impossible to ascertain [the probans] as being qualified by the exclusion of those specific instances. Consequently, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in a probans delimited by that form is untenable.
Furthermore, this would result in the non-arising of the valid cognition of pervasion at a time when no exception is manifest.

Since the collection of all such individual exclusions where an exception might occur is difficult for anyone but an omniscient being to grasp, there would follow the collapse of the valid cognition of pervasion for those who are not omniscient and lack such knowledge.
Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

For it is observed that certain foods cause death and other such outcomes due to defects in the sight [of the food] and so forth, while others are observed not to produce satisfaction due to the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like. Consequently, for those who—based on the knowledge that the mere act of eating possesses the property of being pervaded by "being a means to a desired end qualified by not producing a powerful undesired result"—proceed toward eating after inferring that very quality, or for those non-omniscient persons who possess an inference of satisfaction based on the mark (*liṅga*) of eating due to the knowledge that mere eating is pervaded by satisfaction, there would follow the undesirable consequence of their cognition being erroneous (*bhrama*). Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence.
A discerning person can only act for the sake of fulfilling their own stated intention.

If causality were based on the knowledge of a cause characterized by a multitude of diverse attributes, the delimiting condition of that causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) would result in an excessively cumbersome body; therefore, the aforementioned method alone is correct.
One should not raise the objection that this same [over-extension] would apply even to cases where there is a natural deviation (*svarasa-vyabhicāra*).
Because one resorts to the aforementioned method immediately after establishing the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the form of the stated fitness by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, what was stated in the *Sudhā* is indeed correct.

Furthermore, the word "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) in that passage also refers solely to subsisting in that which lacks the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavadvṛttitva*), and not to the absence of the stated fitness.

Therefore, since there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) whatsoever in the scope of the exception (apavāda), the objection that [the reason] is a defect because it is admitted [as such] has no basis; thus, there is no room for such a doubt.
Now, even so, this inference is still flawed.

Since the subject (dharmin) is introduced in its universal form as "the state of being a substratum" (āśrayatva), and since a difference of the same ontological order as the pot-subject—namely, a conventional (vyāvahārika) difference—is already established in the case of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, both inferences suffer from the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā).

Furthermore, if the respective subjects (*dharmi*) are specifically included within the body of the probandum (*sādhya*), there is simply the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If the subject in the form of Brahman is specifically included, then because a difference co-existent with it (*tatsamānasattāka-bheda*) is unestablished, there is again the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*). Even if one includes "one's own subject" (*svadharmī*), if by the word "own" one grasps the difference from insentient matter (*jaḍa*) residing in the subjects that are merely Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*), there is again the same fallacy of an unestablished qualifier as before.

If it is argued that when one grasps the difference from consciousness (cit) with respect to a locus such as a jar alone, there is sublation (bādha) in both inferences because [such a difference] is absent in both the individual souls (jīva) and Brahman;
and that by taking a difference common to both the conscious and the insentient, the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā) is unavoidable—[we reply]: no.

For in the view of the ancients, since "one's own-ness" (svatva) is somehow pervasive, if the difference is introduced as "by way of one's own-ness," there is no lack of the probandum (sādhyāprasiddhi).

However, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking a difference that is common to both Brahman and the insentient (*jaḍa*), one must adopt one's own position—that there is no single difference residing in both [entities] by virtue of the difference being the very nature of the thing (*vastusvarūpa*) as it relates to each respective substrate.

Regarding the method of establishing a probandum (*sādhya*) that is unestablished even in the subject (*pakṣa*) when it is introduced as "by its own nature" (*svatvena*), the procedure has been demonstrated in the *Dvaitadyumaṇi* and should be consulted therein.

The solution proposed by modern Naiyāyikas and others, however, is that the probandum (*sādhya*) is indeed a difference qualified by the locus (*dharmin*), through the dual relation of "subsisting in itself" and "having the same ontological status (*samānasattākatva*) as existence.
Since the difference subsisting in a jar possesses the qualification of the locus "jar-form" through both relations, the probandum is established (*prasiddhi*).
Furthermore, by establishing the aforementioned probandum in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), the ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*) is proven.

Just as that which is qualified by the absence of occurrence elsewhere does not occur elsewhere, so too there is an absence of occurrence elsewhere of that which is qualified by another [locus] through the relation of being-located-in (*ādheyatā*). Consequently, since the existence of the probandum (sādhya) qualified by the locus (dharmin) through both relations must be established by taking the locus consisting of the individual soul and Brahman—which constitute the subject (pakṣa)—as the basis, it necessarily follows that [the difference] possesses ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*).
Whether difference is distinct according to the distinction of its loci, or whether it is one, there is no loss [to our position].

If one accepts that the appearance of the two properties as delimited by "bothness" (*ubhayatva*) as a relation is without scriptural authority, then what is intended here by "existence on the same level of reality as the locus" (*dharmisattāsamānasattākatva*) is simply the absence of both "ultimate existence" (*pāramārthikavṛttitva*) and "not being ultimate" (*pāramārthikānyatva*).

In this way, the probandum (*sādhya*) is the possession of a difference characterized by such an absence of both. Alternatively, the probandum is the state of being the locus of a difference characterized by the absence of both "being related to what is other than the ultimate" (*pāramārthikānyanirūpitatva*) and "ultimate existence."

If one does not accept that difference is distinct according to the difference in its substrata, then since the difference between a cloth and a jar existing in the cloth would also exist as residing in the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, the absence of both [properties] would not exist there. However, in the case of the difference between the insentient and the sentient—which resides solely in the insentient—the absence of both is well-established, because it lacks ultimate existence (*pāramārthika-vṛttitva*).

This is because, even if difference itself is not distinct according to the difference in its substrata when locus-ness (*adhikaraṇatā*) is taken as the probandum (*sādhya*), the locus-nesses themselves are distinct according to the difference in their respective substrata.

The property of being the absence of both [the absence of ultimate existence and the absence of its counter-positive] is well-established in the loci-residences (adhikaraṇatās) residing in cloth and so forth, as determined by the differences such as the pot;
thus, there is no lack of establishment of the qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).
However, the aforementioned probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) does not reach its final conclusion without the ultimate reality of difference.

Whether one considers difference (*bheda*) or its locus (*tadadhikaraṇatva*), since there is only the existence of ultimate occurrence (*pāramārthikavṛttitva*), one must state the absence of both [the absence of non-ultimacy and the absence of being defined by the ultimate]—either because it is not caused by non-ultimacy or because it is not caused by the absence of being defined by the ultimate. This is the direction in which the argument should be carried out; such is the general method.

Now, one might object: "Since Lakṣmī lacks the status of being a living being (*jīvatva*) here, she is not part of the subject (*pakṣa*); yet, if she were somehow included within the category of the subject on the grounds of possessing some slight power and so forth, there would follow the fallacy of partial unestablishedness (*bhāgāsiddhi*), because the reason—defined as 'the state of being a recollector of suffering' (*duḥkhānusandhātṛtva*)—is absent in her. Alternatively, if she were treated as a similar instance (*sapakṣa*), the reason would be absent there, resulting in the fallacy of the unshared (*asādhāraṇya*). This is not so.

Even if she is included in the subject, since we accept the reason as simply 'the state of being a recollector' (*anusandhātṛtva*) in its general sense—which is common to her as well—the charge of partial unestablishedness is avoided.

In the case where the exclusion from that [dissimilar instance] constitutes the auxiliary factor for the reason (*hetu*), even though it is outside the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no lack of "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇya*) despite the reason not occurring therein; for, since there is no seed for ascertaining the stated probandum (*sādhya*) in that mere [instance], it is equivalent to the subject due to having a doubtful probandum, and thus lacks the status of a similar instance (*sapakṣa*).

If the establishment of the probandum in that [subject] is required, there is no fault, because the stated probandum—such as "having little power" and so forth—can be established by the very example of the living being (*jīva*) proven through this inference.

Fearing that the absence of the probans (*hetvabhāva*) is not established in Brahman, which serves as the negative instance (*vyatirekadṛṣṭānta*), he refutes this [with the words] "And of Brahman. Alternatively, fearing the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the probans in the inference whose subject (*pakṣa*) is Brahman—specifically the probans consisting of the fact that [the world] is not conceived of as Brahman—he refutes it [with the words] "And of Brahman. [He further states] "lest there follow the consequence of [Brahman] not being a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*)."

It should be understood that in the state of *saṃsāra*, there is the experience of one's own suffering alone; however, in the state of Brahmanhood, since there would arise the experience of the suffering of all living beings through attaining identity with them, it follows as a consequence that liberation would be something utterly to be rejected. Regarding the phrase "the scriptural texts on stainlessness" (*nirañjanatva-śruti*):

the meaning is that there is a contradiction [with the opponent's view] because the scripture, "The stainless one attains supreme equality," uses the term "stainless" (*nirañjana*) to express the absence of all defects, such as being an experiencer of suffering.

The ablative ending in *pañcamyantat* and *dvamavat* indicates necessity; [the phrase] *nāsiddhiḥ* means that there is no lack of proof. In accordance with the two preceding introductions, one should understand the two meanings: "no failure of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*) and "no failure of the reason" (*hetvasiddhi*).
Regarding the phrase *anumānāni ca*, the word *bheda* and so forth follows; the word *ucyante* (are stated) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Although, according to the order of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the inference establishing the plurality of selves (*ātman*) in general should have been stated first, nevertheless, with the thought that "if the principal [point] is established, the subordinate points are all the more easily established," he says: "The individual soul (*jīva*). Here, the term "suffering" (*duḥkha*) is a mention of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), and not a constituent of the logical reason (*hetu*).

And thus, the phrase "not recollected by Brahman" is meaningful for the purpose of excluding any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to Brahman, who is the recollector of eternal bliss and so forth.
Nor is there a lack of proof regarding the non-recollection of Brahman, since Brahman is omniscient;
for "recollection" consists precisely in experiencing [an object] as one's own.
And being "one's own" consists in its causing one's own degradation and so forth,
but not in being a property of oneself. Therefore, the suffering that is a modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) is not included [in this definition].

And it should be meditated upon that this [state] is a ground of suffering for the sake of attaining that [bliss]. Although there is no logical necessity [for the argument], since non-difference is established here as well— just as in the case of Indra, who, while not keeping Arjuna in mind, was identified with him due to his recollection of some slight pleasure— the fault does not arise, because the probandum is merely the object of the conventional usage of "non-difference," which is common to both actual non-difference and its specific representative.
Because there is no sublation of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, that very difference is established;
