furthermore, since the cessation of the other [Brahman] is established through the proof of an inherent distinction (*svābhāvikaviśeṣa*), [the author] says "by way of negative concomitance" (*vyatirekeṇa*), because there is no illustrative example for positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) in this case. Although it would have been more appropriate to state the inference first regarding the difference having God as its locus, since perception was already stated therein, [the author proceeds as follows].

Nevertheless, because the difference having the individual soul (*jīva*) as its locus is established through the perception of that soul, inference is easier to formulate therein; therefore, that very point was stated first.
Furthermore, following the sequence of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), perception regarding the difference having God (*īśvara*) as its locus was demonstrated earlier.
And since the opponent rejected that very point first—given its primacy—there is no inconsistency.

Regarding the phrase "brahma vetti" (he knows Brahman): here, the probandum (*sādhya*) is the difference whose counter-positivehood (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the state of being a living soul (*jīvatva*).
Consequently, even though the difference having a living soul as its counter-positive is common to all living souls, there is no lack of establishment of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
Some also say that the probandum is simply the difference having each respective living soul as its counter-positive.

In this reason as well, the term "duḥkha" (suffering) is merely a mention of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Nor should it be argued that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because even Brahman possesses the quality of being a cognizer of the absence of suffering associated with living beings;
for it is only the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of suffering that are associated with living beings.
Furthermore, because the Lord possesses the quality of being one who does not identify with suffering due to the absolute absence of suffering in Him, there is no defect [in the reason].

Thus, since the mere state of non-identification is absent in Brahman, [the qualification] is not unestablished (asiddhi); therefore, the phrase "identified by the individual soul" (jīvānusaṃhita) is meaningful.
Nor should it be suspected that this qualification is useless because it does not exclude any instance of deviation (vyabhicāra).

Since unestablishedness (*asiddhi*), like inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*), is equally an obstacle to inference, it has been established in the treatises that qualifiers such as "body" in arguments like "the subject of dispute is not produced by an agent because it is not produced by a body" are not useless, even though they serve to exclude unestablishedness.
Furthermore, the fact that they serve to establish an indivisible absence (*akhaṇḍābhāva*) is equal in both cases.
Some, however, maintain that in this context the probans consists simply of the presence or absence of being a cognizer of suffering.

They say that the statement regarding [the reason] "not being associated with Brahman" (*brahmānanusaṃhitatva*) in the case of suffering (*duḥkha*) is intended solely to demonstrate the existence of the absence of the reason in the counter-example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). This, however, is to be questioned;

for since the demonstration of that [absence] is already obtained by the subsequent passage beginning with "of suffering and so forth" (*duḥkhādīnām*), the futility of stating "not being associated with Brahman" is unavoidable.
Although it is indeed possible for a jar or similar object to serve as a positive instance (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*) in the second inference, nevertheless,
the phrase "like the individual soul" (*jīva-vat*) was stated by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) precisely to strengthen the positive concomitance. Furthermore,

although it is possible for the reason in the first [inference] to be "not being a cognizer of omniscience and so forth associated with Brahman," and in the second, "being a cognizer of omniscience and so forth not associated with the individual soul," nevertheless, such an approach is not followed because, according to the opponent's view, there would be the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*), since the pure [Self] lacks the status of a cognizer.
Nor should it be argued that, because the first [reason] is well-known as being connected with Brahman, the reason is unestablished for the opponent;

for by the phrase "not connected with Brahman," what is intended is the state of being an object of reflection that is the counter-positive of the absence of abiding in Brahman, and thus there is no fault.

Here, by manifesting the exclusion of the qualification "having the same ontological status as the existence of the subject (*dharmisattāsamānasattākatva*)" within the body of the probandum (*sādhya*), he demonstrates that there is no room for the defects mentioned in the prima facie argument—namely, the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) and proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)—due to the qualification of "difference" (*bheda*) as being ultimate (*pāramārthika*). The word "here" (*atra*) means "in these two inferences.

And this [phrase] is connected with the two statements: "there is no unestablishedness of the qualification" (*nāprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatvam*) and "no proving of the already established" (*na siddhasādhanam*).

Now, if one were to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking a conventional difference that possesses the same ontological status (*sattā*) as the Brahman-existence—such as the existence of "being-ness" (*sattātva*) and so forth—one would have to intend "sameness" specifically in terms of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*).
In that case, the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) for the opponent remains exactly as it was.

However, if one speaks of sameness in the form of either ultimate reality or conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*), then according to the Siddhāntin’s own position, since conventional reality is not admitted [as ultimately real], there is again the unestablished nature of the probandum.

And if that [existence] is intended in the sense of a form pervaded by existence-in-general (*sattātva*), then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because it would involve equality with the existence of Brahman by way of being either ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) or conventional (*vyāvahārika*).
As for the claim that such equality is indeed non-difference—

since, according to the final position (*siddhānta*), difference is the very nature of the substratum (*dharmin*), and thus in that case there is an absence of any existence over and above the existence of the substratum itself.
That is not so;
for in the view of the opponent, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) in respect to a jar and the like is untenable.
It is not thus.
This is because it is accepted that "equality" consists in existing for as long as the locus [of the world] exists;
and since the empirical [world] does not exist beyond the time when worldly transaction ceases, there is no room for objections such as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Alternatively, "equality" should be intended in the sense of being either non-different from the existence of Brahman or identical with it.

Since a difference whose ontological status (*sattā*) is equal to that of the substratum (*dharmin*)—by virtue of being non-different from the existence of Brahman—is well-established in the case of jars and the like, there is no fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

In the case of Brahman, since it is impossible for it to have an existence equal to its own through a difference non-different from the existence of Brahman, a difference whose ontological status is equal to it, established as non-different from it, is proven to be non-different from Brahman and thus ultimately real (*pāramārthika*); this is the general direction of the argument.

Furthermore, because a difference whose ontological status is equal to that of jars and the like is admitted in the case of Brahman, the argument would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); hence the inclusion of the term "substratum" (*dharmin*).
Although a jar and the like indeed possess the status of being the locus (*dharmin*) with respect to their being objects of cognition (*meyatva*) and so forth,
nevertheless, what is intended here is their being the locus of themselves. And since the word "self" (*sva*) refers to each respective particularity (*bheda*), there is no fault.

Nor should it be argued that, according to the opponent's view, there is a lack of establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) because a distinction characterized by the self does not possess the same ontological status as its own substratum;
for the inference is successfully established precisely because a probandum of the same class is well-known in instances such as a jar.
Otherwise, since the fire in the subject (*pakṣa*) would be unestablished prior [to the inference], it would follow that inference itself is abolished.

In reality, the probandum (*sādhya*) is difference (*bheda*) qualified by the locus (*dharmin*) through both relations: being resident in itself (*svaniṣṭhatva*) and having an existence equal to the existence resident in itself (*svaniṣṭhasattāsamānasattākatva*).
And thus, because the probandum is uniform (*anugata*), its establishment in jars and the like is indeed easy.

By this, even if one accepts in the self a difference whose locus has an existence equal to the existence of jars and so forth—under the view that difference is uniform—there is no room for the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

This is because, just as existence (*sattā*) qualified by subsistence in a substance does not exist in qualities and so forth, so too difference (*bheda*) qualified by subsistence in a jar and so forth is absent in the Self (*ātman*).

Now, an objection may be raised: since there is a rule of co-inherence (*aikādhikaraṇya*) regarding knowledge, pleasure, pain, and so on, there is likewise an absence of the experience of those [pleasures, etc. in a living being (*jīva*) that is not the locus of pain; thus, the first inference suffers from the fallacy of unestablished nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*).

Otherwise, since there would be no distinction for Brahman either, the consequence of its experiencing suffering would follow; thus, the objection against the second [alternative] remains. To this he says: "Of suffering and so forth. Because knowledge, pleasure, and the like—which consist of mental modifications (*vṛtti*)—are necessarily restricted to a single substratum, and because their experience is a direct perception by the Witness (*sākṣin*), there is no sublation if that experience resides in the individual soul (*jīva*); therefore, there is no lack of proof regarding the first [alternative].

Furthermore, if Brahman were a subject who experiences suffering, then even one who has attained that state would necessarily experience it; consequently, the state of being Brahman—which is accepted by others as liberation—could not be established as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Moreover, this would lead to the invalidation of scriptural passages such as "free from all evil" (*niraniṣṭaḥ*). Therefore, since it is necessary that Brahman does not experience suffering, there is no fault in the second position either. This is the intended meaning. Thus, having stated the evidence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) for the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), as well as among individual souls, he states the inferences (*anumāna*): "And the inferences... The word "exist" (*santi*) is to be supplied to complete the sense regarding their difference.

In this regard, he first states an inference concerning the difference whose counter-correlate is Brahman and whose locus is the individual soul (jīva)—beginning with the words "the individual soul" (*jīva*). Regarding the phrase "having the same level of reality as the locus" (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*): the locus is the individual soul;
the meaning is that it is the substratum of a difference which possesses the same level of reality as the existence of that locus.
This is because [the soul] is the experiencer of that suffering which is not experienced by Brahman.
The meaning is: "because of being the experiencer of that.

Here, what is called "experience" by the term *anusandhāna* (recollection/identification) is not mere cognition; rather, it is the very modification (*vikriyā*) in the Self characterized by the states of lowness or highness produced by that [suffering], due to the conceit of ownership (*svātmīyatvābhimāna*) regarding suffering and so forth.
Thus, one should not raise the objection: "How can there be an absence of the experience of suffering for Brahman, who is omniscient?"

Because there is no positive example (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*), he says: "by way of negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*). In the case of Brahman, since there is an absence of difference having Brahman as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is to be understood; and since there is an absence of being a subject of the experience of suffering, the absence of the reason (*hetu*) is also to be understood. Now, he states an inference regarding the difference whose locus (*dharmin*) is the Lord and whose counter-correlate is the individual soul (*jīva*): "Or else, Brahman... Here, Brahman is the locus. The remainder is as before.
"Connected with the individual soul" (*jīvānusaṃhitam*):

that suffering which has been connected with, or experienced by, the individual soul; [it is not present here] because of the absence of such connection, meaning because of the absence of being its experiencer. Regarding the phrase "by way of contrast" (*vyatirekeṇa*): in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*), there is an absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) due to the absence of a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the individual soul.

Furthermore, since the very quality of being a cognizer of the suffering associated with living beings is present, there is an absence of the reason [adduced by the opponent], namely, the lack of such cognition; this is how it should be understood.
Regarding these two inferences, is the probandum (sādhya) ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*) or conventional difference (*vyāvahārika*)? It cannot be the first.

Because the qualifier would be unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). Nor is the second [alternative] correct, because it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). To avoid these objections, the qualification "having the same level of existence as the existence of the subject" (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*) has been introduced for both parts of the probandum (*sādhya*).

To show how both defects are avoided by that [reasoning], he demonstrates the avoidance of both in sequence, beginning with "here" (*atra*) and ending with "there is no proving of what is already established" (*na siddhasādhanam*). By the force of the cognition "the jar is not Brahman," there exists, first of all, a difference having Brahman as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogika-bheda*) in the jar.

The jar is the locus (*dharmin*) of that [difference]. It is well known to the Māyāvādin that the jar possesses a conventional existence (*vyāvahārikī sattā*) of the same order as that [existence] of the difference itself.
Therefore, in the first inference, there is no fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇatva*).
Likewise, by the force of the cognition "the jar is not the living being" (*jīva*), the difference between the jar and the living being is established.

Since it is well known that this [difference] possesses the same level of reality (*samasattāka*) as its substratum (*dharmin*), namely the jar, there is no fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) in the second inference.

Similarly, since the living being, the subject (*dharmin*), is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), the difference established as having the same level of reality as it must itself be established as ultimately real; thus, there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in the first inference.

The meaning is as follows: since difference is established as having the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as Brahman, the substratum (*dharmī*), which is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), that difference is itself established as ultimately real. Therefore, there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*) in the second inference. Now, an objection is raised: since suffering (*duḥkha*) is a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), suffering does not exist in the individual soul (*jīva*) at all; consequently, because the soul lacks the capacity for experiencing it (*anusandhātṛtva*), the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*). To this, he replies with the words "of suffering and so forth. This connects with what is to be stated later: that there is no lack of establishment regarding the quality of being an experiencer (*anusandhātṛtva*).
The fact that suffering is experienced by the individual soul (*jīva*) is not the cause for [the soul] being the locus of that suffering;
the point is that we observe the experience of objects such as a jar, even though they do not reside within the soul.

Now, one might object that since there is no sublation to Brahma’s being an experiencer of suffering, the second reason [for the argument] is unestablished in its essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*). To this, he says: "Of Brahma. In the Māyāvāda system, liberation is accepted as nothing other than the soul’s attainment of the state of Brahma.
In that regard, if even Brahman were subject to the experience of suffering, then that would also apply to the individual soul (jīva) who has attained that state.

Consequently, since such liberation would not be something desired by persons, it would lack the status of being a human goal (puruṣārtha). This is the meaning. Regarding the term "nirañjana" (stainless): the meaning is that it contradicts scriptural passages establishing the absence of suffering and so forth, such as "He is without blemish, without fault," and so on. Regarding the phrase "tadabhāve" (in the absence of that): the meaning is the absence of being an experiencer of suffering.

Now, if by the word "jīva" one intends unconditioned consciousness (*anavacchinna-caitanya*), then because such consciousness does not experience suffering, it would follow that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Therefore, one must intend either consciousness conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) or consciousness conditioned by ignorance (*ajñāna*).
But that is not tenable;

for since the conditioned is false, the difference established as having the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as it cannot be ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). If this is argued, then what, according to you, is the meaning of the word "jīva"?
If it is argued that [consciousness] is indeed limited, then the liberation of the individual soul (*jīva*) would be illusory.

If it is objected that the state of being a *jīva* alone is illusory while consciousness itself is truly real, we say no; for that very consciousness in which the illusory state of being a *jīva* exists must itself be real.
One should be satisfied with the fact that it is precisely this consciousness that we intend by the term "individual soul."
And since that very consciousness is the one who experiences suffering, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*).
If it is argued that the state of being an experiencer of suffering is merely illusory, then what is the point of this groundless outburst?
For we have not made "truth" (*satyatva*) a qualifying attribute of the reason.
If it is objected: "But how can there be the status of subject and example prior to the establishment of the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman?", we say no;
for the status of subject and example is established by means of that very conventional difference (vyāvahārika-bheda) which you yourself accept.

Now, one might object: "Even if the distinction [between the individual soul and Brahman] is qualified by the phrase 'having the same ontological status as the subject' (*dharmisamasattāka*) in the first inference, this does not establish the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) you intend. With this intention, he raises the objection with the words "nanvatratra," etc. To indicate the method of resolution through the very mouth of the opponent, he asks: "What then?"—that is, for you who assert the non-difference (*abheda*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.

The word "is considered" (*mata*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Precisely that which is delimited" means that it is precisely consciousness (*caitanya*) as delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth. "In that case" implies the following thought:

since the delimited [consciousness] is admitted to be false, and since liberation—which consists in the true state of being Brahman—is impossible for that which is false, the liberation of the individual soul (*jīva*) described in the scriptures would have to be false.
Now, even if the conditioned self (*jīva*) is illusory, the liberation being described for it does not thereby become illusory;
for that would only be the case if the entire referent of the term "jīva" were illusory,
and such is not the case.

He raises an objection with the thought that the consciousness (*caitanya*) upon which the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) is superimposed is indeed real, and that its liberation is therefore possible: "But surely... (*nanu*). He answers with the thought: "In that case, we too shall say that very same consciousness is what is denoted by the word 'living soul'—that upon which you say the state of being a living soul is superimposed": "Upon which consciousness... (*yatra caitanye*). Thus, since such consciousness alone is obtained by the term "substratum" (*dharmipada*), once it is established that [the difference] has the same ontological status as that [consciousness], the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) of the difference itself is established; this is the sense.

[Objection: But if this is so, and since it is intended that consciousness (*caitanya*) itself—possessing the status of a *jīva*—is the meaning of the term *jīva*, then in my view, because such [consciousness] lacks the quality of being a perceiver of suffering, the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished (*asiddhi*). To this, he says: "That very [consciousness]" (*tadeva*). The meaning is: consciousness to which the state of being a *jīva* has been superimposed (*āropita*). The point is that its being a perceiver of suffering is indeed admitted even by you. [Objection: Even if its being a perceiver of suffering is admitted, in my view it is not real (*satya*).

But how is it that the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*) on the grounds that [the quality] is false? He raises this objection: "duḥkhānusandhātṛtvam" (the state of being a synthesizer of suffering). The meaning is: "it is indeed false," i.e., merely superimposed (*āropita*).

However, you yourself have admitted that even a superimposed synthesizing capacity exists in consciousness (*caitanya*); therefore, how can there be an "unestablished" reason merely by your non-acceptance of its reality?

With the thought that "we have not provided 'truth' as a qualification there," he replies: "What is the use of this? [The phrase] "by this untimely dance" means by this useless description of its falsity, which is like a dance performed without musical instruments and the like. [The phrase] "the status of subject and example" means that in the first inference, the individual soul (*jīva*) is the subject (*pakṣa*) and Brahman is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*);
in the second inference, Brahman is the subject and the individual soul is the example.

"Indeed, here" means: "in both types of inference. "Or by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)"—this alternative position is adopted because mere ignorance (*ajñānamātra*) is not a cause for the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*), nor is it useful for the process of recollection (*anusandhāna*). He causes the opponent himself to state the refutation: "What then?"—the words "in Vedic transactions" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Liberation would be false"—the sense is that since the limited entity (*avacchinna*) is false and thus sublated even in its own nature, of what would there be liberation?
"One should be content" means that one should not undergo the useless distress of attempting to refute the aforementioned inference.

To the objection that "the same refutation applies here as well," he replies: "That very [point]. The sense is that you yourself have stated that the false state of being a *jīva* is superimposed upon the real consciousness (*caitanya*), since the meaning of the word *jīva* is precisely the state of being the experiencer of suffering.

The sense is that if liberation is not admitted for the pure [Self], then the connection with the contemplation of suffering would belong to that same [pure Self] alone; otherwise, there would be a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyyadhikaraṇya*). Regarding the term *akāṇḍa*: it means "uninterrupted. Regarding the question "How?": the sense is that it would result in mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Regarding the term *vyāvahārika*: the sense is that the opponent accepts [this status] merely by virtue of its distinction from the apparent (*pratibhāsika*).

In reality, however, even with a difference that is itself doubtful, the status of subject (*pakṣa*) and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is established—as in such cases as "earth is distinct from others. This is because such a doubt, being one regarding the object of apprehension (*grāhya-sandeha*), does not constitute an obstacle [to inference]; this and other points should be inferred accordingly. Furthermore, since there is no evidence for the difference between Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*) to be anything other than [the difference already under discussion], the conventional difference between the individual soul and Brahman exists even in a conventionally real jar. Thus, because that difference possesses the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as the substrate (*dharmin*) relative to the jar, the argument is once again rendered superfluous (*anyathāsiddhi*) by that very fact.

"Now, here... means by the word "jīva," which expresses the subject (*pakṣa*) in the first inference. "...the non-establishment of ultimate reality" means that, in that case, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). With a hidden intention, he asks: "What then? [The answer is:
liberation residing in the *jīva* would be false.
The meaning is that it is not tenable to claim that a property residing in a false substratum— which is distinct from properties that are either false or similar to the false— is itself not false.
Alternatively, the statement "the soul has liberation" would be false,
because it lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇya*).
If the individual soul (*jīva*) were illusory (*mithyā*), then it would be sublated by the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*).

Consequently, the statement that "the soul is liberated through the knowledge of Brahman" would be invalid, because of the non-existence of the soul as the substratum of liberation; this is the intended meaning. [Objection: "But surely..."—the sense is that since the soul is the substratum of liberation, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

He reveals his intention with the words "where... [in the verse]. Now, one might object that because it lacks the capacity for recollection (*anusandhātṛtva*), its existence as a subject is unestablished; to this he replies: "That very same... The point is that since an insentient limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) cannot possibly be a recollector, it must be admitted that recollection resides in consciousness itself, using the adjunct merely as an instrumental cause. He raises an objection in order to clarify the position: "Now, if... [the term] "unconditioned" (*anavacchinna*) means not limited by ignorance (*avidyā*) or by the limiting adjuncts of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
This connects with the phrase "it should be intended," which follows "lest it follow [absurdly]" (*prasaṅgāt*), and applies to the words "even for you."
"In all else there is no suffering; rather, it is the individual souls (jīvas) alone who suffer.

This scripture proceeds for the sake of their removal of suffering," and so forth—in such passages, [the soul] is presented as being characterized by suffering and as possessing the removal of suffering in the form of liberation.
The meaning of the question is: what is that which is the referent of the word "jīva"? [The answer is: "It is precisely that which is conditioned (avacchinna)."
The meaning is "by ignorance" (avidyā) and by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
By referring specifically to those very things denoted by the word *jīva*, liberation is described as consisting in the abandonment of suffering.
That [liberation] would be false; it would be merely apparent (*prātibhāsikī*).

This is what is meant: the very removal of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause for the destruction of the suffering that constitutes the state of bondage for the individual soul (*jīva*). However, upon their removal, since the soul is defined by those attributes, the soul itself—whose nature is qualified by them—is destroyed. Consequently, because there would be no liberation residing in the soul, the aforementioned scripture would be invalid, like the statement "the consciousness of a jar. [Objection: "But surely... [Response: "The state of being a soul alone... This means that the status of being a soul is superimposed upon Consciousness, or that it is the qualified entity which has attained identity with that [Consciousness].

"But consciousness is real. And so, by the statement "that which was a child is now old age," etc., just as old age is perceived in the very body characterized by childhood—and not in that [body] as qualified by it, because that would involve contradiction—so too in the present case, having referred to those [beings] as characterized by being individual souls (*jīvatva*), liberation is stated.
The sense is that there is no lack of authority for that sentence, because the connection with liberation is not contradicted therein.

He now reveals that which was asked with a hidden intention—in order to establish the impossibility of entering into a debate with him to explain [the nature of] samādhi to another—by means of the passage beginning with "yatra" (wherein).

The phrase "the living being (jīva), characterized by the state of being a living being (jīvatva), is false and superimposed" expresses the relationship between the subject and the predicate in reverse order. Regarding the term "that consciousness" (tac-caitanya): thus, the subject (*pakṣa*) is consciousness itself as qualified by the state of being a living being. The point is this: since the state of being a living being—which is superimposed there through identity with that which is qualified by the state of being a living being—is also superimposed there as its attribute, it possesses the status of being an attribute (*dharmatva*).

[Objection: Since the property of having a living soul (*jīvavattva*) exists only in that which is conditioned by itself (*svopahita*), it follows that only such a conditioned entity can be the subject (*pakṣa*). Consequently, because one accepts the probandum (*sādhya*) as stated therein [of being free from transmigratory existence], there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). [Reply: This is not so. For, if the relation of having a living soul were absent in the pure [Self], the previously cited statements regarding the liberation of the living soul (*jīvamukti*) would result in being invalid; thus, the connection with having a living soul is necessary in that [pure Self]. Therefore, when "having a living soul" is taken as the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) by way of identity (*tādātmya*)—which has the conditioned [Self] as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and does not reside in the conditioned [Self] itself—it both excludes the conditioned and includes the pure [Self]. Thus, there is no fallacy.

Because the absence of identity— qualified by having that which is superimposed as its counter-positive— is present in the superimposed, whereas it is absent in the pure [Brahman], and because that absence exists in the pure; and because, in accordance with both schools of thought, "being superimposed upon that" must be defined as "having a subjectivity that pervades the subjectivity of itself while possessing that [superimposed] mode," it should be understood that even though the superimposed (upahita) as something distinct from the qualified (viśiṣṭa) is not established in the Siddhānta, there is no failure of the locus (*pakṣāsiddhi*).

In that case, it might be argued that the quality of being a "connector of suffering" (*duḥkhānusandhātṛtva*) is unestablished in consciousness (*caitanya*); therefore, he says: "That very [consciousness]... Since an insentient entity (*jaḍa*) is incapable of knowledge in the form of connection, otherwise—just as in the Sūtra *īkṣaternāśabdam* (Brahma Sūtra 1.1.5)—it would be impossible to exclude the Pradhāna by virtue of its being the locus of seeing (*īkṣati*). The intention is that since the quality of being a connector must also be predicated of consciousness alone, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*).

He raises an objection with the intention of showing that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*): "Regarding 'suffering'... [The phrase] "only false" (*mithyaiva*) means being perceived only where its absolute non-existence resides;
thus, the sense is that [the reason] is unestablished.

Is the intention here that there is a failure of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) because [suffering] is in fact false? Or must "truth" (*satyatva*) necessarily be stated as a qualification of the reason, since otherwise—by taking into account the fact of being a synthesizer of superimposed suffering—there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in Brahman itself, and consequently the proof (*sādhana*) would be unestablished? It is not the first [alternative].

In your view, even in the case of a valid inference (*savānumāna*), since both the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*) and sublation (*bādha*) are unavoidable, the very discourse on the validity of inference would be destroyed. Therefore, in order to avoid this, the definitions of *asiddhi*, *bādha*, and so forth must be refined by incorporating conditions such as "non-coexistence with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivaiyyadhikaraṇya*). With the intention of asking how one can point out *asiddhi* [in such a context], he says: "What is the use of this? This means: by a statement that is irrelevant and useless at this juncture.
The sense is that it is incoherent to discuss the nature of falsity (*mithyātva*), which is irrelevant here, when the occasion for describing the defects of inference has arrived.
He refutes the second [position] with the words "Not indeed" (na hi).
That the nature of being a synthesizer (anusandhātṛtva) resides in consciousness (caitanya) is agreed upon by both you and me;
however, regarding whether that [consciousness] is false or true, there is once again a dispute between us.

The point is this: since, regarding the subject of dispute, one does not qualify the property as being either "real" (*satyatva*) or "unreal" (*mithyātva*), but rather adopts the mere state of being an object of inquiry (*anusandhātṛtva*) as the probans (*hetu*), it is impossible to raise the objection of the "unestablished nature of the probans" (*sādhanāprasiddhi*) from the perspective of either party.

In your own view, in order to avoid the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of "smokeness" (*dhūmatva*)—which is delimited by smoke that is merely superimposed—with respect to fire, you maintain that the delimitor of the probans is "smokeness" as it exists only in empirical smoke (*vyāvahārika-dhūma*), which is excluded from the illusory (*prātibhāsika*).
In my view, since that [smoke] is non-existent, the property of being smoke (*dhūmatva*) itself is absent therein; thus, *dhūmatva* serves as the delimitor of the cause (*hetutāvacchedaka*).
Now, one might object: "The qualification of 'reality' (*satyatva*) must be added to the smoke."

The point is this: likewise, in the present case regarding Brahman, since the superimposed agency (*anusandhātṛtva*) is unreal according to my view and merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*) according to your view, there is no possibility of a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) between our two positions based on that [agency]. Therefore, why should the qualification "real" (*satyatva*) be added to the reason (*hetu*)? Regarding the phrase "the state of being the subject and the example": the sense is that if you proceed from the perspective of absolute reality alone, then because you and I would be one and the same, the very relationship of proponent and opponent (*vādiprativādibhāva*) would be untenable.

He raises an objection in order to refine the subject (*pakṣa*) of the first inference, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*). Regarding the term "unconditioned" (*anavacchinna*): although the status of being the subject (*pakṣatva*) is impossible because it is impossible to convey that which is unconditioned by any qualifiers whatsoever—and because, according to the final doctrine (*siddhānta*), such a subject is not established—nevertheless, there is no fault. This is because the word "unconditioned" refers to being unconditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth; thus, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is that the subject consists in being unconditioned by those [limitations].

In the view that there are many individual souls (*bahujīva-pakṣa*), [the world] is [superimposed] by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); in the view that there is only one individual soul (*ekajīva-pakṣa*), it is by ignorance (*ajñāna*).
"Determined" (*avacchinna*) means "qualified" (*viśiṣṭa*).
And its falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in its being non-ultimate (*apāramārthikatva*), which is to say, its being merely empirical (*vyāvahārikatva*).

The intention [of the opponent] is as follows: since a difference co-existent with its own existence (*tatsattāsamānasattāka-bheda*) is already established, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); furthermore, because an ultimately real difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*) is not established, there is the fallacy of shifting the subject matter (*arthāntara*). Anticipating this, and intending to provide a solution by accepting that only the substantive portion (*viśeṣyāṃśa*) constituting the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), [the author] asks—"What then is yours?"—in order to clarify the absence of the aforementioned *siddhasādhana* and other fallacies. "The delimited" (*avacchinnam*): this is a neuter form used for the general category (*sāmānya*), or it may mean "delimited consciousness" (*avacchinna-caitanya*). "It would be false" (*mithyā syāt*): the meaning is that it would be non-existent, like the horn of a hare and so forth.
The sense is that because the individual soul (*jīva*), which is submerged in ignorance due to its state of false-identification (*mithyātva*), cannot possibly attain the nature of Brahman.

Thus, it should be understood that there would follow the undesirable consequence that the Vedāntas are not to be commenced, as they would serve no purpose. Furthermore, the meaning of the term "liberation of the individual soul" (*jīvamukti*) is precisely the attainment of the status of Brahman by the substantive element (*viśeṣyāṃśa*) that constitutes the referent of the word "individual soul."

And regarding that, he raises the objection that the aforementioned fault does not apply: "Now [nanu]... He provides the resolution with the intention that there is no fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*) and so forth, because the subject (*pakṣa*) is consciousness as characterized by the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*): "Where... By the phrase "one should be satisfied," this has been stated merely for the sake of argument;

in reality, it is indicated that even the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) possesses reality alone. "That very same... The sense is that the quality of being a perceiver of suffering is necessarily restricted to the state of being a living soul. Now, one might object: since the quality of being a perceiver of non-ultimate suffering is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to Brahman, the reason must be qualified by the attribute of being ultimate (*pāramārthikatvena*).

Thus, he raises the objection that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*) according to the opponent's view, stating: "the state of being a cognizer of suffering. This would indeed be so if the reason were qualified by ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), but it is not so; for the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) based on the phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*) level is not a defect. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the total destruction of all inference. With this intention, he says: "What is the use of this? The meaning is: what harm is done to us by this irrelevant, frantic display of criticism against something that was never even mentioned?
Now, this is the intended sense of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Because the property of being followed by suffering is false, it does not possess the status of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*),
since a connection between the real and the unreal is impossible.
Even if there exists a relationship in the form of the superimposed and its substratum (*adhyasta-adhiṣṭhāna-bhāva*), [it is still not a valid reason].
Nevertheless, that [connection] is not the determinant of causality;
for in our established doctrine, since the quality of being a cognizer of suffering is non-superimposed, it would be untenable [otherwise].
Rather, it is the relationship of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*).
And thus, [the reason] would be unestablished for others.
To this we reply: here, the state of possessing suffering (*duḥkhavattva*) itself is the logical reason (*hetu*), by virtue of its connection with the state of being a synthesizer (*anusandhātṛtva*).

Furthermore, according to the opponent's view (*paramata*), the status of being the "investigator" (*anusandhātṛtva*) resides in the self-superintending principle (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) alone; whereas in our own system (*siddhānta*), it is the substrate itself (*svādhāra*) that regulates the occurrence of suffering and so forth. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Regarding the question, "How can there be the status of being the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)?"—although in the present case, because difference is doubtful due to the disagreement among disputants, there is no impossibility of its being a subject characterized by having a doubtful probandum (*sandigdhasādhyaka*) and so on;
nevertheless, since what is intended is the impossibility of being an example while simultaneously possessing the status of a subject, there is no fault.

Alternatively, the intended meaning is this: just as it is untenable for the individual soul (*jīva*) to be the subject (*pakṣa*) when non-difference has been ascertained prior to the establishment of difference, so too is it untenable for Brahman to be the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) when there is doubt regarding that [non-difference]. For this very reason, the phrase "prior to the establishment of difference" is also appropriate; otherwise, since the untenability of being the subject would persist even after the establishment of difference, that [phrase] would be inconsistent.

In this regard, even though there is doubt regarding the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, the aforementioned defect does not arise because there is no certainty of non-difference with respect to Brahman. Nor is that [non-difference] untenable; rather, it is established precisely by means of empirical difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*). With this intention, he provides the resolution: "By you. Although the opponent does not accept a difference in pure consciousness (*kevala-caitanya*), nevertheless, the difference of the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-bheda*) has as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) the consciousness that constitutes the substantive element (*viśeṣya*). Thus, that very [difference] serves to establish the relationship between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). This is the intended meaning.
Alternatively, the very consciousness qualified by omniscience and so forth may serve as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*);
since the probandum (*sādhya*) is simply the difference having that [consciousness] as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), there is no fault whatsoever.

Now, even so, for those who maintain the non-difference (*abheda*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because the quality of being a perceiver of suffering exists even in the consciousness of Brahman.
If it is argued that even though non-difference (*abheda*) is doubtful due to conflicting views, the fallacy of "inconclusiveness through doubt" (*sandigdhānaikāntya*) is unavoidable—this is not so.
For a doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*), which arises from a doubt regarding the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) in the locus of the reason (*hetumat*), is not a defect.

In the present case, such a doubt resides in the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the locus of the reason, and is rooted in a doubt regarding its non-difference from Brahman; otherwise, since a doubt regarding deviation would be universal for every subject (*pakṣa*), it would follow that inference (*anumāna*) itself is destroyed.

He raises an objection with the words beginning "But" (*nanu*) and ending with "the non-establishment of ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatvāsiddhi*), [arguing that] even if the qualification "having the same level of existence as the subject" (*dharmisamasattāka*) is added to the inference on the side of the individual soul (*jīva*), the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) is not avoided. It should be understood that the phrase "by the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇena*) refers to the view of those who maintain the plurality of souls (*bahujīvavāda*), whereas "by ignorance" (*ajñānena*) is common to the view of those who maintain the unity of the soul (*ekajīvavāda*).

Here, he provides a rebuttal by way of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*), from the words "Then what... up to "...should be satisfied. This is directed at you, who maintain that liberation is the state of the individual soul (*jīva*) becoming Brahman. The word "then" (*tarhi*) means: if the referent of the term "individual soul" (*jīva*) is something limited (*avacchinna*), then, because it is illusory (*mithyā*) and because that which is illusory is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman, the individual soul itself would cease to exist at the time of the immediate realization of the identity of the soul and Brahman. Consequently, the claim that "liberation is the state of the soul becoming Brahman" would be false.

One might object: "Is it not the case that everything characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, which constitutes the referent of the term 'jīva', is false? However, only the qualifying portion (*viśeṣaṇabhāga*) is false, whereas the qualified portion (*viśeṣyabhāga*), being real, does not cease to exist. Therefore, liberation as the state of being Brahman for that [qualified part] is entirely appropriate. Thus he raises the objection with "nanu" (is it not the case). The phrase "jīvabhāvaḥ" means "the state of being a jīva" (*jīvatva*). Regarding the phrase "yatra caitanye": the point is that since the jīva is ultimately real, the difference established as having the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as that [jīva] must itself be ultimately real; thus, there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*). The statement "the state of being a jīva is false" is a restatement of the opponent's view.

It should be understood that, in our own view, the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) is real. Now, one might object: "If, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), you accept that the very meaning of the word 'living soul' is true consciousness (*satyacaitanya*), then—since such [pure] consciousness lacks the capacity for the experience of suffering—there would be a failure to establish the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) of your subject. To this he replies: "That very [consciousness]" (*tadeva*). The intention is that in the cognition "I am suffering," it is consciousness itself that is the referent of the word "I" (*asmacchabda*). Regarding the phrase "like an untimely *tāṇḍava* dance": here, by the word *kāṇḍa*, the limbs and so forth of the *tāṇḍava* dance are intended.
And thus, even in the absence of the [actual] stalk (kāṇḍa), the meaning is: "Why [is there] the falsity of being a pursuer of suffering?

Just as dancing is appropriate when there is the presence of musical instruments such as the mṛdaṅga—which are the limbs of the dance—but inappropriate in their absence, so too here: the description of the falsity of being a pursuer of suffering is appropriate only if we have previously described its reality; in the absence of that [prior description], its mention would be entirely inappropriate.
This is precisely what he says with the words "nahi" (not). [The word] "hetau" refers to the cause, namely, the state of being a pursuer of suffering.

The intention is that by this [argument], the description of its falsity would be consistent. If it is argued that, in reality, the "truth" (satyatva) favored by you has been refuted, we say no; for the core point is that since that constitutes a different incidental argument (prasaṅgāntara), it does not resolve the inconsistency with the subject at hand.

An objection is raised: "Indeed, it is not possible for the individual soul (jīva) to be the subject (*pakṣa*) and Brahman the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) in the first inference, nor for Brahman to be the subject and the individual soul the example in the second; for the relationship between subject and example depends upon difference, and the difference between the individual soul and Brahman remains unestablished even now. One should not say that the relationship of subject and example is established by the very fact that their difference is proven by this same inference.

The point is that if difference were established, the operation of inference would be possible through the validity of the status of the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); yet, if inference operates, difference is established by it—thus there arises the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). For in the case of the existence of the subject and the example, only difference is required, not its ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*).

If that were the case, then according to your own view, since there is an absence of ultimate difference between the mountain and the kitchen, the impossibility of the status of subject and example would follow as a consequence.

He offers a rebuttal, stating that since even you yourself have admitted a mere difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, the relationship of subject and example is established—this is expressed by the words "by you."

Alternatively, the individual soul (*jīva*) is not the locus of a real identity (*tāttvikatādātmya*) with respect to Brahman as its counter-correlative, nor is Brahman the locus of a real identity with respect to the individual soul as its counter-correlative.
The formulation of the probandum (*sādhya*) should be understood as being based on the very same two reasons mentioned previously.
Furthermore, this does not constitute the fault of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

For that [non-establishment] is a defect either by way of subverting the "subject-property" (*pakṣadharmatā*) through the subversion of "subject-hood" (*pakṣatā*), because when the probandum is not established, no doubt can arise as to whether the locus possesses the probandum or its absence; or else, it is a defect by way of subverting the "pervasion" (*vyāpti*), since when the probandum is unestablished, it is impossible to grasp the pervasion of the reason; or perhaps by way of subverting both. It is not the first [alternative].

Even though there is no doubt as to whether Brahman has attained (or is delimited by) a real identity with the individual soul (*jīva*), the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) is established by the mere doubt as to whether such a real identity with the individual soul exists in Brahman or not—just as in the inference establishing denotability (*abhidheyatva*).
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for in a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped precisely through the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).
In this case, since the absence of the probandum—the identity with the living self—is well-known in relation to the living self;

where, in a negative inference (*vyatirekin*), a positive entity is the probandum, there the non-existence [of that entity] depends upon the knowledge of its existence for the sake of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*), and thus the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) constitutes a defect. However, in the present case, because it is a non-existence that is the probandum, there is no such defect.

Not the third [alternative], because it is not a refutation since it does not subvert either [of the two]. For a refutation consists precisely in subverting either the pervasion (*vyāpti*) or the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

Because there is the disadvantage of complexity (*gaurava*) due to the inclusion of the qualification "having the same ontological status as the subject" (*dharmisamasattāka*) in the two previously mentioned inferences, he says "or else" (*yadvā*) out of dissatisfaction. "By the very same previous reasons" means by the two reasons stated previously.

The sense is that in the first inference, the two previously mentioned reasons are to be understood as "because of not being the one who experiences the suffering experienced by Brahma," and in the second, "because of not being the one who experiences the suffering experienced by the individual soul (jīva). Nor does this result in the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*); for the sense is that the Advaitin accepts in all cases only a real identity (*tādātmya*) between Brahma and the individual soul as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*).

Although there is indeed an unestablished qualification, nevertheless, with the intention that there is no defect in the form of an obstruction to the inferential cognition (*anumiti*) on that account, it was stated: "for the sake of [avoiding] the defect."

The construction is as follows: for that [fault] is a defect either by way of subverting the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), or by way of subverting the pervasion (*vyāpti*), or by way of subverting both.
To the question "How is there a subversion of the property-of-the-subject?", it is said: "by way of subverting the status of being the subject (*pakṣatva*).
To the question "And how is that [subversion of the subject's status]? it is said: "in the category of the probandum (*sādhyakoṭi*)," and so forth.
The meaning is that there is only one side, namely the form of the probandum (*sādhya*).

Thus, since only a subject (*dharmin*) possessing a doubtful probandum qualifies as a "locus" (*pakṣa*), and since the reason (*hetu*) must reside in that very locus to possess the property of being a "locus-feature" (*pakṣadharmatā*), the property of being a locus-feature for the reason is not possible if doubt is absent and the status of the locus is consequently unestablished.
This is what is meant by the statement beginning with "not [being] unestablished" (*aprasiddhatvena*), which is stated in order to demonstrate the failure of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

In the inference "the individual soul (jīva) is not the locus of real identity having Brahman as its counter-correlate," the difference between the soul and God—which has God as its counter-correlate and the soul as its qualificand—is directly perceived by the soul.

With the thought that since the first position—that "I am not free from suffering" and "I am not omniscient"—was already established through direct experience (*anubhava*), what was the point of laboring to refute the status of the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) merely by accepting the opponent's own admission? He demonstrates that the unestablished nature of the probandum is not a defect specifically in the second inference, which has Brahman as its subject, with the words beginning "Not the first.

Although, as previously stated, the difference between the Lord (the subject) and the individual soul (the counter-correlate) is perceptible to the Lord, and thus the probandum is not unestablished even in the second inference; [he nevertheless proceeds to explain].

Nevertheless, since the cognition of another person is not perceptible (*apratyakṣa*), one might object that even with the scriptural statement of the Lord (*īśvara-vākya*)—namely, "But the Supreme Person is other"—there remains the suspicion that the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*) in both perception and inference; considering the excessive labor required to refute such a suspicion, this [text] should be understood as stating that the non-establishment of the probandum in the second inference is not a defect.
Some, however, say that this is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) to show that the "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇatva*) is not a defect in the second inference.
Although this is not the standard path of our own system (*siddhāntika*).

The defects of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), the unestablished substratum (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*), and the unestablished probandum (*sādhyāsiddhi*) are [raised by some]; however, it has been stated that "these are not defects in any way when pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this is said in accordance with the views of others. Regarding the term "Brahman": therein, the phrase "possessing a real identity (*tādātmya*) whose counter-correlative is the individual soul (*jīva*)" demonstrates the side of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).
The phrase "or not" (*na vā*) indicates the alternative side of the probandum (*sādhyakoṭi*).

Thus, even though a doubt regarding the two alternatives of the existence or non-existence of the probandum as residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmika*)—namely, Brahman—is impossible, the status of being a subject (*pakṣatva*) is established by a mere doubt concerning the two alternatives of the presence or absence of the reason's subsistence in that subject (*pakṣavṛttitva*). Consequently, the reason’s property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is established.

It should be observed that in some cases, the status of being a subject is also established by a doubt concerning the two alternatives of the presence or absence of the reason's subsistence in the subject as residing in the property to be proved (*sādhyadharmika*).

One should not think that this method is inconsistent with the treatise; with this intention, he provides an illustration here: "as in the inference establishing denotability. The sense is as follows: in the case of the argument "Sound is denotable because it is knowable," since denotability is a purely positive (kevalānvayi) property, its absence is unestablished. Consequently, while a doubt such as "Is sound denotable or not? may not arise, there still exists a mere doubt as to whether "denotability resides in sound or not. Just as the status of sound as the subject (*pakṣatā*) is established by that alone, so it is here as well.
Furthermore, this establishment of the subject-status is strictly in accordance with the views of others, and not according to our own system.

In our own system (*svamata*), since the nature of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) consists merely in possessing the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—which is the object of the cognition produced by a logical mark (*liṅga*)—there is no rule that the subject must necessarily possess a doubtful property to be proven. Otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence that a subject would lack the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) in the following cases: (1) when one infers a cloud from hearing its thunder; (2) when an inference is employed against someone who, having already known [the conclusion] through observation, asks for the sake of verification; and (3) when an inference is employed for the sake of strengthening a fact already ascertained through perception and other means, because in these instances there is an absence of doubt regarding the property to be proven.

Furthermore, since an inference arises dependent upon its own causes, it cannot be obstructed prior to the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*). Moreover, the absence of [prior] establishment is not a factor in the production of an inference; for the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is not sentient such that it could deliberate, "Since this which was to be done by me has been performed by another, I shall remain indifferent."
For this very reason, doctrines such as "the subjecthood (*pakṣatā*) consists in the absence of proof accompanied by a desire to prove" are indeed too crude.
This is because it is established by experience that when someone who has seen fire on a mountain and has walked some distance away suddenly perceives smoke, an inference of fire occurs;
for in that case, there is no desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*).
Nor is there an absence of proof. Regarding the term "purely negative" (*kevalavyatirekin*):
for when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason with the probandum is grasped, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*) is useful;
however, when the pervasion of the absence of the probandum by the absence of the reason is grasped, the establishment of the probandum is not useful.

The sense is that this reason (*hetu*) is a purely negative one (*kevalavyatirekī*). Now, [one might object]: although the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyaprasiddhi*) is not required for the apprehension of negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) in a purely negative inference, the establishment of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvaprasiddhi*) is nonetheless indispensable. How, then, is that established here? To this he says: "In this case" (*atre*). Since the probandum is precisely the absence of identity with the living self (*jīvatādātmyābhāva*), its absence—namely, identity with the living self—is indeed well-established in the living self (*jīva*). This is the sense.

One might object: "In the inference 'the living body possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth,' since the knowledge of the probandum (*sādhya*) as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is necessary for grasping the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), how can that [knowledge] not be useful? To this, he says: "But where... and so on.

And likewise, although in an inference for the sake of proving "having a self" (*sātmakatva*), the non-apprehension of the counter-positive—namely, "having a self"—is required when grasping the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) because "having a self" is a positive entity, and since such non-apprehension is impossible if that [counter-positive] is unestablished, the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) constitutes a fault; nevertheless, in the present inference, the non-establishment of the probandum does not constitute a fault.

The point is this: although the absence of identity with the living self (*jīva-tādātmyābhāva*) is unestablished because it is the probandum (*sādhya*), in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), identity with the living self—which is the absence of the absence of identity with the living self—is well-established in the living self; therefore, it is easy to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of that [identity] being absent where the reason (*hetu*) is absent.
[The phrase] "of the absence" refers to the cognition of an absence.

[It is said to be so] because the cognition of an absence is dependent upon the cognition of a positive entity (*bhāva*), specifically, dependent upon the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) which constitutes the probandum. [The phrase] "by the disintegration of both" means that among the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), such as unestablishedness (*asiddhi*), one does not observe their status as defects through the disintegration of both *pakṣadharmatā* (presence in the subject) and pervasion (*vyāpti*).
To the question "Why is that?", he says: "Because of pervasion" (*vyāpteḥ*).

The status of being a refutation (*dūṣaṇatva*) arises merely by the fact of subverting one of the two [factors], and not even by the subversion of both, because that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
Therefore, the point here is that even in this case, one should not accept the status of being a refutation on the grounds of subverting both.

Thus, since this applies even to the second application, he employs another method to indicate that the pervasion of the object holds only when the resolution [of the objection] is indeed present. "Or else" (*yadvā*): the resolution, however, is not a single non-difference having Brahman as its counter-correlate (pratiyogin) that applies simultaneously to both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the jar;
for, being of the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*), it is distinct in each respective case. To explain:

Mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) is of the nature of the locus (*dharmisvarūpa*), having as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) that which is superimposed as non-different from the locus; it itself, therefore, does not exist apart from that locus. This is just as relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), which has as its counter-correlative that which is superimposed as different from the locus, is distinct from the locus. Against the contrary position (*vipakṣa*), there is the supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*) that an infinite regress of differences would result.
Or, let it be granted that difference is one and the same, namely, non-existence (*asan*).
Nevertheless, there is no fault because of the qualification "having an existence equal to the existence of the subject" (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*).
It should not be argued that there is a contradiction due to the mutual exclusion of two contradictory existences belonging to the two subjects, the living being (*jīva*) and the pot;
for by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), the [apparent] contradictory meaning does not result as a final conclusion.

Furthermore, by this [definition], it is also established that the soul (*jīva*) and the insentient (*jaḍa*) possess existence (*sattā*) of a single nature in terms of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*).
Nor should it be argued: "In that case, why could the soul not also result in being merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*)?

For it is only logical that the final determination occurs precisely when there is doubt. If it is asked: "Since difference is nothing other than the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*), what is the distinction here from the previous inference?"—the answer is as follows: [The response would follow here.]
Because difference consists precisely in that which is superimposed as identity,
and because here the absence of identity is what is to be proven.
Nor should it be said that, if this were so, there would be an inconsistency in establishing difference.
Because, at the outset, the term "difference" (*bheda*) was intended to signify merely that which is opposed to identity (*tādātmya*).

The qualification "real" (*tāttvika*) is used to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), since conventional identity (*vyāvahārika-tādātmya*) is absent [in the ultimate sense]. The phrase "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*) is employed because the underlying intention is that everything is admitted to be, in reality, of the nature of consciousness (*caitanya*) denoted by the term "Brahman. With the thought that the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāsiddhi*) is not a defect, he says: "For that... (*taddhi*).

There is one type of alternative [regarding the refutation]: by way of refuting the status of being a subject (*pakṣatva*), which is to say, by way of refuting the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

This means that since a doubt whose alternatives are unestablished is impossible, there is an absence of the status of being a subject in the form of being "doubtful. Regarding the term "both": it means the two forms mentioned, namely pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property-of-the-subject.
The sense is that it is impossible for it to be a defect without these three modes.

He says, "In Brahman, does it exist or not? because even when there is no doubt having both the probandum and its absence as alternatives with the subject (pakṣa) as the qualificand due to the non-establishment of the probandum, the doubt is sufficient provided it has as its qualificand either the probandum or its absence, and as its alternatives, the presence or absence in the subject.

The underlying sense is that, in this way, only existence-in-Brahman and non-existence-in-Brahman serve as the alternatives, and these two are well-known in such cases as [the doubt regarding] the existence of knowledge in Brahman.

The meaning is as follows: regarding the statement "sound is denotable," although a doubt of the form "is it denotable or not" is impossible—because the property of being denotable (*abhidheyatva*) is a *kevalānvayi* (universally present) and thus the negative alternative (*neti koṭi*) is unestablished—there is still a mere doubt of the form "does denotability exist in sound or not.

The point is that some kind of doubt regarding the co-presence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) is a necessary factor for inference; however, there is no requirement for that doubt to have the same qualificandum or the same mode (*prakāratā*) as the resulting inferential cognition.
In reality, however, doubt is a constituent factor only when an inference is directed toward one who desires to know;
it is not so when there is a desire to prove [a point] against an opponent,
because the proponent, the opponent, and the neutral arbiter each possess certainty regarding their own respective tenets.
Furthermore, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is the cognition of the limit itself that serves as the cause for doubt;
therefore, non-establishment in the form of a superimposition (*āropa*) is appropriate in all cases.
Nor should it be argued that this is not tenable for an opponent who possesses the perception of the specific characteristics (*viśeṣadarśana*).
For even that [doubt] can be produced artificially (*āhārya*).
Furthermore, when proceeding against an opponent, it is accepted that even doubt can serve as an artificial reason (*hetu*).
Moreover, let the establishment of the alternatives (*koṭi*) arise from the very statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*), namely: "It does not have identity as its locus."

The cognition of inappropriateness (*ayogyatājñāna*) is an obstacle specifically to the validity of the knowledge of the sentence-meaning. However, that cognition [of inappropriateness] arises precisely through the perception of specific features (*viśeṣadarśana*), by virtue of the causal complex for the direct perception of the moon's digit-length as being its actual digit-length. [The phrase] "because of the apprehension of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)" means that, in this way, the non-apprehension of the pervasion of the probandum is not a defect, because [the probandum] is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).
And this [explanation] is strictly according to the perspective of the opponent.

In reality, even though a specific locus (*adhikaraṇa-viśeṣa*) may not be well-known, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) itself is easily grasped through the connection with the locus in general: "This is pervaded by that, because it is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of that [pervader].

This is merely an illustration; for even when the specific [locus] and its probandum (*sādhya*) are unknown, the general pervasion—"whatever is the locus of a property that does not reside in x is not the locus of identity with x"—is easily grasped. Since the establishment of the counter-positive (*pratiyogi-prasiddhi*) is necessary even for the apprehension of the pervasion of an absence, he says "where... and so forth. The phrase "for the sake of the fault" implies the remainder of the sentence: "in some way."
The sense is that, in this case, it is possible to establish [the reason] because both [the locus and the property to be proved] are well-known.

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction in the claim that the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) is not a defect. "The probandum being a non-existence" means that there is no need for a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) because the non-existence of a non-existence is understood as a positive entity (*bhāva*). And this is said provisionally; even if the non-existence of a non-existence is a positive entity, the negative cognition (*vyatirekadhī*) does not occur in an affirmative manner (*vidhimukhena*).
However, it is by virtue of being the absence of an absence;

for only such [an absence] is opposed to the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). In reality, however, non-establishment (*aprasiddhi*) should be understood as consisting in superimposition (*āropa*), according to the manner already stated. To the objection that there might be defectiveness through some other mode, he says: "In the case of pervasion... (*vyāpti...*).
[Objection: But surely the property of being a subject (*dharmitva*) is not a single, recurring [property].

Thus, if the qualification "difference" is of the same ontological status as the existence of the pot (*ghaṭasattā*), then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) and the uselessness of the qualification (*viśeṣaṇavaiyyarthya*).

If, on the other hand, it is of the same ontological status as the existence of Brahman (*brahmasattā*), then the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*). To this, he says: "Or else... [and] "Brahman, or that which has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*). This is with reference to the second inference.

Thus, even though in the first inference a doubt as to whether the individual soul (*jīva*) is the locus of a real identity (*tāttvikatādātmya*) having Brahman as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*) is impossible, a doubt as to whether "real identity having Brahman as its counter-correlative" resides in the individual soul is possible; therefore, the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) should be understood [in this way]. Nor can it be argued that if the status of being a subject were to arise from any doubt other than one whose alternative branches consist of the probandum (*sādhya*) and its absence, with the subject as the qualificand (*viśeṣyaka*), then the status of being a subject would undesirably apply even at the time when the conclusion has already been established—because such a doubt, which does not preclude the present inference, serves to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

The intended meaning is that the inference under discussion, even though it has a different subject as its qualificandum, serves to remove such doubt because it contradicts [the content of] experience.
This is merely an illustration;

in reality, however, following the inference of clouds and so forth from the thundering of clouds, "subjectness" (*pakṣatā*) consists in the absence of the establishment of the qualified [conclusion], and that remains intact even in the absence of doubt.

However, "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*) does not mean being a property of that specific subject; rather, it is simply the occurrence of the property in what is intended as the subject (*pakṣatā*). Furthermore, since this [occurrence] is independent of doubt, it should be understood that the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) cannot obstruct it.
In this regard, the reading "because the cognition of absence, which is useful for pervasion (*vyāpti*), is dependent upon presence" is correct.
In some places, there is a reading: "because the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the absence-pervasion (*abhāvavyāpti*) therein is dependent upon presence (*bhāva*).

In that context, the meaning is: "because the counter-positive of the pervasion—that is, the locus of the pervasion—is dependent upon the cognition of absence. Regarding the phrase "by the disintegration of both": although the obstruction of inference certainly occurs when both are disintegrated, the intention is that the state of being a disintegrator of both is not the actual ground for being a defeater (*dūṣakatābīja*), due to the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*) and because it would result in over-extension (*avyāpti*).

For the sake of instructing the student and for the sake of strengthening the stated meaning, he states further inferences, beginning with "Or else" (yadvā). Some, however, say that if [the subject] is introduced as the locus (*dharmin*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking a conventional difference whose existence is of the same order as the existence of the locus, such as a jar.

Others say that if one introduces it as "one's own locus" (*svadharmī*), the single probandum (*sādhya*) common to both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) cannot be obtained; therefore, out of dissatisfaction with these views, he says "Or else."
