This means that the statement of the probandum (*sādhya-nirdeśa*) must be formulated according to the reason previously stated: "It is not the locus of a real identity (*tāttvika-tādātmya*) whose counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is Brahman. Now, an objection may be raised: the qualification "real" (*tāttvika*) in the case of identity is redundant;
for the intended object is established even by proving merely that it is not the locus of identity in general.

This is because if it were the locus of that identity in any way whatsoever, there would be a contradiction with its not being the substratum of that [identity] in general, which would result in the establishment of absolute difference (*atyanta-bheda*).

Nor should it be argued that its purpose is to prevent sublation (bādha) by virtue of the existence, within Brahman, of the superimposed identity with the individual soul (jīva), and the existence, within the individual soul, of the identity with Brahman;
for there is no single property called "identity" (tādātmyatva) that exists in both the superimposed and the non-superimposed simultaneously.
Furthermore, since the superimposed is non-existent, there is no possibility of sublation occurring on the grounds of possessing a property that does not reside in its own locus.
Nor should it be said that this is for the purpose of avoiding *bādha* (contradiction) and *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) with respect to an opponent.

For, since you yourself accept real identity (*tāttvikatādātmya*) in your own system, the absence of identity in general is not accepted by you; thus, there is no room for the charge of *siddhasādhana*. Furthermore, for one who accepts real identity, contradiction (*bādha*) is inevitable whether or not [the qualification of] "realness" is granted; therefore, that [charge of *siddhasādhana*] cannot serve as a valid objection.

Otherwise, since everything not accepted by the opponent would have to be proven, sublation (*bādhā*) would be inevitable, leading to the undesirable consequence that the discourse on inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) would be abolished. Furthermore, even if identity (*tādātmya*) were granted, one could not avoid the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by resorting to its mere conventional absence.
Therefore, it is impossible for reality (*tāttvikatva*) to function as a qualification of identity.
Nor should it be said that its being a qualifier of the absence [of the probandum] is non-ultimate,

in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*). This is because a word situated within a compound cannot convey a connection with the meaning of a *nañ* (negation) that stands outside the compound and is not co-uttered (*asamabhivyāhṛta*) with it.

Furthermore, the difference in the form of the absence of identity qualified by ultimate reality (*paramārthatva*) is unestablished for the opponent. Even through an inference based on negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), although the reason possesses the capacity to infer the absence of that property which is delimited by the delimitor of the pervasion of the locus of the reason's absence, there is no basis for inferring such an absence as qualified by ultimate reality. Therefore, the term "real" (*tāttvika*) is indeed fruitless. If this is argued, we reply: no.
In this context, the term *tāttvika* does not refer to the ultimate (*pāramārthika*), but rather to the primary (*mukhya*).
It serves as an indicator of the intended meaning of the term *tādātmya* (identity) as referring to oneness (*ekatva*).

Otherwise, since terms such as *tādātmya* and *aikya* (unity) are frequently employed in the scriptures with the intention of expressing similarity, non-difference, and so forth between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman.

If only "identity" (*tādātmya*) were stated, there might arise a suspicion of sublation (*bādha*) in the present context due to the misconception that the probandum (*sādhya*) is either the mere absence of those [identities]—which would include both primary and secondary identities—or the absence of identity as delimited by a form common to both primary and secondary identities.

However, when the word "real" (*tāttvika*) is added, the meaning obtained is "primary identity"; since this yields the absence of that [primary identity] alone as the probandum, the suspicion of sublation does not arise.

And thus, in the two inferences, the respective probanda (*sādhya*) are: the absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by oneness having the individual soul (*jīva*) as its counter-correlative, and the absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by oneness having Brahman as its counter-correlative. This absence has a counter-correlativity delimited by an essential relation (*svarūpa-saṃsarga*) residing in identity (*tādātmya*); it is indeed an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*), distinct from difference (*bheda*). According to the opponent's view, it is established as ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), since it is of the very nature of the substrate, such as Brahman. Therefore, there is no possibility of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking that [absence] to be merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).

Difference (*bheda*), however, is either that whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the relation of identity (*tādātmya-sambandha*), or that whose counter-correlativity is delimitated by identity itself, or difference-ness (*bhedatva*) is an impartite adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).

With the intention that—under the opponent’s position that the general category of non-difference (*abheda-sāmānya*) is not ultimately real—we have achieved our purpose merely by proving absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), this inference has been set forth; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
For this very reason, in the subsequent texts, the qualification "ultimately real" (*tāttvikatva*) is not applied to identity when dealing with conventional usage.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction between what was stated previously and the present position—since previously non-existence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*) was treated as being identical to difference (*bheda*), whereas here its distinctness is accepted—the answer is no.

This is because there is no contradiction, as that usage was intended according to a specific philosophical view which maintains the identity of difference and that [non-existence] through their complete equivalence.

However, some maintain that since inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) must be preceded by a formal dispute (*vipratipatti*), and in such a dispute the opponent must state his own position as having real identity (*tāttvikatādātmya*).

Otherwise, since the conclusion would result from taking the identity with the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), there would be the fallacy of shifting the subject matter (*arthāntara*) for the opponent. Thus, they say that the term "real" (*tāttvika*) is meaningful because the category of the established doctrine (the position favored by the proponent), which consists of the absence of that [identity], is indeed defined by reality. Nor can it be argued that this constitutes the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). It should not be said: "Since the identity of Brahman or the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) is absent in things like a jar, their absence is well-known in the jar itself; so how can there be the fallacy of an unestablished qualification?"
Identity (*tādātmya*) and oneness (*aikya*) are not different in meaning, because the unique property residing in that [substratum] is itself the nature of identity;

and because oneness, which consists in the absence of difference, ultimately resolves into that very [property], as it is the nature of the counter-correlative's delimiting condition (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*).

Thus, prior to the statement of the definition of earth as "possessing fragrance" (*gandhavattva*), since the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*) would apply everywhere, there would be no knowledge of an object distinct from water and the rest; consequently, since the difference from water and so forth is not established anywhere, one might suspect that a cognition of the presence of a property pervaded by such differences is impossible. However, because the inference of the difference from water is accepted by others—based on the cognition "it possesses fragrance, which is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the nature of water (which is the absence of the probandum in a negative inference where non-existence is the probandum)"—therefore, [the nature of] Brahman belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*).

Furthermore, at the stage when [earthness] is suspected of being present everywhere, there is no certainty regarding the absence of identity (tādātmyābhāva) in any particular locus; thus, the objection that the qualifier is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) can be resolved by that very same reasoning, and so it is not a fault.

Just as, at the stage when earthness is suspected of being present everywhere, one cannot determine a specific individual as the locus of the exclusion of any one of the thirteen [categories] such as water and so forth—because of which the exclusion of water and the rest is not present there—even here, in a particular state, it is possible for such an absence of identity not to be present.

Alternatively, according to the view of Bhāskara, the proponent of non-dualism (*advaitavādin*), since it is accepted that the entire world is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of Brahman, which possesses the power of existence (*sacchaktimat*), there is identity with Brahman throughout the entire world; and likewise, because the individual consciousness (*jīvacit*) itself is Brahman, there exists identity with the individual self (*jīvatādātmya*) everywhere as well, by virtue of being its material cause (*upādāna*).

Even in the Māyāvāda system, since existence (*sattā*)—in the form of a unique attribute of Brahman which is the substrate for the superimposed phenomenal world—is accepted everywhere as being identical with Brahman-consciousness, it is therefore accepted that this identity and the identity with the individual soul (jīva), which is non-different from it, are purely positive (*kevalānvayin*). Consequently, it is indeed possible to raise the objection of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) against [the opponent's position].

Furthermore, the fact that existence (*sattā*) is a unique attribute of Brahman is established by the statement in the *Pañcapādikā*: "Bliss, the experience of objects, and existence—these are the three attributes; although they are not separate from consciousness, they appear as if distinct from it. Thus, there is no difficulty whatsoever. [Regarding the phrase] "and for the sake of a fault": the word "not" (*na*) is to be construed here with this clause.

The meaning is that it does not constitute a defect in the form of subverting the inference under discussion. "By subverting both" means by accomplishing the two [requirements] through the subversion of the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in each case and the subversion of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), respectively. "Brahman" refers to that which has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its counter-correlate.

Although the inference having the individual soul (*jīva*) as its subject (*pakṣa*) was stated first—on the grounds that, since the soul possesses the nature of being a living entity, it is an object of perception, and therefore the probans (*hetu*) and other factors are easily apprehended therein, leading to an immediate inference—the doubt is now established in the second inference alone. This is because, following the principle of priority, the doubt regarding the subject is more easily produced here; for the identity (*tādātmya*) with the individual soul, which serves as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), is established by perception in the case of the subject of the doubt. Thus, the justification for the status of the subject (*pakṣatopapatti*) is provided.

The point is this: since it is accepted that *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject) consists merely in a doubt that is capable of being removed by the inferential cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*), even a doubt whose delimiting property of the locus (*dharmitāvacchedaka*) is not identical [to that of the inference] possesses the status of *pakṣatā*, because such a doubt is experienced as being removable by the inferential cognition.
This, however, is said while accepting that the doubt itself constitutes *pakṣatā*.

However, in the view that the state of being a subject (pakṣatā) consists in the absence of proof (siddhyabhāva), there is no fault whatsoever. [The phrase] "non-existence is the probandum" (abhāvaḥ sādhyaḥ) means that, in that case, because the cognition of the probandum—which is of the nature of an absence—is dependent upon the cognition of its counter-positive (pratiyogin)—which is of the nature of a positive entity—therefore the presence of the probandum (sādhyopasthiti) is necessary; this is the intended meaning. [The phrase] "useful for pervasion" (vyāptyupayoginaḥ) means: of that which has become the object of a cognition which serves as the cause for the cognition of pervasion by way of being a cognition of a qualifier (viśeṣaṇajñānamudrayā). [The phrase] "of the absence" (abhāvasya) [is to be understood].

The point is this: although the presence of the probandum (sādhya) is required for the cognition of the absence of that [absence]—since the absence of an absence has the nature of a positive entity and thus constitutes the absence of its own probandum—nevertheless, it is accepted that within the body of the pervasion (vyāpti), it appears precisely in the form of the delimiting property of the counterpositiveness (pratiyogitāvacchedaka-rūpa) belonging to the absence that constitutes the probandum. Consequently, the presence of the probandum itself is not required there. Nor should it be argued: "In a state where the difference from water (jalabheda) is not present, if one apprehends 'water-ness' (jalatva)—which consists of identity with water—in all instances, one would be able to apprehend the absence of odor as being pervaded by it; for even in that which possesses odor, there is the contingency of [apprehending water-ness], and thus a grasping of deviation (vyabhicāra) occurs. This is not tenable.

At the time when water-ness (*jalatva*) is perceived in water through direct perception, the absence of odor (*gandhābhāva*) therein has already been grasped previously as its pervader (*vyāpaka*), and so forth; therefore, the aforementioned inference is possible through the *parāmarśa* (reflective judgment) consisting of the recollection of that [pervasion]. Even if it was not previously grasped, although there may now exist a doubt regarding the relation of the counter-correlate (*anuyogitva*) to earth with respect to the identity with water (*jalatādātmya*)—which is over-pervasive (*atiprasakta*)—such a doubt ultimately results in a doubt regarding water-ness itself as being non-deviant (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the absence of odor. Nevertheless, because a doubt concerning the probandum (*grāhya-saṃśaya*) does not constitute an obstacle to the ascertainment of the subject (*pakṣa-niścaya*).

Furthermore, since it is possible to remove that [doubt] by any means whatsoever through a favorable *tarka* (reductio), its inclusion in the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed appropriate.
Likewise, even in the case of verbal certainty (*śābdaniścaya*), the aforementioned doubt regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) does not act as an obstacle;

on the contrary, because it functions as a cause under the guise of the cognition of semantic competency (*yogyatājñāna*), its ascertainment via authoritative speech (*āptavākya*) and the like is also appropriate—thus, there is no fault whatsoever. This is because it is not a defect, as it does not subvert both [pervasion and the subject], specifically by way of subverting the subjecthood (*pakṣatā*) through the subversion of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

The meaning is that since there is an absence of that which constitutes a defect—namely, both the sublation of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) and [the sublation of the subject itself]—there is no fault.

This is because, even if one holds the view that "being a subject" (*pakṣatā*) consists in doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhyasaṃdeha*), and thus the sublation of that [doubt] would constitute a sublation of the property-of-the-subject, that position has been refuted; rather, it has been established as a tenet that "being a subject" consists simply in the absence of proof (*siddhyabhāva*). Consequently, since it is impossible to effect a sublation of that [absence of proof] by means of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*), the two-fold sublation is untenable.

In the view that "being the subject of doubt" (saṃśayapakṣatā) constitutes a flaw, even though both [types of] disintegration exist, they do not constitute a fault by way of being combined; for if they were raised as a combination, it would result in the fallacy of defeat (*nigraha*) for the one who points out the "inconstancy qualified by sublation" (*bādhaviśiṣṭavyabhicāra*), due to its superiority [as a distinct fault].
Rather, the meaning is that, like sublation and inconstancy, they must be pointed out separately, and thus they are defects independently.

As for their inclusion within the categories of alternatives (*vikalpakoṭi*), it should be understood as being merely on account of some degree of possibility. "Either pervasion or subsistence in the subject" (*vyāptipakṣadharmatānyatarat*) means by way of being the disintegrator of each one individually.
And thus, the meaning is that only one [of the three] should be pointed out at a time.
The refutation of the third alternative is intended solely for the instruction of the student,
not because it is useful for the subject at hand.

It should be understood that since both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) have been established in the present case, there is no deficiency even if both together constitute a defect.

Even without positing that the difference [between the two] possesses an existence equal to the existence of the substratum (*dharmin*), he begins the method for proving ultimate difference with the words "Or else" (*yadvā*). The phrase "respectively" (*krameṇa*) is to be supplied to the previously stated reasons. Thus, it is stated: "The individual soul (*jīva*) is not the locus of identity having Brahman as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), because it is an experiencer of suffering not experienced by Brahman; the negative instance (*vyatireka*) being like Brahman itself.

Or, Brahman is not the locus of identity having the individual soul as its counter-correlative, because it is not an experiencer of suffering experienced by the individual soul; the negative instance being like the individual soul itself."

Nor should it be argued that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because a conventional difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is Brahman—standing as the locus of identity with Brahman—is admitted in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*);
for what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by being the locus of identity with Brahman.

Even if one admits a difference between the space within a jar and the great space (mahākāśa), since there is no perception of the jar-space not being identical with the great space, there is no defect; for just as a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by being the locus [of the great space] is not admitted by others, so too, even in the case of the individual soul (jīva), a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by being the locus of identity with Brahman—though it be merely empirical—is likewise not admitted by others. Thus, there is no fault.

[Objection: But if this were so, according to the opponent's view, since everything would indeed be the locus of identity with Brahman, the probandum—in the form of a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by that [Brahman]—would be unestablished (*aprasiddhi*). To this, he says: "And it is not so. Although, as in the case of a probandum such as "fire made of gold," the non-establishment of the probandum in the form of the absence of the delimitor of the probandum-ness (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) is indeed a flaw, because it directly contradicts the inference;
nevertheless, in the present case, such a non-establishment cannot be raised as an objection.

Because, given the difference [of the world] due to misconception, there is doubt as to whether it possesses a counter-correlativity delimited by being the locus of identity with Brahman; consequently, that [identity] is not determined.
Furthermore, since such doubt generates doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), it is not a contradiction [to the reason].
Rather, because the aforementioned probandum has not been apprehended in some cases, only the fallacy of unestablishedness (*asiddhi*) consisting in ignorance (*ajñāna*) should be raised.
The point is that this is not a defect in a negative inference (*vyatirekīnumāna*) where the probandum is a non-existence (*abhāva*).

He demonstrates this very point with the words "For that... (*taddhi*). The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: the defect consists either in the sublation of the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), or in the sublation of the pervasion (*vyāpti*), or in the sublation of both.

Now, one might object: even if the probandum is unestablished, the reason can still possess the property-of-the-subject; so how can the [non-establishment of the probandum] sublate that? To this he says: "By sublating the subjecthood (*pakṣatā*). But how is that so? To this he says: "In the category of the probandum," and so forth.

Now, it might be argued that the cognition of the subject’s being qualified by the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*) is not the cause of inference, because *pakṣatā*, as a real entity, is itself a distinct cause. Rather, the cause is simply the cognition of the reason’s presence in that which is delimited by the subject-delimiter (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*). Thus, how can that which subverts *pakṣatā* be considered a subverter of the subject-property (*pakṣadharmatā*) necessary for inference? This is true.

Nevertheless, even if the state of being the subject (*pakṣatā*) were an independent cause [of inference], since the property of being a predicate of that subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) qualified by it would still remain a necessary factor for inference, the fact that the destruction of one part necessarily entails the destruction of the whole remains unassailable.
The passage ending with "because of the impossibility of [the reason] being unestablished" (*aprasiddhena... ayogāt*) is the reason for the destruction of the pervasion (*vyāpti*);

the meaning is that if the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, it is impossible to grasp the pervasion as defined by it. "By the destruction of both" means, according to the aforementioned method, by the destruction of both the pervasion and the property of being a predicate of the subject.

He establishes that there is no fault in the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) in that case—because the inference based on the distinction of the Brahman-subject (*brahmadharmika*) is primary and serves as an indicator for others—by means of the passage beginning with "Not the first," and so forth. Now, one might object: since *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject) consists precisely in a doubt regarding the presence or absence of the probandum within the property-possessor (*pakṣadharmika*), how can *pakṣatā* be established by a doubt of a different kind? To this he replies: "In the inference where 'nameability' (*abhidheyatva*) is the probandum. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "by means of a doubt as to whether nameability exists in sound or not."

The point is this: just as in cases such as "sound is expressible because it is knowable," where—due to the non-establishment of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*)—a doubt regarding the two alternatives of the probandum and its absence is impossible, yet a doubt regarding the two alternatives of the presence or absence of the probandum's subsistence in the subject (*pakṣaniṣṭhatva*) is accepted as being the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*); so too here, in the case of the absence of the probandum consisting of identity with the living self (*jīvatādātmya*), a doubt regarding the two alternatives of the presence or absence of that [absence] subsisting in the subject is adopted as the state of being a subject, since there is no distinction [between the two cases].
This is merely an illustration.

It should be understood that the status of being a *pakṣa* (the subject of inference) belongs both to a doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) dependent upon a misconception, and to the absence of established knowledge (*siddhi*) qualified by the absence of a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*).
Now, one might object: "If the probandum (*sādhya*) is not previously established, how can there be a grasp of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) even for the absence of the probandum?

For the cognition of an absence requires the prior establishment of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). To this, he says: "In cases such as... [The example follows: "Sound is a specific quality of space, because it possesses sound-ness; otherwise, like color. And so forth.
Because the absence— which serves as the basis for grasping the pervasion (vyāpti) defined by the non-existence of the reason (*hetu*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent—
is dependent upon the cognition of the probandum;
that is, it is necessitated by the cognition of the probandum.

The meaning is that the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) constitutes a defect by way of obstructing the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), which in turn obstructs the inferential cognition (*anumiti*).
This is the underlying intention:

in the case of a negative inference (*vyatirekin*), for an inferential cognition whose probandum is the absence of a property delimited by a specific attribute (*taddharmāvacchinnābhāva*), the knowledge of pervasion as the absence of the absence of that property delimited by that attribute is a cause; likewise, the knowledge of pervasion with respect to that attribute is also a cause.

For it is observed that even from the cognition of a pervasion by way of "fire-ness"—just as from the cognition of "the absence of the absence of fire"—there arises an inference of the absence of fire.

Thus, in the present case, since the apprehension of pervasion occurs by way of identity with a well-known living being (*jīva*), the inference whose probandum is the absence delimited by that [identity] does not depend upon the prior establishment of the probandum.

If it is objected: "In your final system (*siddhānta*), since a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) establishes the probandum only through the medium of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), how can it lead to the inference of a pervasion for a probandum that is unestablished?"—we reply: No.
That which is the counter-positive of an absence that pervades [the probans] is itself pervaded by the absence of that [probans].

This is because, through a general pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti)—as in the case of smoke being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of fire—it is possible to infer a pervasion with a probandum not previously established by the force of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā). This is how it should be understood. Regarding the phrase "by not obstructing both": the meaning is that, in the manner described, since it does not obstruct the apprehension of the pervasion and the property of the subject, it does not obstruct the inference.

[Objection: Even so, let it be that non-establishment (*asiddhi*), like sublation (*bādha*) and the rest, is a defect precisely because it is directly opposed to inference; [in response] he says: "Regarding pervasion" (*vyāpti*). It should be understood that sublation and the other defects are also defects by way of destroying the status of the subject (*pakṣatā*), which consists in doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).

Due to dissatisfaction with the introduction of the qualification "having the same ontological status as the existence of the subject" (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*) in the two previously mentioned inferences, [the author] says: "Or else... (*yadvā*). Regarding the phrase "of the two previous reasons": thus, the individual soul (*jīva*) is not the locus of that identity or oneness which has Brahman as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogika*), because it is a cognizer of suffering not cognized by Brahman; for instance, unlike Brahman (in the case of the negative concomitance).

Two inferences have thus been stated: either Brahman does not possess that identity which has the individual soul (jīva) as its counter-correlate, because it does not experience the suffering associated with the individual soul, like the individual soul itself; or, by way of negative concomitance, [Brahman is not the locus of such identity].

[The author] raises the objection: "But surely, since I accept everywhere that the locus-hood of identity with Brahman as counter-correlative to the individual soul (*jīva*) is precisely what is meant, the probandum—in the form of the absence of that [identity]—is unestablished; thus, in both cases, there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). Anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*). If one were to state the proposition (*pratijñā*) in the manner described above, the fallacy of an unestablished qualification would be evident; how then can it be denied? To this, he replies: "For the sake of the fault" (*doṣāya*). The connection is as follows: even though that fallacy of an unestablished qualification exists, it is considered a "fault" (*doṣa*) because it obstructs the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

To the question, "How does it [the counter-example] undermine the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)?", it is said: "By way of undermining the subject-status (*pakṣatā*). The meaning is that the property-of-the-subject consists in residing in the locus of the subject-status; therefore, in the absence of subject-status, there is also no property-of-the-subject in the sense of residing in its locus. To the further question, "How exactly does it undermine the subject-status?", it is said: "Because doubt regarding its possessing the probandum or its absence does not arise. For subject-status is indeed the state of possessing a property whose status as the probandum is doubtful.

The meaning is that in the absence of doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), there is also no "pakṣatā" (the state of being a subject of inquiry) which is constituted by that [doubt]. To the question, "Why does doubt regarding the probandum not arise? it is said: "Because the alternative of the probandum is unestablished. The implication is that, such being the case, there is an absence of recollection of either alternative. Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility of grasping pervasion (*vyāpti*)," the implication is that in the cognition of a relational entity such as pervasion—which possesses a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—the cognition of the probandum as that counter-correlate cannot serve as a cause. Regarding the word "both," the meaning is "both" in the form of pervasion and subsistence-in-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).

With the intention of providing an illustration, he states—beginning with "Not the first," etc.—that in the second inference, the defect of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) does not exist. The sense is: "merely by means of doubt" [is said] because a doubt regarding whether the subject (*pakṣa*) resides in either the probandum (*sādhya*) or its absence—which has as its alternatives the probandum and its absence—is also a constituent factor of the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), just like a doubt regarding whether the property-possessor (*dharmin*) is the probandum or its absence.

Regarding this very point, he states an illustration: "The prover of denotability," etc. In the inference "Sound is denotable because it is cognizable," since denotability is a purely positive (kevalānvayi) property, its absence is unestablished; thus, there is no doubt regarding the presence or absence of the probandum within the locus (the subject), namely, "Is sound denotable or not? Nevertheless, just as the property of being a locus-feature (*pakṣadharmatā*) is established here merely through a doubt concerning the presence or absence of the locus-feature itself—namely, a doubt whose modes are the presence or absence of the locus-feature in the locus of the probandum or its absence—so too is it here.

The meaning is that *pakṣatā* (the state of being a subject of inference) is established by a doubt concerning two alternatives—the presence of the reason in the locus of the subject where the probandum is absent, and its absence there. Regarding the phrase "herein": in the second inference, the probandum is the non-locus-hood of the living self (*jīva*), while its absence is the locus-hood of the living self; since this latter is well-known in the case of the living self, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is possible through the absence of the probans therein. This is the meaning.

Now, one might object: since the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is a cause for the cognition of an absence, if the counter-positive—the probandum (*sādhya*)—is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), the cognition of its absence would be impossible; how, then, can there be a grasp of pervasion (*vyāpti*) in such a case? To this, he says: "Where... In the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatireki-anumāna*): "Sound is a specific quality of space (*ākāśa*), because it is a quality residing solely in space, like color (*rūpa*) by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)," the probandum—being the state of being a specific quality of space—is positive in nature. Consequently, its absence is negative in nature. Thus [the objection does not apply].

The meaning is as follows: since the specific quality of ether (ākāśa), which would serve as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), is unestablished, its absence cannot be known; consequently, it is impossible to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) therein, and thus the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) constitutes a logical defect. In the present case, however, identity with the individual soul (*jīva-tādātmya*) is of a positive nature (*bhāvarūpa*); therefore, the knowledge of that [identity] does not depend upon the knowledge of a counter-positive. Since it is possible to grasp the pervasion therein, the non-establishment of the probandum is not a defect.
[The term] "of the absence" refers to the knowledge of the absence of the probandum.
Because [the cognition of the probandum] is dependent upon the cognition of the entity, and because it is dependent upon the cognition of the counter-positive in the form of the probandum.

Why is this so? To this he says: "Regarding pervasion" (*vyāpti*). For it is well known that fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), such as the unestablished (*asiddha*) and others, constitute defects precisely by way of subverting either the pervasion (*vyāpti*) or the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and not by any other means. Therefore, since the "unestablishedness of the qualifier" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) likewise lacks the capacity to subvert pervasion and so forth, it does not even qualify as a defect. This is the meaning.

Alternatively, non-difference having Brahman as its counter-correlative is neither a non-difference residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) nor a non-difference residing in Brahman that has the individual soul as its counter-correlative;
because it is a non-difference belonging to one who does not experience the suffering associated with the individual soul.
This is by way of contrast, like the oneness that resides in the individual soul and has the individual soul as its counter-correlative.

Unity having the individual soul (*jīva*) as its counter-correlate does not have Brahman as its locus, nor does unity having Brahman as its locus have the individual soul as its counter-correlate, because there is non-difference with respect to one who experiences suffering that has not been experienced by Brahman.
By way of contrast, this is like unity having Brahman as its locus and Brahman as its counter-correlate (or like unity having Brahman as its counter-correlate and Brahman as its locus).
In the same manner, the difference of Devadatta and others from Yajñadatta and others is to be established.

Out of dissatisfaction with the laborious effort required to dispel the doubt regarding the unestablished nature of the qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) even in these two inferences, he says: "Or else... [He explains: "Because it is non-difference from that which does not contemplate" means because it is non-difference belonging to that Brahman which does not contemplate.

Furthermore, the relationship should be understood as being of the nature of the counter-correlative and the substratum (*pratiyogyanuyogibhāva*) in the first case, and of the nature of the property and the locus (*dharmidharmabhāva*) in the second.

The same applies hereafter. [Regarding the phrase] "by way of exclusion, having the individual soul (*jīva*) as its counter-correlative": for in that case, there exists the state of having the individual soul as its locus and the state of having the individual soul as its counter-correlative, but not the absence thereof.

Thus, there exists only the state of being connected to the soul that experiences suffering associated with living beings, and not the state of being unconnected to that which does not experience it; therefore, the absence of the relationship between the probandum and the probans should be understood.
The same applies to what follows.

Having thus stated the eight inferences regarding the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), he extends that same method to the mutual difference between individual souls as well, [saying] "In this way" (*evam*). The meaning is that the difference is to be established in such forms as: "Devadatta is the locus of a difference whose counter-correlate is Yajñadatta and which possesses the same ontological status as its substratum, because he is an experiencer of pain not experienced by Yajñadatta; otherwise, like Yajñadatta. If it is asked, "What is the fault in [an inference] such as 'The earth is scratched by a hare's horn, because it is an entity'? [the answer follows].
This must be resolved by [the argument] that there is sublation by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇabādha*).

Even one who considers it a fault for the qualifier to be unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) should be satisfied with this; thus, he employs another formulation: "Or else" (*yadvā*). Since the absence of being a property of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth is well-known in relation to omniscience and the like, there is no fault. Regarding the phrase "because of non-difference for one who does not reflect," here the meaning of the genitive case is merely a relationship indifferent to the status of being either the locus (*dharmin*) or the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); that is, [the relationship] is either having Brahman as its counter-correlate or having the individual soul as its counter-correlate.

The sense is as follows: if there were non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, then either the soul would be one with Brahman, or Brahman would be one with the soul; thus, in relation to their unity, they would respectively function as the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). If that [distinction] is negated, then unity itself becomes negated. Thus it is said: "In this way"—Devadatta is not the locus of a difference whose existence has the same ontological status as the existence of the substratum that has Yajñadatta as its counter-correlate, nor is he the locus of identity with him.
Because one does not experience that merit, [the argument] is established through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) just like that;
it should be inferred through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of the example of a jar and so forth.

Since it would follow that there would be the loss of what was done (*kṛtahāni*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) if the merit of one person were experienced by another, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddhi*).

He says "or else" (*yadvā*) for the sake of making the establishment of the probandum easy: in the fourfold inference, "reality" (*tāttvikatva*) should be understood as a qualification of the subject (*pakṣa*).
By this, there is no fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
In the phrase "of one who experiences the suffering not experienced by the individual souls" (*jīvānanusaṃhitaduḥkhānusandhātuḥ*), the genitive case is used.

In the first case, the relation between the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and the substratum (*anuyogin*) is to be understood; in the second, the relation between the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and the property (*dharma*). This applies to the subsequent cases as well.

Nor should it be argued that there is a commonality (*sādhāraṇya*) between the two differences—the one having the pot as its counter-positive and the one having the pot as its property-bearer—within a pot or similar object.

Since non-difference consists in being of the nature of the pot, a difference whose counter-positive is the pot and whose locus is the pot would consist in being of the nature of a cloth or the like; thus, because even a difference whose locus is the pot takes such a form, the reason (hetu) exists excessively [in the heterologue].

Although the commonality (sādhāraṇya) of the reason is not easily avoided by means of the subsequent inference alone, nevertheless, because it is supported by favorable reasoning (anukūlatarka), it is impossible for it to function as a sublator (satpratipakṣa) in the case of a negative-only inference (vyatirekin); this is the sense in which it does not constitute a flaw.

He states the proof for the difference [of the self] as a corollary: "In this way. The meaning is: Devadatta is the locus of a difference whose existence has the same ontological status as the existence of the subject (dharmin) that is the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) of Yajñadatta, because he is one who experiences suffering not experienced by Yajñadatta; the formulation is by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), such as "like Yajñadatta," and so forth.

Out of aversion to the aforementioned laborious effort, he shows other inferences: "because of being non-different from the experiencer of suffering. In the first inference, the meaning of the genitive case is "counter-correlativity" (*pratiyogitva*).

In the second inference, it should be understood that the meaning of the genitive case is "the state of being contained" (*ādheyatva*). Regarding the phrase "having the individual soul as its counter-correlative" (*jīvapratiyogika*): according to the purport of the first inference, it means "having the individual soul as its counter-correlative"; according to the purport of the second, it means "having the individual soul as its locus" (*jīvadharmika*). Here too, in the phrase "of the one who reflects" (*anusandhātuḥ*), two meanings should be seen based on the distinction between the two inferences, by virtue of the genitive case.

In all four types of inference, both in our own system and in the opponent's system, non-difference is the very nature of the subject (*dharmin*) and is therefore real. Consequently, for one who accepts that the probandum (*sādhya*)—which is to be established as an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*)—is of the same nature as its locus (*adhikaraṇa*), it is impossible to assert [the falsity of the world]. Thus, there is no opportunity to raise the objection of "proving the already proven" (*arthāntaratā*) by taking a merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) probandum.

He extends this same method even to the proof of the mutual difference between individual souls (*jīvas*). [The text says: "In this way. The method is to be seen as follows: Devadatta possesses the absence of identity with respect to Yajñadatta as its counter-correlate, because he does not experience the pain that Yajñadatta has not experienced; by contrast, Yajñadatta [does not possess such absence]. He states another inference, which is not beset by the suspicion of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*): "Or else. Non-difference (*abheda*) here means identity (*tādātmya*).

Although it has been stated that non-difference having Brahman as its counter-correlative is not [non-difference] having the individual soul (jīva) as its counter-correlative, nor is non-difference residing in Brahman [non-difference] residing in the individual soul, the difference between the individual soul and Brahman is established by implication.

Nevertheless, since the sentences such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), which are accepted by others as proving non-difference, must establish either non-difference having Brahman as its counter-correlative in respect to the individual soul, or non-difference having the individual soul as its counter-correlative in respect to Brahman,
and since it is precisely the aforementioned inferences that directly contradict those [sentences], one follows those [inferences].
In this regard, it should be understood that the first and fourth [alternatives] are opposed to the second, while the second and third are opposed to the first.

Since mere identity (*tādātmyatva*) in the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and since identity not followed by [the knowledge of] the living being (*jīva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), the phrase "followed by the living being" (*jīvānusaṃhita*) and so forth has its meaning already explained.

In this context, because there is no positive example (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*) due to the identity with insentience being equivalent to the subject (*pakṣa*), he says: "by way of negative concomitance" (*vyatirekeṇa*). Nor should it be argued that, according to the opponent's view, since the oneness having the individual soul (*jīva*) as its counter-correlative necessarily also has Brahman as its counter-correlative, a negative example is likewise impossible.

Because the absence of the reason—namely, the state of not being a cognizer of suffering—is established for both parties in the case of the identity of souls and so forth, since that [identity] consists in the very nature of being a soul. "In this manner" means by such a method as: Devadatta is the locus of a difference whose existence has the same ontological status as the existence of the subject (the dharmin) having Yajñadatta as its counter-correlative, because he is a cognizer of suffering and so forth that are not cognized by him, unlike Yajñadatta.

Out of dissatisfaction with the laborious effort required to refute the objection of *aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva* (an unestablished qualification) in the two previously mentioned inferences, he states another alternative: "Or else (*yadvā*)... [The example is] "like that which possesses oneness having a living being as its counter-correlative and a living being as its locus. For in that case, the property of having a living being as its locus exists; a living being is one who experiences the suffering experienced by other living beings, and it is precisely the state of non-difference having such a being as its counter-correlative that exists there, not the state of non-difference from one who does not experience that [suffering].
Likewise, the property of having a living being as its counter-correlative exists;
a living being is one who experiences the suffering experienced by other living beings.
The intended meaning is that the non-difference having that [Brahman] as its substrate is established.

Having thus stated the inference that negates the relation of the non-difference from Brahman to the individual soul (*jīva*), he now states the one that negates the relation of the non-difference from the individual soul to Brahman: "possessing the connection with the pleasure of the individual soul. This means: "like the oneness whose substrate is Brahman and whose counter-correlate is Brahman. For in that case, the state of having Brahman as its substrate exists. Brahman is the non-perceiver of suffering that is not perceived by itself.
And there exists the state of non-difference having that as its counter-correlative;
it is not otherwise.

Likewise, the state of having Brahman as its counter-correlative exists; for one who does not contemplate suffering and does not contemplate [it] while being Brahman, there exists precisely the state of non-difference having that as its substrate, and not otherwise. Such is the sense in which the absence of the probandum and the probans is established.

He extends the method for proving the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) to the proof of the mutual difference between individual souls as well, stating: "In this same way. The sense is that by substituting terms such as "Devadatta" and "Yajñadatta" in place of the words "individual soul" (*jīva*) and "Brahman," all formal arguments (*prayoga*) are to be understood here, such as: "Devadatta is the locus of a difference whose counter-correlate is Yajñadatta, and which possesses a substratum with a reality-level identical to its own, because he is the experiencer of pain not experienced by Yajñadatta; otherwise, it would be like Yajñadatta himself. This is the intended meaning.

If it is argued that since the capacity to experience suffering and the incapacity to experience it can be accounted for merely by a difference due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*), there is no logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*) for establishing an ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*), we say: not so.
For even in the case of a difference due to limiting adjuncts, we observe that a yogin experiences the pleasure and other states produced by multiple bodies;
this is because the limiting adjuncts—the body and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—are distinct in each case.
For the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) situated in one body cannot be situated in another body.
If it is argued that in that case there is only one limiting adjunct consisting of ignorance (avidyopādhi),
then here too, for the proponent of the doctrine of a single soul (ekajīvavādin), there is only one.

However, for those who maintain that there are many individual souls (bahujīvavādins), who assert that even during sleep the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) persists in its causal form, the limitation by ignorance (avidyāvaccheda) is not the cause of the state of being an individual soul (jīvabhāva). Rather, it is the internal organ itself.
Consequently, that [internal organ] alone must be declared the regulator.
And it has been stated that this [distinction] exists even among yogis (or is found even in a yoginī).

Now, an objection: whether between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, or between individual souls themselves, the presence or absence of the experience of suffering and so forth is not the cause of an ultimate difference;
for even while essential identity (*svarūpa-ekya*) exists, such [experiences] are possible through mere adventitious difference (*aupādhika-bheda*).

Anticipating the objection that "therefore all these reasons are non-conclusive," he refutes it with the words "But if [it be argued]... The phrase "merely by the difference of limiting adjuncts" (upādhibhedamātreṇa) means merely by the difference created by limiting adjuncts;

or alternatively, "merely by the difference of the limiting adjuncts" (upādhīnāṃ bhedamātreṇa). The expression "even though there is a difference consisting of limiting adjuncts" (aupādhikabhede'pi) means even though there is a difference produced by limiting adjuncts.
This statement is made for the sake of argument (*abhyupagamya*).
In our own system (*svamata*), the adjunct (*upādhi*) lacks the capacity to act as a cause with respect to difference.
"Belonging to the adjunct" (*aupādhika*) means related to the adjuncts; that is to say, it resides in the adjunct (*upādhiniṣṭha*).
Or, [it may mean] "even in the presence of such a difference.
[This refers to] yogis such as Saubhari and others.

Thus, the meaning is that an adventitious difference (*aupādhika-bheda*) is not the determining factor; rather, it must be accepted that only an ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*) is the determining factor for the lack of mutual recollection between individuals.
But is it not the case that the body alone is not the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), but rather the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as well?
And thus, even when there is a difference of bodies—as in the cases of Śauri and others—recollection is possible because the internal organ is one;
this is not so in the present case.

Because the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are distinct, he says: "of the body. Even in the case of the body of Saubhari, the internal organ is not one, but rather distinct. Otherwise, how could the internal organ situated in one body be the delimiting factor for experience in another body? This is the sense. Now, it might be argued that it is not proper to accept the mind as being distinct from the body, because like the body, it lacks origination.
The mind is eternal because it is beginningless, according to scripture.
For it is not possible for a single, beginningless mind to be distinct in every body.
Therefore, if it is asked: "How then can its distinctness be asserted?"

True. Nevertheless, it should be understood that this statement regarding their difference is like the acceptance of a distinction between Sītā and her ornaments; for although the mind is one, it is divided into many parts and augmented by various material (bhautika) components.

For this very reason, in the second chapter of the *Nyāyamṛta*, while presenting the supporting arguments for the plurality of selves, the author raises the objection: "It should not be argued that the difference in the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the determining factor in the non-recollection of pain and so forth, since the yogi possesses only a single internal organ. Anticipating this, he states: "Because even when there is unity of consciousness (*caitanya*), the difference in the internal organ is irrelevant (*aprayojaka*)."
However, a difference in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has not been established even for yogis.
Therefore, it is inferred that the internal organ of yogis is indeed one and the same.

[Objection: Even if there is a difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the internal organ, there is mutual recollection among yogis because they possess oneness with respect to the limiting adjunct characterized by ignorance (*avidyā*).
But regarding the present case, he raises the objection that there is no recollection due to the difference in ignorance, saying "therein" (tatra). This means "by the Yoginī.
He states the answer: "here too" (ihāpi);
this means "even in the case of Devadatta and others. "Of the proponent of the single-jīva theory" (ekajīvavādinaḥ); the word "view" (mata) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
It is indeed one.
The term "limiting adjunct" (upādhi) is understood to carry over.
Since the individual soul (jīva), which is the delimited entity, is one, the ignorance (avidyā) that serves as the delimiting adjunct is also one.

The sense is that, in such a case, the pursuit [of the argument] would be unavoidable. Regarding the phrase "for those who maintain the doctrine of many souls," the word "view" (mata) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
This is the underlying intention:

Although there is a distinction of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the doctrine of the plurality of souls (*bahujīvavāda*), nevertheless, that [ignorance] is not the cause of the state of being a soul; rather, it is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone.

If the internal organ were not intended as the cause for the state of being a soul, then the persistence of the internal organ in the form of its causal substrate during deep sleep would not be admitted.
For it is precisely because of the non-cessation of ignorance that the persistence of the state of being a *jīva* is logically established even during deep sleep.

Furthermore, he accepts this in order to dispel the doubt that liberation in the form of the nature of Brahman might occur at that very moment due to the disappearance of the state of being a *jīva* through the dissolution of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) during deep sleep;
for even though [the internal organ] has dissolved in its form as an effect, it persists in its form as a cause.

And thus, although the limiting adjunct of ignorance (*avidyopādhi*) is one, because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the cause of the state of being an individual soul (*jīva*), is distinct in every body, the absence of recollection (*anusandhāna*)—just as in the case of Devadatta and others—is indeed logical.
Yet, such recollection does exist.

Therefore, it is known that identity of essential nature (*svarūpaikyam*) alone is the cause of recollection, not the absence of difference in limiting adjuncts. Consequently, the presence and absence of the capacity for recollecting pain and so forth imply only a real difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*).

"But surely these reasons are inconclusive. [The opponent] raises this objection with "But surely" (*nanu*), suggesting that the logical argument—which holds that if there were no difference, there would necessarily be a recollection of pleasure and so forth—is rendered otherwise possible (*anyathāsiddhi*) by means of a false difference. [The author] replies: "Because it is non-deviant from that," meaning that because that [false difference] deviates from the conclusion, the argument cannot be established otherwise. The sense is that a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*) is not a valid reason because it deviates from the positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Regarding the word "here" (*atra*): he shows the difference based on limiting adjuncts in the case of a yogin with "here" (*atra*). The meaning is: in a yogin who has assumed many forms.
Let there be only a difference [in state], not a difference in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); therefore, he says: "For not...
The sense is that this is because of their atomicity (*aṇutva*).
[Objection: In that case, there would be an absence of the internal organ in the Lord (*īśvara*) and the individual souls (*jīva*).
If it is argued that this is because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is accepted as being produced at that very moment, we say no;
for even that [internal organ] is admitted to have a distinct portion (*aṃśabheda*) together with consciousness (*caitanya*),
and because the portions of the internal organ are mutually distinct from one another.
Even so, if it is asked what the cause is for the existence of such synthetic awareness (*anusandhāna*) in a yogi, we say:
it is because otherwise the desire to assume a multiplicity of bodies would be impossible.
Now, one might object that even in the absence of mutual synthetic awareness among the parts, there must certainly be a synthetic awareness in the whole (*aṃśin*) regarding all its constituent parts.

Because the parts [of the Lord] constitute the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there is also non-difference between the part and the whole; thus, due to the identity of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is the desire for many forms by that much alone. In the state of separation, however, there is no identity of the limiting adjuncts.
He raises the objection regarding the identity of the adjuncts with the words "therein" (*tatra*). [He answers] with "here too" (*ihāpi*).
The meaning is "among those who are not yogis.
The intention is that there is only one single *jīva* imagined by the *māyā* of the Lord (*īśvara*), while others are considered to be its parts (*aṃśas*) imagined by His ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is because [the author] accepts that there is such a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*).

And thus, since that [ignorance] is not the cause of the connection or non-connection [with the internal organ], the sense is that for its explanation, a real difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*) must be accepted.

Regarding the phrase "even in deep sleep, they assert the persistence of the internal organ in the form of its cause," there is a variant reading: "In order to avoid the [objection] that the internal organ is not present during deep sleep, some assert the persistence of the internal organ; [they hold] that the limitation by ignorance (*avidyāvaccheda*) is not the cause of the state of being an individual soul (*jīvabhāva*), but rather the internal organ itself.
In that context, *bahujīvavādinaḥ* is a nominative plural.

In an alternative reading, however, the word "they say" (*vadanti*) does not appear. In that case, it should be understood that *bahujīvavādinaḥ* is in the genitive singular. He raises the objection of the argument being inconclusive (*aprayojakatā*) regarding the inference: "But [the difference] is due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*)," and so forth. The sense is this: since the logical reason (*tarka*)—namely, the impossibility of accounting for the distinction between the retention and non-retention of memory if there were natural unity—is not produced, the argument is inconclusive. [The opponent replies: "Difference is due to limiting adjuncts. [This means: in the case of the retention of memory, natural unity alone is the cause, and not the absence of difference caused by limiting adjuncts.

The meaning is that [the proposed definition] fails because it is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of those who, through the grace of yoga, experience a unification (*aikya*) together with that [body], being the synthesizers of pleasure delimited by various bodies; for that [synthesis] has been established elsewhere as existing even without such a body.
Now, one might object: "Is it not rather the absence of difference caused by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone that is the determining factor?"

And because that [internal organ] exists within yogis, he refutes the identity of the internal organs [with the self] by saying, "And of the internal organ... He says, "Not so," for since bodies are mutually distinct, if one were to admit the existence of a single internal organ therein, it would follow that it must be long, and consequently, it would have to reside even in the body of another person; such is the sense.

[The author] raises an objection—namely, that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is not the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), but rather ignorance (*avidyā*); and since that [ignorance] is partless and non-demonstrable, its unity across all bodies is logical—and then refutes it with the words: "If ignorance were the adjunct... and "for the proponent of the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavādin*). The sense is that, in the doctrine of a single soul, the refutation is indeed difficult to avoid.
Furthermore, this has been stated while provisionally accepting the avoidance of the refutation in the case of a yogin.

It should be understood that, just as there is a distinction such as "the space within a jar" due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi) like jars and cloths, so too, because of the simultaneous connection with various bodies, a distinction within ignorance itself is unavoidable; consequently, the distinction among individual souls (jīva-bheda), which is rooted in that [ignorance], is also unavoidable.
Regarding the phrase "even in deep sleep": "in the form of the causal self" means in the form of latent impressions (saṃskāra) consisting of a subtle state.

Thus, since the status of being a jīva belongs only to consciousness delimited by either the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) or its latent impressions as limiting adjuncts, the existence of the jīva is established even in deep sleep.

Otherwise, the consequence would be the dissolution of the *jīva* itself; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "not [merely] ignorance" (*nāvidyā*): if that were the case, since the *jīva* could exist in deep sleep precisely because of the presence of ignorance, it would be improper to speak of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) existing in a subtle form during deep sleep, as it would be redundant; such is the sense. Now, one might argue: "Ignorance itself is the cause of the internal organ.

Since it remains in the form of the internal organ, it follows that it is indeed ignorance, and thus the status of having ignorance as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is established. To this it must be replied: [this is not so].
True;

ignorance alone is the cause of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Nevertheless, even at that time, it remains in a state of effect precisely through its imagined differentiation, for it is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Otherwise, at the time when Caitra and Maitra both sleep simultaneously, there would follow the absurdity of each remembering the other's deep sleep, due to their attaining oneness by virtue of the single limiting adjunct of pure ignorance.

And likewise, in the doctrine of many souls (*bahujīvavāda*), since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the soul, the aforementioned objection remains quite firm.
If it is argued that this fault does not apply in the doctrine of many souls when one accepts distinct cognitions for each individual,
we reply that there is no evidence for such a position and that objections such as unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) do indeed exist.
Furthermore, since the previously mentioned defect—that the distinction [of ignorance] is contingent upon the distinction of bodies—has not been avoided, enough [with this discussion].
Regarding the reading "atrāntaḥkaraṇavṛttiṃ vadataḥ," the genitive singular *bahujīvavādinaḥ* is used; however, in the reading *vadantaḥ*, it is simply the nominative plural.
Following the phrase "tasya kiṃ tarhyantaḥkaraṇameva," one must supply the words "ityāhuḥ" (thus they say) and state that its connection is with that [supplied verb].

One might object: "In the aforementioned inferences, since there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), the reasons are inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). Nor does this imply that a single entity would simultaneously be both the one who does not reflect upon itself and the one who reflects upon it; for this can be explained by the mere difference relative to its own counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), without the necessity of an ultimately real difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*). Thus he raises the objection with the words, "nanu" (But...). [The reply is: Even if there is no ultimately real difference due to the mere difference of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is still a difference produced by limiting adjuncts such as ignorance (*avidyā*).
The phrase "of suffering," etc., refers to "of the individual soul and the Lord," and so forth.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the stated reasons lack probative force.
In regard to [the attributes of] not being aware of that [difference] and being aware of it, one must state that the ultimate difference having that as its counter-correlative is the actual cause.

Otherwise, it would be impossible for those such as Saubhari, who have attained yoga-siddhi, to possess the quality of being a synthesizer (anusandhātṛ) who unifies the consciousness delimited by various bodies assumed at will.

Thus, with the intention that the non-occurrence of the reason in the counter-example (vipakṣa) serves as the subverting factor (bādhaka), he provides the resolution: "Not so," ending with the phrase "because of the difference due to limiting adjuncts" (upādher bhinnatvāt). This constitutes the reason for the difference based on limiting adjuncts (aupādhika-bheda).

Now, one might argue that since it is only the difference created by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) that serves as the cause for the lack of recollection, there is no logical impossibility of recollection even when there is a difference of bodies. To this, he says: "And of the internal organ... One might further object: "Let there be identity of the internal organ even when there is a difference of bodies. To this, he says: "For not... The sense is that the internal organ is not all-pervading (*avyāpin*), like space and other such entities.

If it is asked, "What is the fault if it were to pervade the entire body?"—then, because another person residing within that same body would also be swallowed up by that same internal organ, the distinction created by it would be absent, and consequently, the recollection belonging to that other person would result [inappropriately].

Furthermore, regarding the identity [of the self], is it the identity of consciousness that is the regulating factor for the identity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), or is it the identity of the body?
It cannot be the former, because it would entail the absurd consequence that even non-yogis possess a single internal organ.
Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable, because that too is untenable even for yogins.

Nor should it be argued that there is no such fault because the recollection of experiences occurring in various bodies is the regulating factor for the unity of the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) residing in those respective bodies.
Because the continuity of experience is based on the unity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

In our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, although the parts of the internal organs are distinct due to the difference in bodies, the unity of the Self (*ātmaikya*) serves as the regulator of the continuity of experience; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Let it then be that the distinction created by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) alone is the regulator of the lack of continuity.

For Caitra, Maitra, and others, although there is a difference of bodies, non-connection [of experiences] is possible due to the difference of their respective ignorances (*avidyā*), while connection is possible for the non-yogi due to the unity of ignorance. Nor should it be asked how there can be a difference of ignorances when there is no cause for such difference; for that [difference] is accepted as being beginningless (*anādi*). With this intention, he raises the objection: "In that case" (*tatra*). This means: "in the case of a yogi who possesses multiple bodies."

Is the fact that the differentiation of ignorance (avidyābheda) is the regulator of non-connection asserted on the basis of the doctrine of a single soul (ekajīvavāda), or rather on the basis of the doctrine of many souls (bahujīvavāda)? Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "In this world," etc. The meaning is: "in Caitra and others who are not [yogis]. "Only one," etc.; the phrase "having ignorance as its limiting adjunct" (avidyopādhi) is understood from the context. The word "in our view" (mate) is to be supplied.

Thus, in the view that there is only one *jīva*, namely Hiraṇyagarbha, while all others are false by their very nature—like pots and other objects—the mutual non-connection [of experiences] is untenable; for it is difficult to specify the mutual difference conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopahita*) which serves as the cause of such non-connection among Caitra, Maitra, and others. This is the sense. Regarding the second [position], he states the defect: "In the case of many *jīvas*. During deep sleep (*suptau*), because the functioning of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) in its effected state (*kāryātmanā*) is impossible, it is said to exist in its causal state (*kāraṇātmanā*).

The sense is this: if the state of being a *jīva* (individual soul) were caused solely by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), then since that very adjunct would persist during deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the persistence of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) would be useless.

Now, one might object: "Even if the limiting adjunct of ignorance is not the cause of the state of being a *jīva*, it may still serve as the regulator of the aforementioned distinctions. To this, he says: "And therefore... [The phrase] "the regulator of the distinction" means: even though consciousness is one, that very adjunct—by being the cause of mutual difference which regulates the non-experience of each other's enjoyments—ensures the regulation that "only that [specific adjunct] experiences," thereby maintaining the consistency of those distinctions.

The sense is that, in the doctrine of non-duality (*aikyavāda*), for the sake of maintaining the established definitions, the distinction between individual selves (*jīva-bheda*) is merely imagined; thus, it follows that the very factor which governs [the experience] of one must be the governor of the other as well. Regarding the phrase "And that": the meaning is that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which serves as the mutual cause for the lack of recollection due to the difference in bodies with which one is connected, is what is meant. Consequently, the objection—that the yogin’s recollection of experiences occurring in various bodies remains untenable—persists; this is the intended sense.

Now, regarding the doubt that in all the aforementioned inferences proving ultimate difference, the reason (hetu) may exist while the probandum (sādhya) does not—therefore rendering them inconclusive due to the absence of a subverting factor (bādhaka)—it cannot be argued that there is a subverting factor as follows: "If there were no ultimate difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, nor among the souls themselves, then there would be no such systematic distinction as the soul's experience of suffering versus Brahman's non-experience of it, or the happiness of one soul and the suffering of another. [This is because] such a distinction can be accounted for even in the absence of ultimate difference, through the mechanism of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Thus, the charge of inconclusiveness remains.

He raises an objection, [arguing] that even if there is no ultimate difference in the state already described, the reasoning (*tarka*) is otherwise established because it is possible through a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*): "But surely, by a mere difference based on limiting adjuncts... This means: "by a mere difference produced by limiting adjuncts. Regarding the phrase "even in the case of a difference based on limiting adjuncts": for instance, yogis such as Saubhari, through the power of yoga, simultaneously sustain many bodies.

In that situation, when one body situated in a particular place experiences pain, another body situated elsewhere also experiences pain; and when one experiences pleasure, the other also experiences pleasure—such is the nature of things.

The meaning is this: even though a distinction produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) exists there, the distinction based on such adjuncts cannot be the regulator of the aforementioned rule, because we observe a lack of mutual awareness of suffering. Thus, the argument is not rendered otherwise-established (*anyathāsiddhi*). Now, one might object: "In the case of a yogi, there is no distinction at all produced by limiting adjuncts; therefore, mutual awareness is logical due to non-difference. To this, he says: "In this case... The connection is: "because the body, which is the limiting adjunct, is distinct [in each case]."

[Objection: But surely, even though the limiting adjunct (upādhi) characterized as the body exists there [in the other world], mutual recollection occurs because the limiting adjunct of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is one; therefore, it is said: "of the internal organ. He establishes the very distinction of the internal organs with the words: "for not... The sense is that since the internal organ consists of the mind (manas), and the sense organs such as the mind are distinct in every body.

An objection is raised: "In that case," meaning in the context of the yogis. Even though there is a difference in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body and internal organ, because the limiting adjunct called ignorance (avidyā) is one, there would be mutual recollection among the yogis; however, in the present case, there is no such recollection due to the plurality of ignorances.

Is this stated according to the view of the proponents of a single soul (ekajīvavāda), or according to the view of the proponents of many souls (bahujīvavāda)? Regarding the first, he says: "Even here. In that view, since the soul delimited [by ignorance] is one, its delimiting ignorance must also be one. Thus, by the reasoning already stated, mutual recollection would be unavoidable. This is the sense.
In the second [verse], he says: "But for the proponent of many souls (*bahujīvavādin*)," etc. "Limitation by ignorance" (*avidyāvaccheda*) means the demarcation of ignorance.
It is true that, according to the doctrine of many souls, the adjuncts of ignorance (*avidyopādhi*) are distinct;

nevertheless, because limitation by ignorance is not the cause of the state of being a soul (*jīvabhāva*), the distinction between ignorances does not serve as the regulator of the aforementioned systematic arrangement—this is the meaning. "The internal organ alone," etc., means "only the limitation by the internal organ. To the question "Why is this so?", it is said: "Even in deep sleep," etc.
The proponent of the doctrine of many souls (Bahujīvavādī) has established in his own work that even during the time of deep sleep, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) persists in the form of its cause;
and this is consistent with the view that the limitation by the internal organ is the cause of the state of being a soul (jīvabhāva).
