If the limitation by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) were the cause of the state of being an individual soul (*jīva*), then one might raise the objection that at the time of deep sleep, due to the dissolution of the internal organ, the absence of a limiting adjunct would lead to the cessation of the state of being a soul, resulting in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of liberation in the form of the experience of identity with Brahman at that very moment. This objection can be refuted by the possibility of the following response: although the internal organ dissolves in its *effect-form* (*kāryātmanā*) during sleep, it continues to exist in its *cause-form* (*kāraṇātmanā*); therefore, since the state of being a soul dependent upon it does not cease, there is no such consequence of liberation at that time.
However, this [refutation] is not consistent if the limitation by ignorance (*avidyā*) is held to be the cause of the state of being a soul.
The sense is that, if that were the case, it would follow that ignorance alone persists during the state of deep sleep.
That very [mind] is the differentiated internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
For it is not the case that one [aspect] serves as the cause of the state of being a living individual (*jīva*), while another serves as the regulator of the specific conditions; such is the sense.

To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And that" (*tacceti*). The meaning is that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) which is distinct [in each case] is the regulator of the established order (*vyavasthā*).
This has been stated in the passage beginning with "another body" (*anyadeha*), etc.
Thus, even though a distinction of internal organs exists among yogis, it does not possess the capacity to regulate the established order, because no such fixed order exists [among them].

Therefore, the sense is that because an ultimately real distinction (*pāramārthika-bheda*) is necessary as that which determines the established order, there is no lack of a probans (*aprayojakatva*).
Furthermore, earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) is distinct from the genus directly pervaded by [the others of] water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, mind-ness, and substance-ness other than itself;
this is because it is a genus (*jātitvāt*) or because it is cognizable (*prameyatvāt*), like water-ness.

Nor is "otherness than earth-ness" (pṛthivītvetaratva) a limiting adjunct (upādhi), because it is "otherness than the subject" (pakṣetaratva); furthermore, favorable arguments (anukūlatarka) will be stated hereafter.

In this manner, four inferences are to be formulated by taking water-ness (*jalatva*), fire-ness (*tejastva*), air-ness (*vāyutva*), and mind-ness (*manastva*) as the subjects (*pakṣa*). Regarding the previously stated argument that "self-ness (*ātmatva*) resides in multiple individuals because it is a genus (*jāti*), like earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*)," its unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) was pointed out. To that end, he states the inferences—beginning with "Moreover" (*apica*) and ending with "these inferences establish the plurality of the self"—in order to prove the plurality of the self by first establishing that self-ness is a genus. These inferences proceed precisely on the basis of the Nyāya school's doctrine;
for such is their methodological system.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind are the nine substances (*dravya*).
Among these, "ether-ness" (*ākāśatva*), "time-ness" (*kālatva*), and "space-ness" (*diktvā*) are not universals (*jāti*),
because each exists in only a single individual instance (*ekavyaktikatvāt*).

The group of six beginning with earthness (*pṛthivītva*) is indeed a genus (*jāti*). In that context, once it is established that earthness is a distinct genus directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*) and different from the four [genuses] beginning with waterness (*jalatva*), such a genus cannot exceed [the scope of] selfhood (*ātmatva*); thus, for that genus to be established as a genus, one must necessarily accept a plurality of selves (*ātman*) in order to account for it. In this way, the distinction between selves is established. The same applies to the subsequent cases. Regarding "waterness, etc.": [it refers to] that which is other than the four beginning with waterness and is directly pervaded by substanceness.
"Jāti" (universal) means that which is different from it (the particular).
In the example, the conclusion of the probandum is reached by way of being different from the universal "earthness.
In the probandum, the qualifier "pervaded" (*vyāpya*) is included to exclude the universal "existence" (*sattā*).
Nor should it be said that [the property] is nevertheless pervaded by knowability (*prameyatva*) and so forth; for what is intended is pervasion by a *jāti* (universal),
and knowability and the like are not *jāti*s.

If it were stated merely as "different from a pervading genus," there would be the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), since it would be proven that [the subject] is different from the genus *rūpatva*.
Therefore, the term "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is included.
If only that much were stated, there would again be the fallacy of *arthāntara*, because [the subject] could be taken as being different from the genus *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness).
Therefore, it is said "directly.
Since pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) is pervaded by earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), which in turn is pervaded by substance-ness (*dravyatva*), it is not directly pervaded by substance-ness.
This is because something is directly pervaded by another only when it is itself pervaded by that [other] while not being pervaded by any genus that is itself pervaded by that [other].

If only that much were stated, there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), because it would establish merely the difference from the genus "water-ness" (*jalatva*) and so forth.
Therefore, the qualifier "other than water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, and mind-ness" is added to the genus.
[Objection: But surely, it is also necessary for "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) to be pervaded by "substance-ness."
Otherwise, in the argument "sound is non-eternal because it is produced," *kṛtakatva* (the state of being produced) itself would result in being a pseudo-reason (*upādhi*),
because it possesses a pervasion equal to that of the probandum (*sādhya*) and is thus a pervader of non-eternality;
furthermore, if one does not admit its own pervasion [by the probandum], it would follow that it is not a non-pervader of the probans (*sādhana*) which is non-different from itself.

Therefore, even if there is non-difference, by accepting the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*), one must accept that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is a pervader of the probans (*sādhana*).

If it is argued that here too, since "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) must be accepted as being pervaded by substance-ness, this results in the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntaratā*) because its difference [from itself] would have to be proven—
this is not so, because the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader is necessarily restricted to having different loci (*bhinnāśrayatva*).
For this has been stated in exactly the same way in the *Tattvodyota-ṭīkā* and in the *Prapañca-mithyātva-anumāna-khaṇḍana-ṭīkā*.
Nor does it follow that, if such were the case, "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) would become a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the inference for the non-eternality of sound;
for there is no undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa*) [in that].

Because there is a contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the probans (*sādhana*) as being pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*), it is a rule that when the probans exists, its pervader—the probandum—must also exist; therefore, [the reason] cannot lead to the fallacies of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) regarding the subject (*pakṣa*), nor can it lead to sublation (*bādha*) or a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*).
Consequently, since "substancehood" (*dravyatva*) lacks the property of being pervaded by substancehood itself, there is no "shifting the topic" (*arthāntara*) by taking that difference into account.
This has been stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position].
In reality, however, *kṛtakatva* (the state of being produced) cannot be an *upādhi* (limiting condition) in that case at all,
because it lacks the very quality of not pervading the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*).
For *sādhanāvyāpakatva* is not merely the absence of pervading the probans, but rather the state of not occurring where the probans occurs.
For "being produced" (kṛtakatva) does not reside in sound,
because it is impossible for that [property] to be absent in what possesses it.

However, some, while accepting the relation of pervader and pervaded even in the absence of numerical difference, maintain that although "substance-ness" (dravyatva) is pervaded by substance-ness, it does not possess the status of being directly pervaded by it.
For direct pervasion (*sākṣād-vyāpyatva*) consists in being pervaded by that [the higher genus] while not being pervaded by what is pervaded by that [the higher genus].
And this does not exist in the case of "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*).
This is because, in the case of "substance-ness," which is itself pervaded by "substance-ness," there is an absence of non-pervasion by it.
Therefore, they say that it is not a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). "Because it is other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratvāt*) means because its nature consists in being other than the subject.

The underlying sense is that if "being other than the subject" were also considered a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total destruction of all inference.

Now, one might ask: why should "being other than the subject" not also function as a limiting adjunct—just like "being other than fire" in an inference such as "fire is not hot, because it is a category" (*padārthatvāt*)? To this, he says: "of the favorable arguments" (*anukūlatarkāṇām*). [The reason is] "because it will be stated later," meaning by the argument beginning with "there is parsimony (*lāghava*) if one accepts that *ātmatva*, the ground for the application of the term 'self', is a universal (*jāti*)," and so forth.

Furthermore, if one were to accept that *ātmatva* (selfhood) is not a universal (*jāti*) residing in the counter-correlate of the difference located in earthness (*pṛthivītva*), but rather an adventitious property (*aupādhika-dharma*), then there would follow the fault of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), since its cognition would depend upon the cognition of its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Because such favorable reasoning exists, the fact that *ātmatva* must necessarily be accepted as a universal means that "being different from that" (i.e., being different from selfhood) is present in earthness. Consequently, "being other than earthness" fails to be a pervader of the probandum even within the subject (*pakṣa*), and thus it cannot be an adventitious property (*upādhi*).

The point is that in the inference of the non-heat of fire and so forth, since there is no favorable *tarka* (reductio), it is possible for "being other than fire" (*vahnītaratva*) and the like to function as a limiting condition (*upādhi*). The phrase "in this manner" (*evam*) means that one should infer [the following] by way of such arguments as: "Water-ness (*jalatva*) is distinct from the genus directly pervaded by earth-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, ether-ness, and being-other-than-substance (*dravyatva*), because it is a genus, because it is knowable (*prameyatva*), just like earth-ness. Etc.

He employs the inferences conceived by the opponent, beginning with "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "distinct from a genus" (*jātibhinna*): the sense is that once the genus "self-ness" (*ātmatva*) is established as the counter-correlate of difference, the plurality of selves is established by the rule that [a genus] must reside in multiple instances.

Since earth-ness cannot be distinct from itself, and since water-ness and the others are excluded by the inclusion of the other term [in the compound], and since there is no dispute regarding the fact that ether, time, and direction are each single substances (so the argument does not terminate there), and because it would be cumbersome to postulate another genus given the rule that substances are ninefold, there is no alternative explanation (*anyathāsiddhi*).
The term "pervaded by substance-ness" (*dravyatvavyāpya*) is used to exclude [the definition's over-extension] by means of being a quality (*guṇatva*) and so forth.

The term "directly pervaded" (*sākṣādvyāpya*) is used to exclude that same [over-extension] by means of pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth. The term "universal" (*jāti*) is used to exclude that same [over-extension] by means of being a quality of cognition (*buddhiguṇatva*) and so forth.

If it is argued: "But since we accept a difference whose counter-correlate is non-existent, even if that stated genus (*jāti*) is non-existent, [the probandum] is otherwise established by virtue of being different from it," we say no;
for what is intended is precisely the difference from such a genus of existence (*sajjāti*).
Furthermore, there is no fault, as this inference proceeds according to the system of the Nyāya school.

For this very reason, the existence of [qualities such as] substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth is established. According to our own view, however, it should also be understood that "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) includes properties such as "I-ness" (*ahantva*) and "egoity" (*ahaṅkāratva*). Regarding the phrase "like water-ness" (*jalatvavat*): it should be understood that this [water-ness] is distinct from the "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) which has been made the subject (*pakṣa*). Regarding the phrase "because it is other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratvāt*): the intention is that if this were a limiting condition (*upādhi*), it would result in the undesirable consequence of the total collapse of all inference (*anumāna-mātroccheda-prasaṅga*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that in arguments such as "heat is non-hot because it is a category (padārtha)," the property of being distinct from heat—induced by sublation—is indeed an *upādhi*? Furthermore, in the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka*), it is logical for the property of being "other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) to be an *upādhi*. To this, he says: "of favorable tarkas," etc. "In this manner": it should be inferred that "the nature of water (*jalatva*) is distinct from the genus directly pervaded by earthness, fireness, airness, and mindness, yet other than the nature of substance (*dravyatva*), because it is a genus, like earthness," and so forth.

With the intention that the plurality of selves will be established by proving the genus "selfhood" (ātmatva), he says: "Moreover" (api ca). In the example (dṛṣṭānta), the probandum is to be understood by taking "earthness" (pṛthivītva);

and in the subject (pakṣa), it is by taking the genus "selfhood" that the plurality of selves is established. Nor is there the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (arthāntaratā) by taking distinctions such as "time-ness" (kālatva) and so forth.
The identity of that [substratum] is established by the means of knowledge apprehending the subject (*dharmigrāhakamāna*), aided by the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghavatarka*).

However, the qualification "other than water-ness and so forth" is included to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking the difference from those [qualities] as the basis.
To prevent that same fallacy by taking the difference from existence (*sattā*) as the basis, the term "pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvavyāpya*) is added.
The term "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used to exclude [the fallacy] by taking the distinction of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth into account.

Now, one might object: "In the absence of a supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*), even the 'being other than the subject' (*pakṣetaratva*) would indeed be a defect, as it could give rise to a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*). To this, he says: "of the supporting arguments" (*anukūlatarkāṇām*). "In this way" (*evam*): in that case, "otherness from earth-ness" (*pṛthivītvānyatva*) should be included in the probandum (*sādhya*), and "water-ness" (*jalatva*) and so forth should be made the subject (*pakṣa*).

The intention is that "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth should be taken as the illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the phrase "Moreover" (*api ca*): "earthness," etc. Earthness is the genus (*jāti*) that is directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*) and distinct from [the genera] such as water-ness (*jalatva*). The state of being distinct from that [earthness] exists in the example, namely water-ness, and also exists in other genera residing in the locus of the reason; therefore, there is no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) anywhere.

And when the stated probandum is established by the force of the reason in the subject (*pakṣa*), since it is possible to establish it by taking its own internal difference within the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*), the difference between selves is established by way of proving the existence of a universal (*jāti*) consisting in the nature of being a distinct self (*atmatva*).

Here, the inclusion of "water-ness" (*jalatva*) and so forth is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacies of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratā*), as the differences from water-ness and so forth are not yet established.

If the universal were not introduced as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), then the aforementioned fallacy would occur again by taking the difference between the three-ness or many-ness residing in ether, dimension, earth, water, and so forth; therefore, the universal is introduced by way of its being a universal (*jātitvena*).

To exclude that fault by taking into account distinctions such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, [the definition] specifies "directly pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvasākṣādvyāpya*). This [direct pervasion] consists in being a property that resides in a collection of exclusions delimited by each of those universals (*jāti*) which are distinct from substanceness, distinct from itself, and do not reside in non-substances; and it must also reside in what is other than substances while not residing in non-substances. This is clear in the case of "water-ness," "earth-ness," and so on.

In the case of potness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like, because they do not subsist in that which possesses the earth-exclusion (*pṛthivībhedavat*) included within such a collection of exclusions (*bhedakūṭa*), they do not possess direct pervasion (*sākṣādvyāpyatva*).
Nor is this difficult to establish for earthness (*pṛthivītva*), water-ness (*jalatva*), and so forth.

[For instance,] there are certain universals (*jāti*) distinct from earthness and distinct from substanceness (*dravyatva*), such as potness and others, which are pervaded by earthness and pervaded by water-ness.
The state of possessing a collection of absences delimited by this or that [specific property] exists neither in earth nor in water and so forth;
for every instance of earth and every instance of water is pervaded by some universal (jāti).

Therefore, it must be stated that such a collection [of absences] belongs to ether and the like, or to qualities and the like, because the property of "earthness" (pṛthivītva) and so forth does not subsist therein.

This is because it is possible to provide a justification by taking atoms themselves, since one does not accept any genus (jāti) that is pervaded by a sub-class of substantiality (dravyatva) within atoms. However, some maintain that there is no fault, as one must simply include the entire collection (kūṭa) of co-presences with the respective delimited absences.

In the state of being earth (*pṛthivītva*), there exists a co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the collection of differences delimited by potness (*ghaṭatva*), including cloth; and a co-occurrence with the collection of differences delimited by clothness, including pots. In this manner, there exists a collection of co-occurrences with the collections of differences delimited by each respective genus (*jāti*). Thus, earthness, waterness, and so forth, are the direct pervaders (*sākṣād-vyāpya*) of substanceness (*dravyatva*); however, potness and the like are not so. When "potness" is explicitly mentioned by its own term, it is included among those genera that reside in neither substances different from itself nor in anything other than substances.

They say that because earthness (*pṛthivītva*) is also included [in the definition], it lacks co-occurrence with the difference delimited by itself; thus, there is no violation of the direct pervasion of earthness by substanceness (*dravyatva*), as the properties of being different from itself and being different from substanceness are included within the genus (*jāti*) that does not subsist in non-substances. Furthermore, by including the property of not subsisting in non-substances, the aforementioned fault regarding the inclusion of existence (*sattā*) is avoided.

Because the term is introduced as a *jāti* (universal), there is no occurrence of the aforementioned defect, since there is an absence of co-occurrence with a difference delimited by a number consisting of all that subsist in earth alone.

The qualifier portion [of the definition] is included to exclude the cases of *sattā* (existence) and *guṇatva* (quality-ness), which are directly pervaded (*sākṣād-vyāpya*) by *dravyatva* (substanceness).

Alternatively, due to the complexity (*gaurava*) of introducing a collection (*kūṭa*) of such differences, the meaning of the qualifier portion is: "subsisting in that which possesses the absence of being delimited by the universal of *jāti* that does not reside in anything other than substance, provided it is distinct from substance and distinct from itself."

Since the property of "having a jar" (ghaṭavattva) occurs in that which lacks some particular genus such as "cloth-ness" (paṭatva), the inclusion of the absence of the general class of such genera is intended to exclude [the genus] from being a direct subordinate (sākṣādvyāpyatva). Because the genera that are subordinates of the subordinate of "substance-ness" (dravyatva) are absent in atoms, the substance-ness itself possesses the aforementioned form of being a direct subordinate of substance-ness; thus, this is indeed accepted for the sake of establishing the stated definition.

In the inference under discussion, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) as the subject, one must introduce "the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in substance-ness" as an additional qualification. Such pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) must then be excluded from substance-ness itself. Now, an objection may be raised: since the aforementioned direct pervasion involves the term "itself" (*sva*), it lacks uniformity (*ananugatatva*). Consequently, in accordance with the requirement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) alone would have to be substituted for the referent of the term "itself. If that were the case, how could "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) be established? On the contrary, because there is no absence of its own difference within the subject—which is earth-ness—there would instead be a contradiction (*bādha*). This is not so.

The property of being a genus directly pervaded by *dravyatva* (substance-ness) is the property of being a genus (*jātitva*) that is coextensive with *dravyatva*. This is defined as follows: it is the state of possessing a genus (*jātimattva*) qualified by itself through the dual relation of "not occurring in what lacks itself" (*svābhāvavadavṛttitva*) and "being different from itself" (*svabhinnatva*). Furthermore, the state of possessing the absence of itself (*svābhāvavattva*), where the counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of possessing a genus qualified by itself through the dual relation of "not occurring in what lacks itself" and "being different from itself," and the state of not occurring in what lacks itself—these two relations together constitute the definition. It should be understood that within the body of this definition, the property of possessing a genus (*jātimattva*) is determined by the dual relation of "not occurring in what lacks itself" and "being different from itself"; thus, both this great composite relation and the second relation [of absence] are to be applied to the genera that constitute the definienda of *dravyatva*.
In this context, [the definition of a universal] consists in being a genus directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*), by virtue of its commonality with substanceness.

To exclude that [genus, i.e., existence (*sattā*)] in the present case, one must either introduce—by means of the third relation—the property of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference residing in its own substratum, or state that it is a genus qualified by substanceness through the three aforementioned relations, or a genus directly pervaded by that [substanceness].
Following the literal reading, the final formulation and the purpose of the relations should be investigated accordingly.

When one considers the counter-argument resulting from the fact that "ownership" (*svatva*) is not included within the body of the relation, it should be understood that—in place of the condition "not occurring in what lacks ownership"—the condition "possessing a difference whose delimitation is its own occurrence, as delimited by the relation of 'occurring in what lacks [the property]" (*abhāvavadvṛttitvasambandhāvacchinna-svavṛttyavacchedakatākabhedavattva*), is the constituent of the relation. This is the general direction. Regarding the phrase "because of being a genus" (*jātitvāt*): here, the inclusion of another reason, namely "knowability" (*prameyatva*), which is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) property, is intended to indicate that no suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the aforementioned probandum should ever be raised.

The absence of defects such as the uselessness of a qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇakatva*) in the reason (*jātitva-hetu*) should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Tattvodyota-ṭīkā* in the passage beginning with "that which excludes the [other] reasons" (*yaddhetuvyavacchedakatva*). Anticipating the objection that even "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) possesses the status of a limiting condition (*upādhitva*) even in the absence of a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*), he says: "of favorable arguments" (*anukūlatarkāṇām*). This means [arguments] such as: "if *jāti* were the ground for the application of the term 'self' (*ātmapada-pravṛttinimitta*), there would be parsimony (*lāghava*); if it were a limiting condition (*upādhi*), there would be prolixity (*gaurava*)," and so forth.

Now, desiring to remove the defects stated by the opponent in such inferences as "Selfhood (ātmatva) resides in multiple individuals because it is a genus (jāti), like potness (ghaṭatva)," [the author] first states the proof for the genus-status of selfhood in order to dispel the suspicion of unestablished reason (asiddhi) regarding the initial inference—beginning with the words "Furthermore" (api ca). The connection [of the sentence] is that these inferences establish the plurality of the Self by means of proving the genus of selfhood.

Here, by taking the difference of "earthness" (pṛthivītva) as the example, the presence of the probandum (sādhya) is established; however, since that [difference of earthness] is not applicable to the subject (pakṣa), the intended conclusion is achieved by establishing the probandum through the difference of the genus of selfhood alone.
Nor should one suspect the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara) by means of establishing other universals such as "space-ness" (ākāśatva) and so forth;
for it will be stated later that such [universals] are not established due to their contradiction with reasoning (tarka).
Furthermore, the reasonings that grasp the identity of the Self are merely fallacious (ābhāsa), as they are contradicted by stronger means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
By this, the objection that there is a "different subject matter" (arthāntara) due to the establishment of another genus such as "omnipresence" (vibhutva) is refuted;

for [the claim] contradicts such reasoning as: "A genus subsumed under substancehood that does not subsist in ether and so forth [is impossible], because it is a genus distinct from existence (sattā) and substancehood (dravyatva), like earthhood.
Furthermore, they say that the genus should be qualified by the property of "not subsisting in that which is devoid of impression" (saṃskāra).

In this context, the qualification "distinct from water-ness (*jalatva*) and so forth" is added to the genus (*jāti*) in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking water-ness and other such genera as the subject. To avoid that same fallacy by taking pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and other such genera, the phrase "directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*)" is included. Being directly pervaded by substantiality means: being pervaded by substantiality while not being pervaded by any genus that is itself pervaded by substantiality.
The first part of the definition (the locative absolute clause) excludes pot-ness and the like.

The term "jāti" (universal) is included there in order to include earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and the like, which are subsumed under [universals] such as "being an element" (*bhūtatva*) that are themselves subsumed under "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*).
The qualifying portion [of the definition] is for the purpose of excluding "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and the like.

Now, since "being pervaded" (*vyāpyatva*) consists in not occurring in that which lacks it [the pervader], substance-ness itself could also be considered "pervaded by substance-ness"; thus, by taking its own difference [from itself], there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

As for the claim that *dravyatva* (substanceness) is not directly pervaded [by a lower genus] because it is pervaded by the genus *dravyatvarūpa*, which is itself pervaded by *dravyatva*—that is not correct.

For if that were the case, then even *pṛthivītva* (earthness) and the like would be pervaded by the genus *dravyatvarūpa*, which is pervaded by *dravyatva*; consequently, there would follow the impossibility of establishing any genus that is directly pervaded by *dravyatva*.

However, if one intends to mean "not being pervaded by a genus that is distinct from substancehood yet pervaded by substancehood," then even substancehood itself would not be excluded, as it remains directly pervaded by substancehood.

Likewise, if "not being pervaded by a genus pervaded by substancehood" is defined as "subsisting in that which lacks a genus pervaded by substancehood," then earthness and the like would not be included;
for since a genus pervaded by substancehood exists in earth, its absence (the lack of such a genus) cannot be established there.

If it is argued that by intending [the definition] to mean "subsisting in that which lacks any universal whatsoever that is pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatva*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of including even "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and the like, we say: not so. For what is intended is a pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) consisting in being of lesser extension (*nyūnavṛttitva*).

And being of lesser extension means: while having the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as that [universal], it is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference that is co-locus with that [universal].

The inclusion of the positive (sat) portion and the qualificand (viśeṣya) portion [in the definition] is for the purpose of excluding existence (*sattā*) and quality-ness (*guṇatva*) from being pervaded by substance-ness (*dravyatva*).

Furthermore, substance-ness itself is not pervaded by substance-ness because it lacks the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference that is co-locational (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with substance-ness.

And within the body of the definition of "not being pervaded by a genus that is pervaded by substance-ness," the term "pervasion by substance-ness" consists merely in being a delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference co-locational with substance-ness.
Because [the property] would be redundant (*vaiyarthyāt*).

And its non-pervasion (*tadavyāpyatva*) consists in being other than that which, while being co-locatable with it, is a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference co-located with it.

In other words, it is being other than that which is qualified by such a genus through the two relations of being a delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of a difference co-located with itself and being co-located with itself.

Since earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and the like are the delimiters of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of a difference that is co-located with waterness (*jalatva*), which is pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*), and since they are also co-located with potness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like, there would be the undesirable consequence (*asaṅgraha*) of their non-inclusion; therefore, both parts [of the definition] are introduced.
In this way, earthness and the like are pervaded by substanceness;
potness and the like are pervaded by those [earthen things].
And since "otherness than that" (tadanyatva) applies to earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth,

the term "genus" (*jāti*) is included to exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), by taking into account the difference in properties such as possessing specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) that do not reside in space (*gagana*).

Although there is still the fallacy of *siddhasādhana*— because the difference from both earth-ness and a pot, which has as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) a property residing in such a genus, exists in earth-ness itself— [the term "genus" is necessary].

Furthermore, if one were to attempt to prove that earthness (*pṛthivītva*) is not the locus of such a genus, there would be a contradiction (*bādha*), because earthness itself is indeed the locus of such a genus.
Nevertheless, this fault does not apply if one proves a difference that has as its counter-positive something residing in the counter-positive of such a genus;
for the difference from both [the genus and its locus] resides in the counter-positive.
And "jātitva" (the state of being a universal) is an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*).

Therefore, there is no defect even if a cumbersome property (*gurudharma*) cannot serve as a delimitor of the probans (*hetutānavacchedaka*), because it is impossible for [the property of] "inhering in multiple eternal entities" to be the probans;
or rather, mere "being located in" (*ādheyatvamātra*) is intended as the probans.

In the phrase "or because of being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatvāt*), the prefix *pra-* is intended to indicate that the probans under discussion is established by valid means of cognition (*prāmāṇika*).

Regarding the words "but not" (*na ca*): although it is impossible to ascertain the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*) by the state of being other than the subject (*pakṣetaratva*)—since there is doubt regarding the probandum in the subject (*pakṣa*)—nevertheless, its status as a doubtful extraneous condition (*sandigdhopādhitva*) remains unimpeded.

Nor should it be argued that [the property of being] "other than the subject" (pakṣetaratva) lacks the capacity to lead to the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*), or that there is no contradiction because doubt regarding the counter-position—dependent on that [property]—is itself a doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*).
The point is this: while a natural doubt does not constitute a contradiction, a doubt induced [by a fallacious reason] does contradict inference.
Furthermore, even if "being other than the subject" is a suspected pseudo-reason (*upādhi*), it possesses no subverting power (*dūṣakatva*).

With the intention that otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of inference (*anumiti*), he says: "of that" (*tasya*). Now, one might object: a suspected extraneous condition (*sandigdhopādhi*) is non-defective only when a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*) exists; otherwise, in cases such as "fire is not hot because it is produced," it would be impossible for the extraneous condition "being other than fire" (*vahnītaratva*) to be defective. To this, he says: "of the favorable arguments" (*anukūlatarkāṇām*). This refers to [arguments] such as "the contingency of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)," and so forth.

"Thus" means in the following manner: "Water-ness is distinct from the genus directly pervaded by earth-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, mind-ness, and [the property of] being a substance other than these, because it is a genus, like earth-ness," and so forth.

This is merely an illustration. One may also argue: "Earth-ness does not reside in that which resides in a certain genus residing in substances but not residing in water and the rest, because it is a genus pervaded by substance-ness, like water-ness and the like."

One should also infer that the universal *pṛthivītva* (earth-ness) is distinct from any genus directly pervaded by substancehood (*dravyatva*) that subsists in either smell or cognition, because it is knowable (*meyatva*), like potness (*ghaṭatva*); this and similar arguments are to be understood as proving the existence of the universal *ātmatva* (selfhood).

Now, by means of proving that *ātmatva* (the nature of self) is a universal (*jāti*), he states the inferences that establish the plurality of selves, beginning with "Moreover" (*apica*) and ending with "establishes the difference of selves" (*ātmabhedaṃ sādhayati*). Here, once it is established that the universal "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) is distinct from the four universals such as "water-ness" (*jalatva*) and is a universal directly pervaded by the property of being a substance other than those [four], then—since such a universal is not different from "self-hood" (*ātmatva*)—it follows that *ātmatva* is established as a universal. To account for this, one must admit the multiplicity of selves; thus, the difference between selves is established.

In the same way, the application [of the definition] should be understood in the subsequent cases as well. Regarding the term "jalatva" (water-ness): the meaning is that which is different from those [qualities] such as water-ness, which are themselves distinct from the genus directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*).
In the example, the conclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) is reached through its being distinct from earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*).

If, in the probandum, one were to say merely "distinct from a genus," there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), because it would establish only the distinction from the genus existence (*sattā*).

Hence, "pervaded" (vyāpya). Since that [property] is pervasive because it subsists in things other than substances and so forth, it is excluded. Nor should it be said that even that [property] is indeed a genus pervaded by knowability (*prameyatva*); for what is intended is being pervaded in relation to a genus.

If it were stated simply that "it is distinct from a pervaded genus" (*vyāpyajātibhinna*), there would be the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), because the fact of being distinct from *rūpatva* (the genus of color) is already proven; for that [distinction] resides only in *rūpa* (color), which is indeed a pervaded genus.
Therefore, the term "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is added. And since that [substance-ness] is pervaded by the genus "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), that [fallacy] is avoided.

If it were stated that [the property] is distinct from the genus (jāti) pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*) because it is already established that it is distinct from "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Therefore, it is specified as "directly" (*sākṣāt*). And "pot-ness" is not a genus directly pervaded by substantiality. For being directly pervaded by X is defined as being pervaded by X while not being pervaded by any genus that is itself pervaded by X.
For example, "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) is directly pervaded by substantiality.
That is substantiality (*dravyatva*).
That is a genus pervaded by it, such as "water-ness" (*jalatva*) and so forth;
for, while being pervaded by that [substantiality], it is itself pervaded by substantiality.
Pot-ness is not so;
that is substantiality (dravyatva);
and earth-ness (pṛthivītva) is pervaded by that.
Because there is no absence of being pervaded by that [the genus *dravyatva*] due to its being pervaded by it;

for if one were to say "different from the genus directly pervaded by *dravyatva*," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*), since even *jalatva* (water-ness) and so forth are genera directly pervaded by *dravyatva*, and thus their difference from it would be proven. Therefore, the phrase "other than *jalatva*, *tejastva*, *vāyutva*, and *manastva*" is included.
Consequently, everything [in the definition] is purposeful.

But even so, since "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is a genus directly pervaded by something other than "water-ness" (*jalatva*) and the like, the proof of its being distinct from that [water-ness] results in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*).
Nor is it the case that substance-ness is not pervaded by substance-ness;
for we do not accept the relation of pervader and pervaded when there is identity.

Otherwise, in the argument "Sound is eternal because it is produced," there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is itself a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because "being produced" is pervaded by "non-eternality," and because,
since identity does not admit the relation of the pervaded and the pervader, "being produced" is not pervaded [by the probandum].
Therefore, if that [pervasion] is accepted, this fault does not arise;
for "being produced" (kṛtakatva) is a pervader of the probans, since it pervades the property to be proven.
If it is asked, "How so?"—no.
This is because, although *dravyatva* (substancehood) is pervaded by *dravyatva*, it lacks direct pervasion (*sākṣādvyāpyatva*). To explain:
direct pervasion of X by Y consists in being pervaded by Y while not being pervaded by any genus that is itself pervaded by Y.

And that [pervasion] does not exist in substanceness (*dravyatva*). That is, substanceness; that which is pervaded by it is "being pervaded by substanceness" (*tadvyāpyatva*), and this resides in substanceness, but not in that which is pervaded by it. Therefore, there is no fault, as in the case of "water-ness" (*jalatva*). Regarding the phrase "and not" (*na ca*): because water-ness is a pervader of the probandum (*sādhya*) and is a non-pervader of the probans (*sādhana*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*) for fluidity (*taratva*); the meaning is that it is not so.

Why is this so? To this he says: "because it is other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratvāt*). If it is asked, "Why should 'being other than the subject' not also be a limiting condition (*upādhi*)?"—the implication is that if that were the case, then in the inference "The mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke," "being other than the mountain" would be a limiting condition, since it pervades the probandum (*sādhya*) in the kitchen (the example) but does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*) in the subject (the mountain).
And if that were so, there would be the total destruction of all inference.

Is this not an unequal comparison? For in the case of "the mountain possesses fire," when fire is established on the mountain by the force of a favorable *tarka*—namely, that "if fire were not there, then smoke would also not be there"—then because the property of being other than the mountain (*parvatetaratva*) is absent from the mountain, it does not pervade the probandum (*sādhya*) and thus cannot be an *upādhi*.
As they say:
"When the probans (*sādhana*) is accompanied by a favorable *tarka*..."
"There is no possibility of an *upādhi* (limiting condition) in the subject (*pakṣa*) because the pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatā*) is destroyed," [it is argued].
This means that when there is a probans (*sādhana*) that has a protector—that is, one that possesses its own owner—the pervasion of the probandum is destroyed in the subject.
And in the present case, this is because of the absence of a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*).

In the argument "Fire is not hot because it is a category" (*padārthatvāt*), just as "being other than fire" (*vahnyitaratva*) [or "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*)] is considered a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), so too would "being other than earth-ness" (*pṛthivītvetaratva*) be appropriately considered a limiting adjunct. To this, he says: "of favorable arguments" (*anukūlatarkāṇām*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in accepting that the ground for the application of the term 'self' (*ātmapada*) is a universal (*jāti*)," and so forth. Thus, the point is that since the probandum (*sādhya*) is established in the subject (*pakṣa*) by the force of such favorable arguments, "being other than earth-ness" is not a limiting adjunct here, because it does not pervade the probandum due to its absence in the subject.

Because a separate presentation would be cumbersome, he says: "In this way. The meaning is that one should infer as follows: "Wetness (jalatva) is distinct from the universal directly pervaded by earthness, fireness, airness, mindness, and substanceness, because it is a universal, like earthness," and so forth.

Substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is the direct pervader (*sākṣād-vyāpaka*) of the universals other than earth-ness, water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, and mind-ness, because it is a universal that is directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*), just like quality-ness (*guṇatva*).

All minds are distinct from substances that possess a universal which is the direct pervader of substance-ness yet is not the locus of touch, because they are substances, or because they are loci of existence, or because they are objects of cognition, just like earth.
However, for those who maintain the plurality of directions (*digbheda-vādin*), one must include the qualification "not being the locus of direction-ness" (*diktvānadhikaraṇatva*) in every case.

The entire earth is distinct from that which possesses a genus directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*), yet is not the locus of the properties of water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, or mind-ness, because it is a substance and because it is the locus of existence (*sattā*), like water.
Existence (*sattā*) is other than the genus residing in itself that is different from substanceness, because it is a genus and because it is knowable (*prameya*), like pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*).

Alternatively, substanceness is other than the genus residing in itself that is different from existence (i.e., other than the genus residing in itself that is different from existence), because it is a genus, like pot-ness.

For those who maintain that the self is atomic, however, the following inferences establish the plurality of selves: "The self is the locus of a genus (jāti) subsumed under the category of substance (dravyatva), because it is a non-omnipresent substance, like the earth," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "like the quality-ness" (*guṇatvavat*): here, one should understand that by taking the genus "color-ness" (*rūpatva*), the conclusion of the probandum is reached through its being a pervader of that [quality-ness].

If one were to state in the probandum simply that [the self] is a pervader with respect to a genus, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntaratā*) by taking "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as the instance.
Therefore, it says "directly" (*sākṣāt*).
If only that much were stated, there would be the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntaratā*) by taking the five [properties] beginning with earthness;
to exclude that, the word "other" (*itara*) is included.

If it were stated simply as "because it is a genus (*jāti*) in the reason," there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to existence (*sattā*). Even if it were stated as "because it is a pervaded genus (*vyāpyajāti*)," there would still be a deviation with respect to existence itself,
because existence is pervaded by knowability (*prameyatva*).

Therefore, [the reason is] "because it is a genus pervaded by existence" (*sattāvyāpyajātitvāt*). If only that much were stated, there would be a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth; to exclude that, the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is added. Regarding the phrase "all minds" (*sarvāṇi manāṃsi*): if the reference were simply "minds," since it would be possible for only a few minds to constitute the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be the fallacy of proving the irrelevant (*arthāntaratā*), because one could establish the exclusion of those remaining minds which possess the genus "mind-ness" (*manastva*)—which is directly pervaded by "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*)—and which are not substrata of touch. Therefore, the word "all" is used.
And thus, the term "genus" (*jāti*) culminates precisely in the genus "selfhood" (*ātmatva*).
This is because the qualification "not being the locus of touch" excludes earth and the other elements, which possess the genera of earthness, water-ness, fire-ness, and air-ness;
furthermore, since all minds are included within the subject of the inference, it is impossible to include those minds that possess the genus "mind-ness" (*manastva*).
Because it is impossible for something to be distinct from itself;
and because ether, time, and space are not substrata of any genus (jāti) that is pervaded by the property of being a substance (dravyatva).

If, in the probandum, one were to state merely "distinct from that which possesses a genus," there would be the fallacy of proving the already established (arthāntara), since it would follow that [the categories] are distinct from qualities and actions, which also possess genera such as "existence" (sattā).
Hence, [the author] says "pervaded by" (*vyāpya*).

Even so, there would be the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*), because it would establish the state of being distinct from qualities and actions that possess the universals (*jāti*) of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and action-ness (*karmatva*), which are themselves pervaded by the universal of existence (*sattā*).
Therefore, [the author] says "by substantiality" (*dravyatva*).

Even so, there is the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*), because it would establish the distinctness of things such as jars—which possess the genus *jar-ness* and the like, which are themselves subsumed under the genus *substance-ness*—from [the subject].
Therefore, the term "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used.

Nevertheless, there remains the fallacy of *arthāntara*, because it would establish the distinctness of the four [elements] beginning with earth—which possess the genus *earth-ness* and the like, which are directly subsumed under the genus *substance-ness*—from [the subject].
Therefore, [the definition] is "that which does not have touch as its locus.

Now, one might object: if this is so, it would suffice simply to say "that which possesses a genus subordinate to substanceness (dravyatvavyāpyajāti) that does not have touch as its locus, and is distinct from the four [elements] beginning with earth";
the word "directly" (sākṣāt) is redundant.

If it is argued that pots and the like—which possess universals such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) that are pervaded by a series of substance-hood (dravyatva)—are already excluded by the very term "not being the locus of touch," [the author replies:
True.
Nevertheless, some say that this [term] is intended to establish that "self-hood" (ātmatva) is directly pervaded by substance-hood.

However, some [opponents], while accepting the relation of pervader and pervaded even in the case of non-difference, argue that since *dravyatva* (substance-ness) is indeed pervaded by *dravyatva*, it is possible for the term "the genus pervaded by *dravyatva*" to refer to the genus *dravyatva* itself; thus, its establishment would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Therefore, to exclude this, the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used.
And being directly pervaded means: being pervaded by that [genus] while not being pervaded by anything pervaded by that [genus].

And because *dravyatva* (substance-ness) is itself pervaded by [the property] "being pervaded by *dravyatva*," it lacks the state of being unpervaded by what is pervaded by that; thus, it lacks direct pervasion (*sākṣād-vyāpyatva*) by *dravyatva*.
It is said that the function of the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is to ensure that the definition culminates in the universal *ātmatva* (selfhood) alone.

However, in reality, since there is no relationship of pervader and pervaded between identical things, it should be understood that the word "directly" is unnecessary in this context. Regarding the phrase "like earth": in that case, taking the universal *manastva* (mind-ness) as the instance, the probandum should be understood as being distinct from that mind.

[Objection: But surely, for those who maintain that the distinction between directions is inherent (*svābhāvikabhedavādin*), since they admit that "direction-ness" (*dik-tva*) is a universal (*jāti*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntaratā*) in the following ways: (1) in the inferences where "earth-ness" (*pṛthivī-tva*) and so on are the subject (*pakṣa*), by establishing that [the subject] is distinct from direction-ness; (2) in the inferences where "substance-ness" (*dravya-tva*) is the subject, by establishing that it is the direct pervader (*sākṣād-vyāpaka*) of the universal direction-ness; and (3) in the inferences where "mind" (*manas*) is the subject, by establishing a distinction between directions possessing the universal direction-ness. To this, he says: "But for those who maintain the distinction of directions... This means: with reference to them. "...the apprehension of not being the locus of direction-ness."
This is an elliptical indication;
it should also be understood as including the apprehension of direction (*dik*). This is because the word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) has been stated here.

And likewise, in the inference where the mind (*manas*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), just as "not being the locus of touch" is used, "not being the locus of direction-ness" (*diktvānadhikaraṇa*) should be supplied.
The sense is that in the other inferences, "direction-ness" (*diktvā*) should be supplied as being on an equal footing with "water-ness" (*jalatva*) and so forth.
In the same way, in the inference where the earth (*pṛthivī*) will be mentioned as the subject, it should also be understood as "not being the locus of direction-ness."

For this very reason, it is stated here that "in all cases. Regarding the phrase "the entire earth": here too, the function of the word "all" (sarva) should be understood as before—namely, the exclusion of the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara)—by taking any portion of the earth as the subject and establishing the exclusion of the remaining earth that possesses the aforementioned class-property of "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva). The term "non-abode" (anadhikaraṇa) at the end of the definition is included to prevent the fallacy of proving something else by taking the difference from water and so forth as the probandum.
To exclude the possibility of proving the difference from qualities (guṇa) and so forth, the class-property (jāti) is qualified by the term "pervaded by substanceness" (dravyatvavyāpya).

In this context as well, they say that the word "directly" (sākṣāt) is for the purpose of establishing that selfhood (ātmatva) is directly pervaded by substanceness (dravyatva). "Like water-ness" (jalatvavat): here, the conclusion of the probandum is reached by taking the difference from earth (pṛthivībheda). "Existence" (sattā): the meaning is "other than that genus which resides in the self and is distinct from substanceness."

In this context, the phrase "other than substance-ness" (*dravyatvānyeti*) is intended to exclude the universal *substance-ness* (*dravyatvajāti*) which resides in the self (*ātman*). The phrase "residing in the self" (*ātmaniṣṭha*) is used to exclude [universals] such as *earth-ness* (*pṛthivītva*). The underlying idea is that this universal cannot be anything other than *selfhood* (*ātmatva*). Regarding the example "like pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvavat*): here, it should be understood that the probandum (*sādhya*)—being other than that [universal]—is established by taking the universal of existence (*sattājāti*) as the referent. Regarding the phrase "or substance-ness" (*dravyatvaṃ vā*): here too, the conclusion of the probandum in the example is reached by taking the difference from substance-ness (*dravyatvabheda*). [The reason given is] "because it is a non-pervasive substance" (*avibhudravyatvāt*).
Here, the term "non-omnipresent" (*avibhu*) is used to exclude the lack of pervasion (*anaikāntya*) with respect to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth;
the term "being a substance" (*dravyatvāt*) is used to exclude that same fallacy with respect to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth.

Since the Naiyāyikas and others do not accept the atomicity (*aṇutva*) of the self (*ātman*), the phrase "of those who maintain the atomicity of the self" is stated at the very outset to prevent the suspicion that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*) according to their own system. Thus, regarding the phrase "such inferences as these": here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), one may include: "Selfhood (*ātmatva*) is a universal (*jāti*), because it is the ground for the application of a word conventionally established in its own substratum, like potness (*ghaṭatva*)."

The word "ātman" has as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) a universal (*jāti*) other than existence (*sattā*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*), which resides in that which is denoted by itself, because it is conventional (*rūḍhatvāt*), like the word "jar. Alternatively, the self (*ātman*) is the substratum of the universal that is the basis for the application of the word "ātman," because it is the conventional meaning of that word. Whatever is the conventional meaning of a word is the substratum of the universal that is the basis for the application of that word.

Inferences such as "the object denoted by the word 'pot' is a pot" and "it is the substratum of the universal *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness), which is the ground for the application of the word 'pot'," are to be understood here. Regarding the phrase "directly pervading": the sense is that the universal *ātmatva* (selfhood) is established by virtue of being pervaded by that [consciousness].
The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is included in the proposition (*pratijñā*) to preclude the possibility of its being otherwise established as a pervader of *ghaṭatva* and other such universals.

The term "directly pervaded" (*sākṣādvyāpya*) is included in the reason (*hetu*) to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as being a "bowl" (*śarāva*) or a "ladle" (*udañcana*), which are final pervades that lack any further pervader.

The word "universal" (*jāti*) is used merely for the sake of defining its own nature. The phrase "distinct from those possessing universals" implies that the universal "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is established by way of being a qualifier of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the negation. The qualification of the subject (*pakṣa*) as "all" is intended to prevent the charge of being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) with respect to the internal organ (*manas*).
If it is argued that there is an alternative proof for the mutual difference of minds [based on other reasons], we say no;
because the probandum (sādhya) is the state of being the locus of the absence of that which is delimited by "mind-ness" (manastva).
And thus, there is no deficiency in the probandum.

In place of "delimited by the nature of mind" (*manastvāvacchinna*), it is appropriate to adopt the term "directly pervaded by substantiality" (*dravyatvasākṣādvyāpya*). Alternatively, the phrase "distinct from those possessing a genus directly pervaded by substantiality" means "loci of the absence whose counter-correlate is delimited by the aforementioned genus.
The term "not the locus of touch" (*sparśānadhikaraṇa*) is included to exclude the four [substances] beginning with earth.

The term "possessing a genus" (*jātimat*) is used to exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) regarding that which is distinct from genus and so forth. The term "pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvavyāpya*) is used to exclude [the same fallacy] regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. The phrase "like earth" (*pṛthivīvat*) should be understood as "that which is distinct from the mind (*manas*) of the aforementioned nature. Since for those who maintain the doctrine of difference (*bhedavādin*), even that [existence] is a genus, it would be unestablished elsewhere; therefore, he says "existence" (*sattā*). Here, in order to exclude the fallacy of being otherwise established (*anyathāsiddhi*) by virtue of residing in the self (*ātman*) which is pervaded by substanceness, he specifies "other than substanceness" (*dravyatvānya*).
It should be understood that this [substance-ness] is non-different from the existence (*sattā*) of the aforementioned form.

"Substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is as explained previously. Regarding "self" (*ātman*): the term "pervaded by substance-ness" (*dravyatvavyāpya*) is used to exclude other categories such as existence and substance-ness itself.
The term "non-omnipresent" (*avibhu*) in the reason (*hetu*) is used to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in respect to space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.

The phrase "lest this [reason] be unestablished" and so forth was stated with reference to those who maintain that the self (*ātman*) is atomic. Regarding the phrase "and so forth": 1. Earth-qualities are distinct from qualities that do not coexist with the universals (*jāti*) of water, fire, air, or mind, while yet coexisting with a universal; this is because they possess the nature of being a quality (*guṇatva*), like color (*rūpa*). 2. Cognition (*buddhi*) coexists with a universal other than existence (*sattā*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*); this is because it is a quality other than sound, like color. 3.

Earth is distinct from that which possesses a universal different from the substratum of specific qualities other than those of water and so forth; this is because it is an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), like water.

The nature of selfhood (*ātmatva*) is co-extensive with that which has a counter-correlate residing in the same locus as itself, because it is a property (*dharma*), like cloth; this and other such arguments are to be inferred.

Regarding the term "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*): the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking as the pervader [of the probandum] properties such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).
The word "other" (*itara*) is used to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established by taking as the pervader [of the probandum] something else [such as existence].
Pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) consists in subsisting in a wider locus.
Therefore, by taking the pervasion of [the property] "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) with respect to itself, there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
Pervasion with respect to a genus (*jāti*) is precisely what constitutes pervasion of a specific genus.

Therefore, by taking as the pervader [of the subject] the existence (*sattā*) qualified by its being other than quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), and earth (*pṛthivī*), there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). The phrase "directly pervaded by existence" (*sattāsākṣādvyāpya*) is included to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to lower genera (*aparajāti*). Being directly pervaded by that [existence] means: being pervaded by it while not being pervaded by any genus that is itself pervaded by it. [The example] "like quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and so forth" indicates that the probandum (*sādhya*) should be understood as the state of being the direct pervader of quality-ness and the like.

Even though [the property] is an action (*karman*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the probandum (*sādhya*) exists by taking as its direct pervader (*sākṣād-vyāpaka*) the property of being an upward motion (*utkṣepaṇatva*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "all minds" (*sarvāṇi manāṃsi*): the word "all" is used to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), which would occur if one were to take only a few minds as the subject (*pakṣa*) while asserting their distinction from other minds.
The phrase "not having touch as its locus" (*sparśānadhikaraṇa*) is a qualification of that which possesses a genus (*jātimat*).

The phrase "directly pervaded by substantiality" (*dravyatvasākṣād-vyāpya*) is used to exclude [the probandum] from being established by means of [the property of] being distinct from color and so forth.

The term "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is for the purpose of establishing that "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is directly pervaded by "substancehood" (*dravyatva*). "Like earth" (*pṛthivīvat*): the probandum (*sādhya*) should be understood as including the exclusion of the mind (*manas*). "Of those who maintain the distinction of directions" (*digbhedavādinām*): for those who maintain the natural distinction of directions, in an immediate inference, the probandum must be formulated as: "they are distinct from those substances which possess a genus directly pervaded by substancehood, yet do not reside in direction (*dik*) that is not a substratum of touch (*sparśa*)."

The intention is that, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking the difference from "directionness" (*dik-tva*) as the basis, the qualification "other than directionness" (*dik-tvetaratva*) must be added to the probandum (*sādhya*) in all inferences. Regarding the phrase "all earth" (*sarvā pṛthivī*): if one were to take only some particular earth as the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established by taking the difference from other instances of earth; hence, the word "all" is used. The inclusion of the term ending in the locative case (i.e., "in all") is to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established by taking the difference from water and so forth. To avoid the same fallacy by taking [the difference] from properties such as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), the qualification "directly pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatva-sākṣād-vyāpya*) is added.

The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is for the purpose of establishing that being-selfhood (*ātmatva*) is directly pervaded [by the probans]. "Like water-ness" (*jalatvavat*): the probandum should be understood as referring to the exclusion of earth (*pṛthivībheda*). "Existence" (*sattā*): the phrase "other than substance-ness" (*dravyatvānya*) is included to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), since the exclusion of substance-ness is present in existence. The phrase "residing in the self" (*ātmaniṣṭha*) is included to avoid that same fallacy by taking the exclusion of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and so forth. The word "universal" (*jāti*) is included to avoid that same fallacy by taking the exclusion residing in the self, even though there is no exclusion of the self itself. "Like pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvavat*): the probandum should be understood as referring to the exclusion of existence (*sattābheda*). "And substance-ness" (*dravyatvaṃ ca*): the functions [of the qualifiers] are exactly as before.

In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), however, the probandum (*sādhya*) is to be understood by taking "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) as the property. The phrase "of those who maintain the atomicity of the self" is intended to avoid the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the subject (*svarūpāsiddhi*). The term "non-omnipresent" (*avibhu*) is used to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of space and so forth. The qualifier [“non-omnipresent”] is used to exclude deviation in the case of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. The phrase "proving the diversity of selves" means by means of proving the universal "selfhood" (*ātmatva-jāti*).

Regarding the phrase "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*): it is "directly pervasive" (*sākṣād-vyāpaka*). The meaning is: being pervasive of that [entity] while not being non-pervasive with respect to anything distinct from itself that is pervasive of that [entity]. Furthermore, the term "directly pervaded" (*sākṣād-vyāpya*) is included in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking the pervasion of [lower categories] such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) into account.

The mention of "being a genus" (*jātitva*) in the reason is for the purpose of avoiding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of "pot-ness" and so forth, and to secure the state of being pervaded as defined by existence (*sattā*) through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).

Otherwise, since "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) exists in all produced things by virtue of its temporal relation (kālika), and since no universal subsumed under existence (sattāvyāpyajāti) exists everywhere through inherence (samavāya), it would follow that pot-ness possesses a direct subsumption (sākṣādvyāpyatva) characterized by not being subsumed by any universal subsumed under existence. Furthermore, if the property of being subsumed under existence were introduced by way of a general relation, there would be a lack of proof (asiddhi) because such a state does not exist through the temporal relation; therefore, that [specification] is necessary. [The phrase] "all minds" (sarvāṇi manāṃsi).

Prior to this inference, the following reading is observed: "Substantiality (*dravyatva*) is distinct from the genus directly pervaded by substantiality that is different from earthness, water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, and mind-ness, because it is an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*).
In this context, being "directly pervaded by substantiality" must be defined as being common to all substances.

Consequently, there is no room for the objection that the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished prior to the proof of the genus "self-ness" (*ātmatva*), nor that this inference is fallacious due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the very genus "self-ness" established by the inference under discussion.

Nor should it be argued that, because the universal *ātmatva* (selfhood) has not yet been presented prior to the arising of the inference, there is no opportunity to apprehend a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) therein; and that after its establishment, since that universal is already established, it is useless for the apprehension of deviation to disrupt it, as it is merely subservient to the apprehension of deviation. For even after its establishment, the aforementioned apprehension of deviation—by way of producing an apprehension of the invalidity of the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection)—generates an apprehension of the invalidity of the said inference, and thus its capacity to disrupt the non-establishment of the subject matter (*prakṛta-sādhya*) remains unimpaired.

In the phrase "all minds" (*sarvāṇi manāṃsi*), the word "all" is used so that the status of being the object of the inference (*uddeśyatā*) may be obtained through the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) by way of the delimitation of "mind-ness" (*manastva*).

If the object of the inference were the establishment of the probandum by way of its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [mind-ness], then after the inference, since the doubt regarding the absence of the probandum would not have been removed by way of co-referentiality with mind-ness, there would arise a doubt about the invalidity of the original consideration (*parāmarśa*)—a doubt induced by the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason in that very instance—and consequently, a doubt regarding the invalidity of the inference itself would occur.

In this way, there might arise a suspicion of the reason being irrelevant (*aprayojakatā*), namely: "Even if other minds besides that [specific mind] possess causality just like that particular mind, why should the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) not occur? To dispel this, a further effort must be made; for it would be improper according to the maxim of "washing away [stains with water]" (*prakṣālanāddhi*) to establish the probandum and the probans merely by delimiting them as "mind-ness" (*manastva*).

However, the claim that the word "all" (*sarvāṇi*) was used to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*)—since the exclusion of some particular mind exists in another mind—is not correct.

Even if that were the case, the fallacy of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) would not be avoided, because the probandum—in the form of the difference of this mind from that mind—exists in this mind, and the probandum—in the form of the difference of that mind from this mind—exists in that mind.

Nor can it be argued that there is only one single difference that is absent in all the positions; for even so, the fallacy of *siddhasādhana* necessarily arises simply because each individual instance among those individuals encompassed by the delimiting property of the probandum exists in each respective subject (*pakṣa*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that when fire is ascertained as delimited by "mountain-ness" (*parvatatva*), there would be no case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

Nor should it be said that the probandum (*sādhya*) is simply "oneness of difference" (*ekabheda*); for since the quality (*guṇa*) consisting of the number "one" (*ekatvasaṅkhyā*) is absent in a difference (*bheda*), the probandum would be unestablished (*sādhyāprasiddhi*).

Even if one were to accept a different kind of quality (*guṇa*) or admit such a quality there, the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*)—namely, "the state of being a single difference"—would remain unimpaired across all differences, since oneness would not serve as its differentiator. However, it is impossible to establish a different kind [of oneness] that is useful for the present context; for in the case of the view that "oneness of the probandum belongs to a restricted single individual," neither the subject (*pakṣa*) nor the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) includes a single difference.

Furthermore, even when the proof is formulated with the property of "mind-ness" (*manastva*) as the delimiting condition, the various individual minds (*tattanmanobheda*) indeed possess differences whose counter-correlates are non-locuses of those specific types of touch; thus, by taking these into account, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
However, it is not possible to introduce a difference whose counter-correlate is delimited by the property of being a non-locus of such specific types of touch.

This is because there is no sublation (*abādha*), since the difference in the form of a cognition—"the mind is not a non-locus of such specific types of touch"—does not exist in the mind that possesses the genus of mind-ness, which is the probandum (*sādhya*).
Therefore, it must be stated that what is being proved is simply a difference whose counter-positive is not co-extensive with any single such genus.
And so, how can there be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking the difference from that mind after "all-ness" (*sarvatva*) has been introduced?
Alas, then, how could there be the fallacy of proving what is already established even when that [mind] is not included?

In the refinement of the probandum (sādhya) as stated by you, if a difference whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by a property that subsists distributively (vyāsajyavṛtti) is admitted in each individual member, there is simply the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā), because the difference between the mind and a pot is not sublated in the case of the mind. Furthermore, due to the lack of uniformity (ananugama) resulting from the introduction of the term "any whatsoever" (yatkiñcit), there is also the fault of prolixity (gaurava).

Since the probandum (*sādhya*) is defined as a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by such a genus (*jāti*) residing in that which is not the locus of touch (*sparśa*), there would arise the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking into account the difference from that [specific] mind (*manas*) in that case.
Therefore, the aforementioned purpose alone is appropriate.
The phrase "not the locus of touch" is included to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established by taking into account differences from earth and so forth.

Since those [atoms] also lack touch at the time of their production, in order to avoid that same defect once again, the inclusion of "having a counter-correlativity delimited by not being the locus of touch" is made.
