Even if the genus residing in substance (*dravyavṛttijāti*) were included, since existence (*sattā*) is of such a nature, one would have to take into account the difference from the qualities (*guṇa*) which are its substrata; therefore, to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), "being pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvavyāpyatva*) is included. Furthermore, since substanceness itself is pervaded by substanceness, one would have to take into account the difference from ether (*gagana*) and so forth, which are its substrata; therefore, the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is added.
In the present context, what is intended by "directness" (*sākṣāttva*) is primacy (*mukhyatva*).
And that [primacy] is constituted by difference;
for the ancients do not accept a relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) in cases of identity, and thus [difference] possesses primacy.
And thus, it is obtained that [the subject] is the locus of touch possessing a genus that is distinct from substanceness (*dravyatva*) and is pervaded by substanceness.
Since ether (*gagana*) and so forth are not such, there is no room for the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

However, this [formulation] is merely preliminary, following the literal sense of the probandum (*sādhya*); for it is necessary to include a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a genus residing in a substance that is not the locus of touch, whereby the aforementioned faults regarding the collection [of properties] do not apply to existence (*sattā*) or substanceness (*dravyatva*).

However, some say that in order to exclude defects by taking into account the distinction between qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, one should simply attribute "subsisting in a substance" (*dravyavṛttitvamātra*) to the universal (*jāti*).

Others, however, maintain that because they do not accept a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by a property that subsists distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), the probandum (*sādhya*) consists precisely in a difference whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a possessor of such a universal.

As for the avoidance of the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking into account the difference from each respective mind, this is because it is necessary that the pervasion (*vyāpakatā*) of the property delimiting the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) appears in the difference that constitutes the probandum (*sādhya*). In that case, the pervasion—consisting precisely of the difference characterized by the non-delimitation of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the difference residing in that which possesses the nature of "mind" (*manastva*) as the delimitant of the subject—is either present in the probandum itself or in the relation that delimits its probandum-ness;
it is not, however, of the form "possessing the delimitor of probandum-ness that is the non-delimitant of the counter-correlativity of absolute non-existence residing in the mind."

Furthermore, because each individual instance lacks the pervasion (vyāpakatva) constituted by such a difference, there is no room for the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā).

Thus, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established by taking as the counter-positive the difference from ether (gagana) and the like—which possess universals (jāti) such as "substance-ness" (dravyatva) and "existence" (sattā) that do not reside in touch—one must indeed specify that the universal [in question] is directly pervaded by substance-ness.

However, they say that since the aforementioned defect is not avoided even by [defining] "being directly pervaded" (svasākṣādvyāpyatva) as non-different from "being pervaded by itself" (svavyāpyatva), one must rely on the primary sense of the word "directly" (sākṣāt) and conclude that it means "being pervaded by it while being distinct from substance-ness" (dravyatvabhinnatve sati tadvyāpyatva).

Others, however, maintain that in an inference where the object is delimited by a specific delimitor (*avacchedaka*), the pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) that appears either in the probandum (*sādhya*) or in the relation delimiting the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*) does not depend upon the appearance of that [pervasion] in the consideration (*parāmarśa*)—whether in the probandum or in its relation—but rather depends solely upon the consideration’s grasping of the reason (*hetu*) as delimited by that same delimitor.
And it must be accepted that this is exactly as it is established in other cases here as well.

Furthermore, since it must be admitted that in all inferences—such as "the pot possesses the destruction of its color" (*ghaṭo rūpadhvaṃsavān*) and "the mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*)—the manifestation of pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) consisting of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is necessary to prevent the resulting inference from being invalid, it follows that here too, only that manifestation occurs. Consequently, even when proving a probandum (*sādhya*) by means of a prover (*sādhana*) under a specific delimitation (*avacchedaka-avacchedena*), the fallacies of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*) are unavoidable.
For this sentence [of yours] does not function such that an inferential reflection (*parāmarśa*) could generate an inference that apprehends an object in accordance with the speaker's intention.

Furthermore, since the intended object is established simply by proving the difference [of the self] from substances that do not possess touch as delimited by a genus, it would be inappropriate for the authors of the treatise to employ numerous efforts—such as the non-acceptance of differences delimited by properties existing in multiple loci (*vyāsajyavṛttidharma*), the inclusion of the term "directly" (*sākṣāt*), and the consideration of the intention regarding other categories (*padārthāntara*) and so forth.

Therefore, it is not appropriate to state this as a direct explanation of the purpose of the term "pervaded-ness" (*vyāpyatva*); rather, [the point is that] while the inclusion of a redundant qualification in the reason (*hetu*) results in the fallacy of unestablished pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), there is no such redundancy in the body of the probandum (*sādhya*). This is because the qualifications of the probandum serve the purpose of making known the intended object (*uddeśya*). One might ask: "From what does this status of being the intended object arise? To this we reply:

it is with the intention of stating that [the qualification arises] by means of dispelling other doubts regarding whether [the property] shares the same status as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, both in terms of its establishment and non-establishment.

There is another doubt: just as in the case of a jar and so forth, the ancient masters have accepted that even in ten jars produced by Caitra—which are pervaded by the universal *ghaṭatva* (jar-ness)—there exist universals (*jāti*) that delimit Caitra’s productivity;

and these are established by experience in the case of scripts and the like, because of a usage well-known to all people, such as: "I know this script belongs to Caitra, not to Maitra, for his [script] is distinct.
Furthermore, objects that perish in the very second moment after their moment of production are treated in the treatises of the ancients.

Likewise, regarding a substance composed of fragrant and non-fragrant parts, there arises a contradiction in the production of fragrance in the effect by means of the fragrance of the parts; for there is no determining factor as to whether two fragrances would result in the effect or only one would arise. Furthermore, since even "variegated fragrance" (*citragandha*) is not accepted in our own system (*siddhānta*), there is no fragrance at all in that composite whole (*avayavin*); rather, it is simply the fragrance of the parts that is perceived. Nor should it be argued that, on these grounds, variegated color (*citrarūpa*) is likewise unestablished.

In the perception of external substances, since the causality of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) has been established, and because the perception of that [substance] would be untenable in the absence of color in the locus (*dharmī*), the "variegated color" (*citrarūpa*) is accepted for the sake of establishing it; such is the conventional usage in the treatises of the ancients.

Thus it is stated in the *Tarkadīpikā*: "In a substance composed of fragrant and non-fragrant parts, because fragrance is not produced due to mutual opposition, a variegated fragrance is not admitted. Consequently, the definition of 'possessing fragrance' is under-extended (*avyāpta*) to a jar at its first moment of existence, as well as to a jar that has been produced and subsequently destroyed."

And thus, in the present case, even among those ten jars produced by Caitra that have arisen and perished, [the existence of variegated touch] is impossible; for in certain substances produced by both water and earth—such as those produced by Caitra and Maitra which are neither cold nor hot—the variegated touch (*citrasparśa*) is contrary to established doctrine. Consequently, since there is an absence of any touch whatsoever in those substrates lacking touch, one cannot deny the existence of those universals (*jāti*)—established by experience—which serve as the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the states produced by Caitra and Maitra. By taking those universals as the subject, the argument commits the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because those universals reside in substrates that lack touch.
Because the exclusion (*bheda*) delimited by that [quality] does not exist in the mind (*manas*) (i.e., because it is not sublated).

By this, since *dravyatva* and *sattva* are excluded simply by including the lack of co-existence with touch (*sparśa*) within the definition of a genus (*jāti*), it is refuted that the qualification "being pervaded by *dravyatva*" need even be adopted, let alone the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*).
This is because, if those aforementioned genera were admitted, the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) would remain unprevented.

The removal of that doubt occurs either by refuting the natures of such categories through powerful arguments, or by refuting such universals (*jāti*), or by accepting them and adding the qualification "directly pervaded by substance-ness" (*dravyatva-sākṣād-vyāpyatva*) to the universals in the inference under consideration; for among these options, since the refutation and so forth would be misplaced as they are irrelevant to the present context, one accepts them [the universals] as they are. Thus, in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), because excellence exists in the co-referential [category], there is the universal of "self-ness" (*ātmatva*) as intended by us.

They say that the inclusion of "being directly pervaded by substantiality" (*dravyatvasākṣādvyāpyatva*) is intended with the thought that this alone is logical, since "having the same nature as earth-ness" (*pṛthivītvasamaśīlatva*) is also established [for the opponent]. Regarding the phrase "according to those who maintain the distinction of directions" (*digbhedavādinām*): the meaning is "according to the Prācīna-Ekadeśin Siddhāntin.

Here, in all cases, the phrase "not being the locus of direction-ness" (*diktvānadhikaraṇatva*) is intended with reference to this inference combined with the preceding and following inferences. It should be understood that, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) when formulating inferences to prove a difference between universals (*jāti*), the specific difference from "direction-ness" (*diktvabheda*) must also be included within the universal. "The entire earth," etc. *Note: The provided text contains a mix of Sanskrit and English commentary. The translation above focuses on the philosophical argumentation regarding the definition of "earth" and the role of "direction-ness" (*diktvam*) in the context of Navya-Nyāya logic.*

In this context, the purpose of every word is exactly as before. Regarding the phrase "directly pervades" (*sākṣād-vyāpnoti*): some say it is for the sake of indicating the mere subject (*uddeśya*) according to the manner stated by the words "others, however" (*anye tu*), or according to the manner stated by the words "others, moreover" (*apare tu*);
thus, they hold that [the term] is meaningful.

In reality, even when the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by the delimitation of earth-ness (*pṛthivītvāvacchedena*), it has been established in the case of inference that what appears as the delimitation of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) must be precisely that which is defined by the absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the state of being a delimitation of the pervader of the subjecthood-delimiter (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

It should be understood that the qualification "directly pervaded" (*sākṣād-vyāpyatva*) applied to the genus (*jāti*) is meaningful for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). This is because the various differences—whose counter-positives are delimited by potness, clothness, and so forth, which reside in earth-substances that do not possess the four genera such as water-ness—are pervaded by earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*), since they reside in earth-substances that do not possess those same four genera. Without this qualification, the probandum would be already established. Therefore, the specific qualification of being directly pervaded is necessary within the definition of the genus.

Others, however, argue that in the case of the proposition "all minds," if the probandum were the difference between individuals possessing such a genus (jāti), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because one could take the difference from each respective mind as the probandum. Furthermore, if one were to prove a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the state of possessing such a genus, there would be a contradiction (*bādha*), because the nature of being a mind (*manastva*) is also included within the body of that genus.

Therefore, the probandum (*sādhya*) is the absence (*bheda*) whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by some property that is co-extensive with any such genus (*jāti*) and is distributed over multiple loci (*vyāsajyavṛtti*).

Since such an absence exists in each and every mind (*manas*), the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) would be unavoidable; hence, the phrase "all minds" is used so that the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) is a property distributed over multiple loci that is not co-extensive with the nature of mind (*manastva*).

In the view that accepts the difference [of a whole] from each of its parts as qualified by a property residing in each part individually (pratyekavṛttidharma) while being delimited by a property that resides distributively (vyāsajyavṛttidharma), the probandum would be established even through the proof of a sub-genus of *manastva* (the nature of mind); thus, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntaratā*). To prevent this, "genus" (*jāti*) is qualified by being directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva-sākṣād-vyāpyatvena*).

Even with that inclusion, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth as the subject, the phrase "residing in that which is not the locus of touch" (*sparśānadhikaraṇavṛtti*) is added.
Furthermore, the state of being the locus of touch (*sparśādhikaraṇatva*) should be understood according to the general relation accepted by all disputants.

Therefore, even if the self is one, there is no room for the objection that the probandum’s existence is established through a different meaning (*arthāntaratā*)—by admitting a plurality in the triad of space, time, and direction (distinct from the self and the individual self), and thus establishing the universal [of touch] in each of those two, or in space and time, or in time and direction, or in space and direction.

This is because, while time possesses touch through the temporal relation (*kālika-sambandha*) and direction possesses touch produced by spatial location (*dikkṛta-viśeṣa*), the aforementioned universals lack co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with touch.

Since it is accepted that [the mind] exists in the limiting adjuncts of space (*dig-upādhi*) by virtue of being qualified by space, it is possible to include it within the category of "mind-ness" (*manastva*); thus, the presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is established.

Nor should it be argued that even so, a different conclusion (*arthāntaratā*) remains unavoidable because the existence of a genus (*jāti*) for both ether (*gagana*) and the self (*ātman*) is also possible;
for the lack of co-inherence with sound (*śabda-asāmānādhikaraṇya*) is also a qualifier of the genus.

Nor should it be argued that even if the self were one, since it is possible to accept "mind-ness" (*manastva*) as a genus (*jāti*) common to all, the fallacy of proving something other than the intended subject (*arthāntara*) remains unavoidable;

for the intention is that if that were the case, corporeality (*mūrtatva*) would also result in being a genus, and since such a confusion (*sāṅkarya*) would arise, it would be impossible to postulate such a genus. Alternatively, the definition may be given as "being distinct from that which subsists in both the corporeal and the incorporeal."

In reality, however, according to the literal reading, since earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and other such properties are pervaded by both substantiality (*dravyatva*) and incorporeality (*amūrtatva*), the qualification "directly pervaded by substantiality" alone would render the phrase "not having touch as its locus" and so forth entirely redundant.
Therefore, the term "directly pervaded" is merely intended to characterize the property that serves as the differentiator of substance (*dravyavibhājakopādhi*).
Thus, the probandum (*sādhya*) is a difference whose delimitation is resident in a genus that is a differentiator of substance and which does not reside in the same locus as touch.
In this context, the phrase "all minds" (*sarvāṇi manāṃsi*) is stated to indicate that there is no fault even if one accepts each individual mind as the subject (*pakṣa*).
The meaning is "all minds indeed.
Just as in expressions such as "every auspicious time," it is possible for the minds to be presented in their specific individuality (*tadvyaktitvena*).

They say that in cases such as "the entire earth," the purpose should be inferred in exactly the same way. The term *avibhu* (non-omnipresent) is included to prevent the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*) with respect to the atomic nature of the self (*ātman*) which will be mentioned later; and the two components—the qualifier and the qualified—within the reason are included to prevent the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, as well as in the case of qualities (*guṇa*). Regarding the phrase "and such inferences":
the self possesses a genus (*jāti*) that subsists in a domain narrower than "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), because of its conjunction with a jar, like a jar itself.
In the view that the self is non-atomic, [arguments] such as "because of the conjunction of the body and the self, [the self is subject to change], like the body" are to be understood.

However, in the case of the atomic view, the very probandum previously stated is established by the reason of either atomicity or possession of action, with the mind serving as the corroborative example.
And possession of action is indeed established by scripture, as in: "Having departed from this body... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.2).

In the view that the self is atomic (*aṇu*), it could be argued that [the conjunction] occurs only within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) due to its contact with the self; therefore, this [objection] does not hold.
This is because, like the explicitly stated inferences, these [inferences] also establish their objects through the support of favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*).

Regarding the term "substantiality" (*dravyatva*): here, one should understand that the presence of the probandum (*sādhyasattva*) exists in the example by taking the genus "color-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth, and in the subject (*pakṣa*) by taking the genus "self-ness" (*ātmatva*).

The term "other" (*itara*) is included to exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), since *substance-ness* (*dravyatva*) is the direct pervader (*sākṣādvyāpaka*) of earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth.
The word "universal" (*jāti*) is used to avoid that same fallacy by taking as the pervader a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) residing in eight substances.

Since the pervasion of such a universal as delimited by the property of being a universal (*tādṛśajātitvāvacchinna-vyāpakatva*) is contradicted in the case of a universal itself, the compound is disregarded to obtain the pervasion of some single such universal; thus, the word "universal" is separately presented with a singular ending (*jātiṃ prati*) rather than in a compound.

Since there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking as the pervader of "pot-ness" (which is distinct from "earth-ness" and so on) the property of being a pervader [of pot-ness] in general, the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is included.
Direct pervasion (*sākṣādvyāpakatva*) means not being a pervader of any genus that pervades that [property].
And pervasion (*vyāpakatva*) means subsisting in a wider locus.

And that [the definition] consists in being present in that which possesses the exclusion (bheda) delimited by it, while simultaneously being present in that which possesses it. Since *guṇatva* (the property of being a quality) is a pervader (*vyāpaka*) with respect to *rūpatva* (the property of being color/form), which resides in that which possesses *rūpatva*—which is distinct from *pṛthivītva* (earthness) and so on—and with respect to *asattva* (non-existence), which resides in that which possesses the exclusion delimited by those [earthen things], there would arise a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Therefore, both the restrictive clause (*satyanta*) and the substantive member (*viśeṣyadala*) are introduced.

If "not being a pervader of such a property" were the probandum (*sādhya*), then since *guṇatva* (the nature of quality) is a pervader of such properties as *viśeṣaguṇatva* (the nature of specific qualities), there would be a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). Therefore, "not being a pervader of such a genus" was adopted [as the probandum]. Nor should it be argued that this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because it is already established in the case of *dravyatva* (substance-ness) that it does not pervade *guṇatva*, which itself pervades *rūpatva* (color-ness) and other such properties distinct from *pṛthivītva* (earth-ness) and so on;

for that non-pervasion consists in not occurring in that which possesses a difference delimited by that [genus], and thus the non-pervasion of such *guṇatva* is sublated (*bādhita*) in the case of *dravyatva*.

Nor should it be argued that there is a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) by taking as the probandum the property of not occurring in that which possesses a difference from the universal *sattā*, which pervades the category of quality (*guṇatva*) and is distinct from earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth.
This is because what is intended is the state of not being inherent (*asamavetatva*) in that which possesses a difference from that [universal] *sattā*.
Since the state of being inherent in something that possesses a difference from the universal *sattā* is itself unestablished (*aprasiddha*), there is no room for the charge of *siddhasādhana*.

The final conclusion (*niṣkarṣa*) is as follows: the probandum (*sādhya*) is the state of not being inherent (*asamavetatva*) in that which possesses a difference delimited by some genus other than "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, qualified by a genus [itself] related to it through both of the following relations: (1) residing in its own substratum (*svādhikaraṇavṛttitva*), and (2) residing in that which possesses a difference delimited by itself (*svāvacchinnabhedavadvṛttitva*).

Because both relations are introduced, there is no deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*); for although quality-ness pervades those genera such as "taste-ness" (*rasatva*) which reside in that which possesses a difference delimited by "form-ness" (*rūpatva*)—which is distinct from "earth-ness" and so forth—and which also reside in that which possesses such "taste-ness," it does not reside in that which possesses a difference delimited by a genus other than "earth-ness" and so forth. Thus, the probandum is absent in the example.

Thus, the objection that the example lacks the probandum—defined as non-pervasion—because *guṇatva* (the state of being a quality) is pervasive with respect to *rūpatvavyāpakaguṇatva* (the state of being a quality pervading the nature of color) since it is not the counter-positive of an absence residing in its own locus, is refuted; for what is intended by "pervasion" here is precisely the state of occurring in a greater number of loci (*adhikadeśavṛttitva*). Furthermore, in the reason (*hetu*), the term "pervaded by existence" (*sattāvyāpya*) is used because the mere state of being a genus (*jātitvamātra*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to existence (*sattā*).
And pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) should be understood, as before, in the sense of having a smaller extension (*nyūnavṛttitva*).
Therefore, there is no fault in taking a thing’s own self as being pervaded by itself.
The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is included to prevent the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).

Although there is no room for the charge of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the probandum—in the form of being a pervader of potness (*ghaṭatva*) and the like, which are distinct from earthness (*pṭhivītva*) and the like—is present in potness and so forth, nevertheless, that term [“directly”] is employed with the intention that the pervasion must be specified as "being a pervader of that [the subject] while not being a pervader of any genus that pervades that [the subject]," in order to exclude the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*). This is because one could otherwise establish another property, such as "being either a substance or a quality" (*dravyaguṇānyataratva*), which is a pervader of substanceness (*dravyatva*)—distinct from earthness and the like—but is not a pervader of potness and the like. Otherwise, it should be understood that the word "directly" need not be included at all.
The inclusion of "being a genus" (*jātitva*) is for the purpose of avoiding a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), which has as its substrate properties residing in space.
This is merely an illustration.

Substance-ness (*dravyatva*) resides in that which possesses a genus not residing in corporeal things (*mūrta*); this is because it is a genus directly pervaded by existence (*sattā*), or because it is a genus residing in incorporeal things (*amūrta*), like quality-ness (*guṇatva*) and so forth.

"Substantiality (*dravyatva*) pervades the genus that resides in the self (*ātma-vṛtti-jāti*), because it is a genus residing in both the self and the non-self (*ātmānātma-vṛtti-jātitvāt*), like existence (*sattā*)," and so forth—this should also be inferred. Regarding the phrase "all minds": it should be understood that in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the conclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) is reached by way of being distinct from that which possesses the genus *manastva*, while in the subject (*pakṣa*), it is reached by way of being distinct from that which possesses the genus *ātmatva*.

On this point, some maintain that if any single mind were taken as the subject, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking its distinction from other minds; therefore, the word "all" was used.
That is to be considered:

since all minds possess the property of being distinct from a mind that possesses such a universal (jāti) by way of the "shaking sieve" (cālinī-nyāya), even if the term "all" is employed, the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana) is not avoided.

Furthermore, if the meaning of the probandum (sādhya) were the possession of a difference whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by such a universal, then the word "all" would be redundant.
Nor can it be argued that there is no fault because the probandum is the difference from some single thing possessing a counter-positive characterized by such a genus,
since the difference from one mind exists in all minds by their very nature;
for [the reason] would be inconclusive with respect to the counter-positive of such a difference.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the word "directly" (sākṣāt) being redundant in the probandum (sādhya).

Since the exclusion of that which possesses a single difference from the substratum of the lower genus *manastva* is established by the very nature of all minds (*manas*), there is no room for the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

As for the claim that the word "directly" is used to avoid *siddhasādhana* by taking as the counter-positive the exclusion of ether (*gagana*) and so forth—which possess substanceness (*dravyatva*) and are pervaded by substanceness—that is incorrect.
And since there is no absence of being pervaded by that which is pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*) within substanceness itself, there is no fault.
That is not so;

for if one intends to mean "pervasion by substanceness" as common to all substances, then—given that it is not pervaded by what is pervaded by substanceness—the universal (*jāti*) that is pervaded by substanceness would be unestablished, and thus the probandum (*sādhya*) would be unestablished.

As for the claim that the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used in order to establish that the property of selfhood (*ātmatva*) is directly pervaded by the property of substancehood (*dravyatva*), that too is not correct; for its establishment is irrelevant to the present context. Therefore, the probandum (*sādhya*) must be simply the difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is delimited by such a genus (*jāti*).
The inclusion of the term "all" (*sarva*), however, is for the purpose of making known the validity of the probans (*sādhana*) by way of its delimitation (*avacchedaka-avacchedena*).

The phrase "not having contact as its locus" (*sparśānadhikaraṇa*) is intended to exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking as the subject something distinct from earth and the other elements.

The phrase "possessing a genus subsumed under substantiality" (*dravyatvavyāpyajātimat*) is intended to eliminate the charge of proving what is already established by taking as the subject something distinct from universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), and so forth.

The word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used to avoid that fault by taking [the property] of being distinct from those possessing intermediate universals such as "mind-ness" (*manastva*) and "cognition-ness" (*cittatva*).
To indicate this, it is said "all minds" (*sarvāṇi manāṃsi*); the meaning is that they belong to various classes due to the distinctions between cognition (*citta*), and so forth.
Therefore, since there is no authoritative evidence for a sub-class within the genus "manas-ness" (*manastva*), there is no room for the objection that the term "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is redundant.

Although there might be the possibility of proving another genus common to the self (*ātman*), earth (*pṛthivī*), and so forth— which would constitute a different conclusion (*arthāntara*)— nevertheless, because by the phrase "not the substratum of touch" it is intended that the genus [in question] does not have touch as its common locus (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), there is no fault.

Earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and the like are directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*), because they are universals that subsume substance, just as mindness (*manastva*) is; thus, such other universals are not established due to contradiction with this inference. Furthermore, the establishment of another universal common only to self (*ātman*), ether (*ākāśa*), and so forth, has already been refuted previously. Now, even if this were so, one might argue that for those who maintain that the divisions of space (*digbheda*) are intrinsic, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking as the probandum the state of being distinct from that which possesses the universal "spatiality" (*diktva*). To this he says: "of those who maintain the divisions of space. This refers to the inference where the subject (*pakṣa*) is substance.
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

In the aforementioned inferences where "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so forth are the subjects (*pakṣa*), one must also include the apprehension of "direction-ness" (*diktvā*) and "otherness" (*itaratva*).
[The phrase] "all earth" implies a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with water, fire, air, and mind by way of the suffix *-tva*.
The rest is as before.
In this very manner, the individual inferences having water and so forth as the subject (*pakṣa*) are to be inferred.

Likewise, the inference should be understood as follows: "Earth and the other substances are distinct from that which possesses a genus residing in the self, because they are non-self, like qualities and so forth."

Regarding the term "existence" (*sattā*): here, in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), one should understand the presence of the probandum (*sādhyasattva*) by taking the difference from existence (*sattānyatva*); and in the subject (*pakṣa*), by taking the difference from selfhood (*ātmatvānyatva*).

The inclusion of both "difference from substantiality" (*dravyatvānyatva*) and "residing in the self" (*ātmaniṣṭhatva*) within the category of "universal" (*jāti*) is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking differences such as "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) or "earthness" (*pṛthivītva*). Furthermore, the inclusion of "difference from quality" (*guṇabheda*) within the universal is for the purpose of removing that same fallacy.

Although it might be argued that before the establishment of selfhood (*ātmatva*), the inclusion of "residing in the self" is impossible; [this objection is addressed by the aforementioned qualification].
Because the manifestation of an individual cannot occur without a genus (*jāti*).
Nevertheless, there is no fault, as that [genus] is included either as that specific individuality (*tadvyaktitva*) or as a substance other than the eight substances.

Nor should it be argued that even so, there is the fallacy of proving something extraneous (*arthāntara*), because another genus common to both the self (*ātman*) and earth would thereby be established.

Since there is no decisive evidence [to determine which one it is], if it were to subsist in as many substances as exist, it would not be distinct from "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) due to having the same number of individual instances.
By this, the argument beginning with "or substanceness" is essentially explained. Regarding "the self": the meaning is the individual soul (*jīvātman*).
Therefore, there is no "partial unestablishedness" (*bhāgāsiddhi*) with respect to God (*Īśvara*).

Here, the term "pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvavyāpya*) is stated for the purpose of excluding the fallacy of the probandum being already established (*siddhārthatā*) by means of universals such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*).
The word "universal" (*jāti*) is used to exclude that same fallacy [of *siddhārthatā*] by means of [accidental properties] such as oneness (*ekatva*).
The term "non-omnipresent" (*avibhu*) is used to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of space (*gagana*) and so forth.
Omnipresence (*vibhutva*) consists either in being conjoined with all corporeal things or in possessing the quality of infinite magnitude (*paramamahattva*).
Since the property of non-omnipresence—defined as the absence of that [omnipresence]—is present in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, the term "substance" (*dravya*) is added.
The phrase "of those who maintain the atomicity of the self" was stated precisely to avoid the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*) for such [opponents];
it was not because no other reason is possible under the view that the self is omnipresent (*vibhu*),
since reasons such as "being a perceptible substance" (*pratyakṣadravyatva*) are indeed possible.
Thus, a cloth is devoid of any genus residing in either the cloth or the nature of cloth, because it is an object of cognition, like a jar.

The inference establishing the universal *ātmatva* (selfhood) should be understood as follows: "This [entity], which was previously known through its existence (*sattā*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*), is not now known by a universal residing in the self, because it is a real entity (*vastu*), like any other real entity. Regarding the phrase "a universal subordinate to substantiality" (*dravyatvavyāpyajāti*): the meaning is that by the establishment of a tenth substance qualified by such another universal, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*) in the inferences where earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth are the subjects (*pakṣa*). Regarding the phrase "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*): the sense is that the postulation of a mere property (*dharma*) is simpler than the postulation of both the property and the substratum (*dharmin*).

Nor should it be argued that because the postulation of a genus (*jāti*) is impossible within a single individual, the postulation of another individual is necessarily required; for there is no loss of parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating a genus as being included within an already established individual, rather than postulating multiple unestablished individuals.
Regarding the term "existence" (*sattā*): the meaning is that it is a genus directly pervaded by the genus "existence" (*sattājāti*).

In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the conclusion of the probandum (*sādhyaparyavasāna*) is established by way of being the pervader of "form-ness" (*rūpatva*). If, in the probandum, it were merely stated that [the property] is the pervader of the universal (*jāti*), there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratva*), because it would establish pervasion with respect to "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Therefore, the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is used. Direct pervasion, moreover, consists in being the pervader of that [universal] while not being the pervader of its pervaders. Since "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is the pervader of "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), which is itself the pervader of "pot-ness," it lacks the quality of "not being the pervader of its pervaders"; thus, due to the absence of direct pervasion, there is no fault.

If it were stated that [the probans] is the direct pervader of a genus (*jāti*), there would be the fallacy of proving the already established (*arthāntara*), because [the probans] is the direct pervader of the five [substances], such as earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth.
Therefore, [the term] "other than earthness, waterness, fireness, airness, and mindness" is included.
Consequently, everything [in the definition] is purposeful.

In this case as well, following the previously stated method, since substantiality (*dravyatva*) does not possess direct pervasiveness (*sākṣād-vyāpakatva*), one should not suspect the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*) by taking substantiality as the probandum.

If it is stated that "because it is a genus" (*jātitvāt*) as the reason, or "because it is a pervaded genus" (*vyāpyajātitvāt*), or "because it is a genus pervaded by existence" (*sattāvyāpyajātitvāt*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).
This is because, although it is a pervaded genus, it lacks the probandum in the form of being pervasive.
Therefore, it says "directly" (*sākṣāt*).

It should be understood that there is no fault [in the definition], because *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) is pervaded by *sattā* (existence) through the intermediaries of *pṛthivītva* (earth-ness) and *dravyatva* (substance-ness). Regarding the phrase "not the locus of touch" (*sparśānadhikaraṇa*): the meaning is those things other than that which possesses a genus directly pervaded by *dravyatva* and which is not the locus of touch.

In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the conclusion of the probandum (*sādhyaparyavasāna*) is by way of being distinct from a mind possessing such a genus (*jāti*). In the subject (*pakṣa*), if the word "all" (*sarva*) were omitted, any particular minds would fall under the scope of the subject; consequently, there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), namely, the establishment of being distinct from that mind which possesses a genus directly pervaded by the property of being a substance that is not a locus of touch (*sparśānadhikaraṇadravyatvasākṣādvyāpyajātimanmanas*). Therefore, the word "all" is used. If it were stated in the probandum that they are "distinct from that which possesses a genus," there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant, as it would result in establishing their distinction merely from action (*karma*) which possesses the genus of existence (*sattājāti*).

Therefore, [the term] "pervaded" (*vyāpya*) is used. If it were stated that they are "distinct from those possessing a genus pervaded by [existence]," there would be the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), because it would be proven that they are distinct from actions (*karma*) which possess the genus "action-ness" (*karmatva*)—which is itself pervaded by existence (*sattā*). Therefore, [the term] "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is added. If it were stated that they are "distinct from those possessing a genus pervaded by substance-ness," there would again be the fallacy of *arthāntara*, because—as explained above—it would be proven that they are distinct from substances which possess the genus "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*)—which is itself pervaded by substance-ness. Therefore, [the term] "directly" (*sākṣāt*) is added.

If it were stated that [the subject] consists of things distinct from those possessing a genus directly pervaded by *dravyatva* (substanceness), there would be the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), because the four [substances] beginning with earth—which possess the genera such as *pṛthivītva* (earthness) directly pervaded by *dravyatva*—would be excluded.
Therefore, the qualification "not being the locus of touch" is added.
Since the four [substances] beginning with earth are loci of touch, this fault does not apply.

But surely, in the inference where "earthness" is the subject (*pakṣa*), there is the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*)—namely, that the genus "directionness" (*dik-tva*) is distinct from the four genera beginning with "water-ness"—because its difference from those is established.
This is likewise the case for the inferences where the four genera beginning with "water-ness" are the subjects.

Similarly, in the inference where "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is the subject, there is the fallacy of proving something else, because it establishes that "directionness" is the direct pervader (*sākṣād-vyāpaka*) of the five genera beginning with "earthness."

Likewise, in the inference where the mind (*manas*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), there is the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*) because it establishes the distinctness of that which possesses a genus (*jāti*) directly pervaded by "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and not residing in touch (*sparśa*). Similarly, in the inference to be stated where earth (*pṛthivī*) is the subject, there is the fallacy of proving something else because it establishes the distinctness of that which possesses a genus directly pervaded by "substance-ness" and not residing in water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, or mind-ness.

Nor should it be argued that because direction (*dik*) is one, the genus "direction-ness" (*diktva*) does not exist at all due to the non-difference of its individual instances; for [the genus exists] despite such non-difference.

In the view where an inherent distinction (*svābhāvikabheda*) in space is accepted, [the opponent's objection] remains unrefuted because it results in a different meaning (*arthāntara*). Therefore, he says: "of those who maintain the distinction of directions" (*digbhedavādinām*). Here, in the inference whose subject (*pakṣa*) is the mind (*manas*), one must state: "because it is not the substratum of touch and not the substratum of direction-ness.

In all inferences where the earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) is the subject, one must state: "other than mind-ness and direction-ness. In the inference where substance-ness (*dravyatva*) is the subject, one should formulate it as: "in relation to a genus other than mind-ness and direction-ness."

The meaning is that in the inference regarding the subject (*pakṣa*) of "earth" which is about to be stated, one must add the qualification "not being the locus of *manastva* (the nature of mind) and *ādikatva* (the nature of air, etc.)". Regarding "water-ness" (*jalatva*): the meaning is "that which is distinct from whatever possesses a genus directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*), yet is not the locus of water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, or mind-ness.
In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the conclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) is reached through its being distinct from earth, which possesses such a genus.

Here, if the subject (*pakṣa*) were indicated merely as "earth" (*pṛthivī*), then since anything whatsoever would incur the status of being the subject, there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*)—namely, the establishment of the fact that earth is distinct from other earths that possess the genus "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva-jāti*), which is directly pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*) and is the locus of the absence of water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, and mind-ness. Therefore, the term "all" (*sarva*) is used.

Regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), the function of the phrase "substanceness... and so forth should be understood exactly as it was explained in the inference where the mind (*manas*) was the subject.

If it were stated as "distinct from that which possesses a genus directly pervaded by substantiality" (*dravyatvasākṣādvyāpyajātimadvyatirikta*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*), because one would have proven its distinction from those things possessing the four genera directly pervaded by substantiality, such as "water-ness" (*jalatva*) and so on. Therefore, it is specified as "not having water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, or mind-ness as its locus" (*jalatvatejastvavāyutvamanastvānadhikaraṇa*). Regarding the term "substantiality" (*dravyatva*): the meaning is "other than that genus residing in the self which is different from substantiality. In the example (the probandum), the conclusion is reached through its being other than "existence" (*sattā*). If, in the probandum, it were simply stated as "other than a genus" (*jātyanya*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established, because one would have proven its difference from the genus "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).
Therefore, it is said "distinct from the universal inhering in the self" (*ātmaniṣṭhajātivyatireka*).

If it were stated merely as "distinct from the universal inhering in the self," there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), since the distinctness from the universal "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) would already be established.
Hence, it is specified as "distinct from substance-ness."

If it were stated as "other than a genus other than substanceness," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntara*), by taking as the probandum the state of being other than potness (which is indeed other than a genus other than substanceness).
Therefore, it is specified as "residing in the self" (*ātmaniṣṭha*).

If it were stated as "other than that which resides in the self and is other than substanceness," there would again be the fallacy of *arthāntara*, because the state of being other than pleasure (*sukha*) is thereby established [as residing in the self].

"Thus, [the term] 'jāti' [is used]. "Substantiality (dravyatva)" [is the example]. Here, in the instance, the conclusion of the probandum (sādhya) is reached through its being other than substantiality. If it were stated in the probandum as "other than the genus residing in the self," there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (arthāntara) because it would merely establish its being other than existence (sattā). Therefore, it is specified as "other than existence. The function of the word "jāti," however, should be understood as being like the inference where the subject (pakṣa) is a specific kind of existence (viśiṣṭasattā).
Because the self is all-pervasive (*vyāpta*), the qualification [of the reason] would be unestablished; therefore, it is stated: "according to those who maintain the atomicity of the self.
The word "in the view" (*mate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Since the proof of being the locus of a genus (*jāti*) in the probandum would result in proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*), [the reason is specified as] "pervaded by substantiality" (*dravyatvavyāpya*).

When it is stated in the reason (*hetu*) "because of substantiality" (*dravyatvāt*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because substantiality exists in space (*gagana*), yet it lacks the status of being the locus of a genus pervaded by substantiality.
Therefore, [the term] "non-omnipresent" (*avibhu*) is added.
When "because of non-omnipresence" (*avibhutvāt*) is stated, [there is a deviation] with respect to a quality (*guṇa*); therefore, "because of substantiality" (*ato dravyatvāt*) is added.
To the question of where the aforementioned inferences are of use, he says: "ityādi" (and so forth).

Nor is there the fallacy of proving something other than the intended subject (*arthāntaratva*) here by means of establishing another category possessing a genus subsumed under "substantiality" (*dravyatvavyāpyajātimat*);

for when it is possible to conclude the inference merely by proving a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) in a substrate (*dharmin*) already established, it would be unnecessarily cumbersome (*gaurava*) to conclude the inference with respect to a substrate qualified by that [new] property.
Furthermore, there is no fallacy of an unestablished reason (*asiddhi*) or the like, because the substantiality of the self (*ātman*) is not unestablished.

Since there is no subverting evidence against accepting the existence of conventional qualities such as duality (dvitva) and so forth— which persist as long as the substance exists— even in the absence of qualities like color (rūpa) in the attributeless self (ātman),
and since the inclusion [of the self] among qualities and so forth would entail its being established as a substance (dravya);
nor is there a lack of supporting reasoning, for [the argument] does not share the same status as a fallacy of being non-probative (aprayojakatva).
There is parsimony (*lāghava*) in accepting that "selfhood" (*ātmatva*), which is the ground for the application of the term "self," is a universal (*jāti*);

whereas, if it were held to be adventitious (*aupādhika*)—that is, if its status as an adventitious property were accepted—there would be complexity (*gaurava*) because it would depend upon the cognition of its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). This is because [the former view] is supported by favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*), and because there is an absence of subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) such as the [objection] regarding the identity of the individual instances (*tulyavyaktikatva*).

"And not here" means: in the inference where the mind (*manas*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), and in the inference where the earth (*pṛthivī*) is the subject. "In another category possessing a genus" means: in a case where the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) possesses a genus other than *ātmatva*, there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). The meaning is that this occurs when that other category, distinct from the self (*ātman*), is established. "In the already postulated subject" means: [in the case of the mind, which is already accepted].

The meaning is: "merely by proving a property in the form of a specific genus directly pervaded by *dravyatva* (substantiality) in this subject (*dharmin*) called 'self,' which is included within the nine substances. "And not because *dravyatva* is unestablished" means: since the self is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), how could *dravyatva*, which depends upon possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*), be possible for it? This is the intended sense. "Unestablishedness and so forth" refers to [the fallacies of] *asiddhi* (unestablished reason), etc.

The meaning is as follows: in an inference where the self (*ātman*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), there is the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*); in an inference where existence (*sattā*) is the subject, the qualification "other than substanceness" (*dravyatvānyeti*) is redundant when proving [the property]; and in an inference where substanceness (*dravyatva*) is the subject, there is sublation (*bādha*) in all other inferences as well. Regarding the phrase "even in the absence of qualities such as color" (*rūpādiguṇābhāve’pi*): the sense is that since qualities like color are observed to be essentially concomitant with cloth and other substances, they would necessarily persist as long as the substance exists. If one were to admit them in the self, it would follow—by analogy with the self—that they must be ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), which would result in a contradiction with scriptural texts stating that the self is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). Therefore, those qualities cannot be admitted [in the self]. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the term "duality etc. (*dvitvādi*), numbers such as three and so forth are included.

The point is that since these [qualities] are produced by relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), their destruction upon the destruction of that cognition is logical, and thus they do not endure as long as the substance itself.

Furthermore, if even those qualities that do not endure as long as the substance were ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), there would again be a contradiction with the scriptural texts stating that [the Self] is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*); therefore, it is said that they are "conventional" (*vyāvahārika*). Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of any subverting evidence": the meaning is that the scriptural texts concerning the absence of qualities refer only to the absence of ultimate qualities. And regarding the phrase "because it would entail the inclusion [of the Self] among qualities and so forth": if the Self were accepted as a category (*padārtha*) but its status as a substance (*dravyatva*) were not admitted, it would have to be included among qualities and the like; however, that is not tenable.
It cannot first be included among qualities (*guṇa*), because it is not admitted that a universal (*jāti*) has a quality as its substratum; nor can it be included among actions (*karman*).

It is not [the cause] with respect to conjunction and disjunction, because it lacks the status of being a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) for them; nor is it [the cause] with respect to generality (sāmānya),
because it lacks the property of inhering in multiple things (anekasamavetatva).
Nor [is it] in inherence,
because [inherence] is by nature devoid of relation;
nor is it in particularity.
Because it lacks dependence on an eternal substance;
nor does it reside in non-existence, because it cannot be defined without its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
The sense is that, therefore, the establishment of [the category of] substance (*dravyatva*) follows.

Now, one might object: "In these inferences, there is no subverting argument against the suspicion of being *aprayojaka* (irrelevant/unproving). Since *ātmatva* could be included as being on the same footing as *jalatva* and *tejastva*, it would be possible to prove that [the subject] is distinct from any genus directly pervaded by 'being a substance other than those' (*taditaradravyatvasākṣādvyāpyajātibhinnatva*). Consequently, this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even *ākāśatva* and the like would be established as genera, resulting in an equality with fallacious arguments. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
In this context, "yoga" refers to the perfection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth;

it should be understood that "kṣema," however, means the absence of sublation by valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*). Regarding the phrase "of the ground for the application of the term 'self'": this is the intended meaning.
It cannot be said, first of all, that the property consisting of "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) simply does not exist.

That being the case, in the absence of a basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), the very use of the word "self" (*ātman*) with respect to the self would be impossible. And if that [basis] is not a genus (*jāti*), it must be defined. Nor can it be said that selfhood (*ātmatva*) is simply the state of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*).

According to the opponent's view, since self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) is accepted as being simply the state of not being cognizable by another, it follows that self-luminosity itself becomes an additional property; consequently, because it would depend on the cognition of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the form of others, there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*).
However, if one accepts [self-luminosity] as a universal (*jāti*), there is parsimony (*lāghava*), because, being partless (*akhaṇḍa*), it does not depend on anything else.

And thus, because these inferences are supported by favorable *tarka* in the form of the contingency of excessive complexity (*gaurava*), they do not suffer from the fault of being "unproving" (*aprayojaka*) and so forth. Now, it might be objected that mere simplicity (*lāghava*) is ineffective when accompanied by a sublation; otherwise, even "sky-ness" (*gaganatva*), the ground for the application of the term "sky," would have to be considered a universal (*jāti*). To this, he says: "Because of [the faults of] identity of individuals and so forth. The phrase "the acceptance of *ātmatva* as a universal" is understood to carry over. [The faults are: "Identity of the individual, equality, confusion, or infinite regress."

According to the statement, "The loss of form, lack of connection, and the inclusion [of the definition] among the subverters of genus—these are the six subverters of genus," there are six such subverters, beginning with the non-difference of individuals.
Among these, first, the five subverters beginning with "equality" do not apply to the acceptance of *ātmatva* (selfhood) as a genus. To explain:
What is called "equality" (tulyatva) is the state of having an equal number of individual instances; that is to say, the state of subsisting in the same locations.
And thus, because elephant-ness (karīratva) subsists only in those jars that are the substrata of jar-ness (ghaṭatva), it does not possess the status of a universal (jāti).
*Saṅkara* (commixture) is the coexistence in a single locus of two properties that exist through mutual exclusion;
for example, the case of "being an element" (*bhūtatva*) and "having form" (*mūrtatva*).
"Being an element" exists in space (*ākāśa*), but "having form" does not.
Furthermore, corporeality exists in the mind, but the state of being a primary element (bhūtatva) does not;
yet both of these are included within the four primary elements beginning with earth.
Therefore, those two are not universals (jāti).

Furthermore, if one were to admit the universal "existence" (*sattājāti*) in potness (*ghaṭatva*), it would follow that one must again admit the universal "existence" in that [potness] as well; because this would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*), a universal should not be admitted within a universal.

As for the admission of a universal in the form of "particularity-ness" (*viśeṣatva*) in the ultimate particulars (*viśeṣas*), the loss of their essential nature (*rūpahāni*) serves as the subverting argument. By "loss of essential nature" is meant the abandonment of their own-being (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, the ultimate differentiators of the specific qualities residing in atoms consist in their nature as causes for the cognition of mutual exclusion among those atoms. Their "absolute" nature means that they never serve as causes for doubt or other such cognitive states.
For this very reason, in the case of yogis who perceive atoms directly and observe the specific qualities inherent in them, neither doubt nor error ever arises regarding those atoms.

If the universal "particularity" (*viśeṣatva-jāti*) were to exist even in the ultimate particulars (*viśeṣa*), then, because all particulars would be pervaded by the common property of "particularity," there could arise at some time doubts and the like regarding them—just as it occurs with jars and other objects. Consequently, since doubt and so forth would also reach the atoms that serve as the substrata for those particulars, the unique nature of those atoms would be lost. Therefore, there is no universal in the particulars. Regarding inherence (*samavāya*), the acceptance of a universal "inherence-ness" (*samavāyatva-jāti*) is precluded by the logical defect of non-relation (*asambandha*).

If a universal were accepted in inherence, then, because the rule is that a universal must inhere in its individual instances, another further inherence would have to be accepted for inherence itself.
Furthermore, inherence (*samavāya*) is one and only one.

Therefore, if one were to postulate an inherence within inherence itself, it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*); thus, "inherence-ness" (*samavāyatva*) cannot be a universal (*jāti*) residing in inherence. Likewise, if the universal "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is accepted, the objection that its instances would be identical in number does not apply as a refutation;
for there exists no other property co-extensive with selfhood within the self.
Or, if it were to exist, it would follow that it itself is a genus (*jāti*).
Nor is there any confusion (*saṅkara*),
because the property of selfhood (*ātmatva*) subsists only in selves.
Nor is there an infinite regress,
because that [regress] does not exist;
nor is there a loss of its essential nature.
This is because no self-nature whatsoever can be lost;
nor is there a lack of connection, since inherence (samavāya) is possible— this is the intended meaning.

One might ask: why should the inferences other than the final triad not result in the establishment of a tenth substance possessing a genus (*jātimat*), just as [the inference] results in the self’s possession of a genus? To this, he says: "And not here. This means: regarding the inferences other than the final triad. "Due to non-establishment, etc. means that, according to the direction already stated—namely, "of the self which is devoid of qualities"—there is a lack of establishment (*asiddhi*) in the final inference.

Therefore, since the probandum must be stated in the example as being distinct from the universals residing in the self—namely existence (*sattā*) and substantiality (*dravyatva*)—there would be a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) if substantiality were absent from the self; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "not lasting as long as the substance" (*ayāvaddravya*): if one were to accept qualities that persist for the duration of the substance, then because these [qualities] would never cease, the doctrine of its qualitylessness (*nirguṇatva*) would be undermined.

However, if the aforementioned qualities are accepted, there would be a contradiction with the future state of qualitylessness; this is the intended sense. He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against not accepting substantiality: "of qualities" (*guṇānām*). If it were not a substance, it would have to be one of the categories other than substance, such as a quality and so forth.

"Otherwise, it would follow that it is not a category (*apadārthatva*). [Objection: "But even if it is distinct from the six categories beginning with substance (*dravya*), why should its status as a category (*padārthatva*) not be admitted? What is the fault? [Response:

"In that case, since 'substance-ness' (*dravyatva*) is intended to mean simply being different from the five categories beginning with quality (*guṇa*), how can there be the fallacy of the unestablished reason (*asiddhi*) and so forth? [Objection: 'It is a case of being on the same footing as a pseudo-reason based on lack of necessity (*aprayojakatva*). [Response: Lack of necessity arises because, although concomitance may exist elsewhere, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is possible within the subject (*pakṣa*).

Nor should it be argued that there is a logical warrant (*tarka*)—namely, that if the probandum were absent where the reason exists, the concomitance of the *upādhi* (limiting condition) would be broken, resulting in the total destruction of inference."

Since it is not accepted that "the absence of a limiting condition" (anaupādhikatva) [is the definition of pervasion], because for one who intends to eliminate deviation, there must necessarily be a limiting condition (upādhi) in the case of deviation;
nor should it be said that no limiting condition is observed,
because in the absence of a subverting proof (bādhaka), even "being other than the subject" (pakṣetaratva) and the like would likewise [be considered non-limiting conditions].

Furthermore, in the aforementioned inference, just as one might include "other than water and so forth," one could also include "other than selfhood" (*ātmatva*); this would lead to the undesirable consequence that the tenth substance, which possesses a genus (*jātimat*), would also be established.
If one were to further include "not being a locus [of that genus]" (*anadhikaraṇatva*) therein, it would again lead to the establishment of yet another substance.
Likewise, it would be easy to prove that even ether (*ākāśa*) and the other [substances] possess a genus.

The meaning is that there is a parity of fallacies (*ābhāsasāmya*), such that if one takes the position that [the self] is distinct from the mind, then—given the qualifier "a specific universal" (jāti) which is co-located with the impermanent—the self would have to be impermanent. Regarding "simplicity" (*lāghava*): the intention is that, according to the maxim that "among universals and adventitious adjuncts (*upādhi*), the universal is stronger," [the universal is more fundamental]. Regarding "adventitious adjuncts" (*upādhi*):
the intention is that [the unity of the self] depends on adjuncts such as having the quality of cognition (*buddhiguṇakatva*) or self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).
Although the acceptance of non-adventitiousness is redundant—since the uniform cognition (*anugatapratīti*) can be accounted for by the aforementioned adjuncts alone—[it is nevertheless asserted].
Nevertheless, it should be understood that this is merely a restatement of what has been accepted by others for the sake of establishing the usage of the term as an indivisible whole (*akhaṇḍa*).

This complexity (*gaurava*) is not "result-oriented" (*phalamukha*), which would constitute a fault; rather, it is "cause-oriented" (*kāraṇamukha*). To demonstrate this, it was stated at the outset: "of the ground for the application of the word *ātman*. Now, one might object: "The introduction of the maxim is precisely for the purpose of ascertaining the multiplicity of individuals (*vyakti*)."
If it is argued that here, because of the doubt regarding that [unity], the universal (*jāti*) itself is more cumbersome due to its temporal extension, we say no;
for since the difference between individuals is established by perception, it is not a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

On the contrary, the construction of [the universal] as being merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) entails even greater cumbersomeness, as it ultimately requires the assumption of the non-validity of the perception and other means of knowledge that apprehend the difference between individuals. And thus, if selfhood (*ātmatva*) were not a universal, there would be the fault of conceptual cumbersomeness; however, since this reasoning (*tarka*) exists, there is no such defect.

"Non-establishment, etc. means that in the immediately preceding inference there is a *svarūpāsiddhi* (unestablished nature of the reason); in the inference where existence (*sattā*) is the subject (*pakṣa*), the qualification of the probandum (*sādhya*) is redundant; and in certain cases, there is sublation (*bādha*). This is the sense. "Due to the absence of a subverting factor" means that, since there is no cessation of the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—namely, being the substratum of qualities (*guṇāśrayatva*)—there is no non-establishment of substantiality (*dravyatva*). This is the sense. "Inclusion within qualities, etc. [is the sense].

If the self were not the substratum of conventional qualities such as duality and so forth, but were the substratum of existence (*sattā*), then—since it would be distinct from action and a substratum of mere universals—it would fall under the definition of a quality (*guṇa*) as "that which is a substratum of a universal but not of action," and thus it would be included among the qualities. However, if it were not the substratum of existence, the consequence would be its inclusion among absences (*abhāva*). Therefore, one must accept that the self is the substratum of qualities such as duality and so forth.

And thus, the sense is that the existence of *dravyatva* (substanceness) is established. As for the objection, "because there is a lack of supporting reasoning (*anukūlatarka*)," [the response is as follows]: "Because it is a universal distinct from the universals directly pervaded by *dravyatva*—namely, earthness, water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, mind-ness, self-ness, and [the universal] other than *dravyatva*—just like water-ness. The meaning is that [the argument] shares the same logical status as the fallacious argument: "Existence (*sattā*) is a universal residing in ether that is other than the universal *dravyatva*. Now, one might object: "An absence of sublation (*bādhaka*) renders parsimony (*lāghava*) ineffective; otherwise, even 'ether-ness' (*gaganatva*) would have to be a universal, as it is the ground for the application of the term 'ether' (*gagana*). To this, he says: "Because of having an equal number of instances (*tulyavyaktikatva*), etc."
"Nor [is it so]," etc. "A distinct category," etc.: the meaning is "distinct from the nine substances including the self. "In the case of an already established substratum":
the meaning is that there is parsimony (lāghava) in postulating that universal (jāti) within the selves alone, which are established by all perception;
otherwise, there would be complexity (gaurava) in postulating both the property and the substratum.
One might object: "In that case, [the universal] would be established in respect to space and so forth, which are already established [as entities].

And it should not be argued that the postulation of a genus is improper because those [entities] are established as singular by the very means of knowledge that apprehends their substrata (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*), for this will be stated later. [Response:

This is not so, because even if such a genus is not established in each individual space and so forth through such reasoning, it is possible to accept the genus in them—either in space, time, and direction collectively, or together with the self—once one considers the absence of any decisive factor (*vinigamakābhāva*) among them.
If it is argued that this results in the fallacy of proving something other than the intended subject (*arthāntaratā*) because the plurality of selves is not established, we say no.
This is because, according to the rule of logic, the application of reasoning occurs only where there is doubt, not where there is sublation (*bādhita*).

Since the absence of any genus directly pervaded by "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) has been ascertained in the case of space, time, and direction, there is no dispute regarding them; thus, setting aside those cases where the object is sublated, the genus is established only in respect to the other doubtful selves.

For this very reason, in order to establish the existence of the probandum (sādhya) which is the object of the inference beginning with "all minds," let there be one genus directly pervaded by the property of being a single substance (*ekadravyatva*) in some minds, and another such genus in other minds called "mind-ness" (*manastva*), which pervades both.
Let the state of being the subject (*pakṣatā*) belong to all minds by virtue of their being the referents of the term "mind.

Since the two types of difference constituting the probandum are indeed pervaded by the nature that delimits the probandum in the manner of the delimitant of the subject, there is no inconsistency even in the establishment of the probandum as delimited by that specific delimitant.
Thus, even the suspicion that there is a "shifting of the subject matter" (*arthāntaratā*) due to the non-establishment of [the property of] selfhood is refuted.

This is because it would involve the unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) of postulating two classes (*jāti*) for which there is no evidence, whereas it is possible to postulate four classes; furthermore, such a move would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakti*).

Since there is an absence of such two classes, one must instead accept the class directly subsumed under mind-ness (*manastva*), and only by taking that as the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) can this very suspicion be dismissed as sheer audacity.

If it is argued that because there is no sublation even in the case of space (*gagana*) and so forth, a different meaning (*arthāntara*) arises due to the establishment of the universal (*jāti*) therein, it should be understood as follows: in the formulation of the probandum (*sādhya*) in all the preceding inferences, the qualification "not residing in anything other than sound and being devoid of specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*)" must be added to the universal directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva*). Therefore, there is no possibility of the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended. Furthermore, the objection of "unestablishedness" (*asiddhi*) regarding the term "substantiality" is raised with reference to the inference concerning non-omnipresent substances; however, the word "etc. (*ādi*) is used with reference to the other inferences.

Even in the case of the self (*ātman*), since the universal "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is grasped as being sublated by the absence of its own pervader, "substance-ness," [if one were to argue] that by the force of such an inference another substance possessing that universal would be established as distinct from the self, this would result in the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratā*). Furthermore, if there is a certainty regarding the non-existence of any other substance, there would be a sublation (*bādha*); both of these points are to be understood as the meaning of the word "etc.
(*ādi*). There is no seed (reason) for establishing the absence of the pervading "substance-ness" in the self.

Because the doubt regarding the absence of a seed (nirbīja-śaṅkā) lacks a final resolution, there is no possibility at all of such a doubt being raised. Nor can its establishment be achieved through the mere absence of qualities—which would be the pervader (vyāpaka) with respect to substanceness (dravyatva)—by virtue of its being the definition of substanceness;
for in that very case, the seed [of the argument] is absent.
Surely, by establishing the absence of each specific quality in the self, the absence of the general category of qualities is established;
for you accept that knowledge, desire, and so forth are qualities of the mind because they are transformations of the mind.
Furthermore, there is no evidence for the existence of unmanifest color-form and other such qualities.
If manifested color and so forth were present [in the self], it would follow that the great self (mahān ātmā) would be perceptible by the eye and other senses.
If one attempts to avoid this consequence by not admitting the existence of magnitude (mahattva), then there is no evidence for the very absence of those [qualities] in that [self].
Furthermore, the claim that "previously color resided in the self, and thus visual perception also resided there, but now, due to its destruction, there is no longer visual perception" is incorrect.
In that case, since there is an absence of both the destruction and the production of color and other qualities,
and because the destruction of the substratum— which serves as the cause— is impossible due to the eternity of the self, cooking and the like cannot be established there as valid;
furthermore, if such were the case, the production of another color would necessarily follow.
Furthermore, because causes such as cooking and the like are impossible [in the case of eternal substances],

and likewise because qualities such as oneness and dimension are not objects of perception and thus lack any basis in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their absence is established. Therefore, if it is argued that the absence of the universal is established solely by the force of the aggregate of absences of particulars, we say no.
