Even given that much, since the existence of duality, conjunction, and so forth is established by the force of scriptural usage such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*)—where the word "two" is employed—and because these [qualities] persist as long as the substance exists, it must be admitted that their production and destruction result from relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) and the actions of other [agents]. Consequently, the non-existence of qualities such as duality and conjunction is not proven; thus, the reason consisting of a collection of specific absences (*viśeṣābhāvakūṭa*) remains unestablished (*asiddha*).

Therefore, with the intention that even the suspicion of the absence of substantiality (*dravyatva*) in the Self is utterly baseless, he says: "In the Self" (*ātmani*) and "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇaḥ*). This means that [the Self] is devoid of qualities even in the context of scriptural usage and the like.

The phrase "of duality and so forth" (*dvitvādīnām*) is intended to indicate the following doubt: that the quality-less nature (*nirguṇatva*) is accepted solely on the strength of scriptural statements such as "and this is without qualities.

Thus, because the scriptural statement teaching duality and so forth exists, the scriptural statement regarding quality-lessness is subject to a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*); consequently, it lacks the power to determine its own specific meaning. However, at the stage of inquiry, since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) in accepting duality and so forth, that [dualistic] scripture possesses the power to determine its own intended meaning. Therefore, the sense is that if the scriptural statement on quality-lessness were intended to mean the absolute absence of all qualities (*guṇasāmānyābhāva*), it would be contradicted; hence, it must mean the absence of qualities consisting of form and the like (*rūpādirūpaguṇābhāva*).

[Objection: But since everything is negated here by the Śruti text, "Not this, not this" (*neha nānā*), how can duality and so forth be admitted in the Self? [Reply: To this, it is said, "of empirical things" (*vyāvahārikāṇām*). The sense is that even in the case of earth and other elements, since ultimate qualities are absent, they must possess substancehood (*dravyatva*) precisely by being the substrata of empirical qualities; thus, substancehood is necessary here as well. "Inclusion among qualities and so forth"—the ellipsis is "if substancehood is not admitted. "And because of the logical consequences" (*prasaṅgāt ca*)—this means by the force of the reasoning that would result in their inclusion among qualities and so forth.
Since it is a category (padārtha) while being distinct from substance (dravya), it would follow that it is one of the categories beginning with quality (guṇa);
yet this is not an acceptable conclusion.

For it is impossible to include it within the categories starting with quality and ending with absence (abhāva), because it is not inherent (asamaveta) and because it lacks a counter-positive that exists (sat-pratiyogikatvābhāva).

Therefore, since the consequence (*āpādya*) is absent, let there be the absence of the specific consequence-bearer (*viśiṣṭāpādaka*). Once the absence of the consequence-bearer is established, it culminates in the absence of its substantive attribute (*viśeṣya*), namely "being a category" (*padārthatva*). Since this would result in the Self not being established as a non-entity (*alīka*), it must instead culminate in the absence of its qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*); thus, the meaning is that "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) is established. Alternatively, for the scripture to be authoritative regarding the Self—which is the subject of the scriptural texts teaching "qualitylessness"—the existence of the absence of qualities is required.
And that [absence] cannot abide in something that possesses qualities which persist as long as the substance exists.

The meaning is that even though a quality exists as long as the substance exists (*ayāvaddravyabhāvī*), since the absence of that quality occurs at times other than the time of its existence, there is no sublation—consisting of the lack of authority in scripture—and thus its existence is possible.

He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the total non-acceptance of that [selfhood] as follows: "Because of the qualities," etc. The sense is that they (the selves) are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*) and are momentary (*kṣaṇatva*). And regarding the phrase "nor is there a supporting reason" (*na cānukūlatarka*), etc.: "Equal to fallacies" (*ābhāsasamāna*) means that even after the universal *ātmatva* (selfhood) has been established, one might still attempt to prove other universals and so forth by employing reasons such as: "The self is not possessed of a universal, because it is either the absence of self or something else, like an absence. Such arguments would share the same logical status (*samānayogakṣematva*) as fallacious reasons, because one could likewise posit "being distinct from that [selfhood]" within a universal that is directly pervaded by substantiality (*dravyatva-sākṣād-vyāpya-jāti*) and then employ that to establish the probandum. Thus, the point is that these [proposed proofs] are on par with fallacies.

Although the similarity of fallacies (*ābhāsasāmya*) is a defect only insofar as it results in the [reason] being inconclusive (*aprayojakatā*), otherwise—if mere existence of similarity were a defect—it would follow that even the inference from smoke would be faulty due to its similarity to fallacies by virtue of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*). Nevertheless, it is mentioned separately with the intention that, according to the method stated in the *Sudhā*, it also possesses the capacity to render [the reason] non-probative (*asādhakatva*). Regarding the phrase "by being dependent on the cognition of a limiting condition" (*upādhijñānasāpekṣatvena*): being a property conditioned by a limiting factor (*aupādhikadharma*) means being a property constituted by various distinct entities.

The meaning is as follows: since the knowledge of the various constituent objects is necessary for the knowledge of that [whole], if one were to accept a cognition of *śakti* (denotative power) dependent on a cognition of the *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for application) which itself depends on that [knowledge of the constituents], there would be the fault of "cognitive complexity" (*upasthiti-gaurava*) and "complexity of the delimitors of denotability" (*śakyatāvacchedaka-gaurava*). Thus, by means of this favorable reasoning (*anukūla-tarka*), the suspicion of being non-conclusive (*aprayojakatva*) is dispelled, establishing these [constituents] as the proof. On the other hand, the others [the universalists] lack such favorable reasoning; moreover, they face unfavorable reasoning (*pratikūla-tarka*) such as the introduction of the unauthoritative burden of many universals (*bahujāti-gaurava*). Therefore, they do not constitute proof.

Nor should it be argued that, following the principle of parsimony regarding the delimiting condition (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the denotable meaning of the term "all-pervasive" (*vibhu*), a universal of all-pervasiveness (*vibhutvajāti*) would also be established by the aforementioned inference and other means.
For pure inference, being independent of desire, establishes neither any object nor refutes any;

rather, it is our established doctrine for both ourselves and others that when there is doubt regarding an object already established through perception and other means, reasoning, acting as its aid, becomes the establisher of that object.

Thus, since the universal *ātmatva* (selfhood) is the object of such perceptions as "I, I," when doubt arises regarding it, the aforementioned inferences serve as determinative factors by way of supporting that perception.

However, this is not the case for the locus of omnipresence (*vibhutva*), because it is not perceptible; for if one were to postulate a universal based merely on the parsimony of the delimitors of capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka-lāghava*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the collapse of all polysemous terms—this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: In that case, having seen a tree, people employ the conventions "this is a jar" or "this is a *karīra* (mango-tree)," and from this usage, universals such as *karīratva* (mangoness) would be established.

Anticipating the objection that "since there exist subverting (or proving) factors, those [qualities] lack the status of being a universal (jāti), let it be the same in the present case as well," he refutes this with the intention that having an equal number of individual instances (tulyavyaktikatva) does not constitute a subverting factor. He says: "na ca" (and not). He dispels the Māyins' doubt in their own manner: "na ca" (and not). The meaning is that since the possession of qualities in the Self is not established due to contradiction with the scriptural texts on the qualityless (nirguṇa-śruti), the universal "substance-ness" (dravyatva-jāti), which is pervaded by that [quality], is also unestablished. Regarding the phrase "asiddhyādi" (unestablished, etc.): in the immediately preceding inference, there is unestablished nature of the essential form (svarūpāsiddhi) and subversion (bādha);
in the inference prior to that, there is non-establishment of the probandum (sādhyāprasiddhi).
In those preceding inferences, the qualification "other than substanceness" (*dravyatvānyat*) is redundant.

The meaning is that in those preceding inferences, since the conclusion cannot be established by taking the proof of a genus pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatvavyāpyajāti*) in the self (*ātman*), the intended object remains unestablished. Regarding the phrase "in the self": this is the underlying point.
Even though scriptural texts denying qualities (*nirguṇa-śruti*) negate ultimate qualities, there is no sublation to the acceptance of conventional qualities (*vyāvahārika-guṇa*).
Nor does it follow that qualities (guṇas) possess ultimate reality (pāramārthikatva) simply because they persist as long as the substance (yāvaddravyabhāvitva) exists;

for although it is impossible to accept qualities such as color (rūpa) as persisting as long as the substance, there is no subverting argument against accepting duality (dvitva) and so forth produced by relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi).

To the objection that here the very absence of a proof is itself a subverting argument, he says: "Because of its inclusion among qualities and so forth. The meaning is that since it is not included among qualities and so forth due to its non-inherence (avṛttitva), the nature of being a substance (dravyatva) is established by the method of elimination (pariśeṣāt).

One might object: "In the aforementioned inferences, let the reason (hetu) exist, but let the probandum (sādhya) not; thus, due to the absence of a *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) that wards off the suspicion of being 'unproving' (*aprayojaka*), they lack proving power. Furthermore, there is a parity with fallacious arguments (*ābhāsa*), such as: 'Earth-ness is distinct from a genus directly pervaded by substanceness that is different from established genera like water-ness, because it is a genus'; or 'Existence (*sattā*) is other than the genus residing in ether which is different from substanceness, because it is a genus—just like pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*)'. He refutes this objection with the words "And not... (*na ca*). Regarding the phrase "parity with fallacies" (*ābhāsa-samāna*): the meaning is that there is a parity between the "acquisition and preservation" (*yogakṣema*)—that is, the presence or absence of a proving or subverting factor—in these cases.
The sense is that since the aforementioned inference is fallacious, this one is also fallacious due to there being no distinction [between them].

Wishing to dismantle the equality of these fallacies, he establishes a favorable *tarka* (logical argument) with the words "ātmapada... etc. "Of the delimitor of the denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word 'self' (*ātmapada*)" is the meaning. "Lightness" (*lāghava*) means that because a universal (*jāti*) is partless, it does not depend on the cognition of qualifiers and so forth. "Being adventitious" (*aupādhikatva*) means having the nature of a qualified attribute (*viśiṣṭadharma*).

The meaning is that [the property of] being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*), which is constituted by multiple entities (*anekavastu*), serves as the basis for the application of the term "self" (*ātmapadapravṛttinimitta*). Regarding the phrase "there is prolixity" (*gauravam*): although there is no room for parsimony (*lāghava*) because even if self-luminosity and so forth were not the basis for the application of the term "self," they would still possess the quality of having a cognition dependent on the knowledge of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that constitute them; and indeed, there is prolixity precisely from the postulation of a distinct universal (*jātyantara*), nevertheless, one should understand that prolixity arises from the assumption that the knowledge of the word "self" and so forth depends on the knowledge of multiple limiting adjuncts, and from the assumption that the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) includes those multiple adjuncts within its scope.

Having thus established the existence of evidence for the universal *ātmatva*, he now establishes the absence of any subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) with the words "tulyavyaktikatvādīnām" (due to having an equal number of instances, etc.). If *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) and *kalaśatva* (jar-ness) were distinct universals, then having an equal number of instances (*tulyavyaktikatva*), which consists in being co-extensive with the universal, would be a subverting argument against their being distinct.

If *bhūtatva* (elementality) and *mūrtatva* (corporeality) were universals, there would be the fault of confusion (*sāṅkarya*), consisting in their being co-located while being co-located with the mutual absence of each other.
If a universal itself possessed a universal, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to a succession of universals.

If a particular (*viśeṣa*) possesses a genus (*jāti*), then since the genus alone would be the differentiator, its essential nature—which consists in being self-differentiated—would be lost. Alternatively, if it were other than a genus and devoid of a genus, its defining characteristic—which consists in inherence (*samavāya*)—would be lost.
Furthermore, if non-existence (*abhāva*) possessed a genus, its lack of inherence would constitute a sublation.
And if the genus "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) were accepted, [the genus] would be absent in these [particulars]. This is the meaning.

Now, it may be argued that when all the aforementioned inferences establish the existence of a genus directly pervaded by earthness, water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, mind-ness, and other-substance-ness, and since such a genus is not distinct from selfhood (ātmatva), the establishment of its status as a genus proves the plurality of selves.

Anticipating the objection that this would lead to a different conclusion (*arthāntara*) because it would establish a tenth substance distinct from the self, characterized by a specific genus different from those [already known], he refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*). The meaning is that there would be a different conclusion if one were to establish an individual entity other than the self, possessing a genus directly pervaded by the five [genuses] such as earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and so on, yet distinct from the category of substance. Regarding the phrase "established" (*klṛpta*): the self is already established as the subject (*dharmin*). Therefore, when the inference culminates in a specific property in the form of the genus "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) residing therein, there is parsimony (*lāghava*), because only a property is being postulated. On the other hand, if the inference were to culminate in another individual entity qualified by a specific postulated property, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*).

The meaning is that since both the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) are equally subject to conceptual construction (*kalpyatva*), the conclusion regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) follows precisely by the stated method, based on the maxim: "It is better to postulate a property than to postulate a substratum.

[Objection: But in the case of the self (*ātman*), which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), the nature of being a substance (*dravyatva*)—defined as being the locus of qualities—is unestablished (*asiddhi*) according to my own view; consequently, the status of *ātmatva* as a genus directly pervaded by *dravyatva* remains unestablished.

Thus, having raised the objection that there is a lack of proof for the substantive (viśeṣya) in inference, he refutes it with the words "And not... and "of those that are empirical...". The sense is that the scriptural text, "He is alone, devoid of qualities," is intended to negate qualities from the perspective of ultimate reality (pāramārthika).

Since qualities (guṇas) exist as long as Brahman does—remaining uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time—they too must be ultimately real; therefore, it was stated that they "exist as long as the substance (dravya) exists. The meaning is that since duality is destroyed by the destruction of the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) while the substance itself still persists, [qualities] are non-existent only for as long as the substance remains. The phrase "due to the absence of a sublater" implies "even in your own position. [The term] "qualities and so forth" [is used].

If the self (*ātman*) were not a substance (*dravya*), then it would have to be stated either that it is included within the categories such as quality (*guṇa*) and so forth, or that it is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*).
Regarding the first alternative, it cannot be included among qualities, because it does not inhere in a substance (*dravya*).
For that very same reason, it cannot be included among actions (*karman*), and furthermore, because its nature is not that of motion.

Nor can it reside in a universal, because a universal lacks the property of being followed by many [individuals]. Nor can it reside in inherence, because inherence is by nature a non-relational entity.
Nor can it reside in a particular, because a particular does not depend upon eternal substances.
Nor can it be non-existence (*abhāva*), because [non-existence] cannot be defined without reference to its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
Nor is the second alternative possible, because there is a fixed rule that categories of existence (*padārtha*) are seven in number.
Therefore, the sense is that by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), its status as substance (*dravyatva*) is established.

Now, regarding the inference (*anumāna*) set forth by the words "nanv api ca" and so on, which aim to prove the universal (*jāti*) of "selfhood" (*ātmatva*), there may be a suspicion of the reason being "unproving" (*aprayojaka*)—namely, that the reason might exist while the probandum (*sādhya*) does not, due to the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhakatarka*). Furthermore, there is a parity with fallacious inferences that attempt to prove the "universality" (*jātitva*) of [the property] "ether-ness" (*ākāśatva*) and so forth, such as: "Earth-ness is distinct from the universals directly pervaded by substance-hood other than water-ness, fire-ness, air-ness, mind-ness, and self-ness, because it is a universal. To address this, he says: "And not... (*na ca*). The analysis of the compound "aprayojakatva" is as follows: it is both "unproving-ness" and "sharing the same fate as a fallacy" (*abhāsa-samāna-yogakṣema*).
By the word *yoga*, the perfection of the means that establishes pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth is intended;
and by the word *kṣema*, the absence of sublation by valid cognition (*pramāṇa-bādha*) and the like is intended.
Thus, the meaning is: the state of possessing neither fallacious evidence nor a sublation that is equivalent to the evidence establishing [the conclusion].

Regarding "of *ātmatva*, which is the ground for the application of the term 'Self'": the meaning is that there is simplicity (*lāghava*) because a universal (*jāti*), being partless, does not depend on the cognition of anything else. Regarding "being adventitious" and "having the nature of self-luminosity": the meaning of "due to an adjunct" (*upādhi*) is that, according to your view, self-luminosity consists in being unknowable by another, and thus it depends upon the cognition of the adjunct in the form of "the other."

The meaning is that without the condition consisting of the substrate (*upādhi*), the condition consisting of the superimposed (*upahita*) cannot be established. Thus, [the argument] is "because it is equipped with a supporting reason (*anukūlatarka*) that acts as a protector. This means that the inferences are equipped with a protector known as a supporting reason, which consists of the "complexity of postulation" (*kalpanā-gaurava*) regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

Nor should it be argued that there is complexity if one does not accept that the ground for the application of the term "space" (*ākāśa-pada-pravṛtti-nimitta*) is a universal (*jāti*); for in that case too, such a claim cannot be made.

The point is that since there exists a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) against the status of being a universal in that instance, it is unfit to be accepted as a universal, and therefore the complexity is not a defect.
When Udayana says,
"Because there is no difference from the individual, because of equality," and so forth,
the meaning is that there are no five objections— such as equality and the rest— to accepting that *ātmatva* (selfhood) is a universal (*jāti*).
This section appears as follows: "As Udayana said:
'Non-difference from the individual, equality, confusion, infinite regress, loss of form, and lack of connection—this is the summary of the factors that invalidate a universal (jāti).'"

In that regard, among many jars, a universal in the form of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) is accepted in order to account for the occurrence of the inclusive cognition and linguistic usage, "This is a jar; this is a jar.
Otherwise, those two would result in being without a basis.
Nor can it be said that their basis consists of the individual jar, its color, and so forth.
Because they do not follow [accompany] those [individuals],
a universal (*jāti*) that does follow them must be admitted.
Thus, since the multiplicity of individuals is the cause for something to be a universal, the non-difference of individuals is a sublater (*bādhaka*) of universality.
Just as, because space is one, "spaceness" is not a genus (*jāti*),
since there is an absence of the inclusive cognition and other factors that would establish it as a genus;

whereas, because existence (*sattā*) subsists in a wider domain than substantiality (*dravyatva*), it is considered higher (*para*), and because earthness (*pṛthivītva*) subsists in a narrower domain, it is considered lower (*apara*), and thus both are accepted as genera.

And thus, since the state of being related as prior and posterior with respect to some genus is the very cause for that genus, "equality"—defined as subsisting in the same locus—is a sublater of genus.
For example, "humanity" (*karīratva*) is not a genus when it subsists in the same locus as "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*).
"Confusion" (*saṅkara*) is the coexistence in one place of two things that normally exist by mutual exclusion.
As in the case of "elementality" (bhūtatva) and "corporeality" (mūrtatva):
elementality exists in space (gagana) while excluding corporeality,
and corporeality exists in the mind (manas) while abandoning elementality.
Because those two would both reside in the earth;
if one accepts a genus (jāti) in a genus, there is the subverting consequence of infinite regress (anavasthiti);
if one accepts a genus in the ultimate particulars (viśeṣas), there is the subverting consequence of the loss of the very nature of the particular.
For instance:

since water-atoms (*āpyaparamāṇu*) and so forth are pervaded by their own common genus (*jāti*), it is impossible for that genus and the like to serve as differentiators; therefore, in those atoms, "particularities" (*viśeṣa*)—defined as having the nature of being ultimate differentiators—are accepted by yogins as producing the cognition of mutual exclusion among them.
And their status as ultimate differentiators consists in never being a cause of doubt or other such cognitive states.
Furthermore, this [definition] is not possible if a genus (*jāti*) is admitted in the case of ultimate particulars (*viśeṣa*).

For if that were so, since all particulars would possess the common property of "particularity" (*viśeṣatva*), they would occasionally become objects of doubt; consequently, they would result in being causes of doubt regarding their own substrates, which are eternal substances.
Therefore, if a genus is admitted in the case of ultimate particulars, the loss of their nature as final differentiators (*antyavyāvartaka*) is unavoidable.
If one accepts the universal *samavāyatva* (the nature of inherence), its lack of a relation [to the individual instances of inherence] constitutes a subverting argument (*bādhaka*).

Since inherence is a single entity, if one were to admit an inherence within that very inherence, it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*); thus, there is an absence of a relation between the inherence and the universal residing therein. — Thus [it is argued]. However, the non-difference of the individuals [of inherence] is not a subverting argument either.
For instance: the diversity of the self is the probandum to be established by means of proving the genus "selfhood" (ātmatva);
and that [diversity] is [currently] doubtful.
Furthermore, a doubt regarding the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva-saṃdeha*) does not obstruct inference (i.e., it is not contrary to inference),
for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total abolition of inference itself.
If it is argued that, in that case, even "sky-ness" (*gaganatva*) and the like would constitute a universal (*jāti*), we say no.

In their case, unity is established by the means of knowledge that apprehends the substratum (*dharmin*), which is assisted by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*); [and in the absence of such establishment], there would be sublation [of the contrary].
But this is not so in the present case, because the perception that apprehends the substratum is demonstrated to be a grasper of difference.
Nor is there the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*)—namely, the proof of a universal "selfhood" (*ātmatva-jāti*)—by means of an explanation based on a non-ultimate difference.
Because a universal (jāti) resides in an individual (vyakti) that possesses a difference whose existence is co-extensive with the existence of the substratum (dharmin).
Otherwise, even "sky-ness" (gaganatva) would result in being a universal.

To the objection that even in the absence of the five subverting arguments (bādhaka), the non-difference of the individual might still serve as a subverting argument, he says: "Even the non-difference of the individual... (vyaktyabhedo'pi).
Even though the proponent of oneness (aikyavādin) accepts the non-difference of individual selves,
nevertheless, even now that [non-difference] is not certain but rather doubtful.
For this very reason, the difference between selves is established by means of proving that "selfhood" (ātmatva) is a universal (jāti).
And non-difference consists in the absence of difference.
Furthermore, doubt regarding the absence of the probandum is not an obstacle to inference,
for that would entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of inference itself.
On the contrary, by virtue of being a constituent of the state of being the subject (*pakṣatā*), it is a factor in inference;
therefore, the meaning is that even the non-difference of the individual (*vyakti*) here does not constitute a sublation.
This too is according to the Nyāya system alone.
In the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the non-difference of individuals and so forth do not constitute sublaters of a universal (*jāti*).
To explain: first of all, the non-difference of individuals is not a sublater of a universal.
As it has been stated in the *Tattvanirṇaya*:
"Since [the self] is different by its very nature, by birth, by Vedic lineage, and by purpose,
how could there be an inseparable relationship such that 'I am he'?"

And this has been explained in its commentary (*ṭīkā*) as: "by way of genus (*jāti*), that is, by way of the distinction between genera such as 'being a living being' (*jīvatva*)," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), "Viṣṇu-hood" (*viṣṇutva*) is included.

Thus, since Viṣṇu-hood is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as a genus, and since there is an absence of a plurality of individuals (*vyakti*) therein, it is understood that the non-difference of individuals does not constitute a sublation of [its status as] a genus.
Thus, even equality is not a subverting factor;
for there is no subversion in accepting that both [categories] possess the status of a universal (jāti) when they have an equal number of individual instances.
Nor does it follow that "elephant-ness" (karīratva), like "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva), would incur the status of a universal.
Because there is no such thing as "karīratva" (the state of being a *karīra* tree) that is distinct from "ghaṭatva" (the state of being a jar),
these two words are synonyms, just like the words "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and "*karīra*.
Thus, even the confusion of categories (*saṅkara*) does not constitute a sublation.

If it is argued that this is because, although asceticism (*yati*) and householdership (*gārhasthya*) exist among humans in mutual exclusion, their commingling (*sāṅkarya*) among the gods is established by scripture—
and therefore they [the gods] are not castes— then it would follow that even Brahminhood and the like lack the status of being castes.
Nor should it be argued that those [categories] lack the status of a universal (*jāti*) due to the absence of commingling (*sāṅkarya*);
for this conceptualization occurs only after the fact that commingling has been established as an obstacle to being a universal.
Furthermore, it does not follow that "elementality" (*bhūtatva*) and "corporeality" (*mūrtatva*) would also incur the status of a universal in this way.

Since corporeality (*mūrtatva*) consists in having a limited dimension (*paricchinnaparimāṇa*), it is an adventitious property (*aupādhikadharma*) and thus cannot even be suspected of being a universal (*jāti*).

For this very reason, there is no inconsistency regarding its status as either higher or lower [in a hierarchy of universals]. Furthermore, infinite regress (*anavasthiti*) does not constitute a sublation [of its status as a universal].
Even if one accepts that a genus (*jāti*) possesses a genus, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
As it has been stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "In our view, qualities and the like, as well as those things possessing them, are indeed [distinguished] by their specific characteristics."

"Because there is no difference, there is no infinite regress. This is the summary: since the very nature of *viśeṣa* (particularity) and *samavāya* (inherence) does not exist, the properties of "particularity-ness" (*viśeṣatva*) and "inherence-ness" (*samavāyatva*) are also absent; therefore, the attempt to establish "loss of form" (*rūpahāni*) and "lack of relation" (*asambandha*) as subverting factors for the purpose of refuting their status as universals (*jāti*) is utterly discarded. "If that is so... means: the absence of the non-difference of individuals from being a subverting factor. "...the nature of space (*gaganatva*), etc."—the word "etc. includes the natures of time (*kālatva*) and direction (*diktva*).
He refutes [the objection] with the words "of those" (*teṣām*). This means "of space, time, and the directions. The neuter gender in "of those" (*teṣām*) is due to the general reference;

alternatively, it refers to the categories consisting of space, time, and the directions. Regarding the phrase "by the grasper of the locus" (*dharmigrāhaka*): when, by the inference "sound is supported by something because it is a quality, like color," a substance as the general substratum of sound is established, and since its being any one of the eight substances such as earth is sublated, that which is established as a substance distinct from those is precisely what constitutes space (*ākāśa*).

Furthermore, since there is no evidence for its being manifold, and because such a hypothesis would lead to unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), one must accept its unity on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*).
This applies equally to time and space as well.

Thus, since unity alone is established by the means of knowledge that apprehends the substratum (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*)—aided by parsimony—and since there is no plurality of individual instances (*vyakti*) such as "ether" (*ākāśa*), the non-difference of the individual serves as a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the acceptance of a universal such as "ether-ness" (*ākāśatva*) therein; this is the intended meaning.

To the objection that "let it be the same way in the case at hand as well," he says: "And not so. [The phrase] "because of the demonstration" means because it has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "To this we say.
Now, even if perception apprehends difference, it does not apprehend ultimate (pāramārthika) difference, because that would contradict the non-duality (advaita) scriptures and other authorities.

Therefore, even by means of a non-ultimate (apāramārthika) distinction, since the universal of "selfhood" (ātmatva-jāti) is established, there is once again the fallacy of proving what is already established (arthāntaratā). To this, he says: "And not... [referring to the phrase] "of the universal. This is because, even in your own view, you admit that the universals such as "potness" (ghaṭatva) reside in those individual instances (vyakti) in the form of pots and so forth, which possess a conventional (vyāvahārika) distinction from their substrates (dharmin) that is co-existent with the existence of those substrates themselves.

The point is as follows: even in the present case, since the individuals that constitute the self—which possess a difference from the self that has the same level of reality (*samasattāka*) as the existence of the self, the substratum (*dharmin*) of the universal *ātmatva*—must be admitted to be the locus of that [universal], it follows that the difference from the self must also be ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), just like the self itself.

One might argue that the qualification "having the same level of reality as the substratum" is irrelevant, because the status of being a universal (*jātitva*) is established in an individual merely by the presence of difference; to this he says: "Otherwise.

For even in the case of the sky (*ākāśa*), since a difference that is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*) exists according to your own view, if the mere presence of such [difference] were the cause for being a universal, then the universal "sky-ness" (*gaganatva*) would be unavoidable.

Therefore, the qualification of "having the same level of reality as the locus" (*dharmisamasattākatva*) is indeed necessary. Consequently, since the sky (*gagana*), which serves as the locus, is of a conventional nature (*vyāvahārika*), it is impossible for a difference from it to be of an illusory nature (*prātibhāsika*); thus, "sky-ness" (*gaganatva*) cannot be a universal (*jāti*).
One must likewise accept here that such a [same-level] difference alone is the determinant of being a universal; this is the sense in which there is no "shifting the subject matter" (*arthāntara*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that the very absence of any sublation of the universal (*jāti*) is what allows the aforementioned logic to apply? [Reply: Therefore, he states "even the non-difference of individuals" (*vyaktyabheda*) because in the present case as well, there is no such thing as having identical individuals (*tulyavyaktikatva*) and so forth. The point is that since [the subject] is doubtful by virtue of being of the nature of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), this doubt—being a doubt regarding the probandum itself—does not constitute an obstacle [to inference]. [Question: Since the universal itself is the probandum, how can this be so? [Reply: He says, "by the nature of selfhood" (*ātmatva*). This is the sense: The meaning is as follows.

In this context, the proof for the genus "selfhood" (ātmatva) does not have that alone as its intended purpose, because it would be redundant; rather, by means of that, the very distinction between individual instances (vyakti-bheda) is what is to be established.

And thus, since non-difference is the probandum through a traditional lineage of inference, doubt regarding difference is not an obstacle to inferential cognition; on the contrary, it is actually an aid. If it is objected that only doubt regarding the probandum itself is a non-obstacle, we say no, because it is precisely any doubt necessarily restricted to the probandum that functions as such.
Otherwise, even doubt regarding the causal complex for fire (*vahni-sāmagrī*) would be an obstacle.

If it is objected: "But surely, in cases such as a counter-balanced argument (*satpratipakṣa*), even doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) obstructs inference," we reply: True. Although that is the case for a doubt induced by a conflicting [reason], natural doubt (*svārasika-saṃśaya*) is actually a merit [for inference]. "Such as 'the nature of space' (*gaganatva*)," etc.: the sense is that this follows from the very logic already stated. "By the grasper of the locus" (*dharmigrāhaka*): the meaning is "by means of [the reason] being the effect of the material cause of sound," and so forth. "And not ultimately real" (*na ca pāramārthika*): the meaning is that even though difference exists in an ultimately unreal thing like a jar, it is established in its "jar-ness. "The existence of the locus" (*dharmisattā*): [refers to the aforementioned reason].

The sense is this: since difference is established as being of that nature precisely because the substrata (*dharmin*) themselves are conventional (*vyāvahārika*), it follows that the Self, as a substratum, is established as ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).

And thus, regarding the definition of a universal (*jāti*), the property of "subsisting in many" means subsisting in a difference that possesses the same ontological status (*sattā*) as the existence of the substratum; therefore, by the very establishment of the universal, the ultimate reality of difference is established.
Or else: [the phrase] "even of the nature of space (*gaganatva*)"...
The point is that even in that case, it is possible for only the difference between apparent individuals (*prātibhāsika-vyakti*) to constitute the basis for the genus (*jāti*).

"Otherwise" means that even there, the difference between the illusory substrata (*prātibhāsika-dharmin*) exists; this is the intended sense. Having revealed the opponent's intention, he refutes it with the words: "Even the non-difference of individuals. "Doubt regarding the absence of the probandum" means natural doubt (*svārasika-saṃdeha*);
whereas induced doubt (*āhita*) certainly does exist, but that is not present in the present case.

The point is that [the objections] such as the grasping of that [object] are rooted in the suspicion of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya-śaṅkā*), and those [suspicions] do not arise in the present case due to the fear of a counter-reasoning (*anukūla-tarka*). "By the means of knowledge that apprehends the locus" (*dharmigrāhakamānena*): the establishment of space (*gagana*) is by virtue of its being the substratum of the quality of sound (*śabda*).
In that regard, by reflecting upon the complexity (*gaurava*) involved in postulating four [elements] such as earth and so forth, space is established as one and all-pervading (*vibhu*).

Thus, in cognitions such as "the jar here," by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*), a single, all-pervading (*vibhu*) time is established as the factor that constitutes the relation between the sun's movement and the jar and so forth.

Similarly, for the sake of accounting for cognitions such as "the jar here," a single, all-pervading space (*dik*) is established as the factor that constitutes the relation with corporeal objects, again due to parsimony.

The meaning is that if one were to accept [space] as a genus (*jāti*), it would result in the contradiction of the means of knowledge that apprehend its substratum (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*), because [a genus] would then have to reside in multiple entities such as various instances of ether (*ākāśa*).
The word "na" (not) is connected with the phrase "it is not another object.
Now, even so, the non-difference of the individual [from the universal] remains a subverting factor,
as it has been stated:

"Non-difference of individuals, equality, confusion, infinite regress, loss of form, and lack of relation—this is the summary of the subverters of a universal (*jāti*). To this, he says: "non-difference of individuals. It should not be argued that if *ātmatva* (selfhood) were a universal, its contradictory would be the non-existence of difference from its own substratum—that is, being non-existent in that which possesses a difference having itself as the counter-correlative.
For there is no evidence that such a property directly contradicts the inferential cognition of its being a universal.

And since the ascertainment of that [difference] would act as a sublation (*bādhaka*) by way of contradiction against the inference of the difference between selves established as results, and since such [ascertainment] is absent in the present case, he says: "Regarding selfhood" (*ātmatva*), etc. "Difference between selves" (*ātmabheda*) means the occurrence of selfhood in something possessing a difference whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is its own locus.
And that [difference] is doubtful. The point is that the doubt regarding it does not constitute a contradiction, because it is itself a doubt regarding the non-difference of individuals (*vyakti*).

[Objection: "But surely it is that very doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhyasaṃdeha*) which will be the obstacle to inference. To this he says: "And not... [The phrase] "the consequence of the total abolition of inference" means that doubt regarding the probandum exists everywhere; such is the sense.
And this was stated according to the view that "doubt regarding the probandum constitutes the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*).

However, under the view that the state of being a subject consists in the absence of certainty (*siddhyabhāva*), since doubt regarding the probandum is not necessarily present immediately prior to the inference, one should understand that the consequence is the abolition of inference where the probandum is doubted.

One might object: "Is it not the case that the mere cognition of the non-difference of an individual from its common locus of doubt acts as an independent obstacle to the inference of *jāti*-ness—just like a jewel or a mantra [which neutralizes poison]—because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of establishing *jāti*s such as 'space-ness' (*gaganatva*) by the aforementioned method?

And thus, the *jāti* 'self-hood' (*ātmatva*) would not be established? Thus he raises this doubt with the words "In this way" (*evam*). The meaning is: if the doubt regarding the non-difference of the individual does not act as an obstacle to the inference of *jāti*-ness.
This would indeed be the case if the non-difference from the individual ether were as doubtful as it is in the case under discussion;
but it is not so,
for it has already been established by valid cognition.

And thus, with the intention that there is no evidence for the aforementioned contradiction because the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is already prevented by that very [reason], he provides the resolution: "By the grasper of the locus" (*dharmigrāhaka*). The meaning is as follows: when the inherence of sound in eight substances—earth and so forth—is sublated by the inference "sound is dependent on a substance because it is a quality, like color," aided by the apprehension of parsimony (*lāghava*) that sound's dependence on a single substance is simpler, then the inherence of sound in a single substance distinct from the eight is established; consequently, there is the ascertainment of the non-existence of "sky-ness" (*gaganatva*) and other such properties as being a universal (*jāti*).
By the term "grasper of the locus," its superior strength due to its status as a foundational requirement (*upajīvya*) is indicated.

Therefore, there is no room for the suspicion of error. Regarding the phrase "of perception": the meaning is that the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), in the form "I am not free from suffering" and so forth, has already been stated previously as being precisely the grasper of difference.
And thus, the intention is that there is no equality with the aforementioned fallacious arguments.

He raises the objection that there is a "shifting of the subject" (*arthāntara*)—since in the resulting inference, "selfhood resides in multiple individuals because it is a genus," the inclusion of both difference (*bheda*) and generality (*sāmānya*) within the body of the probandum allows the inference to conclude even by establishing a superimposed difference—and he refutes this with the words "Not so" (*na ca*). [The phrase] "by the establishment of selfhood as a genus" means by the establishment of selfhood's status as a genus. [The phrase] "of a genus" [is used].

And thus, since it is only a difference whose existence is co-extensive with the existence of the locus (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*) that constitutes the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no "shifting the subject" (*arthāntara*), because the probandum would remain unestablished in the case of the Self (*ātman*) without an ultimately real difference. Now, one might object: the rule is simply that a universal (*jāti*) resides in individuals that possess difference, but its co-extensiveness with the existence of the locus is not included therein. To this he says: "Otherwise... [The phrase] "because it would result in being a universal" means that even in the case of space (*gagana*), there exists a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*).
And this has been stated according to the view of the Māyins.
Because the proponents of the Siddhānta do not accept difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*).

If it is argued that, in that case, the non-difference of the individual (*vyaktyabheda*) must be the subverting factor, he says: "Even the non-difference of the individual is not a subverting factor. The meaning is this:
for even now, the non-difference of the individual is not established, since we are in dispute precisely on that point.
But [the opponent argues that it is] doubtful.

For in this case, since difference (*bheda*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), and non-difference (*abheda*) consists in the absence of that [difference], a doubt regarding it would be a doubt whose alternatives are the probandum and its absence. Since such a doubt is universal, it would undermine the very nature of inference by acting as a defect; on the contrary, as a constituent of the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), it is an auxiliary to inferential cognition and does not obstruct the inference of difference. Therefore, the non-difference of individuals is not a sublation (*bādhaka*) here. [The author replies: "In that case, then... (*evantarhi*).

The point is that even in that case, it is possible to avoid the objection regarding the distinction between individuals (*vyaktibheda*) by means of the method already stated. Regarding the phrase "by the grasper of the locus" (*dharmigrāhaka*): space (*ākāśa*) is the locus (*dharmin*).

By the inference "sound is supported by something, because it is a quality," once the substratum of sound is established in a general sense, and its identity with any one of the eight [substances] such as earth is refuted, a ninth category distinct from those—called space—is accepted.
Furthermore, due to parsimony (*lāghava*) and the absence of evidence for plurality, its oneness is also determined.
The point is this: since the absence of the probandum—in this case, unity—is thus ascertained, the non-difference of individuals (*vyaktyabheda*) indeed serves as a sublation (*bādhaka*) there.

[An objection: "In that case, let it be exactly the same here too. To this he replies: "And not so" (*na caivam*). The meaning is that the direct perception of the witness (*sākṣipratyakṣa*), which grasps the self, is precisely a grasper of difference, as was previously established by such statements as "I am not omniscient," and so forth.
Therefore, the sense is that [the universal] does not share the same status as an appearance (*abhāsa*).

[This is established] by reasoning regarding the universal of selfhood (*ātmatva-jāti*). Regarding the word "of the universal" (*jāteḥ*): for it is a necessary rule that a universal depends upon those individuals which possess a difference having the same ontological status (*sattā*) as the existence of its own substratum, the individual.

This is because we observe that the universal of potness (*ghaṭatva-jāti*) depends upon individual pots which possess a conventional difference having the same conventional status as the conventional existence of its substratum, the pot.

Similarly, regarding the universal "selfhood" (*ātmatva-jāti*), if it were to reside in the selves—which possess a reality equal to that of the ultimate reality of the self—then, by the establishment of an ultimate difference between the selves, there would be no fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntaratā*).

[The opponent objects: Let it be that the mere difference of individuals is the determinant for being a universal (*jātitva*), but not that the difference must have a reality equal to the reality of the substratum (*dharmin*). To this, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). For it is precisely due to the absence of a difference between individuals that the status of "space-ness" (*gaganatva*) as a universal is abandoned;
yet such an absence is not tenable.

Even there, because of the existence of a phenomenal difference (*prātibhāsika-bheda*), "sky-ness" (*gaganatva*) would also have to be a universal (*jāti*). Therefore, the intended meaning is this: although a phenomenal difference exists here [in the case of space], since there is no difference possessing the same ontological status as the conventional existence (*vyāvahārikī sattā*) of the substratum (*dharmin*)—namely, space—"sky-ness" is not a universal. Consequently, one must necessarily admit that for something to be a universal, it depends upon a difference that possesses the same ontological status as the existence of its own substratum.

But surely, by this much, only the generic nature (*jātitva*) of "selfhood" is established, not the plurality of selves. And if that were the case, the non-difference of individuals would not constitute a sublation;
for such [non-difference] is a defect only insofar as it negates the means of valid cognition regarding a universal, by way of the absence of a corresponding inclusive linguistic usage.

Furthermore, there is no inclusive linguistic usage regarding the genus "selfhood" (ātmatva), such that by refuting it the genus itself would fail to be established; thus, the non-difference of individuals would not constitute a valid objection.
Rather, the objections are precisely the inferences you yourself have stated.
If it is asked, "In that case, how is difference established?"—
it is true;
here, the non-difference of the individual from the universal is not refuted by a failure of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
We do not apprehend it in this way;
rather, we do so by means of the dismantling of its defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
For its definition is: "eternal, unitary, and pervading many."
In that case, when there is no difference between selves,
the non-difference of individuals does not directly sublate the universal;
rather, it does so by way of undermining the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the universal.
And the proof [for the existence of a universal] is precisely the uniform linguistic usage consisting of the addressing of individuals through a single qualifier applied to various qualificanda.

For this very reason, there is an admission of the universal "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and so forth in pots and the like, but not of the universal "sky-ness" (gaganatva) and so forth in the sky and the like.
Furthermore, in the present case, such linguistic usage does not exist with respect to the self (ātman).
Because there is no perception of a self distinct from one's own self,
and because inference and other means of knowledge remain deeply obscure even now,
how could the non-difference of individuals serve as a sublater of the universal by way of contradicting it?
Nor should it be argued that, even in the absence of a pervasive linguistic usage (*anugata-vyavahāra*) there, inferential arguments (*anumāna*) establishing it have indeed been presented;
for the opponent replies with the intention that, even if those [arguments] establish the mere existence of a genus (*jāti*), they do not establish the difference between selves (*ātma-bheda*).
He does so with the passage beginning with "For he... and ending with "...how is the difference established?"
The locative case in "ātmatvajātāv" (in the universal *ātmatva*) is a locative of the object (*viṣayasaptamī*).
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the evidence is the uniform linguistic usage.

Thus, if one were to accept a uniform universal in the form of *ātmatva*, there would be no such uniform linguistic usage—characterized by a single qualifier in the form of *ātmatva* and having various individual selves as its subjects—in the form "this is a self," "this is a self."

Therefore, the meaning is that it should not be said that the inclusive linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*) regarding the genus "self-ness" (*ātmatva*) is itself the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[The phrase] "your stated inferences alone" is the ellipsis for "are the means of valid cognition. [The phrase] "by which we might perceive thus" [is the conclusion].

The meaning is that by the absence of any sublation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the nature of inclusive linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*), the non-defectiveness of the non-difference of individuals is understood. "Inclusive of many" (*anekānugatam*) means "inhering in many" (*anekasamavetam*).

After the word "inclusive" (*anugatam*), the word "it" (*iti*) is to be supplied. Consequently, the resulting meaning is that the definition of a universal (*jāti*) consists in its being inclusive of many while being both eternal and unitary.

The point is this: likewise, if the plurality of selves is not accepted, then since it would be impossible for "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) to be co-inherent in multiple instances, it could not even be a universal (*jāti*).
Here, "being co-inherent in multiple instances" means being inherent in more than one thing;
otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of space, which is also co-inherent in many things.
However, because inherence (samavetatva) does not exist in the absence [of the substratum], there is no over-extension (ativyāpti).
If only that much were stated, there would be over-extension to sound, which inheres in space (ākāśa);
therefore, the term "multiple" (aneka) is used.
The term "one" (*eka*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the particularities (*viśeṣa*) inherent in atoms.
The term "eternal" (*nitya*) is used to exclude that [over-extension] to conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
Now, one might object: even so, it would suffice simply to say "eternal" and "inhering in many."

If the term "occurring in many" (*anekānugatatvam*) is intended to mean "occurring in that which possesses the number 'many'," then it would be under-extended (*avyāpti*) to universals such as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*), because one must intend [the definition] to be "inherence in something distinct from its own substratum. For by this, unity (*ekatva*) is obtained by itself;
indeed, it is impossible for that which is distinct in each individual instance to inhere in something distinct from its own substratum.
Therefore, if it is argued that "let there be no [such thing as] 'one' (*ekam*)," [we reply: no.
True;

nevertheless, the proponents of the Nyāya tradition maintain that this statement is intended merely to describe the essential nature [of the universal], namely, that the universal is not distinct for each individual like a particular (viśeṣa), but is indeed one and the same, serving as the cause for the consistent application of a term across all instances. The phrase "by this much" means: by the aforementioned collection of inferences, which are uncontradicted and supported by the principle of parsimony (lāghava). Regarding the statement "the difference between individuals is a sublater": in this way, the universal, while itself being established, necessarily sublates the non-difference of individuals which would otherwise contradict it.

The sense is that, according to the logical principle (*nyāya*) that "whatever [is required] without which the conclusion regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) cannot be established is all obtainable by the force of the property of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*)," there is a sublation of that [universal] only in the case of a genus (*jāti*) whose validity is based on inclusive linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*), and not elsewhere; hence he says, "For that... The sense is that inclusive linguistic usage is impossible with respect to a single [individual].

The phrase "subsequent usage" (*anugatavyavahāra*) implies that it has been established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the words "as stated by you": the point is that if the universal (*jāti*) is established through the very inferences such as "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) and so forth, without relying on subsequent usage, then what utility would there be for the distinction between individual instances (*vyaktibheda*)?
"In that case" (*tathātve*) means in the absence of a difference between the substrata (*dharmibheda*). "For that" (*sa hi*):

subsequent usage, which consists of a single cognition having multiple subjects (*viśeṣya*) and a single qualifier (*prakāra*), is indeed the proof for the universal insofar as there is no confusion (*saṅkara*) and so forth.

"For if there were no difference between individuals, that [universal] would not exist"—this means that the non-difference of individuals is a defect because it undermines the proof [of the universal]. However, in the present case, even though there is no such proof as a uniform linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*), the very inferences you have cited do serve as proof; therefore, that [non-difference of individuals] does not constitute a sublation. This is the collective meaning.

At the occasion of investigating the distinction between the self, he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*) etc., on the grounds that the [universal] is unestablished by the aforementioned inferences, resulting in the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratā*).

The point is this: since a uniform cognition (*anugata-pratīti*) directed toward a single individual can be accounted for simply by having that individual as its object, a universal (*jāti*) is not established for the sake of explaining such a cognition.

However, when there is a plurality of individuals, the uniform usage (*anugata-vyavahāra*) such as "pot, pot" cannot be explained by a single individual alone; therefore, a single entity appearing in all such cognitions is established as the universal. Thus, the identity of the individual is what subverts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the universal.

The meaning is: "we apprehend [the object] in this way," that is, we become the objects of such a conceptual projection (*ākṣepa*). But what then? [The answer is: "by means of the definition" (*lakṣaṇa*). Thus, in order to avoid the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition of a genus (*jāti*) to the nature of space (*gaganatva*), which possesses an imposed difference between individuals, one must define "genus-ness" (*jātitva*) as consisting in subsisting in multiple individuals possessing a difference of the same ontological status (*samānasattāka*) as itself. That very [definition] should be inserted into the body of the probandum (*sādhya*). Otherwise, since there is no evidence for genus-ness being an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*), it would be improper to insert it in that form.

Nevertheless, the point is that the universal *ātmatva* (selfhood) is established by taking the ultimate difference between selves (*pāramārthikātmabheda*) as the basis, solely through the force of the aforementioned inferences.

Now, an objection may be raised: even if the universal *ātmatva* is established by the collection of aforementioned inferences assisted by the stated favorable arguments (*anukūlatarka*), the difference between selves is not thereby established;
nor can that difference be inferred from those very [inferences].
Because it lacks a probative force (*aprayojakatva*).

With the intention that the aforementioned rule is baseless, he shows [the objection] with "But surely" (*nanu*). "In that case" (*tathātve*) means in the absence of a difference between selves. "A subverting factor" (*bādhaka*) means that which opposes the establishment of the universal *ātmatva*.
Thus, the underlying thought is that since a subverting tarka is possible regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there is no lack of probative force.
For the non-difference of individuals does not directly contradict the establishment of a genus, because there is no evidence [for such a contradiction];
rather, it does so by way of subverting the cause [of that establishment].
And the cause [of this] is, in some cases, a uniform linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāra*), and in other cases, inference (*anumāna*).
In the present case, however, it is only inference.

Nor is there any contradiction between that [inference] and the non-difference of individuals (*vyaktyabheda*) therein, because there is no evidence for such a contradiction; thus he says: "For that... Uniform linguistic usage means the cognition of a single property (*ekadharma*) in many [individuals].
Because the property [of being a universal] that would follow [from the cognition] is not established prior to the establishment of that [universal];
rather, there is only a single-form cognition regarding many individuals.

Furthermore, the non-difference of individuals—by bringing about the absence of such a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which is constituted by the non-difference of individuals—is contrary to the establishment of the genus (jāti). This is the meaning. [The phrase] "na ca" [means]: otherwise, inference would be useless; this is the intended sense.

As for what was stated—that "there is no [such thing] as the universal *ātmatva*," and so forth—that is indeed true. However, he provides the following resolution: because the non-difference of individuals is incompatible with the definition of a universal (*jāti*), it brings about the cognition of that [universal's] absence, and thus stands in opposition to the establishment of the universal. He says: "True. Here, "of the universal" means of the universal *ātmatva*, which is the subject of the argument currently under consideration. Although the non-difference of individuals is also directly opposed to the establishment of a universal, since it is pervaded by the absence of being a universal (*jātitvābhāva*).

Nevertheless, it was stated [in the text] that "by way of subverting the definition," because such pervasion (*vyāpyatva*) is difficult to grasp when a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*) does not occur.

It is well known that a definition must be a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the delimitor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*), and that the absence of a pervader establishes the absence of the pervaded.

Thus, since there exists a favorable argument—namely, that the status of being a genus (*jātitva*) would be untenable due to the resulting absence of a definition if there were no difference between individuals—the intention is that the proof of the self's difference must necessarily follow from the aforementioned inference based on the reason of being a genus.

Now, if it is asked how the non-difference of individuals (vyaktyabheda) constitutes a flaw in the definition of a genus (*jāti*), the answer is that it is because [non-difference] is constituted by the difference of individuals; with this intention, he states the definition of *jāti* as propounded by the logicians: "Eternal" (*nityam*). The term "eternal" is used to exclude over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like. The term "inhering in many" (*anekānugata*) is used to exclude over-extension to the dimension of space (*gaganaparimāṇa*) and the like. This means "inhering in many"; therefore, there is no over-extension to absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Furthermore, "inherence in many" is not defined by way of a property (*upādhi*) that serves as a differentiator of categories (*padārthavibhājakopādhi*).

If that were the case, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because that definition—consisting in possessing a property that is a differentiator of categories (*padārthavibhājakopādhi*) which delimits multiple occurrences—is present even in a particular (*viśeṣa*).

However, it is intended that [the definition] amounts to "inhering in each [individual] as something distinct from its own inherent substratum. To make this known, the word "one" (*eka*) was stated. The word "one" (*eka*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).

They also say that by means of this single relation—namely, inherence (*samavāya*)—the quality of subsisting in many [individuals] is obtained. Having previously accepted the establishment of the mere difference of selves through the aforementioned inferences, and having rejected the objection of "shifting the subject matter" (*arthāntara*) on the grounds that its ultimate reality was not established, [the author] now raises the objection that the subject matter has shifted because the very non-difference [of selves] is unestablished: "But surely... (*nanu*). By "this much," he refers to the entire collection of the stated inferences.

In that case, having not accepted a plurality of selves (*ātman*) while accepting that "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is a universal (*jāti*), he refutes its status as a subverting factor in the present context with the words beginning "For that... (*sa hi...*). That [universal] is established by a uniform cognition (*anugata-pratyaya*); and since a uniform cognition is itself established by a uniform property (*anugata-dharma*), a universal such as "non-potness" (*aghaṭatva*) and so forth is accepted. Thus, uniform usage (*anugata-vyavahāra*) is the proof (*pramāṇa*) for the acceptance of a universal here.

Indeed, the flaw in the argument regarding the non-difference of individuals lies in its subverting the very proof that constitutes the universal—namely, the uniform linguistic usage—by asserting that such usage would be impossible if there were no difference between individuals; thus, the acceptance of a recurring universal would be rendered futile. However, in the present case, the status of "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) as a universal is not accepted on the strength of uniform linguistic usage, such that the non-difference of individuals could serve as a refutation by undermining the proof for that universal.
However, the definition of "selfhood" as a genus (jāti) is established solely by the force of inference;
and since, according to the method stated above, there is no identity of individuals that would contradict this, such is the meaning of the collective [statement].
After the word "usage" (vyavahāra), the word "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

"Jāti alone" means the genus *ātmatva* (selfhood) alone. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "your own inferences alone are the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The question "Then how? [is asked]. The meaning is: if the non-difference of individuals is a defect, then a difference must be admitted within the individual self in order to establish the generic nature (*jātitva*) of *ātmatva*; but in the absence of that [difference], since there would be no basis [for it], how could the distinction between selves be established? Regarding this context: "by way of subverting the definition. The sense is that if there were no difference between individuals, the definition consisting of "subsisting in many" would be untenable.

What is that definition of a universal (*jāti*) by virtue of which we recognize the invalidation of the non-difference of individuals as a flaw? Therefore, he sets forth the definition of a universal as stated by the Naiyāyikas: "eternal," and so on.
"Residing in many" means inhering in many [substances].
Otherwise, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of space (*ākāśa*), because in that case,
while it is eternal and unitary, the property of residing in many would still be present.
And by stating "inherence in many," there is no over-extension;
for although [space] possesses eternity and unity, it lacks the quality of inhering in many,
since an absence does not inhere anywhere at all.
Thus, the definition of a universal (*sāmānya*) is that which, being eternal and unitary, inheres in many.
If one were to state here merely that it "inheres," there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to sound (*śabda*),
because sound also inheres in space (*ākāśa*).
Therefore, it is said "not inhering in many.
Since space is a single entity, sound lacks the quality of inhering in many; thus, this serves as a refutation.
When it is stated that [the universal] "inheres in many," this refers to the particulars (*viśeṣas*).
Because even those [atoms] are composed of many atoms;
therefore, it is said to be "one.
Because they are infinite.
When it is stated that "the one is inherent in many," this refers to conjunction (*saṃyoga*); for, as a quality residing in two things, it is inherent in many and yet remains one.
Therefore, [the definition] specifies "eternal" (*nitya*).
Because that [generality] is impermanent;
for when "eternal" is stated, it refers to the particulars.
Therefore, it is said to be "one."
When "eternal" and "one" are stated, [the referent] is space (*ākāśa*).
Therefore, when "inhering in many" is added, it refers to that which inheres in many while being eternal; when this is stated, the referent is the ultimate particulars (*viśeṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "therefore, one" (*ata ekā*): here, those who know the tradition (*sampradāyavid*) maintain that this oneness is not included within the body of the definition itself.

Rather, it is intended merely as a statement of the essential nature (*svarūpa*), meaning that the universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed one because it is the cause of a uniform application (*anugatavyavahāra*) across all instances; it is not distinct for each individual instance like a particular (*viśeṣa*).

In this regard, the following must be considered: what is this so-called "inherence in many"? Is it inherence in that which possesses the number "many," or is it inherence in that which possesses mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) whose counter-positive is its own substratum? In the first case, there is non-pervasion (avyāpti) regarding the nature of color (rūpatva);

because the number "many" is absent in color itself, the property of "inherence in that which possesses the number many" is absent from the nature of color. In the second case, the word "eka" (one) is redundant.
Nor is that [definition] intended to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the *viśeṣas* (particularities);

for since they are restricted to each individual instance (*prativyaktiniyatattva*), there is no over-extension whatsoever, because in no *viśeṣa* is there the property of being inherent (*samavetatva*) in something that possesses mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) relative to its own substratum.
Nor should it be said that this exists in the collection (*samudāya*) of *viśeṣas*.

Because there is no aggregate distinct from its constituents; or, even if such an aggregate existed, because it would lack inherence (*samavāya*) [in its parts], there would be no over-extension (*ativyāpti*);
and furthermore, since the aggregate is itself a single entity, the over-extension would not be avoided even if the qualification were applied.

[Objection: But surely, since the conjunction between time and space (*kālākāśasaṃyoga*) is unproduced, it is eternal; and since it is unitary, it inheres in multiple things consisting of time and space. Therefore, the complete definition [of a universal] would over-apply (*ativyāpti*) to that [conjunction]. [Reply: This is not so, because such a conjunction does not exist at all. Furthermore, since time and space are formless (*amūrta*), their conjunction is not admitted; thus, there is no loss of pervasion (*vyāpti*). This is the summary.

And thus, such arguments as "The self (ātman) is the locus of a difference whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is the self, and which has the same ontological status (samānasattāka) as the existence of the subject (dharmin), because it is a substance, like a jar," are well-established even if they were previously considered otherwise unestablished (*anyathāsiddha*).

In the argument, "Caitra’s body actually has an owner different from the owner of Maitra’s body, because it is a body possessing movements contrary to that [body]," Maitra’s body serves as the negative instance (*vyatirekadṛṣṭānta*).

[Furthermore: "The individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) possess a difference whose ontological status is the same as the existence of the subjects, because they are loci of contradictory attributes, like the two [men] commonly agreed upon."
Furthermore, contradiction is not defined by the rule of non-coexistence; for that is unestablished for one who maintains identity.
What then? It is defined by the relationship of the slayer and the slain, as in the case of permanence and impermanence and so forth.
And such a property consists of omniscience, non-omniscience, and so forth.
Nor can its establishment be justified by a mere difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), because that is not observed in the case of a yogin.

Thus, having raised a doubt regarding the refutations of the opponent's arguments—which were previously shown to be fallacious—by demonstrating that those inferences are actually faultless and established, he says: "And thus" (*evañca*). This means: when it is established that the self is a substance and that "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is a universal (*jāti*), and when the qualification of "difference" is intended to mean "having the same level of reality as the substratum" (*dharmisamasattāka*).
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi-padena*), one includes such inferences as: "Selfhood (*ātmatva*) resides in multiple individuals, because it is a universal (*jāti*), like earthness (*pṛthivītva*).

He dispels the defect in the inference where Caitra’s body is the subject (*pakṣa*) by stating: "Caitra’s body... [The term] "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) is used to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), by taking into account conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*). Here, the words "provided there is no powerful cause" (*balavat-kāraṇābhāve sati*) and "simultaneously" (*yugapat*) should be supplied to the reason (*hetu*).

Consequently, it should be understood that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of Arjuna’s body—which was intent on burning the Khāṇḍava forest against Indra's will—or in Maitra’s body, which undergoes movement and lying down at different times.

If [it is argued that] the Lord’s will and so forth are powerful causes, [we reply: this refers to a negative instance (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, by intending to show the absence of a positive instance (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*), the objection regarding the absence of any instance is thereby refuted. Now, he removes the defect in the inference [presented as] "the two under dispute are distinct"—namely, "the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*)"—by providing the qualification of difference as "having the same level of existence as the subject's own existence" (*dharmisattā-samāna-sattāka*); for if one were to prove an ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*), there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇatā*).

It should be understood that there is no room for the objection that "proving conventional difference results in proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*). Regarding the phrase "for those who maintain oneness": the sense is that in the view of those who maintain the oneness of the Self (*ātmaikyavādin*), attributes such as ignorance and omniscience are accepted as residing in one and the same locus. Regarding the phrase "characterized by the relationship of the victim and the slayer": here, being a victim (*vadhyatva*) means being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absence brought about by another;
and being a slayer (*ghātukatva*) means being the cause of an absence whose counter-positive is another.
This [relationship] is common to cases such as the cow and the tiger, eternity and non-eternity, and omniscience and non-omniscience.
But is it not the case that they are not similar?
For in the case of the cow and the tiger, or darkness and light, there is a rule that the relationship between the prey and the predator must reside in a common substratum;
however, such co-residence in a single substratum does not exist in the case of permanence and impermanence.
For indeed, there is never any impermanence in the eternal sky,
nor is there any lack of omniscience in the omniscient Lord.
Likewise, if it is argued that there is never any permanence in an impermanent object such as a jar, nor any omniscience in a non-omniscient individual soul;
