True. Here too, there is no contradiction because we accept that eternality and non-eternality—or omniscience and non-omniscience—are the counter-correlates of absence precisely when they are applicable by virtue of having a common substratum.
However, this much is the distinction:
In the case of the cow and the tiger, etc., the non-existence that has entered into the relationship between the victim and the slayer is of the nature of *dhvaṃsa* (destruction).

In the case of eternality and non-eternality, etc., it is of the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Now, if this is so, one might object: "Since there is a rule that the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of absolute non-existence must be unestablished by valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*), it would follow that either eternality and non-eternality, or omniscience and non-omniscience, are themselves unestablished. Consequently, how could space and a jar, or the individual soul and the Lord, possess these as their substrata (*adhikaraṇa*)?
This is true.

Even though properties such as eternality and non-eternality, or omniscience and non-omniscience, are not established by valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*) as being the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of non-existence when they are attached elsewhere, they are nonetheless established by valid means of knowledge within their own respective substrata (*svasvādhikaraṇa*), such as ether and a pot, or the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Nor is there any inconsistency in the aforementioned relationship of "slayer and slain" (*vadhyaghātuka*) between them; for that relationship consists in the inability to tolerate the existence of another instance of the same class within one's own substratum.
For permanence, as it occurs in its own locus, such as space (*ākāśa*), does not tolerate impermanence;

nor does impermanence, as it occurs in its own locus, such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), tolerate permanence. In the same way, omniscience also, as it occurs in its own locus, namely God (*īśvara*), does not tolerate non-omniscience.
Nor is non-omniscience applicable to the individual soul (*jīva*) which is its own substratum; rather, it is that very omniscience which is intended here as the counter-positive (*vadhyam*),
for that alone is the relevant similar class (*sajātīya*) which is applicable.

Consequently, even if that which is considered the object of destruction (the soul) lacks scriptural authority, that which is considered the destroyer (the attribute of non-omniscience) certainly possesses scriptural authority.

Thus, what inconsistency could there possibly be? For, while omniscience is attributed to the soul, it is precisely non-omniscience—which is considered its destroyer due to its intolerance of that [omniscience]—that is intended to be the contradictory attribute in that context.

Thus, regarding God as well, the non-omniscience that was previously attributed [to Him] is intended to be destroyed by the omniscience which cannot tolerate its own existence; for it is precisely that omniscience which is intended to be presented as a contradictory attribute (*viruddhadharma*) in relation to God. [Objection: But if contradiction is thus accepted as being characterized by the relationship between the slayer and the slain (*vadhyaghātakabhāva*), this is self-contradictory. For, in the *Nyāyāmṛta*, in the second chapter during the discussion of the inference establishing the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, [it was stated]: "And although contradiction is not 'incompatibility of coexistence' (*sahānavasthāna*), because that is unestablished (*asiddhi*) against the Advaitin..."
Nor is there the relationship of the slayer and the slain;

for, according to the principle that "one who is unborn cannot kill another, nor can one kill based on a different substratum," that [relationship] fails to prove non-difference. Having stated this and more, [the opponent] says: "Nevertheless, contradiction (virodha) consists either in being of the nature of mutual absolute non-existence, or in being pervaded by mutual absolute non-existence, or in the impossibility of coexistence even at different times. Thus, having negated the contradiction characterized as the relationship of the slayer and the slain in that context, how is it that there is no self-contradiction in accepting it here? It is replied:
For the state of being the killer and the killed is indeed twofold:
that which consists in being the cause of mutual exclusion in general,
and that which consists in being the cause of mere mutual destruction.

In this regard, the composition of this text proceeds with the intention of the first [position], while its refutation in the *Nyāyāmṛta* is based on the intention of the second; thus, there is no self-contradiction. Here, some [commentators] observe that according to the maxim that "one who is unborn does not kill another, nor does one reside in a different locus," if omniscience and non-omniscience were to have different substrates, the very relationship between the victim and the slayer would be untenable. Considering this, they explain that here the term "the state of being victim and slayer" (*vadhyaghātukabhāva*) is intended to signify "mutual exclusion" (*parasparaviraharūpatva*) through the figurative indication of exclusion (*jahallakṣaṇā*).
Others, however, say that it is the state of being pervaded by mutual exclusion; both of these views are to be considered,
for as stated above, there is no lack of logical justification when the primary meaning is possible.
Furthermore, this is because neither the relationship of the seed of the secondary sense (*lakṣaṇā*) nor the purpose for employing such a figurative usage can be established;
and because, if by the term "non-omniscience" one intends to mean "limited knowledge," it would be impossible for that to consist in the absence of omniscience.

Now, as for what was stated here—that by the word "victim" (*vadhya*) one intends only that which is unestablished (*aprāmāṇika*) as the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
That is not so;
for one must admit that even the counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) possesses some degree of ontological reality (*prāmāṇikatva*).
Otherwise, the cognition "there is no limited power in Īśvara" would be devoid of an object. If this is argued, we say no.
Otherwise, even the cognition that "there is no rabbit's horn on the ground" would result in being objectless.

Furthermore, while limited power in the individual soul (*jīva*) may be authoritative, it must necessarily be considered non-authoritative when applied to the Lord (*īśa*), as that would entail equality between the Lord and the individual soul.
Now, it might be argued that existence and non-existence are indeed established by authority.
And since these two are of the nature of absolute mutual non-existence, they stand as mutual counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).

Thus, one might ask: "How can there be a determination of the lack of epistemic warrant for that which is the counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence? If this is asked, we say no; for even though the existence of a jar, for instance, is of the nature of the absolute non-existence of its own non-existence, the non-existence that serves as its counter-correlate does not possess epistemic warrant.

Thus, although the non-existence of things such as a rabbit’s horn consists in the absolute absence of existence therein, the existence that serves as its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) is not established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).
This being the case, how can one entertain any hope for the counter-correlative of an absolute absence to be established by valid means of knowledge?

For this very reason, the objection regarding contradiction raised in the *Nyāyāmṛta* and other works—when "the subject under dispute is false" is taken to mean that both the absolute absence of existence and the absolute absence of non-existence are the properties to be proven (*sādhya*)—is logically consistent.

Furthermore, in the *Nyāyāmṛta*, it is stated: "Existence (*sattā*) is defined as the state of not being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitā*) of negation across all times and all places; whereas that [existence] has both the superimposed (*adhyasta*) and the non-existent (*tuccha*) as its counter-correlatives. This is because that very text, in its section on examination, states that according to the view that in cases such as "cowness never exists in a horse," it is only the relation (*saṃsarga*) that is negated, the word "place" (*deśa*) would be unnecessary.

From this it is known that, in his own view, the term "occurring in all places" (*sarvadeśīya*) is required in order to avoid the fallacy of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) regarding the cowness (*gotva*) being negated in a horse.
Consequently, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is of two kinds;
one is of the nature of being both universal in space and universal in time.
The other [type of absence] is merely spatial.

In that regard, it must be said that the status of being a counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) belongs to both the superimposed and the non-existent only with respect to the first type of absence; however, with respect to the second type of absence, even established categories such as "cowness" possess the status of being a counter-positive.
But this cannot be accepted, because there is no evidence for a twofold classification of absences.
Because it is impossible for the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) to be established as a valid object of cognition when it is being negated in a horse.
To explain: is the cowness being negated in the horse while it is present there, or while it is not present?
In the first case, that [negation] would be merely superimposed;
not the second,
because it is impossible to negate what has not been previously apprehended.

If it is argued that the demonstration of a negation necessarily depends upon a prior presumption (prasakti), whereas the cognition of that [negation] itself does not, even so, one must consider whether what is cognized is that very "cowness" which resides in the cow as being absent in the horse,
or whether it is something else entirely belonging to the same class.
Even regarding the first [alternative], does "cowness" reside in all cows or in a single cow?

It cannot be the first, because since all instances of cowness are unknown, it would be impossible to cognize their non-existence; furthermore, it would lead to the absurdity of the cognition that "there is no cowness in horses."
Not the second [alternative],
for if that were the case, it would result in the cognition that "that cowness does not exist.
As for the last [alternative], however, this is simply a non-entity (*tuccha*).
Because there is no other [entity] belonging to the same genus as the entire reality of "cowness" (*gotva*),

therefore, in the case of a horse, that which is negated— the cowness— is simply non-existent. Consequently, it is precisely our own view that it is the connection (*saṃsarga*) with cowness that is negated in the horse, and not cowness itself.
In this context, the term "belonging to all locations" (*sarvadeśīya*) is indeed unnecessary.

Since the relation that serves as the counter-positive of the absolute absence of relation is itself not established by valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*), its absolute absence is necessarily restricted to all locations. The inclusion of the term "belonging to all locations" in the verse, however, is merely for the sake of argument (*abhyupagamavāda*).
And [the plural] is for the purpose of stating the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with what is clearly stated in the *Mandāramañjarī*, a commentary on the *Tattvaviveka*, where it is said that the plural "of the rabbit's horn and so forth" (*śaśaviṣāṇādīnām*) was employed to indicate the recurrence of unestablished counter-correlates (*aprāmāṇika-pratiyogitva*) across all absolute non-existences.

Furthermore, this is because it has been stated in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa-ṭippaṇī* composed by Śrī Rāghavendra Tīrtha that, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), only that which is unestablished (*aprāmāṇika*) can be the counter-correlate of a negation.
This has been explained by us at length in the *Nirdoṣatvavāda*.

Therefore, since even the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) in our final position (*siddhānta*) can have both the insubstantial (*tuccha*) and the substantial (*atuccha*) as its counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), it follows that even if one accepts that omniscience and non-omniscience, etc., are of the nature of mutual exclusion (*parasparaviraharūpa*), there is no loss of their status as being grounded in valid cognition (*prāmāṇikatva*). Thus, the argument is established.

Regarding what has been stated by some—namely, that having raised the objection of contradiction with the *Upādhikhaṇḍana-mandāramañjarī* and having pointed out certain difficulties therein, that work was composed merely as a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*)—that appears somewhat unconvincing and should be reflected upon.

The phrase "na ca" [is explained as follows]: Even though there exists a natural unity, because a difference is postulated by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the form of *māyā* and *avidyā*, the systematic distribution of contradictory attributes such as omniscience and non-omniscience between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is established on that basis alone.
And thus, the meaning is that by this [argument], an ultimate distinction is not established. Regarding the phrase "the yogi who possesses that":

it means that since we observe only the mutual coordination of parts in yogis such as Saubhari—who possess distinctions based on limiting conditions (upādhi)—there is no observation of a fixed arrangement of knowledge, ignorance, pleasure, pain, and so forth [between those parts].

Regarding the phrase "and so": the sense is that because [properties] such as substantiality (*dravyatva*) have been established, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*) or other such defects; therefore, even those points previously refuted in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) are once again established.

The meaning of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "ātmatvaṃ nānāvyaktiniṣṭhaṃ jātitvātpṛthivītvavat" (Selfhood resides in multiple individuals because it is a genus, like earthhood) and so forth is as follows. Regarding the term "Caitra": the inclusion of "bodily nature" (*śarīratva*) in the reason (*hetu*) is for the purpose of avoiding the aforementioned defect of being over-extended to all [bodies].
To the objection that this would result in a lack of a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*), it is replied with the words "by way of negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*).
The remainder has been investigated.

If it is argued that the reason is unproving—since desire is observed to be contradictory in the case of bodies such as those of Indra and Arjuna despite the identity of the owner, yet non-contradictory in the case of bodies such as those of Rāvaṇa despite their difference—and furthermore that there is a deviation in the case of a single person’s own bodies across different births, we say no.

This is because the word "difference" (*bheda*) in the proposition denotes the general property of possessing a characteristic that establishes duality; thus, while such a specific [distinguishing] quality exists in the case of bodies delimited by Indra, Arjuna, and so forth, [the reason remains valid].
Nor does this imply that Caitra and Maitra are distinct entities by virtue of their specific differences,
for that would lead to the collapse of the doctrine of non-difference (*nirviśeṣavāda*).
In reality, however, because oneness is established in the bodies of Indra, Arjuna, and others, there is a total absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for difference.
Just as there is a specific acceptance of *pūtīka* in the absence of *soma*,
here too, the natural tendency is toward difference alone.
Furthermore, since objections will be refuted by the word "and" (*ca*), it is appropriate to accept primary difference itself.

The deviation of the pervader (vyāpaka-vyabhicāra) with respect to the bodies of Rāvaṇa and others is not an obstacle for us; nor should it be argued that, in this way, deviation with respect to bodies belonging to other births remains well-established,
because there is no distinction in their respective owners.
Because "simultaneity" is specified as a qualification of the reason (*hetu*),
or alternatively, because the primary distinction (*mukhyabheda*) is what is to be proven (*sādhya*).
In that case, what is intended by the term "possessing contradictory activities" (*viruddhaceṣṭākatva*) is the state of not being the locus for the mutual recollection of pleasure and so forth.
Since there is indeed a continuity of reflection (*anusandhāna*) in the cases mentioned, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or similar fault.
This is because we accept that some form of reflection exists even regarding the bodies and so forth of other births, as evidenced by the activity toward breast milk and the like.
If it is argued that there is a deviation because there is no reflection upon the pleasure, pain, and so forth residing in a future body while one is in the present body, we say no.

Since even the apprehension of either one [of two contradictory properties] constitutes the meaning of the term "contradiction," enough with further elaboration. Regarding the phrase "the individual soul and the Lord": if one were to attempt to prove an ultimate difference [between them], there would be the fallacy of the subject being unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).
To avoid the aforementioned fault—namely, that it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)—the author specifies the locus (*dharmin*) and so forth.

If "contradiction" is defined as the rule of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-niyama*), then such a rule is necessarily restricted to distinct loci; thus, it would only serve to establish the difference between the individual soul and the Lord.

To the objection that [this reason] was previously unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "And there is a contradiction" (*virodhaśca*). Now, if this is so, the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because according to the principle that "one who is unborn does not kill another, nor does one kill based on another's locus," there must necessarily be a single locus for both the victim and the killer.
Furthermore, the stated contradiction between omniscience and non-omniscience is unestablished.

If it is argued that because there is no stated contradiction between permanence and impermanence, the application of the example is improper, we say no; for here, "the state of being the slayer and the slain" is intended to mean "the absence of the counter-correlative. This has been stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position].

Let contradiction (*virodha*) be precisely non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*), and let the property possessing that [contradiction] be precisely the nature of being a living being (*jīvatva*), lordship (*īśvaratva*), being governed (*niyamyatva*), and being a governor (*niyāmakatva*).
Nor is there a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) in this case; for it has been stated that doubt regarding the reason (*hetu*) induced by doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) is not a logical fault.
The rule of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-niyama*) means that two things cannot exist together, which constitutes a state of being subject to sublation.
This sublation will be refuted later.

Alternatively, contradiction consists merely in dependence upon the distinction between ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*), and neutrality; and this is not unestablished for one who maintains the existence of conventional distinctions.

Alternatively, for the sake of the non-confused usage of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), [the property in question] consists in being the substratum of attributes that are not treated as residing in one another within worldly and Vedic usages—usages which incorporate those unique terms accepted by both parties. This is the direction of the argument. Regarding the phrase "that systematic distinction" (tadvyavasthā): the meaning is the systematic distinction of omniscience and so forth.

Thus, the sense is that since the logical reason would be unestablished (aprasiddha) for the reductio ad absurdum (*hetūcchitti-tarka*) that "if there were no difference, there would be no systematic distinction," the reason is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).

The point is this: although the various portions residing in different bodies possess mutual distinctions based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), no difference in form—such as omniscience versus non-omniscience—is observed among the *yoginīs* due to the division of their constituent parts; therefore, the distinction based on limiting adjuncts is established otherwise (as being non-essential). Now, one might object: "When there is a superimposition (*āropa*), one seeks its cause, but it is not the case that a cause exists simply because there is a superimposition. We reply: No. For in any instance where there is disagreement, we do not observe the aforementioned rule regarding practical distinctions (*vyāvahārika-bheda*); thus, the very status of [the adjunct] as a cause is refuted.

If it is objected that, because two contradictory properties reside in a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), they are not established in the consciousness intended by the terms "jīva" and "Īśvara," we say no;
for the reason consists precisely in the two qualifiers denoted by the word "qualified.
Nor should it be argued that those [contradictory properties] reside only in the two qualified entities themselves.
Because only the two qualifiers of ignorance (*avidyā*) serve as the cause.

"And thus" (*evañca*): the syntactical connection is that when the substantiality (*dravyatva*) [of the self] is established by proving that the self is the locus of the quality of duality (*dvitva*). The meaning is: when substantiality is established by proving that it is the locus of qualities. "Caitra’s body": the phrase "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) is used to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), which would occur if one were to rely on conventional distinctions (*vyāvahārika-bheda*).

Nor should it be said that the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished; for, in reality, the probandum consists in the absence of being owned by one who has attained identity with Maitra’s body, and as was stated previously, the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) in such a case is not a defect. "Because of having contrary activity" (*viruddhaceṣṭākatvāt*): this means "because of having a body whose activity is contrary to the activity of Maitra’s body.
And thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a jar and a cloth that have a single owner.

Accepting the previously mentioned absence of a positive instance (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*), he states a negative instance (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*): "the body of Maitra," and so forth. Nor should it be argued that there is an inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*) because of the observation of two contradictory activities—going and coming—within the very same body of Maitra at different times; for the reason is qualified by the phrase "delimited by a single time. Nor should it be argued that even so, there is an inconstancy regarding the bodies of Indra and Arjuna, due to the observation of contradictory activities conducive to the perception of ignorance regarding the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest; [for that too is delimited by a single time].
That which is accepted by both disputants as having a single owner is qualified by the condition "provided it is empty";
thus, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the bodies of Indra and Arjuna, because we both agree that they have a single owner.
For this very reason, there is no deviation in the case of the bodies of Saubhari and others.

Nor is the reason unestablished (*aprayojakatā*), because it is supported by a subverting argument (*bādhakatarka*) against the counter-position (*vipakṣa*), namely the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the mutual experience of suffering.

For this very reason, there is no suspicion of an equalizing fallacy (*sāmyaśaṅkā*) regarding a limiting condition (*upādhi*) or a counter-argument based on a fallacious probans (*satpratipakṣābhāsa*). Regarding the phrase "the individual soul and the Lord" (*jīveśvarau*): one should not argue that the proof is already established (*siddhasādhana*), on the grounds that since the individual soul (*jīva*) is also the subject (*dharmin*), the opponent (the Advaitin) accepts that it possesses a difference whose existence is of the same order as the existence of the soul itself.

Because an answer has already been given. Regarding the phrase "characterized by the relationship between the victim and the slayer": this means characterized by being of the nature of mutual absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), or characterized by being pervaded by that [non-existence].

Therefore, by the principle that "one who is unborn does not kill another, nor does one kill based on another's locus," there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the locus of knowledge and desire which have attained the state of victim and slayer, nor in the locus of darkness and light which have attained that same state. However, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and its absolute non-existence do not share a single substratum (*ekāśrayatva*), there is no deviation in their respective loci.

For this very reason, the phrase "as in the case of permanence and impermanence, etc. is appropriate; for in that case, a relationship between the destroyed and the destroyer is not possible. For this same reason, it should be understood in this very manner in the *Nyāyāmṛta* as well.
"Having little power, being non-omniscient, dependence, incompleteness, and being dependent for sustenance—these constitute the state of being a *jīva*; lordship (*īśatva*) is the opposite of these.
This is not unestablished, because of such scriptural texts as: "This [nature] of those two is innate; it cannot be otherwise by any means whatsoever."

But surely, according to the Siddhānta, since absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) has only the "void" (*tuccha*) as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), if omniscience and the like were of the nature of mutual absolute non-existence or were pervaded by it, they would themselves incur the status of being void. Furthermore, the property of being their locus (*tadādhāratva*) would be unestablished (*asiddhi*) both in the subject (*pakṣa*) and in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Moreover, it would be impossible for the void to be pervaded by either the other [mutual] non-existences or by the probandum (*sādhya*).
Nor should it be argued that this formal argument follows the method of logicians (tārkika) and thus the aforementioned defect does not apply;

for this would contradict the subsequent statement in the *Nyāyāmṛta*: "However, conjunction and its absolute non-existence do not have the same substratum for us, and therefore there is no deviation (vyabhicāra).
If one asks how this is so:
It is said:

absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) does not have a mere non-entity (*tuccha*) as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), but rather has a non-entity as its counter-correlative; however, this is not real in the same way that [the counter-correlativity] here [of other absences] is not merely a non-entity, nor is it a relation characterized by inherence (*samavāya*). It is precisely with this intention that this formal argument (*prayoga*) is stated.
For this very reason, according to the definition: "Absolute non-existence is always existence without a limit."

But it is not a case of having a non-existent (tuccha) counter-correlative as its object. Indeed, the absence of omniscience in the individual soul (jīva) is indeed absolute; likewise, the absence of the attributes of the individual soul in the Lord (īśa) is also absolute.
Otherwise, cognitions such as "there is no limited power in the Lord" would be devoid of an objective referent (nirviṣaya).
Nor should it be argued that this cognition has as its object the absence of a relation between the Lord and limited power.
Because association is not mentioned within the category of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*);
because it is impossible to provide an explanation for the intellect (*buddhi*) being like sound (*śabda*);
and because this would contradict the cited scripture stating that "lordship" (*īśatva*) is the opposite of that [non-lordship].

Otherwise, since cognitions such as "there is no jar here" or "it will exist here later" would also have to have the prior absence of a relation (*saṃsarga-prāgabhāva*) as their object, jars and the like could not even possess the status of being counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of prior absences and so forth.

Therefore, the author’s intention is that in the final system (*siddhānta*), absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) indeed exists even when its counter-correlative is not a void (*atuccha*). For this very reason, in the *Nyāyāmṛta*, the objection regarding contradiction when both existence and the absolute non-existence of existence are proposed as the probandum (*sādhya*) is set aside; for, by virtue of parsimony (*lāghava*) and necessity, it is accepted that existence itself is simply the absolute non-existence of non-existence.

This is consistent with the logical principle that "two negatives convey the original meaning in an intensified sense," because the negation of one alternative constitutes the affirmation of the other.

Furthermore, the objection that this is a contradiction—like saying "my mother is barren"—is refuted by the fact that I accept existence and non-existence as being respectively the non-counter-correlates and counter-correlates of negations pertaining to all times and all places. Thus, the argument holds together.
However, the absence of a jar that is perceived at a later time on a spot of ground where it was previously present is not "absolute non-existence" (*atyantābhāva*) according to our system.

This is because, being incorporeal, it is impossible for it to move from one place to another; consequently, the cognition of its absence even where the jar is present would result in a false cognition (*apramā*). Nor should it be argued: "How can that be a valid cognition, given that [absolute non-existence] is related [to the locus] through a specific inherence (*samavāya*) as its relation? For [if it were so], it would follow that such a cognition is invalid.
This is because there is no evidence for a specific inherence relation to function as a connector;
otherwise, everything would exist everywhere.
Furthermore, it would follow that even a cognition contradicted by experience could arise simply due to the absence of a specific inherence relation as a connector.
However, there is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the contact between the jar and its locus (the ground), and so forth, according to their respective natures.

Nor should it be argued that the explanation of the cognition of that [non-existence] is untenable in the same way as [the cognition of] sound; for such an acceptance is made in that case only as a last resort (*ananyagatyā*).

It is precisely with this intention that the object of the cognition of the absence of a jar on the ground need not be stated by the ancients; for where there has never been a connection between that jar and the ground, to claim that the object is the absolute non-existence of that relation would lead to an infinite regress, since—according to the reasoning already stated—it is possible for even the absolute non-existence of the jar itself to be the object there.
Alternatively, one need not explain the cognition in that case either.

The existence of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of a jar and so forth in a location other than that where its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) inheres—just as it exists in time and so forth—is not contradictory for those two [absence and inherence].
This is because of such cognitions as: "There is no jar here on this ground now," "It will exist in the future," or "It existed previously.

Nor does it follow from this that only a jar or the like which is currently non-existent can be the counter-positive of a prior absence or a destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) residing in a location other than its own inherence-location, and not something residing in another location.
It should not be argued that the explanation of its meaning—that counter-positiveness belongs only to what is present because it is opposed to antecedent non-existence and so forth—is unavoidable;
for [one can say] regarding this ground: "that jar will be" or "that jar was."

Whether [the jar] will become whole for us or has already become so, there is no difference in the cognition of its being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like, even while it exists. Therefore, just as in the case of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) in Nyāya, one must postulate that in each respective locus, at each respective time, and by each respective relation, the very status of being a counter-positive constitutes the contradiction with prior non-existence and the like; for it is not explained away by saying that it is not perceived there due to a contradiction with that [prior non-existence]. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*apāta*) of multiple prior non-existences having a single jar as their counter-positive, because such a perception would be impossible to observe.
If it is argued that [this is not so] because the object is the prior non-existence of the relation (*saṃsarga-prāgabhāva*), we say no.
Because it is impossible to explain [the cognition] through common consensus, the authority of those who accept the tradition must be respected.

Otherwise, just as in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), one might assume that even in absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) the contradiction consists solely in the presence of the counter-positive; who then could prevent the cognition of that [absolute non-existence] from being considered a cognition of the absolute non-existence of a relation (*saṃsargātyantābhāva*)?

Some maintain that by postulating, with extreme parsimony, that the mere existence (*sattvamātra*) itself is opposed to absolute non-existence, one can prevent anyone from objecting to the following: that the cognition of an absolute non-existence everywhere has as its object the absolute non-existence of a relation (*saṃsargātyantābhāva*) whose counter-positive is "being" (*sat*), while the absolute non-existence itself has as its counter-positive "mere non-being" (*asanmātra*).
Now, an objection is raised: if the author’s intention is described in this way, it contradicts the *Mandāramañjarī*.

For instance, in that work, on the occasion of establishing the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*) regarding perception that apprehends difference (*bhedagrāhipratyakṣa*), it was stated: [text follows].
The absence of sublation of itself (*sva*) alone is the reason. And the word "itself" (*sva*) refers here to the perception that apprehends difference.
Nor should it be argued that the absence of that [perception] cannot be established because of the difficulties arising from its being either known or unknown.
Because absolute non-existence does not depend upon the existence of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*),
it has already been established that even a non-existent thing can be an object of cognition.
If it is asked, "How can a non-existence be without a counter-correlate?"— it is not so.

What is this "absence of a counter-correlative" (*niṣpratiyogikatva*)? Does it mean independence from the cognition of a counter-correlative, or being devoid of a counter-correlative that is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*)? It cannot be the first.
Because this is an unspoken objection.
For we have not stated that the cognition of absolute non-existence is independent of the cognition of the counter-positive;
rather, we have stated that it is the negation of what was previously applicable.

Not the second [alternative], because non-existence (*abhāvatva*) is established as being devoid of a counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*) by the following inference: "It is like existence (*bhāvatva*); for it is a property directly pervaded by existence. Thus, non-existence is proven to be without a counter-correlate.
Now, when a jar exists in another part of the ground, the absence of the jar is inferred by the cognition "there is no jar here on this ground.

This is either prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or non-existence through destruction (*dhvaṃsābhāva*), because these two do not coexist with their counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); nor is it mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), for that would lead to the absurd conclusion that "the ground is not the jar."
Therefore, by process of elimination, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) alone is understood.
If it is asked, "In that case, how can absolute non-existence be without a counter-correlative (*niṣpratiyogika*)," we say no;
for in such cases as "there is no jar on this ground," it is precisely the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between the ground and the jar that is being negated.
And this must necessarily be accepted even by you;
for it is impossible to negate a jar in its own nature by virtue of its existence elsewhere on the ground.
If it is argued that it is negated in the form of being conjoined with *this* particular ground, [we reply:]...
In that case, it follows that by distinguishing between what is already attained and what is not yet attained, it is conjunction itself that is negated;
for according to the maxim, "when a prescription or a prohibition contains a qualification, if the qualified object is sublated, the operation transfers to the qualification.
If it is asked, "How then is the word 'jar' employed in the statement 'the jar does not exist'? [the answer is as follows:]

When the locative case in the word *bhūtale* (on the ground) expresses that the ground is the locus (*āśrayatva*), the state of being the located (*ādheyatva*)—which is the correlative of locus-ness—is implied by the sense of the matter. Then, when the expectancy arises as to "located in what?", the word *ghaṭa* (pot) is employed to indicate that [the location] is "located in the pot. Thus, it is established that even in the sentence "there is no pot here on the ground," the relationship of locus and located between the ground and the pot is negated. In that regard, if indeed such a relationship of locus and located previously existed between them, then this experience has for its object the destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) of that [relationship].
If, however, it will come into being, then [the cognition] has prior non-existence as its object;
if it has neither arisen nor will arise, then it has absolute non-existence as its object.
And thus, one need not even postulate that [cognitions] such as "a rabbit's horn does not exist" have as their objects things like a rabbit's horn.
Even in that case, it is logically possible for something lacking any basis in valid cognition—such as a rabbit's horn—to function as a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
Therefore, since absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is devoid of a counter-correlate, the reason (*hetu*) is the absolute non-existence of its own sublation; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
If it is asked: "In that case, how can you describe the intention [of the opponent] in this way?"

It is replied: First of all, there is no contradiction with inference; for since even an absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is a mere conceptual fiction (tuccha) is admitted, the property of being a non-existence (abhāvatva) resides in that which lacks a counter-correlate.
The state of resting solely in that which is without a counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*) is not the meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*),
because it would be contradicted [by experience] and because there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even in the case of existence (*bhāvatva*).

Although being a property that is directly pervaded by the subject (sattva) which has been made the reason (*hetu*) consists in being pervaded by that [subject] while being pervaded by *sattva*, this is not the case;
for it would result in the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the absence of that [subject], given that it is pervaded by either its own absence or earth (*pṛthivī*).
Nor does it consist in being pervaded by that [subject] while not being pervaded by a genus (*jāti*) pervaded by that [subject].
Because there is a deviation [in the argument] regarding the state of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
Nevertheless, it remains the case that existence (*sattva*) is a direct differentiator (*vibhājaka-upādhi*).

Furthermore, one should not think that this is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because, in the view of one who effects a division of existence into the categories of being (*bhāva*) and non-being (*abhāva*), it would follow a doctrine of a division opposed to independent existence.
And thus, there is no contradiction with inference.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "atha bhūtalāntare" and so forth is not a well-composed composition. To explain:

The property of being an absence (*abhāvatva*) does not reside in that which lacks a counter-correlate (*niṣpratiyogika*), nor does it reside in that which has a non-existent (*tuccha*) as its counter-correlate; for [the property of being an absence] exists only when there is either an absolute absence having a non-existent as its counter-correlate or something other than that.

Since the "how" of the property of being an absence—when the subject under discussion, namely the absence of a sublater (*svabādhaka*), is taken as the reason—is resolved by its being *niṣpratiyogika*, the purpose of the inference is not the mere *niṣpratiyogitva* of an absolute absence, such that the textual composition would remain pure [in that sense].
Furthermore, the claim that "this must necessarily be admitted even by you" and so forth does not strike fear into the Naiyāyika;
for he himself accepts in another context the negation of an existing jar in another location by its very own nature (*svarūpeṇa*).
The only difference is this much: [the manner of negation].
It is said that things such as a rabbit’s horn are negated by the wise in all respects, but it is not said that a jar is negated in its own nature within a particular locus.
This is because, unlike in cases such as "the handsome Devadatta is not here," there is no admission of a specific property such as "being conjoined with the ground" as a qualifier;
rather, it is accepted that the counter-positiveness (pratiyogitā) delimited by the intended relation merely appears through the mediation of that relation.

If the inclusion of the word "pot" were intended merely to indicate that the property of being located (ādheyatā) resides in the pot, then in cases such as "there is no pot here" or "the pot will exist later," the inclusion of the word "pot" would have that same result; consequently, even antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) and the like would not have the pot as their counter-correlate (pratiyogin), but rather would have the locus and the located as their counter-correlates. Therefore, this passage must be explained—by way of a bold assertion (prauḍhivāda)—as having the intention of establishing the non-existence of absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) through the previously mentioned collection of reasons.

For this very reason, it has been stated in the *Mandāramañjarī* during the discussion on the definition of truth: "If it is argued that [truth] is the state of not being the counter-positive of negation, we say no;
for even a balance-scale (*dhaṭa*) and the like are counter-positives of negation, and thus the definition is untenable.
If it is argued that [truth] is the state of not being the counter-positive of a negation at all three times, we say no."
The passage beginning with "Because horse-ness is the counter-positive of a negation [of itself] in a cow across the three periods of time, there is no over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) in that case;
for a cow is never at any time the locus of horse-ness," etc.,
is seen to be intended to establish that horse-ness and the like are indeed the counter-positives of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

Otherwise, there would be an internal contradiction within that very [text] according to the logic already cited, as well as a contradiction with the statements of the *Nyāyāmṛta*. For this very reason, in the *Nyāyāmṛta*’s refutation of the "inexplicability" (*anirvācyatva*) argument based on the impossibility of the counter-correlativity of negation otherwise, it is demonstrated that the cognition "there is no jar here on the ground," etc., has for its object only a relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*)—specifically the occasional absolute non-existence (*sāmayikātyantābhāva*) accepted by the opponent—and not the non-existence of the property of being visible (*dṛśyatva*). To explain:
Furthermore, regarding the cognition "there is no jar on this ground," its object is the *saṃsargābhāva* (non-existence of relation), not the *ghaṭābhāva* (absence of the jar).
This is because Udayana stated that in the case of "there is no jar on this ground," it is the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that is negated;
and since the cognition "the jar exists on the ground" has that relation as its object, the cognition "it does not exist" must likewise have the absence of that relation as its object.
Furthermore, this [absence] cannot be the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) or the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of the jar, because it exists at the same time as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
Nor can it be absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*),
because the jar exists there at some time or other.

If this [absence] were an absolute absence (atyantābhāva) delimited by time, then antecedent absence (prāgabhāva), emergent absence (dhvaṃsa), and so forth—being distinct from absolute absence—would not be established. For instance, in the case of a conjunction on the ground, there is emergent absence when the ground exists [and the conjunction has ceased], antecedent absence when the conjunction is yet to come, and absolute absence when the conjunction never occurs; thus, the status of being a counter-correlate (pratiyogitva) is established for a non-existent relation.
Furthermore, it is not the case that a relation which is already existent in the jar is what is negated here.
For that [non-existence] as well, there would follow the proliferation of conceptualizing prior non-existence and so forth, since it would be equivalent to a jar.

As Vardhamāna stated: "In that case, the absolute non-existence of a jar would not be established as distinct from absolute non-existence, and prior non-existence and the others would not be established;
rather, this [non-existence] belongs only to the conjunction [of the jar] with the ground."
However, at the time when the jar exists, [the absence] does not occur because there is no relation;
for the relation between the absolute absence of the jar and the ground consists in the destruction of their conjunction and so forth.

Alternatively, since absences differ according to the difference in their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*), they also differ according to the difference in the delimiters of counter-correlation (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*).

"This absence of a conjoined jar is indeed something distinct [from the jar], even though it possesses production and destruction, just like other qualified absences. To this, we reply: not the first [alternative].

For, rather than abandoning the established relation—which consists in the locus of the absence having a nature that is inherently connected with it without requiring another relation—and instead postulating "conjunction-destruction" (saṃyoga-dhvaṃsa) and so forth as the relation, it is more appropriate to hold that the cognition of that [absence] has the necessary destruction of conjunction and so forth as its object.

Otherwise, since there would be no relation—such as the nature of destruction consisting in the locus-located relationship between the time of the jar and its substratum—the absolute non-existence of the jar in the potsherds could not even be perceived. Consequently, the absolute non-existence of the jar would be a purely positive (kevalānvayin) entity.
Nor is the second alternative [tenable], because conjunction (*saṃyoga*) falls within the category of what is to be negated, and thus the desired conclusion is not established.

Even when a staff exists, there is an absence of the person to be punished; likewise, even when there is contact with the ground, there is an absence of the jar. Since we do not observe an "absence of what was in contact" (saṃyuktābhāva) [as a distinct category], and since all instances can be accounted for by the destruction of contact and other well-established factors, it is improper to postulate another type of "absence of what was in contact" characterized by arising and perishing. For this very reason, in the *Nyāyāmṛta*, during the discussion on the definition of existence (*sattva*), existence is defined as the state of not being the counter-positive of a negation that applies to all times and all places.

Having stated the definition of existence (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*) as being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) with respect to that which is superimposed as something insubstantial (*tuccha*), it was said that at the time of examination—in such cases as "cowness never exists in a horse"—it is the very relation (*saṃsarga*) [of cowness] that is negated; thus, according to this view, the word "place" (*deśa*) is unnecessary.

Nor should it be argued that even that [definition] is merely his own opinion, and that while the word "place" is required according to the method of Nyāya, it is not required in my own view, and that therefore [the word "place"] has that [negation of the relation] as its meaning.

If that were the case, since it has been stated that even space (*ākāśa*) and the like possess an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) that is "only-positive" (*kevalānvayin*), one might argue that there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding space and so forth, just as one might say that horses and the like are not the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute absence, and thus there is no lack of pervasion there.
However, one should not introduce the term "existing in all locations" (*sarvadeśīya*) for the sake of rescuing that [definition].
Otherwise, in the Nyāya system, one would have to introduce yet another term to rescue the definition from the lack of pervasion regarding space and the like.
Therefore, it is indeed the author’s intention that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) has only the *tuccha* (the void) as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
However, some who seek to establish that absolute non-existence has only the *tuccha* as its counter-correlative say the following:

"It is agreed even by the opponent that for destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), there is a temporal contradiction with their respective counter-correlatives. In that regard, one must state that the delimiters of this temporal contradiction with the counter-correlative are manifold—namely, 'destruction-ness' (*pradhvaṃsatva*) and 'prior-non-existence-ness' (*prāgabhāvatva*)."

Therefore, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is better to maintain that there is only one single nature of non-existence as mutual absence (*saṃsargābhāvatva*). Thus, the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of that [jar] at the time of the jar is established.

For when a single form of opposition can be logically postulated, it is untenable to adopt the "half-old-woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) approach—namely, that spatial opposition applies to absolute absence, while temporal opposition applies to the other two [types of non-existence].
[Objection: In that case, for the sake of even greater parsimony (*lāghava*), let "non-existence-ness" (*abhāvatva*) itself be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of opposition.

If this were so, then even at the time of a jar, the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the jar would not be established; rather, like absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), mutual non-existence too would have a non-existent counter-correlate (*asat-pratiyogika*). [Reply: This is not so. In my view, since mutual non-existence lacks the property of non-existence (*abhāvatva*), non-existence is of three distinct kinds.

Since the production of an undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpādana) brought about by that [reason] is impossible due to the absence of a probans (*āpādaka*), and because non-existence itself is the most parsimonious (*lāghava*) determinant of contradiction (*virodhitāvacchedakatva*), it is precisely our desired position that is established.
As it was stated by the venerable teacher (Bhagavatpāda):
"Non-existence is held to be threefold: prior, subsequent, and eternal."

"Because its nature consists of both existence and non-existence, mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is not distinct [from them]. Now, one might object: "Even by this much, since mutual non-existence has the substratum (*dharmin*) as its essence, it exists within that which is grounded in existence; yet, does it not also exist within that which is grounded in non-existence? To this we reply: even by that much, it would have been stated that the three types of non-existence—namely antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the others—do not possess the nature of mutual non-existence, and therefore they do not share the same time as their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).
This is precisely what we maintain, as we have already stated.
If it is objected that, in this case, there would be no absolute absence of color in air, we say no; for such a consequence is accepted.
Nor does it follow from this that color actually arises in air.

Is it being established that there is the existence of mere form, or the existence of the form of air? Not the first, because it would result in the undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) that form exists in things such as jars.
The second [alternative] is not tenable.

Because of the mention of the locative case-ending (*vibhakti*) denoting the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in the word "in air" (*vāyau*), and because kārakas are construed only with an action, there is—by the very nature of the linguistic expression—the cognition of a specific action consisting in the existence of air as the locus-subject. Since the generative cognition has the same form as the verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), it has as its object a particular relation in the form of air; and since that [relation] is insubstantial (*tuccha*), its absolute non-existence is also possible in air. Thus, there is no room for any objection.
If it is asked: "Since such a relation is timeless (*akālika*), how can there be a cognition of it by which even an objection (*apādana*) could be raised?
[The answer is: It is because the imaginative cognition (*utprekṣājñāna*) that serves as the basis for a poet's poem is voluntary (*āhārya*).

For this very reason, your own traditionalists maintain that the superimposition (*āropa*) of a relation between the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) and its locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is also the cause in that case.
The only difference, however, is this:
they accept that such knowledge is produced independently,
whereas we maintain that it is precisely that knowledge of the counter-positive.

For this very reason, even the cognition of non-existence—namely, "there is no color in the air"—takes as its object the existence of color, which has the air as its locus and is the agent of the action [of being], precisely because it is the negandum; for the cognition produced by the employment of words has the same form as the verbal cognition itself.
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
From the word, however, the cognition is simply that "that which [one might think] exists as color in the air does not exist."
This is because the locative case is prescribed for the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).
However, since the existence of a substrate such as air—which serves as the locus for the metaphorical agent—is unreal, it is logical that it possesses absolute non-existence everywhere.

For this very reason, even in cases such as "one should not drink liquor," you yourself agree that the negation connects only with the meaning of the verbal root (the action) ending in the optative suffix (*liṅ*), which consists in its not being connected with a powerful undesirable consequence.
Even in such cases as "air possesses the absence of color," the color perceived as the object of negation is specifically the color belonging to air itself;
for there is no cognition that "air lacks its own color.

If that cognition were to arise by taking the absence of a color residing in one thing (e.g., a jar) in another thing (e.g., air), then it would follow that there would also be a cognition such as "there is no color in a jar" [when applied to air].
For this very reason, in such a case, the negative particle implies a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (non-presuppositional negation).
And it has been said:
"Where the affirmation is subordinate and the negation is primary..."
"This is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), where the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with a verb.
For this very reason, those who wish to convey the absence of conjunction [of a jar] have been refuted by saying "there is no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭo nāsti*).

By this, those who employ the expression "no jar on the ground" (*bhūtale ghaṭo na*) are also refuted; for, according to the rule "an indeclinable [is compounded] with case-endings, etc.," when an indeclinable denotes the absence of something, it is taught that it must always form a compound with it, and thus the use of the non-compound (*avyasta*) is not grammatically correct.

In cases such as "ghaṭo nāsti" (the pot does not exist), since the rule *sup supā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4) continues to apply, there is no possibility of a compound with a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), and thus there is no room for the suspicion that it is ungrammatical.

Nor does the ungrammaticality arise in instances like "ghaṭaḥ ghaṭo na" (the pot is not a pot), because the formation of negative compounds (*nañsamāsa*) is prescribed specifically within the section governing optional rules (*vibhāṣā*).
Nor does the contingency of this being an *avyayībhāva* compound arise there;

for by the power of employing the word "artha" in the rule "absence of meaning" (*arthābhāve*), the formation of the compound is prescribed only with the negative particle (*nañ*) that denotes a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), and thus its application is precluded in cases of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*).

Therefore, the cognition produced by the words "there is no color in air" has as its object precisely the negation of existence whose agent is color residing in a different locus (*vāyvadhikaraṇaka-rūpakartṛka-sattvaniṣedha*). Consequently, it is established that even perceptual cognition bearing such a description takes as its object a real entity, and thus absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) possesses a non-existent counter-correlate (*asat-pratiyogika*).
And this must necessarily be so;

otherwise, there would be no established linguistic usage for such expressions as "the jar does not exist," "the two jars do not exist," or "the jars do not exist. Furthermore, there would be no established personal usage such as "Devadatta does not exist," "you do not exist," "I do not exist," or "we do not exist."

[Objection: Existence [cannot be the cause] of the absence of perception, because it would follow that one could always employ the expression "it does not exist" [even when it does exist], since the grammatical rule prescribes the middle and highest persons respectively for the second person (*yuṣmad*) when it is coreferential, and likewise for the first person (*asmad*). [Reply: To this it is said:

First, as for what was stated—that the delimiters of temporal opposition with respect to the counter-positive are neither "prior-absence-ness" nor "destruction-absence-ness," because these are manifold and [the assumption of such] would involve prolixity (*gaurava*); [this is incorrect].

However, due to parsimony (*lāghava*), the nature of non-existence as a relational absence (*saṃsargābhāvatva*) is one and the same. Thus, it is established that there is a temporal contradiction among the three [types of absence] by means of a single form, and not a spatial contradiction for absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) while the other two have only temporal contradiction; this avoids the "half-old-woman" fallacy (*ardhajaratīya*). Therefore, the absolute absence has a non-existent counter-positive (*asat-pratiyogika*). That is not so, because the property of being a relational absence—defined as the state of being an absence that is the object of a cognition of negation preceded by a superimposition (*āropa*) of a relation between the counter-positive and its locus—is more parsimonious than the property of being an absence-in-general (*abhāvatva*) which is common to both [relational and absolute absences], and thus serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of contradiction.

Since there is an absolute absence of any relation between threads and cloth and so forth, antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) cannot be considered types of relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*); for the commentators have denied that these two possess the nature of relational non-existence, and thus it is impossible for them to serve as the delimiters of opposition (*virodhitāvacchedaka*). Furthermore, in the doctrine that cause and effect are distinct, it is difficult to maintain a temporal contradiction with the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). Even if such a contradiction were somehow established through their difference, one could not avoid including the threads within the category of the counter-positive.

Since counter-positiveness (pratiyogitā), unlike duality and other such properties, does not possess a distributive existence (vyāsajyavṛttitva), it is also impossible for there to be a contradiction with the locus of the complete inherence (paryāpti) of that counter-positiveness.

This is because we have such cognitions as "now there is no wealth in me" and "there will be [wealth] in me hereafter"; furthermore, it has been shown that even a present entity can be the counter-positive of a prior absence (prāgabhāva).

Even if one accepts that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) possesses temporal contradiction (*kālikavirodha*), one must necessarily also admit spatial contradiction (*daiśikavirodha*); otherwise, one cannot avoid the "half-eaten-curd" logic (*ardhacarvitanyāya*).
For if this were not so, the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) would exist in the locus of absolute non-existence just as it does in the locus of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
Nor should it be argued that because absolute non-existence exists at all times, how could the counter-positive exist in that same locus at that time?
Since this is so, temporal contradiction (kālika-virodha) merely reinforces spatial contradiction (daiśika-virodha); it does not, however, sublate it.

Furthermore, as for the passage beginning with "But surely, because of even greater parsimony than that... and ending with "...we have stated that this is our desired position," that too is not satisfactory.
To explain: [The argument continues: ...For instance:
Is non-existence (*abhāvatva*) that which delimits the opposition to the substratum of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitāśraya*) of anything whatsoever?
Or is it all those [non-existences] such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) residing in that [counter-correlate]?
Not the first.

That being the case, even in the case of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is existent, there is the possibility—according to your own view—of a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the "void" (*tuccha*); and since that [void] is of the nature of that [absence], it is possible for the void—which is the locus of some counter-correlativity defining the mutual absence residing in that [absolute absence]—to possess the status of a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of opposition, despite its temporal opposition to it. Consequently, the status of having an existent as its counter-correlate (*sat-pratiyogikatva*), which you intend to establish, cannot be maintained. Nor is the second alternative [tenable].

Even though non-existence (*abhāvatva*) is the delimiting factor of the opposition residing in that which is the locus of the counter-correlativity defining mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāvatva*) residing in that [non-existence]—despite its being the delimiting factor of the opposition residing in the locus of the counter-correlativity defining the nature of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāvatva*) residing in prior non-exclusion and so forth—it cannot be the delimiting factor of opposition for non-existence itself, because it lacks the status of being the delimiting factor of the opposition residing in jars and the like, which are the loci of the counter-correlativity defining mutual non-existence residing in that [prior non-existence].
As for the passage beginning with "But surely, in this way, in air... and ending with "...is accepted," that is not correct.

Even in the case [of the argument], "If the mountain were fireless, then it would be smokeless," one might argue that since the mere absence of smoke is what is being led to as a consequence (*apādya*), and since that [absence of smoke] exists in water and so forth, there is the fallacy of "proving the already accepted" (*iṣṭāpatti*).

Nor should it be said that in this case too, either the absence of smoke residing in the mountain or the mountain itself as possessing the absence of smoke is the thing to be led to as a consequence; for that [latter] is not water, and thus there is no "proving the already accepted."
For it is impossible to establish that [consequence] merely by the absence of fire;
nor should it be said that a mountain devoid of fire, etc., alone is the subsumer (*āpādaka*),
because there is no apprehension of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between a mountain possessing the absence of fire and a mountain possessing the absence of smoke.

For, in the absence of an undesired consequence regarding a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*), it would be impossible for that [property] to eliminate the cognition of its opposite which is fixed upon it;
furthermore, from this day forward, such a relationship between the subsumed (*āpādya*) and the subsumer (*āpādaka*) has not been heard of.
Nor should it be argued that there is no "undesired consequence" (*iṣṭāpatti*) because the absence of smoke is not desired on the mountain, just as it is in water.

Here too, since air lacks color (*rūpa*) due to its being devoid of it, the following reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*) is perfectly sound: "If air were not absolutely devoid of color, then it would possess color"—just as one might say, "If the mountain were devoid of fire, then it would be devoid of smoke. This is because the relationship between the consequence (*āpādya*) and the reason for the consequence (*āpādaka*) is established through a difference in their respective delimitors (*avacchedaka*).

Alternatively, the form of the reductio (*tarka*) is as follows: "If the absolute non-existence of color were not a property of air, then it would have color as its counter-positive (i.e., it would reside in color).
Furthermore, that which was proposed as an alternative in the second [section]—namely, that the locative case in "in air" (*vāyau*) functions as a *kāraka* case—is also incorrect.

It is more appropriate to say that such an objection is untenable because the existence of color in air is false, whereas the absolute non-existence of color in air is real; therefore, it is impossible to logically entail that [non-existence].

For in the case of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is no dependence on a material cause (*upādāna*). Moreover, the demonstration of that [dependence] is untenable, because in the two forms of the argument (*tarka*) cited, the locative case and so forth are absent;
and furthermore, as in a well-known *tarka*, the property to be established (*āpādya*) and the establishing property (*āpādaka*) are not constituted by a substratum (*dharmin*).

Furthermore, even if absolute non-existence (*tucchātyantābhāva*) were to reside in air, because it is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) entity, it would not be incompatible with color; thus, there is no room for the objection that it would entail [the presence of] color.
Moreover, even if a false object could be an object of cognition, it is impossible to grasp a pervasion (*vyāpti*) by means of it.
Finally, at the stage of investigating *tarka* (reductio), an inquiry into whether the instrument for the cognition of absence is distinct or non-distinct is irrelevant.
As for the argument beginning with "for this very reason" and ending with "because of the instruction that there is no color in air," that too is not correct.
For instance,

by the phrase "for this very reason," either the state of being a non-occurrent relation (*saṃsargābhāvatva*) or the delimiting factor of opposition (*virodhitāvacchedakatva*) is referred to as the supporting ground.
Is it that verbal cognition possesses the form of that [object], or both? Not the first, because that has already been refuted.
Not the second [alternative], because it is unestablished. To explain:
There is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that the connection of grammatical factors (*kāraka*) occurs solely with an action (*kriyā*).

For the case endings denoting grammatical factors do not have their semantic power (*śakti*) restricted only to an object connected with an action; rather, they denote their own meaning as connected with something else that is compatible [with it].

In this context, that *kāraka* which is directly capable of being connected with the action—such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth—is what possesses the connection with the action. However, not every locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is directly capable of being connected with the action.

For example, in such cases as "Devadatta walks on the road," "He gives a cow to Devadatta at the Ganges," and "A leaf falls from the tree onto the ground," the road, the Ganges, and the ground do not possess the status of being the substratum for the actions of walking, giving, and falling, respectively.
Nor should it be said that the substratum-ness (*adhikaraṇatā*) of actions [resides] through Devadatta and others;
for it is more appropriate to state that Devadatta and others are necessarily connected [to the action] itself.
Therefore, they say:

"Whatever is required and appropriate presents itself in proximity; by that very thing, the word's own meaning is expressed as being endowed [with it]. And so, in the present case as well, since the action of existence—which is synonymous with the *bhāvanā* of subsistence residing in form—is incapable of residing in air, air cannot be construed in that manner. Furthermore, the universal of existence (*sattājāti*) is not an action, because in our own system there is no such thing as a universal that is pervasive [and yet an action].
And in this way, the component of the inferential cognition (*anvaya-bodha*) "the existence has wind as its agent" is not tenable;

nor is the component "having wind as its agent" [tenable], because when the agent is expressed by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*), there is an absence of the case-ending for the agent (*kartṛ-vibhakti*) following the other word (the object), which would be required to negate [the existence] having form as its agent.

Furthermore, as for the agent being the meaning of the verbal suffix, according to the rule that "the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) together express a single meaning, and among those two, the meaning of the suffix is primary," it is not possible for it to be subordinate to the action (*kriyā*).
For this very reason, even the portion consisting of the negation of existence is not tenable;
for it is not possible [in this way].

If that were the case, the meaning of the verb would connect with the meaning of the negative particle as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), whereas the meaning of the verb [as a whole] would assume a subordinate status (*upasarjanatā*) toward the meaning of the verbal root. Furthermore, if such a cognition were admitted, then even when it is said, "There is no color in the air," there would again be an expectation for another locus (*adhikaraṇa*).

To prevent that [undesired consequence], the statement "in all cases" (*sarvatra*) would also be necessary. Therefore, the form of the verbal cognition is not a negation of existence (sattā) having the wind-locus (vāyvadhikaraṇa) as its agent;

rather, just as in the case of "This wealth belongs to Caitra, not to Maitra," where there is a cognition of "wealth possessing the absence of Maitra’s ownership" through the connection of the meaning of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhyartha*), namely Maitra’s ownership, with the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), so too in cases such as "Color is in earth, not in wind," there is a relational cognition (*anvayabodha*) of "color possessing the absence of being located in wind and so forth," through the connection of the meaning of the locative case (*saptamyartha*), namely location (*ādheyatva*), with the meaning of the negative particle.
In this way, both the formal arrangement of speech and the arrangement of persons are correctly established within the context of positive concomitance (*anvaya*),

because it is accepted that even things such as jars possess the status of being the agent of action through their relationship with action, factors of action (*kāraka*), and agents (*kartṛ*). To explain:

Since it is impossible to negate jars and the like in their entirety, it is necessary to establish a specific locus; therefore, it is appropriate that the substratum (viśeṣya) be the nature of the self (*ātmatva*), characterized by the negation of being contained within that [locus], just as the nature of a jar or cloth is so characterized.
Nor should it be argued that, in this way, the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar would not be the object in the cognition "there is no jar on the ground.

It is simply not so in the case of verbal cognition; however, in perceptual cognition, when there exists a qualified objective reference (*viśeṣyatā*) connected with the sense organs, it certainly does become the object.

Let there be a distinct cognition—whether mental or otherwise—that has the same form as the verbal cognition and serves as the cause for the employment of words with that specific intention (*tātparya*); thus, there is no confusion whatsoever.

Alternatively, let there be a cognition in the case of a sentence such as "there is no color in air" which has the form of a negation of existence whose locus is air and whose agent is color; even though this serves as the cause for the employment of such a word, it may be a mental or other type of cognition having that very form.
Nevertheless, there is no rule that all perceptual cognitions must necessarily possess that same form.
For there is the possibility of other forms as well, which are witnessed by one’s own after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*) and obtained through the power of their respective causal complexes (*sāmagrī*).
Indeed, there is no rule that all such forms must be expressible by words,
because some forms are incapable of being expressed by words.
For example, the forms of cognitions such as the awareness of the voice or script of a son distinguished by a particular caste;

or, for instance, the form of a perceptual cognition having "the ground" as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and "a jar" as its qualifier (*prakāra*), which cannot be expressed by a word that produces a verbal cognition of the same form—
because the expression "the ground possessing the absence of a jar" brings about the cognition that "the ground is non-different from that which is related to the absence of a jar."

In this way, it is well known to those who understand the process of verbal cognition that even an expression such as "having the earth as its qualificandum and the jar as its qualifier" produces a cognition of a distinct form.
If one were to accept a cognition in the form "color is that which lacks the property of being located in air," then those who say "there is no color in air" would be refuted;

for since the meaning of the locative case itself would be construed as the counter-positive of the negative particle (*nañ*), there would be a lack of semantic competency (*sāmarthya*) with the following word, and thus a compound would not be applicable.
However, since the seventh case-ending (*saptamī*) is not a word ending in a nominal suffix (*subanta*), there is no possibility of a compound with it either.
For this very reason, there are many usages by Vyāsatīrtha, the author of the *Ṭīkā*.

Alternatively, let there be some obstacle in the case of "there is no color in the air" (*vāyau rūpaṃ nāsti*) due to its being understood as an absolute non-existence having something as its counter-correlate (*sat-pratiyogika-atyantābhāva*); however, in cases such as "this belongs to Caitra and not to Maitra," there is no such obstacle.
For even in that case, there is no case-ending denoting a *kāraka* (participant in an action), because the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) does not signify a *kāraka*.
Otherwise, even in the expression "the king's servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the meaning of the genitive would not be construed with the servant.
For this very reason, the third alternative is also untenable.

Furthermore, this being the case, there would be no dispute regarding the fact that in such statements as "Now the pot does not exist, but it will exist later," "Now you do not exist, but you will exist later," or "Now I exist, but I shall not exist later,"— as well as in "In this way, now the pot did not previously exist, you did not previously exist, I did not previously exist"— a cognition of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) relative to the pot arises. Yet, according to your own method of explanation, even that [cognition] would not be possible.

Even there, by hearing the case-ending of the agent (*kāraka-vibhakti*), one would perceive only the negation of the existence of a jar or similar object at a subsequent time, having that [subsequent time] as its locus;
