yet this is not the case, because it contradicts experience.

Furthermore, if the destruction of a jar and so forth were caused by the existence [of the agent], then even if there were no contradiction in speech due to the multiplicity of individual instances of destruction, prior non-existence, and so on, there would certainly be a contradiction with common experience (*puruṣavirodha*).
For in all cases, it would simply have to be "it will be" or "it was";
nor, in that case either, could the distinction between persons be established merely by the distinction of the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of the destruction and so forth.

In rules such as *yuṣmadyupapade samānādhikaraṇe*, "samānādhikaraṇya" (coreferentiality) is intended to mean simply the possession of that property which serves as the delimiting condition for the possibility of non-difference (*abheda*) between the agent (*kartṛ*) or other meanings of the verb and the word expressed by the first-person singular ending;
it should not be said to extend to the state of being qualified by non-difference (*abheda-anvaya-upahitatva*).
For if that were the case, the same [definition] would apply even to sentences such as *bhūtale ghaṭo nāsti* ("There is no pot on the ground").
And in this way, the forms of cognition such as "the absence of a jar exists on the ground" or "existence is the agent" also become consistently established;
for the rule governing linguistic expression shares the same security of status as the rule governing the person who speaks.
Furthermore, what would be the recourse in cases of expressions such as "air possesses the absence of color," or "in air there is the absence of color, which is colorless"?
For in those cases, the aforementioned objection does not apply:
because in the first instance, there is an absence of the locative case ending;
and in the latter, the word *puruṣa* is compounded with the negative particle (*nañ*) and so forth.
Nor should it be argued that even here the word "form" (*rūpa*) refers to the form of air;

for otherwise, since there is an absence of the form belonging to another [element], such a cognition or verbal expression would result in respect to earth and the other elements as well, as has already been stated.

This is because, by the force of grammatical convention (*vyutpatti*), the status of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) is understood as being delimited by the delimiting factor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedakāvacchinna*); thus, since the undesired consequence of such a cognition or verbal expression regarding earth and the others does not arise from this alone, it is futile to accept a figurative sense (*lakṣaṇā*).
The cognition of the absence of a specific difference is indeed intended.
Furthermore, in the case of "the jar is not the cloth," by construing it as "that which is not that," there is understood only the negation of the existence of the cloth having the jar as its agent;
it is not the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) of the cloth.

Nor should it be argued that because the word *paṭa* (cloth) lacks the case-ending of a kāraka-word, its meaning cannot be construed with the sense of the negative particle (*nañ*), and thus there is no cognition of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of cloth; for even in cases such as "there is no color in the air" (*vāyau rūpaṃ nāsti*), the word *rūpa* likewise lacks a kāraka-case-ending, and there is no obstacle to its meaning being construed with the negative particle. Thus, the two cases are equal. This is the general direction [of the argument]. Therefore, it is established that there is no objection whatsoever to describing the intended meaning in this manner.

And this being the case, the status of the Lord's defining characteristics (*bhagavallakṣaṇatā*)—namely, the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of defects such as dependence (*pāratantrya*) and so forth—is also properly established.

However, if absolute non-existence were to have only a non-entity (*tuccha*) as its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), then because such absences would be purely positive (*kevalānvayi*), it would be impossible for them to serve as defining characteristics of the Lord.
Or, even if in our system (*siddhānta*) absolute non-existence does indeed have only a non-entity as its counter-positive, there is no harm [to our position].
For instance: omniscience resides in Hara alone, while its absence resides in another;
likewise, non-omniscience resides in the individual soul (jīva) and so forth, while its absence resides in Hara alone.

Thus, the cognition that "cowness exists only in a cow" and "its absence exists only in what is other than that," and so forth, is established for all people, uncontradicted, and universally accepted.

However, that [cognition] cannot be resolved if omniscience, non-omniscience, cowness, and their absolute absences are either superimposed as being merely illusory (tuccha) with their respective counter-correlates, or if they have as their counter-correlates the relation of such illusory entities; for in those cases, due to the relation of "qualifier-of-absence" (abhāvīya-viśeṣaṇatā), these would be purely positive (kevalānvayi) properties, making resolution impossible.
This is because the absences of superimposed omniscience and the like exist even in Viṣṇu (Hari) and others.

Therefore, for those [properties], another relation is necessary to establish their negative concomitance (*vyatirekitā*). For example, even though the knowledge of God is a purely positive entity (*kevalānvayin*), a relation other than inherence (*samavāya*) is required to establish its negative concomitance through the relation of objecthood (*viṣayatā*).

Or, as in the view of the opponent, although the absolute absence of ether (*ākāśātyantābhāva*) is a purely positive entity, the relation of counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*) is required so that it may reside solely in ether by means of the relation that delimits its counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakasambandha*).

Furthermore, regarding that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), whether its state of having the superimposed cowness (*gotva*) residing in horses and so forth as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) has as its locus of the counter-correlate something distinct from and excluded from what resides solely in horses and so forth—or whatever else it may be—it must nonetheless have as its locus of the counter-correlate something distinct from and excluded from the cow; for without that, the aforementioned cognition could not be accounted for. On the other hand, if it has as its counter-correlate the relation whose counter-correlate is cowness and whose locus is horses and so forth, then its state of having the horse and so forth as the locus of the counter-correlate must likewise be something distinct from and excluded from the cow; for without that, the aforementioned cognition could not be accounted for. And thus, an essential relation residing solely in the individual soul (*jīva*) is necessary for the non-existence of omniscience.
The absence of non-omniscience resides solely in Īśvara,
and that [absence] is his very nature due to parsimony (*lāghava*).
Thus, the uncommon relation is the nature of mutual absolute non-existence, because it consists of that [nature].

Because, through that relation, absolute non-existence possesses the pervasion (vyāpti) as defined by its being a pervader; thus, it is logical that [the absence of defects] has the nature of mutual absolute non-existence and is pervaded by that [Lord Nṛhari].

In this way, even for the absolute non-existence of all defects, a relation residing solely in Nṛhari is necessary; therefore, its status as a definition (lakṣaṇa) is also appropriate through that relation.

In this way, since a relation of the absolute non-existence of color (rūpa) that resides solely in air and so forth—while being excluded from earth and the other elements—is necessary, color does not arise in air and the like because of its opposition to color through that very relation. Thus, although there is an absolute non-existence of the association with defects, it is designated as the "absolute non-existence of defects" because it is indirectly related to defects; therefore, nothing is untenable. If it is asked: "How is it accepted in the established doctrine (siddhānta), which lacks justification, that absolute non-existence has only a non-entity (tuccha) as its counter-positive (pratiyogin)? It is replied as follows:

The state of having a non-entity (tuccha) as its counter-correlative is established in every case by the force of the cognition "the horn of a hare does not exist," because the horn of a hare is a non-entity,
and its status as a counter-correlative is established by the force of that very cognition.
Nor should it be argued that the rabbit’s horn is not the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) there, but rather the horn alone— which is not a non-entity (*tuccha*)—
and that while the counter-positiveness residing in that horn is delimited by the "rabbit-ness" belonging to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*),
the absence grasped by this cognition is one whose counter-positiveness is delimited by that [rabbit-ness] and has the horn as its counter-positive.
If that were the case, the form of the cognition would be "this does not belong to the hare";

for it is impossible for the property of being a horn (*śṛṅgatva*)— which serves as the delimiting factor of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*)— to appear in the direction of the counter-correlative [the hare],
since such is not observed elsewhere.
Furthermore, it is because the spontaneous cessation of the cognition of a qualified counter-correlate (*viśiṣṭa-pratiyogitā*) cannot occur in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*).

Otherwise, even in a cognition such as "Devadatta, who possesses a staff, does not exist," the counter-correlate would be Devadatta alone, and "staff-possessor-ness" (*daṇḍitva*) would be its delimiting property (*avacchedaka*); thus, the qualified entity itself would not be the counter-correlate. Whether the qualified entity is identical to the staff and Devadatta or is something distinct is another matter.
If it is argued that the distinction lies in the fact that "existence" (*sattva*) is qualified there, whereas "non-existence" (*asat*) is not here, let it be so;
what does this matter?
If you say, "It is not the case that cognition cannot be the cause for the apprehension of non-existence," [we reply: no.
For even that which is non-existent can be apprehended through the appearance of a word and so forth;
otherwise, even for you, there would be no cognition of the counter-positive qualified by the delimiting property of counter-positiveness.
Now, it may be argued that the non-apprehension of the perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*) is the cause for the perception of absence.

And fitness (*yogyatā*) consists in the presence of all those factors that cause its apprehension—excluding those pervaded by it—and which constitute the conditions for the apprehension of an existent;
for if these are present, non-apprehension is impossible, and if they are absent, there is no fitness.
Thus, it is not the case that the absence qualified by a non-existent is perceptible. If this is argued, we say: no.
For even when perception is impossible, verbal cognition itself is possible.
Furthermore, regarding compatibility (*yogyatā*), one must state that its being distinct from defects (*doṣa*) alone constitutes the ground for censure;
otherwise, even the absence of a jar would not be perceptible.
Because the reasoning is equal.

Furthermore, in a case where there is the perception of the destruction of a conjunction caused by the destruction of its conjoined relatum, there is an absence of the non-apprehension of this [required] fitness (*yogyatā*).

It must be stated that the cause for the perception of absence is the non-apprehension of a counter-positive whose existence has been hypothetically projected by the undesirable consequence of the existence of that counter-positive.
And since that [non-apprehension] certainly exists here, there is nothing at all that is untenable.
As for the investigation into the non-apprehension of the capable (*yogyānupalabdhi*), it has already been conducted previously, and thus it is not elaborated upon here.
This has been explained in detail in the *Nyāyāmṛta* in the section titled "The Refutation of the Impossibility of the Theory of Non-apprehension" (*akhyātivādānyathā'nupapattibhaṅga*).

And in the refutation of the impossibility of being negated, it is thus established that absolute non-existence has a non-entity (*tuccha*) as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). If it is asked: "Even so, why does it have that alone as its counter-correlate?"
Listen:

there is a temporal contradiction between absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) whose counter-correlative is a non-entity (tuccha) and a temporal counter-correlative, just as there is a spatial contradiction.
Even in that case, the delimitor of temporal contradictoriness is not "the state of being a non-entity" (tucchābhāvatva), because that would be overly complex (gaurava).
However, for the sake of parsimony, it is simply the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvatva*).
And thus, there is no counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) at the time of absolute non-existence;

since absolute non-existence is beginningless and eternal, every moment of time is its locus. Consequently, once it is established that its counter-positive does not occur at any time whatsoever, it follows that its counter-positive is merely a non-entity (*tuccha*).

Alternatively, in your view, the contradiction of absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) in a given locus consists in the existence of the counter-positive—delimited by its own counter-positiveness-determinant (pratiyogitāvacchedaka)—in that locus at that specific place and time through its respective relation.

In this context, for the sake of parsimony (lāghava), one discards the portion delimited by the counter-positiveness-determinant and postulates merely the existence of the counter-positive as the contradictory factor; thus, the impossibility of absences delimited by distributed properties (vyāsajyavṛttidharma) and absences delimited by extrinsic properties (vyadhikaraṇadharma) is asserted.

Thus, for the sake of even greater parsimony (*lāghava*), we maintain that the mere existence of a counter-positive (*pratiyogi-sattva*) anywhere constitutes a contradiction with absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*); it is on this basis that we assert the impossibility of an absolute non-existence having an existent counter-positive. As for the cognition "cowness does not exist in a horse" and the like, it will find its object—just as the cognitions of absences qualified by a distributed property (*vyāsajyavṛtti-dharma*) or absences qualified by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa-dharma*) do—in a distinct category of absence.
And that distinct object is simply the absolute non-existence of the relation of cowness and so forth in the horse.
Nor should it be argued that such an explanation of the cognition is improper, as it would be in the case of sound.
In your view, this is because there is no other alternative, just as in cases such as the absence delimited by a property that exists distributively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*).

Otherwise, even now, on the strength of cognitions such as "the wealth does not exist [now], it will exist later," or "it existed previously," one would have to accept prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and posterior non-existence (*dhvaṃsābhāva*) as having present counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).

And if, in those cases, the objects were the prior non-existence and posterior non-existence of the relation of essential identity (*svarūpasaṃsarga*), then by parsimony (*lāghava*), the mere presence of the counter-correlate would suffice to oppose prior non-existence and posterior non-existence.

However, if one accepts that there is a contradiction when the counter-positive exists in that locus at that specific time through that specific relation—on the grounds of excessive complexity (gaurava)—then let the same logic be applied to the present case as well; this is the summary. Regarding the phrase "And not...": the meaning is that since the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is established by their respective adjuncts (upādhi)—namely, ignorance (avidyā) and māyā—the systematic arrangement of omniscience and non-omniscience is logically consistent. Regarding the phrase "In the case of a yogin...":

the meaning is that in the case of a counter-positive possessing an adventitious distinction, such as Saubhari and others, we do not observe both knowledge and ignorance regarding various objects simultaneously.
"And thus" (evañca): some explain this as meaning that once the substancehood (*dravyatva*) of the self is established by proving its status as the substratum of qualities.

However, in reality, the meaning is: "once it has been established that [the property of] residing in multiple [substrata] must necessarily have the same ontological status (*samānasattāka*) as the existence of the locus (*dharmin*), and that in that very case, the non-difference of individuals (*vyaktyabheda*) acts as a subverting factor. The phrase "and so forth" (*ityādīni*): by the word "etcetera," one should include such arguments as: "Selfhood (*ātmatva*) resides in multiple individuals, because it is a genus (*jāti*) residing in multiple individuals that possess a difference whose counter-correlate is its own locus and which has the same ontological status as its own locus, just like potness (*ghaṭatva*)."
The meaning is that [the distinctions] are well-established and culminate in ultimate, real distinctions between selves.

If a universal (*jāti*) were to reside in multiple individuals merely by virtue of having superimposed distinctions—as is the case with universals such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) or "self-ness" (*ātmatva*) in relation to other selves or other pots—then it would be logically possible for those universals to exist even without real, ultimate distinctions from other selves or pots; they would not be capable of establishing an ultimate distinction of that self from other selves, pots, and so forth.
Furthermore, if the identity of the individual is challenged as a flaw because it does not obstruct valid means of cognition such as perception, [then the following applies].

In that case, the fact that the selfhood established through inference would not establish a real (pāramārthika) difference in the self relative to another self as its counter-correlate (pratiyogin) could not be proven. However, if that [real difference] were established, then this [inferential selfhood] would be proven; such is the connection with the supporting argument (*upaṣṭambha*). Regarding the phrase "Caitra’s body": here, the reading is actually *maitraśarīrasvāmibhinnasvāmikam* ("having a master different from the master of Maitra’s body").

This is because an ancient marginal note states that the word "actually" (*vastutaḥ*) is used to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*) into account.

And since this [inference] is undertaken with the intention of proving the ultimate mutual difference between individual souls (*jīva*) against one who maintains the doctrine of many souls (*bahujīvavāda*), it cannot be argued that there is the fallacy of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) by the proponent of the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvavāda*) on the basis of conventional difference (*vyāvahārikabheda*), when this inference is being employed for the purpose of refuting that doctrine.

Because they accept either that there is only one body possessing a living soul while all other bodies are devoid of life like bodies seen in a dream; or, even if all bodies possess life, that there is only one living soul named Hiraṇyagarbha presiding over all bodies; for they do not admit even a conventional difference relative to another owner in the case of a single owner of bodies.

Therefore, in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking recourse to a merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*) difference, the term "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) is used here to mean "non-apparent."
For this very reason, in some manuscripts, a reading not containing that word (*vastutaḥ*) is observed.

In that case, one need not state "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking into account a merely apparent difference (*prātibhāsika-bheda*).

This is because words are capable only of presenting an object as qualified by a property that excludes the merely apparent, and thus there is no presentation at all of such a thing by means of a word like "difference" (*bheda*).
The intention is that otherwise, one would be forced to employ the formal argument: "In reality, the mountain possesses fire in reality.

[Now, an objection: Here, by the phrase "in reality," if one introduces either ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) or non-illusory appearance (*aprātibhāsikatva*) according to the previously mentioned differences in opinion, then—just as in the case of a real difference having Maitra’s body as its locus and its counter-correlate—the property to be proven (*sādhya*), which is the nature of the owner, would be unestablished due to the difference [from the subject].
This is because, since this [inference] has a positive entity as its probandum (*bhāvasādhyaka*), the unestablishment of the probandum must necessarily be considered a logical flaw (*doṣa*).

Nor should it be argued that what is intended here as the probandum (*sādhya*) is simply the absence of ownership by one who has attained identity with the body of Maitra in reality— that is, this is merely a negative inference (*vyatirekin*) where the probandum is an absence;
for if that were so, the qualification "in reality" would have to apply either to the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) or to the absence itself.
Not the first [alternative],
because since a qualified counter-positive is itself unestablished, it is impossible to apprehend the pervasion determined by it in the absence of the reason (*hetu*).

Even if one were to accept the establishment of the counter-positive here [in the reason], the fault of *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) remains unavoidable, whether the probandum in the form of that absence is considered to be of a conventional (*vyāvahārika*) or an illusory (*prātibhāsika*) nature.
Because this probandum, though established as having the body as its locus, cannot be ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), it is more appropriate that it be merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).

If one adopts the view that every absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is indeed ultimately real, then even if the term "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) were not mentioned within the category of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such an ultimate reality of the general absence of ownership belonging to a dreamer would still be established; thus, [the qualification] would be redundant in the category of the counter-correlate.
For in that system, only an ownership that is ultimately real in fact is admitted as established.

By this [argument], the objection is refuted: that if "ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatva*) is not included as a qualification for the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), then the absence of the general property of ownership would result in the falsity of such ownership and ultimate reality; since this would establish exactly what the opponent intends, there would be the fallacy of proving the already established (*arthāntaratā*). Therefore, its inclusion is necessary. However, if it were included in the counter-correlate, then because that [counter-correlate] is apprehended precisely as ultimately real, the conclusion would not be the falsity of that [ownership]. Even if the ultimate reality of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) is established, its having such an owner [remains unproven].
Furthermore, because the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) prevents the conclusion that [the world] is false;

and according to the view that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is necessarily characterized by having an unestablished object of negation (*aprāmāṇika-pratiyogitva*), it is impossible for the non-existence that constitutes the stated probandum (*sādhya*) to have an ultimately real object of negation (*pāramārthika-pratiyogitva*).

Nor is the second alternative mentioned previously tenable—that this qualification, "only as a non-entity in reality," is intended to avoid the charge of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

For let [the absence] be established by means of the absence of that property whose pervasion by the absence of the reason has been apprehended, specifically as the absence of that property delimited by that [particular] attribute; however, there is no basis for its establishment as being ultimately real (*pāramārthikatvena*). Otherwise, why should it not be established as being conventionally real (*vyāvahārikatvena*)?
Nor should it be argued that the general category of erroneous inference does not apprehend its own object as being ultimately real (*pāramārthikatvena*);
for if that were the case, the inclusion of the qualifier "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) would be entirely purposeless.
This is because, just like other inferences, this inference too could establish the ultimate reality of the aforementioned probandum by its own inherent power. [To this objection, we reply: No.

For this very reason, a reading not containing the word *vastutaḥ* is also seen in manuscripts; however, if that [word] were included, since it would be understood as having ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), it would not result in the conclusion of falsity (*mithyātva*).
Even if that [word] were present, this remains a probandum exactly as it is heard in the text, and is not a probandum for a fallacious argument (*abhāsa*).

In that context, the term "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) is meaningful for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking conventional objects of proof (*vyāvahārika-sādhya*) and so forth as the basis.
And this term connects with the difference between the owner of Maitra’s body.
Nor is there the fault of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇatā*).

This is because that very [position] is accepted by the Naiyāyikas themselves. Furthermore, its non-defectiveness within the Vedānta system has been demonstrated with great precision in the *Anuvyākhyāna* on the *Bhaktipāda* and in the *Sudhā*, through such passages as: "The defects of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and the unestablished nature of the probandum (*sādhyāsiddhi*) are indeed not defects for some, provided that pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists in some way."
The author of the *Advaitacandrikā* has also demonstrated in two or three places that the non-establishment (*aprasiddhi*) of the probandum (*sādhya*) is not a defect;

for at that time, by whatever means possible—such as through the words of the proponent—the mere presentation of the probandum allows for the apprehension of doubt regarding the probandum and the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), provided it is accompanied by favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) and so forth. Thus, while the work might proceed in some instances by adopting the method of the Naiyāyikas, there is no obstacle to its proceeding here by adopting the method of the pure proponent and respondent (*śuddhavādiprativādi*).

Furthermore, if you insist that even this text must be explained by resorting solely to the fault of "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), then the following would occur: first, after establishing "self-possessed-ness" (*sātmakatva*) in a general sense through such arguments as "nairātmya is the counter-positive of some non-existence residing in something, because it is an exclusive property (*vyatirekidharma*)," the negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*)—"the living body is self-possessed, because it possesses breath and so forth"—would then proceed.

Likewise, here too, the distinction between the body and its owner (the self) possesses both the property of being a mental modification (*cid-vṛtti*) and ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), because, while not being defined by anything non-ultimate, it is a mental modification—just like bliss, existence, and so forth, which reside in consciousness (*cit*). The phrase "while not being defined by anything non-ultimate" (*apāramārthikānirūpakakatve sati*) is included to exclude fallacies regarding purity and other qualities that reside in consciousness; for these [qualities], being of the nature of being unmixed with the insentient (*jaḍa*), lack the state of not being defined by anything non-ultimate.
Existence (*sattā*) also possesses the very nature of Brahman; therefore, it is not defined by space, and thus there is no lack of proof for the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Furthermore, even if that [existence] were such [as defined by space], bliss (*ānanda*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) can still serve as the illustrative examples.

The qualifying portion of the definition is included to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the sky, which—being non-substantial due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*svābhāva*) and so forth—is not ultimately real and cannot be definitively described.

Since even opponents accept that difference— which is imagined by the ignorant— is ultimately non-existent within consciousness (citi), there is no lack of establishment of the subject (*pakṣāsiddhi*).
Nor is there a lack of establishment of the reason (*hetvasiddhi*),
because it has been demonstrated that [the reason] resides in consciousness, which serves as the substantive (*viśeṣya*).

Because the term "owner" (*svāmin*) refers exclusively to a conscious entity characterized by reality (*tattva*), and because that [consciousness] exists as the ultimate reality, it also possesses the qualifying attribute of not being a non-ultimate non-apprehender. Thus, after the establishment—by means of the aforementioned inference—of a real difference having as its counter-correlative the owner of Maitra’s body, such consciousness itself is primarily established in Caitra’s body through the mark of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), by way of the relation of being the determiner of ownership (*svāmitā-nirūpakatva*), for the purpose of establishing the difference between individual souls in each respective body; therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.

Alternatively, it is established that the owner of Maitra’s body possesses, in relation to Caitra’s body, a state of ownership characterized by a difference whose counter-correlate is itself, through the relation of being the owner of a difference possessing the absence of both "having a counter-correlate that is ultimately real" and "having a counter-correlate that is not ultimately real.
And this relation of another jar to a jar owned by Maitra is well-known;

for, in the difference residing in Maitra (as its locus) which has another jar as its counter-correlate, there exists the absence of both [properties], necessitated by the absence of having an ultimately real counter-correlate.

By this connection, since the owner of Maitra’s body is the probandum, and because the absence of both [the owner and the difference] must be stated as being caused precisely by the absence of non-ultimate reality (*apāramārthikatva*) regarding that difference which constitutes the relation, the state of having an owner who possesses an ultimately real difference relative to the owner of Maitra’s body is established by the force of the aforementioned inference alone.

In the opponent's view, although it is admitted that the aforementioned relation stands in a relation of different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*) with respect to the aforementioned probandum, and that the absence delimited by that relation is *kevalānvayin* (universally present), yet—at the stage of the aforementioned investigation—since [the existence of such a relation] is doubted in all things other than Maitra’s body, the absence of that [relation] (or the absence of the reason) is established as being agreed upon by both the proponent and the opponent in Maitra’s body alone. Thus, even if there were a certain concomitance, there would be no real distinction between the two; for if that were so, there would follow undesirable consequences such as the mutual experience of pleasure and pain, supported by favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) of this kind.
Since the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established even by disregarding doubts regarding deviation (*vyabhicāra*),
there is not even a suspicion of the reason for inference being "unproven" (*aprayojaka*), precisely due to the force of the aforementioned reasoning (*tarka*).
Further details should be investigated through the exposition of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

The statement regarding the absence of an example based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) is due precisely to the absence of an investigation into the favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) already mentioned. Here, however, there is no contradiction between the preceding and the following, because the mention of a negative example (*vyatirekadṛṣṭānta*) is intended to establish an example by accepting that [reasoning]. Regarding the phrase "contrary to that" (*tadviruddha*): it means being the locus of an activity that is opposed to the production of the result to be accomplished by that action, within the delimitation of a single time; this constitutes "possessing an action contrary to that.
In the present context, Caitra and Maitra are to be understood as precisely those possessing such an activity, and thus there is no lack of proof (*asiddhi*).

The property of being a body (*śarīratva*) is included in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a pot belonging to Maitra, which possesses an action contrary to the action of friendship due to factors such as injury by wind.

When only that much [i.e., "possessing an action contrary to the action of friendship"] is stated, the qualifying portion [of the definition] is included to avoid deviation in the very body of Maitra himself.

Since all components of the qualifiers serve to establish the grasp of pervasion (*vyāpti*) by way of generating a favorable logical argument (*anukūlatarka*)—namely, that if there were a single owner, contradictory actions would not arise—there is no redundancy whatsoever.
Even because this [reason] is supported by such reasoning, the reason is not "inconclusive" (*aprayojaka*).

As for the objection raised here—that there is an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because Indra and Arjuna, who simultaneously engaged in the contradictory acts of burning and extinguishing the Khāṇḍava forest, were nonetheless under a single master—that is not so.
For the aforementioned inference, which is based on a negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) involving the reason and the probandum at hand, no such deviation is possible.

Since an inference based on a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*)—namely, that "whatever body exhibits activity contrary to the activity of its own [usual] body belongs to a master different from its [usual] master" does not fail to function, the objection regarding a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) within that general pervasion is ineffective.
Nor should it be argued: "If this is so, how can the difference between the living selves (*jīva*) of the bodies of Ḍittha and Viṣṇumitra be established?

For even in that case, once that difference is established by such a negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*), its establishment becomes possible through a positive inference (*anvayyanumāna*) using those very cases as examples.
One might object: "In that case, it must be said that the reason stated by means of the example of the bodies of Arjuna and others is indeed inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). [We reply:
No, because two favorable logical arguments (*anukūlatarka*) have been stated.

Among them, in the case of two things sharing a single master, even if contradictory movements occasionally arise due to the power of a specific cause in the form of the Lord’s will—which produces efforts conducive to those opposing actions—it would be impossible to account for this elsewhere without the condition of having different masters.

This is because it has been stated that this pervasion (*vyāpti*), being general (*autsargika*), can only be set aside by a powerful subverting factor (*balavad-bādhaka*); thus, a deviation based on an adventitious condition (*sopādhika-vyabhicāra*) does not constitute a flaw.
Otherwise, since sacrificial violence (*yāgīya-hiṃsā*) does not produce sin, it would be impossible for the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*) itself to possess the capacity to produce sin.

If it is argued that the qualification "being distinct from sacrificial violence" (*yāgīyahiṃsābhinnatva*) must be supplied there [in the general rule], then here too, by supplying the qualification "being known to be dependent on specific causes such as the power of the Lord (*bhagavat-śakti*), which generates the effort that produces contradictory actions in a single instance," the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*) and so forth can indeed be established.

As for the specific pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*), it is employed for the sake of ease, since the general pervasion cannot be demonstrated at any time when the absence of proof for distinct ownership has not been established; enough of this.

To this extent, relying on the fact that difference (*bheda*) subsists collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), he presents an inference having "the two" delimited by duality as its subject (*pakṣa*) in order to establish it: "The individual soul and the Lord... [jīveśau]. Since the difference is established between the individual soul and the Lord, it is possible to take the pair as the subject by means of their duality. Furthermore, there is no room for the objection that this would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because a single difference is not established by way of the delimitation of duality.

The establishment of that [difference] occurs by virtue of duality being the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), just as in the case of the inference: "A jar delimited by the second moment possesses odor.

Here, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is as follows: whatever two things are substrata of mutually contradictory properties, those two possess a difference in their mutual relation as delimited by the duality residing in themselves. This establishment [of difference] is necessitated precisely by the fact that the aforementioned knowledge of pervasion generates an inferential cognition of difference only as delimited by duality.

By this [argument], namely that "establishment occurs by virtue of being the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of the subjecthood (*pakṣatā*)," it follows that the manifestation of that [delimiting condition] is not the delimitor of the effect-ness of the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*).
If that were the case, there would be the generation of an inference of difference even with respect to what is merely characterized (*upalakṣita*) by the aforementioned duality.

This is because, when there is a sublation (*bādha*) regarding a qualified jar, an inference is observed to arise through the force of the inferential consideration present in that instance with respect to a jar characterized by its time of production.

In that case, if you accept this [consequence], then in the inference "Caitra and Maitra possess the exclusion of Caitra" (*caitramaitrau caitrabhedavantau*), such an inference would occur with respect to that which is merely indicated (*upalakṣita*) by duality at the time when there is a grasping of a sublation (*bādhagrahaṇa*) regarding that very duality.
Yet, an inference of that specific form is not established by experience for anyone.
Likewise, there is no room for the suspicion that someone might have inferred, "That same principle (*nyāya*) applies here as well."

Because in the state of the aforementioned knowledge, there exists precisely the capacity to produce an inference. "Like the consensus" (sammatavat) means "possessing both water and fire. There is no room for the suspicion that the probandum is absent in the example, because by the phrase "like the consensus," it is indicated that the inference proceeds precisely at the stage when there is a disagreement regarding the difference between the individual soul and the Lord, having already accepted their difference as delimited by duality elsewhere. "Characterized by the relationship of the slayer and the slain" means either being of the nature of mutual non-existence or being pervaded by mutual absence.
Furthermore, even by one who maintains the doctrine of non-duality (*ekatva*), this must be accepted based on worldly convention;
otherwise, if all boundaries were transgressed, the very status of being a speaker would be untenable—this is the intended meaning.

Although in the final system (*siddhānta*) there is a necessity for the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of absence to be established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), it has been demonstrated previously (in the *Dvaitadyumaṇi*) how this [non-dual position] is nonetheless consistent with that requirement.
[Objection: But surely there is an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), since duality exists even in a single object when two contradictory properties are superimposed upon it.

To avoid this, if one qualifies the reason (*hetu*) by adding "having the same level of reality as the substrate" (*dharmisattāsamānasattākatva*), then the opponent would incur the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*).

[Reply: This is not so, because there is no such defect if one accepts as the qualification of the reason the absence of "phenomenality" (*prātibhāsikatva*), which consists in the absence of being an effect of ignorance that is merely adventitious (*pallavājñāna*).

Furthermore, in my view, since the ignorance of a sprout is not established, there can be no possibility of a deviation (vyabhicāra). This is because the absence whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is constituted by that [ignorance] would have a real entity as its counter-correlate; thus, even if two contradictory properties were superimposed, they would not exist [therein], and since the state of possessing those [properties] is absent in anything at all, no deviation can arise—this is how it should be understood.

Alternatively, even under the view that this difference (*bheda*) is a property residing in multiple substrates (*avyāsajyavṛtti*), since the inference having Brahman as its subject and the inference having the individual soul (*jīva*) as its subject were previously stated separately for the purpose of establishing their mutual ultimate difference, [the author] now says "from the individual soul and the Lord" (*jīveśāt*) in order to establish that [difference] by means of a single [inference]. Here, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of the probans (*sādhana*) through the delimitation of duality (*dvitva*) consists in establishing it by way of being its pervader (*vyāpakatva*).
This is because, in that position, the status of being a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) in the form of an essential relation (*svarūpasambandha*) is indeed sublated.

It should be understood that pervasion (vyāpakatā) exists even for two individual occurrences that are mutually distinct, precisely in the form of the delimitor of the probandum (sādhyatāvacchedaka)—namely, the state of possessing a difference where each is the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) of the other and each is the substratum (anuyogin) of the other—just as it does in other inferences.

Since it has been established in the *Dvaitadyumaṇi* that the status of being the locus of conjunction and its absence is accepted only through a distinction of parts—such that there is only the existence of conjunction in the substratum in the form of a tree, and not the existence of the absence of conjunction there as well—the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not violated by taking both of those [conjunction and its absence] together. Regarding the phrase "not...": "by means of a mere limiting adjunct" (*upādhimātreṇa*) means "by way of a medium that brings about difference," and so forth. "Its counter-positive" (*tatpratiyoginī*) means "the absence of that [conjunction] in the counter-positive of the limiting adjunct.
"Because that is not seen" means "because the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the limiting adjunct is not observed."
It might be capable of establishing a contradiction between two things— even while they reside in a single locus— by means of producing a distinction in their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
if it were possible for something to possess its own absence within itself, and for both [the thing] and its own absence to coexist in one and the same place.
But this is not the case.

The space delimited by a jar is not designated as "mere space" because it does not adopt a distinction between the states of being occupied by the jar and not being occupied by the jar; for such a designation occurs only when the limiting adjunct (upādhi) is absent.
There is no conjunction of the jar with space [in general], because there is no cognition that "there is no conjunction of the jar with the space delimited by the jar."

However, since space in its internal state is natural (*svābhāvika*), it cannot be produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); therefore, one is unable to establish either the coexistence in a single locus of what is not-self and what is self-nature, or their mutual contradiction.

The intention [of the objection] is: according to the maxim that "one who has not descended himself," how could he establish an arrangement elsewhere? Regarding the reading "merely by the difference produced by limiting adjuncts" (*upādhikṛtabhedamātreṇa*), the meaning is as follows: since omniscience and limited knowledge—which you accept as being the counter-correlates to that [difference]—are not observed to possess the nature of being counter-correlates to a difference that has as its own counter-correlate and relatum something produced by limiting adjuncts, [the difference] must be the cause of the difference produced by limiting adjuncts.

In the reading *tadvati yoginī*, the meaning is that in the case of a yogin such as Saubhari, who possesses distinctions based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*), one does not observe both omniscience and limited knowledge [simultaneously].
The phrase "if this is so" (*evam ca*) means: once the first inference has been established according to the aforementioned method.

The term "having the same level of reality as the existence of the subject" (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*) is included in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by way of a non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*) distinction.
By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), there is an inclusion of such arguments as "pleasure resides in multiple individuals because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*).
To suggest that the word "and so forth" includes the argument "selfhood resides in multiple individuals because it is a universal" (*jātitvāt*) is weak;
for that very point has already been established by this extensive discussion.

And because, due to its being the primary [subject], it is appropriate to state that very [property] explicitly. Regarding the term "susthāni" (well-established): since the existence of *dravyatva* (substantiality) in the self (*ātman*) has been established by the aforementioned method, there is no room for the previously mentioned fallacy of unestablished reason (*asiddhi*). Furthermore, by introducing the condition that [the property] must have the same ontological status as the existence of the locus (*dharmisattāsamānasattākatva*) when there is a difference [between the property and the locus], there is no room for the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is the intended meaning. If it is asked, "In that case, how is the previously mentioned defect avoided in the inference where pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth are the subject (*pakṣa*)?", the answer is as follows:
Since there is no sublation to the acceptance of pleasure and the like as persisting as long as the substance exists within the self (*ātman*),
and because, being perceptible, it is impossible for them to be qualities of the mind (*manas*) which lacks the dimension of magnitude (*mahattva*) that is the cause of perception;
it is inferred that pleasure resides in multiple entities distinct from the mind, because it is a quality, like color (*rūpa*).
And thus, there is no proving of what is already established; nor is there a deviation from one's own tenets,
because this formulation follows the method of the logicians (tārkika).
Alternatively, there is no fault because the relation of either being the substratum (*āśrayatva*) or being the synthesizer (*anusandhātṛtva*) is included within the probandum (*sādhya*).

Since it is logically impossible for a mental modification (*manovṛtti*) to have a substratum other than the mind, the probandum is ultimately established by [the subject] having a synthesizer other than the mind; thus, the intended object is proven.
This meaning is already obtained by the very passage beginning with "of duality and so forth" (*dvitvādīnām*), and therefore it is not stated separately.

[Objection: But since the previously mentioned defects have not been avoided in the inference beginning with "Caitra’s body," how can this [inference] be well-established? To this, he says: "Caitra’s body... [and so on]. According to the stated method, the qualification "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) is added as a distinction for the sake of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Its meaning is: "having an existence equal to that of the locus (*dharmin*).
This is the intended sense (*bhāva*).

The state of performing an action contrary to that [intention] consists in possessing an action produced by an effort that is not perceived by one who perceives the effort producing that [intended] action;
therefore, there is no aforementioned deviation,
because actions produced by effort are absent in things such as jars.
And it is for this very purpose that the term "activity" (ceṣṭā) is employed.
Nor should it be argued that, in such a case, things like a jar cannot serve as an example;
for by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka), the body of Maitra himself can indeed serve as the example.
As for the claim that "possessing contrary activity" means possessing an action that obstructs the effects of that [intended] action,
and that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of jars and the like because the reason is qualified by "being a body"—
that is not correct.
Because there is an inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as the burning of the Khandava forest, where Indra and Arjuna performed contradictory actions despite being under a single master;

nor should it be argued that there is no fault because of the qualification "provided there is an absence of a single acknowledged ownership for both," for such a qualification is both redundant and irrelevant to the proof.

To ward off the aforementioned defects in the argument—"The two subjects of dispute are distinct, because they are the substrata of contradictory properties, like fire and snow"—the author states the intended meaning: "The individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). Now, one might object that the reason—"being the substratum of contradictory properties"—is unestablished (*asiddhi*), since, according to the Māyā-vāda view, the properties of the individual soul and the Lord reside in a single substratum. To dispel this doubt, he clarifies the nature of contradiction: "And contradiction... Contradiction is the rule of non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna-niyama*), which consists in not residing in the same substratum (*parasparādhikaraṇāvṛttitva*).
And the relationship between the executioner and the one to be executed is not of the nature of a destroyer and the destroyed;
for that [relationship] is absent in cases such as omniscience and non-omniscience.
Rather, it is stated "as in the case of permanence and impermanence" in order to indicate that it is of the nature of existence and non-existence.

Now, if it is asked: "In the Siddhānta, since there is a rule that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) must have an unreal (*aprāmāṇika*) counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), how can non-omniscience be of the nature of the absolute non-existence of omniscience residing in God? Or how can omniscience be of the nature of the absolute non-existence of non-omniscience residing in the individual soul (*jīva*)?"—the answer is as follows: Non-omniscience is simply the absolute non-existence of omniscience, which has as its counter-correlate the omniscience superimposed upon the individual soul. And this [non-existence], according to other systems, is opposed by the counter-correlate itself; however, in our own system (Siddhānta), it is opposed by the primary reality (*pradhāna*).
Because it is not perceived that omniscience is absent in the Lord who possesses omniscience;

rather, the designation of "counter-correlate" (pratiyogitva) regarding the omniscience residing in the Lord is used precisely because that omniscience is the primary factor relative to non-omniscience.
Thus, non-omniscience is the negation of identity with omniscience.
And since identity with omniscience is simply omniscience itself, non-omniscience has that [omniscience] as its counter-correlate;
for it is established that mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) has a real entity as its counter-correlate,
and the absence of that [non-omniscience] is indeed omniscience itself.

This is because it is established by valid means of knowledge that only an absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) distinct from positive existence can have a negatum (pratiyogin) that is itself a real entity;
as the saying goes: "The negation of a negation must necessarily result in a positive existence.
Further details should be sought elsewhere.
Regarding the term "omniscience" (*sarvajñatva*): Now, what is this omniscience?
It cannot, first of all, consist in possessing knowledge whose objects are all things;
for, in a general sense, knowledge having all things as its object—such as [the knowledge that] "everything is knowable" (*meyatva*) and so forth—is common to all individual souls (*jīva*).
Nor does it consist in possessing a cognition whose objects are all things in their respective individual capacities (*tattadvyaktitvena*);
for this would result in being difficult to know for non-omniscient beings and others, since they lack a cognition specifically directed toward that many objects.
It is said in reply:
Omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) is the state of possessing a cognition that is not the locus of an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of subject-objecthood (*viṣayitā*).

Even though a cognition may have all things as its objects in the sense of being an object of knowledge (*meyatvena*), there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) because, since a pot does not appear under the aspect of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvena*) in such a cognition, there exists only an absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by "pot-ness" and delimited by the relation of subject-objecthood.
Furthermore, this omniscience is not difficult to ascertain, for even one who is not omniscient can possess the cognition of such omniscience.
By the phrase "and so forth," [the author] includes independence (*svātantrya*), non-independence (*asvātantrya*), and the like.
An objection is raised: "The reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*);

for even in the absence of a difference possessing the same ontological status (*sattā*) as the substrate (*dharmin*), the possession of contradictory attributes can be established by means of a difference possessing a lower ontological status. To dispel this doubt, he says: "Not so" (*na ca*). The meaning is that the possession of the aforementioned contradictory attributes by the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is established solely through the difference created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as ignorance (*avidyā*).

The *yoginī* possesses various bodies acquired through yoga. "Because that [difference] is not observed" means because the possession of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmavattva) in the manner described is not observed.

Thus, the sense is that if the difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*) were to necessitate the possession of contradictory properties, then that same consequence would apply to the *yogin* as well.
Previously, it was specifically refuted that the distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*) could serve as the basis for both the experience of suffering and its absence.
Now, however, it is refuted in a general sense that it can serve as the basis for two mutually contradictory attributes; thus, there is no tautology.

Now, he rescues the inferences that were previously rejected by the opponent: "If this is so," etc. This means: provided that the self's status as a substance (*dravyatva*) and the status of *ātmatva* as a universal (*jāti*) have been established.
The meaning is that [the reason] is not unestablished (*asiddhi*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), one includes such inferences as "selfhood (*ātmatva*) resides in multiple individuals because it is a genus (*jāti*)," and so forth.
Anticipating the objection regarding the defects mentioned in the inference where Caitra’s body is the subject (*pakṣa*), he says: "Caitra’s body... This has already been explained above.
The phrase "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) is used to exclude the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Here, the intention is that even if the word "body" (*śarīra*) is inserted into the reason (*hetu*) to avoid the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) found in the case of a jar and a cloth owned by the same master, there is no lack of a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭāntāsiddhi*). Avoiding the defect mentioned regarding the inference whose subject (*pakṣa*) is the matter under dispute, he says: "The individual soul and the Lord" (*jīveśau*). Since the proof establishes a difference possessing the same ontological status as the substrate itself (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*), there is no fault of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) when proving an ultimately real difference (*pāramārthikabheda*).
The sense is that there is no room for the objection that proving a conventional distinction would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

As in the case of fire and snow [cited by] Sammita. Refuting the undesired position, he states the accepted position: "contradiction" (*virodha*). Regarding "the rule of non-coexistence" (*sahānavasthānaniyama*): the meaning is that it consists in the necessary absence of coexistence in a single location.

Why is this? To this he says: "of those who maintain [the doctrine of] unity. The meaning is that, according to their view, since the selves are one, if contradictory properties were to exist, they would necessarily reside in a single locus; thus, because it is impossible for them not to reside in one place, the essential nature [of the distinction between the properties] would be unestablished (*svarūpāsiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "killer and the killed": [one might object] that according to the maxim, "that which has not yet arisen does not kill another, nor does that which lacks a substratum," we observe in the world that scorpions and the like become killers of their mothers and others through their own birth, and that soldiers and the like become killers when they have taken their positions on the battlefield.

In this regard, since the relationship between the slayer and the slain—such as omniscience and so forth, which will be discussed later—cannot exist within a single birth due to the absence of another life, it must be asserted that they share a single locus, just as pots and other objects do. Furthermore, since that [shared locus] requires the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), who are its substrates, how can difference be established on the basis of being the locus of contradictory attributes characterized by the opposition of the slayer and the slain? If this is asked, we say no; for here, by means of *jahallakṣaṇā* (exclusive indication), the term "the state of being slayer and slain" is intended to signify their nature as mutual exclusions (*parasparaviraharūpatva*).
This is because the aforementioned attributes such as omniscience and so forth are likewise of that same nature.

Furthermore, it is our shared view that there is no co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and its absolute non-existence (*tadatyantābhāva*); thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the locus of that [conjunction].

For this very reason, he cites such a property qualified by contradiction as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the phrase "eternity" (*nityatva*), since pleasure, pain, and so forth lack the aforementioned qualification by contradiction, he states—anticipating the question of what such contradictory properties are—"such" (*tādṛśa*). This refers to the establishment of those contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmavyavasthā*).

And thus, since a difference co-existent with the existence of the subject (*dharmin*) is not established, the sense is that there is the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*). Regarding the term "yoginī": although a difference produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as the body and internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), exists among yogins, the distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth—which are contradictory attributes—is not observed; therefore, the establishment of that distinction cannot be accounted for by the mere difference of limiting adjuncts.

Likewise, Devadatta’s internal organ is, in reality, a limiter of consciousness distinct from the consciousness limited by Yajñadatta’s internal organ, because it is that which brings about the cessation of what is not brought about by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the latter. This is by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), like Yajñadatta’s internal organ.
Thus, Devadatta’s memory is not, in reality, Yajñadatta’s, because it is not produced by Yajñadatta’s experience;
one should infer similar arguments establishing their difference, such as the counter-example of Yajñadatta’s own memory.
Nor is there a lack of proof (asiddhi).
Because Yajñadatta does not experience the memory of what was experienced by Devadatta,

and because the impossibility of the systematic distribution of pleasure, pain, and so forth— given the natural non-difference of selves— is a subverting argument, as we have demonstrated in the *Mandāramañjarī*, it should be observed there.

Having thus stated the inference regarding the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), he now states the inferences regarding the mutual difference between individual souls as well: "In the same way, Devadatta’s internal organ... The meaning is that consciousness, which is in reality different from [the individual], is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of that [consciousness].
Because the word *bhinna* (different) is eternally dependent [on another term], it forms a compound.

"Because it possesses a vṛtti that removes what cannot be removed by other vṛttis. This means: because it possesses a vṛtti that removes that ignorance which cannot be removed by the knowledge consisting of a vṛtti of Yajñadatta’s internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Likewise, regarding "Devadatta’s memory": if the non-difference between Devadatta and Yajñadatta were ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), then even though Devadatta’s memory is conventionally (*vyavahārataḥ*) not Yajñadatta’s, it would indeed be possible for it to be Yajñadatta’s in reality (*vastutaḥ*).
Therefore, the term "in reality" is used to exclude that possibility. The intention is that by this, the actual difference between Devadatta and Yajñadatta is established.

Anticipating the objection that since Devadatta and Yajñadatta are in reality one, the memory belonging to Devadatta might simply be produced by the experience of Yajñadatta, the author refutes this with the words: "Nor is [the reason] unestablished. An objection is raised: "But the fact that Devadatta’s memory is produced by Yajñadatta’s experience is compatible even with their empirical difference; therefore, it does not contradict their natural oneness. To this, he replies: "And of selves... [The reference is] to the *Mandāramañjarī*: specifically, at the occasion of explaining the commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the root text which begins, "The experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth is observed to be due to identity of nature or else due to difference."

"Because it is that which removes what is not removed by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of that [person]" means: because it removes the ignorance that veils the object and whose prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) cannot be removed by the mental modification of Yajñadatta.
Nor is there a lack of proof for the qualification;

for when knowledge arises in Yajñadatta, the ignorance residing in Devadatta is not removed. "In reality, it does not belong to Yajñadatta" means that the phrase "it does not belong to Yajñadatta" is intended in the sense of "in reality."

By this, the objection that for one who asserts the falsity of everything, the property of "belonging to Yajñadatta" is also unreal—and thus the argument commits the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*)—is refuted.
The phrase "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) is used to exclude the charge of *siddhasādhanatā* based on the conventional absence of belonging to Yajñadatta. Regarding the phrase "and so forth":
Devadatta’s desire does not, in reality, belong to Yajñadatta, because it is not produced by the knowledge of that [Yajñadatta].
And because it does not cease upon the enjoyment of that [result]:
the killing of a Brahmin committed by Devadatta does not, in reality, belong to Yajñadatta;
for it does not cease upon his seeing the Setu bridge, and so forth—this should be inferred accordingly.
Because there is no subverting argument against the contrary position, these reasons are non-conclusive; therefore, he says: "of selves" and "in the *Mandāramañjarī*. To explain:
if selves were not distinct, then there would be a mutual recollection of each other's pleasure and so forth.
Nor can this be accounted for by the difference of bodies.
Nevertheless, it is perceived by yogis;
yet even in its absence, it is not perceived by those situated in the mother's womb or within the bodies of Rāvaṇa and others.
Nor can this be accounted for by a difference in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
This is because [the state of] *yoginī* has been established for that [consciousness] as well;

for even in the case of a single person who sleeps day after day, the dissolution of the cause is accepted. Consequently, there would be no recollection on a subsequent day of what was experienced on a previous day.
Nor is it untenable for there to be a distinction between instances of ignorance;
for if the liberated one possessed an ignorance distinct from the ignorance of transmigratory existence, it would follow that he would experience its suffering and so forth.
Furthermore, the unity of ignorance is not the necessary factor for such experience.
[Otherwise] there would be the consequence that even for one who is liberated, there would be an absence of the experience of one's own bliss.

Thus, "Devadatta’s internal organ" (devadattāntaḥkaraṇam) [is used]. It is "the delimiting factor of a distinct consciousness" (bhinnacaitanyāvacchedakam). The compound should be understood as being formed due to its constant requirement of a correlative (nityasāpekṣatvāt). "Because it possesses a function that removes what cannot be removed by the functions of that [internal organ]" (tadvṛttyanivartyanivartakatvāt); the meaning is: because it possesses a function that removes ignorance, doubt, error, and so forth, which are not removed by the functions of that [internal organ]. Thus, "Devadatta" [is mentioned]. "In reality distinct" (vastuto bhinna); when this is employed against a proponent of the doctrine of a single soul (ekajīvavādin), the meaning of "in reality" (vastutaḥ) is precisely "not merely illusory" (aprātibhāsika).

In that view, even though the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is not the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), it is possible for even a single [soul] to be delimited by various internal organs which are transformations of that one Great Illusion (*mahāvidyā*), since they share the same Great Illusion as their adjunct.
However, against the proponent of the doctrine of many souls (*bahujīvavādin*), the phrase "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*) already means "from the perspective of ultimate truth" (*paramārthataḥ*).
Alternatively, for the sake of establishing the subject matter, even in the case of the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīvapakṣa*), the meaning may simply be "from the perspective of ultimate truth."

The method for resolving the objection regarding the unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) should be understood according to the sequence set forth in the commentary on the inference beginning with "the body of Caitra" (*caitraśarīram*). Regarding the phrase "subsisting therein" (*tadvṛtti*):
this refers to cognitions such as the absence of a jar, which take the form of a mental modification (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) belonging to Yajñadatta.

The meaning is that [this cognition] acts as the remover of doubts and errors concerning a cloth—doubts and errors which are not removed by that [prior cognition of the jar's absence]—by way of producing the cognition of the cloth.

In the reading "because it follows the non-cessation of their activity," the meaning is: because [the self] produces happiness and so forth—which cannot be produced by those activities such as the perception of objects like garlands and sandalwood—by means of enjoying other objects.
"Not belonging to Yajñadatta in reality" means possessing an ultimate absence (pāramārthika-abhāva) whose counter-positive (pratiyogin) is the state of belonging to Yajñadatta.

Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), for the proponent of falsity (*mithyātvavādin*) accepts an ultimate absence of that [state of belonging to Yajñadatta], even while that state exists, in order to establish falsity.

Even if one does not include "ultimate reality" (*pāramārthika*) in the formulation, there is still the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because that very non-difference [of the self] is admitted.
Furthermore, even in the case of the memory of Yajñadatta, there is a lack of negative concomitance (*vyatirekāsiddhi*), since the ultimate absence of belonging to Yajñadatta exists [in that memory].

Even if the probandum (*sādhya*) is defined as that [absence] qualified by the non-co-referentiality with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*), it remains nothing but the fallacy of proving what is already established.

It should not be argued that, upon the recollection of Devadatta, an ultimate absence whose counter-positive is the state of belonging to Yajñadatta is admitted as existing in exactly that same [body].

For "not actually belonging to Yajñadatta" means: "possessing a lack of ownership by consciousness characterized by non-enjoyment delimited by Yajñadatta’s physical body. And such ownership by consciousness, as qualified by those [attributes], is admitted even by the opponent in the case of the recollection of Devadatta.
Otherwise, the term "identity-in-difference" (*anyathā-aikya*) would result in being merely technical (*pāribhāṣika*).

Thus, since that [identity]—as delimited by the non-co-referentiality with the counter-positive (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*)—is the probandum (*sādhya*), one should observe that there is no such thing as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) and so forth, nor is there a lack of proof for the negative concomitance (*vyatirekā-siddhi*). Regarding the phrase "and so forth": this means [inferences] whose subjects (*pakṣa*) are Devadatta’s pleasure and so on. Regarding the word "should be observed": the sense is that, because it is supported by favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*), there is no lack of a proving factor (*aprayojakatā*).

He states another inference that establishes the mutual difference between living beings with the words "In this way" (*evam*). Here, the probandum (*sādhya*) is specifically qualified by a difference whose ontological status (*sattā*) is equal to that of the locus (*dharmin*), which is the consciousness delimited by Yajñadatta’s internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

The inclusion of the term "delimiting factor of consciousness" (*caitanyāvacchedaka-pada*) is for the purpose of securing the relation of being a delimiting factor—defined as having its occurrence within the sphere of what is experienced by the consciousness—as a property of that which is determined by consciousness.
Therefore, there is no lack of establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*).
Because a jar or the like, as qualified by such a distinction, is well-established;

and because it is impossible for that [distinction] to subsist in it through the aforementioned relation, the conclusion of the probandum (sādhya) is reached only by taking its status as a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of consciousness, whereby the intended object is established. "Because it is the producer of a function that removes what is not removed by functions of that [consciousness]" means: because it initiates a function that removes that ignorance (*ajñāna*) and so forth which is not removable by the knowledge consisting of the internal organ-function (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) of Yajñadatta. "Devadatta’s memory" refers to... [the end of the passage].

The meaning is as follows: the recollection having Devadatta as its agent is distinct from any recollection whose agent stands in a relation of real identity with Yajñadatta; this is because it is not produced by an experience whose agent is Yajñadatta.

Although in this context a jar or similar object could serve as a positive example (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*), nevertheless, because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) is easily grasped through the fact that Yajñadatta’s own recollection is produced by his own experience, that [negative example] is followed here.

And here, the distinction between Devadatta and Yajñadatta is established by way of their respective fruits. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of such arguments as: "Devadatta’s experience is not, in reality, Yajñadatta’s, because it does not produce recollection in Yajñadatta, unlike the case of Yajñadatta’s own experience. One might raise the objection that this reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*) because Devadatta’s recollection is actually produced by Yajñadatta’s experience; he dispels this doubt with the words "na ca" ("nor..."). Nor should it be said that, according to the Māyāvāda view, the unestablished nature of the reason is unavoidable, since Devadatta’s experience itself would belong to Yajñadatta.

Even though there is no difference in pure consciousness (*caitanya-mātra*), for you [the opponent], the state of "belonging to that" (i.e., being the experience of a specific person) is impossible due to the difference between individual qualified entities (*viśiṣṭa-bheda*).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of Yajñadatta remembering what was experienced by Devadatta.

He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position in the aforementioned inferences: "of the selves" (*ātmanām*). This refers to the impossibility of the established order of pleasure and pain, and the impossibility of the restrictive rule that "that pleasure is experienced by that very person alone," and so forth.
The meaning is that it would follow that Caitra and others would experience the pleasure and so forth of Maitra and others.
Now, one might object: if the distinction between pleasure and so forth were ultimately real, then it would depend upon an intrinsic difference [between individuals];
but this is not the case.
It is stated that this has been established in the *Mandāramañjarī* in order to dispel the doubt that [the distinction] is merely conceptual (*kālpanika*).
For instance:
does a conceptual arrangement not depend upon anything at all that establishes it?
Or is it ultimately real?

In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence that the postulation of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth would be useless for the sake of establishing the conventional status of the individual soul (*jīva*) and other such entities as being merely conceptual.
In the second case, even a conceptual regulator cannot be logically established without an intrinsic difference (*svābhāvika-bheda*); these and other points should be examined therein.

He states the inferences that establish the mutual difference between living beings with the words "In this way" (*evam*). Here, when the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of Yajñadatta is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for a consciousness distinct from the consciousness delimited by the internal organ of Devadatta, the difference between Yajñadatta and Devadatta is established. [He says] "Devadatta."

The meaning is as follows: the consciousness delimited by Yajñadatta’s internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the limited consciousness that is Yajñadatta-consciousness; the consciousness of Devadatta, which is in reality distinct from that, is its delimiting factor—that is, its defining boundary. Regarding the phrase "by its modification" (*tadvṛtti*): it means because [the knowledge] removes that ignorance of Devadatta which cannot be removed by the knowledge consisting of a modification of Yajñadatta’s internal organ. "Like Yajñadatta’s internal organ" [is the comparison].

In that case, there exists the state of being the delimitor of the consciousness delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) of Yajñadatta, which is of the nature of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).
Such consciousness is indeed the very consciousness of Devadatta,
because [Yajñadatta's internal organ] does not delimit it.
