Likewise, there is an absence of the state of being a non-remover of that which is not removable by its own mental modification (*vṛtti*), and there exists the state of being a remover of that which is removable by its own mental modification.
It should be understood that "by its own mental modification" refers to the knowledge that is the mental modification of Yajñadatta’s internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
it is because [the Lord] is the remover of that ignorance of Yajñadatta which is to be removed.

Right here, he states another inference: "In this way" (*evam*). Here, one might raise the objection that because Devadatta and Yajñadatta are non-different, the recollection of Devadatta is also produced by the experience of Yajñadatta; thus, the second reason would be unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*). Anticipating this, he refutes it with: "And not so" (*na ca*). Now, it may be argued that in an inference establishing the mutual difference of individual souls (*jīva*), there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), and therefore the reason is irrelevant (*aprayojakatva*). Nor should it be said that the impossibility of the distribution of pleasure and pain (*sukhaduḥkhavyavasthā*) serves as such a subverting proof.

Since there is no ultimate distinction, even if an ultimate systematic arrangement is untenable, there is no contradiction in accepting a systematic arrangement based on what is distinct from that; therefore, he says: "of the selves. If it is argued that even when an ultimate systematic arrangement is impossible, a conceptual systematic arrangement is possible, [we ask]: does that [conceptual] arrangement not require a basis for its arrangement at all, or does it require something ultimate? Not the first, because—as with the offering corresponding to the Yakṣa—a basis for arrangement consistent with the object must necessarily exist.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to accept ignorance (*avidyā*) in order to establish the non-ultimate status of the individual soul (*jīva*) and other categories.

Nor is the second alternative [tenable], because even a non-ultimate regulator will be refuted as being nothing other than an intrinsic difference (*svābhāvikabheda*). Thus, the meaning is that one should observe the untenability of an imaginary arrangement (*kālpanikavyavasthā*), as demonstrated in the *Mandāramañjarī*.
And as for the scriptural passages such as "Two birds...
and so forth—if it is argued that these are intended to convey a difference that is merely conventional (vyāvahārika), [we reply: no.
Is that [conventional difference] to be sublated? If you say, "Certainly," [then proceed].
In that case, the authority of the Śruti would not exist,
because it would be apprehending a sublated object, like the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
If it is argued that its authority is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), [we reply:]...

But what, then, is the ultimate invalidity [of scripture]? Who has any doubt about this? There is indeed great doubt for one who does not know how to take refuge at the feet of the Tathāgata (because he has not attained refuge at the feet of the Tathāgata).
Is it not the case that the invalidity of scripture would follow only if one did not accept the objects established and presented by scripture?
And we do not fail to accept the distinctions taught by scripture.
Nor is it the case that we do not accept its truth as being established in the Śruti,
on the grounds that the word "satya" (truth) is not heard there.
This is not a fault.
For validity consists in the non-sublation of the object within its own sphere; invalidity, conversely, consists in its sublation.
Therefore, if difference—which is known through scripture—is sublated, how can there be validity for that scripture? [This would result in the loss of its validity.]

If non-acceptance [of non-duality] were based merely on not hearing the word "real" (*satya*), then even in passages such as "Brahman is one only, without a second," non-duality would likewise not be ultimate, since the word "real" is not heard there either.
If it is argued that the meaning of the scriptural texts on non-duality is ultimate because they possess the sixfold marks of intentionality (*tātparya-liṅga*), we say no;
for the opening statements (*upakrama*) and so forth indicate intentionality only toward their own literal sense.
And thus, by virtue of the marks of purport (*tātparyaliṅga*), it is established that [the Upanishads] have non-duality alone as their primary subject matter;
they do not have the reality of that [duality] as their primary subject matter, because duality is not their intended meaning.
We have demonstrated elsewhere that it is precisely difference (*bheda*) that is endowed with the sixfold marks of purport.

Having thus stated the perception and inference regarding the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), he states the scripture as well with the words "and the Śrutis. The ellipsis to be supplied is "the proof for the difference between the individual soul and the Lord. Keeping in mind the dilemma—whether this empirical difference is sublatable (bādhya) or non-sublatable (abādhya)—he asks, "Is that [difference] sublatable? in order to refute the first position. The opponent (pūrvapakṣin) accepts that position with the word "Certainly" (bāḍham).
This means that it is indeed firmly established that the difference is sublatable.
He refutes this with the words "In that case" (*tarhi*).
Even though the Veda, like the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, grasps an object that is sublated, it does not follow that its authority is entirely non-existent.
Rather, just as there is a difference in what is being taught, its authority is likewise merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).
The perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is not like that;

rather, its lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*) alone [is real]. With this intention, he raises an objection: "Validity" (*prāmāṇyam*). Accepting that the validity of the Śruti is merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*), he asks sarcastically—"But what then?"—with the thought that if the invalidity [of the perception] is also empirical, then their non-difference must be ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). Not understanding the mockery, the opponent accepts that very position and objects: "What doubt could there be?"—meaning that there is no doubt whatsoever regarding the ultimate reality of the invalidity.
He states the answer: "It exists.
To the question "Why? he says: "By the Tathāgata. Here, "Tathāgata" refers to a Buddhist. [This is said] regarding one who does not know and does not reflect.
"Of oneself"— the word "your" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
This is the intended meaning.
For you do not, like the Buddhist, maintain that the Veda is entirely invalid (*apramāṇya*).

Rather, you accept the validity of the non-dual portion as characterized by its revelation of reality (*tattvāvedakatva*), while accepting the invalidity of the dualistic portion as characterized by its failure to reveal reality.

If it is now asserted that invalidity alone is ultimately real, then your entry into the Buddhist school of thought becomes quite evident. [The opponent] objects: "That which is presented by the Veda..."—that is to say, that which is propounded by the Veda.
The meaning is that difference is not denied, but rather, having accepted difference, its reality is not accepted.
To the question, "How is it known that the reality of difference is not what is taught by the Śruti? he says: "Therein. This means "in the Śruti.
The intention is that words such as "two" (dvi) and so forth merely denote duality, which is pervaded by difference.

He states the answer: "Not this" (*naiṣa*). Even though the word "truth" (*satya*) is not heard in the scripture (*śruti*), its truthfulness is unavoidable; the meaning is that if one does not accept its truthfulness, the resulting loss of the scripture's authority (*aprāmāṇya*) is unavoidable. He demonstrates this very point with the words: "Regarding its own object" (*svagocarārtha*). This means "regarding its own subject matter. Thus, authority consists in the communication of an uncontradicted object, while lack of authority consists in the communication of a contradicted object.

The sense is this: if you accept that the difference established by scripture is sublated by you, how could it not be invalid? He refutes the aforementioned objection—that [the word "true"] is not heard—by means of a *pratibandi* (reductio ad absurdum): "By the word 'true'... If one does not accept that [difference], then one does not accept its reality. For a *pratibandi* is employed when there is equality regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*).

With the intention that there is no equality of objects of knowledge (*prameya*) here, he raises an objection: "Now [atheti]. [The answer is: "Because it is endowed with the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*). The opening is "One only, without a second" (*ekamevādvitīyam*);
the conclusion is "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*);
and the repetition is "That thou art, That thou art," stated nine times.

The meaning is that non-duality possesses novelty (*apūrvatva*) because it is not established by any other means of valid cognition; its fruit is expressed in the passage "for him there is delay only so long"; and there is the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) "by which the unheard becomes heard. Thus, it is endowed with these six kinds of indicators of the intended meaning (*tātparya-liṅga*).
This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Since unity has been established through analogies such as that of the lump of clay and so forth, "logical proof" (*upapatti*) is also to be understood here. Furthermore, since the method of initial statement (*upakrama*) and the others are specific forms of logical proof, they are not intended to be mentioned separately from "proof," and thus the expression "sixfold" is used.

Thus, even though the word "truth" (satya) is absent in the scriptural texts on non-duality (advaita), the truth of non-duality is established by the force of the indicators of intent (tātparyaliṅga).
The sense is that, because the scriptural texts on difference lack such indicators of intent, there is no truth to the difference that is their object.

With the thought that this disparity is irrelevant to the truth of the meaning, he says: "The introductory passages and so forth," [meaning] with respect to its own object, which is the literal meaning of the scripture.
"Because it does not have that as its object" means because it lacks the status of being the meaning of the sacred scripture (*śruti*).
This is stated as a concession (*abhyupagamya-ukti*).
In reality, however, the lack of parity (*vaiṣamya*) is indeed unestablished; thus he says: "Even though there is difference. "Elsewhere" refers to the second chapter of the *Nyāyāmṛta*.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of indicators of the purport (*tātparya-liṅga*) even for the scriptural texts concerning difference. To explain:
in the *Atharva-veda*, the opening passage begins with "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*).
"He attains supreme equality" is the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*).
"One of them does not eat, while the other rules over the other" is the repetition (*abhyāsa*).

Since a difference characterized by that [Self] or having that [Self] as its counter-correlative—which is the Lord knowable solely through scripture and is uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time—is not attained without scripture, this constitutes novelty (*apūrvatā*).
The phrase "having shaken off merit and demerit" refers to the result.
The phrase "his greatness" is an explanatory passage (arthavāda) in the form of praise.
The meaning is that this has been established by such arguments as "eating without eating."

Here too, although it should have been stated that [the Sūtras] possess the sevenfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*), the fact that they are said to possess "sixfold" [marks] implies the very same intention already expressed.
Regarding the phrase "and the Śrutis," one should understand this as meaning both the Śrutis and the Sūtras.

Regarding the term "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*): although it was the status of being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) that was asserted by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), that very point must be refuted first.
Nevertheless, this statement is made in this manner for the sake of brevity in refuting that [position] as a secondary consequence (*prāsaṅgika*).

With the thought that even with a hundred efforts, if one does not accept the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) of the Veda, there would be no distinction from the Buddhists—since the meaning of "invalidity" (*aprāmāṇya*) is simply the state of having a sublatable object (*bādhyārthatva*)—he says, beginning with "Why... [and so forth]. [Regarding the phrase] "because it grasps a sublatable object": if it is objected, "Is this not itself invalidity?", we say no; for here, invalidity consists in the absence of being a producer of valid knowledge (*pramā*).
The meaning is this: when you say, "Who accepts [this], for what doubt could there be? and we then raise that point, you must admit that there is indeed a great doubt.
Now, one might object: since the scripture, its meaning, and its validity possess a single existence, the validity is accepted as having the same ontological status as the subject (the scripture).

Thus, even if one accepts that both the scripture and the world are merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*), and accepts the established order of the world exactly according to the method taught in one's own tradition, yet still accepts the absolute invalidity of the scripture—what is the point of this untimely frantic display?
For it cannot avoid the consequence that its object is sublated, just like the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
If it is argued that a means of valid cognition can have as its object something sublatable by the knowledge of Brahman alone, we say no;
for then even the superimposition of momentariness and other such qualities upon Brahman would result in being a valid cognition.

Furthermore, if it is argued that there is no complexity (gaurava) in accepting a twofold nature of validity—namely, that validity consists in having an object that is not sublated by any cognition other than a non-modal (niṣprakāraka) and inclusive (anugata) cognition—that is not so.

For, in that case, since duality and non-duality would both possess the same form of validity as described, the distinction between their objects as being merely conventional (vyāvahārika) and ultimately real (pāramārthika) would be untenable.
Validity in its primary sense consists in having an object that is absolutely unsublatable.

If it is argued that even though [the Vedas] have as their object that which is sublated by the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*), they possess a secondary degree of validity (*amukhyaprāmāṇya*) because their object is not sublated by anything other than that, and thus there exists indeed an internal distinction within validity—then, since mere intention (*vivakṣā*) is unrestrained, even a Buddhist who asserts that the meaning of the Veda is sublated by a particular cognition would be a proponent of the Veda (*vedavādī*). [Objection: Validity consists in having an object that is uncontradicted prior to its own sublation. In the case of silver [mistaken for mother-of-pearl], however, because the perception of silver is merely illusory (*prātibhāsika*), the silver is sublated even before the perception itself is sublated. [Reply: This is not so.

There is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the case of an error regarding silver and the like, which arises immediately prior to the immediate perception (*aparokṣa*) of Brahman as devoid of all modes (*niṣprakāraka*).
Furthermore, what is meant by "sublation of the object" (*arthabādha*)? Is it the destruction of the object, the cognition of its non-existence, or the perception thereof?
It cannot be the first.

The first [alternative] is not tenable, because it is accepted that the phenomenal world (prapañca), such as a jar which constitutes the literal meaning of the scripture, is destroyed even before the sublation by the scripture occurs.
Nor is the second;
for one who has known the Vedānta already possesses the direct knowledge of the non-existence of objects through such [scriptural passages] as "here there is no diversity."
For this very reason, the third [alternative] is not tenable;
for it would follow that the perception of the moon as being the size of a thumb would be valid, since there is no such sublation (bādhā) against it—enough of this.
Now, an objection: indeed, a fault arises only when one fails to accept exactly what is stated by the scripture.

But here, everything stated in the Śruti is accepted. One might object: "Its ultimate reality is not the meaning of that Śruti. [The author] anticipates this with the words "śrutīti" (regarding the Śruti). With the words "svagocara" (within its own scope), he means: thus, the statement that "everything stated in the Śruti is accepted, but its ultimate reality is not" is empty;
for the very meaning of the word "acceptance" is the cognition of something that is not sublated. This is the intended sense.

Furthermore, since it is impossible to establish a meaning through indifference toward both existence and non-existence, it is established by linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that all sentences, in the absence of the word "real" (*satya*), terminate in the existence of their own referents.

Otherwise, even in such cases as "Truth is knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*), although the word "real" is present, there would be only "reality" (*satyatā*) and not the "reality of reality" (*satyatāyāḥ satyatvam*); thus, the demoness of doubt would be difficult to exorcise.
Moreover, the word "real" is indeed observed in expressions such as "the real division" (*satyaṃ bhidā*).
One might object: "Even without a word expressing truth, since intention (*tātparya*) is impossible toward that which is unreal, the reality of identity is established;

and that intention is understood from its indicative marks (*liṅga*). To this, he raises the following objection: "Now, [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad], 'one alone' is the opening statement (*upakrama*), and 'That thou art' (*tat tvam asi*) is the concluding statement (*upasaṃhāra*)."
The repetition "That thou art, that thou art" occurs nine times.
Its novelty (*apūrvatā*) arises because oneness is not established by any other means of valid knowledge.
The result of the knowledge of oneness is expressed in the words "Then you will become [the Supreme]."
It should be understood that the statement, "By which the unheard becomes heard," is an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*) intended to establish identity.

Regarding the term "its own meaning" (*svārtha*), this means that the purport (*tātparya*) extends only as far as what is stated within its own specific context (*prakaraṇa*), and not merely to the literal expression itself; this is what the indicators such as the introductory context (*upakrama*) and so forth make known.
And thus, the sense is that there would be only the intended meaning (*tātparya*), but not actual reality (*satyatva*).

If it is argued that "reality" is also obtained through the connection with the intended meaning—expressed by the word "nanu"—then [we reply]: in that case, even the speech of one who is deluded and so forth would be possible, provided it possesses an intended meaning understood through indicators such as the opening statement (*upakrama*) and the rest.

In reality, since the phrase "one only, without a second" has been stated elsewhere as the absence of anything equal or superior, the negation of specific attributes implies the affirmation of the remainder. Furthermore, because the opening [of the passage] concerns difference, even the conclusion must be consistent with that illustration. Therefore, for the sake of accounting for the neuter gender, one must either accept that the word *tat tvam asi* is a single compound by means of a pause [between the words], or rely on the etymological analysis (*vigraha*) where *tattva* is taken as "the state of being that" (*tasya bhāvas tattvam*), or else recognize that the term *tat-tvam-pada* refers to the world through the phrase "all this," or else that it signifies similarity and so forth; thus, it is intent upon difference.

For this very reason, since the [Upaniṣadic] repetition (*abhyāsa*) is intent upon difference, and since even the difference between the Lord and that which is knowable through the Vedas alone is unprecedented (*apūrva*), it should be understood that because the context (*prakaraṇa*) is intent upon difference, the fruit (*phala*) is also connected to it; furthermore, because there is the hearing of words such as "tat" (That) and so forth regarding the cause of the knowledge of difference, the purport (*tātparya*) lies in difference alone. Thus, "it is indeed difference. And if [the opponent argues] that the establishment of reality [of difference] follows from these marks of purport, the sense is: "then it is the same for me as well. This is stated elsewhere in the *Nyāyāmṛta*. To explain:
In the *Atharvaṇa*, the opening is "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*);
the conclusion is "he attains equality" (*sāmyam upaiti*); the repetition is "of those two, one does not eat" (*tayor anyaḥ anaśnan*) and "the other is the Lord" (*anyam īśam*);
and there is novelty according to the manner described.
"Having shaken off merit and demerit" is the statement of the result (*phala*).

"Its greatness," and "free from sorrow," are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*). Having considered the dilemma in one's mind as to whether conventional duality is sublatable (*bādhya*) or unsublatable (*abādhya*), he raises the first alternative with the words: "Is that...? He points out the error with: "But surely... He reveals the nature of that error with: "For [it is] the non-cognition of an object within its own domain..."

The meaning is that if one accepts the authority of the Vedas (*śruti*), it is necessary to accept the existence of their object; this is the point. He raises an objection regarding inequality: "Now, [this is] because of this Vedic text. Then he states the motivating factor for the inequality: "By means of the introductory passages (*upakrama*) and so forth.
And thus, by the force of the introductory passages and other criteria, the purport (*tātparya*) of the non-duality (*advaita*) scriptures will be established.
But that is not the case, because even though there is a statement that deceives regarding truth for that purpose, there is an absence of truth in its intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*).
This is the statement from the *Parabhāṣya*: "Let there be non-duality alone, but not truth.
And he says that the disparity is unestablished: "Even in the case of difference... etc.
"Except in the *Nyāyāmṛta*.

Regarding the verse beginning with "dvā suparṇā," the fact that these [scriptural passages] convey difference by way of authoritative tradition (*āgama*) was established during the exposition of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*). "What then?"—when it is said that their authority is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), the meaning is that there is only conventional usage therein, and not that it exists in reality. "The Tathāgata"—this means the Buddhist. "It has been demonstrated"—the meaning is that the absolute non-existence of that substratum (the qualified entity) in which a certain attribute is taught by scripture.

The sense is this: otherwise, if the non-acceptance of anything understood by a sentence within the Śruti were a cause for its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*), then because of the absence of that which is understood by words such as "existence" (*sat*) and so forth within the Veda, your own [scripture] would also be lacking in authority. Regarding the phrase "it is not accepted": the ellipsis is "but it is admitted as being false" (*mithyātvena*).

With the intention that, since the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) is stated in such passages as "Two birds... by taking them as the subjects of the proposition, it would be unavoidable to conclude that those texts lack authority if such a distinction were not accepted, he says: "This is not a fault. Anticipating the objection that a fault occurs only when that which is taught as a qualifier (*prakāra*) by way of existence (*sattva*) is actually non-existent, whereas that is not the case here, he says: "By the word 'satya'...

The statement that [the truth] is sixfold is made either because the logical justification (*upapatti*) is an external factor and one intends to speak of the internal factors, or by relying on the identity between the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) and the result through their relationship of general and particular.

The points regarding the *upakrama* (initial statement) and so forth are to be seen in the *Nyāyāmṛta*. "Its truth is not [established]" means that otherwise, by means of the *upakrama* and other criteria found in the texts of the Śūnyavādins, the emptiness (*śūnya*) which is the intended object of those texts would have to be real. "Difference alone" means that, according to your own logic, truthfulness has instead become something established by the Śruti.

Having thus stated the perception and inference regarding the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), he also cites scripture: "But the Śrutis... He raises an objection, fearing that the Śrutis might not be a means of valid knowledge for ultimate difference: "In a conventional sense... He asks—"What is that?"—in order to refute [the opponent's position] through the dilemma of whether the difference stated in the Śrutis is sublatable or unsublatable. Validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in having an unsublatable object. [The opponent objects: "But surely the validity of the Śruti is merely [concerning what is] superimposed."

However, one might suspect that [the world] is fit for empirical usage because it is not sublated by the knowledge of Brahman; thus he says: "validity" (*prāmāṇyam*). "Invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyam*) means the absence of validity. "Ultimate" (*pāramārthika*)—the sense is that when one of two opposites, existence and non-existence, is sublated, the other is necessarily unsublatable. Here, he anticipates the objection of an "admitted consequence" (*iṣṭāpatti*) by saying: "What doubt is there? He replies: "It exists," for in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of entering the Buddhist position. The meaning is that the Tathāgata is a Buddhist, and [the opponent] does not admit his own adherence to that [Buddhist] doctrine.

Not understanding the intended meaning of the example stated—"like the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell"—the opponent objects with "But surely... [nanviti]. This is because no word signifying reality (satyatva) is heard; that is, because no word is heard that attributes reality to the difference.
For it is indeed the lack of informative content (*abodhakatva*) that is the cause of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).
And since the scriptures do inform us of the very nature of difference, they possess no invalidity regarding that aspect.

The meaning is as follows: its ultimate reality, however, is not taught by the Śruti; therefore, it is indeed accepted that [the scripture] lacks authority regarding that aspect. "In its own domain" means: the quality of making known an object that is not sublated.
This is the intended sense.
Just as non-cognitiveness (*abodhakatva*) is a cause of invalidity, so too is the cognition of a sublated object (*bādhyārthabodhakatva*).
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the defective sense organs and other factors that apprehend nacre-silver would possess validity.
And since this [cognition of a sublated object] is no different in the case of the Veda as well, its invalidity is indeed unavoidable.
Nor should it be argued that validity consists solely in being a cognition that is not sublated by anything other than the knowledge of Brahman,
and that this [criterion] is common to the Śruti;

for one could equally well say that validity consists solely in being a cognition that is not sublated by anything other than the cognition of mother-of-pearl, and that this [criterion] is common to defective sense organs as well.
Furthermore, since the authority of the Śruti would be sublated, the consequence of its lack of authority—defined by that absence [of truth]—remains exactly as it was.

He refutes the claim that "the reality of difference is not stated by the Śruti" with the words: "because the word 'real' (satya) is not heard. This refers to passages such as "Two birds... and so forth.
If that were not accepted—that is, if the reality of difference were not accepted—it would not be possible. This is the underlying intention.

Since difference is perceived as a reality even by the aforementioned scripture—given that it arises from the dependent existence of the existent, the non-existent, and the indifferent—it is possible for the scripture to possess authority regarding its truthfulness.
Otherwise, because the scripture would result in grasping only the nature of non-duality and thus fail to grasp its truthfulness, non-duality itself would be sublated for you.

[Objection: Even if the scripture grasps only the nature of non-duality, its truthfulness is determined through the indicative marks of purport, such as the introductory statements (*upakrama*) and so forth.

But one might raise the objection that difference is real; thus he introduces the [next] section with "Now" (*atha*). "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second" is the introduction (*upakrama*).
"All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) is the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*).
"That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) is the repetition (*abhyāsa*) nine times.
The meaning is that because oneness is not established by any other means of knowledge, it possesses the quality of being "unprecedented" (apūrvatā);

"then one will be perfected" is the fruit; and "by which the unheard becomes heard" is the explanatory praise (arthavāda). Thus, it is endowed with the sixfold marks of purposive significance (tātparya-liṅga).
Although there are seven kinds of indicators of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*) along with logical justification (*upapatti*),

and although there exists scriptural justification for non-duality (*advaita*)— such as, "O dear one, by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay becomes known," and so forth— nevertheless,

since all [the other indicators] such as the introductory statement (*upakrama*) are established in meaning through their very nature as forms of justification, that [justification] is not mentioned separately.
It might be so,
if the truth of identity were what was established by the introduction and other parts;
but it is not so.
Rather, there is merely identity; therefore, its reality is not established. Thus he says: "The introductory passages and so forth."

Now, one might argue that even if the opening passage and so forth do not explicitly establish the identity and reality [of the Self], their capacity to prove it remains unimpeded by virtue of being pervaded by it; to this, he says: "Difference. The opening is "Two birds... (RV 1.164.20);
the conclusion is "...attains the highest equality" (MuU 3.1.3).
The repetition of the word "other" is seen in "One of them... (MuU 3.1.1), "The other does not eat... (ŚU 4.6), and "The other is the Lord" (ŚU 4.7).
Its "novelty" (*apūrvatā*) consists in its being devoted to the distinction of the Lord, who is to be understood solely through the scriptures.
Its "result" (*phala*) is expressed by the words, "having shaken off merit and demerit.
Its "eulogy" (*arthavāda*) is expressed by the words, "his majesty."

The fact that even the scripture concerning difference possesses the sixfold marks of purport (*tātparya-liṅga*)—including the logical justification (*upapatti*) expressed by the phrase "not eating"—has been demonstrated in the *Nyāyāmṛta*.
Consequently, the intention is that the reality of difference is thereby established.
Alternatively, the meaning is that the scripture concerning difference itself is endowed with the sixfold marks of purport.
For instance,
the opening statement, "One only, without a second," refers specifically to the absence of a second of the same class;
for since the existence of time and other factors is heard [in scripture], it is impossible that there be a negation of every kind of second.
The conclusion "of this nature" (*aitadātmyam*) is made by way of its being the owner (*svāmikatvena*), and not by way of its being identical in essence (*svarūpatvena*),
for otherwise the secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) would be redundant.
By the statement "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) as well, it is precisely its similarity to That and so forth that is being reiterated.

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two words is appropriate only insofar as it is secondary, given that it requires a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) for both words by subverting the non-difference characterized by their primary referents.
However, if the text were divided as "That, you are not" (*atat tvam asi*), its focus would clearly be on difference.
Its status as "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) follows from its focus on the difference between the self and the Lord, which is not accessible through other means of knowledge.
Now, the phrase "it will be attained" refers to the attainment of Brahman as the fruit;
and the explanatory passage (arthavāda), "by which the unheard becomes heard," is justified through similarity and so forth,
as it is likewise established by the analogies of the lump of clay and the rest.

It should be observed that [the opponent’s argument] fails because, since all clay objects are not transformations of a single lump of clay, it is impossible for the text to intend their non-difference. Having thus stated the perception and inference regarding the difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), he now cites scripture—“The Śrutis,” etc. The ellipsis is to be supplied as “the means of knowledge for the ultimate difference between the jīva and the īśvara. [The opponent replies: “Regarding conventional [difference],” etc. The point is that it is inappropriate to cite these scriptural passages as evidence for ultimate difference.

Keeping in mind the dilemma as to whether conventional difference (*vyāvahārikabheda*) is sublatable (*bādhya*) or unsublatable (*abādhya*), he asks—beginning with "sa kim" (What is that?)—in order to refute the first alternative. He anticipates the answer with "bāḍham" (Certainly). This means that the conventional difference is indeed firmly sublatable. He refutes this with "tarhi" (In that case). To the question "Why?", he says "śuktirūpya" (shell-silver). For even the perception of shell-silver is seen to lack validity precisely because it grasps an object—the shell-silver—that is itself sublatable.
The point is that, in the same way, it would be difficult to establish the validity of scripture (*āgama*) if it were to grasp an object that is sublated by its nature as a conventional distinction.

Now, one might object: "Even if such [scriptural] validity is impossible because grasping a sublated object contradicts ultimate validity (*pāramārthika-prāmāṇya*), nevertheless, since it does not contradict conventional validity (*vyāvahārika-prāmāṇya*), such validity is possible for scripture. To this, he raises an objection with the words "prāmāṇyam" (validity). If that were so, even the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of silver upon mother-of-pearl would possess conventional validity; thus, while this fault remains, he asks another question to state a further defect: "kintarhi" (but what then?).

The meaning is that the negation of one of two mutually contradictory things is necessarily pervaded by the affirmation of the other. [The question] "Of what? means: for me, who asserts that the authority of the Veda is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), there is indeed a certainty regarding its ultimate lack of authority (*pāramārthika-aprāmāṇya*), and not a doubt. He refutes this with the words "It exists. "Tathāgata" refers to a Buddhist. The Buddhist accepts that the lack of authority of the Veda is ultimate; if you also accept that, it would follow that you are accepting his doctrine.

And thus, since the authority of the Veda is merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*), there arises a doubt as to whether its lack of authority is ultimate (*pāramārthika*) or not; for if one were to accept it as ultimate, it would follow that one accepts the Buddhist doctrine. Therefore, the meaning is that there can only be doubt—that it is not ultimately real—and no certainty that it is so. Alternatively, "doubt" (*sandeha*) means apprehension, which is to say, something undesirable. "Established by Śruti" means "expounded by the Veda."

[Objection: "But surely, even if one accepts the difference propounded by the Śruti, since one does not accept the reality of that difference as propounded by it, there would indeed be a lack of authority [for the scripture]. To this he says: "Nor... (nāpi). Why? To this he says: "In that regard, the word 'real'... (tatra satyapada-). The point is that words such as "two" (dvi) and so forth denote merely duality, which is a synonym for difference.
Furthermore, the acceptance or non-acceptance of the subject matter propounded is not the determinant of authority or lack of authority;
rather, it is precisely the sublation or non-sublation of the propounded meaning that constitutes them.

For instance, the validity of the statement "fire is hot" arises precisely from the non-sublation of its expressed object, while the invalidity of the statement "fire is not hot" arises precisely from the sublation of its expressed object. Now, in the present case, if one were to admit that the difference—the object propounded by the Śruti—is subject to sublation, then its invalidity would be unavoidable; thus he refutes [this objection] with the words beginning "This is no fault. [The term] "svagocara" means: "its own," i.e., that which is intended as valid; the meaning is "that which is to be understood by it."
"Of that which is known through scripture" means of that which is propounded by scripture.

He refutes this by means of a *prativandī* (counter-argument), stating: "In the case of 'truth' (*satya*). This refers to the non-acceptance of that; namely, the non-acceptance of the reality of difference. [Objection: Even though the word "truth" is not heard in the scriptural passage "One only, without a second," the oneness propounded therein is indeed ultimately real.
Because that scripture possesses the sixfold marks of intention (*tātparya*)—beginning with the introduction (*upakrama*)—which establish its unity.
To explain: "One only, without a second" is the introduction.
The conclusion is "That thou art.
The repetition is nine times: "That thou art, That thou art.
Its novelty consists in the fact that oneness is not established by any other means of knowledge.
"Now, it will be attained" refers to the fruit.
"By which the unheard becomes heard" is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) in the form of praise.

Furthermore, because it has been established through analogies such as that of the single lump of clay—"Just as, my dear, by one lump of clay [all that is made of clay is known]"—the argumentative support (*upapatti*) is also additional.

Furthermore, there is no sixfold intentionality regarding difference in the scriptural texts on difference, by which the reality of that object [of difference] would be established; thus he raises an objection with the word "atha" (now/if). Although there are seven types of indicators of intentionality when including "logical consistency" (*upapatti*), as it has been said:
"The introduction and conclusion, repetition, novelty, fruit,..."

This is stated in passages such as, "The indicators [of meaning] are the explanatory statements (*arthavāda*), logical consistency (*upapatti*), and so forth, which determine the intended purport (*tātparya*).
Nevertheless, there is no fault in saying this because the specific types of logical consistency, such as the introductory context (*upakrama*) and others, are sixfold.
The introductory context and other factors in the passage "One only, without a second" indicate that the scriptural texts on unity have their purport in unity.
But this is not the case regarding the reality of oneness. Why? Because oneness is the meaning of the scripture, whereas the reality of that [oneness] is not the meaning of the scripture.

He provides the rebuttal with the passage beginning "upakramādīni" and ending with "tadarthatvāt," on the grounds that the introductory statements (*upakrama*) and so forth possess the inherent nature of indicating the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the scripture itself. "In its own sense" means that the scripture (*śruti*) [indicates] its own meaning;
the ellipsis is "the intention (*tātparya*) of the scripture.

The ellipsis is "the sentence concerning unity has non-duality alone as its ultimate purport. Regarding the word "tātparya": the meaning is that the sentence of unity is endowed with the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of intention, such as the introductory statement, regarding that very unity.
He states what is excluded by the word "only" (mātra): "not so. This is because it does not have that as its meaning; that is, because it lacks the status of being the meaning of the Śruti.
And this has been stated provisionally.

In reality, however, on the strength of the analogies of the bird, the thread, and so forth, it is more appropriate that the sentence "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) establishes difference by means of the word-division "Not that thou art" (na tat tvam asi).
For it is not logical to state an example of difference after having asserted non-difference.
Therefore, the statement "one only, without a second" aims at difference by establishing the absence of any equal or superior;
the same applies to the phrase "having that as its self."
It must be accepted that the passage beginning with "Just as, my dear" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.1) teaches creation in order to make known its preeminence.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the indicators of the purport (tātparya-liṅga), such as the introduction with "Thus, one only, without a second," the conclusion with "All this has that as its self," the ninefold repetition of "That thou art," the novelty (apūrvatva) since the difference between the individual soul and the Lord—who is accessible through scripture alone—does not otherwise arise without scripture, the hearing of the fruit in the words "Then he becomes merged," the eulogy (arthavāda) stating "By which the unheard becomes heard," and the supporting illustrations such as the bird and the thread—all these point toward non-difference alone.

If it is accepted that the meaning of the scriptural texts on unity is ultimate because they possess the sixfold marks of intentionality even though the word "real" (satya) is not heard therein, then one must likewise accept that the meaning of the scriptural texts on difference is ultimate because they are endowed with the sixfold marks of intentionality even though the word "real" is not heard therein; thus he says: "In [the case of] difference, the sixfold... etc.

In the *Atharvaṇa* [Upaniṣad], the opening is "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), the conclusion is "...he attains the supreme equality" (*paramaṃ sāmyam upaiti*), and the repetition is "Of the two, one eats while the other does not eat; [the former worships] the other, the Lord" (*tayor anyaḥ pippalaṃ svādvatty anaśnann anyo abhicākaśīti*). Since a difference characterized by or having as its counter-correlative the Lord—who is knowable solely through scripture—is not established without scripture, this constitutes novelty (*apūrvatā*). The fruit is expressed as "having shaken off merit and demerit" (*puṇyapāpe vidhūya*). The explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is "his greatness" (*asya mahimānam*). The logical justification (*upapatti*) is provided by the statement of contradictory attributes: "he eats" and "not eating. Thus, there is a difference based on the scriptural testimony of difference.
The meaning is that the possession of the marks of *tātparya* (intentional focus) has been established in the second chapter of the *Nyāyāmṛta*.
If, on the other hand, difference were non-sublated (*abādhya*), then there would be no dispute;
for what reason, then, would [the text] have the conventional difference as its intended purport?

If it is argued that this is because of contradiction with the scriptures on non-duality (*advaita-śruti*), then let the scriptures on non-duality have as their purport a merely apparent non-duality (*prātibhāsika-advaita*);
for the resolution of the contradiction is equal [in both cases].
Now, it may be objected that there can be no invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) due to the sublation of what is propounded by scripture (or established by scripture).
Rather, it is [the case] regarding that which is intended;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the non-authoritativeness of the portion consisting of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) according to the Mīmāṃsaka school.
Furthermore, in this context, difference is not the object of the Vedic revelation’s intended meaning.
If it is argued that the scriptural statement "not here, manifoldness" (*neha nānā*) merely restates a difference already established by perception for the purpose of negating it, we say no.

For there is the possibility of the opposite being the case (the consequence of the reverse): the Vedic passages stating "not here, manifoldness" might instead be restating a non-difference already established by inference—namely, that the disputed individual selves are not ultimately different from the Supreme Self because they possess selfhood, just like the Supreme Self—in order to negate [that non-difference] through the verse "two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*).
This is because difference consists in the negation of identity, and therefore statements establishing difference are themselves of the nature of a negation of identity.
By this, the claim that non-dualistic statements are more authoritative because they are prohibitive in nature is refuted.
For it is not the case that in the context of a restatement (*anuvāda*), only what is already established by perception serves as the basis for that restatement.

If that were so, then a statement such as "Fire is the remedy for cold," which explains that fire is the cause of the removal of cold (or the cessation of chill) based on what is established through inference in the form of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), would not be accepted by all as a restatement.

Having thus refuted the position that conventional difference is sublatable (*bādhyatva*), he raises the possibility of its being non-sublatable (*abādhyatva*) and then refutes it with the words, "If, however... The phrase "there is no dispute" means that if one accepts its non-sublatability, then that itself constitutes ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*); therefore, there is no disagreement between us—this is the sense. Thus, having provisionally accepted the opponent’s claim that the scriptures refer to conventional difference, a refutation was stated by means of the dilemma of its being either sublatable or non-sublatable. Now, with the intention that this very [conventional status] is untenable, he says, "From what? He anticipates the reply.

"Advaiteti" [means]: Since non-duality (advaita) is ultimately real, it is impossible for difference (bheda), which is its opposite, to also be ultimately real; therefore, the intention is that the contradiction between the scriptural texts on difference and those on non-difference will be resolved by accepting that difference is merely conventional (vyāvahārika).
[The opponent objects: "In that case, let it not be that these texts on difference have non-duality as their purport; rather, let them simply have meanings such as similarity.

And thus, with the thought that there would be no contradiction with the texts on non-duality even if the texts on difference were intended to convey ultimately real difference, he asks: "What then? [The author replies: "Because the resolution of the contradiction is the same."

The meaning is as follows: just as when a contradiction arises between the scriptures on duality and non-duality, that contradiction is resolved by maintaining that non-duality is ultimate (pāramārthika) while duality is conventional (vyāvahārika), so too, by accepting that duality alone is ultimate and interpreting the non-dual scripture as having the sense of non-difference based on similarity and the like, there is no contradiction between the scriptures on duality and non-duality; thus, the resolution of the contradiction is the same in both cases.
Now, one might object: "It is indeed true what was said—that validity consists in the non-sublation of the object within its own scope.
Nevertheless, the scripture on difference lacks validity."

The "object within its own scope" (svagocarārtha) means precisely that which is the object of its own intended meaning (*tātparya*), not merely that which is expressed by it. Furthermore, difference (*bheda*) is not the object of the scripture's intended meaning;
for if it were, the consequence would follow that the scriptures lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*) upon the admission that such difference is sublated.

With the intention that the Śrutis merely restate the distinction already apprehended through perception—such as "Am I not omniscient?"—in order to negate it, he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). He asks why there is no lack of authority even when there is a contradiction of what has been stated, and answers with the words "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). If the lack of authority of the Śruti were admitted on the grounds of contradicting what was declared by the Śruti itself, then the portion consisting of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) such as "The divine cows indeed carry [the gods] while standing on their backs" would also be devoid of authority;
for the upward-carrying of divine cows declared by the Śruti is contradicted by its non-observation in worldly cows.

Therefore, in that context, according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, during the commentary on the sūtra *prayogacodanābhāvārthakatvamavibhāgāt* (PMS 1.3.24) in the third pāda of the first adhyāya, the sense intended—that this sentence is merely for the purpose of praising those cows belonging to humans which are connected to the gods as sacrificial materials—was established precisely by demonstrating its authoritative validity; this is the underlying point.

However, some say that [the word "contradiction" (bādha) in the sūtra] means the contradiction of those meanings which, though presented through their own expressive power in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and mantras—such as "He wept; because he wept"—are not the actual intended objects (*atātparya-viṣayībhūta*). Regarding the phrase "because of the possibility of the reverse": the meaning is that if one were to accept, without any basis and without any specific reasoning or refutation, that the non-difference texts are prohibitive while the difference texts are merely reiterative, then by that same logic, there would be the undesirable consequence of accepting the reverse as well—that is, that the difference texts are prohibitive and the non-difference texts are reiterative. Thus, since the reverse is equally possible, the former position cannot be maintained.

Now, one might object: since the scriptural texts concerning difference (bheda-śruti) merely establish difference, how can they have the purpose of negating non-difference (abheda), such that the opposite conclusion would follow? To this, he says: "Of difference" (bhedasya). Difference is indeed mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva), and that has identity (tādātmya) as its counter-correlate (pratiyogin).
And thus, the sense is: how could there be an absence of the purpose of negating non-difference in those scriptural passages that establish such difference?
Some might argue that because it is a negative statement, the non-dual (advaita) passage is more powerful, whereas the dualistic (bheda) passage is not negative and is therefore weaker;
that too is refuted by this [argument].

He says, "By this," because even difference consists in the negation of identity. Now, it cannot be argued that just as the scripture concerning difference is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*), so too the scripture concerning non-difference must be reiterative; for in the case of reiteration, the sole determinant is the prior attainment [of the object] through perception. And it cannot be said that non-difference, unlike difference, is not attained through perception but only through inference; therefore he says, "For not... and "That being so... [Note: The provided text contains Sanskrit fragments and logical arguments regarding the status of scriptural testimony on difference and non-difference.]
The point is that because the relationship of cause and effect is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), fire’s status as the cause of the cessation of cold is not established by perception.

Now, one might object: "The distinction stated in scripture is indeed non-sublated; therefore, there is no lack of authority [in it]. To this, he says: "If... The sense is that the abandonment of the ultimate reality of a perceived distinction is baseless; thus he says: "apparent" (*prātibhāsika*). The meaning is that for one of two contradictory things, another meaning must be expressed, rather than it being appropriate to imagine that the perceived meaning possesses primary existence (*mukhyasattā*).
As one Mīmāṃsaka might say: "In the case of a mutual contradiction between two scriptures, one would be authoritative while the other would be non-authoritative.
Furthermore, if the world described by the Śruti were thus unreal, Brahman too would be unreal.
If it is argued that there is a contradiction with such passages as "Truth, Knowledge," we say no;
for this is intelligible in the same manner as the statement "the universe is true.

If it is further argued that the non-existence of the world is expressed by the phrase "for [the world] is veiled by the untrue," while the supreme reality of Brahman is expressed by the phrase "non-duality is the ultimate truth," we say no.

This is because it is logically consistent with such passages as "the meanings according to reality" (*yāthātathyato'rthāni*). Furthermore, it would follow that even Brahman possesses that same nature, based on texts such as: "In the beginning, this was non-existent; it was neither existent nor called non-existent"; and "It is neither existent nor non-existent, but Śiva alone is the absolute Existent; may He, who remains as the negation of both existence and non-existence, be victorious in His entirety."
If it is argued that the non-existence of Brahman is censured by the passage beginning with "they say it is non-existent" (*asad*), we say no;
for even in the present context, the ignorance of those who say "this world is unreal" is censured in such passages as "those [who say] this is unreal and without foundation.
If you argue that this is a censure of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), [we reply:]...
The same applies to you as well.
If it is argued that a single Brahman is necessary for the sake of knowledge regarding the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*),
then for the sake of primacy, the world alone would likewise be such [a substratum].
If you accept a Brahman that is devoid of *pradhāna*, why not also accept one that is devoid of a substratum (*anadhiṣṭhānaka*)?
If it is argued that scripture declares that in liberation only Brahman remains,
[we reply] that scripture also declares that in liberation the world remains, whether in the form of women, vehicles, or kinsmen.
If it is argued that the world remains as a residue only in liberation with attributes (*saguṇa-mukti*) and not in liberation without attributes (*nirguṇa-mukti*), [we reply:
Brahman remains as a residue only in the liberation of the real (*sat-mukti*) and not in the liberation of the unreal (*asat-mukti*).
If it is argued that liberation of the real is not supported by authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇika*), [we reply as follows].

If it is argued that liberation devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa-mukti*) is likewise [taught] because liberation without qualities is heard in the scripture beginning with "But when for him the Self alone has become all," we reply:

by the knowledge that Brahman is non-existent— as in "He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent"— liberation into non-existence (*asan-mukti*) is also heard of as a supreme human goal.
If it is argued that the non-existence of one's own nature (*svarūpāsattva*) is not the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*), we say no;
for the absence of qualities (*nairguṇya*) is exactly the same.

If it is further argued that because there is an abundance of authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) establishing the existence of one's own nature in liberation (*mukti*), this statement must be interpreted otherwise, [we reply:]...

Thus, because there is an abundance of statements that establish [the existence of] enjoyments and so forth, even the statement regarding the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa*) must be interpreted otherwise; enough of this.

Furthermore, do the meanings of the Śruti naturally suggest a merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) status, or do they naturally suggest an ultimate (*pāramārthika*) status like that of Brahman? It is not the first case.
Because it contradicts direct experience; because it would result in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*vaiyyarthya*) regarding the falsity of the subject under dispute;
and because even identity and so forth would not naturally be established as ultimately real.
In the second case, we have won.
For everywhere, that which is universally recognized as having ultimate reality is abandoned when it is sublated;
but here, if you argue that the statement of difference is sublated by the statement of identity, we say no.

There is no proof by another means (anyathāsiddhi), because it is possible that [the world] is either a misconception (vaiparītya) or merely apparent (prātibhāsika), or that there exists a second ultimate reality, or a third kind of existence distinct from the three [levels of reality].

Furthermore, since even "conventional reality" (*vyāvahārikatva*) is difficult to define, the truth of the Śruti is like the eighth flavor—non-existent. He raises an objection, [saying] "The Śruti... [etc.], on the grounds that even if difference is accepted, there is no lack of authority because it is not the object of the [text's] intended meaning (*tātparya*). [He answers with] "Arthavāda... etc. The point is that in cases such as "The divine cows indeed carry [the burden] while lying on their backs," although the literal meaning expressed is sublated, authority is admitted simply because the intended meaning—in the form of a suggested excellence—is not sublated.
The connection is: "[The Śruti] restates the sentences... etc.

If it is argued that there is thus a lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*), he says: "Of difference" (*bhedasya*). "By way of being negative" (*niṣedhātmakatayā*) means by way of having mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as its object. "Because it is of the nature of negation" (*niṣedharūpatvāt*) means because it is of the nature of refutation.

The point is that since the demonstration of a non-existence proceeds precisely by first presupposing the possibility of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and then negating it, it is appropriate for it to function as a negator.

By this, it should be understood that the status of being a mere restatement (*anuvāditva*) asserted in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is refuted. "By this" means: by demonstrating that the sentence expressing difference has the nature of a negation. "Because it is a negative sentence" implies the thought that the term "non-duality" (*advaita*) does not contain an [independent] meaning [of its own].

Alternatively, it implies the thought that the non-duality sentence, such as "there is no diversity here," does not contain an [independent] meaning [of its own]. "It is refuted" implies the thought that, because it takes the form of a verbal negation, the state of being a negation in terms of its actual meaning (*arthataḥ*) is more powerful [than a mere restatement].

To the objection that since oneness, like difference, is not established by perception, how can it be a mere restatement (anuvāda), he says: "For not... The point is that the criterion for being a restatement is simply the fact that another means of knowledge (*māna*) has already established the object independently of oneself. "Established by inference" means that the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is beyond the reach of the senses.

Anticipating the second objection, he states the acceptance of the desired conclusion with the words "yadi punar" (if, however). He states that the claim that the scriptural texts concerning difference have as their purport conventional difference is without proof with the words "kutaśca" (and from where?). Regarding the phrase "of the portion consisting of arthavādas and so forth": the meaning is that there is a sublation of those objects which, though expressed through the primary power (*śakti*) in arthavādas such as "He wept; because he wept... and in mantras, do not constitute the intended purport (*atātparya-viṣaya*).

He states that the opposite is indeed appropriate: "because difference consists in the negation of identity. For this very reason, he says "by this," [referring to] the refutation of Vācaspati’s claim that the non-duality statement is more powerful because it is a negative statement. Now, one might object: since difference is apprehended through perception, it is logical for a statement of difference to be merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*), whereas a statement of non-difference is not, because non-difference is not apprehended by perception. He dispels this doubt by showing its lack of probative force: "for it is not so."
"There is no dispute between us"—this is the ellipsis; the sense is that we also accept it in exactly that way.

Anticipating the objection that difference (*bheda*) is merely uncontradicted during the time of empirical usage (*vyavahāra-kāla*) and not in reality, [the author] asks "From what? with the intention of refuting this by pointing out that although both duality and non-duality are equally taught by the Śruti, why should the former alone be subject to the aforementioned sublation? Previously, the doubt that even if difference were the meaning of the Śruti, it would not be its meaning in the sense of being real, was already set aside.

The passage beginning with "nanu" (but surely) is intended to dispel the doubt that the status of being the literal meaning of the Veda (*śrutyarthatva*) does not exist at all. "Of that which is intended by the Veda" means: of that which appears as not being the counter-correlate (*apratiyogin*) of a negation within the cognition produced by the Veda, which is dependent upon the ascertainment of its purport (*tātparya*). "Of the portion consisting of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*)" means: of such passages as "Prajāpati cut out his own omentum.

Even though the cutting out of Prajāpati’s omentum—the subject matter of the purport—is non-existent, those passages possess authority (*prāmāṇya*) because they indicate excellence (*prāśastya*) through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

The meaning is that this alone is the intended object (*tātparyaviṣaya*). Regarding the phrase "not here" (*na ceha*), the ellipsis is to be supplied as "by not being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of a negation.

The sense is that if one were to admit the non-existence of that [duality] itself, there would be a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*); however, the dualistic statements convey duality precisely as the counter-correlate of a negation.

It was stated that "restatement" (*anuvāda*) is based on perception (*pratyakṣa*) which has [already] obtained [the object]. [Objection: Let it be then that the difference spoken of in the Śruti is indeed non-sublatable (*abādhya*). To this he says: "If, however... (*yadi punar*). [Regarding the term] "without dispute" (*avivāda*): the intention is that since non-sublatability itself constitutes ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), our own desired position is thereby established.

Having stated the objection against the scriptural texts on difference being intended to express only empirical difference, he states the absence of any proof [for their ultimate validity] with the words "kutaśca" (from what?). Because non-duality cannot be merely empirical, it is described as "prātibhāsika" (illusory).

If it is argued that this would result in the scriptures concerning non-duality becoming invalid, the sense is that this is equivalent to the consequence that, in your own view, the scriptures concerning duality would likewise be invalid.
This might indeed be so.
If validity were the state of conveying an uncontradicted object,
it would not be so;
rather, it is the state of having an uncontradicted object as its ultimate purpose.

Furthermore, the validity of passages such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*)—which merely restate duality—is established precisely because they have the purpose of negating that [duality]. With this intention—that the duality propounded by them is likewise sublated—he raises an objection with the words "But surely" (*nanu*). Regarding the phrase "of the portion consisting of an explanatory passage" (*arthavādabhāgasya*): the point is that even though there is no rule that the meaning propounded by such a passage must be non-sublatable, its validity is accepted solely on the grounds that it is subordinate to the injunctive content of the ritual action (*kārya*), which is itself non-sublatable. It is specified as "in the Mīmāṃsaka view" because, in other systems, validity is admitted even for the propounded meaning itself.

With the intention that even if the scriptures on the non-duality of reality (*satyādvaita*) have as their purport a merely apparent non-duality (*prātibhāsikādvaita*), there is no consequence of their being invalid, he says: "Not here" (*neha*). The syntactical connection is: "they repeat the [scriptural] sentences. He says "the disputed ones" (*vimatāḥ*) because difference, unlike non-difference, is not established by perception. Now, one might ask: how can passages such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*) have as their purport the negation of non-difference, given the absence of words to that effect? To this he says: "of difference" (*bhedasya*). This is because [the negation of non-difference] consists in the negation of identity (*tādātmya*), and because it takes the form of the absence of non-difference.
Thus, since the meaning of those [passages] is precisely the meaning of difference, the aforementioned fault does not apply; this is the sense.

By thus establishing that the scriptural texts on difference serve to negate non-difference, the position asserted by Vācaspati is also refuted; this is what he means by saying "by this" (*eteneti*). [He says] "it is more powerful" (*prabalam*): the sense is that, in that case, the scriptural texts on difference themselves would be sublated by it; otherwise, since the strength of even the perception "this is not silver" would not be established, its capacity to sublate the perception "this is silver" would be untenable. [He says] "refuted" (*pratyuktam*): the sense is that if the scriptural texts on difference were equally negating, it would be impossible for them to be weaker.

Now, if it is argued that even though difference consists in the negation of non-difference, since it does not convey difference as such—merely being a negation of non-difference—passages such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*) are indeed weak, then the following must be said: Does the cognition of difference oppose the cognition of non-difference solely by virtue of being a negation of non-difference, or also by virtue of being a difference? In the first case, there is a contradiction with experience.
For at the time of cognitions such as "the pot is different from the cloth," a cognition of their non-difference never arises.
As for the second [alternative], however, how could passages such as "two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) be weak? For there is no difference in their being sublated.
Nor does this lead to the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Because it possesses greater force due to its established validity; because that validity is ascertained through investigation;
and because the mere fact of being prohibitive is not a sufficient reason [for its sublation].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that [the general injunction] "one should not kill" and so forth would subvert specific Vedic texts such as "the Agniṣomīya [animal is to be sacrificed].
Nor does this result in an inability to determine the relative strength or weakness of statements regarding difference and non-difference;
for that determination is made on the basis of criteria such as the lack of scope (niravakāśatva) for one or the other.
Furthermore, it has been elaborated elsewhere that it is precisely the statements regarding difference that lack any scope [for application].
Now, one might object: it is not possible for the scriptures concerning non-difference to be merely reiterative (anuvādaka), because non-difference is not established by perception.

Moreover, mere attainment [of a fact through other means] is not the cause for a statement being a restatement (anuvāda), because since attainment could occur for everything through inference, it would follow that even a mere scriptural statement would be a restatement. Therefore, he says: "For not... The syntactical connection is: "Thus, this sentence would not be a restatement."

This is universally accepted as being merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*) for the purpose of refuting the objection that [the definition] would lead to an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*). Since there is no fault in explaining what is already established by perception, it explains the nature of causality as obtained through inference in the form of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The underlying intention is that causality cannot be perceived because it involves factors such as time.

The inclusion of "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*) is because positive concomitance alone—expressed as "when X exists, Y exists"—is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), as seen in the cases of "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and "nameability" (*abhidheyatva*).

Regarding the formulation of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as "in the absence of X, there is the absence of Y," since this would otherwise be subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—as in the case of a human horn and a rabbit's horn—the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) must be included. Nor does deviation occur even in such a case where the positive and negative concomitances are established otherwise;
for [the definition] must also be qualified by the condition of being "not established otherwise" (*ananyathāsiddha*).

In reality, however, since the property of possessing positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekavattva*) is pervaded by being a necessary antecedent (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*), when that [necessary antecedence] is established by means of it, the status of fire as a cause—defined as being a necessary antecedent that is not otherwise accounted for (*ananyathāsiddhaniyatapūrvavṛttitva*)—is established, because the fire’s necessary antecedence with respect to the cessation of snow is sublated by its being otherwise accounted for (*anyathāsiddha*). This is how it should be understood.

Having thus refuted the first position—that conventional difference is sublatable—he restates and refutes the second position with the words "If [it be said]... The phrase "there would be no dispute" means that if one accepts the unsublatability—which is synonymous with ultimate reality—of the difference taught by the Śruti, then one would be accepting exactly what we ourselves maintain; consequently, there would be no dispute between us.
In this way, a refutation has been stated while provisionally accepting the opponent’s claim that difference is merely conventional.

Now, he states that the difference is not merely conventional by means of the passage beginning with "From what [reason]? and ending with "due to equality. The meaning is: for what reason is the difference propounded by the Śruti accepted as being merely conventional?

He anticipates the following objection: "Advaita" means ultimate non-duality. Regarding the phrase "of the resolution of the contradiction": if both scriptural passages were to establish ultimate difference and non-difference respectively, they would indeed be mutually contradictory; therefore, the resolution is effected by accepting that the scripture concerning difference has a conventional (vyāvahārika) difference as its purport, while the scripture concerning non-duality has ultimate non-duality as its purport.

The meaning is that this is equally applicable even if one accepts that the scriptural texts concerning difference intend ultimate difference, while the scriptural texts concerning non-difference intend merely apparent non-difference, as a way to resolve the contradiction.
Now, it might be argued: "We accept only the first position—that conventional difference is sublatable;
and it should not be said that in such a case the scripture would lack authority because it apprehends a sublatable object."

He raises an objection, saying "But surely" (*nanu*), on the grounds that it is precisely the sublation of the object that constitutes the purport of the scripture (*śruti-tātparya-viṣaya-artha-bādha*) which is the cause of its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*), whereas the sublation of what is merely expressed by the scripture (*śruti-pratipādya-bādha*) is not such a cause; furthermore, although difference (*bheda*) is indeed expressed by the scripture, it does not fall within the scope of the scripture's intended purport. [The author replies: "[Of] that which has been established as the object to be taught"—that is, of that which is intended and constitutes the object of the purport. "[Otherwise]"—if one were to admit the lack of authority of the scripture due to the sublation of that [intended object], then even the portion consisting of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), such as "The divine oxen carry [the gods] while standing on their backs," would likewise be devoid of authority.
Because the upward movement of the gods' cows, which is declared in the Śruti, is sublated;
and because in other systems the non-authoritativeness of arthavādas is accepted, it is specified as "in the Mīmāṃsaka view.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Of the Śrutis... The connection is: "because the Śrutis merely restate distinctions [already established]."

Since there can be no restatement (*anuvāda*) of that which has not been previously apprehended, he says: "apprehended through perception" (*pratyakṣaprāpta*). This means: "apprehended through perception such as 'I am not omniscient'.

He states the purpose of the restatement: "not here, not manifold" (*neha nānā*). He provides the resolution by way of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*): "no. [The opponent objects: "But surely, since the sentence 'not here, not manifold' negates difference—meaning that there is no difference either in Brahman or in the world—it is appropriate for it to serve as a restatement of difference for the sake of its own negation, [just as] the passage beginning with 'two birds' (*dvā suparṇā*) functions as a restatement of difference."

Regarding the verse beginning with "dvā suparṇā" (Two birds...), since it establishes only difference and does not negate non-difference, how can it serve as a restatement of non-difference for the purpose of negation by the passage "neha nānāsti kiñcana" (There is no diversity here)? To this he says: "Of difference... For difference consists in mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
And that [non-existence], having identity (*tādātmya*) as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), is itself of the nature of a negation of that [identity].

Thus, since a sentence establishing such a difference is of the nature of a negation of identity, it is entirely appropriate that the passage "neha nānāsti kiñcana," etc., which serves for negation, should be a restatement of difference. This is the meaning. By the phrase "by this" (*etena*), [he refers to the following:]...

The meaning is as follows: when there is a doubt as to whether the abandonment of the meaning of the non-difference scriptures (*abheda-śruti*) should occur because of conflict with the difference scriptures (*bheda-śruti*), or whether the abandonment of the meaning of the difference scriptures should occur because of conflict with the non-difference scriptures, the Advaitin has argued that since the non-difference scripture is stronger as a prohibitive statement, the very thing prohibited—namely, difference—must be abandoned in conflict with it. That argument is refuted by showing that the difference scripture is likewise prohibitive.
[Objection: But it is not proper to say that the non-difference scripture is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*), for non-difference is not established by any other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Nor should it be said that attainment [of the object] occurs through inference; for in the case of a restatement (*anuvāda*), attainment through direct perception alone is the determining factor, whereas attainment through inference is not. Therefore, he says: "Not so" (*na hi*). Regarding the phrase "that being the case": the logical connection is that if attainment through direct perception alone were the cause of a restatement, then the sentence "Fire is the remedy for cold" would not be a restatement.
To the question "Why?", he states the passage beginning with "of fire" and ending with "establishing."

For fire’s status as the cause of the cessation of cold is established by the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)— namely, that when fire is present, cold ceases, and otherwise it does not— and thus it is reached through inference that the cessation of cold is produced from fire because it follows its positive and negative concomitance.
It is precisely this fact that this sentence is accepted as restating (*anuvādaka*).
Nor should it be said that even in that case, it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) of what has already been apprehended through perception;
