for the meaning is that the relation of cause and effect, being composed of factors such as time, is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). To avoid the objection that this might be an unintended consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he states that it is "accepted by all" (*sarvasammatam*).
It has been stated that the attainment of oneness through the inference based on the statement "not here, not manifold" occurs;
or alternatively, let there be the attainment of non-duality due to a lack of understanding of the meaning of the Śruti text "That thou art.
And indeed, there is a negation by another Śruti text of that which has been attained through a lack of understanding of the Śruti's meaning.
There is a negation of the view that *iṣṭāpūrta* (sacrificial and charitable works) constitutes the supreme human goal.
Alternatively, let the attainment of non-duality occur through a beginningless succession of false scriptures (*duḥśāstra-paramparā*) by way of tradition;
for there exists a negation of what is attained through such erroneous intellects.
Regarding this, some indeed say: "In the beginning, this was non-existence alone, one only, without a second; from that non-existence, existence was born.
To this [the teacher] said: "But how, my dear, could it be so?
How could existence be born from non-existence? and so forth.
For here, the Buddhists' position that non-existence can be a cause is refuted.

Therefore, scriptural passages such as "Two birds... are the authority for the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). However, passages such as "He attains supreme equality with the wise Brahman" and "Having attained My own nature" cannot even be suspected of being intended to convey a conventional distinction.
The difference [between liberation and bondage] exists because it establishes a distinction;
indeed, the difference between a jar, a cloth, and so forth is easily perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

To establish that the Śruti concerning non-duality (*advaita*) is merely reiterative (*anuvādaka*), he shows the attainment of non-duality by another method—namely, "or else" (*yadvā*). The meaning intended as the primary purport (*tātparya-viṣaya*) of the Śruti "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) has been shown by the Author of the Sūtras himself to be of the nature of a similarity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—like the expression "Devadatta is a lion"—on the grounds that [the soul] has that [Brahman] as its essence by virtue of having its qualities as its substance (*tad-guṇa-sāratvāt*); the sense is that this was not fully understood [by the opponent].

To the question, "Where is a negation seen of that which has been established by one scriptural passage through a lack of understanding of its meaning? he says: "There is [such a case]. The scripture states: "The deluded, considering sacrificial rites performed for desire (*kāmyakarman*)—such as *iṣṭāpūrta*—which concern non-supreme objects, to be the best, do not know any other higher good. Having experienced [the fruits] on the back of the firmament (*nāka*) produced by their good deeds, they enter this world or even a lower one. This refers to that which was established by the intent of such scriptural passages as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," etc., due to a lack of understanding of its true purpose.
Having restated [the subject] with the first half-verse, he refutes its being a means to the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha) with the second half-verse;
for censure has as its purport prohibition.
Furthermore, there is no other source from which such an action could be obtained.
Therefore, it must be said that the very failure to understand the purport of the scripture is what leads to that [result].

The sense is that the same applies here as well. Regarding the phrase "of *iṣṭāpūrta*": *iṣṭa* means sacrifice (*yajana*), and *pūrta* means such things as the giving of food; the meaning is "of those two.
The lengthening of the vowel [in *iṣṭāpūrtayoḥ*] is according to the Vedic usage, based on the rule "it is seen in others as well" (*anyeṣām api dṛśyate*).
And in the Śruti, there is the singular form for a *dvandva* compound, according to the rule:
"Every *dvandva* optionally becomes singular. It is the most excellent means for attaining the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*).
Anything else that is superior is the worshipful Supreme Brahman; that is to say, they do not perceive— that is, they do not know— His grace.
The word “supreme” (variṣṭham) is understood [to carry over].

He shows that the attainment of non-duality occurs even by another method—namely, with the words “or else” (athavā). To the question, "How can there be a negation by the beginningless Veda of that which has been obtained through a modern succession of false scriptures? he says: "by way of a stream that is beginningless.
The sense is that, according to the statement, "for conventions (samayas) that have existed from beginningless time are indeed 'by way of a stream'."
He clarifies what is established by this scripture and what is being negated with the words "atra hi" (for here).
The word "iti" indicates the conclusion of the section demonstrating [the opponent's] position.

He concludes with "tasmāt" (therefore); the meaning is that, according to the reasoning stated, since difference lacks even a conventional status, it cannot be the object of a restatement (*anuvāda*).

He states that "the highest" [is the state] because it is impossible even to suspect that the scriptural and traditional texts concerning liberation refer to a conventional distinction; for the sense is that a conventional distinction is not tenable in liberation.

Having thus presented three proofs for the difference between selves, he addresses the previous objection raised in the passage beginning with "by this, the proof for the difference between jars, cloths, and so forth, is refuted"—namely, that [the difference between objects] is easily established. The sense is that no further demonstration is required, as both the substratum and the counter-correlate are perceptible, leaving no room for the previous doubt.

[Objection: But surely the Lord is not attained through inference alone, because the Lord is to be understood solely through scripture (*śāstra*). If [the scripture] is rooted in tradition (*āgama*), then since it does not depend on itself, how can it be considered a restatement (*anuvāda*)? To this, he states another way of attaining [the knowledge]: "Or else... [He says] "due to non-comprehension," which means due to a failure to comprehend the intended meaning (*tātparya*), that is, from mere superficial cognition (*āpātapratīti*).
To the question, "How can an object obtained through the knowledge of a modern person be a restatement (*anuvāda*) by the beginningless Śruti?", he says: "It exists.

The sense is that even ignorance is beginningless by way of its continuous flow (*pravāha*). Regarding the phrase "negation," the words "regarding sacrifices and works of public utility" (*iṣṭāpūrtaṃ manyamānāḥ*) are to be supplied as the remainder.
It should be understood that although a direct negation is heard here, [the meaning] is understood from a deprecatory explanatory passage (*nindārthavāda*).

[Objection: Is it not the case that this attainment [of the goal] results solely from a failure to understand the meaning of the scripture? [Response: No, because it is possible through the scriptures and other means as well. [Objection: If so, why is that? [Response: Because of the designation [in the scripture]: "That flowery speech which the learned proclaim... To show the pervasiveness of the subject matter, he states another form of attainment: "Or else" (*athavā*). Anticipating the doubt—how can this be so given that the convention (*samaya*) is recent—he says: "by way of a continuous stream" (*pravāhataḥ*). Some, namely the proponents of Śūnya (the Śūnyavādins), say: "Prior to this world, before its manifestation, there was only the non-existent, the void, without a second; from that non-existent, this existent world came into being."
They say, "It was born.

To this, the teacher said to the disciple, "O you who are worthy of the Soma, for what reason could it be so?"—the meaning being that [he spoke] with the thought, "How could the existent be born from the non-existent?

Furthermore, because there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence of sentences concerning difference and non-difference, and because in the sentence concerning difference there is the presence of the words "yat" and "tat" as well as the hearing of another thing to be enjoined.

The point is that since the statements regarding difference and non-difference are not in proximity [to one another], and because the statement of difference is recited alongside an accepted alternative meaning, it is not a case of a prohibition based on a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
As for the claim that the statement of difference is weak because it merely restates what is already established—
that is not so.
Because the corroboration by many authorities is a quality (*guṇa*) insofar as it serves as a cause for strengthening [the truth],
the charge that the statement of difference is redundant is thereby refuted.
Furthermore, even if it were redundant, there is no fault, because its meaning does not contradict its truthfulness.
In reality, however, there is no futility even if it is a restatement (anuvāda),

because there is deviation [from the rule] in the case of other recensions (śākhāntara) that have set forth the same subject matter for different classes of qualified practitioners (adhikāribheda). Furthermore, if one were to add the qualification "provided it has not set forth [the same matter] for different classes of qualified practitioners," the reason would be unestablished (asiddhi).
Furthermore, it is directed against one who does not accept that perception grasps the determination of difference through the faculty of speech;
moreover, there is a deviation [in the argument] in the statement "one should not harm any living beings," because for no one is there the possibility of engaging in the harming of all beings.
If it is argued that there is novelty (apūrvatā) regarding a single part [of the object], this is the same for me as well, since every particular distinction is unattained by perception.

Furthermore, there is a deviation [from the rule] in the statement "Brahman is bliss" (*ānandaṃ brahmaṇaḥ*), which restates what is already established by the experience of happiness during deep sleep.

If it is argued that the word "that" (*tat*) is used for the purpose of prescribing its existence across the three periods of time (past, present, and future), this is equally applicable to the case at hand as well;

for, according to the reasoning already stated, the perception of difference depends upon the Veda. Thus, he cites an unambiguous scriptural text regarding the reality of difference, beginning with the words "The Supreme," and so forth.
Now, it might be argued: "In this case, only similarity and so forth are mentioned, not difference;
nor can that [difference] be inferred by stating its pervader. If it is then asked, "In that case, the citation as scriptural authority (*āgama*) would be untenable," we say: no.

Similarity consists in possessing many properties belonging to that [object] while being distinct from it; thus, because it contains the element of difference, one cannot argue that "residing in that" alone should be the definition. For if that were so, it would lead to the absurd consequence that a thing itself could be conventionally designated as similar to itself.
For this very reason, they say that in such passages as "the sky has the form of the sky," the intended meaning is precisely the negation of any other similarity.

Now, one might object: "Even so, your [position] regarding the similarity of Brahman contradicts your own established doctrine. This is not so; for we apply a restriction by following the definitive scriptural determination: "excluding the activity of the world" (*jagadvyāpāravarjam*).

And thus, even for coexistence (*sahabhāva*), when there is a difference from that [other], there is the connection with its activity. "Those beginning with 'containing difference' (*bhedagarbha*)," etc.: "Having attained the supreme light, he manifests in his own form; where Māyā does not exist, how much less others who are followers of Hari"—this and so forth should be inferred. Nor should it be said that this is liberation with attributes (*saguṇa-mukti*).
There is no evidence for a twofold nature of liberation;
if one were to postulate it on the grounds that one's own action would otherwise be inexplicable, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Or, let such twofoldness exist, since the statement regarding equality—“having shaken off merit and demerit” (*puṇyapāpe vidhūya*)—speaks of being stainless (*nirañjana*).
Because in the statement regarding attendance (*upasatti*), which consists of affection, there is a mention of abandonment in the form of a false appearance;

and because in the final [statement], where it says "this is illusion" (*māyā*), there is a mention of the absence of illusion, it does not have as its purport liberation characterized by qualities (*saguṇa-mukti*). Having thus established the difference between selves, he establishes the difference between insentient objects—starting with "pot, cloth," etc.—meaning that the perception "this is not a pot" [establishes such difference].

"By another Śruti passage" means by such passages as: "Thinking that sacrifice and public works (iṣṭāpūrta) are the highest, the deluded know of no other good. "After liberation" means because that which is rooted in ignorance cannot persist once liberation has occurred. "It is indeed easy" means because [the two] are fit to be the counter-correlates (pratiyogin) of dharma.
"Of sacrifice and public works" refers to: "Thinking that sacrifice and public works are the highest, the deluded know of no other good."
The meaning of this Atharvaṇa Śruti—"Having experienced [the fruits] on the back of the firmament (nāka) resulting from their good deeds, they enter this world or one even lower"—is as follows:
*iṣṭa* refers to sacrifice (*yajana*), and *pūrta* refers to the giving of food and so forth.

Regarding the lengthening of the vowel after the word *iṣṭa*, it is stated in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*: "The rule 'it is seen [to apply] after other [words] as well' [Pāṇini 6.3.137] applies here."

They cause others to know— that is, they find— the other [kind of] excellence, which is liberation characterized by the attainment of the Supreme Self, or Brahman (using the causative suffix *ṇic* in its own sense).
Having experienced happiness on the back of the firmament, in the place of heaven achieved through good deeds,
they [return to] this world, and so forth.
The word "vā" (or) indicates an alternative arrangement (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*).

Having performed optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) directed toward Viṣṇu—preceded by the knowledge that He is the supreme among all like a king, yet preceded by a lack of full knowledge regarding His specific attributes—they also eventually dedicate even those rites intended for other deities to Viṣṇu alone.
Having enjoyed heaven, they enter this world, that is, the world of human beings.

Those who possess such knowledge as "others are equal to the Blessed One" or "the Blessed One is inferior to others"—unworthy persons such as Duryodhana and his ilk—are the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Having enjoyed heaven through the spiritual power (*tejas*) of the teachers Drona and others to whom they were offered, they subsequently enter, in succession, a state even more degraded than that—consisting of darkness (*tamas*) and the like—which is devoid of rebirth.
For this has been stated in the *Atharvaṇa-bhāṣya*:
"He who considers Viṣṇu, who is superior to all, to be like a king..."
"He who performs sacrifices goes to the human world, being the most ignorant of those lacking equanimity. Regarding this, the specific detail is to be understood from the *Gītātātparya-nirṇaya*.
Likewise, by means of censure, the Śruti negates the status of sacrificial rites (*iṣṭāpūrta*) and the like as the supreme goal of man for those who know them to be such;
for it is impossible for an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) to terminate its purpose anywhere other than in the context of an injunction or a prohibition.
And a prohibition must be preceded by a prior attainment;
that attainment must be stated, and it occurs through either perception or inference.
Since heaven and so forth, as well as their status as human goals and their capacity to produce them, are beyond the senses, perception is not applicable.
Because it is impossible to apprehend the subject, the probandum, the reason, and so forth, inference itself cannot function.

Thus, for those who do not understand the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of statements defining heaven—such as "that which is not mixed with suffering"—and of injunctions such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma," there exists an attainment consisting of the delusion that heaven and the like, which are actually to be accomplished through sacrifices and other rites, constitute the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*).

The intention is that just as that which has become its object is negated by Śruti, so too should it be here. Regarding the phrase "as beginningless by way of a continuous flow" (*pravāhato'nādirūpayā*): this is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt as to how this adventitious [property] can be restated by Śruti, which is beginningless.

Furthermore, "beginninglessness by way of a continuous flow" must be defined as consisting of a form (*rūpa*), namely: being the locus of such a form at a time common to all [its] substrata, while possessing the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) relative to the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) which is the locus of such a form; thus, it is beginningless by way of a flow in terms of that specific form.

The conclusion of the definition-statement beginning with "of that which is joined with a *mandāra* flower" and ending with "in a single stream," etc., regarding the aforementioned meaning, has been demonstrated by us elsewhere; however, for fear of making this work too voluminous, it is not presented here and should be inferred by the wise themselves. Regarding the passage, "Now, some say... (*taddhaika āhuḥ*): In the sixth chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, after stating his own view—that "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second"—the Buddhist doctrine is restated through the words "Now, some say... and so forth. This is for the purpose of refuting it with the subsequent passage, "How indeed, my dear, could that be so? and so on.

Likewise, here too, the beginningless non-duality—which, in its continuous flow, has not yet attained the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)—is negated by the Śruti that teaches difference in the form of a denial of such identity; this is the meaning.
In this regard, although all living beings harbor the delusion of being independent masters with respect to their own bodies, homes, and so forth.

And since that [perception] possesses a nature common to both existence and non-existence, it is indeed of the nature of an error consisting in the identity with the Blessed Lord; thus, its occurrence is established even in the fourth case.

That this perception is of the nature of direct experience has been demonstrated by the Teacher himself in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya*. Nevertheless, it should be understood that although such [perception] exists, because it is so subtle and can only be known as an error of identity through the requirement of many supporting arguments, the demonstration was performed for only the first three cases. "It could not even be suspected" means that there is no possibility of sublation for those things existing in liberation; this is the intended sense.

"Pot," etc. Among the Advaitins, in the Māyāvāda view, since difference is admitted to be within the scope of error (*bhrānti*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) if one seeks to prove mere difference.

In the Bhāskara view, since it is admitted that even pots, cloths, and so forth are non-different insofar as they have the nature of Being (*sad-rūpa*), while difference exists only in the form of "pot-ness" and so on, there is the fallacy of *siddhasādhanatā* if one seeks to prove only that [latter] difference.
For both [schools], the non-co-referentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) with identity (*tādātmya*)...

Since difference (*bheda*) is not admitted anywhere [in our system], proving absolute non-difference would result in the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*). However, because the Māyāvādins admit that the unreal nature of jars, cloths, and so forth is none other than Brahman, the qualification "ultimately real" (*pāramārthika*) regarding difference does not result in the fallacy of an unestablished qualification for the Māyāvādin; rather, for Bhāskara, it results in the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*). Therefore, setting aside the proof of difference, the absence of ultimate identity (*tādātmya*) alone has been proven. And since that is precisely what the Advaitins do not accept, there is no fallacy of proving the already established.

Although it appears that the qualification "ultimately real" (*tāttvikatvam*) is meaningful [only] in the sense that the proof of the general absence (consisting of the absence delimited by identity) can be accomplished even without it,
nevertheless, the absence of that [identity] which is to be established must be established as being ultimately real itself.

This is for the purpose of indicating that an absence of lower ontological status lacks the capacity to contradict [the presence of identity], and thus an inference based on such an absence would be incapable of removing doubt regarding that [identity].

Alternatively, it should be understood that [the author] has included that [identity] within the scope of the counter-correlate of the absence which constitutes the probandum (sādhya), out of a distaste for the laborious effort involved in demonstrating that the opponent's objection—namely, the impossibility of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) due to the breakdown of the pervasion of the absence of the reason by the identity with the absence of the probandum based on an apparent identity (*prātibhāsikatādātmya*)—is untenable because the locus of such an imposed entity is unestablished due to its non-existence.

Although, according to the opponent, the identity consisting in possessing the status of being real is established as being the very nature of Brahman, and that is also accepted by them even in the case of a jar and so forth.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the occurrence of the two subsequent inferences located at the conclusion of this very text.
Thus, it may be asked: how can the apprehension of pervasion (vyāpti) occur in the case of negative concomitance (vyatireka)?

Nevertheless, it should be understood that because the negative concomitance is ascertained in the case of a jar, even if there is doubt regarding it in another jar, the ascertainment of pervasion occurs by setting aside that doubt through the force of favorable reasoning (anukūlatarka), such as: "If the jar were identical with a cloth, it would have to produce the effects of a cloth."

Because it is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) whose probandum is non-existence, there is no charge here of an "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*). This is made explicit in the root text itself immediately following with the words "but [the charge of] an unestablished qualification. Therefore, there is no room for that doubt. Having thus stated the attainment of non-duality through inference, he states its attainment through scripture as well, beginning with "Or else," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because of a failure to understand the meaning of the scripture": this means because of a failure to understand the meaning that constitutes the intended purport (*tātparya*) of the scripture. This is because if the non-duality established by one scripture were negated by another scripture, it would result in the invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) of that scripture. Thus, [the objection is raised]: "Because of a failure to understand the meaning of the scripture. This means: because of a failure to understand the meaning that is the object of the scripture's purport.

This means that it is because the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the scripture regarding such objects as "similarity to that" has not been understood. Regarding the phrase "of *iṣṭāpūrta*": the meaning is that there is a prohibition—such as in the passage, "The deluded, considering sacrifice and works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*) to be the highest, know nothing else that is better"—against the status of being a means to a heaven characterized by impermanent pleasure. This [prohibition] applies to one who has failed to understand that [heaven] is actually a means for attaining knowledge of the Supreme Self, which is the referent of the word "heaven" in the intended scope of scriptures such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice.
Here, *iṣṭa* refers to sacrifice, and *pūrta* refers to giving food and so forth.

He states that non-duality (*advaita*) is attained even from a mere semblance of words accompanied by reasoning, saying: "Or else" (*athavā*). [This refers to] a succession of false scriptures (*duḥśāstra-paramparā*), wherein each subsequent illusory scripture depends upon its predecessor.

Now, one might ask: how can non-duality, which is established by a modern scripture, be negated by the beginningless Veda? To this he replies: "In the form of being beginningless through its continuous flow" (*pravāhato'nādirūpayā*). Regarding the state of being beginningless through its continuous flow, it is stated in the *Mandāramañjarī* that it is "the state of being a flow which is the counter-positive of a destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) that does not reside in a time delimited by a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) whose counter-positives are multiple flows falling within a single continuous stream."

And therein, in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to actions such as the production of a jar that belong to a beginningless continuum, the phrase "not being a locus of non-existence in time" (*kālāvṛttitvānadhikaraṇa*) has the sense of "pervading time. Furthermore, the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of an object belonging to a beginningless continuum does not pervade time; for even though it exists throughout all time subsequent to that continuum, it does not exist throughout all time delimited by the prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*) of the many objects constituting that continuum. It is for the sake of obtaining this [distinction] that the term "delimited" (*avacchinna*) is included.
However, this [definition] does not include the constituent elements of the definition because they are purposeless.

If one were to state merely "the state of being a continuous flow that pervades time," there would be no inclusion of mental modifications (*manovṛtti*) that constitute an impermanent beginningless flow; therefore, the qualification is extended to "being the counter-positive of such a destruction.

Although it is true that even the destructions of desire, karma, and so forth—which constitute an beginningless flow—cannot individually possess the property of pervading all time, [the definition remains valid].
Nevertheless, the word "streaming" (*pravāhin*) is used to indicate that pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) is intended in the sense of being the destruction of the entities constituting that stream.
Even so, this does not include the stream of destructions of desire, karma, and so forth;
for the destruction of the entities constituting those [desires and karmas] is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*).
Nevertheless, there is no fault here, because only positive entities (*bhāva*) are the objects of definition.

Even if non-entities (*abhāva*) were also objects of definition, "beginninglessness in terms of a stream" should be understood as the state of being a stream that pervades the time delimited by the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of the individual members constituting that stream.

By this, it is shown that the literal definition [of beginninglessness] suffers from the defect of under-extension (*avyāpti*) with respect to the final individual member constituting a beginningless stream.
Because its destruction does not occur during the time delimited by the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the entity that constitutes a member of that stream.

Likewise, since the state of not being the locus of non-occurrence during such a time is equivalent to occurring during such a time, and since this [property] is common to all entities constituting a stream that has a beginning, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*).
If one intends the state of not being the locus of non-occurrence during *any* such time—which effectively amounts to occurring during *all* such times—then there is impossibility (*asambhava*).

The objection that [the definition] is redundant because no destruction whatsoever exists throughout such an entire duration, and that the term "delimited" (*avacchinna*) is therefore superfluous, is hereby refuted.

Some, however, maintain that by the phrase "belonging to a single stream" (*ekapravāha*), what is intended is the state of being the counter-positive of a destruction occurring at a time delimited by the prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*) of all those individual streams that constitute a single stream. In that context, the inclusion of the term "delimited" serves to exclude streams that have a beginning (*sādi*).

And since the destructions of the constituent parts of that [jar] exist during the time delimited by the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the first individual instance of those constituents, there is no fault.

Although it would be possible to avoid that fault even by stipulating existence during a time delimited by all prior non-existences in a general sense, nevertheless— because it would be redundant to include an infinite number of non-distinctive prior non-existences— only the prior non-existences of the members of that specific stream are to be included.

Nor should it be argued that the definition is impossible because even the destructions (*dhvaṃsa*) of the entities constituting an endless stream do not each exist during the time delimited by all such prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*). This is because what is intended is: being the counter-positive of a destruction which is the locus of a destruction existing at a time delimited by its respective prior non-existence, and which itself is a destruction belonging to that very stream. Furthermore, one should not argue that such a formulation is redundant—that it would suffice merely to state "existing at a time delimited by its respective prior non-existence and belonging to that stream"—and thus the inclusion of the term "counter-positive of a destruction" is fruitless. This is because [the latter alone] would fail to exclude cases where an entity belongs to a stream but does not possess the nature of a destruction.
They say that this is because there is no room for futility [in the arrangement].

And thus, since even false doctrines (duḥśāstra) possess the aforementioned beginninglessness, non-duality (advaita) could indeed be established from time immemorial; therefore, it is logical that it should be negated by the Veda—this is the intended meaning.

Regarding the term "negation" (niṣedha): the meaning is that after restating the opponent's view with the words "it is indeed non-existent" (*asadeva*), etc., its negation is carried out with the words "but how [could it be]? (*kutastu*), etc.

In response to the inquiry, "According to whose opinion is this [duality] attained, and what is being negated here?", he says: "For here... (*atra hi*). He concludes that the scripture beginning with "Two birds" (*dvā suparṇā*) has as its purport ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*), saying: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that the sublation of the non-dual scriptures (*advaita-śruti*) is established by the aforementioned method.

To easily dispel the suspicion that [the scripture] might have as its purport conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*), he cites other scriptural passages as well: "The supreme... (*paramam*). "When the seer sees the golden-hued one, the agent, the Lord, the Person who is the source of Brahman... (*yadā paśyaḥ paśyate rukmavarṇam kartāram īśam puruṣam brahmayonim*).
Then the wise one, having shaken off merit and demerit, becomes stainless and attains supreme equality:
"He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the cave of the heart, in the highest heaven—he, together with the all-knowing Brahman, enjoys all desires."

The meaning of the passage beginning with "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature" is as follows: [The phrase] "after liberation" implies that since the meaning of words such as "equality" (*sāmya*) consists in possessing qualities of the same class while being distinct from that [Brahman], and since the state of being in the same location as that [Brahman] while being distinct from it is precisely what constitutes "co-existence" (*sahabhāva*), and since this [co-existence], having been stated as the fruit of the vision of Brahman, cannot be of the nature of ignorance (*avidyaka*) because it occurs subsequent to the cessation of ignorance; such is the intended sense.

Having thus established the difference between selves, he also establishes the difference between non-selves—referring to "pots, cloths, and so forth. The phrase "is indeed easy" means that since both the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) are perceptible, there is no room for the aforementioned doubt.
However, in the case of a difference involving supersensible objects (*atīndriya*), one should cite the perception of the Lord (*Īśvara*) as before.
Furthermore, perception does not have merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*) objects as its domain.
Because there is a lack of evidence;
and because there would be a contradiction regarding whether this very object is conventional or non-conventional.
Nor should it be argued: "Even if difference were perceptible, what is the proof for its ultimate reality?"

Since difference is perceived solely through existence (*sattva*), and since that [existence] is ultimately real due to the absence of sublation— this is explained at length elsewhere— he shows that its attainment occurs by another method as well, with the words "or else" (*yadvā*). According to the principle stated in the *Brahma-sūtra*— "The designation [of the soul] is based on its having that [Brahman] as its essence because its qualities are essentially those [of Brahman]"— the meaning intended as the primary purport of the Śruti text "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) is either "you are like That," as in the case of "Devadatta is a lion," or, according to the method explained in the *Tattvanirṇaya*, by splitting the words as "not-that thou art" (*atat tvam asi*), it means "you are different from That."

The meaning is that during the state of not fully understanding that [reality], unity is perceived as the actual fact, and the statement "not here is any diversity" merely restates that. One might object that it is unprecedented for what is established by one scriptural passage to be negated by another; therefore, he says: "It exists. The intended meaning of the scriptural injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" is that desireless action directed toward the Lord, who is denoted by the word "heaven," must be performed.

In the state of ignorance regarding that [Reality], deluded people—regarding the optional ritual acts (*kāmyakarman*) pertaining to non-supreme objects, such as sacrifices and works of public utility (*iṣṭāpūrta*), as the highest and perceiving no other good—have their position restated in the words, "They do not know any other good. This is then refuted by the statement, "Having experienced [the fruits] on the back of the celestial vault (Nāka) produced by their good deeds, they enter this world or one even lower.
For the purpose of such censure is to effect a prohibition. The sense is that there is no other source for the attainment of such ritual action.

*Iṣṭa* refers to sacrifice; *pūrta* refers to the giving of food and so forth. He shows the attainment of non-duality by another method with the words "Alternatively" (*athavā*). Now, one might ask: how can the negation of non-duality—already established by the beginningless Veda and the tradition of scriptures composed by contemporary disputants—be effected? To this he says: "by its beginningless nature. Since [the Veda] cannot be beginningless in its essential form (*svarūpa*), he says: "by way of its continuous flow" (*pravāhataḥ*). As it has been said:
"For conventions have indeed proceeded from beginningless time by way of a continuous stream.

Since it is not observed that there is a prohibition by the Śruti against what has been established through a succession of bad treatises, he says: "And it exists" (*asti ca*). He demonstrates that very point with: "In that regard" (*tad dhi*). That is, in that context where the causality of the world is to be investigated;
"some" refers to the proponents of Śūnyavāda.
They say it is well known.
What do they say? "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (asat). Here, by the word "non-existent," the void (śūnya) is meant.

Some maintain that there is nothing else apart from its own effect; they deny a second auxiliary cause for the void other than the void itself, [expressing this as] "without a second. He states another opposing view: "Therefore... That is to say: "Therefore, the existent world arises from the non-existent. They refute the position thus restated with the question: "Why? The word *tu* serves to set aside the prima facie view. "O Somya, how could it be so? How indeed could it be that 'the non-existent was'? It could not be so at all."

"And because there is no means of valid knowledge [for such a claim]," he said. He refutes another contradictory position with the question: "How?"—meaning, how could the existent arise from the non-existent?
For it has never been observed, and thus it is logically impossible for the non-existent to be a cause.
The connection is that there is a negation in such passages as these.

Since it is not clearly understood here what is being negated—given that something has been established according to the opinion of certain [schools]—the author says: "In this regard" (*atre*). "Buddhist" (*bauddha*) means the Mādhyamika, who is a partisan of one school of Buddhism.

He concludes with: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*); the meaning is that, according to the reasoning stated, because [the object] lacks conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*) and because there is no basis for restatement (*anuvādakatva*).

Thinking that the effort required to refute the suspicion that the cited scriptural texts on difference might be referring to conventional difference is overly burdensome, he cites those scriptural texts on difference that cannot possibly be suspected of referring to conventional difference, beginning with the verse "The Supreme... (*paramam*). The meaning of the scripture "When he sees" (*yadā paśya*) is as follows:
one who sees is a "seer" (*paśya*), namely, the individual soul (*jīva*).

When one directly perceives the Supreme Person—the golden-hued creator of the universe, its controller, and the progenitor of the four-faced Brahmā—then that living being, possessing immediate knowledge, destroys both undesirable merit and demerit; becoming stainless, he attains equality with the Supreme Person through his own appropriate knowledge, bliss, and other attributes.

This is also the meaning of the Śruti passage beginning with "He who knows": the qualified seeker who knows the Brahman deposited within the cave of the heart in the supreme ether (parame vyoman) enjoys all desires according to his capacity along with the wise Brahmā.

Regarding the statement from the *Gītā*, "This is knowledge" (*idaṃ jñānam*), the meaning is that by relying upon this aforementioned knowledge, those who have attained a state of having attributes identical to Mine—such as knowledge and bliss—are not born at the time of creation and do not suffer at the time of dissolution.

The point is that since the equality, co-existence, and similarity mentioned here cannot exist without difference, their existence [of difference] is established. As for the phrase "after liberation": since the shaking off of merit and demerit, the enjoyment of all objects, and the non-birth at creation are absent in *saṃsāra*, these serve to demonstrate difference after liberation.

The point is that you do not accept that even that which persists in liberation—which consists in the cessation of ignorance—is pervaded by being either ignorance or its effect, nor do you accept its empirical reality (*vyāvahārikatva*).

Furthermore, the inference is as follows: "A pot is not the locus of a real identity (*tāttvikatādātmya*) with respect to a cloth, because it is the locus of a property that is the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the cloth, which is not delimited by a delimitor of coreferentiality (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇyāvacchedaka*); otherwise [if it were], it would be like the cloth itself."

The charge of "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) is to be refuted just as it is in the inference proving the difference between selves (*ātmabheda*). Furthermore, the relationship of subject and example (*pakṣadṛṣṭāntabhāva*) between a jar and a cloth is to be illustrated (justified) by means of a mere conventional distinction (*vyāvahārikabheda*). Regarding the term "inference": the word "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Regarding the term "counter-correlative" (*pratiyogī*): the meaning is that [the jar] possesses the property of being the locus of the nature of "jar-ness," which is the counter-correlative of that absolute non-existence residing in the cloth which is not delimited by the delimitor of co-location with the counter-correlative.
Here, the term "counter-correlate" (*pratiyogipada*) refers to that which has the same primary status [as the subject].

The meaning is that since non-existence (*asattva*) has been established as the counter-correlate of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), it is impossible for a jar to be its locus (*adhikaraṇa*). "By way of negative concomitance, like a cloth" (*vyatirekeṇa paṭavat*): the point is that in the case of a cloth, because the identity with "cloth-ness" (*paṭatādātmya*) and the non-locus-status of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatvānadhikaraṇatva*) both exist, the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) are absent [therein]. And "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*)...

Although there is no possibility of the objection regarding an "unestablished qualification" (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva) on the grounds that the proponent of Māyā, who asserts the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca), does not accept an unreal identity between a jar and a cloth;

nevertheless, this objection must be understood as intended to demonstrate the extreme worthlessness of that [Māyāvāda] doctrine, since for one who accepts the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—which contradicts all means of valid cognition—this too is a conceivable consequence. This is analogous to the inference proving the difference between selves.

The meaning is that this [objection] must be answered as follows: either by noting that although a doubt such as "Is the pot possessed of a real identity with the cloth as its counter-correlative? is impossible, the pot can still be established as the subject (*pakṣa*) by the mere doubt, "Does identity with the cloth as its counter-correlative exist in the pot or not?", thereby validating the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*); or else, by arguing that in the case of a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*), the pervasion is grasped through the absence of the probans where there is an absence of the probandum, whereas here, since the absence of the probandum—namely, identity with the cloth—is well-known in the cloth itself, it cannot serve to subvert the pervasion.

Now, one might ask: "Before the difference between a jar and a cloth is established, how can there be the status of subject (*pakṣa*) and example (*dṛṣṭānta*)? To this he says: "by means of conventional difference" (*vyāvahārikabhedena*). The sense is that otherwise, since for you (the opponent) there is an absence of ultimate difference (*pāramārthikabheda*) anywhere, the employment of an inference consisting of a subject and an example would not be possible in any case whatsoever.
Here, the term "conventional" (*vyāvahārika*) is used to indicate the acceptance of the other party;
in reality, however, it is sufficient simply to say "by means of difference alone" (*bhedamātreṇaiva*).
It should be understood that there is no room for the objection, "Since you do not accept conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*), how can such a statement be made?

[This is] in the phrase "the pot" (*ghaṭa*). To prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) in the case where one does not accept identity with conventional existence (*vyāvahārika-sattā-tādātmya*), the term "real" (*tāttvika*) is used. [The term] "counter-positive" (*pratiyogin*)... [is used].

The meaning is as follows: it is because [the jar] possesses the property of being the locus of attributes such as having a conch-shaped neck (*kambugrīvādi*), which are the counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence residing in the cloth—an absolute non-existence that is not delimited by (i.e., lacks) that property which serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the counter-correlate, and which consists in the state of not contradicting the cognition of its own counter-correlate within its own locus until the production of immediate (*aparokṣa*) consciousness devoid of all mental modes (*niṣprakāraka-caitanya*).

This is the underlying point: for the opponent, who maintains that everything is illusory (*sarvamithyātva-vādin*), the non-existence of properties such as "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) is indeed admitted even in the jar itself—its own locus—just as it is admitted in a cloth or other objects.
However, the absolute absence of pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) in a cloth is co-located with its counter-positive;
therefore, it prevents the cognition of that counter-positive within its own locus.
In the case of the cloth, however, [the absence] is co-located with the counter-positive.
For this very reason, even though the absence of potness exists in a pot, there is no contradiction in the cognition of potness [in that same pot].
This cognition of the counter-positive (pratiyogipratīti) persists until the immediate, contentless realization of Brahman.
Once that [realization] has arisen, even this [cognition] becomes opposed to its own counter-positive.

And thus, the reason is the state of being the locus of properties such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva), which are the counter-correlates of that absolute absence which is devoid of that property which serves as the delimitor of the co-occurrence with the counter-correlate—namely, the property consisting in the non-opposition to the cognition of its own counter-correlate. If it were stated merely that [the property] resides in the cloth (paṭaniṣṭha), there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of the cloth itself;

for the opponent, who accepts that falsity consists in co-occurrence with one's own absolute absence, also accepts that pot-ness and other such properties are counter-correlates of the absolute absence residing in the cloth.
Therefore, it is specified as "not delimited by the delimitor of the co-occurrence with the counter-correlate."
The absolute absence of cloth-ness (*paṭatva*) in a cloth, however, is indeed delimited by the aforementioned property consisting in its non-contradiction with the cognition of its own locus.

The absolute absence of pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*), on the other hand, is not like that. Nor is it the case that the cognition of cloth-ness and so forth in a pot could only be of the nature of an error; thus, even for that [absence], there is no lack of being delimited by the delimitor of the co-location with its counter-positive (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Nor should it be argued that "cognition" is not intended here in the sense of a valid cognition (*pramā*), because the cognition of "pot-ness" in a pot is not accepted as being valid;
for what is intended by "cognition" is precisely that knowledge which is not sublated by any other knowledge.
If one were to state only "not co-located with its counter-correlative," there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a cloth itself.
For it is possible to state that the absolute absence of clothness has its counter-positive as non-co-located with itself precisely in the cloth. To explain:
"having the counter-positive as non-co-located" indeed means the absence of having the counter-positive as co-located.
The absence of counter-positive co-occurrence (*pratiyogisamānādhikaraṇatvābhāva*) is indeed something distinct.

And thus, it is entirely logical that even an absence which is co-occurrent with its own counter-positive may lack the property of "counter-positive co-occurrence" as it exists in another absence that is co-occurrent with that same counter-positive.
Therefore, it is stated [in the definition] that [the absence] is not delimited by a delimitor of counter-positive co-occurrence (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇyāvacchedakānavacchinna*).

And thus, even though there is an absence of the state of being co-located with a counter-positive that falls within the limit of non-existence (*abhāvāntaragata*), there is no lack of being a delimiting factor for co-location with the counter-positive; therefore, there is no fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
In this context, the term "counter-positive" (*pratiyogi*) refers to that which is not delimited by the delimiting factor of the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakānavacchinna*).
By this, the charge of deviation—on the grounds that even the co-location with the counter-positive might be delimited by the co-location with a specific counter-positive—is refuted.

Alternatively, the qualification "not delimited by the locus of the counter-positive" (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇyānavacchinna*) is added to exclude the fallacy (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a cloth that possesses conjunction residing in that very cloth—since such conjunction co-exists with its own absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

Now, one might object: "The opponent already accepts that there is a difference between a jar and a cloth that exists at the same level of reality as their respective substrates; so what is the point of proving it?
Nor is there any effort here to establish ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*)."
Because it is precisely those substrata (*dharmin*) that are the objects to be proven (*sādhya*).
It is their very state of being superposed upon a single locus that constitutes the oneness of insentient things; such is his [the opponent's] view.

Nor is it the case that this is stated to the student because of the contingency of proving difference, for the text proceeds according to the Māyāvāda perspective, and thus there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatva*) for the student. If you say "no" to this, it is not so.
The statement "the jar is not the locus of identity with the cloth" means that it is not superimposed upon the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) of the superimposition (āropa) of the cloth.
The extracted meaning of the probans (*hetu*)—namely, "because it is the locus of attributes entirely distinct from the attributes of the cloth"—is as follows:
the sense is that superimposition is impossible between two things that are entirely distinct when they share a single substrate.

Alternatively, there is no fault here because what is being established is precisely the absence of that identity with the insentient (jaḍa) which is accepted [by the opponent] on the basis of the meaning of such passages as "beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇam*).

Now, one might object: since the identity of all things is accepted, the qualification is unestablished (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*). To this he says: "unestablished" (*aprasiddha*). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "because it does not obstruct the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth. Since the difference from the insentient is not established prior to this inference, the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be untenable; to this he says: "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*). The difference is a factor for establishing the proof by way of its distinction from that which has a non-existent counter-correlative (*asat-pratiyogika*).
The sense is that this [objection] applies equally even to such cases as "this cloth resides in these threads.

Regarding the phrase "and inference": the ellipsis is to be supplied as "the means of valid cognition for the difference between the jar and the cloth. He states, "and the unestablished nature of the qualifier," because since non-existence (*abhāva*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), there is no fault of the probandum being unestablished (*sādhyāprasiddhi*). If the jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth—which is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of that absolute non-existence residing in the cloth which is delimited by the delimitor of co-location with the counter-positive—were to have as its locus the jar-ness, then only if jar-ness and so forth were not a property residing in the jar and existing in the cloth.
Even that [distinction] at that time—if their ultimate difference remains unestablished even today—[is untenable].
Regarding the phrase "the counter-correlate" (*pratiyogī*) and so forth: the word *pratiyogin* refers to its own counter-correlate.
Otherwise, it would follow that it lacks the capacity to exclude [the counter-positive].
The term "unconditioned" (*anavacchinna*) is a qualifier of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is to be understood as residing in some locus.

But it does not reside in an absolute non-existence that is restricted to the locus of the reason's nature, because in our own system as well as in the Nyāya system, such a non-existence is established as being pervasively present everywhere.

Regarding that co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), its delimiting factor is the common locus of both; for there is the cognition: "In a jar, the co-occurrence with the absence of ether exists, but in a cloth, it does not."

The meaning of the statement expressing that "the coexistence (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with potness, which resides in the absence of ether, is delimited by the pot and not delimited by the cloth" is as follows:

however, in the case of the statement "there is no coexistence with potness residing in the absence of ether in the cloth," it is accepted by the Sārvabhauma [Raghunātha Śiromaṇi] that the absence of the coexistence with potness residing in the absence of ether is delimited by the cloth;

for this is accepted by the author of the *Maṇi* in his definition of the *siddhānta* [of pervasion], namely: "that which is coexistent with [the probandum] but not coexistent with its counter-positive," and so forth.
And this text here proceeds according to that [definition]:

the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of that which resides in the absence of a jar (*ghaṭābhāva*)—namely, the co-existence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "jar-ness" (which is the counter-positive of the absolute absence of jar-ness)—is not the cloth (*paṭa*), but rather the jar itself.

Regarding the phrase "residing in the cloth as not delimited by that," when "non-delimitation" is taken as a qualifier of the absence qualified by its subsistence in the cloth, it effectively results in being a qualifier of the property of co-existence with "cloth-ness" residing in the absence of "jar-ness" (or "cloth-ness") located within the locus-ness (*ādheyatā*) defined by the jar (or cloth).
Because, in the absence of potness (*ghaṭatva*), that [absence] would not be a differentiator.
Thus, the meaning is: an absence which possesses a locus-ness (*ādheyatā*) relative to a cloth that is not delimited by a delimitor of co-occurrence with its own counter-positive.
And such an absolute absence of potness exists in the pot [the subject of the reason], because the property of being the counter-positive—namely, the nature of potness—is present there.

The purpose of this [definition] will become clear in the subsequent section of the text. This is stated in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by taking into account such things as the conjunction between a jar and a cloth, which are counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*) of non-pervasive absences (*avyāpyavṛttyabhāva*). Even though the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the conjunction between a jar and a cloth resides in both the jar and the cloth, there is a co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of that absence with its counter-correlative—namely, the conjunction itself—because the cloth serves as the delimiting locus (*avacchedaka*) for that co-location. Consequently, if one were to take that absolute absence residing in the cloth, a fallacy of deviation would arise with respect to the cloth and so forth.

According to the view of the author of the *Dīdhiti*, who does not accept that co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), the expression "co-location with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth means "the substratum-ness (*ādheyatā*) as determined by a cloth which is itself not determined by anything that determines co-location with the counter-positive.

Furthermore, since the property of being a determiner of co-location with the counter-positive residing in some locus belongs only to the locus of the counter-positive itself—by virtue of the aforementioned qualification—the reason (*hetu*) results in: "because of possessing a property that is the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in a cloth which is not the locus of its own counter-positive."

Regarding the term "non-coexistence with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogivaiyadhikaraṇya*), it should be understood that the locusness of the counter-positive is delimited by the relation that delimits the probans-hood (*hetutāvacchedakasambandha*).
The specific purpose [of this qualification] is to be inferred by oneself.

However, some maintain that the meaning is: an absence residing in a cloth which is not delimited by—that is, not qualified by—that limiting property which consists in coexistence with the counter-positive.

Regarding the qualification of the absence (*abhāva*) as being "co-located with its counter-positive" (*pratiyogisamānādhikaraṇa*), this was stated because, according to the logic to be explained later, the absence of cloth-ness (*paṭatvābhāva*) and so forth do not possess that property.

They say that even the aforementioned statement results in the reason already mentioned—namely, "the absolute absence residing in a cloth which is not the locus of its counter-positive"—and therefore there is no room for the doubt, "How can this [reason] also [be established]?

In this very context, they state the inferences (*anumāna*). As for the phrase "And the inference," etc.: the meaning of "cloth," etc., is "possessing a difference whose counter-positiveness is delimited by the state of being the locus of identity (*tādātmya*) having cloth as its counter-positive."

Regarding the reading *tāttvikatādātmya* (real identity): the term *tāttvika* (real) is included to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking into account a difference delimited by an identity qualified by "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*). Furthermore, it serves to ensure the inclusion of an identity characterized by that [reality]. Any resulting shift in the subject matter (*arthāntaratva*)—due to the establishment of a conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*) delimited by that [identity]—should be avoided in the same manner as the method used for the inference proving the difference between selves (*ātmabheda*). Regarding the term *pratiyogī* (counter-positive): the qualifiers "unlimited" (*anavacchinna*) and "resident" (*niṣṭha*) are introduced as attributes of the absence (*abhāva*) in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a cloth, by taking into account conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), and "cloth-ness," which is pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*).

Nor should it be argued that because the exclusion of [the absence of] conjunction (*saṃyogābhāva*) and the like is already achieved by the qualification "not co-located with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇa*), there is no need for the inclusion of the term "unconditioned" (*anavacchinna*).

For in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, the very absence of conjunction which is not co-located with its counter-positive resides in the cloth; thus, that [absence of conjunction] would not be excluded.

Furthermore, when the term "unconditioned" is included, there is an exclusion of that [conjunction-absence], because the property of being an absence of conjunction (*saṃyogābhāvatva*), which is the delimiting factor for co-location with the counter-positive, lacks the quality of being unconditioned.

Nor should it be argued that, for this reason, there would be a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) even for the absence of potness (*ghaṭatvābhāva*) and the like, because [such an absence] is delimited by "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so on—which serve as the delimiters of co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the counter-positive (potness) in its own form. This is because what is intended is "not being delimited by whatever serves as the delimiter of co-occurrence with the counter-positive that defines itself (*svanirūpaka*). Since no counter-positive defined by "knowability" and the like is established, it is impossible to employ that [knowability] as the referent of the term *sva*. Furthermore, it is precisely "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*), "absence-ness" (*bhāvatva*), and so forth, that possess such a status [of being the delimiter].

[Objection: But since everything indeed possesses the locus-hood of identity with the cloth, the probandum—in the form of a difference delimited by that [cloth]—is unestablished; therefore, he says: "unestablished. [Response: It must be understood as "to be refuted," meaning it should be known as not contradicting the inference under discussion. The point is that it has already been demonstrated that this is not a defect in the case of a negative inference (vyatireki-anumāna) where non-existence is the probandum.

Having thus stated the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the difference between selves, he now establishes them with respect to the difference between non-selves, beginning first with perception (*pratyakṣa*): "A pot, a cloth, etc. Perception—such as "a pot is not a cloth"—is indeed easily established and does not require the effort involved in establishing it through inference.
Nor should it be argued that this perception lacks authority because it is sublated by the scriptural text, "Not here, not there" (*neha nānā*).

The point is that since that scriptural passage negates distinctions such as qualities and actions within Brahman, it lacks the power to sublate the distinction between a jar and a cloth. Regarding the term "counter-correlative" (*pratiyogī*): because the absolute absence of "jar-ness" in a jar does not coexist with its counter-correlative (which is jar-ness itself), the property of "coexistence with the counter-correlative" (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇya*) is unestablished; consequently, its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) is also unestablished. Therefore, the meaning is: because [the jar] possesses the substratum-hood of that jar-ness—which is the counter-correlative of the absolute absence of jar-ness residing in a cloth, an absence which is itself not delimited by that [unestablished] factor.

He himself will explain the function of the qualifiers such as "counter-positive" (*pratiyogin*) with the example "like a cloth" (*paṭavat*). For in that case, the absence of the absence of being the locus of identity having the cloth as its counter-positive resides in the state of being the locus of identity having the cloth as its counter-positive;
and the absence of being the locus of the property consisting of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) of that kind also resides there—this is the meaning.

Now, one might object: "Since I accept only the state of being the locus of identity having the cloth as its counter-positive, the probandum in the form of its absence is unestablished, and thus there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*). To this he says: "And [regarding] the charge of an unestablished qualifier..."

The meaning is as follows: just as in the case [of the inference] "the individual soul (*jīva*) is not the locus of identity with respect to Brahman," because an absence (*abhāva*) is the probandum (*sādhya*), the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) is not a defect; so too here, because an absence is the probandum, it does not obstruct the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other factors, and thus the fallacy of an unestablished qualification is not a defect.

Now, one might ask: prior to the establishment of the difference between a jar and a cloth, how can they stand in the relation of subject (*pakṣa*) and example (*dṛṣṭānta*)? To this he replies: "merely by means of conventional difference" (*vyāvahārikabhedamātreṇa*). The phrase "like an inference establishing the difference of the Self" (*ātmabhedasādhakānumānavat*) is understood to follow here.

And thus, since you do not accept ultimate difference anywhere, if ultimate difference were the determinant of the status of subject (*pakṣa*) and example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it would follow that inference itself is abolished; therefore, you must state that mere difference is the determinant. Since such mere difference exists between a jar and a cloth as well, the relationship of subject and example between them is established—this is the meaning.

[Objection: "But even so, since I—who assert that the difference between a jar and a cloth is non-ultimate—also accept that 'jar-ness' and other such properties reside in the cloth, it remains unestablished that the jar is not the locus of a property that is the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the cloth. [Reply: No.
Is "jar-ness" in the cloth real, unreal, or false? It cannot be the first [option].
Because it would result in a contradiction with your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

As for the second [alternative], how could you not accept the absolute absence of "pot-ness" in a cloth? For [it is said]: "Of all entities whatsoever, which are accepted as having their own substratum..."

Since you accept that "falsity" (*mithyātva*) consists in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) that is co-located with itself—based on the statement that "being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence is [the nature of] the false"—then even if there is no absence of that absolute non-existence in a cloth with respect to potness (because the cloth lacks the status of being the locus of potness), the falsity of potness in that cloth is not contradicted. If this is so, then since it is well-established that the locus of the absolute non-existence of potness exists in a cloth—which is not the locus of potness—how can there be any lack of proof?

He raises an objection with the words "nanu" (but surely): "But surely, if one maintains the identity of the jar and the cloth, since the property of being a cloth (paṭatva) also exists in the jar, it lacks the status of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the cloth; therefore, the jar’s non-being-a-substratum-of-that [absence] is unestablished. The meaning is: even though there is no lack of a well-known qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), and even if the relationship between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) can somehow be established.

He asks by means of an alternative [option]—“On the cloth?”—in order to make one accept the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of potness on the cloth. “Of all” means: the meaning of the statement is that for all entities (*bhāva*), such as the category of a pot and so forth, their very nature of being false (*mithyātva*) consists in their being the counter-correlates (*pratiyogitva*) with respect to an absolute absence residing in their own substratum, such as the ground.

And thus, if potness is unreal on the cloth, then its being the counter-correlate of the absolute absence residing in that [cloth] is unavoidable; what then is unestablished? This is the sense. [Objection: But for this very reason, it was said [above] that it is “accepted as its own substratum.”

And thus, since a cloth lacks the status of being the locus of potness (*ghaṭatva*), even if one does not admit the absolute non-existence of potness in the cloth, it does not follow that potness is real. This is because the coexistence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of potness with its own absolute non-existence exists in the pot, which is accepted as its locus; and by this much alone, the falsity (*mithyātva*) of potness is established. With this intention, he raises an objection: "Of the cloth... He answers: "Then," with the thought that in that case there is no room for the charge of unestablished nature (*asiddhi*).
The meaning of that [objection] is: "the cloth's not being the locus of potness. [The phrase] "is well-known" refers to this.
The meaning is that it is universally accepted that the ground, which is not the locus of the jar, is necessarily the substratum for the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar.

Anticipating the objection that the qualification is unestablished (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*), he provides the resolution with the words "But [it may be objected]... (*nanu*). The phrase "because of the acceptance of non-ultimate difference" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*);
it should also be understood as "because of the acceptance of real identity" (*vāstavatādātmya*).
By the phrase "of potness and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes such properties as having a broad base, a belly, and a specific shape.
The meaning is that if there were identity between a pot and a cloth, then because the pot itself would possess the nature of a cloth, potness and the like would not be non-existent in the cloth.

According to the reasoning stated, if potness and the like were identical with clothness, then potness and the like would have to be the counter-positives of an absolute absence residing in the cloth.

This is because falsity (*mithyātva*) is accepted as consisting in being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) residing in its own locus (*svādhikaraṇa*). And thus, with the thought that "let that alone be the qualification of the reason," he offers the rebuttal: "In the cloth, there is potness. [The opponent asks: "How so? [The author replies: Because that very thing is accepted as the meaning of the word "false" (*mithyā*). He provides the consensus of others on this point: "Of others... The connection is as follows: for entities, their state of being false consists in being the counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence in a locus that is accepted as their own substratum (*svāśraya*).
This might be the case:
if the jar were the locus of non-clothness, then its absolute absence would also have to be admitted therein for the sake of establishing its falsity.
But this is not so.

As for the previous objection regarding the non-establishment [of the identity] of the cloth: although the cloth lacks the status of being a pot—which is a specific property of a pot—because it lacks the status of being the substratum [of that property], one might still assume an identity between the pot and the cloth. Therefore, he says: "the cloth's being a pot. [He adds] "it is well-known" because the meaning of the term "subsisting in something else" is precisely the absolute absence of that [property] in it; this is the intended sense.
As for what was stated—that there is no subsistence in the specific property of being a cloth.
That is not so;
for since the cloth itself is its own nature, there is no other real state for the cloth apart from that.
Indeed, unity through the abandonment of parts is not asserted in the case of insentient things as it is in the case of sentient beings.

However, as for that non-ultimate distinction which has been accepted even by me, it does not preclude the mutual transfer of properties; therefore, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhi*). To this, he says: "But even so... (*nanvathāpi*). This means: even though the defect of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) is absent.

Even if the mutual transfer of properties were difficult to establish due to the absence of a subject (*pakṣa*) and an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), its acceptance would still be unnecessary; such is the meaning of "even so. "Unestablished" (*asiddhi*) means the unestablishment of the logical reason (*hetu*).

In this very manner, since it is unestablished that all things possess the property of being the locus of those properties that are the counter-correlates of absolute non-existences residing in a cloth;
[this applies] to the second case as well, and so forth.
For you accept that the falsity of potness in a cloth consists in its being the counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence that is co-locus with itself.
The absolute non-existence of a jar on a cloth must necessarily be admitted;
thus, there is no lack of proof [for the existence of such non-existence].

Furthermore, if it is argued that the locus of "jar-ness" is the jar itself, and its falsity consists precisely in its being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in that [locus], then [the objection is answered].
The collective meaning is that, at that time, the cloth is the absolute non-existence of pot-ness; this is the sense.

Regarding the term "tathyam" (real): the meaning is whether or not this has become the object of the conventional usage of authoritative persons as being ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). Regarding "mṛṣātmateti":
the meaning is that falsity (*mṛṣātva*) is held [to be the case].

The reading *mṛṣātmā* is correct. Regarding the phrase "well-known": the meaning is, how can there be a refusal to accept that which follows from the force of your own conventional usage, namely, "pot-ness does not exist"? Regarding "unestablished" (*asiddhi*): if by the term "self" (*sva*) one grasps the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of pot-ness, then because the locus of its counter-positive (pot-ness) is unestablished, the probans (*sādhana*) composed of that [non-existence] is unestablished. Alternatively, if one accepts the establishment of the probans composed of the absence of being delimited by that [non-existence]—on the grounds that an absolute non-existence may have a non-existent counter-positive—then since the possession of such a property does not exist in a cloth, there is a "defect of essential unestablishment" (*svarūpāsiddhi*).
"By accepting [the identity] as residing in the cloth. The sense is that the essential natures (*svarūpa*) of the jar and the cloth are one and the same.

Although one might here state the objection to be mentioned later—namely, that this would result in the application of the term "jar" to the cloth—nevertheless, since it is precisely the absolute absence of "jarness" (*ghaṭatvātyantābhāva*) in the cloth that is relevant to the present context, he first causes that very point to be accepted: "In the cloth... The word "being accepted" (*aṅgīkriyamāṇam*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

Now, one might ask: even if the nature of a jar (*ghaṭatva*) is false with respect to a cloth, why do you accept its absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) there? To this he says: "Of all [things]... Since, in reality, the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of jars and so forth is not established, it is stated that they are "agreed upon as their own loci.
This means: "as many as are the qualificands (*viśeṣya*) of a cognition having themselves as its qualifier (*svaprakāraka*).
The connection is with the words "by you," who speak thus.

And thus, the point is that for the sake of conforming to such falsity (*mithyātva*) of potness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth, one must admit the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of those properties in cloth and other such things.
Now, an objection may be raised: "Falsity consists precisely in being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of an absence residing in its own locus (*svāśraya*);
and this 'being its own locus' is not real (*vāstava*)."
Nor is it common to the merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), for that would entail either a contradiction or the status of being an established fact (*siddhārthatā*).

Rather, with the intention that it is only conventionally real (*vyāvahārika*), he raises an objection: "Of the cloth... [and so on]. "It is well-known" means that there is a rule that the negation of one of two mutually contradictory things is necessarily pervaded by the affirmation of the other.

One might object: "Since the jar and the cloth are one, just as 'jar-ness' (ghaṭatva) exists in the jar, it likewise exists in the cloth. Thus, there is no absolute absence of jar-ness in the cloth; consequently, because jar-ness lacks the status of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the cloth, the substratum [the jar] lacks the property of being the locus of an absolute absence residing in the cloth that has jar-ness as its counter-positive. Therefore, the reason is unestablished (asiddhi). This is the objection raised with the words "nanu" (now, an objection). The meaning is that even if the qualification is not unestablished by way of non-existence elsewhere, there is still a lack of establishment in terms of the essential nature (svarūpāsiddhi).

He asks by means of a dilemma—"In the cloth?"—in order to make him admit the absolute absence of "pot-ness" in that very cloth.
