"[Because of] the contradiction with the established doctrine (apasiddhāntāt)" means that if one were to admit the reality of even "pot-ness," it would contradict the established doctrine that Brahman alone is real.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Co-inherent with itself (svasamānādhikaraṇa). "Self" refers to that which is intended as false;
the meaning is "the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute absence that is co-inherent with that [self]."
Just as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is false, so too does this definition apply:
its own nature is that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
That which has the same locus as that [silver]—namely, the absolute absence of silver existing in the mother-of-pearl fragment, which shares a single locus with it—is the absolute absence of silver.
Silver possesses the state of being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*) of that [absence]. In the same way, the falsity of "potness" residing in a cloth is also established.
One's own "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) is the subject.

That which is co-located with it—meaning an absolute absence existing in the same locus as that [pot-ness], namely the absolute absence of pot-ness (*ghaṭatvātyantābhāva*)—must be admitted to have pot-ness as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*). Therefore, the meaning is: how could the absolute absence of pot-ness not exist in a cloth?

And with the intention that this acceptance is known from that very statement, it was said: "of all [things] indeed. The meaning of this is as follows: the falsity (mithyātva) of all entities (bhāva), which consists in being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence existing in their own substratum, would then be contradicted if the nature of a jar (ghaṭatva) were accepted as being the substratum of a cloth (paṭa). But this is not the case; thus he raises an objection: "of the cloth," etc. Therein, in the cloth; that, namely, the nature of a jar.

"In that cloth" (*tatra paṭe*): [this refers to] "of that pot-ness" (*tasya ghaṭatvasya*). "It is well-known" (*suprasiddham*): the meaning is that when it is stated that the cloth is not the locus of pot-ness, the absence of such locus-status follows by the force of the logical principle that two mutually contradictory properties cannot coexist. "How is it unestablished? (*kathamasiddhiḥ*): the meaning is that if the cloth were the locus of the absolute absence of pot-ness, then the pot would necessarily be the locus of a property that is the counter-positive of the absolute absence residing in the cloth.

If it is objected: "In that case, since the nature of being a pot (*ghaṭatva*) is false in the pot, the pot itself cannot be the locus of that *ghaṭatva*; thus, [the definition] is unestablished (*asiddhi*)," we say no.
For even with respect to the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of *ghaṭatva* in the pot, the pot must still be accepted as its locus, and likewise as the locus of *ghaṭatva*.
Otherwise, because *ghaṭatva* would lack a substratum, the falsity of *ghaṭatva*—defined as having the same locus as its own absolute non-existence—would not belong to *ghaṭatva* and the like.
But even so, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of a cloth;
for although the absence of the probandum exists in the cloth, there is no absence of the probans.

If it is argued that because clothhood (paṭatva) is also false in the cloth, the cloth is the locus of clothhood—which is the counter-positive of the absolute absence residing in the cloth—therefore this reason is specified as "not delimited by a delimitor of co-occurrence with the counter-positive. For even though the absolute absence of clothhood exists in the cloth, since that absence is co-located with its counter-positive, which is clothhood itself, it is delimited by a delimitor of co-occurrence with the counter-positive; thus, the absence of the probans (the reason) is present [in the example].
[Objection: In that case, the reason is unestablished (asiddhi).

If it is argued that by asserting the non-difference of a jar and a cloth, one must admit "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) in the cloth as well—since the absolute absence of jar-ness in the cloth would then have a coreferential counter-positive with its own locus—we say no. For you too, in asserting the non-ultimate difference between a jar and a cloth, must admit the absolute absence of jar-ness in the cloth; otherwise, you could not avoid the contradiction of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of "jar" applying to a cloth. This is because, just as the distinction between the reality and unreality of a reflection and its original is established through mere conventional difference, so too must the absolute absence of jar-ness be admitted in the cloth. If it is further argued that although jar-ness is omnipresent, practical usage is restricted due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), we say no.
For even when silver is superimposed by ignorance, it does not produce the linguistic usage "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl and the like;
if it did, it would produce that usage with respect to a jar as well.

Furthermore, if one were to admit the ultimate reality of the identity between a jar and a cloth, then the very nature of the jar and the cloth would have to be ultimately real—just as it is for the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman—and thus the doctrine of the illusoriness of the phenomenal world (prapañca-mithyātva) would be untenable. This is the favorable logical argument (anukūlatarka) to be considered.
But if this were the case, the non-establishment of the probans (*asiddhi*) would indeed be unavoidable; for even a pot lacks the status of being the locus of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*),
since in my view, "pot-ness" is admitted to be false (*mithyātva*) even in the pot.

Since being the counter-positive of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvapratiyogitva*) is itself the very nature of falsity (*mithyātva*), the opponent raises an objection by resorting to a parallel case (*pratibandī*): "But then... This means that if one accepts that the locus of an absolute non-existence is not the substratum of its counter-positive, then when there is the absolute non-existence of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) in a pot, it follows that the pot is not the substratum of that "pot-ness. Thus he objects.

Just as you cannot accept that a cloth—which possesses the absolute absence of potness—is not a locus for potness, so too you cannot accept that a pot—which possesses the absolute absence of potness—is not a locus for it.
For if that were the case, it would follow that potness lacks falsity, defined as the property of having a common locus with its own absolute absence.

And thus, with the intention of showing how there can be no lack of establishment since the pot’s being the locus of potness must necessarily be admitted, he removes the counter-objection with "no. [He says: "Because of the absence of a locus for potness. For a cloth has no status as a locus with respect to potness;
likewise, if potness were not admitted even in a pot, it would follow that potness and so forth would be entirely without a locus—this is the meaning.
He raises an objection in order to state the function of the qualifier "not delimited by a delimitor of co-occurrence with the counter-positive": "But surely... [He replies: "Even so..."

The meaning is: "even in the case of avoiding the fallacy of the unestablished" (*asiddhi*). "There is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the cloth" means that there is a deviation of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) in the cloth, which serves as the instance of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). He explains this very point with the words "the cloth. "Even when the absence of the probandum exists" means even when the real identity (*tādātmya*) having the cloth as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) exists. "Because of the non-absence of the absence of the probans" means because the probans itself is present.

He establishes that very point with the words "on the cloth. Now, one might ask: how can there be room for a counter-positive (pratiyogin) in the locus of an absolute non-existence? To this it is said: "because of the falsity of the cloth on the cloth. The meaning is that, in my view, falsity is accepted as being precisely the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence that resides in the same locus as itself. "For this very reason" means: for the sake of avoiding the aforementioned deviation (vyabhicāra). "The probans" (hetu) means: the absolute non-existence included within the probans.

Regarding the phrase *pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇya*: the meaning is that because the absence [of the probans] is defined by the absence of non-restriction—namely, the state of being delimited by that which delimits the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the counter-positive (cloth-ness), which is the state of being the absolute absence of cloth-ness in the cloth—the probans is not present within that [definition].

Although here it would have been sufficient to qualify the absolute absence residing in the cloth simply as "not co-occurring with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇa*), for by that much alone the exclusion of the absolute absence of cloth-ness would have been established.

Nevertheless, since even the absolute absence of potness (*ghaṭatvātyantābhāva*) is co-located with its counter-positive in a pot, it lacks the property of "not being co-located with its counter-positive" (*pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇatva*); consequently, the property [of being such an absence] would remain unestablished (*aprasiddha*) as a characteristic of that counter-positive. To dispel this suspicion of non-establishment (*asiddhi*), the phrase "not delimited by the delimitor of co-location with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇyāvacchedakānavacchinna*) is stated. When it is stated thus, there is no non-establishment.
For although the absolute absence of potness is one and the same everywhere, in the present context, by the term "absolute absence residing in a cloth," a general form of absence is not intended.
However, [the cloth] possesses an absolute absence delimited by its subsistence-in-the-cloth.

And this nature of being an absolute absence (atyantābhāvatva) is not the delimitor of co-occurrence with potness; rather, according to the Māyāvāda view, it is precisely that which is delimited by subsistence-in-the-cloth which serves as the delimitor.

Therefore, one should not fear the objection that there is no unestablished instance of an absence non-co-occurrent with its counter-positive, by taking the co-occurrence of the absolute absence subsisting in the cloth with potness—which is its counter-positive—within the scope of another pot.

And consequently, how can there be a lack of proof (*asiddhi*) for the reason (*hetu*) constructed from that? Now, one who wishes to reconcile this point falls into another difficulty: namely, that by introducing a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*), a lack of proof arises once again;
because, in the doctrine of the non-difference between jar and cloth, the nature of a jar (*ghaṭatva*) exists even in the cloth.

With the intention that, because that [absence] is false, its absolute absence possesses co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), and thus, being delimited by that delimiting factor, it lacks the quality of being non-delimited, he raises an objection with the words, "But then... (*nanu tarhi*). The connection is as follows: even by you—who asserts the non-difference between a jar and a cloth—the absolute absence of "jar-ness" in the cloth must be admitted.
Here, the phrase "of that which does not co-occur with its counter-positive" (*pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇasya*) is to be supplied.
And thus, the intended meaning should be understood as follows: because "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) cannot be admitted in a cloth.
Otherwise, since even he [the opponent] would have to admit the absolute absence of pot-ness [in the cloth], the fault would not be avoided.
To the question, "Why should pot-ness not be admitted in a cloth by me? it is said: "Because it would result in the undesirable consequence of the linguistic usage of 'pot' applying to a cloth."

The sense is that if "pot-ness" were present even in a cloth, then, for fear that the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of "pot" would apply to the cloth just as it does to the pot, one would not admit [such a nature].
However, if one admits an ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*) between the pot and the cloth, how could the non-admission of "pot-ness" in the cloth be possible?

For the establishment of an object of knowledge (*prameya-siddhi*) is not dependent on utility, such that its non-admission might be intended merely to prevent the unwanted consequence of the usage of "pot" applying to a cloth. Therefore, it was stated [in the verse] that this is said by one who asserts the non-ultimate difference between the pot and the cloth.
The intended meaning is that for this very reason, you have also accepted a non-ultimate (apāramārthika) difference.

Since the consequence of non-ultimacy would be non-existence itself, which would not resolve the fault of tautology, it is stated [in the text] "by mere conventional difference" (*vyāvahārikabhedamātreṇa*).
The intention is that by the word "non-ultimate," only a conventional difference is intended, not non-existence.
But is not this also impossible?

For if there is essential identity (*svābhāvikaikya*), how can the restriction that "the pot-ness resides only in the pot and not in the cloth" be established based on a mere conventional difference (*vyāvahārikabheda*)? To this it is said: "like the original and the reflection," and so forth.

Just as in your own view, even though there is no difference between the original (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*), the status of being the original belongs only to the face in its original state and not to its reflection, despite the mere conventional difference.

The meaning is that here too, the established rule is accepted as follows: in the case of a face, there is only the state of being a reflection and not the state of being the original object; likewise, while the original object possesses only reality, the reflection possesses only unreality, and not reality.
Now, one might object: in the doctrine of the identity of the jar and the cloth, the nature of the jar exists in the cloth just as it does in the jar itself.
Nor does it follow that, if such were the case, the conventional usage of "pot" would apply even to a cloth;

for one might object that specific conventional usages are possible due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*). To this, he raises the following objection: "Of pot-ness," etc. [The word] "everywhere" refers to cloth and so forth;
"even though there is no distinction" means even though existence (*sattva*) is present.

If, due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), there is a cessation of the conventional usage of "pot" despite the existence of pot-ness in a cloth, then—since in your view there is no difference between a cloth and a pot just as there is none between mother-of-pearl and silver—even though silver-ness exists in the mother-of-pearl, you must answer when asked why the conventional usage of "silver" does not always occur there: "It is solely due to the power of ignorance. Consequently, even at the time of the superimposition of silver, the conventional usage of "silver" should not occur, because ignorance, which obstructs such usage, remains fully active.
Now, you might say this:
it is not ignorance alone that establishes or subverts worldly transactional usage; rather, it does so only in dependence upon a superimposition (*āropa*).
Thus, when there is the presence of the superimposition of silver, it produces the transactional usage "this is silver," whereas in its absence, it does not produce such usage.

In that case, it follows that it is only the presence or absence of the cause characterized by the object of superimposition that determines the occurrence or non-occurrence of linguistic usage, and not ignorance alone.

Consequently, if the cause in the form of "potness" were present in a cloth, the linguistic usage "pot" would be unavoidable there, since mere ignorance would be ineffective. With this intention, he refutes [the objection] with the words "For it is not... (na hi).
To the question "Why does it not produce [that cognition]?", he says: "Because of its being such" (*tathātve*). This refers to the linguistic usage [of the form] "this is silver.

Here, he dispels the suspicion that the reason (*hetu*) in this inference is irrelevant (*aprayojakatā*) by stating: "In the case of a jar and a cloth. Since it was stated in the *sādhya* (the probandum) that there is "real identity" (*tāttvika-tādātmya*), it was said that one must accept the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) of that identity in accordance with that statement.

However, some, having raised the alternative as to whether that identity is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) or not ultimately real, state this objection regarding the first position: "of the intrinsic natures of the jar and the cloth. The sense is that if the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) are not ultimately real, it is impossible for their identity (*tādātmya*) to be ultimately real. To avoid the charge of begging the question (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says: "of the world-appearance" (*prapañca*). [The compound] *vācoyukti* is a case of non-elision (*aluk*); it means "the employment of words."

Having thus removed the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the qualification of the reason (*hetu*), he now raises and removes the objection regarding the unestablished nature of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*). Regarding the phrase "in a jar, of jar-ness": the intended meaning of the reason is indeed the state of being the locus of properties such as jar-ness that do not reside in a cloth.
This is because, since cloth-ness and so forth are false in a jar, their absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) exists there;
and the meaning of the term "unestablished" is simply the absence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣa*). Such is the sense of the objection.
Moreover, non-establishment (asiddhi) does not consist merely in the absence of the reason;
rather, it is the absence of the reason that is non-coextensive with its counter-positive.
In the present case, even though the absence of potness exists, potness itself must also be admitted [to exist].
Otherwise, since the absence of cloth would also not exist in a pot, it would follow that [the absence] lacks a substratum;

furthermore, the definition of falsity as "having the same substratum as its own absolute non-existence" would be lost. This is the intended meaning. To clarify the function of the phrase "not delimited by the delimitors of the co-occurrence with the counter-positive," he says: "Now, [if...]"—because, due to the existence of identity in the cloth, the absence of the probandum exists there.

The sense is that because the absolute non-existence of cloth-ness (*paṭatvātyantābhāva*) and so forth are false, the reason—consisting in being the locus of a property that does not reside in cloth—is present [in the subject]. "The reason is qualified" means that the non-existence included within the reason is qualified. By this, he states the manner of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*): "the absolute non-existence of cloth-ness in cloth. He raises the objection regarding the failure of the qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) once again, on the grounds that since pot and cloth are identical, pot-ness also exists in cloth; thus, even in cloth, the absolute non-existence of pot-ness possesses co-location with its counter-positive (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is expressed by: "But then... (*nanu tarhi*).

And thus, even while accepting the non-difference of all categories and the presence of all attributes everywhere, one must certainly accept a specific systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) for the sake of establishing conventional usage restricted to particular instances; therefore, our lack of proof is not at all difficult to avoid. He says: "No. Even though all attributes are accepted everywhere, the absolute absence of "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatvātyantābhāva*) is co-located with its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) only in the pot itself, and not in a cloth; such a systematic arrangement must indeed be accepted.

And thus, the resulting meaning is that the qualification of the probans (*hetu*) is precisely the non-coexistence with such a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); therefore, there is no fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "by the power of ignorance" (*avidyāvaśāt*): the sense is that ignorance is capable of bringing about the occurrence of what is otherwise impossible.

He says "no," [meaning] that even ignorance might produce the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) of something as being present where it is, or produce the linguistic usage of its absence where it is not, but not otherwise, because we do not observe it so. The point is that even when the superimposed silver is absent, the substrate—such as mother-of-pearl—does not indeed produce the linguistic usage that "this is that very silver."
The sense [of the objection] is this: if ignorance were capable of producing the impossible, it would generate the linguistic usage "this is silver" even with respect to what is not silver;

why, then, is the birth of illusory (prātibhāsika) silver accepted for that purpose? Since the occurrence of a property non-inherent in one thing—such as a cloth—in another thing—such as a jar—is possible through mere conventional (vyāvahārika) difference, [the opponent suggests] that a real (pāramārthika) cause must be the determinant. To this, he states the reasoning: "In the case of the jar and the cloth... The sense is that just as the identity between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman is real, and therefore the individual soul and Brahman, which are related to it, are also real, so too [is the illusory silver]. "Vāco yuktiḥ" means the employment of words.
"Now, [one might object]: 'In that case...
This means: just as the absolute absence of "pot-ness" exists in a cloth because pot-ness is false there, so too the absolute absence of pot-ness exists in a pot because pot-ness is false there.
And thus, since the state of being the locus of such pot-ness does not exist even in a pot, there is no lack of proof (asiddhi).

If the cognition of "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) regarding a pot were such that pot-ness did not exist anywhere at all, then its falsity—in the form of having its absolute non-existence as its locus—would not be established. Therefore, it must be admitted to exist somewhere; and since, by the force of its own cognition, it must be admitted to reside in the pot itself, there is no lack of proof (asiddhi). This is the sense. [Objection: "But even so..."

The meaning is that because cloth-ness (*paṭatva*) is also false, its absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) exists even in the cloth; thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) "the absence of the general property of being a counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in the cloth," since this property [cloth-ness] does not exist in the cloth. He says "for this very reason" (*ata eva*), meaning that there is no deviation precisely by virtue of the qualification of the probans (*hetu*) as "delimited" (*avacchinna*). The meaning is that the absolute non-existence included within the probans is qualified by the probans itself. As for the phrase "even though the absolute non-existence of cloth-ness exists in the cloth": although the absolute non-existence of cloth-ness exists in the cloth, that [non-existence] has a counter-positive that is not co-located with it (*pratiyogyasamānādhikaraṇa*).

The meaning is that, according to the stated method, since cloth-ness (*paṭatva*) also exists therein [in the pot], such a general absence of both non-existence and its locus-residence (i.e., the absence of the absence of cloth-ness and its locus) is present in the cloth; thus, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

In this context, if one were to state merely "not being co-located with the counter-positive," then even the absolute absence of cloth-ness would be co-located with its counter-positive in a jar; consequently, a property residing in a cloth that is the counter-positive of an absolute absence not co-located with its counter-positive would be unestablished (*aprasiddha*), resulting in the fallacy of an unestablished reason (*hetvaprasiddhi*).
Therefore, [the definition is] "not delimited by that which delimits the non-co-existence with the counter-positive. Now, one might object: even so, the aforementioned defect does not cease;

for the absolute absence of "pot-ness" residing in a cloth is delimited by that which delimits its co-existence with the counter-positive (the form of the pot), and thus such an absence is unestablished. To this we say: no.

"Because the cloth itself is qualified by being the locus of the counter-positive. [Objection: "But then... [Response: This means that a qualification of the reason (*hetu*) is intended for the purpose of avoiding a fallacy (*vyabhicāra*). "[Even] by you": this means even by one who does not accept the ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*) between a jar and a cloth. "Of the absolute absence of jar-ness in the cloth": the sense is that jar-ness cannot be admitted in the cloth;
otherwise, since he too would have admitted the existence [of that absence], the fault would not be avoided.
Although this much alone should have been stated previously.
By that much alone, the avoidance of the charge of unestablished proof (*asiddhi*) will be accomplished; enough with this investigation into the falsity of "pot-ness" in a cloth.

Nevertheless, it should not be thought that this was not stated previously for the sake of training in the art of inquiry. Regarding the phrase "of pot-ness": I certainly accept "pot-ness" in the cloth.
Nor does it follow that there would be the linguistic usage of "cloth-ness" in a pot.

The meaning is that the cessation of that [superimposition] is possible through ignorance (*avidyā*) alone, which is expert at bringing about the occurrence of what was previously impossible. For it is not [the case that] "superimposed by ignorance" [is redundant]. Ignorance is that which brings about worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) in dependence upon its objects, which are themselves products of ignorance.
Otherwise, even in the absence of an object of ignorance such as silver, it would produce the transaction "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl and the like.
Consequently, the admission of an object of ignorance (silver) in that instance would be rendered useless.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of treating even a cloth as silver.

And thus, the point is that if the illusory (āvidyaka) "pot-ness" exists in a pot, it is not possible for ignorance (avidyā) to obstruct its empirical usage. Although it might be conceivable that ignorance could obstruct the usage of "pot-ness" despite its existence—just as ignorance obstructs the usage of "shell-ness" despite its existence in a mother-of-pearl shell—nevertheless, since the usage of "shell" persists after sublation (bādha), it is accepted that the obstruction of the usage of "shell-ness," though it exists, is caused by ignorance.
But this is not the case;

since the conventional usage of "pot" and "cloth" never ceases in the present context, the sense is that their cessation here is not caused by ignorance (*avidyā*). [The statement] "falsity would not occur" is said according to the view that potness and so forth are powers (*śakti*) of ignorance.
Therefore, since they too possess the nature of Brahman, there is no room for the objection that this would result in an undesired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Our refutation of that view has been set forth elsewhere.

He clarifies the purpose of the qualifiers such as "co-occurrence with the counter-correlative" (*pratiyogi-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) through both doubt and its resolution, beginning with the words "Now, [one might object]... (*nanu...*) and so on. Regarding the term "original" (*bimba*): because there exists a settled distinction wherein the one primary [Self] possesses the status of being the original merely by virtue of its conventional limiting adjuncts (*vyāvahārika-upādhi*), while this [other] possesses the status of being the reflection; and because the original alone is real, while the reflection alone is false.

Since such a state of affairs exists even at the time of formal logical application (*nyāyaprayoga*), the aforementioned objection—that the reason (*sādhana*) you have proposed is unestablished (*aprasiddha*)—does not arise.
It is ignorance (*avidyā*) alone that governs conventional usage; as it produces [cognitions], so does the usage occur.

One cannot conclude from this that the absence of the property of being a pot (*ghaṭatvānadhikaraṇatva*) in a cloth is established; thus, he raises the objection that the non-establishment of the reason is unavoidable with the words "of the property of being a pot" (*ghaṭatvasya*). Even ignorance generates conventional usage independently of the objects it itself projects.

Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); therefore, he states that one must accept the established rule regarding the objects of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-viṣaya-vyavasthā*). "Indeed not" (*na hi*): Even in the absence of the silver superimposed upon the mother-of-pearl, does ignorance (*avidyā*) produce the conventional usage "this is silver" even in your own view? Indeed it does not. He states the refutation of the position that this might be accepted: "If that were so" (*tathātve*). [Objection: But surely, when a superimposition occurs, one merely seeks out its cause.

If it is argued that, according to the principle that "there is no basis for a superimposition," one may assume that worldly transactional existence (*vyavahāra-sattva*) is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*),
but it is not logical to establish such a transactional existence merely by the assertion that "ignorance exists," we say: no,
because that principle applies only to objects that are established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the existence of "pot-ness" in a cloth.

Furthermore, since it could be argued that ignorance (*avidyā*) generates empirical usage even in the absence of all things, it would follow as a logical consequence that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—such as space and so forth—which is of the nature of the Brahman and is indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), would also be non-existent at the very time of empirical usage. [The phrases] "of the pot and the cloth" [and] "of the individual soul and Brahman" [are used].

The meaning is this: just as in that case [of the reflection], by abandoning the contradictory forms of being the original object (*bimba*) and the reflected image (*pratibimba*), there remains a single nature consisting of pure consciousness (*caitanya*) common to both; so too here, by abandoning the contradictory forms of being a jar and being a cloth, there would have to be a single, ultimately real insentient (*jaḍa*) essence common to both.

Nor should it be argued that Brahman alone is the reality constituting the nature of both, on the grounds of Vācaspati’s statement: "In the cognition of mother-of-pearl, silver is known in its true nature (*tattvataḥ*), for she [the shell] is its true nature. This is because [that statement refers to the illusory appearance, not to an underlying common substrate].
This being the case, since a pot and a cloth would consist of the living conscious self (*jīvacidātman*), their insentience (*jaḍatva*) would be untenable;
this has been elaborated elsewhere.

With the intention that the final locus (*adhikaraṇatva*) constituting the reason must be real (*vāstavika*), he raises an objection with "But... (*nanu*). With the intention that the locus common to the empirical level (*vyāvahārika*) alone constitutes the reason, he replies with "Of the pot" (*ghaṭasya*). The point is that the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) based on the illusory (*prātibhāsika*) level does not constitute a flaw.

"Otherwise" means if one does not accept that a pot is the conventional locus (*vyāvahārikādhikaraṇatva*) with respect to its potness. "As being without a locus" means that such a locus is impossible apart from the pot; this is the sense.

Since there is no distinction between "being the counter-positive of an absolute absence co-located with itself" and "being co-located with its own absolute absence," he says: "its own absolute absence... Thinking that the qualification "unconditioned" (anavacchinna) serves to exclude only those absences that are non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), he shows this by saying: "Now, [one might object]... Nor should it be argued that because the locusness of "cloth-ness" in a cloth is also false, its absence exists there, and thus there is no deviation in the negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyabhicāra);
for in a negative inference (vyatirekin), what is the effective determinant is only the pervasion (vyāpti) defined by the absence of the probans as being non-co-located with the counter-positive.
This is because the absence of being the locus of cloth-ness (*paṭatva*) in a cloth is co-locus with its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) would be established in water and so forth, due to their possessing conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which is the counter-positive of the absence that pervades the absence of earth-ness. He provides the solution by stating "precisely for this reason," meaning: precisely because of the occurrence of such an undesirable consequence.
The cause is the absence of that which constitutes the cause. Regarding the term "counter-positive" (pratiyogin):

Now, if it is argued that even the absence of pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth is co-located with its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) in a cloth and other such things, and thus there is no established instance of an absence that is not delimited by a delimiter of co-location with the counter-positive—on this point they say:

what is intended is the possession of a property that is the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in a cloth, which is not delimited by that which delimits the co-location with the counter-positive in its capacity as a determiner (*nirūpaka*).
And since the absence of pot-ness and so forth in a cloth is of such a nature, there is no lack of an established instance.
That is incorrect.

For there is no justification for including the locus of the counter-positive (*pratiyogyadhikaraṇa*) as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the co-occurrence with the counter-positive (*pratiyogi-sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

As for the claim that there is no lack of definition because the phrase "not delimited by the delimiting factor of co-occurrence with the counter-positive" intends to qualify the cloth (*paṭa*) as not being the locus of the counter-positive—that too is questionable.

If that were the case, there would be no reason for stating "not delimited by the locus of the counter-positive" instead of simply stating "not co-locating with the counter-positive," as this would lead to the consequence of lacking a logical basis.
Furthermore, if the locus-hood of a non-pervasive occurrence were itself non-pervasive, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) when considering conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

In reality, however, according to the opponent's own view, since absences are identical with their loci, even though the absence of "pot-ness" residing in a pot is delimited by the delimiter of co-location with its counter-positive, the fact that the absence residing in a cloth is not so delimited remains entirely unimpeded.

Nor should it be argued that because the nature of "absence-ness" (*abhāvatva*), which serves as the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) for co-occurrence with the counter-positive (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇya*), is one and the same, it is impossible for an absence residing in a cloth to be non-delimited by that [nature].
This is because the "absence-ness," which is of the nature of a specific relation of relatum (*anuyogitāviśeṣa*), differs according to the difference between absences.
Alternatively, "non-delimitedness" by that which is the delimitor—the qualifier consisting in co-occurrence with the counter-positive—means simply being different from that which is qualified by it.

According to the opponent's view, although the difference characterized by that [absence] is absent in the absence of "pot-ness" as qualified by subsistence in a cloth (*paṭavṛttitvaviśiṣṭaghaṭatvābhāva*), the difference from that which is so qualified remains entirely intact.

Furthermore, in the case of the absence of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as qualified by subsistence in a cloth, there is no difference characterized by co-existence with the counter-positive (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇyaviśiṣṭabhinnatva*); thus, there is no defect whatsoever.

He raises an objection against the opponent’s view, fearing that there would be no established instance of an absence not delimited by a delimitor of co-occurrence with its counter-positive—expressing this as: "But then... The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: even by you, who assert the non-difference between a jar and a cloth, an absolute absence of jar-ness in the cloth must be admitted as an absence of jar-ness whose counter-positive is not co-occurrent.

An objection is raised: "If there is non-difference between the jar and the cloth, how can the absence of 'jar-ness' in the cloth possibly have a lack of co-location with its counter-positive? Anticipating this, it is said: "Merely by virtue of the empirical difference between the jar and the cloth. Here, the illustration is given: "Like the reflection," and so forth.

The point is this: just as there is a formal determination that, despite the identity of nature between an object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), it is by virtue of conventional difference alone that the original object possesses "object-hood" (*bimbatva*) and existence, while the reflection possesses "reflection-hood" (*pratibimbatva*) and non-existence; so too must one accept that "pot-hood" (*ghaṭatva*) belongs to the pot alone and not to a cloth.
Now, an objection might be raised: "Is it not the case that 'pot-hood' is indeed admitted in a cloth just as it is in a pot?
And if this were so, would it not follow that the conventional usage of the term 'pot' applies only to the pot and not to the cloth—a situation which would be untenable? To this, we reply: no.

He raises the objection that [the appearance] is possible through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), stating "of the nature of a jar" (*ghaṭatvasya*). The sense is that, even so, the aforementioned reason remains unestablished (*aprasiddhi*). He states "for not" (*na hi*) because it is unproven that ignorance, independent of an object, can directly determine such empirical usage; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the objects produced by ignorance being purposeless.
The sense is that its determination of such empirical usage must be accepted only by way of bringing about an object.

To the question, "What follows from this in the present context?", he says: "In that state" (*tathātve*). This means: in the capacity of sustaining worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) by way of providing the object. "It would produce that even in a jar" (*ghaṭe 'pi taṃ janayet*): since the object consisting of the nature of "jar-ness" exists in a cloth, ignorance (*avidyā*) would produce the transaction of it [as a jar]—this is the meaning.

As for the interpretation that, "if in that state—even in the absence of superimposed silver—ignorance produces the transaction of silver, then it would also produce the transaction of silver in a cloth," that is incorrect.

Because it is impossible to impose the conventional usage of "silver" upon a cloth for one who avoids the conventional usage of "pot" on that same cloth due to the power of ignorance—since there is no distinction between a pot and silver—it might be argued: "Just as in the state of superimposing silver onto mother-of-pearl, the conventional usage of 'pot' does not occur even though the object's nature as 'cloth-ness' exists in the cloth, so too the non-usage of 'pot' is justified despite the existence of 'pot-ness' in the cloth. This is not correct.
For in the case of mother-of-pearl, it is possible to obstruct the conventional usage of "mother-of-pearl-ness" by means of the superimposition of its opposite;
whereas in the case of a cloth, one must still account for the occurrence of the conventional usage of "pot-ness" when there is no superimposition of its opposite.
Nor should it be argued that the obstruction of that usage occurs there solely through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*).
For it is impossible that ignorance, which imagines "pot-ness" in a cloth, could be opposed to its conventional usage;

and because imagining that ignorance is opposed to its conventional usage after having imagined "pot-ness" in a cloth is improper according to the maxim of "washing away [the stain] with the very thing that caused it.
This might be so.

Even if defects such as the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the stated inference are avoided, its lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*) remains unavoidable due to the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position; therefore, he says: "In the case of a jar and a cloth... The point is this: if the difference between a jar and a cloth were not ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), then their non-difference would have to be ultimately real.
Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even those two [the jar and the cloth] must be ultimately real.
Otherwise, upon the cessation of the jar and the cloth, their non-difference would also necessarily cease.

He raises the objection of svarūpāsiddhi (unestablished nature) by means of a counter-argument (*pratibandī*) in another way—starting with "nanu" (but...). "Tahiṃ" (then): the meaning is that if, because of the falsity (*mithyātva*) of potness (*ghaṭatva*) in a pot, its absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) therein is accepted, then [the following follows]. "By way of falsity": the sense is that if that were so, the absolute non-existence of potness would result in the pot. "Of the pot": [refers to the aforementioned consequence].

The point is that there is no "unestablished nature" (*svarūpāsiddhi*) [of the reason], because the property of being the locus of the nature of potness—which is the counter-correlate of the absolute non-existence previously mentioned—is present in the pot. Regarding the phrase "otherwise": if the pot's status as the locus of potness is not accepted, then, due to the absence of any other locus, there would be no locus for potness at all.
Consequently, the falsity (*mithyātva*) of potness—consisting in its being the counter-correlate of an absolute non-existence existing within its own locus—would not obtain. This is the meaning.

He raises an objection to state the function of the qualification "not delimited by the delimitors of co-occurrence with the counter-positive" (pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇyāvacchedakānavacchinna)—namely, "But [it may be objected]... (nanu iti). The meaning is that even if the fallacy of unestablishedness (asiddhi) is avoided by the aforementioned method, there would still be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of a cloth. He demonstrates the absence of the probans (sādhanābhāva): "Because of the falsity of cloth-ness (paṭatva) in the cloth. This was stated in order to demonstrate the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) of cloth-ness in the cloth;
thus, the absolute absence residing in the cloth is the absolute absence of cloth-ness.

The meaning is that the property of being a cloth, which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of that [absolute absence], exists in the cloth by virtue of being its substratum (*āśraya*), because the probans—in the form of being the locus of a property that is the counter-correlate of an absolute absence residing in the cloth—is present there. "From this very reason" means: since the reason, in the form of being the locus of a property that is the counter-correlate of an absolute absence residing in the cloth, is thus subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to the cloth, for that very reason it is qualified by the condition of "not being delimited by the delimitor of co-occurrence with the counter-correlate" (*pratiyogi-sāmānādhikaraṇya-avacchedaka-anavacchinnatva*).
Although this is a qualification of the absolute absence, [it serves to exclude such deviation].

Nevertheless, it should be understood that this was stated with the intention that, even if that [property] is a qualifier, it is also a qualifier of the reason qualified by it. To the question, "Even when the qualifier is provided, how is the deviation (vyabhicāra) avoided?", he says: "In the case of a cloth. [The phrase] "by way of being co-located with the counter-positive" means that since the counter-positive, which is the nature of cloth-ness (paṭatva), also exists in a cloth where there is the absolute absence of cloth-ness. [The phrase] "co-location with the counter-positive" means that co-location with the counter-positive, which is the nature of cloth-ness, exists in the absolute absence of cloth-ness.

The delimiting factor for that [non-existence] is the state of possessing the absolute absence of cloth-ness (*paṭatva*); the meaning is "by way of being delimited by that. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of the probans" (*sādhanābhāva*): the meaning is that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because the probans is devoid of the property of not being delimited by the delimiter of co-location with its counter-positive (*pratiyogi-sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

If a qualification is introduced to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), then there is the objection that the reason is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*). He raises this doubt with the words "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "because of co-occurrence with the counter-positive" (*pratiyogisāmānādhikaraṇyāt*): the meaning is that since the absolute absence of potness (*ghaṭatva*) in a cloth is co-located with its counter-positive (potness), it is delimited by the possession of the absolute absence of potness—which serves as the delimitor of co-occurrence with the counter-positive—and thus the reason, which contains the element of being "not delimited by the delimitor of co-occurrence with the counter-positive," is absent [in the case of the cloth].

The meaning is that even by you, who assert the non-difference between a jar and a cloth, the absolute absence of "jar-ness" in the cloth must be admitted. Why? To this it is said: "because of the consequence of the usage of the term 'jar' applying to the cloth. If jar-ness were present in the cloth, then, since the conditions for the application of the word 'jar' would exist, the usage of the term 'jar' would necessarily apply to the cloth as well.
Therefore, the meaning is that in order to avoid this [absurdity], "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) should not be admitted in the cloth.

Since the two are non-different, how is the distinction established such that "the pot is indeed a pot and not a cloth," and "pot-ness is indeed the pot and not the cloth"? To this it is said: "by one who asserts the non-ultimate difference between the pot and the cloth. The meaning is that even by one who accepts their non-difference, the aforementioned distinction is justified because he admits a conventional (vyāvahārika) difference between them. As for the question, "If they are in reality non-different, how can this distinction be based on mere conventional difference?"—it is stated "conventional" (vyāvahārika) to address this.

The meaning is that just as in your own view, in the original object (*bimba*) there is only the nature of being an original object (*bimbatva*) and not the nature of being a reflection (*pratibimbatva*), so too there is the determination that in the original object there is only reality (*satyatva*) and not unreality (*asatyatva*), whereas in the reflection there is only unreality and not reality; it is the same here as well.
Now, one might object: "I certainly accept the nature of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) in the cloth.
And it should not be said: "In that case, because the causal conditions (*nimitta*) exist, the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of 'jar' would result for the cloth."

He raises the following objection: "Even though the nature of 'jar-ness' (ghaṭatva), which is the cause for the conventional usage of the term 'jar,' is present without distinction in all objects such as jars, cloths, and so forth, the restriction that the conventional usage of 'jar' applies only to the jar and not to the cloth is possible through the power of ignorance (avidyā). [The author replies: "It is restricted" means it is restricted to each individual object;
that is, in the case of a jar, the form is "this is a jar" and not "this is a cloth," and so on.

He says that such a capacity of ignorance is unproven: "No," etc. If, having accepted that the presence or absence of a cause is not the determinant for the presence or absence of empirical usage, one instead accepts that ignorance alone is what brings about that usage, then ignorance would produce the empirical usage of silver even in a mother-of-pearl shell during a state when there is no superimposition of silver upon it;
for you yourself have admitted that the cause—the nature of being superimposed silver—is not the determinant.
And if this were the case, it would produce the conventional usage of "silver" even with respect to a jar, since there is no distinction [between the two].
Therefore, [the opponent argues that] because the silverness superimposed as the cause for the conventional usage of "silver" exists in the mother-of-pearl, it produces that usage;

whereas because of its absence in a cloth, it does not produce it. Thus, it is only the presence or absence of the cause that is the determinant of the presence or absence of the conventional usage. The meaning is that if "jar-ness" existed in a cloth, the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the conventional usage "cloth" being called "jar" would be unavoidable.

If it is argued that in the aforementioned inference, let the reason be established and let there be identity between the jar and the cloth rather than the probandum consisting of their non-existence—thus rendering the argument irrelevant—it must be said in reply:
Is this identity ultimate (pāramārthika) or non-ultimate (apāramārthika)?

It cannot be the latter; for according to the maxim "between two mutually contradictory things," if identity were non-ultimate, its opposite, difference (bheda), would necessarily follow as being ultimate.

The first [opponent] says: "In the case of the jar and the cloth. Indeed, the nature of reality is such that the ultimate does not cease, whereas the non-ultimate ceases. In that regard, if the non-ultimacy of the jar and the cloth is admitted, their identity would also cease. And if that were so, how could there be ultimacy?

Therefore, the sense is that if oneness is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), then the ultimate reality of the jar and the cloth becomes unavoidable. Regarding the phrase "of the individual soul and Brahman" (*jīvabrahmaṇoḥ*): the meaning is that just as those two possess ultimate reality by virtue of being the substratum for an ultimately real non-difference, so too is it here.

He refutes the acceptance of this [consequence]—the *iṣṭāpatti*—with the following: furthermore, a jar is the counter-positive of an absolute negation (negation at all three times) residing in a cloth, etc., whose counter-positiveness is not delimited by a relation with the jar, because it is a substance, like a cloth.

Alternatively, the absolute absence of a jar is other than an absence that is simultaneous with [the jar] and has as its locus a cloth or similar object whose counter-correlate is the jar, because it is an absence, like the absence of a cloth.

Or, the relation of a jar is other than a property residing in a jar which delimits the counter-correlativity of an absence that is simultaneous with [the jar] and has as its locus a cloth or similar object, because it is a relation, like a relation residing in a cloth.

Or, the prior absence of a jar is other than a beginningless absence that has as its locus a cloth or similar object and whose counter-correlativity is not delimited by the relation of a jar, because it is an absence, like the destruction of a cloth.

Alternatively, the destruction of a jar is distinct from any eternal absence residing in a cloth or similar object whose counter-correlativity is not delimited by a relation with the jar, because it is an absence, like the prior non-existence of a cloth.

Even for one who maintains the identity of the jar and the cloth, there is no deficiency in the probandum regarding the example; for even if there is no mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) having the jar as its counter-correlative in the cloth, one must still admit that the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) having the cloth as its counter-correlative possesses a counter-correlativity that is not delimited by a relation with the jar.

Even though there is no ultimate difference between these two, one must accept that the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) of a cloth, which has a pot as its counter-correlate, possesses a counter-correlativity not delimited by the relation of conjunction with the pot; this is due to their mere conventional difference.

Otherwise, it would follow that a person seeking a pot would act toward a cloth, and for a person who already possesses a pot, it would follow that they would not employ the causal conditions for a cloth.

Nor does the establishment of a conventional mutual non-existence (*vyāvahārikānyonyābhāva*) result in the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntaratva*), because the mutual non-existence is qualified by such attributes as being "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*); for if it were merely conventional, those qualifications would be incompatible with it.

Since the favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) has been stated right here (and not elsewhere), there is no parity of status with fallacious adjuncts (*upādhyābhāsa*), nor is there a lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*). Having considered the difficulty of avoiding defects such as "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) in the aforementioned inference, he states another inference so that those defects do not apply: "Furthermore... It should be understood that the conclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) is reached by taking mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as witnessed by the perception that "the cloth is not the pot."

If it were stated here simply that "it is the counter-correlate of an absence," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntaratā*), as this would include antecedent absence (*prāgabhāva*), destructive absence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and so forth. Therefore, the term "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*) is used. Although a difference residing in an impermanent thing is itself impermanent, the statement regarding its pertaining to all three times is made by relying on the view of those who hold that "the difference of even destroyed objects never perishes," as well as the view of the Naiyāyikas.

Furthermore, the phrase "residing in a cloth, etc. (*paṭādidharmika*) is included to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established by taking the absolute absence of a jar in a jar—which is perceived in the form "there is no jar in the jar"—as the subject.

If it is argued that there is the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*) because the cognition "there is no jar on the cloth" refers to the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar, [the author] says:

"whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is not delimited by a relation. Since absolute non-existence is a sub-variety of relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*), its counter-correlativity is delimited by a relation; therefore, it lacks the property of having a counter-correlativity that is not so delimited.
This too is according to the system of the Nyāya school.
This is because, in our own system, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is not accepted as a type of relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*);

because the property of being an absolute non-existence is itself a direct sub-classifier of non-existence, and its status as a variety of relational non-existence has been refuted in the *Tattvasaṅkhyānaṭīkā*;
and because it must be understood that a non-existence whose counter-positive is a relation is included, as the case may be, within the categories of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth.

When it is cognized that "there is no cloth on the cloth," there arises an absolute absence (atyantābhāva) residing in the cloth (paṭadharmika) throughout the three periods of time, whose counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) is delimited by connection with the cloth. To dispel the doubt that the probandum (sādhya) is deficient in the example because of the absence of a counter-correlativity not delimited by connection with the cloth, the word "pot" (ghaṭa) is used. Thus, although the absolute absence of cloth in the cloth has a counter-correlativity delimited by connection with the cloth, it lacks a counter-correlativity delimited by connection with a pot; therefore, there is no deficiency in the probandum. This is how the function of the term should be understood.

Considering that even in this inference there is the drawback of complexity (*gaurava*) due to the inclusion of the qualification "having a counter-correlativity delimited by relation" (*saṃsargāvacchinnapratiyogitāka*) for the purpose of excluding absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), he states other inferences beginning with "the absolute non-existence of a jar," and so forth.
Here, it should be understood that the conclusion of being "other than that" (*tadanyatva*) regarding the subject (*pakṣa*) is reached by taking mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) as the basis;
whereas in the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), the conclusion of being "other than that" is reached by taking the absolute non-existence of a cloth (*paṭātyantābhāva*) as the basis.

If it were stated here simply that "it is other than non-existence," there would be the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntaratva*), because one could establish its difference from non-existence by taking *prāgabhāva* (prior non-existence) and *pradhvaṃsābhāva* (subsequent non-existence).
Therefore, the term "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*) is added.

Even with that much stated, there would still be the fallacy of proving something already established, because one could establish its difference from the absolute non-existence of a cloth residing in a jar.
To exclude that [possibility], it says "having the pot as its counter-correlate" (*ghaṭapratiyogika*).

The point is that since there is no other such absence, it is by taking mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) alone—and not by any other absence—that the difference between the pot and the cloth is established.
Or, it may be the relation with the pot (*ghaṭasaṃsarga*).

In this context, it should be understood that the conclusion regarding the probandum—which consists in being other than that property residing in the jar which serves as the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*)—is based on mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), as evidenced by the cognition "there is no jar in this cloth.

Here, if one were to state merely "other than a property residing in the jar," there would be the fallacy of proving the unintended (*arthāntara*), since [the cloth] is already established as being other than color (*rūpa*) and so forth.
Therefore, the phrase "delimitor of the counter-correlativity of non-existence" is included.

When that much is stated, there would be the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntaratā*), because one could take as the property residing in the jar the nature of being subsequent or prior in time—which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and emergent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*)—and since the jar is not different from that [property], the proof fails.
To exclude this, the term "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*) is added.

Furthermore, one might take the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar in a jar—as established by the cognition "the jar does not exist in the jar"—and since the jar’s counter-correlativity is delimited by a property consisting of a relation residing in the jar, the difference from that [delimiting property] is sublated (*bādhita*) with respect to the relation of the jar; therefore, to exclude that, the phrase "residing in a cloth or other [substratum]" (*paṭādidharmika*) is added.

The sense is that such an absence cannot be anything other than mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*); thus, the difference between the jar and the cloth is established. In the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the conclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) is reached by taking the distinctness from the relation residing in the jar—which serves as the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) for the absolute non-existence of the jar perceived in the cognition "the jar does not exist in the cloth. Regarding the phrase "or the prior non-existence of the jar": here, the probandum, which consists in being distinct from that [prior non-existence], should be understood in the subject (*pakṣa*) by taking the beginningless mutual non-existence attested by the cognition "the cloth is not the jar."

In this context, if it were stated merely that "it is other than an absence that is beginningless," there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratā*), as this could refer to the absolute absence of a cloth residing in a jar.
To exclude that, the phrase "residing in a locus such as a cloth" (*paṭādidharmika*) is added.
Even with that much stated, there would still be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant, as this could refer to the absolute absence of a jar residing in a cloth.
To exclude that [possibility], it is stated: "having a counter-correlativity not delimited by a relation with a jar.
Such an absence can only be the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) residing in the cloth, which has the jar as its counter-correlate; thus, the difference between the jar and the cloth is established.

In the illustrative example, the probandum—consisting of being other than that [jar]—should be understood by taking the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) residing in the cloth, which is evidenced by the cognition "the jar is not in the cloth. As for the phrase "or the destruction of the jar," here too, being other than that [jar] must ultimately be understood in the subject (pakṣa) by taking precisely the mutual absence residing in the cloth, which has the jar as its counter-correlate.

In this context, if it were stated merely that "it is other than an eternal absence," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*arthāntaratā*), because one could take the absolute absence of a cloth in a jar as the referent. Therefore, it is specified as "residing in a locus such as a cloth. Even with that much stated, there would still be the fallacy of *arthāntaratā*, because one could take the absolute absence of a cloth in a cloth itself as the referent. Therefore, it is specified as "having a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) not delimited by a relation of connection (*saṃsarga*). Nevertheless, there would still be the fallacy of *arthāntaratā*, because one could take the absolute absence of a cloth in a cloth itself as the referent.

Because that [absence] has a counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) not delimited by contact with a cloth, it is said "therefore, [the absence of] a jar. And such an absence—experienced as "the cloth is not a jar"—is indeed a mutual absence (anyonyābhāva); thus, the intended point is established.

In the example, and in the case of the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of a cloth, the conclusion of the probandum (sādhya), which consists in being other than that [cloth], is reached by taking the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) of a cloth in [another] cloth.

[Objection: But in the previous inference and in this inference, one might take the absolute absence of a cloth in a different cloth or similar locus, where the counter-correlativity is not delimited by contact with a jar; since the property of being other than that [absent object] exists in the subject (pakṣa), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana).

If it is argued that, in order to exclude that [over-extension], the absence is qualified by having "the pot" as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), then the probandum (*sādhya*) is deficient in the example;
for the destruction and prior non-existence of the pot do not have the pot as their counter-correlate.

This is not so, because in the phrase "having cloth, etc., as its locus" (*paṭādidharmika*), the word "cloth, etc. must be intended to denote the universal (*sāmānya*) of cloth and so forth, and thus it is impossible to grasp a specific pot or the like as being distinct from the counter-correlate.
For the difference of a cloth from a jar or other objects has not yet been established even by means of another cloth;
or, if it were established, what wrong would the jar have done?
Some, however, in order to dispel this doubt, qualify the absence as having its own counter-correlate as its counter-correlate.
That is questionable.

According to the reasoning stated, if by the term "cloth" (paṭa) one intends the universal "cloth-ness" (paṭatva), there is no room for the aforementioned doubt, and thus the addition of the qualification would be redundant.

Furthermore, since such an absence cannot be anything other than either mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) or absolute absence (atyantābhāva), it would follow that the terms "non-eternal absence" (anādyabhāva) or "eternal absence" (nityābhāva) would be rendered redundant. Now, in this context, within the fourfold set of inferences where the subject (pakṣa) is the absolute absence of a jar and so forth, the word "other" (anya) in the probandum (sādhya) must be understood as referring specifically to mutual absence.

And thus, for one who does not accept [difference] in mere insentient objects, since that [difference] is unestablished anywhere, how could there not be the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) when proving it? Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of using a formulation such as "a jar is directly different from a cloth" without any mediation. If this is argued, we say no; because in all these cases, by the word "other" (*anya*), only difference in general is intended.

And because that [non-existence] is accepted even by one who accepts conventional difference. Now, an objection is raised: in this inference where the subject (*pakṣa*) is the pot, there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example.

For, in the doctrine of the non-difference between the pot and the cloth, since the absence of the cloth is itself of the nature of the presence of the pot, the absolute absence whose locus is the cloth and whose counter-correlate is the cloth must necessarily have a counter-correlativity delimited by the relation of conjunction with the pot. Consequently, because it lacks a counter-correlativity undelimited by such [a relation], the cloth cannot be the counter-correlate of such an absence.
The same applies to the second inference as well.

In the doctrine that asserts the identity of the jar and the cloth, the absence of the cloth (the property of the cloth) which has been made the example exists even as having the jar as its counter-correlate; thus, it is possible for it to take the form of an absence whose counter-correlate is the jar, resulting in a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example. Furthermore, since the relationship between the example and the subject (*dṛṣṭānta-dārṣṭāntika-bhāva*) is pervaded by difference, it would be untenable for either the cloth or the absence of the cloth to serve as the example in an inference where the jar and so forth are the subject. Therefore, he says: "Of the jar and the cloth... Here, by the first word "etc. (*ādi*), the relation residing in the cloth is intended to be included.

By the phrase "the second and so forth," there is the inclusion of the distinctness from the absolute absence (traikālikābhāva) of the jar—which has the jar as its counter-positive (pratiyogin)—from the cloth—which has the cloth as its locus (dharmin)—within the second and third inferences; and the inclusion of the distinctness from the properties residing in the jar, which serve as the delimiters (avacchedaka) of the counter-positiveness of the absolute absence of the cloth—which has the cloth as its locus—within the [respective] inferences.
By the phrase "due to the deficiency of the probandum (sādhyavaikalya), etc.," the word "etc. includes the impossibility of [those things] serving as examples (dṛṣṭānta).
Now, one might ask: how can this be accepted under the doctrine of non-difference (abheda)? To this he says: "Of those two"—meaning, of the jar and the cloth.
Here too, by the first two words, only those previously mentioned are to be understood.
Consequently, this is the meaning:
first of all, in the initial inference, there is no deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example.

Nor does it apply to the second inference. For, by accepting the conventional difference between a jar and a cloth, there exists the state of having a pratiyogitā (counter-correlativity) in the absolute absence of a cloth—which has the cloth as its locus and the cloth as its pratiyogin—that is not delimited by the relation of conjunction with a jar; thus, the cloth possesses such a pratiyogitā in that absence.

Furthermore, in the case of the second inference, it is impossible for the absolute absence of a cloth to be different from the absolute absence whose locus is the cloth and whose pratiyogin is the jar, merely on the basis of the conventional difference between the jar and the cloth.
Nor does this apply to the third inference;

for, precisely because one accepts a conventional difference between the pot and the cloth regarding the relation residing in the cloth, it is possible for there to be a difference from the property consisting of the relation residing in the pot—which serves as the delimiting condition (avacchedaka) for the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of the absolute absence of the pot residing in the cloth.

For this very reason, it is logical to employ cloth, the absolute non-existence of cloth, and the relation residing in cloth as examples in the inferences whose subjects are a jar, the absolute non-existence of a jar, and the relation of a jar [respectively]. He states two refutations for the contrary position with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). This means that if one does not accept the aforementioned systematic arrangement based merely on conventional difference. The term "of the established jar" (*siddhaghaṭasya*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound;
the word "seekers of objects" (*padārthinaḥ*) is to be supplied as the subject.
The sense is that the ultimate non-difference between the jar and the cloth remains intact.
In the phrase "the cloth, the generality, and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the cloth.
Furthermore, this suspicion regarding the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and its refutation apply only to the subject matter of the first three inferences,
not to that of the fourth and fifth.

In that case, since the destruction of the cloth and its prior non-existence—which serve as the examples—possess precisely the property of being distinct from both beginningless non-existents and eternal non-existents, one might object:
"In that case, this discussion should be conducted as a separate set of three inferences.
True.

Nevertheless, since these five inferences were introduced for the purpose of establishing the difference between a jar and a cloth, it should be understood that an intermediate discussion is inappropriate; therefore, this discussion is properly situated within the proof itself.
Some, however, maintain that this discussion concerns only the subject matter of the inference whose locus (*pakṣa*) is the jar.
In that case, one must consider what the function of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is.

Others, however, intending that this discussion concerns only the second inference whose subject (*pakṣa*) is the absolute non-existence of a jar, maintain that the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example must be established.
Likewise, even in the case of the mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) one wishes to prove, there is no absence of a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) not delimited by a relation with a jar;
for there is no difference between the absolute non-existence of a jar and its mutual non-existence.
And thus, intending that there would be a contradiction (*bādha*), they say that by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "deficiency of the probandum, etc.," contradiction is to be understood.
They further state that the mention of "the example" (*dṛṣṭāntasya*) is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the "subject" (*pakṣa*).

In that case as well, the function of the first two "etcetera" words remains indeed to be considered. Regarding the phrase "and if [it were] conventional" (*vyāvahārikatve*): the meaning is that since the conventional is illusory (*avidyaka*), its cessation upon the cessation of ignorance—namely, in liberation—is necessary; therefore, it cannot possibly exist throughout the three periods of time (*traikālika*).
[Objection: Is it not the case that in all the inferences proving the difference of the insentient (*jaḍa*), "graduality" (*taratva*) is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) in the subject (*pakṣa*)?
Likewise, since it is possible to prove the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) as well, these [inferences] share the same status as fallacious arguments (*abhāsa*).

Furthermore, the reasons (*hetu*) are inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). To this, he says: "of the favorable reasoning" (*anukūlatarkasya*). The meaning is: because this has been stated elsewhere in the *Nyāyāmṛta*.

For in that case, within the first chapter—in the section refuting the argument that dualistic perception sublates non-dualistic scripture—the following errors would follow: (1) delusions such as "this is silver" or "I am fair" would possess validity; (2) the Vedāntas, which teach the difference of the Self from the body and its distinction from falsehood and so forth, would lack authority;

(3) since everything—including Brahman and its non-difference from the Self—would be known by the very cognition of a jar (due to their non-difference), the Vedāntas would be omniscient yet redundant, and liberation would occur immediately.

It has been stated that because pleasure and pain, bondage and liberation, difference and non-difference, defects and ornaments, victory and defeat, error and valid cognition, and so forth, would in reality be non-distinct, there would follow a total confusion (sarvasaṅkara) of all things, as well as contradictions with one's own actions, illogicality, and self-contradiction. Furthermore, a supporting argument was previously stated here: "If the identity of a jar and a cloth were accepted as ultimately real, then the essential nature of the jar and the cloth would likewise be ultimately real, just like that of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman," and so on.
Furthermore, it will be stated that perception which grasps the non-difference between two trees standing at a distance would have to be a revealer of reality (*tattvāvedaka*).
Nevertheless, it should be understood that the phrase "elsewhere" was used for the purpose of indicating many supporting arguments (*anukūlatarka*).

Some, however, having explained it as being "already stated" because it was mentioned in the *Nyāyamṛta*, say: "If there were a real identity (*tāttvikamaikya*) between a jar and a cloth, then upon the destruction of the jar, there would be the destruction of the cloth."
They say that this is because such reasoning exists as, for example: "From the cognition of a jar, there would follow the cognition of a cloth.
[The opponent objects: "In that case, let identity (tādātmya) be false;
however, how does that establish the ultimate reality (pāramārthikatva) of difference?"
For it is not merely by refuting identity that the critique of the opponent's position is undertaken here;
rather, it is precisely for the purpose of establishing one's own position through the proof of the reality of difference.
Nor should it be said that, between two mutually contradictory positions, one will necessarily be established simply by the negation of the other.
If it is argued that even if difference (*bheda*) were established, there would be no means to prove its ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*), we say no.
For wherever there is a negation of something as delimited by a certain existence, there is an affirmation of a property that is its opposite and likewise delimited by that same existence.
Thus, when the ultimate identity (*tādātmya*) is negated, difference of that very same nature is obtained; and this is the formal argument (*prayoga*).

Identity consists in being the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in that which possesses existence—which is the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-positiveness of its own negation—and which is contradictory to itself, as is the case with the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), due to [the latter's] falsity (*mithyātva*).
Nor should it be argued that "possessing such existence" is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) even for the substratum (*dharmin*);
otherwise, if eternity were false in the case of a hare's horn, then non-eternity would follow [for the hare's horn].
In the proof that "the locus possesses the aforementioned property of identity and is the counter-positive of absence," the probans (upādhi) is also obtained within the subject (pakṣa).
Nor is there any deviation (vyabhicāra) in this case regarding the eternality of a hare's horn;
