for the statement "because of its falsity" means "because it is the counter-positive of a negation in a locus that possesses existence. [Objection: Even so, the perception of difference by way of the negation of identity is not direct.
Nevertheless, [this argument] is swallowed by the difficulty of proving the existence of the substratum (*dharmin*).

Nor can it be said that one is directly proving "the pot is distinct from the cloth," because since the category of an entity called "difference" (*bheda*) does not exist, there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
The conventional usage of difference, however, is established solely through the absolute non-existence of each other's attributes.

Nor should it be argued that, in the doctrine of universal non-duality (*sarvādvaitavāda*), even the absolute non-existence of each other's attributes is untenable; for it is accepted that attributes coexist with their own absolute non-existence within the same locus.

Furthermore, if one seeks to prove mere difference, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) regarding conventional difference. If, however, one adds the qualification "ultimately real," the reason becomes unestablished (*aprasiddha*).

Moreover, unlike the proof of the difference between selves, it is not possible to employ the qualification "having the same ontological status as the existence of the subject" (*dharmisattāsamānasattāka*).
Because even the subjects (*dharmin*) are merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*), the author employs another formulation due to this underlying unease.

The intended meaning is that "this" refers to the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the jar, which is an absence characterized by a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) not delimited by a relation with the jar; thus, the meaning is "the counter-correlative of that.

The phrase "having a counter-correlativity not delimited by a relation with the jar" is used to prevent the fallacy of being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*) by means of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of cloth and other things whose counter-correlate is the jar. This excludes such an absolute absence because its counter-correlativity is delimited by the aforementioned relation.

It should be understood that here, in both instances—namely, the case of relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)—this statement is made in accordance with common worldly usage, wherein relation and identity serve as the delimiters of the counter-positive (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*). In reality, however, it has been stated previously that for those two [types of non-existence], the mere relationship of the superimposed object (*āropya*) is not the delimiter.
Thus, the meaning here should be understood as "that which does not have the relation to a jar as its superimposed object."
The same applies in the subsequent cases as well.

If one were to state only "delimited by identity with a jar" (*ghaṭatādātmyāvacchinna*), there would be the two faults of the probandum being unestablished (*aprasiddha*) and the deficiency of the example (*sādhyavaikalya*); thus, this specific formulation was employed. Furthermore, if one were to state only "not delimited by a relation" (*saṃsargānavacchinna*) and so forth, those same two faults would persist; therefore, the term "jar" is first introduced as a specific instance of a relation.

The phrase "having the jar and so forth as its locus" (*ghaṭādidharmika*) is used to exclude the fallacy of *arthāntara* (proving something other than what was intended) by means of the distinction of non-conscious entities that are not relevant to the subject. It should be understood that by the term "ether and so forth" (*viyadādi*), only insentient matter is intended.

The term "pertaining to the three times" (*traikālika*) is used to exclude the possibility of the argument being established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*) through the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of a jar. In this view, since there is no rule that prior absence and destruction must reside in the same substrate (*samavāyideśa*), their exclusion is properly accomplished by the phrase "having the cloth and so forth as its locus" alone; thus, there is no room for the doubt as to why that [phrase] is necessary.

If it is objected that since antecedent negation (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) are types of relational non-existence (*saṃsargābhāva*), they are already excluded by the phrase "not delimited by a relation" (*saṃsargānavacchinna*) alone, and therefore the term "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*) is unnecessary for that purpose—[we reply] no.
For here, the inference proceeds on the basis that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) alone is what constitutes relational non-existence.
As stated by the venerable feet of Jayatīrtha:

Furthermore, others have stated that the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is the absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is a relation; or else, the meaning of "not delimited by a relation" is that it is delimited by a relation alone that does not consist of other qualifiers.

And thus, in this case, there is the exclusion of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) by virtue of its being delimited by that [specific locus] alone. The term "pertaining to the three times" (*traikālika*) is used for the purpose of excluding only the conventional mutual non-existence (*vyāvahārikānyonyābhāva*). Regarding the example "like a cloth": although the absolute non-existence of a cloth is not delimited by a relation, it lacks a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by a relation with a jar; therefore, the probandum must be established by means of a qualified non-existence (*viśiṣṭābhāva*) in respect to the cloth, which is its counter-correlate. Alternatively, "or the absolute non-existence of a jar": this means other than that absolute non-existence which has a jar as its counter-correlate and a cloth or similar object as its locus, and which pertains to the three times.
The point is that this must be stated as *anyonyābhāva* (mutual non-existence) itself.

To exclude the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*) by means of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar and so forth, the qualifiers "having a jar as its counter-correlate" (*ghaṭapratiyogika*), "residing in a cloth and so forth" (*paṭādidharmika*), and "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*) are included, as before. Regarding the phrase "like the absence of a cloth": it should be understood that the subject possesses the probandum (*sādhyavat*) because it is distinct from the aforementioned absolute non-existence of the jar. If it is objected: "Even so, since one absolute non-existence is distinct from another absolute non-existence having a jar as its counter-correlate, there remains the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*)," we say no.

Even though there is a difference between an absolute absence whose counter-positive is delimited by "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and another such absence, they are one because there is no difference in their delimiters (avacchedaka).
Nor should it be argued that the same fault applies because the absolute absence of a pot is distinct from the absolute absence of a blue pot;
for in the proposition, the phrase "having a pot as its counter-positive" means "having a counter-positive delimited by pot-ness."

But even so, the absolute absence of a jar superposed by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is merely established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*) as the absolute absence of a jar superposed by way of some other relation;

nor can it be specified that "it is an absence where no relation other than the relation residing in the superposition of the counter-positive—which is the cause of its own cognition—is superposed. This is because such a specification would be contradicted in the case of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), since it is superposed by a relation distinct from that of absolute absence.
Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned fault does not apply because even absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) alone can be the subject (*pakṣa*);
for [the reason] would be established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*) by virtue of being distinct from all other absolute non-existences.

Nor should it be argued that the intended meaning of the phrase "absolute non-existence is distinct" is "that which possesses a distinctness characterized by a locus delimited by absolute non-existence."
[Objection: "Because this would result in the fallacy of the example lacking the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*). [Reply: Not so;
for the statement "the absolute non-existence of the pot is other" means that it possesses an otherness (*anyatva*) as determined by a single absence that exists in all its own loci (*svādhikaraṇa*).
The term "its own locus" (*svādhikaraṇa*) refers to that which is co-uttered with itself (*svasamabhivyāhṛta*); thus, there is no fault such as the deficiency of the probandum.

[Objection: But surely, at the stage when only mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) has been established, if one says "other" (*anya*), there would be the fallacy of an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) because the probandum (*sādhya*) is itself unestablished. [Response: No; for even by one who accepts mutual non-existence as the meaning of the word "other" in other contexts, the intended meaning here is merely that which is the object of the conventional usage of "other" and so forth. "Or the relation with a jar" (*ghaṭasaṃsargo vā*): the meaning is that "other than that" refers to those two—namely, the jar and the relation—which serve as the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the threefold absences (*traikālikābhāva*) residing in the locus (the jar and so forth). For it is these two properties—the relation and identity (*tādātmya*)—that are intended as the delimiters of the counter-correlativity of the absence.
In this context, the difference from such properties (tādṛśadharmānyatva) residing in the relation (saṃsarga) results in being different from those properties whose nature is identity (tādātmya).
The underlying point is that the absence which has as its counter-positive that which is delimited by those [identities] is precisely the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva).
Here, if one were to state merely "different from the properties residing in the jar," there would be the fallacy of proving something else (arthāntara), namely, difference from color and so forth.
Therefore, the qualification extends up to the "delimitor" (*avacchedaka*).

The term "residing in the jar" (*ghaṭaniṣṭha*) is used to prevent the establishment of a property other than the aforementioned one as residing in the jar. "Like the relation residing in the cloth" (*paṭaniṣṭhasaṃsargavat*): it should be understood that the probandum (*sādhya*) consists in its being different from the relation which constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*).
The remainder is as before.

"Or the prior non-existence of the jar (*ghaṭaprāgabhāva*). The meaning is this: that beginningless absence which has the cloth as its locus and whose counter-correlativity is not delimited by a relation to the jar is precisely the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) of the jar and so forth.

Here, in order to avoid the undesirable consequence that [the definition] would apply to the absolute absence of a wall residing in the cloth, the qualification "having the jar as its counter-correlate" must also be included.
In order to avoid the undesirable consequence that it would apply to the absolute absence of the jar, it is stated that "its counter-correlativity is not delimited by a relation to the jar."
The word "beginningless" (*anādi*) is used to exclude the establishment of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) at the conventional level (*vyāvahārika*).
However, it should be understood that this is intended to show that conventional difference is adventitious (*āgantuka*).
Alternatively, "beginningless" means being non-conditional (*anaupādhika*).
Alternatively, the term "beginningless" (*anādi*) is used to exclude destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).

In this context, it should be understood as before by means of the phrase "not delimited by a relation. Regarding the example "like the destruction of a jar": having taken that [destruction]—which possesses the aforementioned form—as the subject (*pakṣa*), its status as the probandum (*sādhya*) should be understood as being "other than the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that jar. Regarding the alternative "or the destruction of a jar": here too, the phrase "having the jar as its counter-correlate" (*ghaṭapratiyogika*) should also be included.

It should be understood that the term "viyat" (ether) is used either to exclude conventional [entities] as before, or for the purpose of excluding prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Regarding the example "like the prior non-existence of a jar," it should be understood that its possession of the probandum (*sādhyavat-tva*) is due to its being other than the aforementioned form of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).

Now, one might object: in these inferences, the probandum must be established in the examples such as cloth by means of properties like being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) not delimited by the relation of conjunction with a jar.
That is not tenable.

For me, who maintains the doctrine of non-difference (*abhedavāda*) regarding all things, even the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of a cloth would possess a counter-positivity (*pratiyogitā*) that is not delimited by its relation to the jar, because the cloth itself is the jar.

Thus, [the objection] that there is a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) or an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) is avoided; therefore, he says: "of the jar and the cloth. By the term "absolute absence of the jar," the absolute absence of a wall and so forth is intended, but not the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of the jar or cloth.

By the phrase "being a counter-correlate" (*pratiyogitvādi*), the inclusion of such properties as "having a jar or the like as its counter-correlate"—which are intended in the second and subsequent inferences—is indicated. He explains this with the words "of those two" (*tayor iti*). You have accepted a conventional difference (*vyāvahārikabheda*) in order to avoid the confusion of linguistic usage regarding jars, cloths, and so forth;
it is precisely by relying on that established distinction that we establish our proof.

He states an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) for one who, out of impudence (*vaiyātya*), does not accept the established rule: "of the perfected cloth" (*siddhapaṭasya*). The sense is that because the jar and the cloth are identical, there is no distinction between what has already arisen and what is yet to be produced. Regarding the phrase "by virtue of existing in the three times, etc. (*traikālikatvādinā*): here, the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes such qualities as beginninglessness (*anāditva*).
Now, what is this "existing in the three times"? Does it mean being connected with the three times, or being uncontradicted throughout the three times?
Not the first [alternative],
because even in the conventional realm, there is no contradiction with that, just as in the case of space and so forth.
Not the second.
This is because it would result in either a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) or the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).

Likewise, "beginninglessness" (*anāditva*) is itself untenable under analysis, as it could mean either not being the counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or not being produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). Similarly, "eternality" (*nityatva*) is also unable to withstand such alternatives, whether it means not being the counter-positive of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) or not being within the scope of sublation (*bādhāgocaratva*). [The author replies: Not so.
Being uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time is precisely what constitutes "pertaining to the three periods of time.
Nor is there any fault as previously stated,
for this [definition] is tenable even against one who maintains that non-existence is ultimately real.

Nor should it be argued that, since the ultimate reality of that [absence] would be established by itself through the proof of mere mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), the qualification "pertaining to the three periods of time" (*traikālika*) is redundant.
This is because [the qualification] is appropriate for one who, while accepting the ultimate reality of mere relational absence (*saṃsargābhāva*), does not accept mutual absence at all,
and who considers that even if [mutual absence] were somehow possible, it would necessarily be sublated.
Alternatively, "belonging to the three times" (traikālika) means being related to the three periods of time.
Nor is the aforementioned fault applicable;

for this [definition] is logical in relation to Bhāskara, who accepts that difference (*bheda*) arises from a real limiting adjunct (*satyopādhi*), is destroyed by the destruction of that [adjunct], and that everything is real.
In this view, it should be understood that the term "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*) in the root text refers to that which is conditioned (*aupādhika*).

Likewise, its beginninglessness (*anāditva*) must also be explained in this manner. Now, one might object: even in these inferences, the state of being other than a pot (*ghaṭānyatva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*);
and it cannot be argued that it is not a limiting condition because it is merely "otherness from the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*).
Because in an inference where the probandum has not been accepted as belonging to the subject (*pakṣa*) alone, exactly such [a reason] must be stated;

for when the seed of fallaciousness exists, the mere form of being "other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) is irrelevant. Furthermore, these [reasons] share the same status as fallacious reasons (*ābhāsa*).

In the first formulation, just as [the term] "non-delimited by relation" (saṃsargānavacchinna) would lead to the undesirable consequence of establishing a third type of absence distinct from both relational absence and mutual absence, so too would [the term] "non-delimited by identity" (tādātmyānavacchinna).

Furthermore, if one were to say "having a jar as its locus" (ghaṭadharmika) instead of "having a jar etc. as its locus" (ghaṭādidharmika), it would result in the absurdity of a thing being different from itself.
This applies to the second formulation as well.
Moreover, the proponents [of the opposing view] say "no.
Because the concomitance between the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) is not perceived, he says: "anukūla... (favorable...). "Elsewhere" means in the *Nyāyāmṛta*. To explain:

If there were no mutual difference among insentient things, and if their identity were ultimately real, then the perceptual apprehension of the identity of trees standing at a distance would not be an error; rather, its sublation alone would constitute valid cognition (*pramā*). Furthermore, by asserting the identity of one's own and the opponent's positions, there would be a contradiction with one's own practice when refuting the opponent.
If the refutation and the proof were one and the same, then the very refutation of another would constitute its proof.

Furthermore, by virtue of being superimposed as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there could be no distinction between the individual souls (*jīva*) based on those adjuncts. Consequently, one who seeks a jar would proceed toward a cloth.
"Even the perpetual suffering of another would be an ornament," and so forth.

Now, if it is argued that the perception of the identity of the tree is empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and grasps that [identity], and that since such [perception] does not exist, it is an error; [we reply:]

If it is argued that because the apprehension of mere oneness by that [perception] lacks the manifestation of conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*), and since non-manifesting perception has as its nature non-ultimate objects, the oneness being grasped is merely superimposed (*āropita*); then, the cognition produced by the sentence "This is one tree" would have to be valid knowledge (*pramā*).
This is because it is possible for the sentence to have an ultimate object as its domain.
If it is argued that even that [perception] has as its object something superimposed, then the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman would likewise be so.
Furthermore, since a superimposition must be inferred by a sublater (*bādhaka*), the identity of air and trees—which is not sublated—is not a superimposition.
This is because the subsequent perception "two trees" cannot constitute a sublation in the form of the non-existence of an object, given that it is itself an error.

Furthermore, since it is possible to avoid contradictions such as those regarding empirical difference and self-referential activity, there is no consequence of that [absurdity] from an ultimate standpoint (*paramārthatas*).

Moreover, regarding the phrase "the jar" (*ghaṭa*): the meaning is that it is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of that absence which is unconditioned by the relation of being a jar and which pertains to a locus such as a cloth throughout the three periods of time.
The probandum (*sādhya*) should be understood by taking the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of a cloth in a cloth.

In the alternative view (pakṣe), however, because the absolute absence of a jar has a counter-correlativity delimited by its relation to the jar, the conclusion of the probandum (sādhya) is reached by taking that [absolute absence] into account; thus, there is the establishment of mutual absence (anyonyābhāva).
The sense is that since that [mutual absence] has a counter-correlativity delimited by identity (tādātmya), it does not have a counter-correlativity delimited by a relation to the jar.

Furthermore, the qualification "existing at all three times" (traikālika) is for the purpose of establishing the intended object, which is the nature of mutual absence as existing at all three times; this is also for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā) by taking a conventional mutual absence into account, as will be clear later on.

But this is not for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or destructive non-existence (*dhvaṃsābhāva*) as the object;
for since those two have a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) delimited by the relation of conjunction with the jar, there is no room for the charge of *siddhasādhanatā*.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "having cloth, etc., as its locus" (*paṭādidharmika*): although, according to our own system (*siddhānta*), mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) of a jar having cloth as its locus does not possess existence across the three periods of time because it is of the very nature of the cloth and so forth, nevertheless, this [statement] is made according to the method of the Nyāya school.

It should be understood that, by means of a *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna-bahuvrīhi* compound, the intention is either to refer to mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) characterized by permanence, or else to absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*). Regarding the phrase "or absolute absence of a jar": the meaning is that it is other than that which is an absence existing at all three times (*traikālika-abhāva*) whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is a jar and whose locus (*dharmin*) is a cloth.

The phrase "having the jar as its counter-correlate" (*ghaṭapratiyogika*) is included to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the cloth as the probandum. In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the probandum should be understood by taking the absolute non-existence of the jar. The phrase "or the relation with the cloth" (*paṭasaṃsargo vā*) means: that property residing in the jar which is other than the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of that threefold temporal non-existence whose locus is the cloth. The term "residing in the jar" (*ghaṭaniṣṭha*) is included to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established by taking the difference from the relation with the cloth and so forth. The word "property" (*dharma*) is a qualifier for both identity (*tādātmya*) and relation (*saṃsarga*).

The meaning is as follows: by that [inference], an absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the pot and which has cloth as its locus at all three times is established; this is established specifically as a mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), because the property of being other than a relational absence (*saṃsargānyatva*) is sublated in the subject (*pakṣa*).

The intention is that the probandum (*sādhya*) in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is taken as "being other than the relation with the pot. Regarding the phrase "or the prior absence of the pot": the meaning is that it is other than that beginningless absence residing in the cloth which possesses a counter-correlativity not delimited by the relation with the pot.

The phrase "having a counter-correlativity not delimited by a relation" (*saṃsargānavacchinnapratiyogitāka*) is included to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), which would occur if one were to take the difference from the absolute non-existence of a jar (*ghaṭātyantābhāvānyatva*) as the probandum. Since the destruction of a cloth (*paṭadhvaṃsa*), which serves as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), possesses the probandum when one takes the difference from the absolute non-existence of a cloth residing in the cloth itself (*paṭadharmikapaṭātyantābhāvānyatva*), the term "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is specified for that purpose.

Although the absolute absence of a jar has a counter-positivity that is not delimited by a relation, it nevertheless does not have a counter-positivity undelimited by the relation of "connection with a jar"; therefore, the phrase "having cloth, etc., as its locus" is used for the purpose of establishing the difference between cloth and jar. The term "beginningless" (*anādi*) is included to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), which would occur if one were to take as the probandum the state of being other than the destruction of the color and so forth belonging to the cloth (which is a property of the cloth).

To exclude [the fallacy] by taking as the property [of the subject] the "difference from cloth-ness" residing in a cloth or other object whose counter-correlativity is not delimited by its relation to a jar, the term "absence" (*abhāva*) is included [in the definition]. Now, one might object: "Just as in the case of the example—the destruction of a cloth—the probandum is established by taking as the property the 'difference from the absolute absence of cloth,' so too in the case of the subject (pakṣa), the probandum exists precisely by taking that same difference; thus, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Nor should it be said that the qualification "having a jar as its counter-correlative" must be added to avoid this [fallacy].
Because this would result in the fallacy of the probandum being absent from the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Nor should it be argued that the probandum will be established in the example by taking "otherness from the prior non-existence of the jar" as the basis;

for that [prior non-existence] lacks both the property of having a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) not delimited by a relation with the jar, and the property of residing in a locus such as the jar.
And because it would contradict the subsequent text.
If it is argued that this is like a rope with snares at both ends, we say no;
for the non-existence is qualified by its having its own counter-positive as its counter-positive.

The word "own" (*sva*) refers to that which is mentioned in proximity; in the case of the application of the probandum (*sādhya*), it conveys the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a jar, while in the application to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), it conveys the destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) of a cloth.

Thus, there is neither the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) nor a deficiency of the probandum in the example. Furthermore, the term "beginningless non-existence" (*anādyabhāva*) will serve as a qualifier; therefore, nothing is untenable. As for the phrase "or the destruction of a jar," everything here should be understood in the same manner as before.

Now, if it is held that there is in reality no mutual difference between insentient things, then because there would be non-difference between the jar and the cloth, and because there would be non-difference between the absolute absence of the jar and the absolute absence of the cloth, the absolute absence of the cloth would not possess a counter-positiveness (pratiyogitā) not delimited by its relation to the jar; thus, the probandum is deficient in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Likewise, even in the case of the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) intended to be proven, there would be no counter-positiveness not delimited by its relation to the jar, because there is non-difference between the absolute absence of the jar and its mutual absence.

And since there would be a contradiction [in that case], he says: "by one who asserts the non-difference between a jar and a cloth. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood as referring to one who asserts the non-difference between the absolute absence and mutual absence of those two, that is, one who asserts the non-difference between the absolute absence of a jar and the mutual absence of a jar. Regarding the phrase "due to the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes contradiction (*bādha*).

The mention of "example" (*dṝṣṭānta*) is an elliptical expression that includes the "subject" (*pakṣa*) as well. "Otherwise" means: in the event of not accepting conventional difference. Now, since a limiting condition (*upādhi*)—namely, being other than the subject (*pakṣetaratva*) or having a nature similar to it—is possible in every case, the property of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāvatva*) would also be subject to the fallacy of being "vitiated by a limiting condition" (*sopādhika*). Furthermore, because this [condition] enters into the very body of the probandum (*sādhya*), it shares the same status as a fallacious reason and lacks probative force (*aprayojakatva*). To this, he says: "Because of the favorable reasoning" (*anukūlatarkasya*). This is explained elsewhere in the *Nyāyāmṛta*.
Because it has already been stated; that is, because it has been explained almost entirely.
If there were an ultimate identity between a jar and a cloth, then upon the destruction of the jar, there would be the destruction of the cloth;
and upon the cognition of the jar, there would be the cognition of the cloth.
Because there exists the following reasoning: "For a person who possesses a perfected jar (siddhaghaṭa), there would be no acquisition of the collection of materials for a cloth," and so forth;

since the reason (*hetu*) is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*), and because the *upādhi* does not pervade the reason that is itself pervaded by the probandum, while it does pervade the probandum, the reason is not vitiated by the presence of an *upādhi*.

Even the difference consisting in mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāvānyatva*), having entered into the body of the probandum (*sādhya*), results in a non-existence that is of the same nature as a fallacy (*ābhāsa*). Because there is an absence of a supporting reason (*anukūlatarka*) for such fallacies, they do not share the same logical status (*samānayogakṣematā*). For this very reason, there is also no lack of a proving factor (*aprayojakatva*); this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "Furthermore" (*kiñca*): [the term] "not delimited by the relation with a jar" (*ghaṭasaṃsargānavacchinna*) is used to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), which would occur if one were to take the absolute non-existence of a jar residing in a cloth (*paṭaniṣṭhaghaṭātyantābhāva*).

If one were to state merely that [the absence] is not delimited by a relation (*saṃsarga*), then, prior to the establishment of difference, there would be a failure to establish the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) because such an absolute absence (*traikālikābhāva*) residing in a jar would be unestablished. Therefore, it is specified as "relation to a jar" (*ghaṭasaṃsarga*).
In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the probandum is established by taking the absolute absence of a cloth residing in a jar;
for although that [absence] is delimited by a relation to a jar, it is not delimited by a relation to a cloth.
Furthermore, on this alternative view, the establishment of the stated probandum does not reach its conclusion without mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).

This is because the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) and the posterior absence (*pradhvaṃsa*) of a jar reside in the inherent cause of their counter-positive, and thus lack the property of having a cloth as their locus.

According to the older school’s view, since only the prior and posterior time-limited inherences possess the status of being the delimiters of that counter-positiveness, there is no absence [of the jar] that is not delimited by the relation of the jar.

And because it lacks existence across the three periods of time, it must be stated that this is indeed an "other-absence" (*anyonyābhāva*) of such a non-existence; thus, its establishment [as such] follows.
Furthermore, the qualification "having cloth as its locus" (*paṭadharmika*) is not redundant.
This is because [the qualification] is for the purpose of establishing the object to be negated (*uddeśya*), namely the destruction of a jar that is delimited by its cloth-locus.
The term "pertaining to the three times" (*traikālika*) is also for that very same purpose.
Furthermore, the fact that it serves to establish its ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) is made explicit later in the text itself.

Nor should it be argued that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*) by taking as the subject an absolute absence of a jar (*ghaṭātyantābhāva*) residing in a cloth (*paṭa*), where the relation is delimited by a non-co-referential connection (*vyadhikaraṇasambandha*). This is because the intended meaning of the term is "not being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) residing in a cloth [or jar] as delimited by a relation of inherence (*saṃsarga*). Regarding the phrase "absolute absence of a jar": in order to avoid the fallacy of *siddhasādhanam*—which would arise if one were to take the difference from the absolute absence of a cloth (*paṭātyantābhāva*) as the counter-correlativity belonging to the jar—one must admit difference elsewhere. Since this probandum (*sādhya*) operates precisely at the point of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the jar and the cloth, once another difference has been accepted, one should not suspect the unestablished nature (*aprasiddhi*) of the probandum as constituted by difference.
The function of the two properties—being a property of cloth (*paṭadharmikatva*) and being present at all three times (*traikālikatva*)—is exactly as before.
In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the probandum (*sādhya*) must be established by taking the difference from the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar which constitutes the subject (*pakṣa*).
This is because, once that [non-existence] is established in the subject, it would be impossible for the conclusion to terminate in its own difference.
Such is the establishment of mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*).

Nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because it is possible to establish the probandum (*sādhya*) by taking the difference from another among the various absolute absences (*atyantābhāva*) residing in the cloth, which have as their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) jars and are delimited by various relations.

Even when the probandum is established under the delimitation of the nature of the absolute absence of a jar, since the probandum exists in all instances of the subject (*pakṣa*) by taking the difference from another within a single instance, the pervasion of the delimitation of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) by the delimitation of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) remains entirely uncontradicted.

The appearance of a pervasion constituted by difference has already been refuted in the context of inference; therefore, the establishment of difference cannot result from the force of such an appearance.

If it is argued that—when proving a difference whose counter-positive is a pot and whose locus is a cloth, and which has a counter-positiveness delimited by the property of being an absolute non-existence at all three times—there would be a sublation (*bādha*) because the probandum is absent even in the subject (*pakṣa*), since it is occupied by the aforementioned delimitors of counter-positiveness—the answer is no.
For in every inference, pervasion as constituted by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) appears by way of a general rule (*utsarga*).

Because of the parsimony of the entity [involved], it is accepted that in an inference dependent on a causal complex assisted by the apprehension of a sublation (*bādhagraha*), it appears as being constituted by an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). In the present case, since there is no ascertainment of sublation, the desired conclusion is established precisely because it appears as being constituted by a mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Alternatively, the desired conclusion is established by accepting its appearance in the present case through the force of the cognition of parsimony (*lāghavajñāna*).

Alternatively, by qualifying the probandum—the difference (*bheda*)—with the property of being other than that which possesses the nature of the absolute absence of a jar (*ghaṭātyantābhāvatva*), through the two relations of "having a counter-positive residing in its locus" (*āśrayaniṣṭhapratiyogitākatva*) and "co-existence" (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*), those aforementioned differences are excluded because they possess such a nature; thus, the desired conclusion is established. "The relation of a jar" (*ghaṭasaṃsarga*) means the relation belonging to that which is related to a jar.

It means: other than that property residing in a jar which serves as the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence existing at all three times (*traikālika*) in that jar.

In the example, the probandum must be established by taking into account the difference from such a relation of the pot as that which is the delimitor of the counterpositiveness belonging to the absence residing in the cloth. This is because it is impossible for that [delimitor] to terminate in its own otherness. Therefore, one must state that difference by taking into account the identity (tādātmya) with something other than the relation of the pot, which serves as the delimitor of the counterpositiveness of that absence.
For the ancients do not accept that identity (*tādātmya*) is of the nature of a relation (*saṃsarga*);

rather, they admit that such a status belongs only to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), essential nature (*svarūpa*), and so forth, which govern the relationship between locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*).
Thus, the intended object [of the definition] is established: that very [relation] is difference (*bheda*).
For the ancients accept that difference (*bheda*) is precisely the absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by identity (*tādātmya*).

Now, if it is argued that in that case, because the relation of objectivity (*viṣayitā*) lacks the status of being a "relation" (*saṃsarga*) as defined by you, it would follow that there is a fallacy of unestablished middle (*asiddhi*) if it were taken as the subject (*pakṣa*) in its general form; and since its exclusion from the subject is necessary, then by taking the difference in objectivity that serves as the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the absence delimited by the relation of objectivity residing in a cloth, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) regarding [the properties of] objectivity and so forth.

In the view of the ancient Naiyāyikas—who do not accept that a relation which is not a restrictor of occurrence (*vṛttyaniyāmaka*) can be a delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence—it is said that such a relation lacks the status of being a delimiting factor altogether.

Nevertheless, it should not be argued that this results in a "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*), because the difference from the potness that delimits the counterpositiveness of absolute non-existence does indeed exist among the relations of a pot.

This is because the probandum (*sādhya*) is specifically defined as the difference characterized by a counterpositiveness delimited by the possession of that unique delimitation which functions as a relation (*saṃsarga*).

Since the deliminatorship (avacchedakatā) corresponding to the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) defined by mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva) is accepted as residing in identity (tādātmya) alone, it follows that the probandum (sādhya) must be the difference from that [identity].
Alternatively, since potness (ghaṭatva) itself possesses such a nature, there is no "proving what is already established" (siddhasādhanatā) by taking the difference from that [potness] into account.
Nor is there proving what is already established by taking the difference from one relation when another relation is intended.

If it is argued that there is a contradiction (*bādha*) in proving a difference characterized by a counter-positiveness delimited by a unique delimitingness (*vilakṣaṇāvacchedakatā*) corresponding to the counter-positiveness of such an absence—
because the subject (*pakṣa*) itself is also pervaded by the property that serves as the delimitant of such a counter-positiveness— we say no.

Alternatively, according to the previously mentioned method, it may be that the pervasion of the probandum by the absence of the delimitor of such a counter-correlativity—delimited by the relation-ness residing in the jar—is manifested as being constituted by difference; or else, because it is possible to exclude [the over-extension] by incorporating into the probandum-difference the property of being other than that which is qualified by jar-relation-ness through the two relations of having a counter-correlative co-located with itself and having an anuyogi (locus) co-located with itself.

Nor should it be said that the qualification "residing in a jar" (*ghaṭaniṣṭhatva*) is applied to the delimitor of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) in order to prevent a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the relation with a cloth, which serves as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), because there is no absence of the difference from the relation with a jar—which is the delimitor of counter-positiveness belonging to such an absence residing in the cloth.
And that [objection] does not hold;
for the probandum (*sādhya*) exists by taking into account the difference from the relation with a pillar (*stambha*). This is what must be stated.

Even in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*), since the existence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by taking that very [absence] into account, its purposefulness lies in avoiding the consequence of the non-establishment of difference (*bhedāsiddhi*). "Or the prior absence of a jar" (*ghaṭaprāgabhāvo vā*): this means other than that beginningless absence which has as its locus cloth and the like, and whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is not delimited by relation to a jar.

In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there exists the state of being other than that beginningless absence—namely, the prior absence of the form of cloth—which has as its locus cloth and the like and whose counter-correlativity is not delimited by relation to a jar.
And in the subject, such a probandum, when established, results precisely in the apprehension of the difference from cloth.
This is because the absolute absence of a jar lacks a counter-positiveness that is not delimited by the relation of conjunction with the jar;
for this very reason, that qualification is meaningful.
Otherwise, there would be the fallacy of proving something other than the intended point (arthāntaratā) by resorting to the non-difference from absolute absence.

If one were to include merely the state of having a counter-correlativity that is not delimited by a relation (*saṃsargānavacchinnapratiyogitākatvamātra*), then—just as the difference from a cloth (*paṭabheda*) is doubtful during the stage of inquiry, so too is the difference from anything else due to the same logic—the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of color residing in a cloth would also have a counter-correlativity not delimited by a relation. Consequently, there would be no established instance (*prasiddhi*) of an "infinite negation" (*anādyabhāva*) residing in the subject (the cloth) that has a counter-correlativity not delimited by a relation. Therefore, the phrase "relation with a jar" (*ghaṭasaṃsarga*) is included [to specify the relation]. Furthermore, if "beginningless" (*anādi*) were not mentioned, one would incur the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking the difference from the destruction of color (*rūpadhvaṃsabheda*) residing in the cloth; therefore, the term "beginningless" is used.
Is it not the case that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason (*hetu*) in the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of color residing in the cloth?
Nor should it be argued that there is no deviation because of the existence of distinctions such as the prior absence of taste and so forth;

for even so, since the probandum (*sādhya*) exists by taking that very [prior absence] within the prior absence of the cloth which has been made the subject (*pakṣa*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

In proving the difference characterized by such a state-of-being-absence (tādṛśābhāvatvāvacchinnabheda), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because the prior absence of a jar (*ghaṭaprāgabhāva*) lacks the property of having a cloth as its locus; thus, the difference characterized by a counter-correlativity delimited by that state-of-being-absence exists [in the jar]. Furthermore, there is an additional instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the beginningless absences existing in the cloth. If one were to posit the counter-correlativity of the jar in an beginningless absence whose locus is the cloth, then prior to the establishment of the difference, the absence—characterized by the cloth as its locus, having the jar as its counter-correlate, and not being delimited by a relation with the jar—is unestablished, and thus the argument fails due to the lack of a known instance (*aprasiddhi*).
Because the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) having a jar or cloth as its counter-positive lacks the property of being delimited by the relation of conjunction with that jar or cloth;
because it has the cloth as its locus (dharmin);
and because absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) lacks the property of having a counter-positiveness (pratiyogitā) that is not delimited by the relation of conjunction with a jar.

In order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking into account a beginningless absence that has as its counter-positive a jar whose counter-positiveness is delimited by a relation with a different locus (e.g., a cloth), the term "jar-relation" (*ghaṭasaṃsarga*) must necessarily be explained as meaning "other than a counter-positiveness residing in a jar that is not delimited by a relation.
Since [the relation in question] does not even enter into that [definition], the term "beginningless" (*anādi*) is redundant;

for an absence such as the destruction of a conjunction residing in a cloth is already excluded by virtue of having a jar as its counter-positive, and thus there would be no possibility of proving what is already established by taking that difference into account.
Not so;

for it is accepted that the very absence of the cloth, as characterized by the cloth, is the probandum (sādhya) through its relation to both being the counter-correlator of its own counter-correlator and being distinct from itself.
In the instance consisting of the destruction of the cloth, the absolute absence of the cloth characterized by the cloth indeed exists through the aforementioned relation.

And in the case [of the subject], since there is no room for objections such as *siddhasādhanatva* (proving what is already established) by taking into account the difference from another positive entity (*bhāvāntara*) that has a jar as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*),

it cannot be argued that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this regard with respect to the absence of ether (*gaganābhāva*) or the difference from knowability (*prameyatvabheda*) residing in a cloth,
because no other absence having that [ether or knowability] as its counter-correlative exists therein.

Even though knowability (*prameyatva*) exists in the cloth by way of its own nature (*svarūpa-sambandha*), there exist many absences (*abhāva*) therein that are not delimited by relations residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa-sambandha*). Thus, by taking one such absence among these, it is possible for the probandum (*sādhya*) to reside in another [locus].

Similarly, since various absences—unrestricted by relations such as inherence (*samavāya*) or essential identity (*svarūpa*)—exist in a jar, by taking one absence, the probandum can reside in another; therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) anywhere.
Nor are the qualifiers "residing in the cloth" (*paṭadharmikatva*) and "beginninglessness" (*anāditva*) redundant.

It should not be argued that [the definition fails] because the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a jar is absent from those absences whose counter-correlates are jars due to the aforementioned relation,
or because absences of the relation of a jar (or a cloth) are excluded simply by virtue of not being delimited by the relation of a jar;

for the qualification "residing in a cloth" is meaningful as it serves to establish the difference of a jar in a cloth as the intended object, and the qualification "beginningless" is meaningful for the purpose of establishing the falsity (*mithyātva*) of difference— which consists in the absence of its being conceptually constructed by cognition.

It should not be argued that, even if the stated absence is taken as the probandum (*sādhya*) by virtue of the mere relation of having its own counter-positive as its counter-positive, the probandum as stated cannot be established without mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), and thus it is redundant for the probandum to be related to both [the cloth and the absence] through the relation of difference.

This is because, in order to avoid such redundancy, "having its own counter-positive as its counter-positive" must be qualified within the scope of the probandum specifically as the absence of the absence residing in the cloth.

Nor should it be argued that, in that case, the probandum should simply be "having such an absence whose counter-positive is its own counter-positive," and that "being other than such an absence" is redundant.

Since the relation to the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi* compound must necessarily be included, the referent of the term "that-ness" (*tatkatva*) is simply being different from that [the subject]. When one cannot tolerate the lack of a commonality (*ananugama*) regarding "one's own-ness" (*svatva*) in both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject is the state of being qualified by something through two relations: (1) the state of possessing a difference residing in that absence which has as its counter-correlate a jar located in a relation delimited by a connection qualified by itself, via the relation of being the counter-correlative of what is counter-correlative to itself; and (2) identity (*tādātmya*). Since "one's own-ness" serves merely as a defining indicator (*paricāyaka*) within the scope of the relation, there is no lack of commonality.
The purpose of the two relations is indeed clear.
Here, this must be noted:

in order to avoid the aforementioned fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), whether by including "having as its counter-positive the counter-positive of itself" within the body of the definition of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*), or by including it within the body of the definition of the probandum through the previously mentioned two relations, there would result—due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the very mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) established by the inference under consideration—a factual defect in the reason (*hetu*). Therefore, the "difference" (*bheda*) component is simply not to be included, because it is redundant and because it actually produces a logical fault.
Nor is there any contradiction with the root text;

for in expressions such as "another of this cow is to be sought," it is observed that the word *anya* (other) has the meaning of being delimited by a similarity (*sājātya*) that is constituted by difference.

In the present case, even if the aspect of difference is set aside while retaining the relation to the counter-positive that constitutes the similarity, there is no contradiction with the root text, because the essential meaning of the root is not thereby abandoned.

Even when only the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is mentioned, the probandum (*sādhya*) is in fact that very absence related to itself by both the relation of not having its own counter-positive as a counter-positive and the relation of being distinct from itself; thus, there is no defect whatsoever in the previously stated probandum.

(In reality), since the mutual presence of the probandum exists by taking the difference from the general category of pot (*ghaṭasāmānyabheda*) and the difference from that specific pot (*tadghaṭabheda*) as the basis, there is no possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Nevertheless, they say that this effort was made to somehow render meaningful the "otherness" (*anyatva*) mentioned in the root text, in order to avoid its redundancy; so, enough of this.

Others, however, maintain that in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the form of a jar (*ghaṭarūpa*) and so forth as the subject, the qualification "having the jar as its counter-correlate" (*ghaṭapratiyogikatva*) must be applied to the absence (*abhāva*).

One should not suspect that there is a lack of establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) because the absence characterized by the previously mentioned qualifications would be unestablished prior to the proof of a difference whose counter-correlate is the jar and whose locus is a cloth;

for the phrase "having a cloth as its locus" means that which possesses the absence of both [the following]: being non-existent in the cloth and being non-different from the prior non-existence [of that non-existence].
The phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) is intended to include pillars and other such things as well, which must be employed [as examples].

Since the subject (*pakṣa*) under consideration is precisely the prior non-existence of a jar (*ghaṭaprāgabhāva*), it is possible to establish the argument by taking that very thing as the example, because the probandum (*sādhya*)—defined as being "other than that"—is already established therein.
This is because, if one were to take its own difference from itself within the subject itself, the probandum would fail to be established.
This establishes the difference between the cloth (the locus) and the pot (the counter-positive).

If one were to state merely that the pot possesses the aforementioned absence whose counter-positive is the pot and which is not delimited by a relation with the pot, then the very subject—the prior absence of the pot—would possess such a property, since a general property of being qualified by itself resides in itself. Consequently, this would result in the fallacies of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) and proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*). Therefore, the definition is pursued as far as "being other than that" (*tad-anyatva*).

Since it is accepted that the counter-positiveness of destruction and prior absence is not delimited by a relation, there is no longer room for the suspicion that the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*).

Because the absence of difference—whose counter-correlativity is delimited by duality residing in both the pot and the cloth—is absent from the cloth (i.e., it does not reside in the cloth), the locus possesses the absence of that [dual] entity.

Furthermore, since there is the relation of having the pot as its counter-correlate, there is no room for the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking "otherness" (*tadanyatva*) as the probandum.

This is because it is accepted that a difference delimited by a property residing in a composite whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti-dharma*) does not reside in a counter-correlate such as the cloth; thus, the aforementioned absence of the dual entity is lacking [in the cloth].

Or, even if this [definition] is accepted, the absence must be further qualified by being "other than that whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a property that subsists distributively" (*vyāsajyavṛttidharmāvacchinnapratiyogitāka*).

Alternatively, one might suggest that the aforementioned fault can be avoided by including either "having only a jar as its counter-correlative" or "not subsisting in the counter-correlative" within the definition of absence; however, this is not correct.

For, since the difference between two jars is not excluded by the first qualification, one could still incur the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*) by taking that very difference as the probandum.

Regarding the second alternative concerning the qualification, they say that since even the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar would be excluded by this very [qualification], the phrase "not delimited by the relation to a jar" (*ghaṭasaṃsargānavacchinna*) would become redundant.
In reality, however, the analysis (*vigraha*) of "not delimited by the relation to a jar" is: "an absence whose counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the relation to a jar.
The counter-positiveness, which is the meaning of the genitive case following the word "jar," is construed with the absence itself.
The phrase "having a counter-correlativity not delimited by a relation" has the intended meaning of being distinct from absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
This is because it is a necessary rule that the counter-correlativity of an absolute non-existence is invariably delimited by a relation.

This is accepted on the grounds that the counter-correlativity of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is both delimited by a property (*dharma*) and delimited by a relation.
In the expression "cloth, jar, etc.," the property delimited by the scope of the word "etc. (*ādi*) is the state of possessing the absence of jar-ness (*ghaṭatvābhāvavattva*).

Thus, the final form of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the state of being other than that beginningless absence which resides in a locus possessing the absence of jar-ness and is distinct from the absolute absence whose counter-positive is a jar.

Here, the existence of the probandum in all instances, such as the example, is established by taking into account the difference from the antecedent absence of a jar (*ghaṭaprāgabhāva*) which resides in a potsherd that is not a locus of jar-ness.
Since it is impossible for [the definition] to terminate by taking its own difference as the subject, there is the establishment of the difference of the jar residing in the cloth and so forth.

To prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking the difference from the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the form residing in the potsherds, the term "counter-positive of the jar" (*ghaṭapratiyogika*) is used. To prevent that same fallacy by taking the difference from the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar residing in that which does not possess the locus of jar-ness (*ghaṭatvānadhikaraṇavṛtti*), the term "distinct from absolute non-existence" (*atyantābhāvabhina*) is used. To prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established by taking the difference from the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of the jar, the term "beginningless" (*anādi*) is used.
Furthermore, it must be stated that the counter-positiveness resides in the jar and is not delimited by any property other than jar-ness (*ghaṭatvetaradharmānavacchinna*).

Therefore, even though the difference residing in the pot (the subject) is not inherent in the pot itself, there is no "shifting of the subject" (*arthāntaratā*) because that difference resides in the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of the pot, having the pot as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

Since the counter-correlativity of the prior absence of the pot is not delimited by any property (*dharmānavacchinna*), the fulfillment of the probandum (*sādhyatva*) in the example is achieved by taking that very difference into account. Furthermore, the qualification "having as its locus a property that lacks the nature of cloth" (*ghaṭatvābhāvavaddharmika*) is included to ensure the attainment of the intended goal, namely the establishment of the difference from the pot in everything other than the pot. This is the essential point. As for the phrase "or the destruction of the pot," everything is exactly as in the previous inference.

In order to establish that difference is ultimately real, one should consider the qualification "eternal" (nityatva), following the refutation of doctrines such as the view that its nature is to be destroyed by knowledge due to its falsity.

One might raise the objection: "At the time when the non-difference of the jar [from the cloth] is not established for itself, the absolute absence of the cloth also has the property of being the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of the absolute absence of the cloth, by virtue of having a counter-correlativity that is not delimited by its relation to the jar; how then can the probandum exist in the example, which is the nature of the cloth? With the intention of showing that if empirical difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*) is capable of sustaining all worldly transactions, it is also capable of avoiding the aforementioned fault, he provides the following rebuttal beginning with "of the jar and the cloth," and so on.

[The phrase] "and the consequence of faults" [is used] up to that point. The sequence is as follows: even mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is not delimited by connection with a jar. Regarding the phrase "sublation, deficiency of the probandum, etc.," the meaning of the word "etc. (*ādi*) is as follows: [it refers to] "by way of being [present] at all three times, etc."; the word "etc. includes beginninglessness (*anāditva*) and eternity (*nityatva*). Regarding the phrase "if it were merely conventional" (*vyāvahārikatve*), the meaning is: if it were imagined by ignorance (*ajñāna*) and if it were sublatable by knowledge (*jñāna*). Regarding the phrase "of the favorable arguments" (*anukūlatarkāṇām*), the meaning is: [as presented] in the *Nyāyāmṛta* and other such works.
If difference were ultimately real, then upon the destruction of a jar, there would be no destruction of the cloth;

furthermore, because bondage and liberation would become identical, one would have to be liberated even now, which renders practices such as hearing the scriptures (śravaṇa) untenable—this is to be understood as the logical argument (tarka). [The phrase] "not due to limiting adjuncts" (nopādhi) [is explained as follows].
The meaning is as follows: "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) is the *upādhi*.

Furthermore, even if one were to include "having a jar as its counter-correlate, not delimited by identity with cloth" within the definition of absence, this would lead to the undesirable consequence of establishing a fifth type of absence in the formal argument; thus, it functions as a reason for the fallacy of being equivalent to a pseudo-reason (*ābhāsa*).

Regarding the phrase "Moreover, etc.": the meaning is that it is the counter-correlate of such an absence—pertaining to a locus such as cloth—which has a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) that is not delimited by a relation of contact (*saṃsarga*) with a jar, and which is threefold-temporal (*traikālika*).

In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the presence of the probandum (*sādhyasattva*) is established by taking the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of cloth; and in the subject (*pakṣa*), because the contradiction of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of that [absolute non-existence] is ruled out, the conclusion of the probandum is reached precisely by taking the difference between the jar and the cloth, whereby the intended object is proven.

The phrase "not delimited by a relation with the jar" (*ghaṭasaṃsargānavacchinna*) is included to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking the counter-correlativity of the absolute non-existence of the jar.
In this context, the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) is used to avoid the deficiency of the probandum in the example.

Nor should it be argued that because the cognition "there is no cloth due to conjunction" involves an apprehension of the generality of conjunction (*saṃyoga-sāmānya*) itself as the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*), how can the absence of cloth have a counter-correlativity that is not delimited by a relation with a jar?
This is because, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), it is precisely the relation of the counter-correlate that serves as the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity;
or else, there is no fault because we intend to mean that [the counter-correlativity] is not delimited by a relation accompanied by jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*).
The phrase "having cloth, etc., as its locus" (*paṭādidharmika*) is used to exclude other possible meanings by establishing the distinction between self and non-self.
If the establishment of the difference of a jar from a cloth were the intended object (*uddeśyatva*), then "having cloth as its locus" would be the qualifier of the absence (*abhāva*).

And if the establishment of that [difference] in a staff or similar object were the intended object, then "having that [staff, etc. as its locus" would likewise be the qualifier; it is for the sake of indicating this that the word "etc. (*ādi*) is employed.

The term "pertaining to all three times" (*traikālika*) is included in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), which would occur if one were to take as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the destruction of a jar.

Nor should it be argued that this fallacy can be avoided simply because those two [prior non-existence and destruction] necessarily reside only in the inherent locus (*samavāyin*) of their own counter-positive, and thus cannot have cloth or other things as their substratum;
for there is no evidence for such a restrictive rule.

This is because, by the force of our cognition, it is appropriate that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) reside only in things related to their counter-positive (*pratiyogin*),
since even a cloth or similar object is related to its counter-positive through conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other relations.

As for the claim that the exclusion of these two is possible simply because, as relational non-existences (*saṃsargābhāva*), they lack a counter-positiveness that is not delimited by a relation with the jar— [that is incorrect].
This is to be considered:

this argument is advanced according to the view of certain logicians (*tārkikaikadeśin*) who do not accept that destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) have counter-positivity delimited by a relation of inherence (*saṃsargāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva*).

For this very reason, even though the difference residing in a substrate such as a cloth cannot be established as existing at all three times—since, in the final system (*siddhānta*), the difference is of the nature of the substrate itself—there is no risk of contradiction (*bādhaprasaṅga*).

As for the claim that there is no fault because the word "cloth" (*paṭa*)— by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the qualities are not included in the referent (*atadguṇasaṃvijñāna*)— refers exclusively to the eternal [atoms],
that is inconsistent;
for if that were the case, it would follow that the distinction between the jar and the cloth under discussion could not be established.

The word "absence" (*abhāva*) is included to exclude the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*), namely, the establishment of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) of inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth with respect to subjects such as cloth;
the same applies in what follows.

Regarding the phrase "or the absolute absence of a jar": here, the presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the example is established by taking the state of being other than the absolute absence of a jar.

In the case [of the subject], because that [absolute absence] is sublated, the probandum is established by taking up only the difference from mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*); thus, the intended object is proven.

To avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking up the difference from the absolute absence of a cloth (*paṭātyantābhāva*), the qualification "having a jar as its counter-correlate" (*ghaṭapratiyogika*) is included, as before.

Although there would be a sublation [of the reason] because even the absolute absence of a jar—by virtue of being an absence at all three times (*traikālika-abhāva*) having a jar as its counter-correlate and a cloth or other thing as its locus—is impossible to be different from that [mutual absence], [the qualification remains necessary].

Nevertheless, since the compound "other than such a non-existence" (*tādṛśābhāvād anya*) ends in the singular, what is obtained as the probandum is simply the state of being other than some such non-existence; thus, there is no fault. Nor does this result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking as the probandum the state of being other than the non-existence of both such a jar and cloth.
Because it is established that [the subject] is other than that [absence], as delimited by the state of being the absolute absence of a jar (*ghaṭātyantābhāvatva*).

Regarding the phrase "or the contact with a jar" (*ghaṭasaṃsargo vā*): here, the probandum (*sādhya*) in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) should be understood as consisting in being other than that contact with a jar which serves as the delimiter of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the absolute absence of a jar.

In the locus (*pakṣa*), however, since that [contact] is impossible, the probandum is ultimately established by taking as its content being other than that identity (*tādātmya*) which serves as the delimiter of the counter-correlativity of the difference whose locus is a cloth; thus, the intended object is proven.

Nor should it be argued that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking as the [property] the difference from "pot-ness," which is the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) of the absolute absence of a pot;
for the probandum (*sādhya*) is the difference characterized by being delimited by the state of being a delimitor of the counter-correlativity of some absolute absence whatsoever residing in a cloth.

This is because, if the term "some absolute absence" were taken to include the absolute absence of a pot, then the difference characterized by being delimited by the state of being its delimitor of counter-correlativity would be sublated (*bādhita*) in the subject (*pakṣa*); therefore, the establishment of the difference [from the pot] is necessary.

Nor should it be argued that there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because the difference characterized by being the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of an absolute absence delimited by another relation is already established in the case of the jar’s single relation.
This is not a fault, because the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by the nature of being a relation of the jar (*ghaṭasaṃsargatva*).

The phrase "residing in the jar" (*ghaṭaniṣṭha*) is included to prevent the fallacy of *siddhasādhana* that would arise from taking the difference that is the delimiting condition of the counter-positiveness of the absolute absence of a cloth, which is delimited by its relation to a cloth.
The rest is as before.

Furthermore, it should be understood that "relationality" (saṃsargatva) consists in being a relation whose relata (pratiyogin and anuyogin) are mutually distinct, or alternatively, being a relation other than identity (tādātmya).

"Or else, it is the prior non-existence of the jar (*ghaṭaprāgabhāva*). This means: it is other than that beginningless absence which has as its locus a cloth or the like, and whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is not delimited by a relation (*saṃsarga*).
In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by taking the state of being other than the prior non-existence of the jar.

In the subject (*pakṣa*), however, since that [prior non-existence] is impossible, the establishment of the intended object occurs by concluding the probandum through the state of being distinct from the difference whose locus is a cloth.
The term "beginningless" (*anādi*) is used to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by means of the difference from the destruction of a jar.
The phrase "residing in a cloth, etc. (*paṭādidharmika*) is used to avoid the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*) by establishing a difference residing in a different substratum.

The phrase "having a counter-correlativity not delimited by a relation" (*saṃsargānavacchinnapratiyogitāka*) is used to prevent the failure of the argument's purpose by means of the difference from the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar.

The term "pot" (*ghaṭa*) is used to avoid that fault by taking as the basis the difference from the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of color and so forth, which reside in a cloth and other substrates.
Since that [prior non-existence] lacks the pot as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), no fault arises.

Although another type of non-existence could serve as an example here, it should be understood that the destruction of the cloth (*paṭadhvaṃsa*) alone is taken as the example, because the difference from the beginningless non-existence residing in the cloth is more evident in that case.

However, some hold that the meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the "distinctness from that non-existence which has cloth as its locus and whose counter-correlativity is not delimited by connection with a jar.

The phrase "connection with a jar," etc., is included to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), which would occur if one were to take "distinctness from the absolute non-existence of a jar" as the probandum.
In this context, the word "jar" is used so that, in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the probandum may be maintained by taking "distinctness from the absolute non-existence of cloth."
The phrase "having cloth, etc., as its locus" (*paṭādidharmika*) is for the purpose of establishing the intended object (*uddeśya*), namely the form of a jar or a cloth.

The term "beginningless" (*anādi*) is used to exclude the possibility of the definition being already established by taking the difference from the destruction of the form belonging to the cloth, and so forth.

The word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is included to prevent that same defect [of over-extension] by means of taking the difference from "cloth-ness" (*paṭatva*) and so on, which is other than that which has a counter-positive delimited by the relation of inherence in a jar (the first member of the definition).

But surely, in this way, even in the case of the subject (*pakṣa*), one might commit the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking as the probandum the difference from the absolute non-existence of the cloth;
nor can the absence be qualified as "having the jar as its counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*),
for that would result in the probandum being deficient in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Nor should it be argued that the presence of the probandum (*sādhyasattva*) in the example is established by taking as the counter-positive something other than the prior non-existence of the jar;
for that [other entity] lacks a counter-positivity not delimited by relation to the jar, and lacks the property of residing in a substrate such as a cloth,
and because this would contradict the subsequent passage beginning with "of the jar and the cloth."

If it is argued that this is because the argument aims to establish the existence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the example by taking the difference from the absolute non-existence of the cloth, we say no;
for the non-existence is qualified as having its own counter-positive as its counter-positive.

They maintain that there is no fault whatsoever, since the word "own" (*sva*) refers to the subject (*pakṣa*) in the proposition (*pratijñā*), whereas in the example (*udāharaṇa*) it refers to the instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).
That is questionable;
for it would result in the redundancy of the term "beginningless" (anādi).
