Furthermore, even in the fivefold inference, if the presence of the probandum in the example were established by taking absolute non-existence as the basis, there would follow the consequence that the inclusion of distinct qualifiers—namely, "belonging to all three times," "beginningless," and "eternal"—would be rendered groundless.

By this, the argument that the purpose of employing the term "beginningless" (anādi) is to exclude a different object (arthāntara) through the establishment of conventional difference (vyāvahārika-bheda) is refuted.
If that alone were its purpose, then for the sake of parsimony (lāghava), it would have been more appropriate to include "beginninglessness" itself in the previous inference.
Furthermore, the subsequent passage will be explained as being entirely consistent with this view.

Therefore, we consider it logical that this passage intends to establish that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of a jar possess a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) that is not delimited by a relation (*saṃsargānavacchinna-pratiyogitākatva*), and that they reside in substrates such as cloth (*paṭa*).

Regarding the phrase "or the destruction of the jar" (*ghaṭadhvaṃso vā*): the meaning is that it is other than that eternal absence which resides in substrates such as cloth and has a counter-correlativity not delimited by a relation to the jar.

In the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the probandum (*sādhya*) is to be established by taking "otherness from the destruction of the jar," and in the subject (*pakṣa*), by taking "otherness from the difference from the jar."
The term "eternal" (*nitya*) is included to prevent the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) by taking the difference from the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a jar.
The phrase "having cloth, etc., as its locus" (*paṭādidharmika*) is for the purpose of establishing the intended subject.

The term "having a counter-correlativity not delimited by a relation" (*saṃsargānavacchinnapratiyogitāka*) is used to avoid the failure of the proof that would result from taking the difference from the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar.
The word "pot" (*ghaṭa*) is used in order to avoid that same fault by taking as the [reason] the state of being other than the destruction of a cloth.
Here too, although the destruction of a cloth and so forth could serve as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is mentioned—as before—to ensure clear understanding.
Now, one might object: in this inference where the pot is the subject (*pakṣa*), the example is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*).

On the view that the jar and the cloth are non-different, even the absolute absence of the cloth would have a counter-correlativity delimited by its relation to the jar; consequently, the property of being the counter-correlative of an absence other than that [absolute absence] would not exist in the cloth.
Thus, in the inferences where the absolute absence of the jar and so forth are the subjects (*pakṣa*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Since even the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a cloth has the jar as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and since the relation (*saṃsarga*) with a cloth is also a property residing in the jar, and since it is possible for both the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of a cloth to likewise have the jar as their counter-correlate and the cloth as their locus, the probandum—consisting of being other than each of those—would already be established in the subject (*pakṣa*), which is the absolute non-existence of the jar and so forth. To this, he says: "Of the jar and the cloth... By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of the absolute non-existence of the cloth and so forth," there is the inclusion of the relation with the cloth, the prior non-existence of the cloth, and the destruction of the cloth.

By the phrase "of having a counter-correlativity not delimited by relation to a jar," etc., the term "etc. includes the absence of being counter-correlated to a jar, the property of residing in a jar, and the state of being a property of a cloth.
By the phrase "due to the deficiency of the probandum in the example," etc., the term "etc. includes the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

As for the claim that—under the view that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) are identical—the counter-correlativity of the mutual non-existence of a jar cannot logically be delimited by its relation to a jar, and thus the term "etc. includes the fallacy of contradiction (*bādha*)—that is not correct.
Because there is no room for sublation (*bādha*) due to the absence of contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) established for both parties;
and because absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), being real, cannot be identical with mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), which is illusory.

Otherwise, since the absolute non-existence of a cloth would lack the property of existing at all three times, it would follow that the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is deficient, a consequence that is difficult to avoid.

Therefore, it must be stated that this treatise is devoted to the refutation of the non-duality of existence (*bhāvādvaita*). "Otherwise" means: if one does not accept the conventional distinction (*vyāvahārika-bheda*) that sustains the aforementioned systematic arrangement;
the meaning is that there would be no engagement with the causal complex for a cloth (*paṭasāmagrī*) by one who has already established or obtained a jar (*siddhaghaṭa*).
The sense is that the desire for the cloth, which would have to serve as its cause, is untenable.

By the phrase "due to existing at all three times," etc., the inclusion of beginninglessness and eternity is intended. "Because of the impossibility of that" means because of the impossibility of [the cloth] existing at all three times, etc.;
the sense is that the conventional [cloth] is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*).
But even by this much, the charge of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntaratva*) remains unavoidable;
for the property of being "three-temporal" (*traikālikatva*), defined as existing at all times, is possible even in the case of a conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*).
Furthermore, since time itself is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*), its absence necessarily entails the absence of that [temporality] when [ignorance] is absent.
In this way, the possibility of beginninglessness and eternity—characterized by the absence of prior and subsequent time—should also be understood.
Not so;
for beginninglessness consists in not being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

Eternality is the state of not being the counter-positive of destruction. And possessing both of these [properties] constitutes existence across the three periods of time. This, however, is not possible in the case of the conventional (vyāvahārika).
Nor should it be argued that even in the conventional realm, beginninglessness like that of ignorance is not accepted;
for if [the world] were beginningless by its very nature, it would be impossible for it to be an effect of ignorance.
Otherwise, one would also have to accept the cessation of what is eternal.

Furthermore, there is no room for the suspicion of a *arthāntara* (proving something other than the intended conclusion) if one intends to mean by "beginninglessness" the state of having a cognition that is not dependent on ignorance (*avidyā*) and is non-identical with its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). This is the general direction of the argument.
Now, an objection may be raised: in the aforementioned inferences, the property of being "other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) and so forth constitutes a *upādhi* (limiting condition).
For in the absence of a supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*), even the property of being other than the subject can potentially function as a *upādhi*.

For this very reason, because the absence [of difference] is qualified by having a counter-correlate that is not delimited by identity (*tādātmya*), it shares the same fate as a fallacious argument and lacks probative force; therefore, he says: "of the favorable reasoning" (*anukūlatarkasya*). The meaning is as follows: if the non-difference between a jar, a cloth, and so forth were ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), then the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the jar, the cloth, and so on would also have to be ultimately real; since such an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) has already been stated right here.

Alternatively, if the reading is "elsewhere" (*anyatra*), the meaning is that an over-extension—such as the confusion of liberation (*mukti-sāṅkarya*) due to the absence of difference from inert matter (*jaḍa-bheda-abhāva*)—has been stated in the *Nyāyāmṛta* and other works.
This is merely an illustration.
From the Self, space was produced;
from space, air; from air, fire.
Scriptural passages such as "From fire, water;
from water, earth;
from earth, plants," and others, should also be cited as examples of the difference between the insentient.

Regarding the term *prapañca*: because there is excessive effort required to avoid the fallacies of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*), an unestablished nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*), and deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the aforementioned inference, he speaks out of dissatisfaction [with that approach], saying "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). The phrase *ghaṭasaṃsargānavacchinna* means: that whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is not delimited by—that is, is not excluded from—the relation with a jar;

that is to say, its counter-correlativity is not delimited by the relation with a jar. In other words, it is devoid of a delimiting condition for counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) characterized by the relation with a jar.
And that very thing is "residing in cloth and so forth," meaning it exists as a property (*dharma*) of cloth and the like.

The meaning is: that which is the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absence (*abhāva*) that exists at all three times (*traikālika*), i.e., an absence occurring throughout the three periods of time.

Here, if it were stated simply that [the object] is the counter-positive of an absence whose locus (*dharmin*) is a cloth or the like, there would be the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*), because that would include being the counter-positive of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destructive non-existence (*dhvaṃsābhāva*). Therefore, the term "at all three times" is used;
for those two [types of non-existence] exist respectively only during the time preceding and following the existence of the counter-positive.

When that much is stated, there is the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), because [the definition would apply] by taking the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitva*) of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Therefore, it is specified as "having a counter-positiveness not delimited by a relation with a jar.
Since absolute non-existence possesses a delimiting factor for its counter-positiveness in the form of a relation, it does not possess such a nature [of being undelimited].

When that much has been stated, there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example; for the opponent does not admit that the cloth possesses counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) in the form of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). Therefore, [the author] says "of the jar."
And such an absolute absence of the cloth exists in that [locus], while the state of being its counter-correlate (pratiyogitva) resides in the cloth;
for this is accepted by the opponent.

This is because the absolute absence of the cloth has a counter-correlativity delimited by the relation of connection with the cloth, and thus does not have a counter-correlativity undelimited by the relation of connection with the jar.

Thus, when it is established that the pot possesses a counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) to an absence that is excluded from the three types of absence, the difference between the pot and the cloth is established, because such an absence is not distinct from mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*). In the aforementioned inference, one might object that there is unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) due to the inclusion of the qualification "having a counter-correlativity not delimited by a relation with the pot" in order to exclude absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*). To avoid this dissatisfaction, he says: "the absolute absence of the pot. [He explains: "having the pot as its counter-correlative" means: that which is other than any absence—whether pertaining to the cloth or other substrates—that has the pot as its counter-correlative and exists throughout the three periods of time.

Here, the phrase "having the jar as its counter-correlate" (*ghaṭapratiyogika*) is used to exclude the fallacy of proving something else (*arthāntara*), namely, the difference from the absolute non-existence of a cloth that exists at all three times in a locus such as a cloth. The rest is to be understood as before. The phrase "like the absence of a cloth" (*paṭābhāvavat*) means that in that case, there exists the state of being different from the absolute non-existence of the jar in the manner previously described; this is the intended sense. He states the inference where the subject (*pakṣa*) is the delimiting condition of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*): "the relation with a jar" (*ghaṭasaṃsarga*). The meaning is: that property residing in the jar which serves as the delimiting condition of the counter-correlativity of whatever threefold absence exists in a locus such as a cloth, [this relation] is different from that.
This is the meaning:
non-existence throughout the three periods of time is indeed twofold—
absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) and mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva).
In this context, the property that delimits the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of absolute non-existence is "relation" (*saṃsarga*).
The property that delimits the counter-correlativity of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is "identity" (*tādātmya*).

Therein, once it is established that the relation of the jar is distinct from the properties residing in the cloth and other substrates that delimit the counter-correlativity of a temporal non-existence [of that relation], the existence of another property within the jar that delimits the counter-correlativity of such a non-existence is established.
Furthermore, the status of being the delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of such an absence cannot be established without that very absence.

And since such an absence is precisely the mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), the difference between the jar and the cloth is thereby established. In this context, if one were to prove merely that [the jar] is different from the property that delimits the counter-correlativity of an absence whose locus is the cloth, it would result in the unintended consequence (*arthāntara*) of establishing merely that the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the cloth is something other than the relation residing in the cloth.

Therefore, [the qualification] "residing in the jar" [is stated]. In proving that [the absence] residing in the jar is different from the properties residing in the jar that serve as the delimiters (avacchedaka) of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of absences whose loci are cloth and so forth, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (arthāntara), because one would thereby establish its difference from properties such as being prior or posterior in time, which are the delimiters of the counter-correlativity of antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) and destruction (pradhvaṃsa). Therefore, [the qualification] "pertaining to all three times" [is stated]. [The phrase] "relation residing in the cloth" [is used]; the sense is that, in that case, there exists a difference from the property consisting of the aforementioned relation.

He states two inferences by not introducing the qualification of "belonging to all three times," beginning with the words "the prior absence of the jar" (*ghaṭaprāgabhāva*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "not delimited by connection with the jar": the meaning is that it is other than that absence which has as its locus a cloth or the like, and whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is not delimited by connection with the jar.

Here, the term "beginningless" (*anādi*) is used to exclude the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntara*), because [otherwise] one would be proving the difference from *pradhvaṃsa* (destruction), which is not beginningless since it has a beginning.

The phrase "having a counter-correlativity not delimited by connection with a jar" is used to exclude the fallacy of proving something other than the intended point (*arthāntara*) by establishing that [the absence] is different from absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). (Regarding "like the destruction of a jar") and "connection with a jar": here, the term "eternal" (*nitya*) is used to exclude the fallacy of proving something other than the intended point by establishing that [the absence] is different from prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), because the latter is non-eternal. The remainder is as explained previously. (Regarding "like the prior non-existence of a jar"): this has already been largely explained. Now, an objection: in the second inference where the jar is the subject (*pakṣa*), there is a deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example of cloth-form (*paṭarūpa*).

Even though the absolute absence (atyantābhāva) having both jar and cloth as its counter-correlates (pratiyogin) exists, it does not possess a counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) that is not delimited by the relation of inherence with the jar. This is because, due to the identity of the jar and the cloth, even the absolute absence having cloth as its counter-correlate possesses a counter-correlativity delimited by the relation of inherence with the jar; thus, it lacks a counter-correlativity that is not delimited by the relation of jar-ness. For this reason, he says: "of the jar and the cloth. Here, "of absolute absence, etc. is the subject (uddeśya), and "of counter-correlativity, etc. is the predicate (vidheya).

[Objection: But surely, since there is no difference [between them], how can this be accepted? The sense is that it would follow from their identity. [The phrase] "of one for whom the jar is already established" means: he for whom the jar is established; the meaning is "of such a person. [The phrase] "the causal complex of cloth" means: since the jar and the cloth are identical, when the jar is obtained, the cloth is also obtained; therefore, there would be no engagement with the causal complex for the sake of obtaining the cloth. [The term] "empirical" (vyāvahārika) means: because the qualification of "ultimate reality" (pāramārthikatva) is absent from the aforementioned inferences. [The phrase] "because of its impossibility" means...

Since being sublated by the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*) alone constitutes "empirical" (*vyāvahārika*) status, if mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) were empirical, it would be sublated after the knowledge of Brahman.
And thus, the sense is that it would not exist throughout the three periods of time.

Now, an objection is raised: in all the inferences establishing the difference from insentient matter (*jaḍabheda*), the state of being "other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) is a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Since the reason [the probans] would be as fallacious as the point at issue—given that it is easy to establish that a jar is the counter-positive of an absolute negation (traikālikābhāva) residing in a jar itself, where the counter-positiveness is not delimited by its relation to a cloth—and since there is the possibility of abandoning the probandum while accepting the probans (rendering the argument *aprayojaka*), he says: "Because a favorable tarka has been stated elsewhere. For if there were no difference from insentient matter (*jaḍa*), then due to the identity between the presence or absence of the proof of difference and the presence or absence of the defect [in the argument], there would be a contradiction with one's own action (*svakriyāvirodha*).

The meaning is that this is because a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*) has been stated in the second chapter of the *Nyāyāmṛta* to the effect that "there would be a confusion of liberation" (*muktisāṅkarya*).
This is merely an illustration;

one should also observe that this was previously mentioned in passages such as "the acceptance of the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) of the identity (*tādātmya*) between a jar and a cloth," and because it will be stated later in passages such as "the perception grasping the non-difference of two distant trees, or of mother-of-pearl and silver, would have to be a revealer of reality (*tatvāvedaka*)."
(33) As for the claim that perception is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding non-difference, that is incorrect.

Since you yourself admit that the *ahaṃkāra*—which consists of a confluence of consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*)—is distinct, the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) cannot be a means of valid cognition regarding its non-difference [from the Self]. Furthermore, in the first inference, there is a fallacy of the unestablished reason (*asiddhi*), because we do not accept the nature of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) defined as being unknowable by another (*avedyatva*).

If it is argued that "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) consists in being non-sublatable (*abādhyatva*), then there is a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because we accept that the body and so forth are non-sublatable in their own nature. Nor should it be said that even those [the body, etc. are equivalent to the subject of the proposition (*pakṣatulya*); for since you yourself accept that the identity between the body and the self is superimposed (*adhyasta*), that identity is not ultimately real. Consequently, in the ultimate sense, they do not differ from the self, and thus the property to be proven (*sādhya*)—namely, "not differing in the ultimate sense"—is absent in them.
Because non-difference is simply the absence of difference.

If the nature of self (*ātmatva*) is the state of being cognition (*jñānatva*), then it is unestablished for the Naiyāyika. If the nature of self is the state of being the substratum of cognition, then it is unestablished for you yourself.

Under the view that a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) functions as a refutation by way of exposing either a contradiction (*bādha*) or an inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*), the limiting adjunct is "the state of not being a cognizer of suffering that has not been experienced by the Supreme Self.

Thus, having stated the proofs for difference, he says—starting with "As for what was said"—in order to refute perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding the claim that there are three proofs for non-difference. Regarding the phrase "of the ego-sense" (*ahaṅkārasya*): although the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) grasps the unity of the Self, nevertheless, according to your own position, its object is not the Self, but rather the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) itself.
And that [internal organ] consists of a conglomeration of consciousness and unconsciousness;
that is to say, it takes the form of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) which is a mixture of the sentient and the insentient.
Therefore, it is accepted as being indeed distinct from the Self (ātman).

The meaning is that, likewise, it is impossible to state that the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), which has as its object the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) distinct from the Self, serves as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the non-difference of the Self.
This is merely an illustration;

for even if the "I-notion" were to have as its object the identity with the Self, nevertheless, the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) would not be established by it.

It should also be observed that even though a pillar is experienced in a single form as "this is a pillar," its non-difference from a *piśāca* (demon) is not established. Now, he refutes the inferences concerning non-difference one by one, beginning with the words "In the first inference," etc.
The meaning is: in the inference, "The disputed selves do not differ from the Supreme Self in reality, because they possess selfhood, like the Supreme Self."
In this regard, the opponent himself has stated that "selfhood" (ātmatva) means self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).
Furthermore, self-luminosity does not consist in being of the nature of the illumination of one's own object,
because in your own system, you do not admit the coexistence of agency (*kartṛtva*) and objecthood (*karmatva*) in a single entity.
However, it is accepted that [the nature of Brahman] is precisely being the object of non-mediate discourse while being unobjectifiable by the means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
And this is unestablished for us, who accept that it is knowable through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is the meaning.

He states "In that case" (*tarhi*) to show that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because the probandum is absent in the body and so forth, which possess the reason; for although they are sublated in the form of superimposed attributes such as eternity, they lack sublation in their own nature—just like the silver in a shell-illusion.
It was stated by us [the Māyāvādins] that, according to the Māyā-vāda, the body and so forth are admitted to be sublated in their very own nature (*svarūpeṇa*).

Although, in our final system (*siddhānta*), there is no superimposition (*āropitatva*) of the body and so forth upon the Self— either in its own nature or in the form of attributes such as "Self-ness"—
for the cognition "this is my body" indeed exists, whereas the cognition "I am the body" does not.
Furthermore, there is figurative usage [of "I" for the body], as seen in such statements as "I am Kṛṣṇa.

As for the Purāṇic passages stating that dogs were fondled as one's own self through clothes, garlands, ornaments, and ointments, it has already been explained that these are intended to show the lack of clear discrimination between the body and the self.

Nevertheless, in this context, one should understand that while superimposition is admitted in the form of attributes such as eternity, the statement regarding its non-sublation refers to its nature as the true Self.
Nor should it be said that "indestructibility in every respect" alone is intended as the reason (*hetu*).

For since even the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) possess a form of destructibility in terms of their attributes (*dharma*), there would arise the fallacies of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*) and the example being deficient (*sādhanavaikalya*). That [body] and so forth are also like the subject (*pakṣatulyatva*); this means they are those in which the probandum (*sādhya*) is doubtful.
And thus, because there is no certainty regarding the absence of the probandum in that case, there is no room for the objection of inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*). This is the sense.
He establishes the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) in the body and so forth with the words "even by you" (tvayāpi).
This means: even by one who maintains the non-difference of the self (ātmābhedavādin).
"That non-difference" refers to the non-difference of the body and the self (dehātmābheda).

[Objection: Granted that the non-difference between the body and the self is unreal because it is superimposed, yet since the probandum under discussion consists in the absence of difference, its reality is established; how then can there be an absence of the probandum in the body and so forth? To this he says: "Of the very absence of difference. The point is that since "non-difference" and "the absence of difference" are synonyms, the probandum does not exist in the body and so forth. [Objection: If this is so, how is it that in your own system (siddhānta) both difference and non-difference are accepted for cause and effect and the like?
[Reply: True.
Although non-difference (*abheda*) is not of the nature of the absence of difference, but rather its opposite;
and this opposition is of the nature of the relationship between the slayer and the slain;
yet that opposition is, in some cases, obstructed by the force of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).
Where there is absolute non-difference, there can be no particularity (viśeṣa) that constitutes a universal of difference;
thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in our own established doctrine (siddhānta).
Nevertheless, it is impossible to accept this in the view of the opponent.

Because it is impossible for one who does not accept a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) to account for the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of difference and non-difference in any instance, it must necessarily be admitted in that system that the absence of difference itself constitutes non-difference; therefore, this statement is made according to the logic of that very system. [Objection: But even in the Siddhānta [of Advaita], how can non-difference exist outside of the absence of difference?
For difference consists in the negation of identity (*tādātmya*).

If it is argued that this is not so because, by the rule that the nature of the counter-positive of a non-existence of non-existence is the very form of its correlate, identity must necessarily be of the nature of the absence of difference—[we reply] no;

for if that were the case, it would follow that both difference and non-difference, which are the counter-positives of absolute non-existence, would be unestablished by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is because it has already been demonstrated that what is established by valid cognition cannot possibly be the counter-positive of absolute non-existence.
Therefore, what is called "difference" (bheda), even though it consists in the negation of identity (tādātmyapratiṣedha), is indeed simply mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva).
For this very reason, its nature as the very essence of the locus (dharmisvarūpatva) is accepted;
as in the passage beginning, "Because its nature is both existence and non-existence, mutual non-existence is not separate [from them]."

Non-difference, however, is the very nature of the entity itself; it does not consist in the absolute non-existence of difference. For this very reason, its status as the nature of the substratum (dharmin) is accepted, because if it were of the nature of absolute non-existence, it would be impossible for it to be the nature of the substratum.

And thus, the distinction between non-difference and the absence of difference is established; enough of this. Regarding the phrase "if [it were] the nature of cognition": although even in our own system (siddhānta) the Self does not possess the nature of cognition—since it is impossible for a knower to be the nature of cognition—it is for this very reason that, in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa-ṭīkā*, after stating the definition of the Lord’s cognition as "independent cognition" (*svatantra-jñāna*), it is said that the term "cognition" therein serves to exclude the [ordinary] Lord.
Nevertheless, this was stated with reference to the Naiyāyika because [for him] there is an existence characterized by identity-in-difference (*saviśeṣatādātmya*).

This is because he accepts only an absolute difference between knowledge and the self. The phrase "because it is unestablished for you alone" means that the self, being of the nature of knowledge, is not accepted as the substratum of knowledge. Regarding the phrase "the state of not experiencing suffering not experienced by the Supreme Self": here, if one were to say merely "not experiencing suffering," since the state of not experiencing each other's suffering exists even among individual souls (*jīvas*), the qualifying condition (*upādhi*) would be over-pervasive (*sādhanavyāpaka*).
Therefore, the term "not experienced by the Supreme Self" is used as a qualification of the suffering.
Therefore, the meaning is that "non-connection with suffering" refers to not being connected to the suffering of the Supreme Self.

Consequently, although individual souls (*jīvas*) possess the quality of not being connected to one another's suffering, they do not possess non-connection to suffering by virtue of the qualification of "not being connected to the Supreme Self," because each soul possesses connection to its own respective suffering.
Therefore, the sense is that [the probans] is not pervaded by the sādhana (the property to be proved).

Furthermore, if by the word "suffering" (*duḥkha*) mere suffering is intended, then this qualification should be understood as being for the purpose of revealing a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*) when there is a suspicion of the probans being irrelevant (*aprayojakatā*) due to the raising of a sublation (*bādhā*) based on the exclusion of the limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Now, it may be objected: a limiting condition is a defeater only by way of suggesting a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*), and not inherently.
And in the present case, no counter-argument is possible.

One should formulate the following counter-inference: "The disputed individual selves are ultimately different from the Supreme Self, because they experience suffering that is not experienced by the Supreme Self, unlike the Supreme Self.

This has already been stated previously in the argument: "The individual soul (*jīva*) is the locus of a difference whose ontological status (*sattā*) is equal to the ontological status of the subject (*dharmin*) whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is Brahman."
Therefore, this pointing out of the *upādhi* (limiting condition) is futile; to this it is replied with the words "of the *upādhi*" and so forth.
Let it be granted that this *upādhi* does not function as a fault by way of suggesting a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*).

Nevertheless, because the *upādhi* pervades the probandum (*sādhya*), if it is excluded from the subject (*pakṣa*), the absence of the probandum in the subject necessarily follows, and thus there is sublation (*bādha*).

The sense is that there will either be a fallacy of the thesis (*pakṣa*) itself or a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). That very thing is also the fault of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), because in the *Pramāṇalakṣaṇa* and other works, the status of a condition as a defect has been stated precisely through its capacity to suggest a counter-argument (*pratipakṣonnāyakatva*). Thus, it is said that [the condition] functions as a defect by way of manifesting either sublation (*bādha*) or deviation.
The word "either" (*anyatara*) is used to avoid the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) known as "excess" (*ādhikya*).

Having thus established the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding difference, he now refutes the means of valid cognition regarding non-difference, beginning with the words "As it has been said," etc. Regarding the phrase "consisting of the confluence of consciousness and the unconscious": since the notion of "I" has as its object consciousness qualified by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), the pure identity [of the self] is not established by the experience of a single form, namely "I. In reality, even if the notion of "I" had the pure [self] as its object, it would still not have non-difference as its object;
for there is no such experience as, "I, being Caitra, shall become both Caitra and Maitra."
However, it perceives only the state of being pervaded by a single form, which is the very nature of what has been described.
Otherwise, because of the cognition of a single form—namely "pot-ness"—among pots, they would have to be one and the same.
If it is argued that in that case there exists a cognition of distinctions such as grossness and minuteness, [we reply:]...

It has already been stated that even here there exists the cognition of distinctions such as pleasure and pain; by this, the claim that the identity of a qualified [self] is established through the experience of "I" is refuted. Regarding the phrase "in the first": the meaning is in the inference beginning with "the selves under dispute," etc. It has been stated that the nature of selfhood (ātmatva), which serves as the logical reason (hetu), is self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva).
That very state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*) is what constitutes self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).
He says "not the first" by stating "provided that there is non-objectivity" (*avedyatve sati*).
Nor is the second [option] valid.
Because that [reason] is unestablished.
The response—that there is a lack of probative force due to the student’s doubt, and that non-contemplation of Brahman-bliss and so forth constitutes a limiting adjunct (upādhi)—must be considered.

By this, the definition of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) as "the state of not requiring consciousness other than itself for its own empirical usage" is refuted. Regarding the phrase "by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*): the meaning is that even if one accepts that what has been known is sublated in the form of being "perfectly known," one still accepts that it is not sublated by its own nature.

It should also be understood that if one intends to assert sublation in every respect, there is the fallacy of the unestablished (*asiddhi*). Regarding the phrase "by accepting superimposition": it should be noted that otherwise, the refutation of the Cārvākas who maintain the identity of the body and the self would be untenable. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvāt*)": the meaning is that the previously mentioned qualification "in the ultimate sense" (*paramārthataḥ*) is itself sublated. Now, if there is no identity between consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*), how can he be a proponent of universal non-duality (*sarvādvaitavādin*)? To this, he says: "of the very absence of difference. This means: of the absence of the unreality of difference. The ellipsis of the sentence is: "there is no contradiction with being a proponent of non-duality."

Alternatively, since the intended meaning in the statement "they are not different from the Supreme Self" is merely the absence of difference having the Supreme Self as its counter-correlate (*paramātmapratiyogikabhedābhāvamātra*), it might follow that even the body and so forth would be included in the subject (*pakṣa*), resulting in the undesirable consequence of a difference between the body and the self. To this he says: "of the mere absence of difference. The sense is that this is said with respect to the Naiyāyika, because [the author] is refuting all proponents of difference (*bhedavādin*).
In reality, however, since [the self] is an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), its being consciousness (*jñānatva*) is difficult to maintain;

furthermore, it should be understood that [the reason] is inconclusive (*savyabhicāra*). Regarding the phrase "and of the limiting adjunct" (*upādheśca*): where there is difference from the Supreme Self, there is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

The remainder [of the text], however, is for the purpose of making manifest the status of being a *prayojaka* (the instigator). Now, an objection might be raised: since a limiting condition (*upādhi*) functions as a raiser of a counter-inference (*satpratipakṣa*), here too the inference "because he does not contemplate suffering that has not been contemplated by Brahman" would attain exactly the same status; thus, it could not serve to determine one's own position (*svapakṣa*), and consequently, a separate formal application (*prayoga*) of this very inference to determine one's own position would be redundant. To this, it is said: "The defectiveness of the condition (*upādhi*) lies in its capacity to vitiate [the argument] by way of exposing either a sublation (*bādha*) or an inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*)."

The sense is that since being the self as asserted by the opponent is the logical ground [for the objection], and since this [proposition] possesses contradiction, it is established as a sublater of that [objection].
Regarding the phrase "of the ego-sense" (*ahaṅkārasya*): the reason for its being distinct from the Self is that it consists of a confluence of consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*).
This is because, if there were no difference between them, there would be no evidence for the non-difference of the Self [from the ego].
The meaning is "due to the absence of being a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇatvābhāvāt*).
Alternatively, there is a word-division as *pramāṇatvāt* (due to being a valid means of knowledge);
in that case, "in its non-difference" refers to the non-difference from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

The construction is: "Because there is proof for the non-difference of the *ahaṅkāra* alone, there is no difference of the Self. Regarding the phrase "in the first inference": the meaning is that in the argument—"The disputed selves do not differ in reality from the Supreme Self, because they possess the nature of being a self (*ātmatva*), like the Supreme Self"—[the reason is unestablished]. As for "unestablished" (*asiddhi*): you yourself have stated that "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is not a genus (*jāti*), but rather self-luminosity; and you define that in your own works as "being fit for immediate empirical usage while being non-objectifiable. In that case, since in our view the very nature of being a self is absent in what is non-objectifiable, the reason is unestablished. [The opponent asks: "Then..."?
In my view, although there is sublation (bādha) regarding the attributes of the body and so forth—since they are superimposed—their nature is not subject to sublation.
The meaning is that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) because of the absence of any real difference (tattvika-bheda) from the counter-correlative, the Supreme Self.

The point is that one cannot employ "sublation in every respect" as a logical reason (hetu), because there is sublation in terms of attributes even for the subject (pakṣa) and the similar instances (sapakṣa).

[Objection: "Granted that the identity between the body and the self is superimposed (*adhyasta*), why could the absence of the distinction between the body and the self not be real? To this, he says: "Of the very absence of distinction. The sense is that it is due to parsimony (*lāghava*). [Regarding the term] "of the limiting adjunct" (*upādheḥ*): the meaning is that when a pervader of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*) exists neither in the subject (*pakṣa*) nor in its locus, the pointing out of a contradiction (*bādhodbhāvana*) is the means; whereas when it exists in its locus, the pointing out of inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*) is the means. [Regarding the definition] "the state of being a cognizer of suffering not cognized by the Supreme Self": here, the phrase "not cognized by the Supreme Self" (*paramātmānanusaṃhita*) is not a constituent part of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because it does not serve to differentiate [the class].
However, [the mention of this condition] is for the purpose of indicating a favorable *tarka* at the stage of inferring a sublation (*bādha*) apart from the presence of an *upādhi*.

On the other hand, if its status as a defeater (*dūṣaka*) were by virtue of raising a counter-balanced argument (*satpratipakṣa*), then even in the case of a counter-balanced argument, this very thing would be an *upādhi* because it possesses a qualification that excludes the subject (*pakṣa*) alone; thus, it should be understood that one cannot raise a counter-balanced argument by means of this, and therefore that [subject] is abandoned.
Furthermore, the fact that [the reason] is deviant (*vyabhicārin*) in cases such as those who are asleep or in a swoon has already been analyzed previously.

Having thus established the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within his own school, he proceeds to refute in succession the means of valid cognition—such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and others—as stated by the opponent, beginning with the words "As it has been said," etc. Regarding the phrase "consisting of the confluence of consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*"): since the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)-delimited consciousness alone constitutes the referent of the word "I" (*ahaṃ*), and because the internal organs are distinct, a difference between them is necessarily required.

The meaning is that such a cognition is not a means of valid cognition for the oneness of all consciousness; rather, it would be a means of valid cognition only for the oneness of the genus (*jāti*) consisting of being an internal organ.

The meaning is that because there is no distinction from that [object], there is no distinction from consciousness (*cid-abheda*), and thus it lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇatvāt*, i.e., *pramāṇatvābhāvāt*). Regarding "in the first inference": since it was stated during the occasion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) in the inference "the selves under dispute [are self-luminous]" that "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) is "self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatva*), he refutes that by saying "if it were unapprehendable" (*avedyatve*). This is because the opponents have established in their own treatises the definition: "being the object of immediate empirical usage while being unapprehendable. To state the lack of proof for that, he says: "by us."

The claim that [the self] does not depend on a consciousness distinct from itself is also unproven, because at the time of deep sleep there is an absence of any activity whatsoever. Furthermore, even the verbal activity occurring after the period of deep sleep invariably depends upon cognitions distinct from itself— such as the knowledge of the superimposition of identity with the body and so forth, the knowledge of the means for attaining what is desired, and so on.
It should also be understood that there is an absence of any self-transaction (*svavyavahāra*) dependent upon a consciousness other than oneself.
This has been presented merely as a direction (*diṅmātra*) by way of illustration.

Therefore, since such self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) can serve as a valid reason (*hetu*), there is no room for the doubt as to how the inference could be unestablished (*asiddha*). Regarding the phrase "of the body and so forth" (*dehādeḥ*): regarding the phrase "by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*): it is said to be "by its own nature" because [the body, etc. is sublated either in the form of identity with the Self (*ātmatādātmya*), or in the form of being essentially dependent on another (*parānāyattasvasvātmikatva*).

The sense is that [the reason] does not exist even in the self (*ātman*), because there is no sublation (*bādhyatva*) in its entirety; for [the self] is subject to sublation in the form of identification with the body (*dehatādātmya*) and so forth. "Similarity to the subject" (*pakṣatulyatvam*) means that I also accept the absence of ultimate difference—where the counter-correlate is the Supreme Self—even in the case of the body and so on. "By you too" (*tvayāpi*): the particle *api* is used to include the Naiyāyikas and others. "Of the non-difference between the body and the self": [this is stated] because of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvāt*).

The point is this: since you yourself have stated that between the two contradictory properties consisting of difference and non-difference, non-difference possesses ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatā*), the ultimate reality of difference follows by implication; thus, the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is unavoidable. "Against the Naiyāyika" means:
because he too is a proponent of the reality of difference, and the present investigation has proceeded precisely by relying upon his own system.
"For you alone" means: regarding the material cause of the mental modification (*vṛttijñāna*), its locus is the mind itself, not the self which is the subject under discussion (*pakṣībhūta*).

The meaning is that since the self cannot be its own locus, it cannot serve as the locus for the cognition of its own nature; thus, the reason is unestablished (*asiddhi*). Regarding the term "of the limiting adjunct" (*upādheḥ*): the point is that because the absence of the limiting adjunct—which has been apprehended as pervading the probandum—is certain, there is indeed sublation (*bādha*), since such an absence is included within that [category].

As for its being a raiser of a counter-inference (*satpratipakṣa*), there would have to be equal strength; for a counter-inference consists precisely in the contradiction of two equally strong means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And that is not possible here.

It has been stated that this is the "subject" (*pakṣa*) because the quality of being a cognizer of suffering— which consists in the non-apprehension of the Supreme Self characterized by the absence of the aforementioned adjuncts— is established as a determiner of difference through the assistance of favorable reasoning.

Some maintain that since it could be argued that even in the case of the reason for the counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*), which consists in the absence of the adjunct in question and which ultimately results in the status of being "other than the subject," the property of being "other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) itself could be cited as an adjunct (*upādhi*), the position [of the opponent] must be abandoned.

It should be noted that since the reason consisting in the absence of a qualified adjunct (*viśiṣṭopādhyabhāva*) is useful for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) according to the method previously stated, the qualified entity possesses the status of an adjunct; however, it is only the factor of "not experiencing suffering" that constitutes the adjunct, while the other portion is purposeful precisely because it gives rise to a supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*) for the inference of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*).

Having thus established the proof for difference, he refutes the proof for non-difference stated by the opponent, beginning with "As for what was said... [regarding] "of the *ahaṅkāra*. The sense is that since the *ahaṅkāra*—which is the object of the notion of "I" (*aham-pratyaya*) and consists of consciousness delimited by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—lacks the nature of pure consciousness (*śuddha-cid-rūpa*), the cognition thereof cannot serve as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for identity with pure consciousness.

Furthermore, regarding what was said about the inferences (*anumāna*) and so forth, he states that they too are invalid, beginning with "In the first inference... [The argument is]: "The subjects under dispute do not differ from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in reality, because they possess the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*)."
The meaning is that this refers to the inference "like the supreme self" (paramātmavat).

Here, it was stated that the nature of being a self (ātmatva), which serves as the probans (hetu), consists in self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva). He refutes that [position] with the words "avedyatve" (if it were non-cognizable). This means: if [self-luminosity] consists in not being an object of illumination (prakāśa) in general, or if it consists in not being an object of illumination other than itself.

By the phrase "because we do not accept this," it is indicated that [the opponent's] proof is unestablished (*asiddhi*), since others do not accept self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) in the sense of being the object of its own manifestation due to the contradiction between action and its object.
The implication is that any self-luminosity other than this is simply impossible to define.
If that is so, then self-luminosity is not the nature of the Self (*ātmatva*).

Nevertheless, he raises the doubt that it might be something else entirely—namely, "incorruptibility" (*abādhyatva*). Now, one might object: since the body and so forth are subject to sublation (*bādhyatva*) by way of their superimposed forms such as agency (*kartṛtva*), how can there be incorruptibility? To resolve this doubt, the term "in its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*) is stated.
The intended meaning is this:
if "incorruptibility in every respect" were the reason, it would be unestablished (*asiddhi*).
Since even the self (*ātman*) is sublated by way of its superimposed form,

it must be stated that [the definition] consists in being unsublated by way of existence (*sattva*). However, since this [quality]— which ultimately amounts to being the object of a valid cognition (*pramiti*) qualified by existence— is present even in the body, senses, and so forth, which lack the property to be proven (*sādhya*), there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*).

He addresses the objection that there is no fault because the non-difference of the Self is established even in relation to the body and so forth, by stating "na ca" (and not). The meaning is: "equal to the subject" (*pakṣatulya*) means equal to the subject under discussion, that is to say, one in which the probandum (*sādhya*) is doubtful.
The point is that only deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that which possesses a definitely ascertained absence of the probandum constitutes a logical fault.
Furthermore, the status of the body and so forth as being "equal to the subject" is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Regarding that, he says "by you too" because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) in accepting the non-difference of the Self. "In the state of being superimposed" (*adhyastatve*): the sense is that otherwise, the mutual superimposition of the body and the Self could not be established. The meaning is that since the non-difference between the body and the Supreme Self is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), the probandum—the absence of ultimate difference—is absent. Now, even if non-difference is not ultimately real, why is there an absence of such a probandum? To this he says: "of the absence of difference. Furthermore, non-difference is not identity (*tādātmya*).
And it should not be said that this very nature [of the self] is merely the absence of difference;

for then the nature of the self itself would fall into the error of being false (mithyā), since it too would be superimposed (adhyasta). Nor can it be argued that while the superimposed nature of the body and so forth is indeed false, the nature of the self is not.
Because it is illogical to postulate a variety of forms when there is mutual superimposition,
and because, in the absence of an ultimate difference between the body and the self, the two would consequently result in an identity of their essential natures.
This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa).

It should also be understood that even if the body and so forth are treated as being on the same footing as the subject (*pakṣa*), the fallacy of the "uncertain with doubtful exclusion" (*sandigdhānaikāntya*) is indeed unavoidable;
for in the absence of a favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*), that too constitutes a defect.

Regarding the phrase "due to non-establishment" (*asiddheḥ*): since the Naiyāyika accepts only the self (*ātman*) as the substratum of cognition, the meaning is that the probans (*sādhana*), the subject (*pakṣa*), the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) are all unestablished.

Although it can be argued that there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the knowledge of mental states (*vṛttijñāna*) even according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the intention is that [the reason] is so because "being eternal knowledge" (*nityajñānatva*) is the probans (*hetu*). [The opponent replies: "Because it is unestablished for you alone. The sense is that this is because you accept that the self (*ātman*) is nothing but knowledge (*jñānamātra*).
Nor should it be said that being non-inert (*ajaḍatva*) constitutes the nature of the self.
Because insentience (*jaḍatva*) consists in being non-self (*anātmatva*), there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*).
Nor can it be said that selfhood (*ātmatva*) is the state of being other than qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, while being other than substances such as earth;
for to me, the fact of being other than qualities and so forth remains unestablished.
If that [qualification] were not stated, there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth according to the view of the logicians (*tārkika*).

Even if the reason (*hetu*) were somehow defined, because of the absence of a supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*), it is difficult to avoid its being seized by a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and the like; thus he says: "of the limiting adjunct" (*upādheḥ*). Here, the limiting adjunct is either merely the state of not being conscious of the Supreme Self (*paramātmānanusaṃhitānanusandhātṛtva*) or merely the state of not being conscious of suffering (*duḥkhānanusandhātṛtva*).
In the first case, the word "suffering" (*duḥkha*) is a mention of the essential nature (*svarūpa*).

In the second [case], it should be understood that the statement "the Supreme Self is not kept in mind" establishes the pervasion of the probandum by the condition (*upādhi*). Now, one might object that because a condition does not consist of sublation (*bādha*), deviation (*vyabhicāra*), or other such fallacies, it cannot be a defect; to this, it is said: "in the view that it is a defect. Since it cannot be a defect by being directly opposed to inference, it functions as a defect through the manifestation of sublation or deviation. It is stated that it is "manifested" because it arises in the context of an argument for others (*parārthaprasaṅga*). The meaning is: either by way of suggesting sublation or by way of suggesting deviation.

The point is that, in the present case, because there is an absence of a limiting condition (*upādhi*), it is possible to infer the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), and it is also possible to infer the deviation of the probandum from the reason (*hetu*) through the deviation of the reason from the limiting condition.

Alternatively, one might object: "Since there is doubt regarding the probandum in the subject and an absence of the reason in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), it is impossible for a limiting condition to ever suggest deviation; how then can it function as a refutation? To this, it is said: "By way of suggesting deviation based on sublation (*bādha*). This means: by way of suggesting deviation as induced by sublation.

The intention is that, in this way, it is possible for a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) to suggest a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of establishing the certainty of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) in the subject (*pakṣa*). Furthermore, it should be understood here that its status as a defect also arises through its capacity to suggest a sublation (*bādhonnāyakatva*). Having thus established the three proofs for difference, he now refutes the three proofs—beginning with the statement "As for the perception regarding difference which was stated..."—and first refutes perception. This is done starting from the words "As for what was stated... and so on. Regarding the phrase "of the 'I'-notion" (*ahaṃkārasya*): indeed, the perception "I" (*aham*) was stated to be the proof for the non-difference of the Self.
That [knowledge] would be so only if it had the self as its object;
but that is not the case,
because in your own system you admit that it has as its object the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is a mixture of the conscious, the unconscious, and the conscious-unconscious.

And because that [notion] is distinct from the Self, the meaning is that the "I-notion" (ahaṃpratyaya) directed toward that [body] is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the non-difference of the Self.

Now, he refutes the inferences (*anumāna*) that establish the non-difference of the Self, beginning with the words "In the first case," etc. Regarding the argument: "The disputed selves are not ultimately different from the Supreme Self, because they possess selfhood (*ātmatva*), like the Supreme Self"—here, the opponent himself has stated that selfhood is indeed the state of being self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*), and not a specific universal (*jāti*).

In this context, since the opponent does not accept self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva) in the sense of being the illuminator of its own object—due to the contradiction between the agent and the object—it must instead be accepted as the state of not being cognizable by other means of knowledge (pramāṇāntarāvedyatva). And that [self-luminosity] is unestablished for me, because I accept that the Self is cognizable by other means of knowledge; such is the meaning.

If it is argued, "In that case, let the nature of the Self be something else," [the author] holds these alternatives in mind—whether it consists in being non-sublatable (*abādhyatva*), or consisting in being consciousness (*jñānatva*), or consisting in being the substratum of consciousness (*jñānādhāratva*)—and first raises an objection to refute the first: "Non-sublatability" (*abādhyatvam*). The sense is that since this is also accepted by you regarding the Self, the previously mentioned fault does not apply. He refutes it with: "In that case" (*tarhi*). "Inconstancy" (*vyabhicāra*): the meaning is that there is inconstancy because the reason, which is the nature of non-sublatability, exists in the body and so forth, while the probandum—the absence of difference from the Self—is absent there. Anticipating the objection of inconstancy, he refutes it with: "And not" (*na ca*). "That" (*tat*) refers to the body and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: just as the absence of a difference in the self (*ātman*) is established in the subject (*pakṣa*), so too is it established in the body and other such things. Therefore, since the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) there is a matter of doubt, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because the reason (*hetu*) does not occur in that which possesses the certainty of the absolute absence of the probandum.

[Objection: Even if there is no certain deviation according to the method stated above, there would still be "doubtful deviation" (*sandigdhavyabhicāra*). This is because "doubtful deviation" consists precisely in the certainty of the reason existing in that which is doubted to possess the absence of the probandum. [Response: No.

If that were the case, then because all reasons would exist in the subject (*pakṣa*) where there is doubt regarding the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*), it would follow that the entire system of inference is destroyed. Rather, "doubtful deviation" (*sandigdhavyabhicāra*) consists precisely in a doubt regarding the reason in a locus where the absence of the probandum is certain. The point is that such a case does not exist in the present instance.

He states that the very equality with the subject (*pakṣa*) is unestablished, saying "by you. Regarding "from the perspective of ultimate reality" (*paramārthataḥ*): the meaning is that it is because of the absence of that probandum (*sādhya*) which consists in the non-existence of difference having the Supreme Self as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). To the question "Why?", he says "of the non-difference [of the body and self]. This means the non-difference between the body and the self. To the question "Why even that?", he says:

"By you" [means]: "superimposedness" (*adhyastatva*) is the state of being superimposed (*āropitatva*). The sense is that this is based on his own commentary (*bhāṣya*), which states: "having superimposed the nature of one upon the other. Now, an objection might be raised: "In this case, it is only the absence of difference (*bhedābhāva*) that is being established, not identity (*abheda*). Therefore, since I accept that the identity between the body and the self is superimposed, even though that [identity] is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), the absence of difference between the body and the self remains ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). Thus, the probandum (*sādhya*) indeed exists in the body and so forth. To this, he replies: "Of the absence of difference" (*bhedābhāvasya*). The sense is this: if one accepts that identity is superimposed, then the absence of difference must also be accepted as such.

Having raised the second objection, he refutes it with the words: "If [the body] were knowledge... The sense is that since the body lacks the nature of knowledge, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Regarding the Naiyāyika: the sense is that by asserting that "selfhood consists in being the inherent cause of knowledge," that [Naiyāyika] does not accept that the self has the nature of knowledge.

He raises a third objection: "The state of being the substratum of knowledge" (*jñānādhāratvam*). The sense is that the aforementioned fault does not apply because the non-dualist (*ayārikena*) accepts the self as the substratum of knowledge. "The very [point] is unestablished for you": the sense is that in your own system, since the self is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatvena*), the status of being the substratum of knowledge is not accepted; therefore, the aforementioned fault remains. "Not having the Supreme Self in mind" (*paramātmānanusaṃhita*): this means that suffering which is not kept in mind by the Supreme Self—that is, not experienced by Him—is what constitutes "not having it in mind" or "not experiencing it."

The meaning is as follows: wherever there is non-difference from the Self, there is the state of not being a cognizer of suffering that is not cognized by the Supreme Self, as in the case of the Supreme Self itself.

Wherever there is the nature of being a [limited] self (jīvatva), there is not the state of not being a cognizer of suffering that is not cognized by the Supreme Self; for in the case of individual souls (*jīvas*), since they possess the very quality of being cognizers of suffering that is not cognized by the Supreme Self—just as they possess the nature of being selves—the probans (*sādhana*) is over-pervasive (*vyāpaka*).

Now, since a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is not itself a direct defect of the reason (*hetu*), its status as a defect of the reason must be asserted by way of its serving as a basis for formulating a counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*). Thus, one should formulate an inferential counter-argument based on the absence of the adjunct as follows: "The individual selves (*ātman*) are in reality distinct from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because they experience suffering that is not experienced by the Supreme Self; unlike the Supreme Self. This is the inference to be performed by means of the exclusion of the adjunct.

And this [objection] is pointless, because it was already stated at the very occasion of establishing the difference between selves; therefore, it was said: "in the view that the upādhi functions as a refutation by way of manifesting a sublation (*bādha*) or an inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*). When the upādhi does not pervade the probans (*sādhana*), the upādhi—which excludes both alternatives from the subject (*pakṣa*) that possesses the probans—also excludes the probandum (*sādhya*) by virtue of its pervading the probandum. Thus, because there is a certainty of the absence of the probandum in the subject, there is sublation (*bādha*).
This is because, according to that view, only the cognition of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) constitutes a sublation (*bādha*).

Thus, when the absence of the probandum is ascertained in the subject by the aforementioned method, that very subject becomes the counter-example (*vipakṣa*); since the reason (*hetu*) exists there, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), for it is precisely the presence of the reason in the counter-example that constitutes deviation.
It is in accordance with this position that the following objection regarding the "limiting condition" (*upādhi*) is raised.

However, according to the view that it does not give rise to a counter-argument distinct from itself, there is no pointlessness; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, there is an equality of status with a fallacious argument (*ābhāsa*), as in: "The disputed selves do not differ from the Supreme Self in reality (or even in non-reality), because they are selves, like the Supreme Self."
Furthermore, due to the absence of a supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*), there is a lack of logical necessity (*aprayojakatā*).

In the second case, if by the word "Devadatta" one intends consciousness delimited by that specific body, then since the bodies of Yajñadatta and others cannot possibly be dependent upon the consciousness delimited by Devadatta’s body, there is a contradiction (*bādha*) if one attempts to prove that they are the locus of his experience. If, on the other hand, one intends undelimited consciousness, then because that [undelimited consciousness] is not an experiencer (*abhoktṛ*), there is again a contradiction.
There is a deviation [of the reason] in the case of bodies that are asleep or in a state of fainting;
for even these would be included within the class of the subject (*pakṣa*), which would result in a contradiction (*bādha*).
Nor should it be argued that the probandum (*sādhya*) is "not being a locus of the absolute non-existence of being a substrate for experience."

Because, by your admission that the locus of experience is false, you must admit that the body, which is its substratum, is the locus of the absolute non-existence of that [experience]. In the third case, there is a failure to define the probandum (*sādhya*).
Nor can it be defined as "that which is removable by the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum."

If by the word "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) one intends destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), falsity is impossible; and if one intends absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), there is a contradiction with your own position, because even you admit difference during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), which renders that [absolute non-existence] untenable. If it is argued that suchness exists in the form of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), we say no.

Furthermore, since the ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), which consists in being non-sublatable, has its cognition dependent upon the cognition of sublatibility as asserted by you, there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*). Regarding the passage beginning with "the subject of dispute" (*vimata*):

since he [the opponent] accepts a non-ultimate difference between the selves under dispute and the Supreme Self as its counter-correlate, proving the absence of that [difference] would be undesirable for him.

It should be understood that because he [the opponent] accepts ultimate difference in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the inference is fallacious due to the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*). Regarding the second [inference]: "The bodies under dispute are the substrata of experience for Devadatta alone, because they are bodies, like Devadatta’s body.
Here, the probandum (*sādhya*) is the state of not being a non-locus of the absolute absence of being a substratum of experience.

Now, wishing to refute that which was previously stated by the opponent—that there is neither sublation nor deviation in the cases of deep sleep, fainting, or dead bodies—the author himself states the very objection raised and resolved by the opponent as an introduction, saying: "In the case of one who has slept, fainted, etc. He now raises the point for which this refutation was set forth and then refutes it, saying: "And it should not be said," and "by accepting [the world's] falsity."

The sense is that, according to his view, falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in having a common locus with its own absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). "In the third [case]" means: in the argument, "Difference is false because it possesses the nature of difference, like the difference between two moons. He refutes this by raising the very same definition of falsity previously stated: "And not... [as follows]. Regarding the phrase "or if there is an intention to mean absolute non-existence": although here the word "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) cannot be intended to mean absolute non-existence, because the latter is unproduced (*ajanya*).

Furthermore, since being removable by knowledge consists in being the counter-positive of a cessation produced by knowledge, one must here intend by "removability" simply the state of being known as having a cessation for its counter-positive. He establishes the sublation in both cases with the words: "By you also..."

The meaning is as follows: even for you, who maintain that difference is false (*mithyātva*), since you accept the persistence of difference during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*) and during the state of liberation-in-life (*jīvanmukti*) following knowledge, there is no destruction of difference by that knowledge.

Furthermore, because you accept difference during the state of empirical transaction, it is all the more impossible for there to be absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*); and since that [absolute non-existence] is untenable, the aforementioned definition of falsity is inapplicable.

However, some say that in the view where [the term] has the sense of "destruction" (*pradhvaṃsa*), since that which is illusory cannot undergo destruction, the phrase "even by you" is intended to establish absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) after having already established sublation (*bādha*) externally; they argue that the statement is thus directed toward proving absolute non-existence. Accepting the position of absolute non-existence, he raises an objection in order to avoid the charge of sublation: "In the form of ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatvākāreṇa*). "That state" (*tathātva*) means being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of absolute non-existence. "Non-sublatability" (*abādhyatva*): ultimate reality is indeed non-sublatability; and that is known dependent upon the knowledge of sublatability.
This is because the cognition of a non-existence depends upon the cognition of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
Furthermore, "sublatability" (*bādhyatva*) consists in being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence with respect to the form of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*).
Thus, once non-sublatability is established, sublatability—in the form of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence with respect to that [ultimate] nature—is thereby established.

The meaning is that since the establishment of that [non-difference] depends upon the establishment of non-sublatability—which consists in the absence of difference—there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*).

"Even from the standpoint of the non-ultimate reality (*aparamārthataḥ*), they do not differ" means that they are devoid even of empirical difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*). "As in the case of the Supreme Self (*paramātmavat*)"—the sense is that because the Supreme Self lacks difference with respect to any counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), it is devoid of empirical difference. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of a supporting argument" (*anukūlatarkābhāvāt*): if one objects that there is indeed an argument—namely, "if there were no non-difference from the Supreme Self, then there would be no selfhood, because the scripture 'There is no other seer than He' and so forth negates the status of being a knower in anything else"—we reply: no.

If there were non-difference from the Supreme Self, then, because its status as a knower is negated by the statement, "By what means could one see whom?", the reasoning [of the opponent] would, conversely, be favorable to the other side; such is the direction of the argument. Regarding the second [point]: the ellipsis is "the inference that 'the bodies under dispute [are not presided over by a single agent]'"; [it is rejected] on the grounds of the impossibility of being a locus (adhiṣṭhānatva), the sense being that it [the individual soul] is limited.

Regarding the reading *adhīnatvāsambhavena* (due to the impossibility of dependence): the sense is that the bodies of Yajñadatta and others lack the activity conforming to Yajñadatta’s effort, and thus they cannot serve as the locus for his experience (*bhoga*). Regarding the term *bādha* (contradiction): it should also be understood to include the charge of *apasiddhānta* (departure from established tenets). Now, one might argue: "Devadatta’s being the locus of experience consists simply in being another qualified entity whose qualificandum is distinct from the qualificandum already entered [into the definition] as being non-distinct from something other than Devadatta. If this is said, we reply: No. Regarding the inclusion of two contradictory qualified entities within a single qualificandum—is it by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), or is it by way of being reinforced by another qualification?
Because whiteness and yellowness are observed in one and the same thing,
there is no contradiction in the coexistence of being "possessed of a staff" and being "bent.
The second [alternative] is not tenable.

"Because it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and so forth. "Because [the world] is accepted as not being the locus of its own absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). If it is argued that by accepting the definition of falsity (*mithyātva*) as "co-occurrence with one's own absolute non-existence," the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is simply "being the locus of absolute non-existence," we say no.

For in your view, since everything consists of everything else, all properties exist everywhere; consequently, an absolute non-existence that does not co-occur with its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is itself unestablished (*aprasiddha*).
In reality, however, there are two preeminent refutations: the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), and "being acquired through Devadatta’s karma" is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Furthermore, one should consider that it is not possible to establish even the *upādhi* (limiting condition) in the following inference— "The disputed bodies were acquired through the karma of Devadatta, because they are bodies"—
since the status of being the locus of Devadatta’s experience serves as the *upādhi*.
This is because both [the probandum and the *upādhi*] are equally doubtful, and thus it is logical for the *upādhi* to be considered "suspected" (*śaṅkita*).

And if both [reasons] are established simultaneously or by one alone, there is defeat (*nigraha*) due to redundancy (*ādhikya*), because the distinction [between them] is already obtained.
