"The third" means: the inference that "difference is false, because it possesses the nature of difference. "The non-specification of the probandum (*sādhyānirukti*)" means: since neither *vyāvahārikatva* (empirical reality) nor *prātibhāsikatva* (illusory appearance) individually conforms to either the subject (*pakṣa*) or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there is no definition of a common [property] (*anugata*). This is the sense.

One might object that this is merely a verbal definition; anticipating this, he refutes it with the words "na ca" (and not). He states that neither of the two meanings possible for the word "nivṛtti" (cessation) is tenable, saying "tadayogāt" (because of the impossibility of that). The sense is that since difference would be the counter-correlate of absolute non-existence, it would follow that it itself is absolutely non-existent; furthermore, if one were to accept it as a property, then upon the arising of the knowledge of the substratum regarding a single thing, no one would have any cognition of that difference either.

An objection is raised: "Surely, being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of absolute non-existence does not occur by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), which would entail non-existence; rather, it occurs by way of another attribute (*dharmāntareṇa*). [The author replies: "By way of ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatvena*). The sense is that it is impossible to define ultimate reality in any other manner. Ultimate reality consists in being non-sublatable (*abādhyatva*). For you, sublatibility means being the counter-positive of absolute non-existence by way of the form of ultimate reality, while not being negatable by way of its own nature. Thus, because ultimate reality enters back into the definition, there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).

Regarding the phrase "But in the third [case]": the meaning is that it refers to the argument, "Difference is false because it is a difference, like the difference in the [reflected] moon. "That which is to be proven" (*tatsādhyam*): by the word "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), what is to be proven is neither the state of being the counter-positive of a destruction produced by the knowledge of the true nature of the substrate, nor the state of being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence produced by that [knowledge].

This is because you yourself accept the persistence of difference during the stage of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which occurs after the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, those [definitions] are untenable.

It should also be understood that absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) cannot be produced. Furthermore, it should be understood that because the final cognition does not have an object greater than that of the preceding cognitions, it is impossible for it to be what brings about the cessation of those [preceding] states. Regarding the phrase "in the form of ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatvākāreṇa*): in the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), the aspect of ultimate reality ceases; this is the sense behind the expression "acting like a burnt cloth. Regarding the phrase "of the nature of non-sublatability" (*abādhyatvarūpasya*): the point is that since the definition of sublatibility involves the entry of "ultimate reality," there is no circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) based on the inclusion of "non-sublatability" within that definition.

"Selfs are diverse" means "not from the perspective of ultimate reality. The implication is that, in this way, there would also follow the undesirable consequence of proving the absence of a distinction between the conventional self and the supreme self. "The second [alternative]" refers to...
The meaning is that "all bodies" refers to inference; this is because [the opponent] accepts that [inference] has those [bodies] as its locus.
And thus, the sense is that there is a contradiction (*bādha*) in proving that [the body] is the locus of that [experience].

Even under the alternative interpretation of this sentence found in the section on the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), which explains it according to the literal meaning of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the manner of "others, however," one must recognize that the status of being the abode of experience (*bhogāyatana*) and so forth is contradicted by direct experience (*anubhavabādha*). "Thirdly" means: in the inference "difference is false because it is a difference. "The probandum is not defined" means: if one attempts to prove non-existence (*asattva*), there is a violation of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*) and contradiction; if one attempts to prove "being distinct from both existence and non-existence," there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*); therefore, the probandum is not defined. "Contradiction" means: [contradiction with perception].
He establishes this with the words "by you also":

since the determination of the relationship between the produced and the producer and so forth is dependent upon difference (*bheda*), when that [difference] is sublated by the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), it is impossible for the property of being produced by that [Self]—which constitutes part of the probandum—to exist; thus, there is a contradiction (*bādha*).

The meaning is that in the case of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), since the property of being produced by that [cognition] is itself absent, the existence of the probandum (*sādhya*)—which is constituted by that [property]—cannot be established; thus, there is a contradiction (*bādha*). Regarding the phrase "in the form of ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatvākāreṇa*): its meaning is the state of being the counter-positive of a destruction whose counter-positivehood is delimited by ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) as produced by cognition. Regarding the phrase "of the nature of non-sublatability" (*abādhyatvarūpasya*): since ultimate reality consists in the absence of sublatibility (*bādhyatvābhāva*), non-sublatability is included within the very body of the concept of sublatibility; thus, one should also observe that this involves the fallacy of circularity (*ātmāśraya*). Now, [an objection]: surely sublatibility is simply the state of being the counter-positive of a destruction produced by cognition.
Ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) is not included within its [the world's] own constitution;
rather, through knowledge—which is ultimate reality—the destruction of the world occurs as qualified by that [knowledge] superimposed upon it.
For this very reason, the world persists in the state of *jīvanmukti* as something resembling a burnt cloth.
And thus, it must be said that sublation (bādhyatva) should be established by taking such a destruction (dhvaṃsa) as it actually exists;

for if, in reality, such a destruction were included merely as "being such a destruction," then since a jar qualified by the objectivity of a present cognition has now been destroyed, there would follow the undesirable consequence (āpatti) of the conventional usage of its sublation even at this present time.

Regarding the phrase "as in the case of self-knowledge in the substrate" (*adhiṣṭhāne yathā''tmajñāneti*): since the status of being a substrate (*adhiṣṭhānatva*) consists in being the locus of superimposition (*āropa*), and because it is impossible to define anything else that is not over-extended, the cognition of difference [between the substrate and the superimposed] cannot establish its own falsity. Furthermore, because it is unestablished prior [to the proof], one should understand that there is the fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) and so forth.

As for the statement "the selves under dispute" (*vimatā ātmānaḥ*): although here there is the fallacy of an unestablished probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*) because the opponent does not accept even conventional difference (*vyāvahārikabheda*), there is nonetheless no fault, as the probandum is the state of being devoid of difference within the sphere of empirical usage (*vyavahāragocara*).
According to the opponent's view, this is because only that which is ultimately real falls within the scope of conventional discourse.
Alternatively, the probandum (*sādhya*) may be defined as the absence of difference that is not sublated by any knowledge other than the realization of Brahman.
Nor should it be argued that such an inference is impossible because it contradicts perception.

The claim that [entities] do not differ from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) contradicts the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as has already been demonstrated. Furthermore, one cannot argue that the absence of a favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) [is the reason for non-difference], nor can it be said that parsimony (*lāghava*) alone constitutes such favorable reasoning when unity is asserted; for parsimony is itself sublated by the aforementioned means of valid cognition. Otherwise, due to the extreme parsimony [of assuming only one entity], you would have to accept the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*).

Furthermore, there is the burden of complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating that the entire world of reality (*prapañca*), including ether and so forth—which is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is an utterly untenable construction of ignorance (*avidyā*).

Regarding the phrase "being the locus of its experience" (*tadbhogāyatanatva*): the meaning is that there is a contradiction (*bādha*) when one attempts to prove that [the body] is the delimiting factor for the experience of the consciousness delimited by Devadatta’s body. The underlying intention is that otherwise, Devadatta would have the retrospective awareness (*anusandhāna*) such as "this is mine" with respect to the pleasure and so forth belonging to Yajñadatta’s body. Regarding the term "contradiction" (*bādha*): the meaning is that because the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished (*aprasiddhi*), the existence of the probandum in the subject (*pakṣa*) cannot be maintained.

Now, since the property of being the delimiting locus of experience (*bhogāvacchedakatva*)—qualified by the absence of an ultimately real difference having Devadatta as its counter-correlative—is a constituent of the probandum (*sādhya*), this is not a case of sublation (*bādha*).
This is because it is possible for Yajñadatta and others to possess such an absence of difference [from Devadatta].

Alternatively, let the probandum be simply the property of being a delimiting locus of experience, conditioned by the state of not being a delimiting locus of experiences belonging to those distinct from Devadatta.

If it is argued that the status of Devadatta as an enjoyer will be established by implication, even so, the sublation of the aforementioned means of valid cognition— such as perception— which apprehend the ultimate difference between Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and others, remains unavoidable.
Nor can those cognitions be considered invalid,
for there is no subverting evidence against their validity.
"Because no stronger opposing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is perceived.
In this context, one should also observe such [proposed] extraneous conditions (*upādhi*) as "being produced by the karma of Devadatta," and so forth.

Here, in order to refute the solution offered by the opponent regarding the previously mentioned fault, he says: "In deep sleep, in a swoon," etc. This has been explained below. Regarding the words "by you," etc.: the sense is that, in that case, there would once again be a sublation (*bādha*).

Now, although the status of being the locus of Devadatta’s experience (*bhogāyatanatva*) does not exist from an ultimate standpoint (*pāramārthika*), it is accepted as existing conventionally (*vyāvahārika*). Therefore, since the probandum (*sādhya*) is the state of not being a locus for the absence of that [status] in its conventional form, there is no room for the fault of sublation (*bādha*).
Nor is there a lack of proof regarding "conventionality" for the opponent;

for the probandum is simply the state of not being a locus for that absence of the status of being the locus of experience which is itself non-sublated by any cognition possessing a mode (*saprakāraka-jñāna*).

If it is argued that this is because, according to the opponent's own view, "non-sublation by a determinate cognition" is established only in the case of the ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), we say no;
for by the criterion of non-sublation by a determinate cognition, the very absence of being a locus of experience (*bhogāyatanatva*) is unestablished.
This is because those who do not accept absences qualified by extrinsic properties (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*) do not admit the existence of particular absences in a general form.

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because what is intended is the absence of being a locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*) qualified by the state of not being sublated by a cognition possessing its own mode (*saprakāraka-jñāna*). This is because, being more complex than the mere state of being a locus of experience, it cannot serve as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence.

By this, the following argument is also refuted: "If being a locus of experience is false, then the state of being a substratum (*adhikaraṇatva*) of its absolute absence is likewise false; therefore, the state of not being its substratum remains unimpeded, and thus there is no room for the aforementioned contradiction."

This is because the absence of being the locus of that [reality] by way of being empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and so forth is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). If, however, the mere absence of being the locus of that were the probandum (*sādhya*), then the fallacy of proving something already established (*arthāntaratā*) would remain as before, since one could take the absence of that [reality] by way of being illusory (*prātibhāsika*) and so forth. This is the general direction of the argument. Regarding the "third": the meaning is that in the inference "difference is false because it possesses the nature of difference (*bhedatva*), like the difference between two moons," it is impossible to provide a faultless definition of falsity (*mithyātva*).
The sense is that the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is defective.

He states this very point with the words "na ca" (and not). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in the state of being sublatable (*bādhyatva*). [He says] "because falsity is impossible," which means because the negation of reality (*satyatva*) is impossible.
The sense is that, in my view, being the counter-positive of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa-pratiyogitva*) is pervaded by reality.
In this example, one should also understand that there is a deficiency regarding the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*).

Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because the intended meaning is "being the object of a cognition that is the counter-positive of a destruction produced by the knowledge of the true nature of the substratum" (*adhiṣṭhāna-yāthātmya-jñāna-janya-dhvaṃsa-pratiyogi-jñāna-viṣayatva*);
for that [intended meaning] ultimately amounts to "not being an object of error" (*bhrama-aviṣayatva-paryavasita*).

And likewise, since I accept that even an existent thing can be an object of error, the fault of *arthāntara* (proving something other than what was intended) remains as it was. "Because that is impossible" means because it is impossible for [the world] to be the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
The implication is that otherwise, it would follow that the world is absolutely non-existent.

Some, however, explain it thus: if one accepts that falsity (*mithyātva*) consists in being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence produced by the knowledge of the true nature of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), then there would be the contingency of impossibility, because you yourself accept the persistence of difference during the state of worldly activity (*vyavahāra-daśā*) in the case of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).

He raises an objection, suggesting that there is no fault because even a difference that exists conventionally (*vyavahārasat*) is admitted to be the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of absolute non-existence by virtue of its ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*). [The phrase] "pāramārthikatvena" [is explained as follows]: "tathātva" means being the counter-correlative of absolute non-existence; the remainder of the sentence is that this constitutes falsity (*mithyātva*). [The phrase] "abādhyatva" [is explained as follows].

The meaning is as follows: the knowledge that something is sublatable—consisting in its being the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence by virtue of its ultimate reality—is dependent upon the knowledge of its ultimate reality; and since that [knowledge of ultimate reality], which consists in the absence of such subtability, is itself dependent upon the knowledge of subtability, there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*).
This is merely an illustration;
it also serves to show that the probandum is lacking in the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Because, from the ultimate standpoint (*pāramārthika*), the non-existence of a distinction between moons is not established;
and because it is not accepted that what is non-existent can function as a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) by way of having the nature of existence.
Nor is falsity merely the state of being a counter-correlative of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
And it must be stated that this [difference] is established by both systems either as having the nature of existence or the nature of non-existence;

for even if difference exists, its being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of absolute non-existence is possible through its non-existence [in some locus], which would result in the fallacy of proving something other than what was intended (*arthāntara*).

"Disputed," and so forth. It should be understood that because he [the opponent] accepts a non-ultimate difference of individual selves from the Supreme Self, the proof of the absence of such [difference] does not constitute an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭavattva*) for him; furthermore, since he does not accept a non-ultimate difference in the Supreme Self having the Supreme Self as its counter-correlative, there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) regarding the example. "The second" means: "The bodies under dispute are the substrata of experience for Devadatta alone, because they are bodies, like Devadatta’s body. This is the meaning.

In this context, having formulated the following dilemma—whether by the word "Devadatta" one intends consciousness delimited by Devadatta’s body or consciousness not so delimited—the author refutes the first alternative, stating: "By the word 'Devadatta'... [and] "in being the locus of his experience. The meaning is that if the probandum is "being the means for the experience of consciousness delimited by Devadatta’s body," there is a contradiction (*bādha*), because that [status] is absent in the disputed bodies of Yajñadatta and others.

The meaning is that if one seeks to prove that the bodies of Yajñadatta and others are instruments for the experience of consciousness delimited by the body of Devadatta, there is a contradiction (*bādha*), because that [consciousness] is absent in those disputed bodies of Yajñadatta and others.

Regarding the question of why the body of Yajñadatta and others is not an instrument of experience for the consciousness delimited by Devadatta’s body, it is said: "of the bodies of Yajñadatta and others. For that which is an instrument of experience for one must be dependent upon that very [consciousness]; even though there is no difference in the essential nature [of consciousness], because the delimited [consciousnesses] are distinct, you yourself do not accept—since it is contradicted by perception—that the [bodies of others] are dependent on the consciousness delimited by Devadatta’s body. This is the sense. Furthermore, is the status of being an experiencer and so forth merely superimposed upon the Self as delimited by the body, just as [the quality of] agency is superimposed upon the ego?

The point is this: since you yourself accept that there is no superimposition of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) and so forth upon the undifferentiated Self because the proximity of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is simply absent there, your attempt to prove that the undifferentiated consciousness is a means of enjoyment (*bhoga-sādhana*) is contradicted by your own position. Regarding the phrase "of those too": the point is that there is no certainty of the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in those cases; therefore, there is no fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Regarding the word "contradiction" (*bādha*): the meaning is that because the probandum—in the form of being a means of enjoyment—is itself absent there, there is a partial contradiction (*aṃśe bādha*).

To avoid this slight defect, it was intended from the outset that "not being the locus of the absolute non-existence of being a locus of experience" (bhogāyatanatva) is what is meant by the term "being a locus of experience. Therefore, he says: "And not... ("na ca"). [The phrase] "by you" means: for you indeed accept that the state of being an experiencer (*bhoktṛtva*) existing in all bodies is illusory (*mithyā*).
And illusoriness consists in being co-located with its own absolute non-existence.
Thus, in the case of the body, both being a locus of experience and the absolute non-existence of that [locus-hood] must be accepted.

The sense is this: since there is an absence of the probandum—in the form of being a non-locus for the absolute non-existence of the locus of experience—there is a contradiction (*bādha*). "Of that locus" means "of the locus of the state of being a locus of experience. "Its absolute non-existence" means the absolute non-existence of the state of being a locus of experience. "In the third [case]" means that in the argument "Difference is false because it is a difference, like the difference in the moon," the definition of the probandum, namely falsity (*mithyātva*), is difficult to establish. "The substratum," etc., has been explained below.

What, then, is this falsity (*mithyātva*)? Is it the state of being removable (*nivartyatva*), which is the state of being the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of a cessation? In that regard, "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) means either destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) or absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). He refutes the first [option] by referring to the word "cessation": the sense is that what is false cannot undergo destruction.

He refutes the second [position] by restating it: "atyantābhāva... (regarding absolute non-existence). He establishes the contradiction itself: "tvayā... (by you). Even the Advaitin, who accepts the empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*) of the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), must admit that difference exists during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra-daśā*); otherwise, its status as merely empirical would be untenable. The sense is that it is logically impossible for something existing at the time of empirical transaction to be the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) whose negation occurs at another time, such as Caitra’s time.
Because that is untenable; because it is untenable for [difference] to be the counter-correlate of absolute non-existence.

We do not assert that difference is the counter-correlate of absolute non-existence in its own nature (*svarūpa*), by which it would not exist as such for a difference that is real at the time of linguistic usage;
rather, we assert it only in the form of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*).

Even for that which exists as a conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*), it is indeed possible for it to be the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*) of an absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) in its aspect of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*).

With the intention that just as a jar, though existing as dark in color, is the counter-positive of the absolute non-existence of redness, he raises an objection: "in the form of ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatvākāreṇa*). This means: by way of the property (*dharma*) consisting of ultimate reality.

With the intention that such a state is the counter-positiveness of absolute non-existence, he raises an objection: "in the form of ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatvākāreṇa*). This means: by way of the property (*dharma*) consisting of ultimate reality.

"Suchness" (*tathātva*) is the state of being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). Regarding the phrase "of that which has the nature of non-sublatability" (*abādhyatvarūpasya*): falsity (*mithyātva*) consists precisely in being the counter-correlate of absolute non-existence by way of having ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*).
Ultimate reality, moreover, is nothing other than non-sublatability; and that [non-sublatability] is the absence of sublatibility (*bādhyatvābhāva*).

And sublatedness (*bādhyatva*) is indeed falsity (*mithyātva*). Thus, the meaning is that there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*): the cognition of falsity is the cause for the cognition of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), which consists in non-sublatedness; and conversely, the cognition of ultimate reality is the cause for the cognition of sublatedness, which consists in falsity. Regarding the phrase "as being stated by you": the meaning is "as being currently defined by you. Regarding the expression "because of being perceived as difference" (*bhedatvena pratīyamānatvāt*): what is this "being perceived"? (What is this *pratīyamānatvam*?)

Is it the state of being an object of valid cognition (*pramā*) or the state of being an object of invalid cognition (*apramā*); or is it the state of being an object of that which is delimited by the generality of "cognition-ness" (*pratītitva-sāmānya*)? (Is it validity (*pramātva*), invalidity (*apramātva*), or rather the generality of "cognition-ness" itself?
Not the first, because it is unestablished for you.
Not the second [alternative],

because it is unestablished for me; nor the third, because even the perception of the distinction between moons is false and thus lacks authoritative status, and since there is no inclusive universal (*sāmānya*) common to both the authoritative and the non-authoritative, [the reason] remains unestablished.
Furthermore, there is inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding the difference between difference and non-difference;
if that [difference] were also made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*), there would be sublation (*bādha*).
If the difference between difference and non-difference were not ultimately real, then by this very inference, non-difference itself would also be false.

Even though empirical difference exists, if it were argued that difference—which is non-different from Brahman in the ultimate sense (or: which is different from Brahman in the ultimate sense)—must be ultimately real, just as the individual soul (*jīva*) is ultimately real despite being non-different from Brahman in the ultimate sense, then there would be a contradiction (*bādha*) in proving [the world's] falsity.
Furthermore, there would be an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the difference between the ultimately real Brahman and the ultimately unreal phenomenal world (*prapañca*).

If it is argued that Brahman possesses ultimate reality because there is no difference from it whose existence is equal to the existence of the substratum (*dharmin*), whereas such a difference exists in the case of a jar and the like—and thus the jar lacks ultimate reality—then [we reply]:

No. In that case, since there is no difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman whose existence is equal to the existence of the substratum, as there is none in the case of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), the two would lack ultimate reality while the phenomenal world would possess it.

Furthermore, since there is no non-difference from the phenomenal world whose existence is equal to the existence of the substratum in the case of Brahman, Brahman itself would lack ultimate reality just like the phenomenal world.

In the case of the distinction between the moon, appearance-ness (*prātibhāsikatva*) and being a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) [are the probanda]; however, these cannot be established in the subject (*pakṣa*),
because that would contradict the acceptance of its conventional reality (*vyāvahārikatva*).
Furthermore, there is a similarity to fallacious arguments (ābhāsa), such as: "Non-difference is false because it is a non-difference, like the non-difference between the body and the self.
Nor should one suspect that the illustrative example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavaikalya);

for if that were the case, the statement in the *Adhyāsa-bhāṣya*—"having superposed upon each other the nature of each and the attributes of each"—would result in the charge of being the ravings of a madman.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence that cognitions such as "I am fair" or "I am thin" would possess validity as revealers of reality (*tattvāvedaka-prāmāṇya*).

In the fourth [alternative], however, since various distinct entities themselves—like an army or a forest—are denoted by the word "world" (*jagat*) through the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is a contradiction (*bādha*) in attempting to prove the non-difference of jars and other objects from that [world], because no separate entity exists apart from them.

Moreover, if earth and the other elements were the originators (*ārambhaka*) of the entity called the "world," then the properties of earthness and so forth would necessarily result in being mixed (*sāṅkarya*) within the world produced by them.
Furthermore, if qualities and so forth—which are included within the world—were the initiators of that [world], they would themselves incur the status of being substances (*dravyatva*).
Moreover, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that partless [entities such as] qualities could initiate substances.
Consequently, there would be a loss of the absolute partlessness of jars and other such things.

If, however, only objects such as jars and the like are taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), then when one intends to prove the absence of difference from itself—by the term "its own internal difference" (i.e., proving the absence of difference whose counter-correlate is itself)—there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

But if one intends to prove merely the absence of mutual difference (i.e., proving the mere absence of difference), then the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the probandum (*sādhyavikala*). As for the proof of the difference of space (*ākāśa*), it should be consulted as it has been treated by us elsewhere.
(However, the proof for the differentiation of space has been established by us elsewhere; it is not elaborated here for fear of excessive length.
Therefore, inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the non-difference of the self.

In order to avoid the charge of the reason (*hetu*) "because of being a difference" (*bhedatvāt*) being unestablished (*asiddhi*), it was stated that the intended meaning is "because of being perceived as a difference" (*bhedatvena pratīyamānatvāt*). To refute this, he analyzes the alternatives: "as a difference" (*bhedatvena*). [The question is: Is that cognition of the nature of valid knowledge (*pramā*), or of the nature of error (*bhrānti*), or is it a mere general cognition (*pratītisāmānya*)? This is the sense. "In your case, it is unestablished" (*tavāsiddheḥ*): the sense is that you do not accept that the cognition of difference is valid knowledge.
"In my case, it is unestablished" (*mamāsiddheḥ*): the sense is that I do accept its status as valid knowledge.

He demonstrates the lack of proof (*asiddhi*) even in the third position, stating: "Not the third. Just as it was said that the reason (*hetu*) is unproven because the difference between moons is illusory (*prātibhāsika*) and thus lacks authoritative status (*aprāmāṇika*), and because there is no common universal (*sāmānya*) of "difference" (*bhedatva*) that could subsume both the authoritative and the non-authoritative, so too the reason "being perceived" (*pratīyamānatva*) is unproven; for the cognition of the difference between moons is also illusory and lacks authoritative status, and thus there is no universal common to both. The meaning is that, due to the absence of such a universal, the reason is unestablished. In some places, the reading is *pratyakṣapratīteḥ*.
The meaning is: because at that time there is the perceptual cognition of the distinction between the moon and its illusory form.
Furthermore, let other matters rest for now; however, one must state that the distinction between difference and non-difference is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).

And thus, he states that the reason [adduced] therein is inconclusive (*anaikāntya*)—namely, "difference and non-difference. To the question, "Since that too is accepted as being part of the subject (*pakṣa*), how can it be inconclusive? he replies: "Of that too..."
The meaning is that there is sublation (*bādha*) in a partial aspect (*aṃśe*).

If, between difference and non-difference, difference were ultimately real (*pāramārthikatva*), there would either be an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) [of the reason] or sublation in a partial aspect. But this is not the case; rather, it is precisely non-ultimately real. Therefore, he says: "Of difference and non-difference" (*bhedābhedayoḥ*). The sense is as follows: if the difference between those two is non-ultimately real, then by the consequence that non-difference alone must be ultimately real, even difference—which is non-distinct from non-ultimately real difference—would itself be of the nature of difference. Consequently, its falsity (*mithyātva*) would follow by the very inference: "Difference is false because it is difference. Thus, the point is established.

Thus, it has been stated that if difference (*bheda*) between identity and difference is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), then because of the resulting non-difference between them, the non-difference that is non-distinct from difference would be false.

Now, with the thought that by that same logic, if one must also accept that difference is non-distinct from non-difference, then since difference—which is non-distinct from an ultimately real non-difference—would itself be established as ultimately real, there would be a contradiction in attempting to prove the falsity of difference, [the author] says: "vyāvahārika... and so forth.
[Objection: But surely, even if difference is non-distinct from an ultimately real non-difference, it does not follow that the difference is itself ultimately real.

Because the conventional difference between the two is also admitted, it is stated: "even though there is the existence of a conventional difference. Thus, while ultimate non-difference exists, the conventional difference is of no consequence.

Otherwise, even for the individual soul (*jīva*), which is ultimately non-different from Brahman, its lack of ultimate reality would follow merely by virtue of the existence of a conventional difference; this is the intended meaning.

He states another refutation of the reason "because of difference" (bhedatva): "pāramārthika... [and so on]. First of all, the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world (prapañca) must be admitted as being indeed ultimately real (pāramārthika). This is because, in your view, while Brahman is ultimately real, the phenomenal world is not.
Furthermore, since difference is necessarily established between two substrata possessing contradictory attributes, just as in the case of water and fire.

And thus, the meaning is that there would be a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) if there were a difference between those two. Regarding the phrase "or sublation" (*bādho vā*): the intention is that even that [difference] would be accepted as the subject (*pakṣa*), just as before.
In some places, the reading "or sublation" does not exist at all; for this very reason, this sentence has not been commented upon by certain [scholars].
Now, one might object: even if Brahman and the phenomenal world (prapañca) are respectively ultimate and non-ultimate, why should their difference be ultimate?

Nor should it be argued that if the difference between them were non-ultimate, it would follow that Brahman—like the phenomenal world—is non-ultimate, or that the phenomenal world—like Brahman—is ultimate.

Even though difference (*bheda*) is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), it is possible to accept that both Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) possess ultimate reality and non-ultimate reality respectively; for in that case, the non-ultimate reality of difference is not the determining factor (*aprayojaka*), since other causal factors are present. With this intention, he raises an objection with the words "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*). Although there is indeed a difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world, nevertheless, that difference does not have the same ontological status as its substratum (*dharmisamasattāka*);
that is to say, it is not ultimately real.

In the case of the phenomenal world, such as a jar and so forth, however, the difference having Brahman as its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) possesses the same degree of reality as its locus (dharmisamasattāka);
that is to say, it is of a conventional nature (vyāvahārika).
Therefore, the point is that even though the difference between those two is not ultimately real, there is no impairment to its ultimate reality [as a conventional distinction].
He refutes this with "No. Regarding "then":

the meaning is that if, even without a restrictive means of valid cognition (*niyāmaka-pramāṇa*), one were to accept that while the absence of difference possessing the existence of the locus (*dharmi-sattāka-bheda-abhāva*) is non-ultimate, the presence of that [difference] is the determinant of its being ultimate, then [the following would follow]. Regarding "of the individual soul and Brahman": [this refers to the consequence].

The meaning is as follows: since it would be easy to establish a rule that "that in which there is a difference possessing the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as the substratum (*dharmin*) has ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), while that in which such a difference does not exist lacks ultimate reality," then the opposite consequence would also follow—namely, that because the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman does not exist [in that sense], they would lack ultimate reality, whereas because the difference of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) does exist, it would possess ultimate reality. Even so, your position would result in Brahman being non-ultimately real just like the phenomenal world; this is the intended refutation. Regarding the phrase "the difference of the moon": the construction of the sentence is as follows.
In this inference, "phenomenality" (*prātibhāsikatva*) is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). How so? Because in the corroborative instance—the difference between two moons—phenomenality exists.

Therefore, it pervades the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*). Furthermore, that *upādhi* cannot be established in the subject (*pakṣa*), which is the object of dispute, because that would contradict the acceptance of its being merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*).

Therefore, [the reason] does not pervade the probans (*sādhanāvyāpaka*). Why should one not suspect a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*)? To this he says: "In that case" (*tathātve*). The meaning is that if the reality of the distinction between the body and the self were admitted, there would be a contradiction with your own accepted position—just like the ravings of a madman—in your own commentary which describes the mutual superimposition (*adhyasta*) of the nature of one upon the other between the body and the self.

He states another objection: "I am fair-complexioned" (*gauro 'ham iti*). The meaning is that if there were no difference between the body and the self, then qualities such as fairness—which are actually attributes of the body—would [erroneously] become attributes of the self. Consequently, the cognition of such [qualities] would result in being a cognition whose object is reality (*tattva-viṣayakatā*), which would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it is a valid cognition (*pramā*).

The phrase "by way of revealing reality" (*tattvāvedakatvena*) means "having reality as its object" (*tattva-viṣayakatā*). Nor should it be argued that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

The point is that [if one were to interpret the text otherwise], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the Bhāṣya statement "having superimposed the attributes of each upon the other" would be the speech of a madman.

For this very reason, the phrase "having superimposed the attributes of each upon the other" from the preceding sentence is also cited as an example. Regarding the phrase "But in the fourth": the meaning is that it refers to the inference: "The object under dispute, namely the world, is in reality devoid of internal differentiation, because it is an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), like the sky.

In that context, "being devoid of internal differentiation in reality" means the absence of ultimate difference either among the objects contained within the world—such as pots and so forth—or between those objects (pots, etc. and the world itself.
For it has been established in that very manner in the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) section;
therein, in the proof of the non-difference of jars and so forth [from Brahman],
and in the proof of the absence of difference having the entire world as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

The meaning is that there is either a proof of the non-existence of difference between that world and things such as jars, or else there is sublation (*bādha*). To the question "Why is there sublation?", it is said: "Because of the absence of any other category of entity" (*padārthāntarābhāvena*). This means: because of the absence of any other category of entity called "world" distinct from jars and the like.

For when another category of entity exists, it is possible to prove either the difference of some entity from that [other] or the absence of difference; but this is not possible when that very [other entity] is absent.
For the absence of difference between a rabbit’s horn and things such as a jar cannot be established [as a valid example].

Therefore, since there is no manifestation of a world distinct [from Brahman], it is logical that there would be a sublation (*bādha*) in attempting to prove the absence of difference from that [Brahman]; this is the meaning.

As for the question "Why even in the absence of other categories?"—it is said: "Because various categories are denoted by the word 'world' (*jagat*). The particle *hi* has the sense of *eva* (indeed/certainly).

To the question "How is that so?", it is said: "by means of a distinction of limiting adjuncts" (*upādhibhedena*). This means by means of a specific limiting adjunct characterized as time. In this regard, an illustration is given: "like an army, a forest, and so forth. Just as it is precisely elephants, horses, chariots, and the like that are denoted by the word "army" through the limiting adjunct of their being situated in one place; and just as various trees are denoted by the word "forest" by virtue of dwelling in one location; or just as grains and the like, when gathered in one place, are denoted by the word "heap"—in the same way, it is precisely pots and other things, when subsumed under the intended limiting adjunct of a single time, that are denoted by the word "world" (*jagat*). This is the meaning.
Therefore it is said in the *Mandāramañjarī*:
"Those that flow together are called a 'stream' (*pravāha*);
like a forest consisting of various trees, they are swallowed by time as its limiting condition (*upādhi*). This is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

It should also be observed that even if one were to attempt to prove the absence of mutual difference among jars and other such things, there would still be a sublation [of that proof] due to contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge.

Now, an objection is raised: "The word 'world' (jagat) does not refer to jars and the like alone; rather, just as a cloth is produced from threads, the entity called 'world' is produced from entities such as jars—which are themselves composed of parts—just as a cloth is produced from threads. Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. To this, he replies: "Of earth and the rest," etc. Regarding the phrase "the consequence of the confusion of universals" (jātisaṅkaryaprasaṅga): since a composite whole (avayavin) produced from earth and so forth is necessarily characterized by the universal 'earth-ness' (pṛthivītva) and so on, it follows that in a world produced from all categories such as earth and the rest, there would be a confusion of universals. This is the meaning.
This too has been stated according to the view of the Nyāya school;
for in our own established doctrine (siddhānta), even in a substance composed of multiple heterogeneous elements, there is no confusion of universals (jāti-sāṅkarya).
Indeed, even earth and the other elements are not produced from mere earth and the rest alone.
However, even each individual element is indeed composed of all three elements;
for thus says the Śruti:
"He made each one of them threefold. Yet, empirical usage proceeds from the predominance of the respective portions of those elements.

And it is said in the Sūtras: "But because of its predominance, there is that designation; and because of its threefold nature, there is that designation due to its abundance. Furthermore, it has been established that the mixing [of elements] does not constitute a sublation of the genus. As for the phrase "the consequence of being a substance," the meaning is that only a substance can be an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).
This too is based solely on the standpoint of the Nyāya system;

for in the Siddhānta (the established doctrine), it is accepted that the material cause possesses qualities and that the effect is a transformation of that which possesses qualities. As for the phrase "of partless things," this too is according to the method of Nyāya alone;
for in the Siddhānta, there is no such thing as a substance devoid of parts.
As it has been said:

"Therefore, parts of all things always exist, because they are connected even in all directions. And as for the [charge of] over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): the meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence of even partless qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), universals (*jāti*), and so forth, initiating substances (*dravya*). And as for the loss of the status of being a final whole (*antyāvayavitva*): the point is that only a causal substance that does not initiate another substance is considered a final whole.
[Objection: "But surely one does not infer in this manner by taking the world—either as a collection consisting of pots and so forth, or as that which is produced from them—as the subject (*pakṣa*).
Rather, taking only the pots and so forth as the subject, one proves the absence of internal differentiation within them.

Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. To this, he says: "pots and so forth" (*ghaṭādi*) [and] "by the word 'internal differentiation' (*svāntarbheda*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "by means of the word following 'devoid of' (*hīna*)."

Alternatively, it should be explained as follows: by the phrase "difference internal to itself" (*svāntarbhedāśabdena*), one takes a difference whose counter-correlative is itself, and thus establishes the absence of that [internal difference]. Regarding the phrase "establishing the mere absence of difference": by the word "internal to itself" (*svāntaḥ*), the state of having itself as the counter-correlative is not intended;

rather, it is precisely the state of having each other as counter-correlatives. Thus, the sense is: how could there be the fallacy of proving what is already established? Regarding the phrase "the example lacks the probandum": the sense is that in space (*ākāśa*), there exists only mutual difference among its parts.

"Is it not the case that this very charge of the probandum being deficient (*sādhyavaikalya*) was already anticipated and refuted earlier? To this he says: "But as for the proof of the division of space... This means: "But as for the proof of the division of parts within space.
[This was discussed] elsewhere, in the *Mandāramañjarī*.

The meaning is that one should look to the proof of the division of space (*ākāśabheda*) which was presented during the occasion of explaining the *Ṭīkā* passage beginning with "But even so, let there be co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between conjunction and its absolute non-existence by the force of cognition," and ending with "Therefore, it has been well said [that this is] against the proponent of the division of space.
One must not, however, be deluded into thinking that the mutual division of the parts of space is accepted in the final system (*siddhānta*) merely on that account.

When the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that there is no division in space (*ākāśa*), then the word "end" (*anta*) signifies a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). This is because it was stated during the occasion of explaining the root text in the *Upādhikhaṇḍanaṭīkā*: "Even in the ether (*khe*), there is that [distinction] of another location. Furthermore, since the Mandāramañjarī introduces the sentence beginning with "When" (*yadā*) precisely for this reason—that in the established doctrine, because the parts of space (which are specific locations) exist as long as the substance itself, absolute non-difference is accepted, and thus the use of the word "end," which denotes division, would otherwise be untenable—it says: "When... (*yadā*).

It should be understood that the statement, "The proof for the differentiation of space has been provided by us elsewhere," was made with the intention that if someone were to challenge a Naiyāyika—who accepts a difference in space as being merely conditional (*aupādhika*)—by asserting instead a natural (*svābhāvika*) division of parts, the Naiyāyika would have no answer at all.
For this very reason, in that same *Mandāramañjarī*, the opponent is made to accept a conditional difference.

He says this because he intends to make [the opponent] accept an intrinsic difference with respect to that [space]; thus, this very same statement is introduced by way of another method. Some, however, say the meaning is that the proof for the intrinsic difference of the parts of space has been established elsewhere, such as in the *Nyāyāmṛta*.
He concludes the refutation of the inference stated by the opponent with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*); the meaning is: "because it is flawed according to the manner already demonstrated.
The phrase "non-difference of the Self" (*ātmābheda*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The phrase "non-difference of non-self" (*anātmabheda*) should also be understood here.
However, only the non-difference of the self (*ātmābheda*) is mentioned because of its predominance;

otherwise, since the fourth inference would merely exclude the difference of non-self, there would be no means of establishing the non-difference of the self, and thus it would be impossible to conclude by refuting the inference of the non-difference of the self in a general sense.

However, some say that because the term "disputed" (*vimata*) there refers to everything belonging to the class of sentient and insentient beings, the conclusion—that there is no inference for the non-difference of the Self—is valid.

In that case, since it would be unavoidable that the reason of "being perceptible" (*dṛśyatva*) is unestablished in part (*bhāgāsiddhi*) with respect to the sentient being if it were included by the word "disputed," one must consider how the opponent could possibly have intended such a meaning.

Regarding what was stated—that "diversity" (bhedatva) is made the reason because it is perceived as diversity—he refutes that by means of an alternative analysis, stating: "because even the cognition [of it] is false. This means that, according to the opponent, in a case of superimposition, both the cognition and its object are admitted to be merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*). [He further states: "due to the absence of a pervasive universal (*anugatasāmānya*). The underlying intention is as follows:

Regarding the phrase "because of being a difference" (*bhedatvāt*): when there is a suspicion of unestablished reason (*asiddhi*) due to the absence of a common universal (*sāmānya*) that pervades both the false and the true, [the author] states that for the sake of their pervasion—even though "difference" itself does not possess a further pervasive nature—the quality of being a difference (*bhedatva*) consists in being perceived as a difference, because the two cognitions of those [two things] share the commonality of being cognitions of difference. However, this is possible only according to the view that even when an object is false in the case of an error, the cognition is true, and not according to the ultimate reality (*tattvataḥ*). Regarding the phrase "if that too were made the subject" (*tasyāpi pakṣatve*): the meaning is that if the difference between difference and non-difference were also made the subject, there would be a contradiction (*bādha*) due to self-refutation (*vyāghāta*).

He states the objection to the position that the avoidance of contradiction is achieved through a distinction between the conventional (*vyāvahārika*) level: "If [it is argued that] there is no contradiction by means of a conventional distinction... [the text says] "The non-difference (*abheda*) would also be false. The sense is this: since difference and non-difference would, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), result in identity, the very proof for the falsity of difference becomes a proof for the falsity of non-difference. Furthermore, if non-difference were thus not ultimately real, then there would be a sublation (*bādha*) when proving the falsity of all differences;
for there is the pervasion (*vyāpti*): whatever has the same existence as something else is non-different from it.

Alternatively, it should be understood that the intended inference here is: "Difference is real, because it is distinct from real non-difference; for whatever is distinct from something whose existence is real is itself real; likewise, the individual soul (jīva) is distinct from Brahman. Regarding the term "inconstancy" (vyabhicāra): the sense is that if the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world (prapañca) were not ultimately real, then the distinction between them—consisting of their respective statuses as ultimate reality and empirical reality—would be untenable. Regarding the phrase "there is no sublation" (bādho na): the ellipsis is "of that [difference] too being the subject of the proposition" (pakṣatva). This is because even though Brahman is ultimately real, the difference having the phenomenal world as its counter-correlate (pratiyogika) does not possess that same status.

He raises the objection that there is no deviation [from the rule]—namely, "of Brahman. [The meaning is: the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) would be ultimately real. This is because, since there is no difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman that possesses the same level of existence as the existence of the substratum (*dharmin*) relative to the phenomenal world, [the soul] would likewise be false, just like the phenomenal world itself. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:

"Brahman must be false because it is devoid of ultimate difference in relation to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), just like the phenomenal world. Regarding "the difference in the moon": the meaning is that it is the falsity existing in the difference of the moon that is the causal factor (*prayojaka*), not the state of being a difference (*bhedatva*).

Now, one might object: "I shall establish the presence of the *upādhi* in the subject (*pakṣa*) by means of the very reason already stated. To this he says: "And that... Nor should it be argued that there is an absence of pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatā*) in the case of a jar or similar objects;
for that would result in the pervasion of the probandum as delimited by the probans in the form of "the state of being a difference" (*bhedatvarūpa-sādhanāvacchinna-sādhyavyāpakatā*).

There is no fault, because that which possesses empirical difference (*vyāvahārikabheda*) is the subject (*pakṣa*). One should not suspect a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*); the point is that the opponent is an advocate of universal non-duality (*sarvādvaitavādin*). Regarding the term "insane": the point is that if [the identity] were unreal, it would be impossible to speak of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), such as attributing the nature of one thing to another.

Now, if it is argued that while the mention of superimposition in the *Bhāṣya* refers only to the empirical level, ultimate unity (*pāramārthikaikya*) is indeed accepted [by us], then in that case, it is precisely that superimposed unity which has been made the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*); so how can there be a deficiency in the probandum?

[Objection: Even so, there is still the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the ultimate identity between the body and the self (*dehātman*). [Response: No, because that too is included within the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*).
[Objection: Nevertheless, there is a fallacy of deviation in the case of the self’s identity with its own counter-correlative (*svapratiyogikaikya*). [Response: No.
Because the reason is precisely the unity of difference and co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Nor is there a lack of proof regarding the qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*), because that very non-difference which exists in a case where the opponent, having accepted non-difference, accepts a conventional difference (*vyāvahārikabheda*), is what is made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛta*).

Furthermore, it should be inferred that there is a parity of fallacious arguments (*ābhāsa-sāmya*): "Difference is ultimately real because it is a difference, like the difference in the [reflected] moon," and "Brahman is unreal because it is an entity, like the difference in the [reflected] moon. Regarding the phrase "I am fair" (*gauro 'ham*): the meaning is that this is a perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the identity between the body and the self.
Now, one might object: "This perception apprehends the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) identity between the body and the self."
If it is argued that [the cognition] is therefore erroneous, we ask:
does this mean that it perceives a unity that is merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*)?
Or does it mean that it perceives a unity which itself is conventional?
Not the first,
because that [object] does not exist.
In the second case, it would be a valid cognition (*pramā*) with respect to the aspect of identity.

Nor can this be accepted as a desired conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it contradicts the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of mutual identity. "In the fourth" means: in the context of the statement, "The subject of dispute (*vimata*) is devoid of real internal difference.
Here, by the term "subject of dispute," the entity known as the world (*jagat*) is made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*).

In this regard, [the author] refutes the two alternatives—whether that which is said to be "pervading" (anugata) is something distinct from the pot and so forth, or whether it is the pot and so forth themselves—by means of the following sequence:

Just as various dissimilar things such as elephants and horses are called "one place" by virtue of the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being in the same location, or by the limiting condition of being subordinate to a single king, yet there is no part distinct from the elephants and so forth [that constitutes this "oneness"]; so too here.
Likewise, the world is spoken of as "the jar and so forth" by means of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of being mounted upon a single cognition;
thus, since there is no world distinct [from the cognition], there is a sublation (*bādha*) in the proof of non-difference—this is the meaning.
The sense is that for each individual jar and so forth, plurality is impossible.

To the objection that the world might be like a cloth begun by threads, he says: "Of earth and so forth. The meaning is that there would be a confusion of categories (*sāṅkarya*), because earth-ness cannot exist in water without water-ness, and water-ness cannot exist in earth without earth-ness; yet both must necessarily exist in the effect (the world) as well as in their cause, according to the principle that the genus residing in the cause must also reside in the effect. Furthermore, there would be the consequence of [the world] being a substance (*dravya*); this should be understood because the very definition of the category of substance is "being an inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇatva*). And regarding "the state of being a producer of a substance": [this refers to the impossibility of the world being a substance].
The meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence of contradicting the established doctrine if a partless, great substance were to act as the originator of other substances.
Furthermore, do objects such as jars originate the world individually or collectively?
It cannot be the first case.
Because there is a rule that a single [entity] cannot be a non-producer [of multiple effects],
and because it would contradict the cognition of [the universal] as following through many [individuals].
Not the second [alternative].
Because it is impossible for past and future things to coalesce in the production of the world;
furthermore, if the world were something that has a beginning, it would contradict the scriptural statement that "this world is without beginning or end.
If it is argued that although jars and the like are part of the world, they do not contradict its beginninglessness, we say no.
Because the world consists of the continuous flow of jars and other such things;
and because, even at a time when jars and the like are absent, the property of being the world is fully present in space and so forth.
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "of objects such as jars. The meaning is that the word *sva* (self) within the compound *svapratiyogika* appropriately refers to those very objects.
Or let there be only one entity that constitutes the world.
[If you argue that] because there exist distinctions between parts of space within space, the probandum is lacking [in the example], he asks:
"How can there be a distinction of parts therein? and replies: "But the proof for the distinction of space," etc. This is found elsewhere, in the *Mandāramañjarī*.
For instance: space possesses inherent internal divisions, because it is simultaneously in conjunction with multiple corporeal forms.
Nor is there any deviation [from the rule] in the case of time and so forth.
Because they are equal as subjects (*pakṣa*).
Nor is the reason (*hetu*) inconclusive;
for there exists a subverting argument (*bādhaka*), namely: "If there were no distinction between spaces, then there would be co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with material objects."
Nor can the lack of contradiction be maintained on the grounds of difference due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),
because those very adjuncts would themselves entail a contradiction with co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Otherwise, even for objects such as jars, there would arise an internal differentiation of parts based on the adjunct consisting in their being the counter-correlates of conjunction with them.
It is not inherent.

Furthermore, the cognition that "I have come from another country" and "I am going to another country," as well as the cognitions "the bird is here" and "the bird is not here," serve as proof for its distinctness.
Nor does this [cognition] have as its object a distinction based on light and so forth;
for even in darkness, one perceives through touch and other means that "the pillar is here" or "the pillar is not here.
Furthermore, there is a perception of identity of locus in the form: "wherever the vulture is, there [is the pillar], even at night."
Furthermore, since light and moonlight cannot be objects of perception in relation to each other as distinct entities, that [proposed definition] is impossible.

Moreover, the cognition "where there is light, there is darkness" does not tolerate light being the locus [of darkness]. Nor should it be asserted that all cognitions have only adventitious (aupādhika) objects.

In cases such as "a bird is here" and "a bird is not here," no limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is observed; nor can there be a single substratum for both the body of a bird and its absence, because that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
If it is argued that [the ether] is merely an indicator (*upalakṣaka*),

then in the absence of even one part of its inherent nature, the entire ether would become connected with the pot; consequently, every single instance of "pot-ether" (*ghaṭākāśa*) would be identical [to the ether].
Regarding what was said here—"What is the meaning of the statement that there is 'pot-space'?"—the answer is this:
it is simply this very region that is the pot-space and nothing else.

However, the distinction that is perceived—that "this is the great space"—would not exist [if they were identical]. Furthermore, as for what was stated: even though the adjunct (*upādhi*) is related to space just like the object to be reflected (*upādeya*), because the adjunct favors the reflection, its own dimensions and so forth color only the pot-space that has become the reflection.
"It is not the great space (mahākāśa). But that is merely a playful fabrication of a conceptual framework;
for there is no relationship of original and reflection between the space within a jar and the great space.
This is because one does not perceive the arising of a different space in the way one perceives, "Previously there was only one face; now another face has arisen."
However, the perception is that this single eastern region has now become two separate parts; yet,
if it is argued that the division is not intrinsic because it follows the rule of contingent conditions (*upādhi*), we say no,
for those with subtle intellects perceive the division even in the absence of such conditions.

For those of deluded intellect, however, it is possible [to mistake the one for the many], just as one who has fallen into the middle of the ocean fails to perceive the further shore and, due to the mutual similarity of the waters and their specific cohesion, remains unaware of the distinction between different portions of water.
Furthermore, why this aversion toward natural difference?
If it is argued that "if there were parts, there would be impermanence," we say no.

Because, when "substantiality" (dravyatva) is the probandum (sādhya), the presence of a contradictory [property] in the case of "producedness" (kṛtakatva) consists precisely in the sublation (bādhitatva) of "intermediate dimension";
furthermore, even if [the entity] possesses parts, it is not admitted that it has "possessing parts" (sāvayavatva) in the sense of having a material cause (sopādānatva). Enough of this elaboration.
As for what was said—that conjunction (saṃyoga) is co-located with its own absolute non-existence (svātyantābhāva)—[that too is untenable].
That is not so, because of contradiction.
If it is argued that this is accepted on the strength of uncontradicted perception— namely, "the tree is in contact with the monkey at its top, but not at its root"— we say no.
This is because only a difference in loci is perceived in the expressions "at the top" (*agre*) and "at the root" (*mūle*).

Nor should it be argued that in both cases—namely, "the tree is conjoined" and "the tree is not [conjoined]"—it is the tree itself that appears as the substantive (*viśeṣya*), and therefore the tree alone is the locus, while the top and the root are not. For if that were the case, the use of the locative case in "at the top" (*agre*) and "at the root" (*mūle*) would be untenable.
Furthermore, it would follow that the cognition of conjunction and its absence could occur even without the prior apprehension of the "top" and the "root";
moreover, this contradicts the experienced fact that the top and the root themselves are perceived as loci.

Finally, in such cases as "the tree has conjunction with the monkey at its top," the possessive suffix *matup* has as its object the general relation of being connected to conjunction and its absence, and thus does not have "locus-ness" (*adhikaraṇatā*) as its specific object.
Therefore, this cognition does not have the tree as its locus for the presence and absence of conjunction; rather, it is the roots and the tip alone that possess the status of being the locus.

The tree, however, possesses such roots and tips; thus, by way of a mediated relation (*paramparā*), it is precisely the tree’s connection with the presence and absence of conjunction that constitutes the object of the cognition.

Otherwise, based on the cognition "there is no monkey at the base [of the tree] though there is one at the top," even the monkey would possess the property of being co-locatable with its own absolute non-existence.
If it is argued that "being co-locatable with its own absolute non-existence" means simply "inherence in the locus of that [non-existence]," we say no;
for this would result in the absolute non-existence of conjunction itself possessing that same property.
Therefore, it is quite easy to state that for things such as a monkey, there is co-existence with their own absolute non-existence through their respective appropriate relations.

If it is argued that since the conjunction with the monkey itself possesses that property (of being co-existent with its own absolute non-existence), it is sufficient to explain the case thus, and that postulating the same for the monkey itself would be cumbersome; [we reply: then, since the inherence of the conjunction itself possesses that property, it is sufficient to explain the case thus, and the conjunction need not be so postulated.
Furthermore, by the cognition "the tree is the locus of inherence at the top, but not at the root," inherence itself would also be co-existent with its own absolute non-existence.

Moreover, even if [the existence of space] were established in the case of trees and the like through a distinction of parts, it would remain unestablished in the case of the distinction of space itself, since that [existence of parts] is not admitted; so, enough of this.
"Knowability" (*prameyatva*) is the state of being an object of valid cognition (*pramā*);
"unknowability" (*aprameyatva*) is the state of not being an object of valid cognition.
"Being a cognition" (*pratītitva*) means being the object of a cognition (*pratītiviṣayatva*).

In some places, however, the reading is "being cognized" (*pratīyamānatva*), "validity" (*pramātva*), "cognition-ness" (*pratītitva*), or "generality" (*sāmānya*); in those cases, the meaning is that "cognition-ness" is the constituent factor of "being cognized. [The phrase] "even of perceptual cognition" (*pratyakṣapratīter api*)...

The meaning is that even the perception in the form of direct experience (*pratyakṣa*) of the distinction between the moon and its illusory appearance is, according to your own view, merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*); therefore, a common universal (*sāmānya*) applicable to both [the real and the apparent] is impossible. Regarding the phrase "difference and non-difference" (*bhedābheda*): the meaning is that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) because difference and non-difference lack falsity (*mithyātva*).

Now, one might object that since that [instance] is also included within the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no inconclusiveness; to this he says: "tasyāpi" (of that too). The ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) of difference and non-difference must necessarily be admitted.
The meaning is that even in that case, there would be a sublation (*bādha*) if falsity (*mithyātva*) were to be proven.
Why must ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) be admitted? To this he says: "Of difference and non-difference" (*bhedābhedayoḥ*). By this [he means] by the proof of difference and non-difference.

Now, if the difference between difference and non-difference were merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*), then by the very proof of the falsity of difference, the falsity of non-difference would also follow.
But it is not so; rather, it is conventional (*vyāvahārika*). For this very reason, there is no sublation (*bādha*) either.
Since even the conventional is false (*mithyātva*), he says: "even though there exists a conventional distinction."
The meaning is that there is no contradiction between a conventional difference—such as that between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—and ultimate non-difference;
however, if a difference were non-distinct from ultimate non-difference, its ultimacy would necessarily follow, which constitutes an insurmountable contradiction.
The terms "ultimate" and "non-ultimate" are qualifiers of both Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), intended to highlight the ultimacy of their respective differences.

Regarding its being the subject (*pakṣa*) as well, he says: "or there would be sublation" (*bādho vā*). If the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), then both would have to be either ultimately real or not ultimately real;

they could not be such that one is ultimately real while the other is not. Therefore, since its ultimate reality must be asserted, and since "falsity" (*mithyātva*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*) therein, there would be sublation—this is the meaning.

One might object: "Even if the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), the distinction between their respective ultimate and non-ultimate reality can still be established by another means. With this intention, he raises the following doubt: "Of Brahman... [and so forth]. Since there is no restrictive rule (*niyāmaka*) to establish that the difference and its absence must be non-ultimate or ultimate respectively when they possess the same degree of existence (*sattā*) as the substratum (*dharmin*), one might ask:

why could the relationship between the restricted and the restrictor (*niyamyaniyāmakabhāva*) not be the reverse? To this, he replies: "In that case... The implication is that, consequently, the reason does not suffer from the fallacy of being too broad (*sādhanavyāpakatā*).
The mention of "mutual properties" (*anyonyadharmān*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the connection with the preceding term, even though they are separated by intervening words.

In some places, the reading is simply *anyonyātmakamadhyastha*. The phrase "I am fair-complexioned" (*gauro 'ham*) is used because the cognition "I am fair-complexioned" would otherwise result in being invalid (*apramātva*), due to the absence of its object, were there not a false identity between the body and the self; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the "fourth" [reason]: the meaning is "in the [verse] beginning with 'the subject of dispute is devoid of real internal difference, because it is an object of thought'. Here, the universe (*jagat*) is the subject (*pakṣa*).

Furthermore, that [collection] is not a distinct substance produced from the pot and cloth, as is the case with a cloth and so forth; rather, it is subsumed under a specific limiting adjunct such as "knowability" (prameyatva) according to the analogy of an army, a forest, and the like.

If the probandum is the absence of real internal difference within the pot, cloth, and so forth themselves, there is a contradiction (bādha), because a real difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world has already been established. He will state later that if one were to prove non-difference regarding the world in the form of pots and so forth, it would result in the fallacy of proving what is already accepted (iṣṭāpatti).

[Objection: "But could it not be that the category called 'the world' is simply the earth and its substrates? To this he says: "Of the earth and so forth. The meaning is that since there is a restriction such that a whole (avayavin) composed of earth and so forth possesses the property of being earth (*pṛthivītva*) and so on, there would be a confusion (*sāṅkarya*) of the property of being earth and so forth within the world. And [there would be] the consequence of [the world] being a substance (*dravyatva*); the point is that the definition of a substance is "that which is an inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇa*). And [he says]: "Of pots and so forth," meaning [the world would have] the status of being a producer of substances.

The meaning is that an effect-substance which does not initiate further substance is the "ultimate whole" (*antyāvayavin*), because that is its defining characteristic. Regarding the phrase "the proof of the differentiation of space": it means that the proof for the inherent differentiation of the parts of space has been established elsewhere, such as in the *Nyāyamṛta* and other works.
And thus, the meaning is that even the probandum intended by the opponent is deficient in that regard.
Regarding the question "What is this 'being perceived' (*pratīyamānatva*)?": it means the nature of cognition (*pratītitva*) which constitutes the factor of being perceived.

In some places, the reading is simply "pratītatvam" (the state of being perceived). "Tava" (in your view): the sense is that, according to your position, the perception of difference is an error (*bhrama*). "Mama" (in my view): the sense is that I have accepted the fact that such a perception is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*). "In your position": [this refers to] "of the perception."

The meaning is as follows: according to your position, since error consists of a modification (*vṛtti*) of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is an object [of cognition]. Because it is false, there is an absence of even the state of being a cognition (*pratītitva*) therein; consequently, the state of being an object of cognition (*pratītiviṣayatva*) does not exist in the difference between the two moons.
