Thus, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*). The underlying intention is that the notion of a single genus (*ekajāti*) for both valid and invalid cognitions has been refuted elsewhere. Regarding "the difference between difference and non-difference" (*bhedābhedabheda*): the meaning is that it is the difference between difference and non-difference in that context. Regarding "sublation" (*bādha*): the intention is that its ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*) would necessarily follow.

Why is this so? He establishes that point with the words: "Of difference and non-difference. By the phrase "by this very [means]," the intended meaning is that the sublation (bādha) which proves the falsity of difference necessarily serves as the proof for the falsity of non-difference as well.

Since all conventional arrangements are possible even though those two are non-different from the perspective of ultimate reality, he says: "The existence of conventional difference. Regarding the term "from the perspective of ultimate reality" (paramārthataḥ), the syntactical split is: "of that which is different from Brahman, [but only] from the perspective of non-ultimate reality."
And thus, since the individual soul (*jīva*), which possesses non-ultimate difference from the ultimately real Brahman, possesses ultimate non-difference;

and since the difference of the soul—which possesses non-ultimate difference along with ultimate difference—possesses ultimate non-difference along with that difference, it would attain ultimacy. Therefore, the point is that there is indeed a contradiction (*bādha*) in attempting to prove its falsity (*mithyātva*). [The phrase] "because of non-difference in the ultimate sense" means "because of non-difference in the ultimate sense."

Nor does the absence of an ultimately real difference—relative to an ultimately real counter-correlate—within the ultimate reality itself, by its very nature, entail its own ultimate reality; for such a [mutual] difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is observed.
Nor should it be argued that the same applies here because the difference is not ultimately real.

Because it would be cumbersome to include "ultimate reality" (*pāramārthikatva*) within the scope of the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*), and because the probandum (*sādhya*) itself would attain the status of being a probandum at the very time the reason is known—thereby resulting in the absurdity that the means of proof (*sādhana*) would be absent—the pervasion is simply this: wherever there is an absence of ultimate difference from a given counter-positive, there is, in ultimate reality, identity with that [counter-positive]. This is stated with the intention that even in the case of the unreal (*asat*), the difference having that [unreal] as its counter-positive is indeed ultimately real; therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) anywhere. Thus, the aforementioned consequence is established.

In some manuscripts, there is a reading stating that even though empirical difference exists in certain cases, if one were to argue that—just as the individual soul (*jīva*), which is different from Brahman in the ultimate sense, possesses ultimate reality—then difference, which is non-different from ultimate non-difference, would also possess ultimate reality; thus, this constitutes a contradiction (*bādha*) in the proof of its falsity (*mithyātva*). Regarding this, there is no difficulty whatsoever. [This refers to the phrase] "ultimate and non-ultimate."

And this [is stated] to indicate the undesirable consequence that if difference were false, Brahman would lack ultimate reality (while the phenomenal world would possess ultimate reality). "And there is deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) means exclusion from the subject (*pakṣa*). "Or sublation" (*bādha*) means inclusion within the subject. Since the difference whose counter-correlate is the phenomenal world has Brahman as its locus is false, there is neither deviation nor sublation in that case.
Nor does it follow, in that case, that Brahman would be non-different from the world, which lacks ultimate reality.
This is because we accept this as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Nor does it follow that Brahman would then be non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*),
for there is no basis for such an inference.
If it is argued that non-difference whose counter-correlate is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*) alone is the logical ground for the consequence (*apādaka*), [we reply: no;

for it is accepted that only such non-difference which possesses the same level of reality (*samānasattāka*) as itself is the pervaded (*vyāpya*) with respect to being ultimately unreal. Since that [non-difference] is absent in Brahman, it is impossible to draw the consequence against it.

Nor do there exist sublation (*bādha*) or deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the difference residing in the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which has Brahman as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), because that [difference] is admitted to be false (*mithyā*).

If it is argued: "In that case, would not Brahman itself also be false, since it is the counter-correlative of a non-difference residing in the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)?"—we say no. For, when there is a non-difference whose counter-correlative resides in something non-ultimate and possesses the same degree of reality (*samasattāka*) as that non-difference, the status of being a counter-correlative is necessarily pervaded by non-ultimacy (*apāramārthikatva*). Consequently, since the non-difference of the world with Brahman does not possess the same degree of reality as Brahman, it is impossible to apply [the charge of falsity] to Brahman.

Having raised an objection based on the following intention—"Otherwise, just as the non-difference (abheda) whose correlate (anuyogin) is the superimposed silver would be unreal, so too the shell (śukti) itself would become unreal"—he refutes it with the words "of Brahman. "Non-difference having the same ontological status (samānasattāka) as the locus (dharmin)"—here the word "non-difference" is to be separated [from the preceding compound].
The meaning is: non-difference whose counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is unreal.

To demonstrate the concomitance (sahacāra) for the sake of grasping the pervasion (vyāpti), he shows it in the case of "the jar and so forth. "That exists" means: there exists a difference that has the same ontological status as its locus and whose counter-correlate is unreal.

By this, the doubt raised by relying on the falsity of the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is also effectively resolved through the same logic; thus, there is no deficiency [in the argument]. For if that position were not intended even within the context of the doubt itself, it would result in an inconsistency in the doubt, since the fallacies of *vyabhicāra* (deviation) and *bādha* (sublation) have already been stated in the general statement regarding the difference between the phenomenal world and Brahman—where Brahman is the counter-correlative—and the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world—where the phenomenal world is the counter-correlative. Consequently, one could not remove that defect in one case while failing to do so in the other.

Nor should it be argued that if there is an intention to raise doubts such as "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the two types of difference, then the use of the singular number in the phrase "the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world" (*brahma-prapañca-bheda*) would be inconsistent.

This is because, since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is a single entity in its essence, the singular number is used generically to include all specific differences—such as the difference between Brahman and a jar, the difference between a jar and Brahman, and the difference between a cloth and Brahman—in order to encompass them.

This is because the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—"wherever there is an absence of difference belonging to the same level of reality (*svasamānasattāka*) whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by non-ultimate reality (*apāramārthikatva*), there is non-ultimate reality"—is established even for you, as it includes the phenomenal world of jars and so forth within its scope.

If there were a difference (*bheda*) in Brahman that possesses the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as itself and is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) to the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) which is non-ultimate (*apāramārthika*), then the non-ultimacy of Brahman would be unavoidable. Therefore, with the intention that if its reality (*satyatva*) is admitted, both the sublation (*bādhaka*) and the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) are indeed unavoidable, he provides the resolution starting with "Then" (*tarhi*). Regarding the phrase "a difference possessing the same ontological status as itself": here the word division (*cheda*) is *svasamānasattākabheda*.

Others, however, [state]: "Or there would be sublation (bādha). The meaning is this: if the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world (prapañca) were unreal, then both would have to be either ultimately real or ultimately unreal;

it could not be that one alone is ultimately real while the other is unreal. Therefore, since the unreality of the difference must necessarily be asserted, if one attempts to prove its falsity (mithyātva), there is sublation (bādha).

One might object: "Even if the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is not ultimately real, the distinction between their respective ultimate reality and non-ultimate reality could still be established by some other means. With this intention, the opponent raises a doubt with the words "of Brahman" (*brahmaṇaḥ*). They ask: "In the rule that 'the non-ultimate reality or ultimate reality of a difference and its absence is determined by a difference whose existence is of the same order as the existence of the substratum (*dharmin*),' why should the relationship of the governed and the governor (*niyamyaniyāmaka-bhāva*) not be exactly the reverse? To this, they reply with the word "then" (*tarhi*). According to their view, the punctuation should be made after "difference" (*bheda*) in both instances.
The illustration "like the world of phenomenal proliferation" (prapañcavat) intends precisely its lack of ultimate reality;

even that statement is for the purpose of establishing its falsity in terms of its own nature. Otherwise, if one were to accept its falsity only in its conditioned form, it would result in the undesirable consequence (iṣṭāpatti) of proving what is already accepted. This is how it should be understood.
In some manuscripts, the reading "a difference having the same ontological status as the locus" (*dharmisamānasattāka-bheda*) is seen in both sentences;

therefore, it should be understood that this is precisely the intended meaning there. Regarding "the state of being merely apparent" (*prātibhāsikatva*): the meaning is that it consists in being sublated by knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman, and so forth. Regarding "and not": [this refers to] that state of being merely apparent.

The meaning of the *Bhāṣya*—“in each other”—is that, having superimposed the non-self upon the self and the self upon the non-self, within each other—that is, within the objects of the notions of “you” (*yuṣmad*) and “I” (*asmad*), which are the self and the non-self under discussion—all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) proceeds. Regarding the example, “I am fair”: the meaning is that because the non-difference of the fair-complexioned body from the referent of the word “I,” which appears as the self, has been superimposed.

Now, it was stated in the *Tattvaprakāśikā* on the section concerning omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) that since one of the two moons is superimposed, there exists a distinction between the superimposed and the non-superimposed; therefore, the example is deficient in its probandum (*sādhyavikala*).

Nor can it be argued that there is a contradiction [with our position] because, after first establishing in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) the superimposition of another moon—which had been refuted in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*)—we have reinforced the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and stated a different refutation by abandoning that [superimposition]; for the superimposition of another moon is indeed established through reasoning. To explain: [The text continues: "For instance..."

If there were a superimposition [of the finger] upon the moon, it would be impossible for there to be the cognition of the movement of one moon and the absence of the movement of the other moon resulting from the movement of the finger;
for you accept that the superimposition belongs to the action itself, and that action resides only in the moon.
Furthermore, since qualities such as curvature would be equally present in both [the moon and the finger], it would follow that they would be perceived in both places.

Therefore, just as in the case of a rope, one must state that there is a superimposition of a snake characterized by qualities such as being terrifying, or rather, of the moon itself characterized by qualities such as curvature and movement.
Furthermore, there is no impossibility of a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) according to the manner argued in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*),
because the moon situated in front is indeed possible as the substratum.
Nor should it be asked: "How can that which is perceived as distinct from the moon present before one appear as identical with it?
For it is possible for the moon to be the object of error even without appearing as identical with its substrate.
Furthermore, there is no rule that the object of an error must necessarily appear as identical with its substrate.

In the view of the opponent (*paramata*), in cases such as a crystal where there is the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of a reflection of redness, the reflection itself [is unreal]; in all positions, in this very delusion (*bhrama*), the action and so forth appearing therein; in cases of the delusion of motion in stationary objects like mountains, the motion and so forth; and in cases of the delusion of a tuft of hair and the like, the rays and so forth appearing as long—because no other object is established as being identical (*tādātmya*) to these.
This is because the color and other qualities residing in the mountain and so forth appear precisely as distinct from the object being superimposed.

In cases such as a tuft of hair, since they appear only through their relation to the lamp, they are seen to be distinct from it; furthermore, there is no perception of any sensory object appearing in the intervening space as having attained identity with that [lamp]. Even if one asserts that the superimposition of redness occurs upon the form of the crystal due to non-difference, this remains an untenable position in the case of the superimposition of a face, because it appears precisely as being inside the mirror.

Furthermore, neither the proponent of illusion (māyāvādin) nor the Buddhist can accept an error that lacks a substratum (*anadhiṣṭhāna*), as this would entail the fallacy of contradicting their own tenets.

Nor should it be argued: "Since being manifested as identical with that which is the object of the error is itself the nature of the substratum, and since the moon and so forth are not such [objects], how can they be the substratum? [This objection is invalid.]

Because the nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) in the aforementioned error must be postulated as otherwise inexplicable, and because in errors such as that of mother-of-pearl for silver, the reality appearing in the silver must be postulated as the real entity constituting the substratum as otherwise inexplicable, it is accepted that the meaning of the term "substratum" is precisely the state of being the locus of the sensory contact that generates that error. Thus, just as a visual organ in contact with mother-of-pearl produces a cognition in the form of silver due to a defect, so too, by virtue of the contact between the eye and the moon, lamp, or other objects, [the cognition arises] through the visual organ accompanied by the aforementioned defect.

This is because it is accepted that in cases such as the moon-lamp and so forth, there arises a cognition having the form of a distinct moon, a long shape, rays, and so on, characterized by the crookedness perceived therein.
Since the superimposed moon appearing there is non-existent, the distinction from the real moon that appears is itself real.
Nor is there any contradiction with the experience of the sublation of difference, which states, "This is one and the same moon."

This is because there is no such experience as "of these two, one is a mango tree and the other is a jackfruit," which would involve apprehending their individual natures and ownership prior to apprehending their mere identity;

rather, there is an absence of such an experience, and instead, there is an experience of the sublation of the moon itself, preceded by a specific determination of difference, such as: "between these two appearing [objects], there is only this single moon located in this region, and not another.
Furthermore, the objection raised in the prima facie argument—that the recollection required for superimposition is untenable—does not apply here.

Since that [knowledge of the substrate] is required by the condition of being the primary object (*pradhānajñānamudrā*), and since there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) against the fact that the moon currently perceived—the substrate—is also primary, superimposition (*āropa*) is established by the mere knowledge of that [substrate].
And that knowledge may be either of the nature of direct experience (*anubhava*) or, in some way, of the nature of memory (*smaraṇa*).
In your own system, just as in the case of the knowledge of difference which is the cause of the error of difference, there is no fault in either case.
The superimposition of another moon is also accepted by the Buddhists;
for in the *Viṣṇutattvanirṇaya-ṭīkā*, their view is presented as follows: "That which is imagined merely by its own nature is false, just like another moon caused by pressing upon a finger.

Thus, since the second moon is a superimposed entity, its difference [from the real moon] is unreal; therefore, the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the illustrative example cited in the commentary is indeed very firmly established.

As for the absence of an establishment of that [distinction] in this text: since it has already been stated that the reason (*hetu*) of "being a difference" (*bhedatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), and since such non-establishment can be demonstrated even with the intent of relying on the position of the superimposition of difference (*bhedāropa*), no exclusive emphasis is shown upon a single position; therefore, the lack of necessity for establishing that [distinction] should be understood by those with discerning hearts. Regarding the phrase "but in the fourth": the meaning is in the inference "the subject of dispute [is not real] in reality. Regarding the phrase "by the difference of limiting adjuncts" (*upādhibhedena*): the meaning is "by way of being a collection of earth and so forth."

Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of any other entity": nor should one suspect that through *apekṣābuddhi* (relational cognition) a manifold collection termed a "whole" (*samudāya*) is produced; rather, a single qualified [entity] arises. In that case, there is no occasion for the objections that will be stated later.

In this regard, it must be stated that this is because properties existing as parts [of a whole] are not admitted. Otherwise, if a person qualified by a staff were produced from the connection with a staff, there would follow the confusion (sāṅkarya) of the universals "staffness" and "personhood.

This is because, while such a statement might be possible regarding a collection existing only at the present time, in the present case it is impossible for such a collection to arise, since a conjunction of past and future cognitions can never occur. This is the intended meaning.

For if one were to accept that [the world] is composed of earth and other elements just like a jar or similar objects, then the objections to be stated later would also apply. Regarding the term "sublation" (*bādha*): the sense is that difference is ascertained by perception as being precisely real. Regarding the phrase "earth-ness and so forth": if it is argued that this same fault would apply even to houses constructed of wood, stone, and the like, we say no.

Although it might be possible to somehow avoid these defects by asserting that [the existence of qualities] is established through all means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the intention here is that these defects are stated as further arguments precisely because the subject under discussion lacks any basis in valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*). Regarding the phrase "of qualities and so forth" (*guṇādīnām*): the phrase "the consequence of being a substance" (*dravyatvāpatti*) means that being an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of a substance. Regarding the phrase "of those without parts" (*niravayavānām*): one should not object by asking how this can be so, given that partless atoms (*paramāṇu*) are observed to be the initiators of substances.

If the single ether were the originator of other substances, it would follow that there is no entity at all in the world that participates in the conventional usage of "ether," because it would not be perceived separately, just like the atoms that originate a jar.

Furthermore, since being an originator in parts is impossible for that which is partless, the qualification "partless" is employed with this intended meaning. "The proof of the division of ether" means the proof of the inherent division of the parts of ether.
[This is] elsewhere in the *Nyāyāmṛta* and other works.

Thus, the intention is that there is also a deficiency (*vaikalya*) therein regarding the probandum (*sādhya*), which is the state of being devoid of internal differentiation as accepted by the opponent.
He also refutes the reason stated by the opponent with the words "as difference" (*bhedatvena*). The term "this-being-perceived" (*idaṃ-pratīyamānatvam*) is a single compound word.

The meaning is: what is the purpose of the term *pratīyamānatva* (being perceived), which is intended as a qualification for that cognition and serves as an aid for the understanding of the specific and general forms to be described hereafter?

Therefore, there is no room for the objection regarding the impossibility of the [proposed] alternatives. "Because it is unestablished for you": since difference in itself is false, the cognition of it cannot be valid; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished for both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). "Because it is unestablished for me": the sense is that differences such as those between a pot and a cloth, as well as the difference between the superimposed moon and the non-superimposed moon, are real.
Nor is there any complexity (*gaurava*) in the case of the superimposed "other moon."
Because it is impossible for that [second moon] to be perceived in the vicinity of the moon without the superimposition of another moon upon it;
and because there is a recollection, "another moon appeared as a mere illusion.
By this, the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the illustrative example is also indicated.

Regarding the phrase "because of the perception of the difference from the moon": according to that [opponent's] view, since the perception of the difference from the moon is an error (*bhrama*), it is merely apparent (*prātibhāsika*). Consequently, because there is no common universal (*anugatasāmānya*) that encompasses both the empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and the apparent, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

The underlying sense is that otherwise, since fire and so forth would be absent in a place where smoke and the like are superimposed (such as steam), there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the abolition of inference (*anumāna*).

Even having granted the objection, he states the fault: "bhedābheda... (regarding difference and non-difference). The meaning is: "in that which is the difference between difference and non-difference. "Since that too is the subject" (*pakṣatva*) means: because the disputed nature common to that [difference] serves as the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), and because deviation within the subject (*vyabhicāra*) is not a fault. Now, one might object: since even the difference between difference and non-difference is admitted to be false, there is no sublation (*bādha*). To this he says: "bhedābhedayoḥ... (of difference and non-difference). "It would be false" means: because non-difference also possesses the status of being a subject by virtue of its being a difference, and because it possesses the probans (*hetumat*).

Right here, he states another objection: "vyāvahārika... (conventional...). [The phrase] "it would be ultimately real" (pāramārthikaḥ syāt) implies that if non-difference were ultimately real, then difference—which is non-distinct from it—could not possibly be false.

To the question, "Since conventional difference exists between difference and non-difference, how can there be non-difference?", he says: "ultimately non-different" (paramārthato'bhinnaḥ). The intention is that conventional difference does not contradict ultimate non-difference.
The example for this begins with "vyāvahārika... and so forth.

He states an instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in another place: "pāramārthika... [and so on]. The meaning is that since the difference between the ultimate Brahman and the non-ultimate phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is itself ultimately real, there is a deviation even in that case. Regarding the phrase "tasyāpi": this means "of the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world as well.

And if that [difference] were non-ultimate, then because the phenomenal world would consequently become ultimate—just like Brahman—there would again be a contradiction regarding the difference contained within it.
This might be so if the absence of ultimate difference having Brahman as its counter-correlative were the property that brings about the attributes of Brahman;
but this is not the case.

Rather, it is the absence of difference having the same ontological status as the substrate itself and having Brahman as its counter-correlative [that is required]; therefore, the aforementioned defect does not arise. Thus he raises the objection: "In Brahman... (*brahmaṇi*). "Difference" (*bheda*) means difference from Brahman. "It would be like the phenomenal world" (*prapañcavat syāt*): the sense is that, by the same logic, the absence of difference having the same ontological status as the substrate itself and having the phenomenal world as its counter-correlative would necessarily entail the possession of the attributes of the phenomenal world.
The term "distinction from the moon" (*candrabheda*) is intended to demonstrate that [the probandum] is pervaded by the subject.

Although phenomenal reality (*prātibhāsikatva*) does not exist in things such as jars which possess falsity (*mithyātva*), nevertheless, it constitutes a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) because it pervades the probandum as delimited by the property of being a distinction (*bhedatva*). Now, one might object: since this [adjunct] also pervades the probans (*sādhana*), it cannot be a limiting adjunct.

He wards off the objection that "the probans [difference] can also be inferred in the subject (pakṣa) by means of a limiting condition (upādhi)" with the words "na ca" ("and not"). The sense is that this would result in a contradiction with one's own established tenets (apasiddhānta). He explains the very contradiction with Śaṅkara’s Bhāṣya with the words "gauro 'ham" ("I am fair-complexioned"). The sense is that if one does not admit the falsity of the identity between the body and the self, then the cognition "I am fair-complexioned" and so forth—which has that [identity] as its object—would have an unsublated object and would consequently result in being valid knowledge (pramā); thus, there would be a contradiction with the Bhāṣya which describes such [cognition] as an error (bhrama).
However, if the reading is "prāmāṇyaprasaṅgācca," it should be understood that this is the statement of another refutation.
As for the claim that "the falsity of the non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa) is indeed accepted, so there is no occurrence of the aforementioned fallacy;
nor does it follow that difference becomes real,
because scripture determines falsity only as delimited by the property of being an object of perception (dṛśyatva)," that is trivial.

Because the falsity of both difference and non-difference is contradictory, it cannot be established even by scripture; for the meaning of scripture must be logically consistent. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Abhimāny-adhikaraṇa.

In the fourth inference—"The world under dispute is, in reality, devoid of internal differentiation because it is an object of cognition (*meyatva*), like space"—if the world were an independent entity (*svatantra-padārtha*) like space and so forth, then the probandum (the absence of difference) would be established through the well-known existence of its parts or constituent portions.
But this is not the case;

for the world is a referent of the term "world" (*jagat-padārtha*) by virtue of the specific limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being a collection (*samūhatva*), just as the referents of terms such as "army" or "forest" consist of various individual objects.

And since the qualifier of the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished with respect to that which is delimited by that [unreal], there is a sublation (*bādha*); thus he says: "But in the fourth [case]... Now, one might argue: "Let it be then that the world is simply another category of entity (*padārtha*), like the sky and so forth.
And it should not be asked how, on this basis, the non-difference of earth and the other elements is established."

Anticipating the objection that since earth and the other elements are the material causes (*upādāna*) of the world, they would be a part of it, he says: "Of earth and the others. [He states] "the consequence of the confusion of genera (*jātisaṅkara*)," because the meaning is that what is produced from earth and the others would itself possess the nature of earth and so forth. [He says] "of those included within the world"; this is the reason for their being the originators (*ārambhaka*) of the world. [He states] "the consequence of [their] becoming substances (*dravyatvāpatti*)," because the meaning is that the state of being an originator in the form of being a material cause is a property of substances.

It should be understood that if partless, all-pervading substances were to originate the substance called the "world," their all-pervasiveness would be contradicted by the necessity of them possessing a dimension smaller than that [of the world]. Furthermore, there would be the loss of their status as ultimate constituents (*antyāvayavitva*). The sense is that being an ultimate constituent consists in being a substance that does not originate another substance. This is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); one should also understand that since the world originated from earth (as a constituent) is itself included within the world, it would necessarily have to originate the world, leading to the acceptance of yet another world and thus resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

One might object: "Since it is being proven that a specific jar or similar object is devoid of internal difference, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Anticipating this, he refutes it by showing the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavikalpa*)—namely, "of objects such as jars" (*ghaṭādipadārthānām*). The sense is: "The probandum is deficient because I admit the existence of ultimate difference, relative to things like jars, within space. Regarding the proof of the absence of difference even with respect to its own parts, he says: "of space" (*ākāśa*). The sense is: since the proof of the real difference between the parts of space and space itself, as well as among those parts themselves, has been established elsewhere in works such as the *Nyāyāmṛta*, the probandum is therefore deficient in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Thus, in all the inferences intended to establish difference—such as "the two subjects under dispute are ultimately not mutually non-different, because they are objects of cognition, like each other"—there is sublation by means of valid cognitions such as perception.
This is because the perception of difference between the Witness (sākṣin) and the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara) is established by valid means of knowledge in every case.

Furthermore, there is the inference: "The two subjects under dispute are not ultimately mutually non-different, because they possess mutually contradictory attributes, like [the instances of] 'like each other' in the negative concomitance (vyatireka)," as well as scriptural texts such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*).

The state of not being the locus of mutually contradictory properties—even ultimately including "being other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*)—is a limiting condition (*upādhi*). There is a parity of fallacy in the argument: "The two subjects under dispute are non-different from each other according to worldly usage, because they are cognizable, like each other. Furthermore, due to the absence of a supporting reason (*anukūlatarka*), the probans is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*). Thus, because it is vitiated by such initial and final defects, non-duality (*advaita*) is not to be accepted.
Regarding what has been prattled by someone here:
"Is this difference the very nature of the substratum (dharmin) or a property (dharma) thereof?
Not the first."
For it would be impossible for "diversity" (*bhinna*) to function as a qualifier (*prakāra*) in the cognition [of that very diversity];
furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence that there is no distinction between the cognition of a pot and the cognition of the diversity of the pot,
since there would be no difference in their objective referents (*viṣaya*).
Furthermore, because the diversity of the causal complex of the apprehender is untenable;
and because doubt regarding difference is untenable in the cognition of a jar,
since there is no unknown portion [remaining].
Furthermore, it is because difference cannot logically possess a counter-correlative;
for a substratum such as a jar lacks a counter-correlative,
and it would follow that even qualities such as color would themselves become the nature of the substratum.
Furthermore, since non-difference, like difference, is the very nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*), it would follow that difference and non-difference are themselves identical.
Moreover, this would entail the consequence that there is no distinction between the cognitions of those two,
and that the two words denoting them would become synonyms.
By this, it should be understood that the view that causality and other such properties are the very nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpa*) is also refuted.

Regarding the second [alternative], is it a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a negative one (*abhāva*)? Not the first; for if it were of the nature of a universal (*jāti*) and so forth, its having a counter-correlative (*sapratiyogikatva*) and other such features would be untenable.
Furthermore, if [separateness] were of the nature of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) and so forth, the cognition of difference regarding qualities (*guṇa*) and the like would be untenable;
for such a cognition is accounted for by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) alone, and there is no acceptance of a separate quality in the form of distinctness.
Nor is the latter [alternative] tenable.

If difference were of the nature of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), it would follow that a tree possessing contact with a monkey would possess that difference [with respect to its own parts], because of the cognition:
"The tree is not in contact with a monkey at its root.

Furthermore, if it were of the nature of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), it would follow that there would be no distinction between the cognitions "it does not exist" and "it does not become."
Furthermore, since its own absolute non-existence exists even within itself, it would follow that there is a cognition of difference from itself.
Moreover, if that difference were of the nature of the absolute non-existence of its own attributes, the first fault would not be avoided.
Furthermore, because there is no means of valid cognition for either the counter-positive or the locus of negation, difference cannot be established.
For instance, the pot is not the counter-positive (pratiyogin) of the difference from the pot;
because the difference from the pot is impossible where a pot exists,
and because, by the principle of parsimony (lāghava), it is determined that opposition to the counter-positive belongs to the state of being an absence (abhāvatva) alone.
Furthermore, since difference is the absence of non-difference, non-difference itself would have to be its counter-correlative.
Nor can it be maintained that non-difference is simply the very nature of the jar and so forth; for if a jar were present, the difference from a jar would be logically untenable.
Furthermore, it is not possible for non-difference itself to have difference as its counter-correlative;

for the cognition of that [non-difference] would depend upon the cognition of difference, and the cognition of difference depends upon the cognition of the counter-correlative, resulting in a circular dependency.
For this very reason, perception is not a valid means of knowledge in that regard.
Because of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Thus, when there is doubt or certainty regarding the difference or non-difference of a cloth from a jar, one does not observe a certainty regarding the jar’s difference [from the cloth] until there is a certainty regarding the cloth’s difference [from the jar]; therefore, the certainty regarding the jar’s difference must be stated to be the cause of the certainty regarding the cloth’s difference.
This is according to the rule: "That whose doubt and certainty of absence are obstacles to a certain cognition is the cause of that certainty."
Thus, there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*) in that the determination of the difference from a jar depends upon the determination of the difference from a cloth.

Furthermore, since there is no sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*) capable of apprehending the state of being a counter-correlative (*pratiyogitva*), the perception of a difference qualified by that counter-correlativity is impossible.

If it is argued that cognition itself constitutes the sensory contact, then alas, that cognition would require the knowledge of the difference to have the counter-correlativity as its object; thus, there is again a circular argument.
Nor is there inference [to prove it],

because such arguments as "Devadatta possesses a difference from Yajñadatta, because he is a cognizer of that [Yajñadatta’s] suffering" can be accounted for even by means of a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*).
For this very reason, there is no scriptural authority (*āgama*) [either].
Because it does not establish an ultimate distinction, it is logical that every perception of difference is merely the play of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyā-avidyā*).
As it has been said: "For she is clever at making the impossible appear."
All of this is, however, refuted by the acceptance of *viśeṣa* (particularity).
For instance: difference (*bheda*) is both the essential nature of the substratum (*dharmin*) and its attribute (*dharma*).
Even in the case of non-difference (*abheda*), the relationship of attribute and substratum exists through the power of *viśeṣa*.

For this very reason, even the status of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) occurs in the cognition "it is different. Furthermore, the distinction between the cognition of a jar and the cognition of its difference arises precisely from the particular (*viśeṣa*).

Nor does the admission that a neutral particular acts as the regulator of the diversity of cognitions lead to the consequence of Idealism (*vijñānavāda*), because the object would otherwise be rendered purposeless.
It should not be argued that if it were so [i.e., if the difference were apprehended as a qualifier], there would be a contradiction with experience;
for the diversity of cognition arises precisely from the diversity of qualifiers in the form of *ghaṭatva* (pot-ness) and *bhedatva* (difference-ness),
while the distinction between these two qualifiers is merely one of specific character, and thus there is no fault.
For this very reason, the diversity of the causal complex of the apprehender (*grāhaka-sāmagrī*) is also established,
since the diversity of the apprehended (*grāhya*) has already been demonstrated.
By this, the objection that doubt regarding difference would be impossible in the cognition of a jar is also refuted.
Even when that [entity] is cognized as "pot-ness," it is not cognized as "difference-ness";
for although pot-ness and difference-ness are non-different, this is possible precisely because of the existence of a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*).
Furthermore, the fact that difference possesses a counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is also due solely to the power of that specific distinction.

Nor should it be argued that the linguistic usage "the pot is not non-possessing-a-counterpositive" would be untenable because [the pot] is non-different from its difference from that which possesses a counter-positive;
for even though there is non-difference, it is specifically that particularity (*viśeṣa*) which is the object of such linguistic usage.
This particularity ensures the fulfillment of the functions of difference despite the absence of actual difference.
It is indeed accepted that color and so forth constitute the very nature of the substratum (*dharmin*).
Nor does it follow from this that the cognition of taste and so forth would occur upon the cognition of color;
for it is precisely because they are not cognized as "tasteness" (*rasatva*) and so on that this is logically established through their specific distinctions.
The non-difference between difference and non-difference is indeed intended;
for there is no contradiction in difference being [non-different] in relation to itself while being different in relation to another.
Nor does it follow that, in this way, the conventional usage of non-difference would apply to a jar even in relation to another, just as it does in relation to itself.
It should be stated that [this is so] because there is no distinction within its own nature (*svarūpa*).
For if there were no distinction, the very expression "in relation to itself" would be untenable.
But if such a distinction exists, then by virtue of that very distinction, there is non-difference from itself and not non-difference from another.
For this very reason, there is no lack of distinction between the cognitions of difference and non-difference,
nor are those two words synonyms,
since it has been stated that their respective objects of comprehension are diverse.
By this, causality and other such properties are also explained.

As for what was said regarding whether something is a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a negative one (*abhāva*), we reply: whatever distinction is perceived in relation to a given thing, that is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of that thing.

Nor should it be argued that, in the case of the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of a jar, the difference from the jar perceived therein would have the nature of that absolute non-existence; and since that [non-existence] exists in the jar as well, it would follow that there must be a perception of the difference from the jar even in the jar itself. This is not to be said.
Because that [otherness] does not exist in the pot as "pot-otherness.

Nor should it be argued that there is no distinction between "being otherness" (*bhedatva*) and "being absolute non-existence" (*atyantābhāvatva*), given that the nature of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) and the delimitors of the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) are identical;
for there is a distinction: absolute non-existence is the negation of the pot, whereas mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is the negation of identity with the pot.
If it is argued that in the cognition "the jar does not exist," the jar itself appears as the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) directly, then the jar is indeed the counter-positive.
Furthermore, they say that identity (*tādātmya*) is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-positiveness of difference.

By this, the objection that the absolute non-existence of a conjunct in relation to conjunction would result in being a difference—because its counter-positiveness is delimited by the identity of the conjunct with the nature of conjunction—is refuted.

Because conjunction is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence that is co-present with the conjunct; and even if it were its delimiting property (*avacchedaka*), it would be so only as "conjunction-ness" (*saṃyogatva*) and not as "identity-ness" (*tādātmyatva*), which constitutes the distinction.
In reality, there is a great distinction between mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*) and absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) due to their respective positive and negative counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).
By this, the objection that the cognitions "it does not exist" and "it does not become" would result in being indistinguishable is also refuted.

Furthermore, as for the argument in the root-text—that from the cognition "the tree at the root is not conjoined with the monkey," the absence of monkey-conjunction in the tree delimited by the root is established—this is precisely what is accepted by those who maintain the theory of the difference of the qualified (*viśiṣṭabheda-vādin*).
Nor does this contradict recognition (*pratyabhijñā*),
because non-difference also exists between the two [states] as delimited by the branch, the root, and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference.
Because non-contradiction is established through the force of specific distinctions.
Nor should it be argued: "In that case, let there be only the distinction itself; what is the use of [postulating] difference?
For difference is known through valid means of cognition (*pramita*).

As for the claim that the difference from a jar is untenable in a locus containing a jar because the opposition to the counter-positive is determined by the delimitation of non-existence (*abhāvatva*),
that is incorrect; for even in a locus containing a jar, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the jar and so forth would likewise be untenable.

If it is argued that since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like are known to subsist in the locus of their counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), a contradiction consisting in not subsisting at the time of the counter-positive is determined in those cases; then, since difference (*bheda*) is known to subsist in both the locus and the time of its counter-positive, let a contradiction consisting in not subsisting in the very substance that is the counter-positive be determined here. If it is argued that the contradiction consisting in not coexisting with the counter-positive at one and the same place and time is common to prior non-existence and the rest, then let the contradiction consisting in not coexisting with its own absence at one and the same place and time be common to difference and the rest.
In reality, opposition to the counter-positive by means of the relation that delimits its counter-positiveness is common to all absences;
for even difference (bheda) is opposed to its counter-positive by way of identity (tādātmya).
As for the claim that because difference is the absence of non-difference (abheda), a jar or the like cannot be its counter-positive, that too is incorrect.

Just as in the case of antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the like, there is no contradiction in difference being the absence of its own absence even while having a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) such as a jar;
likewise, there is no fault even if non-difference (*abheda*) is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the jar and so forth,
because non-difference exists only in the counter-correlate by virtue of being non-difference.

Precisely because there exists a distinction between the property of being a pot (*ghaṭatva*) and the property of being non-different from the pot (*ghaṭābhedatva*), it is possible for [the pot] to be absent [in a locus] by way of its being non-different from the pot, even while it is present as a pot.
As for the claim that difference and non-difference involve a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) because their cognition is dependent upon the cognition of one another—
that is trivial.
Because the non-cognition of the difference from a jar—which is the cause for the cognition of non-difference from a jar—depends solely upon the cognition of the jar itself as "not being a non-jar.
For this very reason, even the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of difference is logically established.
As for the objection that there is a circularity (*anyonyāśraya*) because the cognition of the difference between a jar and a cloth depends upon the mutual cognition of each other: [this is not so].
That too is not correct.

For the mutual doubt regarding the difference between a jar and a cloth does not obstruct the cognition of each other, just as a doubt regarding the object of perception does not; thus, it is unproven that their cognition is dependent upon the cognition of the other.

Otherwise, it would follow that even the doubt regarding the object of perception acts as an obstruction, leading to the absurd conclusion that every entity whatsoever must have its cognition dependent on its own cognition, which would result in the total negation of all cognition.
Furthermore, because there is no subverting argument (bādhaka) against the contrary position, the rule beginning with "that which is doubted" (*yatsaṃśaya*) and so forth is not a necessary factor.

As for the claim that the perception of a difference qualified by its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is untenable due to the absence of sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) regarding the aspect of being a counter-correlate—
that is extremely weak.
This is because non-conceptual apprehension itself can constitute a means of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*);
and since that apprehension does not depend on the cognition of difference, there is no room for the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Furthermore, since the nature of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*) is identical to the nature of the counter-correlate itself, the apprehension of that [counter-correlate] can indeed constitute the means of contact for it.
Thus, in inference, because the distinction [of the property] is qualified by having an existence equal to the existence of the locus (*dharmin*), the intended object is established.
Nor is there a lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*);

for in the case of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) consisting in the undesirable consequence that Caitra and others would experience the suffering of Maitra and others.
It cannot be argued that because Caitra and Maitra are one, it is acceptable for Caitra’s consciousness to experience the suffering and so forth belonging to Maitra;
for it is not desired that suffering arising in Maitra’s body be experienced by Caitra’s body.
Nor can it be argued that the absence of such experience is due to the difference between the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) residing in their respective bodies.
Because it has already been stated that [the existence of] a yoginī is untenable;
for this very reason, even scripture (*āgama*) conveys only an intrinsic difference (*svābhāvikabheda*),
since the eating and non-eating mentioned in the phrase "eating while not eating" would be unintelligible without an intrinsic difference.
Furthermore, this is because scriptural passages concerning difference in the state of liberation have been cited.

Nor should it be argued that since difference is accepted as the very nature of the reality (*vastu-svarūpa*), and since there is no dispute regarding the inherent nature of that essence, this [scriptural teaching] amounts to nothing more than a restatement of the obvious;
for difference is not merely the bare essence of the reality itself.
Because the relationship between property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) and so forth is untenable;
rather, it has been stated that it is a particularity (*viśeṣa*) of that [entity].

And thus, since there is no fault, because what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is a particular nature of the entity as qualified by properties such as being a property (*dharmitva*) or having another as its counter-correlative (*parapratiyogikatva*).

Now, if it is asked what proof there is for the existence of a distinction within the very nature of the entity itself, [the answer is as follows]: although the nature (*svarūpa*) is non-different from the entity, the distinction of the nature from the entity is established by the very experience of their relationship, expressed as "the nature of the entity. Likewise, the non-difference between Brahman and its attributes is established by such scriptural passages as: "Just as water rained upon a mountain peak flows away in different directions, so he who perceives the attributes as separate runs after them alone"; "It should be perceived as one alone"; and "There is no diversity here. Thus, the identity of Brahman and its attributes is proven.
Furthermore, in such passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" and "The knower of Brahman as bliss," linguistic usage occurs through the relation of qualifier and qualified;
therefore, due to the contradiction between these two [theories], a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is necessarily implied by the sense of the context.

Likewise, since a jar and its properties are not perceived separately, their oneness being established, the relation of property and property-possessor (*dharmadharmibhāva*) and so forth can find refuge only in particularity (*viśeṣa*).
As for the argument that since all worldly and Vedic transactions are possible through the power of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācyāvidyā*) alone, what is the need for a specific [distinction]?
That is trivial;
for if ignorance were independent of an object, it would result in the consequence of the Vijñānavāda (Idealist) doctrine.

And if that [difference] were dependent upon it, there would necessarily be a contradiction between its being of the nature of that [Brahman] and its being non-different from it, as well as between its being the nature [of Brahman] and its being different.

If it is argued that non-difference alone is intrinsic while its being the nature [of Brahman] is merely false, then it follows that the scriptures teaching that [nature] would lack authority because they do not reveal the ultimate reality (*atattvāvedaka*). If it is argued that this fault does not apply because all the scriptures have their purport solely in the ultimately real nature of consciousness devoid of distinctions, we say no.
Because this would entail the conceptualization of abandoning what is seen and accepting what is unseen;
because it involves discarding perceived distinctions to accept an unperceived lack of distinction;
and because a non-distinct experience is not observed from the word itself.

Nor should it be argued that in cases such as "this is that" (*so 'yam*), since the non-difference between the two things qualified by *tattā* (that-ness) and *idantā* (this-ness) is sublated, we observe instead a cognition of their mere essential natures (*svarūpa-mātra*).

For even there, there is a non-difference relation between that which is characterized by *tattā*—in the form of a past connection—or that which is qualified by *tattā* in the form of the destruction of its connection with that time, and that which is qualified by *idantā* in the form of a present connection.
Furthermore, in the Advaita doctrine, even ignorance (*avidyā*) itself is not logically tenable.
Because of the fault of conceptual construction;
for if it were real, there would be the consequence of duality, and if it were false, there would be no basis for its conceptualization.

If it were imagined by itself, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). If it were imagined by another instance of ignorance (*avidyā*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
And thus, how could there be any room for the conceptualization of the falsity of "being a property" (*dharmatva*) and so forth?

If it is argued that this very lack of logical consistency (*anupapannatva*) is actually a proof for falsity (*mithyātva*), since truth would indeed follow from logical consistency, then— by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*)— it should be postulated that ignorance (*avidyā*) is simply the Self (*ātman*) itself. If it is objected that the Self cannot be ignorance because that would entail the cessation of the Self upon the cessation of ignorance— which is logically untenable— it is precisely for this reason that it is easy to say that it is false.

If it is argued that the self’s being ignorance is unproven, then what proof has your long-livedness found for the property [of the self] being ignorance, given that all perceived means of knowledge have been refuted? This is the direction of the argument.
Now, one might object: "In this way, even the distinction [between the self and ignorance] is not tenable, due to the fault of the dilemma."
For instance:

if the distinction (*viśeṣa*) between a property (*dharma*) and its substratum (*dharmin*) is different from the property and the substratum, then let there simply be difference; what is the use of this superfluous "distinction"?
If it is not different, then only the property and the substratum exist, and not the distinction.
If it is argued that, in that case, the relationship between property and its substratum (dharma-dharmin-bhāva) would also not exist, we say: not so.
Even though the particularity (*viśeṣa*) is non-different [from the entity], there is no fault because it does not consist of that [entity] alone.
If it is argued that if the particularity were itself qualified, there would be an infinite regress of particularities, we reply: there is no such fault because it is not a separate entity.
It might be argued as follows:

"Since difference (*bheda*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*) are eternal, they would possess the nature of impermanent things such as jars; and if they were impermanent, there would follow the consequence that after some time, all things would become indistinguishable and devoid of difference. But this is not so.

For even if that which belongs to the impermanent is itself impermanent, there is no consequence of a remainder consisting of an indistinguishable, non-differentiated entity, because after a certain time, the entity itself ceases to exist.
Furthermore, it is utterly illogical that there should be a consequence of universal non-difference for that which belongs to the eternal, due to its very nature of permanence.
Therefore, the fivefold difference between the insentient (jaḍa), the individual soul (jīva), and the Lord (īśvara) is indeed natural and inherent.

For thus says the Śruti: "The distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as well as the distinction between the insentient (jaḍa) and the Lord; the mutual distinction between individual souls, and likewise the distinction between the insentient and the individual soul."
And this fivefold diversity of the phenomenal world is mutually a distinction of the insentient.
This very [reality] is indeed true and beginningless; if it had a beginning, it would meet with destruction.
Yet it does not undergo destruction, nor is it imagined through delusion.
"If the imagined were to cease, it does not so cease;
therefore, the view that duality does not exist belongs to the ignorant," and so forth.

In this context, "the state of being a difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara)" does not mean a difference having both the jīva and the īśvara as its counter-correlates (pratiyogin).
This is because a mutual difference lacks the property of having both as its counter-correlates, and thus would not be included [under that definition].
For this very reason, it also does not mean a difference having both as its substrata (anuyogin).
Because a single entity cannot simultaneously possess both [the property of being a relatum and the property of being a counter-correlative].

Nor can it be defined as "the state of being a difference having either the individual soul (jīva) or the Lord (īśvara) as its counter-correlative," or "the state of being a difference having either as its relatum";
for this would render redundant the separate mention of the difference between the insentient (jaḍa) and the Lord, and so forth.

Nor is it the state of being a difference having either the individual soul (jīva) or the Lord (īśvara) as its counter-correlative (pratiyogin) or its substratum (anuyogin); for it would be illogical to separately mention the mutual difference between souls.
Rather, it is the state of being a difference whose counter-correlativity and substratum-ness are co-located with the duality of both the individual soul and the Lord.

Since the counter-correlativity residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), and the sub-correlativity [residing therein], are co-located with the duality of the *jīva* and the Lord, the difference between the *jīva* and the Lord is included.
Because the counter-correlativity and sub-correlativity residing in the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the Lord do not possess that same property, their difference is not so included.
Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of including mutual differences between individual souls.

It should not be argued that this is because the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) and the substratum-correlativity (*anuyogitva*) are each co-located with the duality of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). This is because what is intended is the state of being a difference whose counter-correlativity is co-located with the duality of the individual soul and the Lord, which resides in its own substratum (*anuyogi*). Furthermore, the mutual difference between individual souls is not included [in this definition], as it lacks the property of having a counter-correlativity co-located with that duality of the individual soul and the Lord which resides in its own substratum.
By this, the distinction between the insentient and the Lord, as well as the distinction between the insentient and the individual soul, should be understood as explained.

Furthermore, the mutual distinction between individual souls and so forth consists in the nature of difference where one soul is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and another soul is the substratum (*anuyogin*).
And in this context, "soul-ness" (*jīvatva*) is simply the state of being a reflection of the Blessed Lord; this is the summary.
If it is argued that, in this way, the status of the Lord as the Supreme Brahman (parabrahman) would be untenable—
since He is defined by the absence of the three kinds of limitations (trividhapariccheda),

and since limitation by another entity distinct from limitations of space and time consists in being a separate entity from Him— we say: do not speak thus, for you are stating what is unauthoritative.

Now, why is it called "Brahman"? Because, as stated in the *Nirukta*—"For great (*bṛhantaḥ*) are the qualities within it"—the very nature of the Supreme Brahman consists in being filled with infinite, entirely faultless, and auspicious qualities.

Therefore, since the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the mutual distinctions between the insentient, the individual soul, and the Lord is ultimately real, it is established that Śrī Nārāyaṇa alone—being the source of all auspicious qualities such as being the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire universe, and thus being the most excellent of all—is to be worshipped at all times for the sake of attaining the supreme grace of the Supreme Lord.

Having thus refuted the probandum (*sādhya*), he now refutes the reason (*hetu*) as well, by means of the phrase "as being a difference" (*bhedatvena*). Since the difference between [the moon and its reflection] is false and lacks epistemic warrant (*aprāmāṇika*), there exists no universal (*sāmānya*) that could subsume both the epistemically warranted and the unwarranted; therefore, the universal "difference-ness" (*bhedatva*) cannot serve as the reason. Consequently, it is stated that the reason is "being perceived as a difference. In this context, "being perceived" (*pratīyamānatva*) means being the object of cognition (*pratīti-gocaratva*).

The meaning is: "And what is the nature of that cognition? [The phrase] "the generality of cognition" means the generality of cognition (*pratītitva-sāmānya*) which is common to both valid (*pramā*) and invalid (*apramā*) cognitions. [The word] "for you" implies that you do not accept the validity of the cognition of non-difference. [The phrase] "even of cognition" [is used].

The meaning is as follows: just as the difference between the moon [in the sky] and [its reflection] lacks a universal (*sāmānya*) that subsumes both valid and invalid instances—because such a difference is false and thus lacks epistemic validity—so too, because the cognition of non-difference is false and thus lacks epistemic validity, there is an absence of a universal in the form of being "cognized" that subsumes both valid and invalid instances; consequently, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). Regarding the phrase "difference and non-difference" (*bhedābheda*): "difference" (*bheda*) and "non-difference" (*abheda*) constitute the pair "difference-and-non-difference"; the meaning is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the difference between these two.

The meaning is that while difference (*bheda*) exists there, falsity (*mithyātva*) does not. Regarding the term "sublation" (*bādha*): the meaning is that it is because of the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*), which consists of falsity.

Now, one might object: "Since difference is indeed false, there is no sublation. To this he says: "Of difference and non-difference" (*bhedābhedayoḥ*). "Non-ultimate reality" (*apāramārthikatva*) means falsity; this is what is meant by the phrase beginning with "difference is false. [He continues: "There would also be falsity of non-difference. If, between difference and non-difference, difference is false, then—since falsity is a synonym for non-existence—it would follow that there is no difference at all between difference and non-difference.
In the absence of difference between the two, there would necessarily be non-difference.
Thus, when difference is established as false by this inference, non-difference—which is non-distinct from that difference—would likewise be false.
Therefore, the point is that if one accepts the existence of both difference and non-difference in order to avoid that fault, sublation (bādha) remains difficult to overcome.

He establishes the sublation [of the opponent's position] by another method—starting with the words "vyāvahārika" (conventional). For the opponent indeed accepts that non-difference (*abheda*) is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).

If, according to the reasoning stated, there were non-difference between difference and non-difference, then difference—which is non-distinct from ultimately real non-difference—would also be ultimately real; thus, there would again be a sublation in the attempt to prove its falsity (*mithyātva*).

[Objection: "But even if there is no ultimate difference between difference and non-difference, since conventional difference is admitted, it follows that while non-difference is not ultimate, difference must be ultimate. To this, [the author] says "conventional," and so forth. The meaning is: although a conventional difference exists between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), because that [difference] is not the determining factor (*aprayojakatvena*), the soul is accepted as being ultimately real by virtue of its ultimate non-difference from the ultimately real Brahman; the same applies here as well. He states an instance of deviation elsewhere: "ultimately real" and "not ultimately real. [In this context,] "ultimately real" refers to Brahman.
The proliferation (prapañca) is not ultimate.
There exists the perception of these two as being distinct;
the meaning is that there is no deviation [from the rule] such that falsity would be absent.

Since that [distinction] is also false, there is no deviation [from the rule]; therefore, the qualification of "ultimate" (*pāramārthika*) for Brahman and "non-ultimate" (*apāramārthika*) for the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is stated so that there is no deviation because that too is false. Consequently, the ultimate reality of Brahman and the non-ultimate reality of the phenomenal world would follow. Thus, the sense is that if one were to assert the existence of a distinction between the two in order to avoid that fault, there would indeed be a deviation. Now, one might object: even if the distinction between Brahman and the phenomenal world is false, the aforementioned fault does not arise.

For instance, in the case of ultimate reality (*pāramārthikatva*), the determining factor is being devoid of difference that possesses the same ontological status as the substratum (*dharmisamasattāka*). In the case of non-ultimate reality, however, it is possessing difference that has the same ontological status as the substratum.
Thus, since in Brahman there exists no ultimately real difference whose status is equal to the status of the substratum itself, its [Brahman's] nature is ultimate.

In phenomenal reality (prapañca), there exists a conventional distinction that possesses the same ontological status as its substratum; therefore, that distinction is not ultimately real (apāramārthika).

Therefore, he raises the objection that it is not logical to deduce that the ultimate reality of Brahman would imply the ultimate reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—stating "Brahman is the substratum" (*brahmaṇo dharmī*). He refutes this by saying "No," meaning: even so, since you do not admit a difference in Brahman having the same ontological status as the substratum relative to the phenomenal world, it follows that in Brahman—which is non-different from the phenomenal world—the phenomenal world must likewise be non-ultimate, just like Brahman itself. The phrase "difference in the moon" was stated in order to demonstrate that the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) pervades the probandum (*sādhya*).

And thus, wherever there is falsity (*mithyātva*), there is phenomenal reality (*prātibhāsikatva*), as in the case of the difference between two moons; therefore, [falsity] is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*). However, there is no such rule that wherever there is the nature of difference (*bhedatva*), there must be phenomenal reality.

The point is that even in the case of the "dissimilar instance" (*vimatabheda*) which possesses a cause, there is a lack of pervasion by the probans (*sādhanāvyāpakatva*), because it lacks the quality of being merely apparent (*prātibhāsikatva*).

Now, one might object: "In the case of the thesis—'the dissimilar instance under dispute is merely apparent, because it is a difference, like the difference in the [two] moons'—it is indeed 'merely apparent' that is being established as the property to be proven (*sādhya*)."

Therefore, because this is not a pervader of the probans (*sādhanavyāpaka*), it is not an *upādhi*; to this he says: "And that... [referring to *sa ca*]. Regarding the phrase "in terms of being empirical" (*vyāvahārikatvena*): the meaning is that by your admission that the difference under discussion is empirical (*vyāvahārika*), there is now a contradiction with your own statement in establishing its illusory nature (*prātibhāsikatva*). Regarding the phrase "deficiency of the probandum" (*sādhyavaikalya*): the sense is that the non-difference between the body and the self is unreal (*asatya*).

To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of its being such" (*tathātve*). The meaning is that if the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the distinction between the body and the self were not established, then the *Bhāṣya* passage demonstrating that falsity would be equivalent to the speech of a madman who asserts what does not exist.

Regarding the *Śāṅkara-bhāṣya* statement, "superimposing the nature of one upon the other," the meaning is that one superimposes the identity of the body upon the self, and the identity of the self upon the body.
It should be understood here that by the word "superimposing" (*adhyasya*), falsity is demonstrated.

He states another objection: "I am fair-complexioned" (*gauro 'ham iti*). If the identity between the body and the self were real, then, since the self would possess a body, the qualities of the body such as fairness and so forth would truly belong to the self; consequently, the cognition apprehending that [identity] would be a revealer of reality (*tattvāvedaka*). But this is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*).

The sense is that [the opponent's position] contradicts the subsequent commentary (*uttarabhāṣya*), which states, "having superimposed the attributes of one upon the other," thereby establishing the falsity of the body's attributes in the Self. Regarding the phrase "in the fourth": the meaning is as follows: "The world under dispute is in reality devoid of internal differentiation, because it is an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), like the sky. Regarding the phrase "not manifold" (*nāna*) and so forth: By the aforementioned inference, the absence of difference between the entity called "the world" and its own parts—such as cloth and the like—is what is being proven.
That would be possible only if jars and other such things were parts of the entity called "the world. But this is not the case.

Since it is precisely various objects such as jars that, through specific limiting conditions (*upādhi*) like time, are denoted by the word "world" (*jagat*), there exists no other distinct entity called "the world" apart from time, jars, and so forth.
Regarding this, the example is given: "like an army, a forest, and so on.

The meaning is that just as elephants, horses, and the like are denoted by the word "army" when residing in a single location, or just as various trees are denoted by the word "forest" when residing in a single location, so it is here as well.

[Objection: Is it not the case that only various distinct entities are denoted by the word "world" (*jagat*), but rather that the entity called the "world" is produced from those various entities—just as a cloth is produced from [threads] which are distinct?

Therefore, since things such as jars can be considered parts of that [whole], the aforementioned fault does not apply. To this, he says: "of earth and so forth. "The consequence of confusion" (*sāṅkarya-prasaṅga*) means the coexistence in one place of two things that exist by mutually excluding one another. For example, the nature of water exists in water by excluding the nature of earth, and the nature of earth exists in earth by excluding the nature of water; yet both would have to coexist in the world produced from them.
The same applies elsewhere as well;

therefore, the meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence of confusion among mere universals (*jāti*). "And the consequence of [universals] being substances" means that their inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) is a substance.
This refers to qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), and so forth, which are themselves partless.

The meaning is that only a composite entity (*sāvayava-padārtha*) possesses the capacity to originate a substance (*dravyārambhakatva*). If it is objected: "But we observe that even partless atoms (*paramāṇu*) originate a substance called a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*); how then can this [position] be undesirable?"—we reply: No, because by the term "originator of a substance," what is intended is the origination of a large substance (*mahaddravya*). And there would be the loss of the status of being a final constituent (*antyāvayavitva*). For the status of being a final constituent consists in not originating another substance while being itself an effect-substance (*kāryadravyatva*).
The meaning is that if jars and the like were also initiators of the substance called the "world," then there would be a loss of its status as a single composite whole (*avayavin*).

Now, it might be argued: we do not take the entity called the "world" as the subject (*pakṣa*) by asserting that it is initiated by entities such as jars; rather, we prove that it is devoid of internal differentiation.
If that were so, the aforementioned fault would not apply.

However, by taking only the jar and so forth as the subject (*pakṣa*), its lack of internal difference is what is being proved; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply. To this he says: "the jar and so forth. The word "lack" (*hīna*) is to be understood as being conjoined with the term "internal difference" (*svāntarbheda*). Thus, since the mere phrase "internal difference" does not prove the absence of difference, there is no room for the objection: "How can this be? [The opponent objects: "This is proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*). The sense is that we too accept the absence of difference in the case of jars and so forth when the difference has itself as its counter-correlative (*apratiyogika*).
"Deficient in the probandum (sādhyavikala)"—the sense is that there exists a mutual difference between the space within a jar and the space within a hut, and so forth.
To avoid the aforementioned refutation in that regard, he says: "Regarding the difference of space. This is stated elsewhere in the *Mandāramañjarī*.
He concludes the refutation of the inference that establishes the non-difference of the Self with: "Therefore," and so on.
As for this which is stated—that inference is the means of valid cognition regarding the non-difference of jars, cloths, and so forth:
