"The jar under dispute and others are the locus of a real identity with the counter-correlative cloth, because they are denotable or because they are cognizable, like a cloth;
or, a cloth does not differ from a jar in reality, because it is a substance or because it is earth, like a jar."
On this point, the following must be addressed:
does a jar perish through the blow of a hammer and so forth, or not?
If it does not, there is a contradiction with the scriptural texts that establish impermanence, as well as a deviation from one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*).

Furthermore, the activity performed for the sake of a jar would be rendered futile (and there would arise the defect that the jar and so forth fail to perform their purposeful functions). Regarding the first [alternative], does the phenomenal world of ignorance—such as space and so forth—perish at that very moment or not?
If the former, it would follow that there is an absence of purposeful activity (such as the production of jars and the like).
Furthermore, because it would be impossible for both the sky and ignorance to be destroyed,
there would follow the consequences of either a great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) or liberation (*mokṣa*).
In the second case, how could there be an ultimate non-difference between a cloth and a jar or other such objects?
For when the silver has perished, there is no ultimate non-difference between it and the persisting mother-of-pearl.

Furthermore, a perception that grasps the non-difference of two trees standing at a distance would have to be a means of valid cognition revealing reality (*tattvāvedaka-pramāṇa*), on the grounds that they are in fact identical in substance; such counter-arguments (*pratikūla-tarka*) are to be inferred.

The common refutations against any inference that seeks to establish non-duality include being sublated by perception, inference, or scripture; being defeated by *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum); having a limiting condition (*upādhi*); and being equivalent to fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*).
Furthermore, the scriptural texts concerning non-duality have been explained otherwise by the venerable Bhagavatpāda himself in another work. || CHA ||
Salutations to Ramānātha, to Hari, whose body is perfect bliss, who is full of faultless qualities, and who is the enjoyer of all sacrifices.
Salutations to Ramanatha, to Rama, the enjoyer of all sacrifices.
To Him who is perfect in faultless qualities, whose body is full bliss—(1).

Thus ends the *Bhedojjīvana* (The Revival of Difference), composed by the ascetic Vyāsa, disciple of the venerable Brahmaṇyatīrtha, who had crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the authoritative scriptures on words and sentences.
(Thus ends the *Bhedojjīvana*, composed by the ascetic Vyāsa, disciple of the venerable Brahmaṇyapūjyapāda.)

Having thus refuted the four types of inference suspected by one [opponent], he now restates the two inferences suspected by another to refute them as well—those which seek to establish the distinction of the non-self (anātmabheda). He says: "And as for this which is said... Here, after the words "like a jar" (*ghaṭavat*), the word "thus" (*iti*) is to be supplied. Regarding the phrase "and it would be a departure from established tenets" (*apasiddhāntaśca*): the sense is that since the opponent also accepts the finitude (*paricchinnatva*) of jars and so forth in order to establish their falsity (*mithyātva*), they must consequently accept their empirical destruction (*vyāvahārikavināśa*). Regarding the phrase "the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of jars and so forth": [this refers to the objection that such efficiency would be impossible if they were not real].
The meaning is that even after the blow of a mallet or other instrument, there would be the fault of that jar performing purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as carrying water.

The term *doṣāpatti* is a reversed compound (*viparītasamāsa*) meaning "the occurrence of a fault" (*āpattiḥ* and *doṣaḥ*). The phrase "at that very time" means at the very moment of the jar's destruction. In the expression "not space, ignorance, etc.," the word "etc. includes pillars and other such objects.

In the doctrine of the non-difference of the world (jagadabheda-vāda), since a jar is non-different from a cloth as well as from space and so forth, its destruction at that very time would be possible; thus, the logical contingency arises: "Is it so, or not?"

The term "must be stated" (*vaktavyam*) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. Regarding the phrase "the absence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) such as that of a jar": the meaning is that the absence of that causal efficiency—consisting of providing space and so forth—which belongs to those things such as space (*ākāśa*), would result as an undesirable consequence (*prasajyeta*). And regarding the phrase "because destruction is impossible for both space and ignorance": the point is that since space is conventionally eternal (*vyāvahārika-nityatva*) and ignorance is removable solely by knowledge (*jñāna-eka-nivartyatva*), their destruction at the time of the destruction of a jar by the blow of a mallet or similar means is not logical.
Some also say it is because their pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) makes destruction impossible.

If it is asked what objection there is to accepting the destruction of even such things as space and ignorance at this very moment, he says: "The great dissolution and liberation would occur [at that very time]. The word "then" (*tadā*) is understood to carry over.
Thus, if the destruction of everything were to occur at the time of the pot's destruction, then the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) would occur right now;

and if ignorance were destroyed, liberation (*mokṣa*) would also occur right now—this is the meaning. Regarding the second case: the meaning is that if space and the rest were not destroyed even when the pot is destroyed. "How so?"—the sense is that it is impossible for there to be ultimate non-difference between that which is destroyed and that which is not destroyed.
He establishes that very point with the words "for not" (na hi). Regarding the phrase "ultimate non-difference," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "by [the silver] whose silver-ness has perished.

Here, since the entire empirical world (vyāvahārika-prapañca) is the object of dispute, it is impossible to cite the examples of a pot and a cloth—one destroyed and one undestroyed; therefore, he cites only the illusory (prātibhāsika) silver and the real (vyāvahārika) mother-of-pearl as examples.

For it is not possible to accept an ultimate non-difference between the illusory silver and the mother-of-pearl, as one might do between a pot and a cloth which are both empirical; thus, he states the refutation by reasoning (*tarka*) against the inference proving the non-difference of insentient things, beginning with the words "dūrastha" (situated at a distance). The phrase "if there were an ultimate non-difference of insentient things" must be supplied to complete the sense.

Having thus refuted each inference individually, he now refutes them with general objections, stating: "of every inference proving non-difference. This means that even the group of six inferences beginning with "the selves under dispute [are non-different]" is subject to these flaws.
By the phrase "due to the security of yoga (*yogakṣema*) and so forth," the term "and so forth" includes the lack of necessity (*aprayojakatva*). To explain:
first of all, the initial inference is not sublated by such direct perception as "I am not omniscient" or "I am not free from suffering."

There is sublation by scripture in the form of the Vedic text beginning with "dvā suparṇā" (Two birds...). There is also sublation by inference in the form: "The individual soul (jīva) is the locus of a difference that possesses the same ontological status as its substratum, which is Brahman as the counter-correlative, because it is the experiencer of suffering not consciously recollected by Brahman," and so forth.
The state of having adjuncts (*sopādhikatva*) exists by virtue of being the Supreme Self (*paramātmatva*).

The argument that "the selves under dispute do not differ from the Supreme Self even in an ultimate sense, because they possess selfhood (*ātmatva*), just like the Supreme Self" shares the same logical status as a fallacious argument (*ābhāsa*). Furthermore, even if selfhood were granted, the probandum might still not follow; thus, the reason is unestablished (*aprayojakatā*).

The inference that "the bodies under dispute are the loci of experience for Devadatta alone" is sublated by the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of Devadatta, who thinks, "Yajñadatta’s body is not my locus of experience.

It is also sublated by scripture (āgama), such as the statement, "Objects are distinct and possess distinct properties. Furthermore, [the inference] is countered by the following counter-inference: "The bodies under dispute are not the loci of experience for Devadatta alone, because they are not presided over by Devadatta, just like Devadatta’s own body in the case of the negative concomitance (vyatireka)."

Nor is there a lack of proof; for its establishment occurs through the inference: "Devadatta is not the controller of Yajñadatta’s body and so forth, because he is non-pervasive, like Īśvara (the Lord) in the negative instance.
Thus, there is a refutation by means of inference.
The upādhi (limiting condition) is "being presided over by Devadatta.

There is a similarity to a fallacious argument (*ābhāsa*) in the following: "The wives under dispute are the objects of enjoyment for Devadatta alone, because they are wives, like Devadatta’s own wives.
Furthermore, due to the absence of a supporting reason (*anukūlatarka*), the logical mark (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).

In the third inference as well—namely, that "difference is false"—there is contradiction with the direct perception of Devadatta, such as "I am not omniscient," "I am not Yajñadatta," and "I am not a jar.
There is contradiction with scriptural authority (āgama) such as "Difference is real.
And there is contradiction with inference such as "Difference is real because it is perceived by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), like the Self."
The state of being superimposed (*āropitatva*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Furthermore, the similarity of fallacious reasoning (*ābhāsa-sāmya*) has already been stated: "Non-difference is false because it is a form of non-difference, like the non-difference between the body and the self.

Alternatively, whether in the case of the difference between difference and non-difference, or the difference between Brahman and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), since falsity is not observed despite the existence of difference, the reason is inconclusive (*aprayojakatā*).
In the fourth inference, since the mutual difference between jars and other objects is established by uncontradicted perception, there is an easy refutation by perception.
Furthermore, the claim that "all objects are indeed distinct and possess distinct properties" contradicts scripture.
[The thesis is: A jar is not devoid of real difference from cloth and other things.

There is a contradiction with such inferences as "because it is a pot, [it must have internal parts], unlike a cloth," and so forth. Furthermore, "being God" (*īśvaratva*) serves as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

Since one could also employ the argument, "The subject of dispute possesses real internal differentiation because it is visible," there is an equality of fallacies and a lack of probative force (*aprayojakatā*).

In the same way, for the fifth and sixth [arguments] as well, one must demonstrate their sublation by perception and other means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣādi*), as well as their being based on a limiting condition (*sopādhikatva*).
Now, he refutes the claim that the scriptural texts (*śruti*) such as "neither here nor there" (*neha nānā*) teach non-duality (*abheda*): "But the non-dual scriptures...

Elsewhere, in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka-bhāṣya* and other works, the scripture "neither here nor there is anything manifold" (*neha nānāsti kiñcana*) has been explained differently, as intending the absence of difference in the Blessed Lord—that is, that within this Brahman there is no "anything manifold," meaning no difference consisting of qualities, actions, and so forth, or any state of plurality.
The meaning is that statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) are explained as being intended to express similarity (*sādṛśya*).

As it has been stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "Whether in independence, in distinction, in location, in absolute identity, or in similarity—the statement of identity is properly applicable according to one's wish. The phrase "of the word 'iti'" is connected with the previously stated proposition: "this is the refutation."
Or it indicates completion;
or this word "iti" has the sense of a reason (*hetu*).

Therefore, the connection is with the remainder of the concluding statement: "Thus, the distinctness of the Brahman named Viṣṇu from the universe consisting of the sentient and the insentient is established."

Thus having concluded this treatise, the venerable king of sages, Vyāsatīrtha, praises and bows to Viṣṇu—who is characterized by the very attributes for the sake of which he has established Viṣṇu’s distinction from the universe in this work—by describing Him as "the Lord of Ramā" (*ramānātha*). The compound is analyzed as "He who is both faultless (*nirdoṣa*) and full of all auspicious qualities (*guṇapūrṇa*).

The mention of "faultless" is made with the intention that just as the establishment of His distinction from the universe serves to prove His fullness of qualities, it likewise serves to prove His faultlessness.
By this, he indicates that in the first verse as well, the phrase "and by being faultless" (*nirdoṣatvena ca*) should be understood as an elliptical inclusion (*upalakṣaṇa*).
As it has been stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna*: "Its distinction [from all else] exists everywhere;

for the sake of establishing its faultlessness, whatever is associated with non-difference [is attributed to it]. To make known that just as bowing to the Lord, so too bowing to the Goddess is a cause of the Lord's pleasure, it is said: "To Ramānātha. Because this work of one's own is of the nature of a sacrifice of speech (*vāgyajña*), it is said: "To the Enjoyer of All Sacrifices," with the intention that by this the Lord, the enjoyer of all sacrifices, may be pleased. As it was stated at the end of the *Nyāyāmṛta*:

"May Keśava, the Lord of Lakṣmī, be pleased by this sacrifice in the form of speech, which was performed for himself by Hari, my inspirer, [with the words]: 'Obeisance to Keśava'. Now, one might ask: if Viṣṇu is bodiless (*aśarīra*), how can he be the enjoyer of all sacrifices?
Conversely, if he possesses a body, he would be subject to an end, like Yajñadatta.
Furthermore, if one were to accept that He is the enjoyer of sacrifices, it would follow that He is incomplete;

for in the world, enjoyment is observed only in those who are incomplete. Therefore, it is said that He possesses a body of perfect bliss (*pūrṇānanda*). Indeed, the Blessed Lord has a body, and that consists precisely of qualities such as bliss and the rest.
Therefore, there is no impossibility of being an enjoyer, nor is there any attachment to defects such as death and so forth.
Nor, in that case, does the enjoyer incur incompleteness;
for the point is that even for one who is full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*), the enjoyment of play is possible. Thus, may all be entirely auspicious. || 6 ||

Salutations to You, who are faultless and an ocean of infinite virtues; who are the sole object of knowledge for all the Vedas; and who are the true cause of the birth, sustenance, and dissolution of the entire universe, as well as of knowledge and all other perfections.

Salutations to Śrī Kṛṣṇa Vṛṣṇi, the enemy of Kaṃsa, who dwells as a swan in the lotus-heart of the illustrious Madhva, and whose form is the very object of their own cherished desire for those who serve him. || 1 ||

This illumination of the reality that revives the distinctions has been composed for the purification of speech and intellect, having reflected upon the words of the former teachers and then extracted their essence in a beautiful manner.
Alas, out of childishness I have indeed displayed my immaturity; let that be forgiven by the wise, who are like those intent on drinking the milk from a mother’s udder for her calves. (2)
It was fashioned by the Blessed One, who possesses the lotus feet of the noble Arhat.
May this *Bhedojjīvana-pañcikā* be for the pleasure of the Blessed One. || 3 || cha ||

Thus ends *The Lamp of the Sentiment that Revives Duality*, composed by the venerable Bhagavannāma, a worshiper at the feet of the holy feet of the illustrious Bhāskara Veṅkaṭavarāhācārya. || Cha || Cha ||

"The jar and so forth are subject to dispute" means that this inference should be understood as belonging to that Bhāskara and others who assert the reality of the world and its constituents, as well as the absence of any inherent difference [between them].

In this context, the term *tāttvika* (real) refers to *svābhāvika* (intrinsic). Alternatively, this inference belongs specifically to the Māyāvādin. Here, the phrase "the locus of real identity" means "that which is not the locus of real difference. [The word] "śruti" [is used].

The passage beginning with "The state of being tomorrow belongs to the mortal" (ŚvB 1.2) should be cited as an illustration. Regarding "the purposeful activity of a jar and so forth": the meaning is that if a jar were to perish due to the blow of a mallet or similar causes, then even immediately thereafter, there would be the occurrence of activities such as carrying water. "At that very time" means at the very moment of the jar's destruction. Regarding "the absence of the purposeful activity of the jar and so forth": the meaning is that upon the destruction of the jar, since things such as cloth would also be destroyed, their purposeful activity would likewise not exist. And regarding "because destruction is impossible": the implication is that this is because [the entity] is eternal.

He says that there would be dissolution and liberation for everything as well—this is expressed by the words "mahāpralaya" (great dissolution). As for the phrase "katham" (how so?), the sense is that even when a jar is destroyed, it is impossible for that which has not been destroyed to be non-different from it.
He provides an illustration for this with the words "na hi" (for not).
The meaning is that even when the silver produced by an illusion is sublated, one does not observe the non-difference of the un-sublated mother-of-pearl from that silver.
But surely, even upon the blow of a mallet, there is no destruction of the jar;
for the scriptural statement is fulfilled by the simultaneous destruction of all things at the time of universal dissolution (*pralaya*).
Nor is there any contradiction with the non-perception of the jar immediately after the blow of the mallet.
This is established by the absence of a manifesting agent.
The statement regarding that specific time, however, refers merely to the non-perception [of the object]. The perception "the jar is destroyed" takes as its object the state of being unmanifest.
If it is argued that this is not so because only the manifest possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) and thus does not fall into the error of [the eternal being] causal efficiency,
do not say so.

For since space (*ākāśa*) and the like, being eternal, never undergo destruction, that which is of the same nature as them would likewise not be destroyed, which contradicts the sacred scriptures (*śruti*).
Furthermore, as for the absence of the manifestor, is it absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) or destruction (*dhvaṃsa*)?
In the first case, the jar would never be perceived at any time.
In the second case, there is the undesirable consequence that all things would perish simultaneously.
Nor should it be argued that even for the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), there is merely non-manifestation and not destruction;
for that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
[Objection: Even so, one might argue that by virtue of conventional difference (*vyāvahārika-bheda*), the destruction of one does not entail the destruction of the other.

For although its destruction is absent from the perspective of conventional reality (*vyavahāra*), it necessarily occurs from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Nor can this be accepted as a desired consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because no distinction is perceived in the ether before or after the destruction of the jar. Enough of this effort spent refuting a system that is too easily ridiculed.

He states the subverting argument (*bādhakatarka*) against the real non-difference of insentient things, beginning with "dūrastha... [and so on]. Regarding "the Śrutis on non-duality": the meaning is those intended by the opponent to have non-duality as their primary purport. Regarding "otherwise": the meaning is that [the texts] would instead have as their subject matter the absence of internal difference within the Lord, His being characterized by sovereignty, His possessing the power of agency, His internal governance, His all-pervasiveness, similarity, the unity of abode, the unity of mind, and liberation through union (*sāyujya*), and so forth.

Thus, Hari, who is distinct from everything else due to His absolute sovereignty and other attributes, is the supreme among all because He is the mine of all virtues; He is therefore infinitely more auspicious than the phenomenal world, which consists of mutually distinct living beings and insentient matter. || 6 || || 6 ||

Enough with these direct perceptions witnessed by all the self-realized ones, which are entirely free from defects; enough also with the collections of scriptural passages accepted as direct perception, and with irrefutable reasonings.

May the illustrious Lord Śrīśa—who is known through the Vedas with their limbs (Aṅgas), the Purāṇas, the Smṛtis, the arts, the Sūtras, the Itihāsas, and the Āgamas, and who is measured by us as higher than the highest—be for my supreme delight.

The excellent wish-fulfilling creeper that is Ramā, honored by rows of flowers, fruits, leaves, and twigs that are no less than the Kalpa tree itself, entwines Murāri, who is the very body of the Kalpa tree.
May the city of the gods, whose inhabitants have Karālambā as their support, grant the fruit of our desire when we ascend to the mountain abode of the slayer of Mura. || 2 ||

For the Lord of the World, who intends to establish [the world], the earth acts as a stage for the drama and other arts of one about to begin his work; and this crown prince freely bears the burden of the universe even while desiring its establishment.
He who was indeed the vanguard, the crest-jewel of heroes, has now become the charioteer of the sun-like Vyāsa, desiring to withdraw [the world], acting as the honey-souled wind.

Indeed, a fool becomes the foremost among the eminent; the deaf becomes a master of speech; the mute becomes an eloquent orator; the one of evil conduct becomes devoid of movement; and the lame becomes a conqueror who overcomes others.

May that Goddess of Speech protect us—she by whose mere glance even a king becomes deformed, bodiless, dull-witted, or impotent, yet who makes one truly skilled in all matters entirely complete and unimpaired.

Victory to the noble speech, which shines forth through various circumstances—its essence being the profound cultivation of the limbs of enlightenment—and which traverses the manifold paths of conduct within the four abodes.
She is a female garland-maker who has skillfully woven together the various compositions of the three Vedas using the firm golden threads of the multitude of jewels spoken by her gurus.

The speech of this man produces for the virtuous the essence of nectar; it is comparable to the very marrow of sweetness, and is like the edge of a great sword-blade sharpened by the hardness of absolute independence for the wise.
May that King Vyāsa—who has been summoned by the fruits of the merit and demerit of people seen and unseen—grant me the crest-jewel that adorns the foremost of the crowns upon his ten heads. || 6 ||

He upon whose tongue the sovereign splendor of the empire of speech sports like the lion-throne, and within whose heart the Goddess of Fortune dwells at night’s end—He is Hari, free from weariness, together with His beloved.

Those eminent Tīrthācāryas, born of the noble Viṭṭhalārya, who were the foremost among the learned commentators on the words of the venerable Madhvārya and most excellent, are indeed my gurus. || 7 ||
By the son of Mudgala Ārya, whose home was in the city of Janārdana.
The speech was spoken according to his wisdom by Śarman Ānandatīrtha.
This *Bhedacintāratna* (The Jewel of Reflection on Difference) has arisen from the ocean of Madhva’s scriptures.
May that which has been polished by the whetstone of intelligence be held within the heart by Hari.
Thus ends the *Bhedacintāratna*, a commentary on the *Bhedojjīvana* composed by the venerable Vyāsatīrtha, who had reached the further shore of the study of words and sentences. || Cha || Cha ||

"And [the charge of] contradicting one's own tenets": since the cessation of that which is produced by ignorance (avidyā) through the knowledge of Brahman is accepted, a contradiction with direct perception (pratyakṣa) should also be understood. "The consequence of the defect of performing the purposeful action (arthakriyā) of a jar, etc.": the meaning is that if the jar were to exist even after the blow of a mallet, it would continue to perform the purposeful action of a jar, and so forth.

In some places, however, the reading is: "there would be the futility of the activity performed for the sake of a jar. Regarding the phrase "of space and ignorance": the meaning is that no destruction of a pervasive entity is observed. Regarding the term "great dissolution" (*mahāpralaya*): the meaning is that if everything included within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—like jars, cloths, and so forth—were destroyed, then there would follow the destruction of both the great dissolution and liberation (*mokṣa*).

In the second case [if space were not pervasive], even though jars and the like are destroyed, how could there be an ultimate difference (*pāramārthika-bheda*) between jars, cloths, and so forth, and space? This is the meaning.

In the argument—"Since there is no ultimate difference between the conch-shell and the silver," [it follows that] there would be an ultimate difference among insentient things—the *āpādaka* (the logical ground for the undesirable consequence) must be supplied.

Having thus stated the specific defects of inference (*prātisvikānumānadoṣa*), he now states the common ones as well: "of every inference establishing non-difference," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the fallacies of being unproving (*aprayojakatva*) and having a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) are included.
The sense is that these have already been demonstrated therein, though some others are to be inferred.

The same applies to other forms of inference as well. Regarding the phrase "the scriptural texts on non-duality": those have been explained and commented upon by us elsewhere, which should be understood there.
Furthermore, the concluding statement—that the Supreme Brahman, known as Viṣṇu, is distinct from the universe—is also to be understood in this way. || ॐ || ॐ ||
Where is the gait of Vyāsa, who moves like a swan, and where is the gait of one such as me? Where indeed can they be found together?
I consider this union of these two here to have been accomplished by Nṛhari. || 1 ||
If this cow, having been shaken by hundreds of whips harsh with logic, returns to her teacher, it is well.
Reflecting thus upon her being a first-calf cow, the virtuous should immediately act there out of compassion. || 2 ||
May the cakora birds of the learned be satiated by this moonlight of non-duality.
Through the examination of the established meaning in the *Bhedojjīvana-ṭippaṇī*. || 3 ||
Thus ends the *Bhedacandrikā*, a commentary on the *Bhedojjīvana*, composed by Vāsudevācārya, son of Śrī Kumbhārī Nārāyaṇācārya. || Cha || Cha ||

Regarding the term "real" (*tāttvika*): the intention is that their identity with the nature of Brahman is real (*vāstavam*), in order to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) by taking into account an identity based on mere appearance (*prātibhāsika*). Regarding the term "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*): the term "non-eternal" (*anityatva*) is used to avoid sublation (*bādha*) by taking into account such a difference [between the two]. This refers to the meaning of the scriptural text, "Everything else but That perishes" (*tato 'nyad ārtaṃ*). Regarding the phrase "and it would be a contradiction of one's own tenets" (*apasiddhāntaśca*): this means that at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the dissolution of all things into the state of their cause is accepted. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of objects such as jars": [this is the context].
The meaning is "for the sake of producing the jar again.
The point is that otherwise, since the jar would already be established, its production would be rendered purposeless.

In the reading "the fallacy of performing the jar’s functional activity" (*ghaṭārthakriyākaraṇadoṣāpatti*), the meaning is that it would follow [absurdly] that the jar performs activities such as carrying water. Regarding "the absence of activity": the meaning is that, due to the absence of space, no activity of that [jar] is ever observed to arise eternally. Regarding "because destruction is impossible": because [space] is partless, there is an absence of the cause consisting in the destruction of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

The meaning is as follows: since the reasons such as "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*) and "being denotable" (*abhidheyatva*) are fallacious (*vyabhicāra*)—because in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and other such things which possess these reasons, there is an absence of being the locus of a real identity (*tādātmya*) with a cloth—the aforementioned reasons could not possibly establish that [identity]. Even regarding destruction (*nāśa*), one might argue that a real identity with space is indeed admitted for the cloth; therefore, he says, "For it is not so" (*na hi*). The point is that if that were the case, a person seeking silver would certainly act toward a mother-of-pearl shell. Regarding the phrase "because they share the same logical status as a fallacy" (*ābhāsasamānayogakṣematvāt*): [it refers to the fact that the reasons are equally subject to the same defects].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the fallacies of being non-conclusive (*aprayojakatva*) and having a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*) are to be understood. Regarding the phrase "the Śrutis": the meaning is that they have been explained; the ellipsis to be supplied is "they have also been commented upon by us. Regarding the word "in brief" (*samāsa*): the meaning is that a summary has been made.
Therefore, the concluding sentence—"Therefore, Viṣṇu is characterized by the qualities of independence and so forth"—must be supplied. Thus, everything is entirely auspicious. *Cha*.
He possesses the nature of the various Siddhas through his innate qualities, such as absolute sovereignty.
May that Vyāsa, the Lord of the Universe, who is distinct from both the conscious and the unconscious, be pleased with me. || 1 ||
By the power of his nectar-like speech, he protects [the world] from the serpent of evil speakers, whose names have vanished at the mere sight of him.
May this speech of mine, which follows the venerable Vyāsarāja Yatīndra, spread joy here among the wise.
By the son of Vāsudevārya, a resident of the illustrious city of Vyāghrapurī.
A commentary titled *Bhedojjīvana* was composed for them by their disciple. || 3 ||
Whatever merit has been acquired in its entirety by this author through the composition of this work—
I offer this to the Lord of my Life, who resides within the lotus-heart of my Guru. || 4 ||
Thus ends the *Bhedasañjīvanī*, a commentary on the *Bhedojjīvana*, composed by Śrī Nātha, whose secondary name is Śrī Vyāghrapurī.
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
May the Sun-like Madhava, who destroys the darkness of the wicked doctrines of the Kali age and possesses the qualities described in the Vedas such as "balittha," be forever pleased with me.
Thus concludes the commentary titled *Bhedojjīvana*, composed by the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya Kāśī Tirumalācārya, based on the work of the illustrious Vyāsarājatīrtha Śrīpāda.

Since the opponent has not yet stated the inferences that establish the non-difference from the non-self, [the author] now raises other objections, beginning with "And as for this... and so forth. Here, the proof of non-difference from the cloth is merely illustrative;
in the same manner, the non-difference of the jar from the entire manifold of non-self must be established.

Just as when silver is destroyed, there is no identity between the silver and the persisting mother-of-pearl, so too, even when a jar is destroyed, there is no identity between the jar and the persisting phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of cloth and so forth; with this intention, he says [the passage] beginning with "In this case, this... and ending with "...the ultimate non-difference of the mother-of-pearl. Regarding the phrase "scriptures establishing impermanence": the meaning is that there is a contradiction with such scriptures as "Into whom the world enters," and so on.

"Apasiddhānta" (contradiction of one's own tenet): The meaning is that since the destruction of a jar by the blow of a mallet and so forth was accepted by the former teachers, your current non-acceptance of that constitutes a contradiction of your own established doctrine. "Ghaṭādyarthakriyā" (the causal efficiency of the jar, etc.): The meaning is that if the jar were not destroyed by the blow of a mallet and so forth, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of its performing causal functions such as carrying water immediately thereafter. "Tadaiva" (at that very time): This means "at the very time when the jar is destroyed. "Arthakriyābhāva" (absence of causal efficiency): If ignorance (*avidyā*) were destroyed at the very moment of the jar's destruction, then the production of another jar and so forth would not occur.

And thus, the meaning is that there would be an abandonment of activities such as fetching water. Regarding the phrase "and because destruction is impossible": since the destruction of that [identity] is admitted only at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) through the direct knowledge of identity, its destruction is impossible now; for if it were destroyed now, the great dissolution and liberation would occur right now—this is the meaning. He demonstrates this very point with the words "for not...": just as when silver is destroyed by a sublating cognition such as "this is not silver," the shell is not destroyed, and therefore there is no ultimate non-difference between the two; likewise, even upon the destruction of a jar, the cosmic manifestation (*prapañca*) consisting of ignorance, space, and so forth—which is not destroyed—is not identical with the jar. This is the meaning.

He states the refutation by reasoning (*tarka*) for the inference that establishes difference as being without self (*anātman*), beginning with the words "of two trees standing at a distance. If a real, ultimate non-difference (*pāramārthika-abheda*) between two insentient objects is admitted, then even the delusion that arises—namely, the thought "this is one and the same tree" regarding two mango and jackfruit trees existing far apart—would have to be considered valid (*prāmāṇya*). The meaning is that because there is actual non-difference between them, that cognition which apprehends it must be a revealer of reality (*tattvāvedaka*).

Having thus stated the refutation of each of the inferences establishing the distinction between the self and the non-self, he now states the [refutation] common to those inferences that establish mere non-distinction, beginning with the words "of the inference establishing non-distinction" (*abhedasādhaka*). Regarding the phrase "perception," etc.: for the inference establishing the non-difference of the self—such as "the disputed selves do not, in the ultimate sense, differ from the Supreme Self"—there is a contradiction with perception, such as "I am not omniscient, I am not free from suffering," and so forth;
there is also a contradiction with scripture, such as "Two birds... (*dvā suparṇā*), and so forth.

The individual soul (jīva) is the locus of a difference that possesses the same ontological status as the existence of the subject (dharmin) relative to Brahman, because it is an experiencer of suffering not experienced by Brahman;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the following inference: [the soul is so] like Brahman.
Furthermore, due to the absence of a supporting reason (*anukūlatarka*), the condition (*upādhi*) of being "other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) applies.

The disputants’ selves do not differ from the Supreme Self even in the ultimate sense, because they possess selfhood, just like the Supreme Self; since this can also be established, [the opponent's argument] shares the same logical status as a fallacy (*ābhāsa*).

Furthermore, regarding the inference proving the non-difference of non-selves—such as "the subject under dispute, the jar and so forth, is the locus of identity with the counter-correlative 'cloth,' because it is denotable" (*abhidheyatvāt*)—there is a contradiction with perception, such as the cognition "the jar is not the cloth."

There is a contradiction with the following inference: "A jar is not the locus of identity with a cloth, because it is the locus of a property that is the counter-positive of an absolute absence residing in the cloth—which is not delimited by a delimitor of co-occurrence with its counter-positive—just like the cloth itself (in the case of the vyatireka). Furthermore, there is a contradiction with scripture stating, "This difference between inert things is mutual. Due to the absence of a supporting tarka (reductio), the status of being "other than the subject" (*pakṣetaratva*) constitutes a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

The distinction is as follows: it can be established that the subject under dispute, such as a jar, is not a non-locus of identity with the counter-correlative of cloth (i.e., it is identical with cloth), because it is nameable, just like cloth; thus, [the argument] shares the same logical status as the proof for non-existence.

Now he refutes the scriptural passages that establish non-duality. "The Advaita-śrutayaḥ" means such passages as "neha nānāsti" (here there is no diversity), and so forth. "Elsewhere" means in the commentary on the Kaṭhopaniṣad and other works, they have been explained by the venerable [Śaṅkara] as negating the distinctions of the Lord’s qualities, actions, and so on. Having thus concluded the section, the venerable sage Vyāsatīrtha performs the concluding auspicious rite (*maṅgalānta-maṅgala*)—recalling that those scriptures which possess auspicious beginnings and middles result in long-lived persons—and he too practices that same custom: "To Ramānātha."
The connection is "salutation to Hari.
The qualification "to the Lord of Ramā" (aramānāthāya) is intended to indicate the purpose of defining [the nature of] difference.
The word "aramā" is an indicator for the entire universe consisting of both sentient and insentient beings.
And thus, the meaning is "to the Lord of the world, which consists of both the sentient and the insentient.

By this, it should be understood that the purpose is to establish the Lordship of the World as stated in the *Sadyapadya* (the verse beginning with *sadyaḥ*), while simultaneously supporting the doctrine of difference (*bheda*).
To state the attributes that differentiate [Him], [He is called] "the enjoyer of all sacrifices" (*sarvayajñabhuj*).
To the objection that [if this were so] there would be incompleteness, it is said: "to the one complete in qualities" (*guṇapūrṇāya*).

The sense is that although He is Himself complete in qualities such as bliss and the like, He enjoys them for the sake of favoring His devotees, and not for the sake of personal satisfaction. To the question, "Since there is a rule that wherever there are qualities there are defects, why is He also free from defects? it is said: "faultless" (*nirdoṣa*).
The analysis of the compound is: "He is faultless and full of qualities. Alternatively, this too is a statement of a distinguishing attribute. Now, does Hari have a body or not?
In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of death and so forth;
in the second case, it would be impossible for that [body] to be an enjoyer. Therefore, it is said: "possessing a body of perfect bliss.
Indeed, such a body exists, and it consists of happiness, not being material (prākṛta) and thus inseparable from destruction.
Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply; thus, may all be entirely auspicious. (6)
O you who are worshipped by the multitude of lotus-born ones, whose eyes resemble the petals of a lotus!
Salutations to Padmanābha, the beloved of Rāmā, who wears a garland of excellent lotuses.
It was composed by Śarkarāśrīnivāsa for the instruction of beginners.
May this commentary, which revives the doctrine of difference, be for the pleasure of the Lord of Ramā.
May the unsurpassed merit obtained from this commentary that revives the Bheḍa [Tantra] [accrue to all].
Having received this, may our teachers be pleased and show compassion toward me.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Bhedojjīvana* composed by Śrī Vyāsatīrtha, written by Śarkara Śrīnivāsa.
